## TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS
## AND MOST HIGH PRINCE AND LORD,

# JOHN ERNEST
# THE YOUNGER,

## DUKE OF SAXONY, JÜLICH, CLEVES,
## AND BERG, LANDGRAVE OF THURIN-
## GIA, MARGRAVE OF MEISSEN, etc.
### To a Prince Great-hearted, Brave, and a most devoted lover of Truth and Fatherland.

->MOST ILLUSTRIOUS AND HIGH PRINCE,<-

When Plato was asked by Dionysius the Younger, King of Sicily, to reveal a more advanced and mysterious demonstration concerning the First Nature <note>original: *de Prima Natura*; this refers to the fundamental essence of reality or the first principles of the universe in Platonic philosophy</note>, he disclosed it through Archedemus in a certain Letter which still survives. Although Plato had ordered that letter to be burned after several readings so that it might not spread among the common people, he stated therein that by the Law of Nature, Wisdom and Power <note>original: *Sapientiam Potentiamque*</note> converge into one and love to be joined; these two always desire, pursue, and meet one another. The reason for this was more obscure at that time, and unless supported by various examples...

<sig>a 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: various</meta>

<summary>A formal dedication to John Ernest the Younger, Duke of Saxony, framing the work within a Platonic tradition where wisdom and political power are naturally destined to unite. The author uses a famous anecdote about Plato’s letters to Dionysius of Syracuse to illustrate this intellectual partnership.</summary>

<keywords>John Ernest the Younger, Duke of Saxony, dedication, Plato, Dionysius the Younger, Wisdom and Power, First Nature, philosophy of governance</keywords>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication to John Ernest the Younger, Duke of Saxony. The previous page ended mid-sentence, discussing the philosophical union of Wisdom and Power mentioned in Plato's letters.</meta>

...explained with various examples, it was scarcely likely or probable enough; however, it is now evident and very clear from the <term>Primalities</term> <note>original: *Primalitatibus*; in this philosophical system, these are the three fundamental attributes of being: Power, Wisdom, and Love</note> and Pro-principles of this philosophy of ours, which have been so beautifully elucidated, as may be seen.

Therefore, when I came into Your presence for the first time several years ago, after a laborious journey, having been summoned by Your Highness <note>original: *C. T.*, abbreviating *Celsitudo Tua*</note>, I wondered at how this secret marriage of the Law of Nature held such great power even in You. You considered nothing more important than to join true Wisdom to the Power inherited by You from the ancient royal blood of Your ancestors. When these two unite correctly, they cannot fail to give birth to a true Love, both for the Fatherland and its subjects, and for the whole Universe. Then I understood what the same Plato meant in a certain place <note>a reference to the "Noble Lie" or "Myth of the Metals" in Book III of Plato’s *Republic*</note> when he ordained that his citizens be persuaded, even through myths, that all in the city are indeed like brothers; but when God formed them, he mixed gold into the generation of whoever was born fit to rule, for which reason they are most honored, while the others partake of at least the cheaper metals. 

For this "Gold" of which I speak shone forth so brightly from Your Soul and Actions that, although You carried Yourself with none of the pride common to a Prince, You were loved by everyone as more than a brother and a Father. To this, even all the foreigners who know You bear witness. I think they would also not unwillingly grant me this: that even if You had been born neither a Prince, nor a German, nor a Saxon, anyone would judge You worthy of the Princedom, of Germany, and of the House of Saxony. With this goodness of nature and through Your great zeal for virtue...

# *Dedication.*

<sig>a 3</sig>

...you were carried toward everything high and genuine, you also came upon this philosophy of Campanella. You had previously tasted it in part in both Italian and Latin, but you did not then know it in its entirety—a work perhaps no less pleasant and dear than Plato's explanation was to Dionysius <note>original: *Dionysio Platonis fuit elucidatio*; referring to Plato’s attempts to teach the tyrant Dionysius II of Syracuse, as described in Plato's *Seventh Letter*</note>, and one which yields to it in no way in truth or the solidity of its reasoning.

Now indeed, since I am permitted by the author's will to present it in a more complete form—properly revised, expanded, and, as it were, refined <note>original: *recoctam*; literally "re-cooked," implying a process of purification or further maturation of the ideas</note> and set in public type—I certainly ought to dedicate it to no one else. Indeed, Your Highness <note>original: *C. T.*, for *Celsitudo Tua*</note> may by your own right demand it from me, for I have been moved by so many of your kindnesses. 

Nor, as I hope, will this appeal for Wisdom be untimely amidst the clash of arms to Fortitude. For I know that your heroic Soul is "never less alone than when alone" <note>original: *minus solum esse, cum solus non sit*; a classical paradox suggesting that a wise person is most active in thought when physically solitary</note>, and amidst these warlike tumults, you think no less of peace and the works of peace, just as your Soul knows that Power can never stand firm without the companionship of Wisdom and Love.

Certainly, when we consider the wondrous and continuous changes of the universe, governed by such great providence, we may in a way find relief even amidst the present public evils that surround us and have oppressed us for so many years in this **Common Combustion of Germany** <note>original: *Communi Germaniæ Combustione*; a vivid reference to the devastation of the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648)</note>. In such matters, true philosophy provides the greatest solace to anyone, second only to the Sacred Scriptures. Of this matter, Magnanimous Prince, after such heavy blows of fortune which you have sustained until now, you will undoubtedly be able to speak from experience, perhaps at times singing that verse of the Poet with your most glorious ancestor:

<meta>catchword: Just</meta>

<summary>The author presents a revised and expanded edition of Tommaso Campanella's philosophy to the Duke of Saxony, arguing that true Power must be paired with Wisdom and Love. He positions this philosophical work as a source of solace during the ongoing devastation of the Thirty Years' War.</summary>

# Dedication.

<margin>
Horace,
Odes,
Book 3,
Ode 3
</margin>

> *The man who is just and firm of purpose,*
> *Neither the heat of the citizens <note>original: "Non Civium ardor"; referring to the irrational fury of a mob or political faction</note>, and so forth,*
> *Should the world break and fall upon him,*
> *The ruins will strike him unafraid.*

You will truly find other excellent things here concerning the actions and institutions of men, which may stir your sublime and praiseworthy thoughts. A time will come when, with hypocrisy driven away, a place will also be left for Sincerity, Truth, and Virtue.

May the First Power <note>original: "Prima Potentia"; a term often used by the philosopher Tommaso Campanella to refer to God's attribute of Power</note>, God the Best and Greatest, deign to preserve Your Highness <note>original: "C. T." for *Celsitudo Tua*</note>—divinely rescued from the hands of enemies—safe for a long time for the salvation of your people and your Fatherland and for the glory of Germany, along with your most Illustrious Brothers. This is my prayer; and at the same time, I most humbly ask—nor do I ask unfairly—that you set before yourself these philosophical contemplations <note>original: *Philosophemata*</note> to be meditated upon many times over.

->Of Your Highness<-

The most bound and
devoted servant,

**TOBIAS ADAMI.**

<image-desc>A rectangular decorative woodcut headpiece featuring symmetrical scrolling acanthus leaves, floral motifs, and a central small oval containing a figure, possibly an angel or a saint.</image-desc>

# TO THE HONEST READER
### AND TO THE PHILOSOPHER WHO
### WISELY UNDERSTANDS, HEALTH AND GREETINGS.

## Tobias Adami

<insert>NATIONAL LIBRARY OF ROME VITTORIO EMANUELE</insert>

*ACCEPT at last, Christian Reader, the long-promised Summary <note>original: "Epilogismum"; here meaning a concise review or systematic condensation of a larger philosophical system</note> of Worldly Philosophy <note>original: "Philosophiæ Mundanae"; the natural philosophy of Tommaso Campanella, which Adami was instrumental in publishing in Germany</note>, which, after so many and such great skirmishes <note>original: "velitationes"; referring to the debates and minor intellectual battles between different schools of thought</note> of the human intellect across all ages, seems to us so far to be the truer version. It is drawn forth from Nature, confirmed by the testimonies of the Creator, and approved by the consensus of the sacred interpreters <note>referring to theologians and biblical commentators</note>. Finally, it is made clear by eternal Reasons and stands unerringly upon daily experiments. Our aim is that if our Christian Religion—which we firmly believe—is true, there should be an all-encompassing uniformity and an inviolable harmony of all truths. Just as there is one God who is the cause of all things, and one Nature which is His work, so too is there one Truth expressing, producing, and declaring the entities of this work, as far as the dim light of our capacity allows.*

<note>The vocabulary listed below highlights the core concepts of this introduction: Summary (Epilogismum), Worldly Philosophy (Philosophia Mundana), Tobias Adami (the editor), Truth (Veritas), Nature (Natura), Christian Religion, and the One God (unus Deus).</note>

<summary>This preface by Tobias Adami introduces the reader to Tommaso Campanella’s natural philosophy, arguing that it represents a "truer" understanding of the world because it harmonizes scientific observation (Nature) with religious doctrine.</summary>
<keywords>Tobias Adami, Tommaso Campanella, natural philosophy, harmony of faith and reason, Christian science, empiricism</keywords>

# PREFACE BY TOBIAS ADAMI.

*You behold, therefore, the World as an object worthy of consideration in all its parts and tiny particles, and then especially Yourself as a small Epitome <term>Epitome: A condensed summary or 'microcosm'; the idea that a human being mirrors the structure of the entire universe</term> of the great World. Into this self you must descend, not only to examine its construction and investigate the guests dwelling within—the Spirit and the Mind—but also their wonderful works, emotions, and habits, both within themselves and with others in the city and the home; until the play of this Comedy of Mortals <note>original: "Mortalium Comœdiæ"; a common Renaissance metaphor viewing human life as a theatrical performance</note> is finished and they retreat behind the scenes, and each returns to where they came from or where they belong, just as we hope the whole Theater <note>original: "Theatrum"; referring to the 'Theater of the World' (Theatrum Mundi), the belief that the physical universe is a temporary stage for God's plan</note> will finally collapse and be renewed.*

*In these many thousands of changes of the entire living mass, wise men of every age have inquired whether there is some Natural and sensory-comprehensible motor and architect by whose service such great labors are performed. Once this architect is found and its nature understood, a reason can be given for everything that follows, once the physical principle is established within it—whether that principle is solitary, or whether it finds joy in performing its duties in the company of others. Since they saw that four causes always concur in artificial and human works—the Efficient, the Material, the Formal, and the Final <note>These are the four Aristotelian causes: the 'Efficient' (the agent that brings something about), 'Material' (the substance), 'Formal' (the design or essence), and 'Final' (the purpose or end goal)</note>—they rightly judged, by ascending through similarity, that these same causes must apply here, whether some or all of them. If they could bring forth these as the primary origins, they would be worthy of the title of "principles." And indeed, according to*

<meta>catchword: of those [illarum]</meta>

<summary>Tobias Adami introduces the concept of the human being as a microcosm (epitome) of the universe and argues that by studying the self and the world, one can discover the underlying "architect" and the four primary causes of all things.</summary>
<keywords>Microcosm, Macrocosm, Theater of the World, Four Causes, Natural Philosophy, Tobias Adami, Human Spirit, Teleology</keywords>

# PREFACE.

b

*...the classes of those causes can be examined according to the opinion of any philosophers and adapted to them, with Place <note>original: "Loco"; referring to the Aristotelian category of space or position</note> being presupposed by some, or reduced as it were to matter.*

*Regarding **Matter**, there has been agreement among all in establishing it as a principle (though they disagreed on the manner of it), because the entire visible machine of the universe consists of corporeality.*

*The **Epicureans** <term>Epicureans: Followers of the Greek philosopher Epicurus, who taught that the world is made of atoms moving in a void</term> even judged that this matter alone, along with the **Void** or **Space**, was sufficient, and that it moved itself. However, this is impossible, since one and the same thing cannot be both active and passive <note>original: "agens & patiens"; the 'agent' that acts and the 'patient' that is acted upon</note> at the same time and in the same respect—especially in corporeal things. Such an idea implies a contradiction, and that **fourfold nature of causes** <note>The four Aristotelian causes: Material (what it's made of), Formal (its design), Efficient (who made it), and Final (its purpose)</note> cannot be removed from Nature.*

*The **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics: Members of the school of philosophy founded by Aristotle, so named because they walked about while debating</term> joined **Form** to Matter, so that it might perform the duties of both the **Efficient** and the **Final** cause at the same time. Yet they do not say what that Form actually is, being content only with a logical term of the "second notion" <term>Second Notion: A technical term in Scholastic logic for concepts that exist only in our minds to categorize things (like 'species'), rather than the actual physical essence of the thing itself</term>. Nor do they explain—since there are so many innumerable forms in the whole **World**—which one is the primary form from which the rest of the secondary ones descend, and where that primary form resides; for surely order is required in such a beautiful piece of craftsmanship.*

*Regarding the **End** <note>original: "Fine"; referring to the Final Cause or the ultimate purpose for which a thing exists</note>, they are truly ridiculous: they think it coincides with form in natural things, and yet they admit that "nature does nothing in vain." They speak much about the "use of parts" <note>An argument from design, suggesting every organ or part has a specific function</note>; from this, if the final cause is denied, **providence** <note>The protective care of God or nature as a spiritual power</note> must also be denied, just as from a false...*

<meta>catchword: believed [credita]</meta>

<summary>Tobias Adami critiques the Epicurean and Aristotelian (Peripatetic) views of nature, arguing that they fail to properly explain the four causes or the role of a primary Form and divine Providence. He asserts that matter cannot move itself and that a logical categorization of "Form" is insufficient to explain the complex order of the world.</summary>

<keywords>Matter, Epicureans, Void, Four Causes, Peripatetics, Form, Efficient Cause, Final Cause, Providence, Aristotelianism</keywords>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the "fourfold nature of causes." The previous page ended with "Final c...", which this page completes as "Final Cause." Adami is contrasting the mechanical views of the Epicureans and Peripatetics with the more purposeful philosophy of Socrates.</meta>

<header>TOBIAS ADAMI</header>

...cause. From the belief in the eternity of the world, the concealment of the **Efficient Cause** <note>The 'Efficient Cause' is the agent or force that brings something into being—in a religious context, this often refers to God</note> flowed forth. How much better indeed did **Socrates** behave in **Plato's** *Phaedo*, when—almost despairing of that which is better in things, or of the **Final Cause** <note>The 'Final Cause' refers to the purpose or "end goal" for which a thing exists</note>—he finally took up Ideal reasons as a support. Yet he ingenuously confesses that he would most willingly be anyone's disciple to learn how that cause of the **End** (which he calls "the good and the fitting") behaves. 

After he was deprived of this, and could neither find it himself nor learn it from another, he attempted a **"second sailing"** <term>Second Sailing: From the Greek 'deuteros plous'; a navigational metaphor used by Socrates to describe a backup plan or a more laborious path of reasoning when direct observation fails</term> for investigating through Ideas. He accuses **Anaxagoras** <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BC) was a Pre-Socratic philosopher who was the first to suggest that 'Mind' (Nous) was the primary cause of the universe's order</note> in this regard: although he had heard Anaxagoras's opinion that **Mind** <note>original: "Mentem"</note> arranges all things and is the cause of all, and rejoiced that he would learn from it how each thing was arranged by Mind in the best possible way for the specific good of each and the common good of all, he was nonetheless cast down from this wonderful hope. For as he continued reading, he discovered that although Anaxagoras had spoken about Mind at the start, in assigning the particular causes of natural things he mostly used **Matter**, and the external shape and figure of that matter. 

Truly, this is a passage most worthy of consideration by a Philosopher on the very verge of death <note>Socrates' dialogue in the *Phaedo* takes place in his prison cell on the day he is to be executed</note> to commend this doctrine of the reasoning of causes about which we speak.

<meta>catchword: Finalis (Final)</meta>

<summary>This page recounts Socrates' disappointment with earlier philosophers who ignored the "Final Cause" (purpose). Adami uses Plato's Phaedo to argue that the universe is organized by a "Mind" toward the "Good," rather than being a result of mere material shapes.</summary>

<keywords>Socrates, Plato, Phaedo, Anaxagoras, Final Cause, Mind, Matter, Second Sailing, Efficient Cause, Purpose</keywords>

Adami is contrasting the author's approach (Tommaso Campanella) with earlier philosophers like Telesio and the ancient Greeks regarding the purpose behind creation.</meta>

# P R Æ F A T I O .

<sig>b 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: instru-</meta>

<margin>
<unclear>The cause of the end</unclear>
</margin>
The **Final Cause** <note>The purpose or "end goal" for which something exists</note> of things, therefore, since it is so obscure—even if it has not been denied by many—has nevertheless been brought into consideration for the explanation of principles by very few, or rather by none of the philosophers. For this reason, our author here is all the more to be admired; having dared to attempt this, he shows the way to others, so that they may strive to proceed with fruit in the contemplation of **this machine** <note>A common Renaissance metaphor for the universe as a complex, divine mechanism</note>, and to wonder more daily at divine works. For everywhere, as far as the human intellect allows, he strives to investigate the reasons of the **Creating Wisdom** or **Art**, by which it was led to fashion things in such a way and no other—a matter in which **Telesio** <note>Bernardino Telesio (1509–1588), a natural philosopher who influenced Campanella but focused more on physical heat and cold than on divine purpose</note> is deficient.

Furthermore, regarding the nature of the **Efficient Cause** <note>The agent or force that brings something into being</note>, almost most thinkers have been more anxious to meditate upon it, whether explicitly or implicitly, whether more deeply and **Metaphysically**, or more closely and **Physically**. Whence, although the **Epicureans** <note>Followers of Epicurus who believed the world was formed by the random collision of atoms</note>, as we have said, thought **Matter** was sufficient for themselves, they nevertheless repeatedly attribute something to it in their consideration of the Efficient Cause, just as the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, known for their focus on "Form" and "Matter"</note> do for **Form**. The **Stoics**, however, assume **God** for the moving of matter; and **Anaxagoras** assumes **Mind** or **Wisdom** for **Chaos**; **Empedocles** assumes **Love and Strife** <note>original: "Amorem & odium"</note> for the four elements; **Parmenides** (as also the **Pythagoreans**) assumes the **immobile One**, and this most loftily—understanding God, of course, to whom he soon attributes **Ideas**, and then **Heat and Cold** in Nature, as

<note>This list summarizes how different schools identified the "Efficient Cause" or the driving force of the universe: for some, it was divine mind; for others, physical forces like heat or attraction.</note>

<summary>Tobias Adami praises Tommaso Campanella for investigating the "Final Cause" (the divine purpose) of the universe, a topic he claims other philosophers, including the influential Bernardino Telesio, ignored in favor of the "Efficient Cause."</summary>
<keywords>Final Cause, Efficient Cause, Tommaso Campanella, Bernardino Telesio, Ancient Greek Philosophy, Stoicism, Peripatetics, divine wisdom</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues from the previous page's discussion of the "Efficient Cause." The text begins mid-sentence, completing the thought that certain philosophers added "instruments" (tools or secondary causes) to their explanation of how the world was built.</meta>

...adds instruments, just as **Archelaus** <note>A 5th-century BCE philosopher and teacher of Socrates; he proposed that mind and matter were both involved in the creation of the world</note>, the teacher of Socrates, as well as **Plato** and **Timaeus** <note>Referring to the narrator of Plato's dialogue "Timaeus," which describes the creation of the universe by a divine craftsman</note> did. Others put forward principles such as water (as **Thales** <note>Thales of Miletus, often called the first philosopher, who argued water was the primary substance of all things</note> did), or air endowed with divinity (as **Diogenes** <note>Diogenes of Apollonia, who believed air was the fundamental, intelligent substance of the cosmos</note> did), or fire (as **Heraclitus** and **Hippasus** did). Although they seem to hint at a *matter* from which they wish to draw the birth of things, it is nevertheless likely that they everywhere understood an **Efficient Force** <note>The active power or agent that causes change or motion</note> to be present as well, whether in the form of a "seminal reason" <note>An ancient concept—*ratio seminalis*—that certain "seeds" or rational principles within matter guide its development and growth</note> or some other mode of action—as is clear in the case of Diogenes, where divinity imbues the air. And from this material modification, using analogous names, also come **Sulfur**, **Mercury**, and **Salt**, which are held as principles by the **Chemists** <note>Refers here to the "Tria Prima" of Paracelsian alchemy, which taught that these three substances were the fundamental components of all matter</note>. These constitute all things from the diverse marriage of **Heat** with **Matter**, and for that reason, they are subordinate to our own principles. However, one can now only guess at the opinions of many of these ancients rather than clearly grasp them, since their teachings have reached us in such a fragmentary state.

For us, after having carefully weighed all their opinions and the difficulties into which they have cast themselves in various ways—one more than another—and being aided at the same time by the holy revelation of the **Eternal Architect** <note>original: *Opifex Æternus*; a term for God as the craftsman of the universe</note>, it is that much easier to strip away the labyrinth of so many divisions to reach closer to the truth, and to form less ambiguous decrees once certain and distinct principles have been established.

<summary>Tobias Adami reviews how ancient philosophers and alchemists attempted to identify the primary forces of nature, arguing that their fragmentary views are perfected by the author's new system, which is aided by divine revelation.</summary>

*These principles, at the beginning of **Time**—which for us does not follow the motion of the heavens, but rather the existence and duration of things—began to perform their duties. This was necessary because one must eventually arrive at one primary **Opposition** <note>The idea that all complex changes in nature can be reduced to the struggle between two fundamental opposites</note> from so many other types of conflict. ***Heat**, therefore, and **Cold** (since we know no higher opposites in the study of Physics) being not imaginary or accidental entities, but Real ones, of the noblest Nature and very much recognizable to our senses, are those **First Inhabitants**...*

# TOB. ADAMI <note>Tobias Adami (1581–1643) was a German scholar and member of the Fruitbearing Society. He was instrumental in publishing the works of the Italian philosopher Tommaso Campanella, who is the "Author" referred to here.</note>

*the World that have been—of Empires, Kingdoms, Communities, and Orders—with their structures or deeds, their works and instruments, and the causes of their lives, deaths, and changes, as well as the diseases and remedies of each, according to the subject matter found within Republics <term>Respublica: The "public thing" or Commonwealth; here referring to any organized state or political body</term>. From these, you will learn to know your own Country and how to provide for it, as becomes a good citizen. In a few Aphorisms <term>Aphorisms: Short, pithy statements or principles intended to be easily memorized and applied</term>, our Author has vigorously embraced a great many things, so that he seems to give you anything rather than mere words. If you desire many and great things, look around at the histories of nations, and enter them armed with these axioms; unless I am mistaken, you will judge most things more correctly from these than from the grand Commentaries of others.*

**And since it has hitherto prevailed in common Philosophy that the doctrine of the Domestic Community <note>original: "Communitate Domestica"; the management of the household or family unit as the foundational building block of society</note> or family is perhaps treated separately as a particle or element of the Civil Community, the author wished to subjoin certain Aphorisms concerning it in the manner of others. He did this so that you might have the operations of the human Spirit in this kind also in a single view, and so that those Moral, Civil, and domestic philosophical ideas should not be separated from their roots, but rather connected with Natural things <note>original: "Naturalibus"; referring here to Natural Philosophy or the laws of nature</note>, from which they take their origin and strength, and their growth, if they are rightly cultivated from them.**

### PREFACE.

*This Poetic Dialogue is placed here like a delightful gem, serving as a model for our Author's Philosophical Republic <term>Respublica Philosophica: An ideal state governed by wisdom and reason rather than mere tradition or force</term>. After so many different forms of government devised by various lawmakers and others, it pleased the author—as a Natural Philosopher guided by Reason—to fashion this one. He modeled it wonderfully according to the great pattern of Nature and its principles; hence it received the name **THE CITY OF THE SUN** <note>original: "Solis Civitatis"</note>. You will see here a structure far more ingenious than the city of Ecbatana described by Herodotus <note>Herodotus, the "Father of History," described the Median capital Ecbatana as having seven concentric walls, each a different color</note>, which likewise shone with distinct colors across seven circuits on a hill. If there are matters that deserve excuse, explanation, or defense, these will be discussed in the Questions <note>Referring to Campanella’s "Politica," which includes a section of "Questions" defending the City of the Sun</note>.*

Adami visited Galileo in Florence in 1613, where he was shown the moons of Jupiter and the phases of Venus through the telescope</note>, revealing the face of the Heavenly Bodies more closely, and in a manner quite different than I had previously believed. # PREFACE.

->TOB. ADAMI<-

...believe it <note>Completing the thought from the previous page</note>, the old opinion surely had to be doubted, especially since many other reasons have come to light—reasons which, following the work of others, you now find in abundance throughout the excellent monuments <note>original: "monumentis," referring here to his lasting scientific publications</note> of **Johannes Kepler** everywhere.

Let no one object to me here by citing the senses or the Holy Scriptures; for I do not demand a "rustic" sense <note>meaning a simple, unreflective or uneducated perception</note>, but one that is optical and judicious, so that it is not deceived. For motion itself does not properly possess an external sense by which it might be perceived; rather, it is inferred through internal sensation, comparison, and judgment. If you look at the Moon and other bodies through a telescope <term>Perspicillum: An early Latin term for a telescope, literally "a thing to see through," popularized after Galileo's discoveries in 1610</term>, you will see they are bodies not unlike our own Earth, and yet you acknowledge that they move. 

Furthermore, the Holy Scriptures (which we surely consider it a sin to contradict) do not define anything certain regarding such motion when they mention these matters in passing while discussing higher, more sublime things. Instead, they accommodate themselves to the understanding of the common people <note>This "accommodation" theory was a standard argument used by figures like Galileo to explain why the Bible speaks of the sun "rising" or "standing still" even if the Earth is moving</note>, as is demonstrated elsewhere. Indeed, no man should be allowed to fabricate a construction of the World from his own imagination, however much it might seem skillfully fashioned with plausible reasoning. Instead, one must investigate and contemplate the World exactly as it was built by the most wise Architect <note>Adami uses the terms "Artifex" and "Opifex" to describe God as the master craftsman of the universe</note>, applying every possible diligence, lest we do an injustice to the Creator by trying to "correct" His handiwork. After a meeting with **Galileo**, I then advised **Campanella** to consider these things more carefully; for this "carrying away" of the first mover <term>Primum Mobile: In the traditional geocentric system, the "First Movable" sphere was the outermost shell of the universe that was believed to rotate at incredible speed, dragging all other celestial spheres around the Earth every 24 hours</term>...

<meta>catchword: than (quam)</meta>

He notes that he urged Campanella to reconsider his geocentric views after meeting with Galileo and studying Kepler.</summary>

# PREFACE.

*...how tyrannical and entirely absurd it was in Nature, but also how it was, in a certain way, repugnant to the senses when they are corrected by reason. **Campanella** replied—as he is a most sincere man—rejoicing that the new discoveries he had already perceived were now confirmed for him. Lamenting his misery, being hindered in prison <note>Campanella spent 27 years in prison for his political and religious views; during this time, he wrote many of his most famous works</note> and thus unable to gaze with us upon that homeland from which the better part of himself had come <note>He likely refers to the stars and the heavens, which he viewed as the spiritual origin of the soul</note>, he again implored me to look carefully into the matter, lest I be moved from the common doctrine of almost everyone by a flighty opinion. He said that he could define nothing else for now; but even if it were absolutely necessary for the Earth to rotate, his own principles would certainly hold firm within our System. He maintained as a manifest dogma that the **Sun** is the Father and the **Earth** the Mother of all beings that are produced on our Earth <note>This "Father/Mother" imagery reflects the Renaissance idea of a living universe, where the Sun provides the active heat (spirit) and the Earth provides the passive matter</note>.*

*As for me, the further I progressed in philosophizing, the more I was confirmed in this. But perhaps he himself began to waver, or at least to be in suspense, as can be clear to you from his **Apology for Galileo** <note>original: "Apologia pro Galileo." Campanella wrote this defense of Galileo in 1616, arguing that the Bible should not be used to suppress scientific inquiry</note> which we published recently, where he strives especially to show that this opinion is not contrary to the Holy Scriptures. However, nothing has been changed regarding these matters in the physical sections <note>original: "physiologicis," referring here to the study of nature or physics</note> of this book; instead, these philosophical points have remained just as they were established long ago. It is hinted at briefly under Article 5 of Chapter 1. It will be clearer from the "Questions" and the **Metaphysics** <note>Referring to Campanella's other major works which delve deeper into the nature of reality beyond the physical world</note>.*

# TOBIAS ADAMI

Indeed, even if all things are understood according to the system of the **Pythagoreans** <note>The Pythagoreans were ancient Greek philosophers who proposed that the Earth and planets revolve around a "Central Fire," an idea that early modern scientists like Copernicus saw as a precursor to their own theories</note>, the aforementioned principles can remain consistent, provided they are explained with a bit more grace and skill. For one cannot deny the presence of **Heat** and **Cold** in nature any more than **Light** and **Darkness**, which are their outward appearances. We therefore say that all bodies in nature move—specifically driven by heat—though each in its own distinct way.

The **Sun** itself, positioned at the center, revolves on its own axis—a fact proven by sunspots <note>original: "maculae." These dark spots on the Sun’s surface, observed by Galileo and others through telescopes, proved that the Sun was not an unchanging, perfect orb and that it rotated on an axis</note>. This motion, because it arises from **primordial heat** <note>term: primordial heat (original: "primordiali calore"); the fundamental, life-giving energy that Adami believes is the primary cause of all movement in the universe</note> within itself and does not depend on any other source, is the most noble kind of movement. Yet, compared to the planets traveling their vast orbits, the Sun appears almost stationary, just like the fixed stars in the heavens.

As for the rest of the **planets**, the **Telescope** indicates they are thick, dense bodies that do not shine on their own but are lit from elsewhere. These planets are **animated and driven by Sense and Love**, stirred by the continuous waves of Solar Heat. They perform their "dances" in wondrous eccentric orbits <note>term: eccentric; orbits that are not perfectly circular or centered, a concept used to explain the varying speeds and distances of planets</note>. These movements follow a law that is constant to itself, even if it varies due to the physical nature of the bodies or higher causes. Do we not also see, in the wood of trees, how the pulsing of a small amount of Heat pushes out annual rings—those wonderfully varied concentric and eccentric circles?

Those things without Heat, however, remain stable and immobile...

He uses the growth rings of trees as a biological analogy for the mathematical complexity of planetary orbits.</summary>

# PREFACE

...the planets may be judged by the degree of density and **Cold** hidden within them, which weighs down and darkens their massive bulks. However, as we can observe on Earth, their outer layers and the areas deep beneath the surface are nourished and brought to life by incoming **Heat**. It is no wonder, then, if they are moved when stirred by this heat. 

In the same way, our own bodies (though of a much different nature) would be motionless if they were without **vital Heat** <note>original: "Calore vitali"; the internal heat thought by early modern thinkers to be the source of life, digestion, and the movement of limbs</note>. It is by this heat that they are raised up and directed. Nor should we fear that the blood in our heads and chests will sink into our feet; for everything remains in its proper place and is supported by a life-giving flow, just as **primordial nature** <note>original: "natura primordiali"; the fundamental order of the universe as established at the beginning of creation</note> intended.

As for **Cold**, which we truly experience in Nature, we cannot assign it any other kingdom or seat than within the most fundamental dense substances. Cold, therefore, appears to be a less noble principle. It dwells within the density of matter and resists the reign of heat to preserve the celestial spheres around the **center of love** <note>original: "centrum amoris"; in the philosophy of Campanella and Adami, this refers to the Sun or a metaphysical point of attraction that binds the universe together through harmony</note>. By opposing heat, cold actually helps promote the creation of all things.

**Heat**, however—which is the true cause of the birth of all created things—spreads its power far and wide in every direction. It is the most noble **servant of the Divine** <note>original: "diuinitatis minister"</note> and the giver of all life and movement. And perhaps, at the **end of time** <note>original: "consummatione seculorum"; the final transformation or conclusion of the current world age</note>, Heat alone will reign over all matter.

Lest their opinion seem <unclear>doubtful</unclear>, even **chemical experiments** <note>original: "Chymica experimenta"; at this time, alchemy was frequently used as physical evidence to prove theological or cosmological theories</note> can lead us by the hand to see the truth, proving great things by observing the small.

This is not the place to say more on these matters, as I refer you to the Author’s *Questions* and his other books for a more extensive treatment. I merely wished to mention these points in passing, since friends have long raised similar objections. I did not want these doubts to disturb you, nor did I want you to think that we had given these subjects too little consideration.

Therefore, kind Reader, take in good part whatever we have now labored upon for your benefit—as if on a foreign soil—by bringing to light these philosophical works of the incomparable **Campanella**. If, as promised, not everything seems entirely consistent or as settled as you might wish, you will nonetheless find few things to criticize, and those of minor importance. # PREFACE

...will consider discourses often woven about such abstruse matters for human **craftsmen** <note>original: "Artifices"; here referring to those who study or work within the mechanics of the natural world</note>. You will find these works to be such that, although they are adorned with **philosophical investigations** <note>original: "Philosophicis indagationibus"</note> and analogies drawn from our own world—insofar as nature can teach us about them from what follows <term>a posteriori|the method of reasoning from observed effects back to their causes, rather than from theory alone</term>—they nonetheless do not contradict the words of the divine **Moses** and others who were taught by the **Author of Nature** himself. Instead, you will find that they explain these things in a skillful, rational, and perceptible way. 

This is certainly what the holy **Church Fathers** <note>the foundational theologians of the Christian tradition</note> also did, each according to his own ability. For who could convince themselves that the ineffable workmanship of the **incomprehensible Master** <note>referring to God as the Great Architect</note> could be adequately captured by formulated words? Even if the progress of this **miraculous texture** <note>original: "Mirabilis texturæ"; the complex, woven structure of the universe</note> were revealed to you as if in a mirror, you would still be unable to describe it with mortal speech. Whatever the case may be, you will certainly find far more solid and true reasoning here than in the decrees of the **Sophists**, the **Peripatetics** <note>the followers of Aristotle, whose dominance in the universities Campanella sought to overturn</note>, or others.

I here challenge a comparison with all authors, whoever they may be, who have until this day published anything regarding **human truths** which are to be derived and reconciled from their sources according to the natural order of things. If, however, you are able to bring forward more correct arguments in certain matters...

# T O B I A S  A D A M I

...even if you should think so, surely for the sake of **Christian Charity** <note>original: "Charitate Christiana"</note> you will not cease to contribute to such a **holy edifice** <note>a metaphor for the collective pursuit of divine and natural truth</note>. Nor would I wish you to think of us as such rigid censors of affairs that we consider everything concluded by these writings, since perhaps there are some points with which we ourselves are not entirely satisfied. We are, however, equally friends of **Truth** and of **Philosophical Liberty**, without which Truth cannot be investigated. Meanwhile, we rest upon these principles as true and solid until you can teach us better things, if you are able.

The condition of the **Author** <note>Tommaso Campanella (1568–1639), who spent 27 years in prison for his religious and political views</note> must also be rightly considered: he is heavily burdened by wretched **envy** and afflicted by necessity, yet he is by no means an evil man—as some falsely suspect of him—but a man of the utmost sincerity and most worthy of a better fate, a true **Philosopher**. This consideration will help explain any other shortcomings, if there be any.

Indeed, in these matters as in all others, I attribute nothing to myself, except that together with others, I too desire with all my strength to help you toward the **Truth**. If we reach this goal together, you yourself will undoubtedly attribute the success not to me, but to these very writings. **Farewell**, and if you love **First Wisdom** <term>Sapientia Prima|Campanella’s term for the fundamental principles of knowledge that unite science, metaphysics, and divinity</term>, imitate it also in your life; consider that you can progress no more through **Knowing** than through **Loving**.

# *On Thomas Campanella, by Tobias Adami*

Hanging and ringing in a corner of the world,
While it happens to please mortals to sleep,
The Little Bell <note>original: *Campanula*, a pun on the author’s name, Campanella</note> awakens many with its loud sounding.
"Who," they ask, "would so boldly bring this restless bronze,
So troublesome to us? Why do we not take it away?"
Now the poor Little Bell <note>Campanella</note> sounds in secret for only a few,
Gathering a heavy rust <term>ærugo|Literally "verdigris" or copper rust; here Adami uses it to represent the neglect, silencing, and physical toll of Campanella's decades-long imprisonment</term>.
O, may my efforts wipe away that heavy rust,
So that, as a purer servant of the Primal Mind <term>Prima Mens|A central concept in Campanella’s philosophy, referring to the "First Mind" or God, the source of all wisdom and natural laws</term>,
The Little Bell <note>Campanella</note> will ring out the sacred truths more clearly.

# F. T. CAMPANELLA’S
## ON MATTERS OF NATURE
### P R E F A C E
<note>original: *Physiologicorum*. In the 17th century, "Physiology" referred to the general study of nature and the physical world—what we would now call "Natural Philosophy"—rather than specifically the functions of living organisms.</note>

->To the Academic of the First Wisdom.<-
<note>Campanella likely refers to a member of an "Academy" (a private intellectual circle) dedicated to "First Wisdom" or Metaphysics.</note>

<margin>a The universe of things and its parts are the Book and the statues of God; rational creatures are his images; irrational ones are his footprints. From St. Augustine, St. Bridget, and St. Anthony, according to Nicephorus.</margin>
<margin>What Philosophy is.</margin>
*Since it is not granted to me to lead my life with you, my Dearest one—as you most eagerly desire, so that you might become close to God through virtue: Lest such great love be utterly frustrated, I have decided to delight you in these pages, where you will be able to drink in my understanding and rejoice at the same time. For lovers often look pleasantly even upon the image of the beloved if the living object is absent: This is what I myself do, while I contemplate the first Divinity <note>original: *Numen*. This refers to the divine power or the presence of God.</note> in his ᵃ footprints, images, and divine statues, and in his own Book <note>original: *Codice*. This refers to the "Book of Nature," a popular concept in the Renaissance suggesting that God wrote two books: the Bible and the physical Universe.</note>, which is the World itself. Moreover, contemplation of this kind is called Philosophy. For where Wisdom is lacking, Love supplies it; since Philosophy is the Love of Wisdom. And indeed, where love grows numb, it is awakened by Wisdom; for Love does not seek out gnats and ants for their own sake, but when the mind considers by what means and for what purpose they were made, it raises us to an affection for such great craftsmanship; And wherever Love is carried, Wisdom offers the occasion for recognizing God in the things loved,*

<summary>This page serves as the introduction to Campanella's work on natural philosophy, defining philosophy as the "Love of Wisdom" and the study of the "Book of Nature." Campanella argues that by observing the world—God's "statues and footprints"—one can cultivate a love for the divine Creator.</summary>

<keywords>Tommaso Campanella, Natural Philosophy, Book of Nature, Wisdom, Divinity, Metaphysics, St. Augustine</keywords>

# FRA TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

*...having been loved and considered. But if it is not possible to attain this completely, in great matters it is enough to have willed it.* <note>original: "in magnis voluisse sat est." This is a famous Latin proverb by the poet Propertius, suggesting that even if a noble goal is not reached, the sincere attempt is virtuous in itself.</note>

<margin>b Knowledge is drawn from the senses. From those objects known beforehand, reason crosses over to unknown things as if they were the same, because they are similar.</margin>
<margin>c Holy men provide indubitable faith when they speak as witnesses of those things they learned from God; they provide science, however, when they speak as witnesses of the living book, which is the World—which we read through experience consisting of many sensations; but they provide only opinion when they speak from their own conjecture.</margin>
*To these things ᵇ I shall lead you with me, from one similarity to another, under the guidance of Science and Faith. This faith ought to be applied to holy men ᶜ when they speak as those testifying to the things they learned in the School of the First Wisdom <note>original: "Sapientia Prima." In Campanella's thought, this refers to Metaphysics or the direct knowledge of God, the "First Teacher."</note>, but not when they are merely forming opinions in human schools.*

<margin>d The sense corrects errors and resolves doubts by its own nature; all knowledge comes from the First Wisdom.</margin>
*ᵈ Senses correct our science, and they resolve and clarify doubts through experience; one sense supplies what is lacking in another. A present sensation corrects a past one, and things already known demonstrate things unknown because of the unity of all knowledge, both with each other and with the First Cause. Whose*

<margin>What Nature is. St. Thomas, [Commentary on] Physics, Book 2.</margin>
<margin>e Nature is an art intrinsic to things. Art, however, is an "extrinsic nature" that imitates nature, just as nature imitates God.</margin>
*ᵉ art, implanted in things and leading them toward their own ends, is called Nature. This word is derived from the "birth" <note>original: "nativitas." Campanella is playing on the etymological root of Natura (nature) and natus (born).</note> of things, referring to the art that is implanted in that very birth. And so, we may ask the Maker of the World to spare us if, concerning*

<margin>f Knowledge of God is obtained through similarities, and discourse [about Him] through metaphors.</margin>
*Himself, we prepare ᶠ a discourse through metaphors <note>original: "translationes." In a theological context, this refers to "metaphorical transfers," where human words are used to describe divine qualities that exceed human language.</note>, rather than according to what He is in His own entity—for He is incomprehensible and infinite. We are most distant from Him, even if He is most near and intimate to us. Therefore, may He help our knowledge and forgive our ignorance, and be content that we are able to be able, to know, and to love within His own systems,*

<summary>Campanella outlines his "sensalist" philosophy, arguing that all knowledge begins in the senses and moves toward God through the study of nature. He defines Nature as "God's art" acting from within objects and notes that our language about the Divine must rely on metaphor.</summary>

<margin>
a Since in Metaphysics we have shown from the construction of the World and its parts that it is necessary for those parts to precede the whole which they compose; nor could this have been constructed from itself out of contrary things; nor arise by chance, since the highest Art shines forth in it; it was necessary to assign to them its principle...
</margin>

I shall say <gloss>a</gloss> therefore through a syllogism <note>A logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note> illuminated by wisdom and faith: the first Being, most Powerful, most Wise, and Best, after (if it is right to assign "after" and "before" in Him) the infinite glories, which He enjoys with every pleasure in the immense spaciousness of His divinity, inclined His will (new toward things producible outside the infinite, but ancient within infinity) to fashion certain statues and images, mimicking His own immense goods. In these we contemplate, admire, and praise Him—we who are also His statues and images. For there was no other Being outside Him to admire them; but His handiwork, since it is alive, admires the Maker within itself, and is raised from itself toward Him.

He who surely <gloss>b</gloss> knows because He can; and He wills because He is wise and can. This sacred Monotrias <note>original: "Monotrias." A term coined by Campanella to describe the Trinity through his philosophical theory of the three "Primalities": Power, Wisdom, and Love.</note>, when it foresaw through its wisdom that a finite entity of things could be produced beneath its infinity—since it was itself good—it did not envy its own power the glorious production of those things; nor did it deny that entity to the handiwork, through which it could be produced in the likeness of the first Being. For indeed the whole World, and every particle of it, is constituted from Wisdom, Power, and Love, and one from...

Being unable to discourse concerning Him through His own proper nature, but rather from the likeness of human Craftsmen, I have assigned this reason for creation; although there are many others most unknown to us, but most known to Him: always adhering to sacred Scripture, and the more illustrious fathers, and to reason by divine light.

But not Paternity, Filiation, and Spiration <note>Theological terms for the relationships within the Trinity: the Fatherhood of God, the Sonship of Christ, and the "breathing forth" of the Holy Spirit.</note>, which are revealed in Theology, which this book serves.

### On Place.

#### ARTICLE II.

<margin>a Time is the successive duration of things. Eternity is the permanent duration of the Author of things. From the Epistle of St. James.</margin>
Thus I seem to see, though from too far away, that the First Creator <note>original: "Primum Opificem"</note>—at the Beginning of the *a* successive duration or the cycle of things which we call Time (an image of the ever-permanent Eternity from which it flows)—extended a space that is nearly infinite, in which He might place this, His statue <note>Campanella frequently describes the physical world as a living "statue" or monument to God's power.</note>.

<margin>b Since every natural being is founded in place, one must begin with place: because a thing in its causes is a cause, in the intellect it is intellect, but in place it is an existing thing. From St. Augustine’s *On the Knowledge of the True Life*.</margin>
<margin>c The term "substance" applies to place and to the underlying matter. It is improper for God, Angels, and the soul—according to Augustine in *On the Trinity*, Book 7—but the name "essence" fits them.</margin>
<margin>d This resolves Aristotle's arguments which try to prove that dimensioned space is not "place" (based on the idea that two bodies would be in the same spot, etc.). It is clear that the dimensions of place, being incorporeal, can embrace corporeal matter; place and the thing placed cannot penetrate each other unless both have physical bodies.</margin>
This is *b* Place, the foundation of existence, in which that beautiful Masterpiece <note>original: "Opificium"</note>—that is, the World—sits. If we imagine that Place does not exist, we must admit that an empty space remains in its stead. Place, therefore, is *c* primary substance, or a seat, or an immobile and incorporeal capacity suited for receiving every body. Therefore, it is a foundation that possesses length, breadth, and depth *d* in an incorporeal way. Through this, it can receive bodies that are long, wide, and deep without any mutual "penetration of bodies" <note>In traditional physics, two bodies cannot occupy the same space. Campanella argues that because Space is incorporeal, it can "hold" a body without violating this rule.</note>. Indeed, Place is similar and proportional to all these things. For this reason, God willed that Place be contrary to no Being, nor even to itself, but rather entirely similar to all things and in every direction. Therefore, "right" and "left," "up" and "down," "front" and "back" are terms assigned by us to the diversity of the bodies placed within it, and not to Place itself. For fire is not carried to the "upper" place because it flees the "lower" place, but because it flees the hostile earth. Every body moves from place to place because it seeks what is similar to it, or flees...

<summary>Campanella defines Space (Place) as an incorporeal, three-dimensional "primary substance" created by God to serve as the foundation for the physical world. He distinguishes between the successiveness of Time and the permanence of Eternity, while refuting Aristotelian views on the nature of space.</summary>

->### ON THE STUDY OF NATURE, Chapter I.<-

<margin>
e. The surface of the surrounding body cannot be an immobile place, as Aristotle thinks; for the surface itself is always moving, while the body located within—such as a tower—always remains at rest. Therefore, the body would simultaneously change its place and not change it. It is necessary that the <unclear>spectus</unclear> <note>Likely "aspectus" (view) or "respectus" (relation).</note> of its immobility be founded in the tower itself, otherwise the tower would be its own place; nor is place found in the surface, which is continually becoming something else. Therefore, place exists in the space within.
</margin>
<margin>
St. Thomas, *Physics*, Book 4.
</margin>
...flees or pursues an opposing body. And while it moves, it physically penetrates a place, and is non-physically <note>original: "incorporaliter." In this context, Campanella argues that while bodies take up space, the space itself lacks physical mass and thus "penetrates" the body without displacing it.</note> penetrated by that place: insofar as place is the foundation and internal basis of the entire corporeal being, and not merely of the $e$ outer circumference which ends at the surface of other bodies. It does not terminate at a "place" unless that place underlies both bodies as a first $f$ immobile substance. Yet, this space does not enter into the composition of things by existing *with* them as a part, but rather by existing *under* them. For rare things <note>referring to low-density materials</note> $g$ are not composed of a mixture of "the full" and "the empty," even if a vacuum were to come between them. $h$ Space—as Place—rejoices so greatly in supporting beings that it abhors ever becoming entirely empty; for this reason, it perpetually draws toward itself the bodies that offer the least resistance, such as rare substances which are more similar to itself, lest it remain a vacuum. Nevertheless, a vacuum can often be created by force, though not by nature; we experience this in the rifts within clouds, and in vessels full of smoke that is suddenly chilled and reduced into a narrower space. We see it also in bellows that are sealed after the air has been squeezed out and then forcibly pulled apart; and in siphons <note>original: "siphonibus." Here referring to syringes or tubes used for drawing liquids.</note> where the end hole is blocked with pitch, so that a piston wrapped in cotton, when pulled out by force, immediately returns on its own to fill the vacuum when released. Not only does Place refuse to remain empty, but the $i$ located bodies themselves do not admit a vacuum, because they enjoy mutual contact, as if they were constituted from a single matter and a single sense and consensus; therefore, they abhor the vacuum that divides them. For this reason, in a clepsydra <note>A water clock. Campanella is describing why water stays in a vessel with only a small opening if the top is sealed.</note>, the contained water does not fall downward when the upper hole is closed so that air cannot enter, unless the substance is of a much heavier mass, such as honey. Often, too, substances are carried upward in a very brief moment to fill a vacuum, as is made clear in the science of pneumatics <note>original: "de spiritalibus." This refers to the study of "spirits" or gases/air, pioneered by ancient engineers like Hero of Alexandria.</note>.

---

...firmly containing it from within and without. $f$ If place moved, it would enter into another place, and then it would be a "located thing" rather than "Place" itself. Likewise, it would interrupt and disturb the entities and motions of bodies rather than supporting them.
$g$ Bodies are not composed of the "located thing" and "Place," as Democritus believes. For Place does not move with the bodies, which it would have to do if it were a part of them.
$h$ Nature allows neither place nor located things to permit a vacuum, but treats it as a force hostile to their mutual love <note>Campanella views the physical world as being held together by "sensuscensus" or a shared "sense" of harmony/love between all parts of creation.</note>.
$i$ Inside a vacuum, motion would not happen "outside of time" (instantaneously), as Aristotle argues, but in a very brief time, because the impossibility of the boundaries resists it; and while something moves from one thing to another, it must pass through the middle.

# On Matter.

## ARTICLE III.

<margin>
a. Matter and the substantial body are one and the same, since this substance is by nature passive rather than active. If it were not so, a physical body would have to be made out of incorporeal matter and incorporeal forms, which is impossible.
</margin>

Inside of "Place," God positioned a certain "whole"—a formless body, without shape, and devoid of action. This substance, however, was fit to be extended, contracted, divided, united, and to receive every shape, action, and craft, just as wax receives every seal. In the imagination, it can be cut into the smallest possible "little bodies" <note>original: "corpuscula"</note> infinitely; however, to the senses, its division finds an end in the tiniest <term>atoms</term> <note>Campanella refers to the smallest physical units of matter, similar to the "dust motes" seen in light.</note> which appear in a sunbeam entering a house through a vent. It was necessary for it to be this way so that <term>quantity</term>—which is the internal limit and measure of this substance—could take on every degree of smallness or greatness, and every position consisting of particles. Thus, it could be transformed as needed by the active powers <note>the "virtues" or forces</note> that were to be sown into it. This is Matter: the second substance, the basis of forms, the passive principle in the composition of things, and a body that is entirely terminable and capable of being acted upon; for physical bodies cannot be made out of non-physical things.

<margin>
I am speaking of the matter found in the nature of things, from which things are composed—not that "imaginary" matter which is neither a "what," nor a "quality," nor a "quantity," as described by Aristotle <note>Campanella is mocking the Aristotelian definition of "Prime Matter" as a pure abstraction.</note>. St. Basil mocks this view, and Averroes confesses that such matter does not exist outside the mind unless it is corporeal, even if it lacks its own specific boundaries. * Solomon and St. Basil testify that God created the world from "invisible matter." The text says: "the earth was invisible and unformed," which is explained as I have done here.
</margin>

* Furthermore, because matter is inert, it is invisible; for it cannot perform any action upon the sight. Therefore, it is black and dark: for darkness is just as invisible to open eyes as it is to closed ones. Nothing in the essence of matter prevents it from having a passive quality, only an active one. Indeed, even burnt things—from which the white color has exhaled and the grim cold has been expelled—reveal that blackness is the true face of matter. **b** Likewise, whenever matter is not fully overcome by a moving power, nor by immobility, and is left to itself, it falls downward toward the support of the earth. This is seen in stones, and even in glowing coals which are contrary to the earth.

---

<margin>
**b** Things do not fall downward by accelerating their motion at the end because of a "likeness to the earth," as some say; for even burning things, which are the opposite of earth, accelerate in the same way. Nor is it because they are weighed down by an ever-increasing amount of air; for the air under a falling weight is compressed more and more, and should therefore support and slow it down more. Therefore, this kind of fall is accelerated because of matter seeking a support <note>original: "fulcimentum"</note>, just as an animal accelerates at the end of its flight. Since all beings have a sense for their own conservation, and matter is preserved while it is being acted upon <note>passive</note>, not while it is acting.
</margin>

<summary>Campanella defines matter as a fundamentally passive, corporeal substance that fills space and serves as the "wax" for all physical forms. He argues against the abstract "prime matter" of Aristotle, asserting that matter is physically real, atomic, and naturally dark and heavy.</summary>

# On the Active Principles and the Origin of the Elements.

## ARTICLE IV.

<margin>
Lactantius, On the Workmanship of God.
St. Basil, in the Six Days of Creation.
a. Formal principles ought to belong to the substance, but active principles [are different], since they do not exist on their own but act [upon others].
b. Since we see that heat and light are continually poured from the Sun onto the earth; and all fires [are derived] from it...
</margin>
In this corporeal mass, the "statue" of so much matter, **GOD** commanded that two incorporeal Craftsmen be born. These forces are not able to exist except within a body; they are not the specialized tools of any specific physical forms, but only of the Creator himself. Therefore, Heat and Cold were born as the primary Active Principles, <margin>a</margin> and thus they are capable of spreading their own power. Immediately they became mutual enemies, as each desired to occupy the entire material substance. <margin>b</margin> Hence they began to fight against one another, with God providing a great good from this kind of discord. And behold, Heat destroyed—that is, it converted a large part of the matter into smoke <note>Campanella uses "smoke" to describe matter becoming less dense or gaseous</note>; it seized it by pulling it apart through its space, wishing to subject the whole to itself. It exhaled everywhere in a circuit toward this portion of space which we call the periphery. And stretching that far, until it fell into a finite place, or until its strength could no longer be extended against the enemy Cold, it began <unclear>faithfully</unclear> to be driven in a circle. It unfolded so much of its mass that it occupied the whole space and the common firmament. And this kind of very thin, expanded mass was called Heaven; the slightly thicker part, Air; and finally, the thick thinness, which is like sweat, was called the Sea.

---

->*Cold*<-

*...to be generated, both within the earth and in the depths of the sea. Likewise, the earth is thinned by it [the Sun], as are our own beings, and vapor is made similar to heaven, and then it is moved and made white: we believe the Sun to be the hottest, brightest, thinnest, and most noble, as its works testify. Also, because we know that heat is concentrated in mirrors; and struck from stones, and rubbed from wood, and gathered in a cloud, it generates fire by itself; we judge it to be the principal acting cause, while light is its "face" or appearance. This is because it shines with the flames in which it is united; but when those flames are scattered and made invisible, it does not shine. It is also clear that its motion is its operation, for whatever mass it occupies, it thins and moves; therefore, thinness is the disposition which it gives to the mass so that it can move it. Hence it was reasonable to think that heaven was established by heat, as the holy Fathers declare from the sacred scriptures, such as St. Basil, St. Ambrose, Origen, Bernard, and others who call it the <term>Empyrean</term> <note>original: "Empyreum", from the Greek 'pyros' meaning fire</note> heaven, that is, fiery.*

<summary>Campanella introduces Heat and Cold as the two "incorporeal craftsmen" created by God to shape passive matter. Their eternal conflict results in the stratification of the universe into Heaven, Air, and Sea.</summary>

<margin>
c. On the other hand, observing that Great Cold is poured out from the earth, and that it freezes and destroys waters; likewise, that it renders the air and things born from heat immobile and black. Likewise, observing that darkness expands from the earth into the sky: We have indicated that Cold is the principle of the earth, though less robust than heat; and that its operation is rest, while darkness is its face.
</margin>

c. <note>original: "Frigus autem"</note> Cold, however, which persisted stubbornly in the conflict, found itself surrounded on all sides by its enemy—the proud, exhaling Heat—which was thinning its mass everywhere. Feeling itself encircled, Cold gathered itself together in the center of the firmament with its own portion of matter. Just as drops of water form a sphere when surrounded by air, every enemy surrounded by many foes tends to pull inward; thus, all the particles of the underlying mass, desiring to retreat from the hostile heaven, converged into a single round globe. This mass moved no further, lest it approach the hostile heaven. It remained dense, hard, and immobile, and for this reason, it was called **Earth** by the First Wisdom <note>referring to God as the source of all knowledge and design</note>. Such was the d. origin of the two primary bodies, the first Elements of the World, established by two contrary active principles and one passive principle <note>Matter</note> that is not contrary to either of them. These active principles bestowed opposite conditions upon the matter, which was split into two parts. For in truth, every opposition is reduced to that e. primary opposition <note>the fundamental struggle between Heat and Cold</note>. And Wisdom said that one primary opposition would suffice to transform one primary matter, and from this, the variety of all things depends. And God said that if other Worlds were to be created, each of them would be allotted one primary matter and one primary opposition, so that from any one thing, another might be made in turn, and not separately. Therefore, in the earth established by cold, Cold reigns as the Sovereign Cause; density exists there as a seat prepared for it by itself; immobility is its useful operation; and blackness is its f. face—

<meta>The text cuts off here at the catchword "tan-" (likely "tandem" or "tanquam"), which leads into the final sentence of the paragraph on the next page.</meta>

---

<margin>
c. Density is the final disposition that the earth bestowed upon itself so that it could remain immobile.
d. Moses testifies that there are two primary elements, and that all other beings are their "ornaments"—namely, the heaven and the earth. St. Basil, Lactantius, and others agree, teaching that at the end of the world, only these two shall remain. Likewise, if there are two active principles, there must be two elements, for they must always remain somewhere. And where do they remain if not in the primary elements? Therefore, there are two elements, as Aristotle concludes in the first book of his *Physics* alongside Parmenides; although he contradicts himself in the second book of *On Generation*, where he posits four Elements, adding moisture and dryness to the primary opposition along with Ocellus and Hippocrates. 
e. <term>Humidity</term> <note>original: "Humiditas"</note> arises from the dilation of matter, which is rarefaction—the work of heat. Therefore, it has no boundaries of its own and easily takes on those of others, which applies to water, air, and fire, according to Aristotle’s testimony.
f. <term>Dryness</term> <note>original: "Siccit as"</note> arises from the constriction of matter performed by cold itself, or by heat by accident. Because of this, it remains united within its own boundaries and does not easily receive others, as Aristotle testifies. Therefore, these material "passions" <note>passive qualities</note> are produced by the active forces of heat and cold; they are not active causes themselves, as the <term>Peripatetics</term> <note>the followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy</note> foolishly assert.
</margin>

<summary>Campanella explains how the Earth was formed when the active principle of Cold retreated from the surrounding Heat, condensing matter into a solid, immobile sphere. He argues that there are only two primary elements (Heaven and Earth) driven by two active forces (Heat and Cold), dismissing the traditional four-element model.</summary>

<header>CHAPTER I. ON PHYSICS.</header>

<margin>
g. Heat and Cold are not accidents <note>original: "accidentia"; in philosophy, an 'accident' is a property that can change without changing the core nature of a thing. Campanella argues they are more fundamental than that.</note>, since they do not exist outside of intention, or will, or nature, nor do they arrive after a being is already complete; rather, they themselves constitute...

f. ...as its face: for it <note>Matter</note> seems to have been contained within the matter g. in which it stands, presenting a face hostile to the light, which Heat bestowed upon the heaven as its own proper element. This element is the hottest, coming from Heat itself as the active principle g. <note>original: "principio actiuo"</note>; it is the thinnest, because its seat is a thinness suited for motion; it is the most mobile through the operation of Heat; and finally, it is the brightest, because the mass conquered by Heat was gifted with its own face, which is called light—a living brightness that amplifies itself. And these two were the primary elements, since the first contraries dwell within them; and they are the greatest bodies of the world and the most active, and therefore the most sensible—meaning they have the greatest power to change our senses. They are self-diffusing. They do all things. They are not made by any other prior corporeal Being, nor from each other, as secondary Beings are; and finally, they possess the most powerful forces, while secondary things are weak.

*...they constitute being. Nor are they absent or present without the destruction of the subject when they are robust and have time to act. Although a weak and brief heat acting on our hand is an accident <note>a temporary sensation</note>, because it arrives after our being is already formed and does not destroy water by turning it into vapor (of which it is afterwards the essence itself). Therefore, native heat is essence; foreign heat is an accident until it destroys the subject and makes a new Being. The same thing is substance—that is, essence—and accident, with respect to different things: just as a garment is to us and to itself. Contrariety exists in active forms by necessity: for from them it is derived into accidents, and not from accidents to forms. But substance, such as a body or a place, has no contrary. Therefore, the arguments of the Peripatetics <note>the followers of Aristotle</note> are void. Similarly, I say that active forms must be intensified and diminished, otherwise only two beings would be made from them, and not the innumerable ones we see. Matter and place, however, do not admit of "more" and "less." Heat and cold are the primary active physical causes, and not merely instruments of other physical forms; though they are certainly the instruments of the Creator of all things. An instrument does not act unless it is moved by a primary cause. But heat creates fire in mirrors, in thunder, and elsewhere in plants and animals, not moved by any active form (since none is there), but by operating through itself, as seen in the Metaphysics, etc.*

## On the Origin of the Stars.

### ARTICLE V.

After these things, when Heat felt that it could be attacked by the united power of Cold, it also gathered itself in the highest region, where the enemy could not disturb its gatherings; and there, copiously united, it reflected its face—that is, light. These many apparent unions were called **Stars**. Heat could not create them in the lower heaven, because although everything that is extended from the earth to the highest periphery is all one ether, a heaven...

a. Therefore, there is no need to posit a terrestrial solidity in the Sun, in which heat would be united and shine, as Plato thought, since abundant light can reside in great thinness <note>original: "tenuitati"; referring to the quality of being thin or rarefied, the opposite of density.</note>.

And because of the mutual similarity of their parts, every collection assumed a spherical shape, and especially because it was most suited for their motion. Light <gloss>a</gloss> indeed, carried through transparent things, is collected in the opposite air, and like fire it shines and burns: indicating that a copious heat could have been placed in the highest and middle parts—pure, and mixed with no weight adverse to its motion. Unless, however, the Stars are systems <note>original: "systemata"; Campanella uses this to mean a complex world-structure like Earth, containing various elements.</note> assembled from all kinds of things. On the contrary, heat shines more in thin matter than in dense matter: just as in flames more than in iron, and in purer things more than in impure ones.

</margin>

Therefore, thickness did not settle in a single center, but while the battle <note>The primal struggle between Heat and Cold.</note> raged, it was divided into several portions and departed: and the stars move around the center of Love <note>original: "Amoris"; for Campanella, Love and Hatred are the metaphysical forces that draw things together or push them apart.</note>, for which they revolve in its service around the center of Hatred. As for what Beings are in the Stars and how they are formed, metaphysical conjecture will reveal. It stands in-

---

*...our own, as Aristarchus and Philolaus <note>Ancient Greek philosophers who proposed heliocentric or non-geocentric models.</note> seem to have thought, and as it is fitting for Copernicus to say, a different method of philosophizing would be needed; nor would earthly density produce light, but rather reflection from the dense into the transparent part of the system, and the union of rarity and equality. * After I read Galileo's observations, I began to hesitate further whether the stars are systems, as it seems to the Pythagoreans, and I have enclosed this parenthesis in the text so that you may understand that even if the stars are not pure fire, our philosophy regarding the things that happen in our system does not collapse. But these things are discussed most extensively in the questions added to this work and in the *Metaphysics*; and Origen <note>A third-century Christian theologian.</note> is praised, who posited that stars were systems illuminated and moved by the light of the Sun: and therefore the world will perish when God turns away and restrains the light of the Sun. For then, as the Sibyl, Seneca, and Lucan write, stars meeting stars will fall with dire motions, etc. See *Metaphysics*.*
