PHYSIOLOGY CHAPTER V. 39

# *That from a single heat, varied by many degrees of weakening and increasing, and from a single matter changed in various ways, a multitude of Beings can arise, and without the mixing of cold.*

## ARTICLE VI.

<margin>
a. Cold itself was created to preserve the Earth, lest it become the heavens and the whole world become a single element, and lest generation should fail. It exists for the sake of diversifying the degrees of heat, from which different things may arise for the beauty of the statue <note>Campanella refers to the universe as a "World-Statue," a beautifully ordered work of art.</note>, etc., but not so that it enters into the composition itself.

b. Two contraries cannot be reconciled; for they would no longer be contraries. Therefore, heat would not be heat, nor cold be cold. Likewise, just as intense heat is contrary to intense cold, so is weakened heat to weakened cold; and the former acts against the latter just as much as this acts against that. Therefore, a mixture cannot occur: for if they remain as they are, it is a gathering of parts, not a true mixture; nor can the same point of matter be shaped by four forms of elements, or even two. Also, if the forms are destroyed, their powers must also be destroyed—indeed, even more so, since they depend on the forms. Also, if the forms are only weakened, they will still be contraries and will not be reconciled, as Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to medieval and Renaissance science.</note> thinks. Also, it is asked whether they are all in the same part of matter; and how, since they are contrary? Or are they in different parts? If so, a mixture would be four distinct things made from their four elements, and not one uniform thing, as Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher who defined "mixture" as the unification of altered components.</note> decrees. But if they were divided into tiny fragments escaping the senses, it would be a mixture according to our perception, not according to truth. Nor could Aristotle solve his own reasoning, but fled to the concepts of "potentiality" and "actuality." But he cannot teach how they exist in potentiality—whether preserved or destroyed—and the aforementioned inconsistencies return. Furthermore, he does not say in what places mixture occurs. For the element within which the mixture happens will always conquer the portions of the others, and generation will occur, but not mixture. Likewise, fire cannot be submerged under the sea or under the earth to generate mixtures—especially those where heat predominates—before it is extinguished. Therefore, etc. Therefore, the Sun, penetrating the lower regions and everything, is the generator, and not through mixture, etc.
</margin>

Furthermore, it is worth considering how such a great variety of Beings is produced from a single solar heat diffused into the earth without the mixture of the contrary cold <a> [for cold itself does not enter the work of nature, because two contraries <b> can in no way be reconciled and set aside their hatred to compose a third single Being; otherwise they would not be contraries, but having forgotten their own Entity, they would possess another]. This, as Wisdom said, is clear to one considering heat and cold pouring themselves out from two elements, acting against each other from within themselves, understanding nothing other than the amplification of their own nature—of which they are naturally diffusive, since they are the active principles of things. Furthermore, whatever degree of heat or cold is produced, it decreases and increases without marked boundaries or fixed steps, so that when one degree is lost it passes into another; it moves as if through an infinite flow without certain fixed degrees.

<margin>
c. The Sun is the origin of all fire. The striking of a stone does not generate fire, but rouses the fire placed within it by the Sun; by opening the packed matter that binds it, the blow provides the fire with the power to manifest and multiply itself. One strike from marcasite <note>A metallic mineral, iron pyrite, often called "fool's gold," known for sparking easily.</note> draws out more fire and ash than ten strikes from other stones.
</margin>

through certain degrees, although for the sake of teaching we indicate as many degrees as there are species of things and the temperaments within them.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Furthermore, any degree of heat generated in whatever matter strives to thin that matter out and draw it upward toward the expansion of the heavens. Therefore, wherever it is impressed, it never desires to remain in the earth, but always struggles to return upward with the "prey" of the matter it has conquered, fleeing its enemy <note>The enemy here is the cold of the Earth.</note> and seeking its friend, the celestial fire, from which it has its origin. Indeed, that all fires emanate from the Sun is also declared by the fire roused from stones that are struck or rubbed together; for this fire lay blunt and "dead" beneath the density of the matter, but once that matter is loosened by a blow, the fire receives the power of acting and manifesting itself. For this reason, a single blow from a flint draws out more sparks—smelling of sulfur and accompanied by ash—than many strikes from a common stone. The same is shown by the fire produced in mirrors from collected solar light, or rather, fire that is made more robust by it. 

<margin>d. The "element of fire" which the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, so named because they discussed philosophy while walking.</note> placed below the Moon is a fiction. For fire is never seen to be poured out except from the Sun; especially that which occurs within the earth and sea, where this "sublunary fire" could not descend to generate fires, sulfur, bitumen, and other beings where heat predominates. Fire also, which is drawn from stones or produced by the Sun in a mirror, is similar to our own fire in essence, action, and operation; it is therefore not "equivocal" <note>In medieval logic, an "equivocal" thing has the same name but a different nature; Campanella argues terrestrial and celestial fire are exactly the same thing.</note> as Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher from Spain whose interpretations of Aristotle dominated university learning.</note> used to say. e. The proper motion of fire is circular, though it can also take on all motions as needed, and it has only rest as its contrary.</margin>

d. Similarly, fires generated within the earth can arise from nowhere else than the Sun itself, which, shut up within the earth, is united, multiplied, and ignited. Nor does heat ever forget this origin of its own, which is why it always lifts itself toward the sky. This movement ought to be called a "return to nature" and to kindred bodies, where it is soon carried in a circle by its natural motion. Indeed, the downward motion of heavy things should be seen as a fall and a sinking of the corporeal matter which is unable to sustain or move itself; it is not, however, an operation or an action of either cold or heat.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Cold, on the contrary, is spread even without certain degrees upwards, and it endeavors to bind and harden the things generated by heat, to turn them into earth, and to return to its own element; concerning which he says, how...

***

*Therefore, fire was enclosed within that matter; it is not born from struck air, nor from motion, nor from nothing—as the Peripatetics dream—but was placed in things by the sun and is forced out of them, as Virgil <note>The Roman poet Virgil, whom Campanella cites as a scientific authority regarding the "seeds of fire" hidden in flint.</note> testifies. The element of fire which they placed under the Moon is a fiction. For fire is never seen to be poured out except from the Sun; especially that which occurs within the earth and sea, where this sublunary fire could not descend to generate fires, sulfur, bitumen, and other beings where heat predominates. Fire also, which is drawn from stones or produced by the Sun in a mirror, is similar to our own fire in essence, action, and operation; it is therefore not "equivocal," as Averroes used to say. The proper motion of fire is circular, though it can also take on all motions as needed, and it has only rest as its contrary.*

<margin>Ecclesiastes 1</margin>
<margin>f. The use of the variety in the earth’s shape and its parts, and of the adjacent bodies.</margin>
Again, the First Wisdom <note>original: "Sapientia Prima." In Campanella’s philosophy, this refers to the Second Person of the Trinity or the Divine Logos, the structural intelligence of the universe.</note> was delighted, seeing that the heat bursting from the bowels of the earth raised it up into mountains; and by generating a wealth of liquids moving through the earth, it established valleys, rivers, and seas. Indeed, if the surface of the earth were perfectly spherical, it would be less capable of sustaining a multitude of things than it is now, being distinguished by mountains and valleys.

<margin>g. Things, whether they will it or not, carry out the will of God.</margin>
He <note>Referring to God/First Wisdom.</note> also approved that when forces are poured out everywhere, acting contrary against contrary, even while one desires to destroy the other, the result is preservation. For while heat hardens the earth, it makes it more solid and tougher, and thus heat blocked its own path from entering further until the earth's final consumption. Likewise, while heat liquefies the earth in other places, it provides moisture to other parts for their restoration. The earth, too, restored itself by pouring out shadow and cold in turn. Likewise God said *g*: "Let the luminaries be carried around in a circle," for they shall be driven to do not what they themselves would desire—while their forces remain within the earth—nor do they stop at the destruction of the earth; therefore, they must do what they would not want. Likewise, without being forced by violence, they will perform what I myself decree through the fate of my will. Hence it happens that since matter exists in a non-uniform state—its thick and thin parts having been separated by ancient action into viscous and slippery, hard and soft, high and flat, large and small, continuous, contiguous, united and divided, etc.—we see the bodies of these portions constituted in number, weight, and measure, <note>A reference to the Book of Wisdom 11:20, "thou hast ordered all things in measure and number and weight."</note> according to the Idea of the First Wisdom. The types of heat also become varied and diverse: for some act differently on different species of matter, as is evident in wax, which they liquefy, and in clay, which they harden; and they act differently in the whole, in the parts, and in the tiny particles of those parts; as is manifest in a single herb, in

## Recognition of the wonderful succession of things in particular, and of all their variety.

### ARTICLE VII.

<margin>
a. The works of nature come from an unerring intelligence.
b. Power, Wisdom, and Love are metaphysical primalities. Fate, Necessity, and Harmony are their influences, as described in the *Metaphysics*, and they precede physical principles such as heat, cold, matter, and place.
</margin>

When the Eternal Intellect **a** sowed Fate, Harmony, and Necessity into the World—which was affected by the Intellect itself—it said: Heat will think it is making the heavens forever, and cold will think it is making the earth, rather than intermediate beings; yet I will let them labor. **b** For Fate, depending on my Wisdom, will correct them through a necessity emanating from my Power, so that they will be tempered into Harmony, which depends on my will.

For the Sun, passing in a perpetual circle by the necessity of its nature (in which it is preserved through motion), cannot impress itself entirely upon the earth, but only a portion of its heat <note>original: "coloris" — likely a variant or error for "caloris" (heat), as the sun's action is defined by heat in this context</note>. This heat, desiring to create another Sun, occupies the interior of the earth and labors there. But the oncoming cold will surround it, thinking to destroy it; instead, it will gather the heat more into a single point and strengthen it. From this it happens that this heat, organizing the Earth, becomes the "seed" of plants, beasts, stones, and other things. Thus, the earth is the mother of these things; in the day, she is stirred by the Sun and receives the seed, and in the night she conceives as the cold constrains it.

In this same way, diverse beings are conceived in every point of the earth. For the rising Sun heats every part of the Earth in one particular way: when it is morning, it acts obliquely and heats the eastern parts more. Then, as it approaches the meridian <note>The highest point in the sky at noon.</note>, it heats the middle parts more and the eastern parts less, regarding them with a second action that transforms the first; and it heats the western parts a little more. From this, it happens that the primary action and the virtue <note>The inherent power or "imprint" of the sun.</note> implanted in all things vary; the being that is to be born, and its individual parts, vary accordingly. Similarly, upon reaching the sunset, the Sun spreads its rays in other ways over the same part of the earth—even onto the very same apple or floweret—and it diversifies the preceding actions and the organization of beings. Soon, the nighttime cold, acting in opposition, introduces further varieties.

# OF PHYSIOLOGY, CHAPTER V.

<margin>c The rising and falling of the planets occurs from an abundance</margin>

The Sun effects this in every point of the heavens. Thus, every given degree—of which there are surely an infinite number—produces the greatest diversity through its turn of increasing and decreasing. Furthermore, the earth is not uniform in its portions; hence, the action of heat will vary within those same particles of dissimilar matter, which is composed of dense, soft, and thin substances. From this it happens that from a single seed, such things as bones, nerves, cartilages, hair, intestines, foliage, stalks, flowers, and bark are formed, due to the diversity of the parts in which the actions and the driving causes must necessarily vary. 

For heat differs from heat in strength and in quantity; thus in moisture, as is evident in flames, heat is more abundant; but in dry things it is more robust because it is more concentrated, as in glowing iron. It is characteristic of the latter to burn sharply, while it is characteristic of the former to warm abundantly and mildly. 

Furthermore, the surface of the Earth is not level, but is high, flat, round, mountainous, and full of valleys; these locations and parts receive the sun's influence in different ways. For plains and valleys collect and strengthen the heat, while mountains and heights receive it but disperse it, whereby they render it weaker. Furthermore, the same portion of earth that appears entirely flat to us is actually divided into almost invisible little mounds and many tiny pits that receive more light. Therefore, these pits obtain more heat than the mounds, and whether they are seen by direct or slanted light, they multiply the variety of effects. 

Furthermore, whatever heat achieves today is altered tonight by the encroaching cold; it is changed again tomorrow by a different heat, and then by cold, in countless successions. Furthermore, as the planets travel on their slanted paths—some slower, others faster—they come to be joined with the fixed stars and with each other in many configurations. In this way, they multiply and vary the forces of heat. Even more so, the Moon, through its waxings and wanings, as well as intervening clouds and varying distances, will diversify the works of heat, resulting in the greatest variety. This is all the more true because the planets **c**, receiving now more light from the Sun and now less, at times become closer to the Earth and at other times more distant; likewise, they become swifter...

Astrology cannot divine things perfectly, but only in part, because it considers common causes, but not particular ones: namely, the individual passions of its subject.</margin> will be able to guess many things through reason, if they will watch these celestial lights—those small statues of the First Idea <note>Campanella refers to the planets as physical representations or "statues" of the archetypal ideas in the mind of God.</note>.

Furthermore, Wisdom said: if the Sun wishes to pour out the highest heat upon the earth, it will burn its surface by suddenly converting the less resistant parts into a fine vapor <note>original: "tenuitatem," referring to a thin, gaseous state of matter</note>, and it will return upward before it penetrates, leaving the earth encrusted, with the harder parts exposed and stripped of that vapor. Indeed, it splits the earth itself while it exhales along with that fine vapor, from which it happens that if any heat is retained in the interior, it might escape outward. And so, where too much heat is present on the surface, the interior parts of the earth are colder—just as waters and caves show themselves to be colder at that time than at others—and all matter that is breathed upon from the outside becomes raw on the inside because of the overpowering heat. 

However, where the Sun has impressed a more languid <note>meaning weaker or more gentle</note> heat, it remains inside because it cannot quickly thin the matter out and return upward with its prize. And therefore, shut in here, this heat disposes the earth into many beings, which create a most beautiful order and distinction in the world, and various delights. For this reason, in whatever way it acts—contrary upon contrary—it will happen that not whatever the sun itself desires is done, but what I prescribe. Therefore, from my providence and from "chance" occurring simultaneously in respect to these things, the World will be tempered; since chance and fortune are events beyond the intention or will of a particular cause. <margin>What chance and fortune are: see Saint Thomas [Aquinas], first part [of the Summa Theologica], and the Metaphysics.</margin> For I have thought out and willed all things: therefore, in respect to me—who am surely the universal cause—nothing happens by chance, but everything happens by art. Therefore, the heat, forced by the necessity of remaining within the mass upon which it acts, will love in...

...the things themselves to live and be nourished by a neighboring and similar being. Indeed, the diversity and multitude which occurs outside the unity of the first being will represent in this statue—for it is colored <note>Campanella frequently compares the created universe to a "statue" or "painting" of God; the "colors" represent the variety of physical forms.</note>—a kind of shadow, as it were, which will be called evil and hatred.

I proclaim the same about all things. Also, the death of one thing, if it is the birth of many things, is not evil. Eaten bread dies so that it may become blood, and blood dies so that it may be turned into flesh, nerves, and bones, and live. Nor does this process displease the whole animal, although to the parts death itself—that is, a painful transformation <term>transmutatio dolorifica: a change accompanied by pain or the breakdown of the current form</term>—is and is perceived as unpleasant. Thus, the transformation of particular beings is useful to the World, though harmful and unpleasant to those individual parts. The whole man is composed of partial deaths and lives, which integrate human life. So the whole World is composed of deaths and lives, which make up the life of the whole. And God said that all things were **very good** <note>original: "valde bona," referencing the Latin Vulgate of Genesis 1:31.</note>: but that evil is nothing except the abuse of good, or a defect. Therefore, it does not have an essence, but draws its origin from non-being. For a good God cannot give entity to evil. Nor can there be two Gods: it is entirely repugnant for there to be two first, maximum, infinite beings. But indeed, men not understanding this will err in their contemplation of me: but I will lead all things into good. Thus he himself spoke, and all these things followed: and the lamp of the World <note>the Sun</note> with its luminaries circled about, and from so many modes of action and the resistances of things acted upon, and from so many various lights and heats distinguished in multiple ways, and from the opposite conditions of Heaven and Earth, there arose such a great variety of Beings as we certainly discern within and without.

# On the Sea & Waters, & Springs, & Rivers.
## CHAPTER VI.
### ARTICLE I.

<margin>a The Sea is not a primary element, as Aristotle thinks, but a secondary body: because it does not possess the quantity of cold and the tastelessness which belong to this element according to Aristotle, Hippocrates, and Plato; nor does it have diffusive powers.</margin>
God commanded the sea to be born first, *a* for as the exhaling heat rose with the *b* thinner parts to expand the heavens, the less thin parts followed as the Earth sweated abundantly, because it was affected by such great heat. And soon that "sweat" <note>Campanella frequently uses the physiological metaphor of *sudor* (sweat) to explain how heat draws moisture out of the Earth to form the oceans.</note> remained upon the Earth itself; for its thickness did not allow it to be carried upward. It happened that there was such a great abundance of this sweat that it surrounds the southern earth, and at the same time, flooding toward the North, it is divided into two hemispheres and is submerged more than a hundred paces in its greatest depth. This occurs because within the earth there is a greater supply of moderate heat than of robust heat: therefore, more water is constituted by the former than other things are made by the latter—even though in the beginning the most robust heat created such a great mass of ether. Soon the waters ran down into the lowest parts of the earth, where indeed the land had been diminished, because liquids cannot sustain themselves on high. Hard stones, however...

*a. Nor can the Sea or waters generate themselves: but they are generated by the Sun from the earth. I say the same of other waters, and even more so. b. Nor does air generate air, but it is generated by the Sun: it does not have the highest heat nor diffusive power; therefore it is not an element, but a more impure part of the heavens under attack by the earth. For this reason it is called the "firmament," on the testimony of St. Basil, because it is written: "He placed the birds in the firmament of heaven," etc. and "the way of an eagle in the midst of heaven," etc. <note>Proverbs 30:19 and Genesis 1:20.</note> since air is a denser, thicker, and firmer part of the heavens.*

...hard substances, from which the highest mountains are composed; indeed, the bones of the **World-animal** <note>original: *Mundani animalis*. <margin>So that the Sun might bring back to life what it had lost in the North <note>original: *Aquilone*</note>, when it first traveled toward the South, it increased its rotations upon returning to the northern region; therefore, it stays for more days in the sign of Cancer than in the sign of Capricorn. This has remained as part of its very nature.</margin>

And because when the Sun was first brought forth [at God's command] at the equator, it began to revolve, descending toward the Antarctic pole until it reached the Tropic of Capricorn. From there, when it returned by divine instinct back toward the Arctic, *c* fearing lest the cold should occupy the entire Arctic region, it happened that much of the earth melted in the Southern region. For this reason, the great Ocean surrounds the entire globe under the Southern tropic beyond the equinoctial line, where the Sun first traveled—not without cause, but for the sake of strengthening a less powerful portion of its heaven. This is because in the Arctic pole there are fewer and smaller stars; for the same reason, the Northern region obtained more land and more mountains. These were undoubtedly formed from thicker fluids by a less vigorous heat, left behind during the first general conflict. The northern sea is more abundant and located further toward the pole, where indeed there is a concentration and strength of stars assisting the heat left in the earth for its generation. 

The Southern sea, however, is located more under the tropic than under the pole for the reasons mentioned. And perhaps from there the waters flowed down into the northern valleys, reaching through the Arctic sea to the straits between Scythia <note>A vast region in Eurasia, often used by early modern writers to refer to the lands of the North and East.</note> and the Polar Land, and through the straits between Japan, Cathay <note>An older name for Northern China.</note>, and China; and between Japan and Quivira <note>A semi-mythical region in North America, believed by Spanish explorers to be rich in gold.</note> from the Southern Sea. 

Thus, the earth remained divided into two distinct hemispheres. One contains Peru-America in the southern position and Mexico-America in the northern, separated from each other by the Isthmus of Panama, which forms peninsulas eight degrees from the Equator. The other contains Africa to the South, entirely within the tropics but extending slightly beyond them; to the East it contains Asia, likewise toward the North, separated from Africa by the Red Sea running inland from the southern ocean and through its own isthmus. It also contains Europe to the West, toward the North, divided from Africa by the Mediterranean Sea, which indeed runs from Gades <note>Modern-day Cádiz, Spain, considered the "edge" of the known world in antiquity.</note> toward the east as far as Cyprus...

# THE WORKS OF BROTHER TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

...the Syrian sea <note>The Mediterranean</note>, which together with the Red Sea <note>original: *Erythraeo*</note> forms the African peninsula, and then flooded toward the North as far as the mouth of the Don <note>original: *Tanais*, the river traditionally considered the boundary between Europe and Asia</note>. Therefore, this river marks the boundary between Europe and Asia. Furthermore, there are two other distinct portions of land, separate from all other parts of the earth, located under the Arctic and Antarctic poles within the northern and southern oceans; thus, there are seven parts of the earth, just as there are seven planets in the heavens. All the seas are therefore connected to one another, except for the Caspian, located at the borders of Armenia toward the North; it is vast and salty like the other seas, unless perhaps it is connected to them underground.

<margin>**On Salt Water**</margin> Wherever it occurs, this kind of salty liquid arises from the earth. For heat collected in the deep bowels of the earth converts the earth into vapor. When this vapor is prevented from escaping—being shut within internal cavities—it mixes with the burnt portions of earth from which it exhaled, thus disposing them toward liquefaction. Afterward, when both are converted together into a fluid, salty springs are formed from the burnt and liquefied earth. 

<margin>*d* The sea is not salty, as Aristotle thinks, because its thin parts are removed by the Sun; for if that were the case, lakes would also become salty. Likewise, as many parts as are removed by the Sun are restored by rivers and rains; therefore, his theory is incorrect.</margin> 

Therefore, salty moisture *d* arises from excessive heat burning and liquefying matter within such enclosures, just as our own urine and salty sweat demonstrate. For this reason, salty springs are frequently found upon the earth, because they arise in its depths from heat increased by its concentration <note>referring to the concept of *antiparistasis*, where heat intensifies when surrounded by cold or confined</note>, liquefying the burnt matter where it resides; nothing escapes outward because the narrowness of the place does not permit it.

<margin>**On Petrifying Waters**</margin> But where the heat is gentle and does not burn the earth, yet is abundant and copiously liquefies the earth, it *e* produces thick and dense fluids. From these, a separated particle hardens into stone; and whatever is submerged in such springs is "clothed" in stone, just as a stylus or hemp fiber <note>original: *stupa*</note> dipped in liquid wax takes on a certain coating. This substance, however, hardens apart from the general mass because the common heat does not preserve it in its fluidity.

Likewise, neither does a hot and dry exhalation falling with the rains make the sea salty. For the rain and the lakes formed from them would then be even saltier. Therefore, Aristotle's reasons are vain; the sea is salty by nature, and not from such accidental causes. *e* When petrifying fluid penetrates the pores of wood, they turn to stone over a long period of time, as we have seen in the Museum of Ferrante Imperato <note>A famous Neapolitan apothecary and naturalist (c. 1550–1625) who maintained one of the most famous "cabinets of curiosities" in Europe</note>. The stakes and beams upon which the Venetians build their houses harden from the penetrating Sun, becoming rot-proof and turning to stone. In this way, iron becomes steel, and tin becomes bronze <note>original: *aramentum*; Campanella is using metallurgical analogies for how substances "harden" or improve through heat and mineral infusion</note>.

<summary>Campanella describes the world's seven landmasses and argues that the salinity of the sea and the existence of petrifying springs are caused by internal geothermal heat rather than the sun's evaporation, as Aristotle had claimed.</summary>

### CHAPTER VI OF THE PHYSICAL WORKS
G

...it preserves; but truly its own [heat] is overcome by the slightly cold air, and it cannot preserve its own softness.

Nor should it be thought that because the earth does not melt on its outer surface, it cannot or does not melt in its bowels. On the surface, the acting heat—as soon as it has dissolved and thinned any portion of the earth—is carried up into the sky. It does not wait for other parts until they melt, nor does it prepare them for thinness by overcoming their hardness. Therefore, on the surface, the heat creates a crust or reduces the earth into tiny <margin>About Dust and Sand.</margin> fragments while it breaks the earth apart so that it can exhale. This is just like what usually happens to roasted chestnuts and eggs: because the abundant internal moisture <note>original: *tenuitas*, referring to the thin, vaporous quality of the substance</note> cannot all exit at once through the narrow pores, it makes a great push and breaks them open. However, <margin>f This is evident in reverberating furnaces <note>A furnace that reflects heat back onto the material being heated</note> where bricks soon melt, showing that heat can melt things when it remains inside the earth for a long time. Therefore, Porta <note>Giambattista della Porta (1535–1615), a famous Italian scholar and contemporary of Campanella</note> was wrong when, in debating with me, he said that earth cannot be melted; he was deceived by Aristotle, who posited water as the primary element of liquidity.</margin> in the cavities of the earth, the acting heat is not carried upward with its thinned matter, but remains to do its work. Therefore, it produces various liquids, just as heat within the enclosure of an animal's belly produces several humors—namely blood, yellow bile <note>original: *cholera*</note>, phlegm, black bile <note>original: *melancholia*</note>, urine, saliva, and fat—which differ in consistency, heat, taste, and color, and which the heat could not produce outside the body. For this reason, heat enclosed within the earth acting upon uniform, unburnt matter produces "stony water" <note>Water rich in minerals that forms stalactites or petrifies objects</note> if the heat is moderate; but if it should burn after it liquefies the matter gently, it generates salt water.

<margin>On hot and mineral springs.</margin> But if the material is ignited too much and is enclosed so that vapors cannot exhale but are instead "suffocated" <note>Condensed or trapped</note> into water while they are still flames, then sulfur is created from that burnt and agitated water within the ignited crusts of the deep earth. Bituminous and nitrous waters are also formed where the earth is converted into nitre <note>Saltpeter or sodium carbonate</note>, alum, or bitumen <note>A naturally occurring oily or tar-like petroleum</note>, and hot water is generated within these areas of ignition. From there, the water flows out affected by the heat and the flavor of the mineral.

<margin>On petroleum oil.</margin> Often, too, thin portions squeezed out from fatty and bituminous earth congeal into oil and oily springs. <margin>On fresh waters.</margin> However, fresh waters do not arise from being burnt and liquefied like salt waters, but from vapors condensed in the caverns of the earth. These are the principle of all liquefactions; yet, because water is itself liquefied and hardened by other things, it is not the ultimate principle.

<summary>Campanella explains that the Earth's internal heat creates minerals, oils, and various types of water (salty, hot, and fresh) through a process of "cooking" and liquefaction, comparing the Earth's interior to a furnace or an animal's stomach.</summary>

# FRIAR TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

<margin>On springs.</margin>
...just as they condense into water on the lids of boiling pots. From these, springs have their origin, and from springs come rivers. Waters emerge at the openings of springs after they have been produced from condensed vapors; they follow the preceding thin exhaling vapor—from which the thicker ones that become water are perpetually generated—as if they were kin, and so that no vacuum is introduced, much like blood follows the spirit <note>In early modern physiology, "spirit" referred to a subtle, active substance that carried life through the body</note> when a vein is cut. For this reason, they even leap out with force atop mountains. Furthermore, springs and lakes are mostly formed in the foothills of mountains, and from these, rivers arise.

<margin>On rivers.</margin>
Indeed, many hollows in which vapors are accustomed to being condensed into water were made inside the mountains while they were being raised up. Moreover, God willed this so that from them, the waters might glide down to irrigate the plains. Southern waters are thinner <note>original: *tenuiores*, meaning less dense or more refined</note> and sweeter than northern ones, since they are made from thin vapors and are filtered through dry and purified earth. For the massive rivers—namely the Indus, Ganges, Tigris, Nile, Eridanus <note>The Po River</note>, Ister <note>The Danube River</note>, Orellana <note>The Amazon River</note>, Maragnon, La Plata, Tanais <note>The Don River</note>, and many others, which expand to a width of seventy leagues and reach a depth almost equal to the Mediterranean Sea—their origin must likewise be assigned to earth converted into vapor and then thickened, or from liquid earth that has not been burned, or from both: since they are neither salty, nor thick, nor **g** bitter, as the sea is.

<margin>**g** God called the gathering of waters the Sea [**Mare**], which is to say "bitter" [**amarum**], because it was created salty and bitter—as the Holy Doctors of the Church say—and it did not become so by accident afterward on its own, as Aristotle thinks.</margin>
Although the sea is continually diminished by the Sun and deprived of its thinner and sweeter parts, it nevertheless never loses its great size, because such a mass of rivers is restored to it. Yet it does not increase, because the earth sucks up a great part of it, from which it supplies moisture to the springs: truly, part exhales upward and returns to the sea itself, and into the earth, in a perpetual circle.

<margin>Why the sea does not grow, nor become sweet by the mixing of rivers.</margin>
<margin>St. Basil, in the *Hexaemeron* <note>A commentary on the six days of Creation</note></margin>
Nor does it ever become sweet: for since it is salt water having a total thickness, a small particle of it is enough to affect and permeate much water incorporated into itself.

<margin>Ecclesiastes 1 <note>"All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea is not full" (Eccl 1:7)</note></margin>
And it is more miraculous that it does not become sweet, nor increase, than the contrary. Salt water, when heated, is made saltier; but sweet water becomes sweeter, because it becomes rarer <note>meaning less dense</note>. Therefore, the Sea was never sweet, nor was it stripped of its sweetness by the Sun: otherwise, springs and lakes would themselves also become sweet <note>Campanella likely means "salty" here, arguing that if the process were accidental, all water would change similarly</note>, which does not happen, since they are composed of similar parts. Nor [does] salt...

He argues against Aristotle, asserting that God created the sea inherently salty and bitter, and explains the hydrological cycle as a "perpetual circle" where the sea neither grows nor loses its saltiness despite the influx of fresh river water.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Tommaso Campanella’s refutation of Aristotelian meteorology. Having previously discussed how springs and rivers are formed by the condensation of vapors within the earth, he now addresses the nature of the sea, arguing that its saltiness and size are inherent qualities designed by God, rather than accidental changes caused by the sun.</meta>

### PHYSIOLOGY CHAPTER VI.

...and that exhalation falls with the rains into the sea, which is why it becomes salty. For lakes and springs similarly disprove this <note>The Aristotelian theory that saltiness comes from sun-dried vapors</note>, as do the rains themselves, which are sweet; moreover, dryness is denied to the thinnest exhalation, and it falls downward. <margin>h The Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy</note> err in asserting that the sea must <gloss>however</gloss> be ten times larger than the land—</margin> **h** By nature, the sea is salty and bitter; for it is born as such from its own springs. It is natural for it to have a magnitude far smaller than the earth, since it is the earth’s sweat and resides in its valleys; it is not <note>original: *non se;*</note> *as they claim; but they say it is diminished by the Sun, when instead it ought to increase more from the inflowing rains and rivers. Likewise, it does not become thicker or saltier because the Sun draws away the sweet and thin parts. For those same parts, and even more, are restored to it, etc. But it must be seen as such a nature and size: for lakes would also become saltier and thicker, as they receive more of the Sun’s action. Likewise, water that has been boiled would become very salty, whereas the exact opposite happens <note>Campanella observes that boiling water purifies it or leaves a different residue, rather than creating seawater</note>. Furthermore, the exhalation that Aristotle claims is brought down with rain to affect the sea with saltiness would affect lakes even more, especially those formed from rainwater, which is otherwise completely sweet. Nor is exhalation pulled downward by them, as it leaps entirely upward. Also, if the Sun diminished the sea so greatly that it made it—from its supposed tenfold size—at least seven thousand times smaller, it would quickly destroy it, and the world—which Aristotle posits as eternal—would end. Indeed, it would have been destroyed already: for if one element is destroyed, the whole World collapses, as he himself says against Heraclitus. Therefore, its smallness, saltiness, and heat are natural; it was made so by God. For what God does in things from the beginning is natural to them, not a new miracle, as St. Augustine testifies in his commentary on Genesis. Those who claim the sea ought to have been cold and sweet, and so much larger than the earth that it covered it, accuse God and nature of ignorance and impotence—as if He did not know or could not make things in the proper size, quantity, and manner. Furthermore, these people do not wish to be investigators, but composers and builders of things—they wish to be the "correctors" of God. Truly, because they erred in positing the sea as an Element <note>One of the four primary building blocks of the universe</note>, they soon noticed it was not of the size, quality, or location required by their theory: hence, clinging to their error, they said the sea was not like this from the beginning, but was changed by the Sun, etc. Others said God ought to have made the sea naturally larger than the earth, cold, and sweet; but that He miraculously made it small so it would not cover the earth, but provide a place for land animals. To these I say: it by no means ought to have been made otherwise than it was made by God—small and warm. For in that way, anyone could compose the world according to his own whim, and then say the World ought to have been composed as he imagined, but that God miraculously did otherwise—which is foolish and impious. Likewise, when the Sacred Scriptures say God placed sand as a boundary and bridle for the sea, they should be seen to indicate a natural law that God gave to it, not a new miracle: for they also say He could place a boundary for the mountains so they would not cover the earth, and for the ages of men. Therefore, the discourse in both cases concerns natural law. Furthermore, Job says the sea came forth from the earth like urine from the womb. And Esdras in his fourth book <note>The apocryphal book 2 Esdras, which suggests the earth is six parts land and one part water</note> places the waters in a sixth part of the earth: therefore, it is much smaller. And in Apocalypse 21 <note>The Book of Revelation</note> it is held that when the Renewal of the world occurs, only a new heaven and a new earth will remain, as if there were only two elements. And it is expressly said that the sea will be no more, and the Glossary <note>The *Glossa Ordinaria*, a standard medieval biblical commentary</note> posits only two elements in the renewal of the age, just as in the beginning Moses posits two things created first: heaven and earth. And so St. Basil and the wiser commentators teach. And if others posit four elements, it is clear that air and water are called elements not as primary ones, but as great portions of things, as Empedocles also intended, and Plato, and as it is explained in the Epistle of St. Peter.*

...but that it [the sea] covers [the earth]: for that which was first given to each thing at its birth constitutes its nature. And it shall perpetually be so, just as the **First Wisdom** <note>God, as the primary source of order in Campanella's theology</note> decreed: that it should exist solely for navigation, as a home for fish, as a restoration for the earth—much like blood in the liver and veins of an animal—and as a bond between heaven and earth. <margin>The Use of the Sea</margin> For if such a great mass of waters were not in the springs, rivers, and seas, no vapors would be drawn from the earth except the thinnest and fewest, and after a short time, almost none at all. Then the heavens would pull away from the earth, and the space where the air resides would become a vacuum; thus the structure of the **Great Animal** <note>original: *maximi animalis*; Campanella's philosophical view that the world is a living, sentient being</note> that we call the "world" would dissolve. Just as when blood fails in an animal—from which the Spirits (the celestial portion) are nourished and the body (the earthly portion) is irrigated—its solidity is consumed by a wasting fever <note>original: *hecticam*; a "hectic fever" associated with physical consumption or drying out</note>, the spirit exhales, and the composite being dissolves. For this reason, in the death of the world by fire, *the sea shall be no more.* <margin>Revelation 21 <note>original: *Apocal 21*; Campanella cites the biblical prophecy: "And I saw a new heaven and a new earth... and there was no more sea."</note></margin> 

There are also waters beneath the flat lands, from which wells are filled, because generated vapors thicken into waters—not on the surface, nor for several paces beneath it, because they evaporate there and dryness remains. Nevertheless, water does not reach a depth of a hundred paces beneath the earth. <margin>The Quantity of Waters</margin> Indeed, even if it extended further, it should by no means be seen to equal the quantity of the earth, just as the blood of the human body does not equal its total size.

Furthermore, the depth of the sea nowhere extends to a hundred paces <note>Campanella’s estimate of the sea’s depth is very shallow by modern standards, likely based on contemporary sounding-line limits</note>—let us say it even reaches a thousand. Yet the depth of the earth's semi-diameter <note>the radius</note> contains 5,500 miles and more, calculating the diameter as a third part of the circle <note>Campanella uses a rough approximation of Pi as 3 to calculate the earth's dimensions</note>, where sixty miles correspond to one of the 360 celestial degrees—or perhaps even more. Therefore, the total depth of the earth exceeds the depth of the water by ten thousand miles or more. And the surface of the earth is six times larger than the surface of the water. <margin>4 Esdras <note>Referring to the apocryphal 2 Esdras 6:42, which states God dried up six parts of the earth for habitation and left one part water. This passage famously influenced Christopher Columbus's belief that the ocean was small enough to cross.</note></margin> Truly, even if the earth were covered by water everywhere to a height of one mile, the mass of the water would be as nothing compared to the mass of the earth. Likewise, one single mountain melting down would nearly create a sea. Moreover, the sea does not have the height of the mountains, although it maintains itself in a spherical shape so as not to be divided (since all division is destructive), just as water forms a sphere in a cup as long as it can. Often, however, it becomes "humped" by the winds from the land...

<summary>Campanella argues that the sea acts as the Earth's "blood," vital for the world's survival as a living organism, and uses scriptural and mathematical reasoning to prove that the Earth's mass far exceeds that of the oceans.</summary>

...driven by force. And since the earth and water form a single sphere, all the waters would hang toward the center unless they held themselves in a globe; otherwise, they would move not toward the center, but toward the circumference, which is impossible. For our beings all have the center as the "bottom," and the heavens as the "top." This is why navigation occurs around the circle of the earth, and feet are always placed opposite to feet <note>original: *pedes pedibus contraponuntur*; a description of people living on the opposite side of the globe</note>, while heads everywhere look toward the sky; the former looking toward the earth and the center, and the latter looking toward the heaven and the summit.

Aristotle and others err in this, but not the most wise Plato and Origen.</margin>

# On the Movements of the Sea.

## ARTICLE II.

<margin>Albertus [Magnus] and others wrongly attribute the flow and ebb <note>tides</note> of the sea to the Moon. For when it lacks light, it would not lift the sea, especially where the Moon itself is absent—that is, in the other hemisphere</margin>
All seas are carried in a continuous motion from the east to the west, because they are thinned <note>original: *rarefiunt*; the idea that heat expands water, making it take up more space</note> and swell up because of the Sun. Therefore they rush forward, just as boiling water in a cauldron swells where the fire is applied and flees to the opposite side; and if the fire is moved in a circle, the water itself will go in a circle. In fact, the sky, the air, and the sea all proceed in this way, one following the other. Nevertheless, where the air strikes against certain mountains, it is twisted into another path. So too the Adriatic Sea, carried into the Venetian Gulf, turns back in a circle because it has no exit toward the west. And the Atlantic Ocean, running between the regions of Peru and Mexico to the "Gulf of the Head of God" <note>original: *sinum capitis Dei*; likely referring to the Caribbean or the Gulf of Mexico</note>, rolls back toward the North as far as Estotiland <note>A 16th-century name for a region in North America, typically identified with Labrador or Newfoundland</note>, and is carried into diverse motions. Similarly, seas meeting here and there create whirlpools in the straits of Sicily, Cadiz <note>original: *Gadum*</note>, Magellan, Anian <note>The mythical "Strait of Anian," believed by early explorers to be the Northwest Passage</note>, and Zembla <note>Novaya Zemlya in the Arctic</note>, while they strike against each other and roll in a circle. While the sea swells from the Sun’s thinning heat, it happens that for six hours it increases,

> for him whom it [the Sun] hangs over. But if the Moon draws the sea like a magnet draws iron and lifts it, why does it immediately depress it? Nor is it true, as they say, that the sea is raised when the Moon is elevated at the meridian, and depressed when it descends to the western horizon. For this ascent and descent of the Moon does not occur in a heaven that is round everywhere, except in respect to us, to whom it seems more depressed when it descends below the horizon, and they think the sea itself ought to be diminished, which they do not want to admit. Furthermore, often where the Moon hangs directly over, there is a depression in the sea; therefore, it is not caused by the Moon, etc.

<meta>This page continues Campanella’s argument that oceanic tides are primarily caused by the Sun’s heat rather than the Moon. He uses the analogy of a boiling pot to explain how the Sun creates two high tides simultaneously—one directly beneath it and one on the opposite side of the globe—while the "sides" of the Earth experience low tide.</meta>

<page-num>54</page-num>

->FRIAR THOMAS CAMPANELLA<-

[...it is increased] and for six [hours] it decreases: since in the four quarters of the day, its active heat can produce these distinctions of warmth in the sea where it is present. In those same parts, when the Sun is absent, depressions occur according to this rhythm: where the Sun hangs perpendicularly, the sea boils <note>The author uses the term "boiling" (*feruet*) to describe thermal expansion or the agitation of water by solar heat.</note>. This rising heat causes the waters to lift high and run down across the lateral parts of the global world until they meet each other on the side opposite the Sun and its heat, where it is, of course, midnight. Therefore, in both this part and that part, the sea is raised during those same six hours: in the latter due to the collision of the waters, and in the former due to the heat. Meanwhile, at the sides of these two opposite parts, the water must decrease and be depressed, for in those places there is neither heat nor a collision of waters.

We see this happen in no different a way in a boiling pot; the waters are seen to rise in that part where the fire is applied, and simultaneously in the part which occupies the diameter of the heat and fire—that is, at the handle of the pot—while at the sides, the water is depressed. As the Sun moves to the following quarter of the sky, which faces the side where the sea was not boiling, the water is raised in this very side, and it is depressed in the previous quarter where the Sun had been hanging, and simultaneously in the part opposite that first quarter where the collision had occurred. This same collision of waters passes to the part opposite the second quarter through the six hours of the day. Thus, as the Sun passes from quarter to quarter, it perpetually happens that the same portion of the sea is raised for six hours and lowered for six hours; just as fire, moving around the rim of a boiling pot, produces two elevations and two opposite depressions.

<margin>
**b** Aristotle wrongly wrote that the sea is raised and depressed because it is narrowed by the land and is balanced back and forth like a scale <note>original: *bilance libretur*</note>. For it is not forced to flow here and there by the earth itself (which always maintains the same position), just as water does not suffer this from a vessel, no matter how narrow. Furthermore, waters are not hard like the wood from which scales are hung, so as to be able to be balanced on both sides; they are fluid and divisible, so they cannot be raised and lowered on both sides in turn. Nor, as Aristotle thinks, do they flow down from islands or reefs and alternately bounce back up. For stones placed inside a lake or a bowl do not affect the waters with this motion, and once they have settled, they stay put, etc. Therefore, [the cause is] from vapors, etc.
</margin>

Nevertheless, these types of flows and ebbs <term>fluxus & refluxus: the tides</term> tend to vary when they run into each other in narrow straits or strike against headlands. Indeed, at the shores of Guinea and the Bordeaux strait <note>original: *Burdegalensis freti*; likely referring to the Bay of Biscay or the Gironde estuary near Bordeaux, France.</note>, the increase and decrease do not happen alternately every six hours, but occur outside the usual order. Furthermore...

<meta>This page continues Campanella’s discussion of tidal movements. On the previous page, he argued that the Sun's heat causes the primary tides through a process of "boiling" or thermal expansion. Here, he explains why some seas lack tides and introduces the secondary influence of the Moon and planets on the waters and biological life.</meta>

<page-num>55</page-num>

<header>OF PHYSIOLOGICAL MATTERS. CHAPTER VI.</header>

<warning>Page heavily spotted with foxing.</warning>

The Pisan and Genoese seas <note>The coastal waters of Tuscany and Liguria in Italy.</note> and almost the entire Mediterranean lack such flux and reflux <note>Tides.</note>: because they are thinner <note>The author uses "thin" (*tenuiora*) to mean less dense or less viscous.</note>, the vapors generated within them—which cause the Ocean to swell—find an easy exit, and therefore do not agitate these seas. Indeed, denser seas swell in the summer but remain calm in winter: whereas, on the contrary, thin seas are agitated in winter. This is because winter heat is small and weak; in denser waters, it cannot generate vapors at all, but in thin waters it can, yet it cannot draw them out to the surface; hence the waters must be disturbed. Summer heat, by contrast, agitates dense waters because it does not draw out the generated vapors as easily as it does from thin ones; this difference is made manifest by the Persian and Indian seas.

The wandering stars <note>term: <term>Erraticæ stellæ</term> refers to the planets, which "wander" across the fixed backdrop of the constellations.</note> bestow a variety of motions upon the seas, to which they stand in oblique motion. The Gothic and German seas <note>The Baltic and North Seas.</note> swell beyond their usual order as the Moon waxes: for the swelling they receive from the Sun is customary to them. Indeed, the power of lunar heat is proportioned and suited to rarefy and agitate the waters, since it is not so great as to be sufficient for drawing out the generated vapors. And therefore the brains of animals, especially marine ones, and all moist beings are moister and fuller during a full moon. Thus, through this rarefaction, they easily admit cold, and they induce an opinion contrary to the truth—namely, that the Moon is cold: whereas when the Moon wanes, the swellings of moist things also fail, etc.

## On Rain Waters. And on Thunder and Lightning.

### ARTICLE III.

<margin>
a The waters above the firmament, according to Saint Basil and Saint Augustine in his unfinished book on Genesis.
</margin>
**From** the seas, the earth, and all things born upon it, solar <sup>a</sup> heat lifts many kinds of vapors into the air: thin ones indeed, thick, pure and impure, and mixed, because they are the matter for all things that occur in this lowest heaven <note>The atmosphere or "sublunary" sphere.</note>. Therefore, if the vapors are somewhat thick,

->they become rain.<-

For the air is called the firmament, because it is a denser and firmer part of the heavens. And *God divided the waters from the waters, because He commanded some to be upon the earth and others to be above the air, as these Saints learnedly speak; they also deny that a crystalline heaven <note>A traditional celestial sphere made of solid, transparent water.</note> can exist alongside the Empyrean heaven <note>The highest, fiery heaven.</note>, for fire and water would not agree except by a miracle.*

<margin>
h Against *Aristotle*. Condensation seems sufficient to make water from vapor without the need for cold, as is evident in alembics <note>term: <term>Alembic</term> refers to an early chemical apparatus used for distillation, consisting of two vessels connected by a tube.</note> and in the coats of animals. Therefore, cold does not create water by granting them their essence, but only by condensing them; nor does it take away the innate heat from the vapor, but rather binds and attacks it. For in baths and on the lids of boiling pots, it is manifest that smoke thickens into hot water without cold, simply by the narrowness of the space.
</margin>

...vapors are lifted up, and when they have been thickened by contrary winds, or by mutual contact <gloss>b</gloss>, or by cold, or by the narrowness of the region, they are converted into rain water. This should certainly be seen as thickened smoke which, being unable to sustain itself in the heights, falls downward, restoring the earth and its beings, just as God spoke. For this reason, water does not form in the summer in our climates near the tropics: for then the vapors become so thin that they are unsuited for condensation. Nor indeed does it rain much in winter; for since the vapors are thick, being generated by a weak, slanted heat, they cannot be lifted upward. Therefore, the earth is often covered with a thick mist and receives only rare, tiny drops.

But in Spring and Autumn, they are moderately thick because the distance of the Sun is moderate, and so they are easy to thicken—all the more so because they are mixed with thin and hot vapors exhaling from the dry and mineral-rich earth and from portions of things. While these try to escape from the thicker vapors by which they are compressed, they break through them, and at the same time, from the crash of the eruption, thunder occurs <gloss>c</gloss>, by the command of the First Wisdom <note>Campanella uses "First Wisdom" (*Prima Sapientia*) as a title for God, emphasizing the rational order and divine intelligence behind natural laws.</note>, either that animals might be forewarned or that demons might tremble. From the light which flashes from the ignited vapors breaking out, lightning is produced. For where they are shut in, they are collected, strengthened, ignited, and they break through and shine. 

Then the remaining thick parts are collected together, fearing division and therefore destruction (for all beings sense their own advantage and disadvantage <note>This reflects Campanella's "panpsychist" view that all things in nature, including inanimate elements, possess a basic form of sentience or "sense" aimed at self-preservation.</note>); deprived of their thinner portion, they are condensed even more. Hence they turn into a quite heavy rain, but not a lasting one: for the thickness falls down suddenly. In winter, the rain is indeed more prolonged, because the thinness established by the faint heat cannot sufficiently escape, and it thickens gradually and by resisting. For this reason, thunders and lightnings rarely occur in the winter time, and the rains are small: for the thinness mixed into the clouds does not have heat powerful enough to exhale, nor to do so quickly: But in Spring and Autumn...

## *On the Flooding of the Nile and Other Rivers.*

### ARTICLE IV.

<margin>The Nile does not flood because it is prevented by the Etesian winds from entering the sea (since other rivers do not experience this); nor because snows melt, as others say, since at its source there is no melting heat, but freezing cold; other rivers also do not experience this.</margin>
Because indeed at the Cafates and Silver Mountains <note>Historical names for the legendary "Mountains of the Moon," long thought to be the source of the Nile.</note>, from which the Nile arises twelve degrees beyond the equinoctial line, when the Sun is on this side in the sign of Cancer during the month of June, huge rains occur there and near other springs of the same river. For when it is summer for us, it is winter there, having begun at the start of April. It happens that its waters overflow excessively, which, running down into Egypt, flood the region and make it fertile, just as Wisdom <note>original: *Sapientia*; likely referring to the Book of Wisdom or a personified divine order.</note> said, since rains do not occur there [in Egypt] because the vapors are perpetually thin in that same place. The Pegu and Menan rivers <note>Likely referring to the Bago and Chao Phraya rivers in Southeast Asia (modern Myanmar and Thailand).</note> in India cause the same flooding, as do other rivers flowing from distant regions, coming from where it is winter to where it is summer. 

Truly, rivers flowing from the North to the South flood for the opposite reason in summer, because the Sun in Cancer undoubtedly melts the Scythian Sea <note>The Arctic Ocean or the frozen northern waters.</note> which was frozen in winter, by which the subterranean rivers having their head nearby are increased. Simultaneously, both the snows and the frozen earth are melted, and many vapors are raised up besides, which, compressed by the peaks of the mountains, are turned into huge rains; thus all the waters together surge with the addition of the Dog-days <note>term: <term>Canicula</term> or the "Dog-days" refers to the hottest period of summer, traditionally associated with the rising of the star Sirius.</note> heat. Therefore, this is also the case for the Caspian Sea, and the springs of the Menan, Pegu, and others that run a very long distance.

### ARTICLE V.

Hailstones, however, are formed from thick and hot vapors in hot places and times *a* for they are not frozen by external cold, but by the union of thicker vapors when they are stripped of the thinner and hotter ones. Thus, as soon as they lose their heat and thinness—while as it were following that heat, being unwilling to be separated from it or from themselves—they are squeezed, compressed, and hardened. And by whatever *b* small amount of cold, they achieve a great density; for cold delights in density, and is multiplied within it. This is why before it hails, the sky thunders and flashes with lightning, because surely the "thinness" <note>Campanella uses "thinness" to refer to the hot, energetic spirit of the vapor.</note> is separated by bursting out from the "thickness," as is well known in <term>Lombardy</term> <note>A region in Northern Italy famous for its violent summer hailstorms.</note> during the boiling summer.

## On Snow.

### ARTICLE VI.

Snow, however, occurs in cold places and during times when cold follows a period of warmth. Furthermore, when the <term>South Wind</term> <note>original: *Auster*; traditionally a hot, moist wind.</note> has brought many hot vapors into the air, and the <term>North Wind</term> <note>original: *Aquilonare frigus*; the cold of the North Wind.</note> simultaneously arrives and begins to attack them, it gradually occupies, overcomes, and freezes them, and consistencies of this sort are seen. For this reason, snow does not form in coastal regions (which are warmer due to the light multiplying as it bounces off the water) in the same way hail does, nor in summer like hail, nor often in Autumn or Spring. Instead, it occurs in the mountains and in winter, with no preceding thunder. This is because the "thinness" does not burst out from the "thickness," but remains with it; its heat is bound by the cold, which makes the snow white, soft, and warm, since it does not allow it to be entirely hardened by the cold.

<summary>Campanella explains that hail is formed when heat rapidly exits thick vapors, causing them to contract and harden, while snow forms when cold slowly traps heat within the vapor, resulting in a soft, white consistency.</summary>

<margin>
*a* Snow seen on the ridges of the Apennines was observed to be formed from sea spray carried up there, and it remained salty rather than becoming sweet. Likewise, its qualities show its innate, mild heat—namely its "fatness" <note>Campanella uses "fatness" (*pinguedo*) to refer to a substance's richness or fertility, which he associates with life-giving heat.</note> and its whiteness, which scatters and thins out the vision, even destroying it, which is the work of heat. This is why Xenophon provided black veils for the eyes of his soldiers who were blinded by the snow while returning from Armenia, *
</margin>

All snow *a*, just like other waters, is composed of a native and mild heat, even though it is felt as cold to our touch because of the external cold attacking it, and because we ourselves are warmer than the snow. Nevertheless, snow enriches the fields; it is white and soft, endowed with the appearance and character of heat. Indeed, neither wine nor oil lose their native heat when they are frozen, even though its action is bound and hindered by external cold. The same is true for any other being or any other liquid. Every liquid is preserved by a mild heat, but is destroyed by a dominant heat, which turns it into vapor; similarly, it is destroyed by cold, which generates a hard, motionless, and dry thing—namely ice, crystal, or earth—from a soft, flowing, and moist liquid. Therefore, liquids derive their essence from mild heat. The entire sea is also hot, as it is salty. Furthermore, all waters are generated by heat from thickened hot smoke <note>original: *fumo*; here referring to vapor or exhalations.</note>; they have a sweet taste close to our own mild heat, or a tastelessness very similar to the heat of the tongue. They delight in motion, which is surely the operation of heat, but they are corrupted by stillness. 

However, *b* water does not extinguish fire by pouring out an "enemy" action <note>Campanella rejects the Aristotelian idea that elements fight each other through "antipathy."</note>; for if that were so, the fire would transform itself into water. Rather, water extinguishes fire by suffocating it with its mass and viscosity—specifically, it blocks the passages <term>pores</term> <note>original: *meatus*; the tiny channels in a substance through which heat and air travel.</note> of the burning wood from which the flame (the thin and smoky part) emerges. Thus, it does not allow the fire to breathe out, and so it must die. This same effect is caused by hot wine, salty water, or oil poured on in large quantities. Yet, fires are seen to burn in bitumen, pitch, and other non-porous materials even when submerged in water,

<margin>
*so that he might hinder the action of that scattering whiteness. 

*a* Green wood does not ignite as easily as dry wood, not because moisture is "the enemy" of fire, but because it abounds with a thick humor <note>fluid or moisture</note> that blocks the pores. This prevents the fire from entering to do its work, and prevents the air from entering; therefore, green wood sinks in water due to its weight. Dry wood is full of air, so it floats and admits heat into its pores. Thus, green wood does not fail to burn because moisture is an enemy to fire, etc. Likewise, bituminous substances burn in water because they do not have pores that can be closed by the water; they are equally ignited and even nourished by the water. Furthermore, great conflagrations turn water into flame before it can reach and block the pores. Finally, every liquid nourishes fire and is generated by fire; it is liquefied by heat and frozen by cold. Because its nature is to be perpetually liquid, its nature is to be always warm with a mild heat—for by a strong heat, it is dissolved into smoke.

...that waters burn and even increase; in fact, the greatest fires are nourished by waters, such as the fires of Mount Etna and the forge of Vulcan <note>Campanella refers to the Roman god of fire, associated with volcanic activity; he is arguing that water contains "fatness" or sulfurous qualities that can fuel flames</note>. These vapors naturally fill the pathways of the head and heart through which the spirits <term>spirits: the "pneuma" or vital vapors that Campanella believed moved through the nerves to facilitate thought and movement</term> travel; they produce sleep while they call the spirit into the internal parts for battle, and the vapors themselves are defeated. But if the vapors win, they suffocate the spirit into a thick substance and bring about death. If indeed these substances induced such conditions through cold, then warm wine would not bring sleep, nor would cold snow kill more effectively than hemlock.

## On Dew and Hoarfrost

### ARTICLE VII.

Dew is formed from a few thin vapors extracted by the heat of the day but captured by the cold of the night. It is truly useful for the crops, just as God said. This occurs more frequently in regions where it does not rain, such as in Arabia and similar climates, where this kind of liquid is produced in abundance. This happens because the heat there is excessive and easily dissolves all vapors into the air, since they are drawn from dry earth and are therefore very thin. Thus, only the remnants left in the evening are suited to be turned into dew, rather than into rain or thunder, since the vapor is either pure or uniform. It can also happen that fumes emerging from beneath the earth in the evening strike against plants and thicken into dew before they rise—

## On Manna and Honey.

### ARTICLE VIII.

Manna, which they gather in Calabria and in Arabia Felix <note>original: "Arabia felici." A historical name for the fertile southern part of the Arabian Peninsula, modern-day Yemen</note>, does not flow down from heaven, like that which God gave to Moses, but from the sun-drenched trees themselves from which it is collected. For indeed, during the day, these trees express a certain well-digested liquid through their stalks to the leaves, which suddenly dissolves into an invisible thinness; then at night, another similar liquid follows the same path as that unseen liquid which exhaled, which is condensed into Manna by the nocturnal cold toward the end of spring, until the Sun in the month of June causes such moisture to vanish, at which time it ceases to be gathered.

It is the custom of peasants to make small incisions in the bark of the trunks of ash trees <note>original: "fraxinorum"</note> in the evening, from which incisions a gum emerges at night that is collected in the morning; this they call "Manna of the body." From this it becomes manifest that Manna comes forth from the sap of the tree, and not from the air. Otherwise, other trees near the common ash and manna-ash trees <note>original: "fraxiſniq; orniſq;"—referring to the *Fraxinus excelsior* and *Fraxinus ornus*</note> would also receive Manna, and even the stones themselves would be covered in it if it were flowing down from the sky.

Honey, too, is a juice consisting of particles qualified for our taste, drawn out from flowers by the work of heat; these are surely constituted from the purer and well-digested smoky part, and all—

## CHAPTER VII.

### ARTICLE I.

<margin>St. Basil in the Hexaemeron <note>A commentary on the six days of creation.</note></margin>

...when they feel themselves squeezed by contact (which is against their nature and is the "death" of their thinness <note>original: *tenuitas*; Campanella views "thinness" or rarefaction as the natural state of heat and vapor, and "density" or *crassities* as the state of cold and matter</note>, just as, conversely, expansion is the death of density), they flee in a circle, seeking a space capable of holding their wide rarefaction. They do this until they either strike against one another or are pushed back by mountains and thicken into water; or, conversely, thinned by their own agitation, they seek the higher, more ample and capacious spaces of the heavens. They are more violent whenever the place of generation—the region where they are born—supplies a greater abundance of smoke to them. In such cases, they feel themselves more constricted and being put to death; thus, they exert greater effort to leap out from that region into others. This is just like the powder of a cannon <note>original: *bombarda*</note> ignited in a cavity: being driven into a state of thinness, it seeks more space and exits impetuously into the air, carrying with it whatever it finds in its path. For this reason, on the open sea and at the mouths of rivers, a wind almost always blows, because an abundance of vapor seeking a space beneficial to its own life is easily drawn out from the waters.

<margin>The second kind of wind generation.</margin>
It is also possible that the air, boiling in the manner of water, expands; and while it expands impetuously, it creates that "wave of air" which we call wind. This does not happen in summer, because then the center of the heat is here, where the Sun hangs perpendicularly, and consequently the air flees elsewhere toward the perimeter. Nor does it happen in winter, because the source of heat is far from us. But in autumn and spring, strong winds blow toward us from their center under the equator with a greater mass, because we are closer to the circle of "boiling."

<margin>Concerning the morning and evening breeze.</margin>
In the morning, from the eastern region where the Sun thins the air or moves the vapors, a light, almost perpetual breeze blows toward us. This stops when the Sun reaches our meridian <note>The highest point in the sky at noon.</note>, because at that time, the center of vapor and heat is right here, and the wind blows away to other places. But in the evening, when the Sun has reached the west, breezes blow from that direction more vehemently than the morning aura, because the western heat flowing toward us is added to the vapor drawn out from the Spanish Ocean <note>The Atlantic Ocean.</note>.

## On the Etesian Winds.
### ARTICLE II.

<margin>On the Etesian winds. *a* Etesian winds do not blow at midday because snow melts on the mountains and the winds evaporate, as Aristotle thinks. For on the shores of Africa and all seas, Etesian winds occur and breathe from places where there is no snow, etc.</margin>

This happens almost constantly in nearly all climates. But in regions near the sea, gentle winds blow at midday in summer, which they call *a* Etesian winds <note>original: *Etesias*; from the Greek word for 'annual,' these are strong, cool Mediterranean winds that blow every summer</note>: these arise not indeed from the heat of the air, which has its center among us on land, but from the sea. For at that time, the sea is struck by the direct rays of the midday Sun; and therefore, it emits an abundance of windy vapors. Furthermore, at midday the sea is then calm, because it is so thinned <note>original: *rarefit*; Campanella follows the classical idea that heat "thins" or expands matter, allowing internal gases to escape</note> by the powerful Sun that it provides an easy exit for the vapors generated within. But in the morning and evening, the sea is struck by slanted rays, and the generated vapors are not permitted to exit because the sea is not sufficiently thinned. Therefore, at those times the winds do not blow, but instead stir up the waters internally. This is why we see the sea disturbed in the morning and evening.

However, in swampy regions—such as Naples—because the sea is "thicker" <note>original: *crassius*; likely referring to the density of the water or the presence of more sediment and organic matter</note>, it is stirred only at midday, because the vapor that is to be turned into Etesian winds is being drawn out. In the morning and evening, however, the sea is seen to be calm, because it does not suffer enough from the slanted light to conceive the amount of vapor required to stir it.

## On the Qualities, Locations, and Names of the Winds.
### ARTICLE III.

<image-desc>A circular diagram representing the world or the sky with wind directions. A vertical axis connects "North Wind" (Boreas) at the top and "South Wind" (Auster) at the bottom. A central horizontal line is labeled "Equinoctial" (the Equator). Two parallel horizontal lines represent the Tropics: "Cancer" above and "Capricorn" below. The horizontal axis is marked "West" (Occidens) on the left and "East" (Oriens) on the right. Diagonal lines indicate intermediate winds: "The Greek Wind" (North-East), "The South Wind" (South-East), and "The Southwest Wind" (Libs). A handwritten note in the upper-left quadrant marks the North-West wind.</image-desc>

Winds receive their names from the locations from which they blow: hence some are Eastern, Western, Southern, and Northern. Likewise, they are named after the intermediate regions from which they seem to us to blow; thus, from Greece they are called the "Greeks" <note>original: *Graeci*; known today in the Mediterranean as the *Gregale*</note>, and from Libya, the "Libyans" <note>original: *Libes*; known today as the *Libeccio*</note>. Indeed, in almost every province they have their own specific names. For in Apulia, they are called "Slavonians" if they blow from Slavonia, or "Calabrians" if they blow from Calabria. But winds often arise even in our own region...
