<header>FATHER TOMMASO CAMPANELLA</header>

<margin>a By the agitation of the returning sea from the Gulf of Mexico, the West Winds <note>original: *Zephyri*</note> blow toward us; though they are also born in nearby regions.</margin>

<margin>b This discussion concerns winds blowing across the width of the earth toward the poles and from the tropics, but not [the equatorial winds], etc.</margin>

...but we, for our part, impose a name from where we see them blowing. Under the equator, a perpetual, uniform wind blows from east to west, but not the other way around, especially at sea. For the Sun *a* carries vapor and heat there, both of the air and the sea. But outside the tropics, they blow from everywhere and in any direction, depending on where the place from which they emerge is found; these seek space in any and every direction; they are thrown elsewhere by mountains and by themselves blowing from other directions. From the *b* four cardinal points of the World and from the four opposite points of the tropics, eight winds are marked, distinguished by different names in different regions; and in their midst, many others are marked, up to thirty-six, which the lore of sailors has divided for use <note>Campanella refers to the "wind rose" or maritime compass, which by his time had been refined into 32 or 36 points for precise navigation</note>. But at the poles, all winds are Southerly <note>A logical observation: if one stands at the North Pole, every direction is South</note>, while under the tropics they are more polar, because from there they blow out across the latitude.

Winds bring with them the qualities of the regions from which they blow toward us. Therefore, Southerly winds <note>original: *Australes*</note>—coming from a sweltering Africa full of serpents and blowing across the sea to us—are thick, poisonous, watery, and damp. Northerly winds <note>original: *Septentrionales*</note>, however, flowing from snowy and cold mountains, are thin and clear; for they freeze the vapors in the air and cause them to fall to the earth, or they drive them toward the south. Easterly winds <note>original: *Orientales*</note> are violent and somewhat warm; but Westerly winds <note>original: *Occidentales*</note> are violent and somewhat cool when they are formed from vapors in regions pushing against us. Indeed, in certain places these are healthy, but in others those are, according to the quality they take on during their passage. In Apulia <note>a region in Southern Italy</note>, the West Wind <note>original: *zephyrus*</note>, which is beneficial to almost all other regions, is harmful and brings the effect of the South Wind <note>original: *Notus*</note>, whose nature is to fill the head, weigh down the hearing, loosen the bowels, and contaminate the crops; which elsewhere the North Wind <note>original: *Boreas*</note> and the West Wind itself—also called *Favonius*—brings to life, clears the head, provides relief for the chest, gathers natural heat for better digestion, and prepares the mind for contemplation.

<margin>c A fan <note>original: *flabellum*</note> does not generate cold, but brings cold air by expelling the air touching us which is already warmed by our own heat. Likewise, new air entering our pores forcefully induces a sensation of cold because the air is cooler than the pores themselves, even if it is not "outside cold." For less warm things appear colder to those that are warmer, just as to a person with a fever, our touch (which is warm to others) seems cold.</margin>

All winds *c* are hot by nature, being born undoubtedly from heat:

...exerted: but when they push cold toward us, they do so by pushing the air. Indeed, any air or water set in motion brings cold to our limbs because it expels the portion of water or air touching us—which is being warmed by our own heat—and immediately brings in another, less warm portion. This brings us a sensation of slight cold through a certain continuation and alternation, just as fans <note>original: *flabella*</note> do.

<margin>On the Whirlwind.</margin>
Where contrary winds blow against one another, meeting head-on, they are gathered together into a mass; unable to be separated, they are whirled into a circle, just as opposing waves in narrow straits create whirlpools <note>original: *voragines*</note>. They lift into the air whatever easily movable thing is found in their midst, just as we often see straw and dust rotating and being carried upward. If such whirlwinds of winds become violent at sea, they almost lift ships into the air, just as Charybdis <note>A legendary whirlpool in the Strait of Messina, described in classical mythology as a ship-devouring monster</note> swallows them downward for a similar reason.

## On Earthquakes.

### ARTICLE IV.

When abundant vapors <note>Campanella uses "vapor" to describe pressurized gases or steam trapped underground</note> are generated within the cavities of the earth, hating their confinement and desiring to escape to a more spacious place, they strike against the solid earth until they find an exit. Therefore, according to the magnitude and quantity of their quality and strength, they shake the earth more or less and often split it open, demolish mountains, submerge cities, and bring other damages. These are seen more frequently in Sicily and in the Puteolan territory <note>The *Agro Puteolano*, now known as the Phlegraean Fields near Naples, a region of intense volcanic activity</note>, where the earth is certainly cavernous and weakened in its inner depths by the internal sun <note>original: *indito Sole*; Campanella believed the center of the earth contained a source of heat or "inner sun" that fueled geological processes</note>.

This happens more on islands than on the continent, because the sea flows into them, providing water that is turned into the vapor that strikes the earth. It occurs even more in regions that are ignited beneath the earth, where hot springs and minerals flow from the quantity of vapors; since these cannot be contained within, and are unable to exit through narrow passages all at once, they cause an eruption. In this way, the vapor of fresh wine breaks a sealed jar. Roasted eggs and chestnuts also conceive so much vapor that, being entirely prevented from exiting through narrow pores all at once, it breaks out and turns the solid obstructing matter into dust.

<header>FATHER TOMMASO CAMPANELLA</header>

Gunpowder <note>original: *Puluis bellicus*, literally "war powder"</note> also, when ignited in tunnels, demolishes mountains and cities as it breaks out from a desire for vital expansion <note>Campanella believed all matter possessed a "sense" or "soul" and that heat causes substances to desire more space, leading to expansion and explosion</note>. By the same reasoning, from thin and sulfurous vapors collected and ignited within a thick cloud, thunderclaps are created in the air; these are prolonged and slow when they arise from a faint vapor and small heat, but short and impetuous when formed from much vapor and robust heat.

### On Lightning Bolts.

->A R T I C L E V.<-

When thin and ignited vapors in the clouds are driven down into lower bodies, they penetrate through their own fineness and consume external moisture with their heat. Passing through the porous parts, they leave the remaining parts dry and upright, as happens to animals struck by lightning. But when the ignited vapors are somewhat thick, they burn the exterior parts, such as hair, leaves, and clothing; however, they are not permitted to penetrate the interior because of their own bluntness <note>In this context, "bluntness" refers to a lack of "subtlety" or thinness in the particles, meaning they are too coarse to pass through pores</note>.

<margin>
* A stone of 3 pounds fell with accidents <note>In the sense of observable phenomena or symptoms</note> of this kind at Castrovillari <note>original: *Castrum Villarum*, a town in Calabria, Campanella's home region</note> in our time. From this, it is obvious that Aristotle is mistaken when he says these stones are carried upward by winds and then fall. For the wind does not pull them into the heights, but into a circle; nor would there be thunder, fire, and the smell of sulfur with a common stone, as we see happening here.
</margin>

While overpowering heat burns earthly materials, the flames (which are ignited vapors) or the vapors (which are dead flames) are generated within the burned things. Emerging from the less resistant parts—namely the thinner ones—and exiting through the pores of the more solid part, they turn the material itself into minute and viscous atoms. Thus, the solidity of the material is converted into tiny particles called soot <note>original: *fuligines*</note> and is carried upward with the exhaling smoke; it could not go anywhere else unless it were cut into the smallest fragments and elevated. This indeed is the matter from which lightning bolts are made. They are formed after much heat from thick, viscous, and sooty vapors, along with many sulfurous vapors, both thin and thick. When these are ignited, the thinness escapes due to the gathering of such a great mass, but the viscous soot is compressed into one while melting from the ignition. They are then compacted into iron, or into stone, or a consisten[cy]...

## *On shooting stars and the fires that appear in the air.*

### ARTICLE VI.

When very thin vapors are ignited on their own, rather than inside clouds, they appear in the <term>ether</term> <note>The upper atmosphere or the region of fire</note> as shooting stars. This happens because the flame runs from the beginning of the vapor to its end, just as firebrands thrown into the night air appear to do. Often, a unified and ignited vapor, by moving faster than the eye can follow, creates the appearance of a long flame, even though it is actually short and concentrated. This is like a burning stick spun rapidly in a circle; although the stick is only in one spot at a time, it seems to be in every part of the circle at once <note>Campanella is describing the "persistence of vision" to explain how a single point of light can look like a line or a shape</note>.

Other fiery shapes are formed depending on the position and density of the vapors: for "burning houses," "Dragons," "leaping Goats," and other such phantoms are observed <note>original: *Dracones, Capræ saltantes*. These were standard scientific terms in the Renaissance for different types of meteors, auroras, or glowing atmospheric gases</note>. Occasionally, it happens that lit lamps are seen at night in the graves of the dead; this is because the hot vapor exhaled from them during the day is concentrated and ignited by the cold of the night. Sometimes, horses and men who are breathing or speaking vigorously emit vapors into the chilly air that are so hot that, when struck and compressed by the cold, they turn into tiny flames.

# FRIAR TOMMASO CAMPANELLA On Comets.

### ARTICLE VII.

<margin>a. Comets are formed from illuminated vapors, not ignited ones, as Aristotle thinks. For they are seen to be eclipsed and persist for a year, which cannot happen to ignited things.</margin>
Vapors raised on high and illuminated by the Sun <a> become a Comet, so named because it sends out a "hair" <note>original: *comam*; the word "comet" derives from the Greek *kometes*, meaning "long-haired"</note> in the direction opposite to the Sun’s illumination, just as a flask full of water shows when exposed to the Sun. For this reason, Comets have been seen to be eclipsed by the shadow of the earth, and they persist until the vapor is completely thinned out into the sky. If the vapor of a Comet were first ignited <note>meaning actually on fire rather than just reflecting light</note>, it would not last until the tenth hour; this is proven by shooting stars and by ignited gunpowder <note>original: *puluis bellicus*, literally "war powder"</note>, which is a substance thicker than the exhalation of a Comet.

<margin>* The decrease in parallax shows that Comets are formed above the Moon, as does their absence in the stellar region.</margin>
Comets are formed both below and above the Moon, and even as far as Jupiter, <*> and the higher ones are often observed through the reduction of <term>parallax</term> <note>The apparent change in position of an object when viewed from different points; a smaller parallax indicates a greater distance from Earth</note>. They are carried along with certain fixed stars with which they have a natural sympathy and resemblance. Mostly they move toward wherever the exhalation is thinnest, whether they are carried by an oblique or some other path. They wander almost perpetually from east to west along with the sky, sending out a tail in the direction opposite to the face that receives the solar light. Often they seem to stand motionless, because while they are carried forward by the force of their own thinness and the solar light preceding them, they are held back by the movement of the sky being driven backward; thus they stand where Eternal Wisdom has foreseen a certain change should occur.

<margin>Wherefore perhaps vapors to be illuminated are raised even from other systems, which our earth does not produce to that extent.</margin>
<margin>b. The significance of Comets and Eclipses.</margin>
When such a great abundance of exhalations is gathered in the <term>ether</term> <note>The region of the upper atmosphere or the heavens</note> as to constitute a star of this kind and one so flashing, <b> unusual changes necessarily happen to earthly things. Just as the failing solar light in an eclipse determines a great variety of effects, the universe of things is tempered like a clock, where any subtraction or addition brings about a change. For this reason, Comets predict scarcity, war, and mortality—which is more conspicuous among the great <note>meaning the nobility or leaders</note>, though common to all—since they cannot be formed except by great heat. <c> Furthermore, adding themselves... <margin>St. Thomas, *Against the Gentiles*, Book 3.</margin>

---

<margin>c. Men are mostly governed by sense and passion generated by the heavens, rather than by free reason, which is also indirectly moved by the heavens, according to the text of St. Thomas; therefore, Astrologers usually divine correctly.</margin>

<summary>Campanella argues that comets are illuminated vapors rather than fires, located often beyond the Moon, and serves as celestial omens of major earthly changes like war and plague.</summary>

By their dryness, they also produce sterility, from which famine and plagues arise. But if they arrange human affairs in a gentle manner, they lead them to a better state. For some lights and some exhalations benefit certain things, while they are harmful to others. Therefore, it is not without cause that they are commonly said to bring about effects similar to the variety of the planets they resemble. 

But whether such a great mass, exceeding the stars and the earth, is carried from our soil all the way up to Jupiter, or whether it comes from other systems unknown to us and hidden by the heavens—just as the Moon, devoid of light, appears no different from the sky—who can understand? Indeed, new stars do arise, such as those in the time of Hipparchus <note>A Greek astronomer (c. 190–120 BCE) who recorded a new star, prompting his famous star catalog.</note> and Tycho [Brahe] <note>Tycho Brahe observed a "New Star" or supernova in 1572, proving that the heavens could change.</note> even in the sphere of the fixed stars, as revealed by the lack of <term>parallax</term> <note>The apparent change in position of an object when viewed from different points; a lack of parallax indicates the object is extremely far from Earth, placing it in the celestial rather than the atmospheric realm.</note>. And we now see small clouds <note>original: *nubeculas*; likely referring to sunspots, which were a subject of intense study in the early 17th century by Galileo and others.</note> revolving near the Sun, which it is impossible to have been drawn out from our earth.

## On the Halo and Parhelia.

### ARTICLE VIII.

<image-desc>A vertical scientific diagram illustrating optical refraction or reflection in the atmosphere. It consists of a crescent-shaped band at the top representing a layer or lens, from which two lines descend to form a tapering cone. A central vertical dotted line serves as an axis, intersected by a horizontal dashed line near the bottom. At the base where the lines converge, there is a small cross-shaped detail.</image-desc>

When the light of the Sun, especially in the morning and evening, penetrates through a multitude of vapors that have been somewhat scattered, it is stretched into streaks of saffron, green, red, or scarlet, depending on how the light is stained by them in its passage.

Vapors positioned beneath the Moon and illuminated by it represent a certain halo <note>original: *aream*; a circular ring of light around a celestial body.</note> of light; sometimes even several, according to how the Moon gazes upon her own reflection in many of their consistencies. The halo appears to exceed the size of the Moon, although it is far smaller, because the halo is closer to the earth while the Moon is more distant. Similarly, the Sun, in one or more clouds of a consistency not so thick that they are not transparent, creates another sun or multiple suns <note>referred to as parhelia or "sundogs."</note> by reflecting itself, just as it is accustomed to showing itself in glass or in water.

<header>FRIAR TOMMASO CAMPANELLA On the Rainbow.</header>

### ARTICLE IX.

But when a cloud is positioned opposite to the **Sun**, rather than beneath it, if that cloud is dewy, it produces a **Rainbow**. This arises from the oblique portions of the Sun reflecting back; it is therefore semicircular because the upper portions of the Sun do not extend direct rays toward the cloud, but elsewhere. It is also circular for the reason that the Sun itself is of such a shape. The Sun pours out light from every point of itself and in every direction, both direct and oblique. From the middle parts of the Sun, which extend direct light into the cloud, powerful and white rays flow down, which do not allow themselves to be "defiled" or colored. However, from the lower parts of the Sun facing the horizon, these types of oblique rays flow into the dewy cloud and are "defiled" <note>Campanella uses the term *fædantur* (stained or defiled), reflecting his theory that colors are produced when pure white light is weakened or "corrupted" by the darkness of matter.</note> by this perpetually darkening matter. Yet the more vivid and direct light is less obscured; thus it happens that the first circle of the Rainbow, because it is closer to the white rays emanating from the middle of the Sun, is **crimson** <note>original: *puniceus*</note>, which is to say, it is only slightly defeated by the presence of the matter. The second, narrower circle of light is **saffron** <note>original: *croceus*</note>, because being weaker, it is stained more. Finally, the last is **green** <note>original: *viridis*</note>, since it is more oblique and even more narrow. It also happens, when there is an abundance of elevated vapors such that they can be struck by the most oblique rays of the Sun, that they are stained and reflect other colors, such as **purple**, **blue**, **yellow**, and so on.

From these middle "warmths" between black and white, many colors are reborn from the mixture, as the variously changing colors of rose wreaths demonstrate by comparison. Indeed, in the triangular glass prism <note>original: *serratili vitro triangulari*; Campanella describes a prism as a "toothed" or "saw-like" triangular glass, likely referring to its angular shape used to refract light.</note> which we mentioned, one may observe this: where the light is closer to the thinner angle, it is **crimson**; following that is **saffron**; then comes **green**, then **purple**; after this **blue**, and finally **dark** <note>original: *fusca*</note>, where the two angles of the triangle's base intercept more matter than the sides themselves. Often another Rainbow is found above this one, but tinted with opposite colors—namely, it has its smallest circle as crimson, etc.—because the rays from the upper oblique part of the Sun pass into the second...

<note>original vocabulary list: Rainbow, Sun, cloud, colors, crimson, saffron, green, purple, blue, yellow, triangular glass</note>

A Rainbow occurs both before and after rain, because the first and last remnants of moist vapors are suited to "stain" the light. A Rainbow also occurs by the **Moon** when vapors are present, though it is whiter. ## On the Milky Circle.

### ARTICLE X.

<margin>St. Thomas [Aquinas], in the first [book of the commentary on] the Metaphysics.</margin>
<margin>The Milky Way is not formed in the air, for then it would not be visible from every region of the earth, nor always in the same position, nor with the same consistency. Therefore Aristotle errs by claiming it consists of vapors.</margin>
When, at God’s command, the heavens were stretched out, a great portion of the "upward" substance exhaled more into this specific location than into others, whence it obtained an unequal consistency. Indeed, this collected matter created a certain glowing path (since light is simply united heat), which is called the **Milky Circle** <note>The "Milky Way" or *Via Lactea*.</note>. It is not perfectly straight, but has certain twists and turn-offs, and varying thicknesses. It was arranged by **Prime Wisdom** <note>God.</note> to produce variety upon the earth, and to show that the heavens themselves—and not just the stars—revolve in a circle, and for other uses known to the inhabitants of heaven, for whom it perhaps marks a path. It is seen perpetually in the same position from all regions of our world, always in the highest starry portion of the sky; it has never changed its position, its arrangement, nor its thinness. For whatever happened to things from the beginning became their nature, both for the Heaven and the Earth, as well as for their parts.

## On stones and minerals.

### CHAPTER VIII.

### ARTICLE I.

<margin>a I always prioritize the **final cause** <term>final cause: the ultimate purpose or "why" for which a thing exists</term>, since it is the true reason for all things produced by skill and intellect. Physical causes, such as heat, cold, matter, and location, are merely the means to achieve that end, which we shall discuss in our *Metaphysics*. Those who believe the world is eternal or created by chance, such as Aristotle and Democritus, ignore this purpose. However, I well recognize that nature, as an active force, does nothing without a purpose, neither producing too much of the unnecessary nor failing in the necessary.</margin>

<margin>b Through ignorance, Aristotle said that stones and minerals are formed from a thick "exhalation" <note>Aristotle's *Meteorology* suggested that dry exhalations from the earth formed stones.</note>; but if that were so, they would all be transparent, and their density would be no greater than that of ice or water.</margin>

For the defense and support of the Earth—acting as its very bones—many mountains were made from various kinds of stone. They were created to serve as dwellings for animals, suited for the multiplication of nests and seeds; to act as a support for forests so they may stand tall; to ensure the Earth can hold many different beings; and so that regions might be bounded and divided. Stones were also made so that **Art**—which is a "second Nature"—might have material to work with (just as God intended), and thus they grew to such great heights. **Metals** were also created for the use of trade and the exchange of goods, for the cultivation of the earth, and as tools for humans to master stones, trees, and animals for their own use, among other reasons. All these things indeed come from the "liquid of the earth," as we have said regarding their origin. 

Stones are born from liquefied earth that has been hardened by constricting cold, as ice and crystal demonstrate; or by heat lifting away the thinner parts, causing the thicker parts to unite into one for their own preservation, as seen in the stones that form in the human kidney or bladder; or by cold and heat acting in turns, as the horns of animals and the "bones" <note>The hard, woody centers</note> of plants show us.

For this reason, stones of this kind become more or less hard, depending on how much or how little fluid <term>fluid: Latin *fluoris*, here referring to a mineral-binding liquid or "cement" that hardens into stone</term> joined them together, as is clearly seen in tufa <note>original: *tophis*, a porous rock formed from volcanic ash or calcium deposits</note> and other gravelly compositions.

This occurs all the more because where the land is now, the sea once was; thus, maritime things are found in such places. This is seen in Egypt, which was once under the sea, and at the mouth of the Po <note>Latin: *Padus*</note>, and in the territory of Padua <note>Latin: *agro Patauino*</note>. We have noted that the Adriatic Sea has receded twenty miles from the time of the historian Titus Livy until our own day. In other places, the opposite is true: where there was once land, there is now sea, such as at the Sea of Azov <note>Latin: *paludem Mæotidem*</note>, where the sea is expanding, just as it is diminishing near Venice. Thus, the world maintains its balance <note>original: *contralibatur*, suggesting a physical counter-weighting or leveling of the Earth's surface</note>. Universal fires and earthquakes have also altered both the Earth and the Sea.

## *On the pregnant stone.*

### ARTICLE III.

While a stone is hardening in its outer layer, it can still remain liquid on the inside, especially when the thinner substance is driven toward the center by cold. When this inner part hardens over a long period of time, it separates from the surrounding outer layer, and so a stone is formed inside a stone <note>Campanella is likely describing a geode or an "eagle stone" (aetites), which was historically called a "pregnant stone" because of the loose piece of mineral that rattles inside it</note>.

This was the origin of the **crystalline humor of the eyes** <term>the lens of the eye, which early anatomists believed was a solidified liquid similar to a gemstone</term>; that is, it arose from non-uniform matter. Salt and other **crystallizations** <note>original: *ingemmationes*, referring to the "budding" or growth of crystals</note> had the same origin, though with this difference: if they melt from abundant and strong heat and then harden spontaneously afterward, the mass was hardened by a heat that was not long-lasting, and it was rather uniform in its nature.

But if a substance does not melt through long-lasting, uneven, and strong heat, but rather through a heat that is mild, uniform, and very long-lasting, then this matter has arisen from dissimilar parts—that is, from compound liquids that are thin, thick, and oily. While the long-lasting heat gradually evaporates the thin parts, the remaining parts are hardened as if they were following and embracing those evaporating elements. For this reason, they do not melt when exposed to great heat; for as the thin parts evaporate even now, the remaining parts must necessarily become harder for the same reason. This is what happens to the **diamond** <note>original: *adamanti*</note> from a mild, long-lasting, and dissolving heat; in this way, all the parts are dissolved equally at once, and the first parts, once overcome, do not evaporate without the later ones. For this reason, it is melted better by **goat's blood** <note>original: *sanguine hircino*. This refers to a long-held classical and medieval belief, famously cited by Pliny the Elder, that the indestructible diamond could only be softened or broken by the blood of a goat.</note>, because it is gradually penetrated and opened by it; whatever grows warm and refined remains mixed with the remaining portion, disposing it toward dissolution, since it is held back by blood of this kind at a proportionate, uncertain degree opposed to its binding.

However, it must be considered that a violent fire reflected within a furnace is able to dissolve every hardness over a long period, even that of a diamond—though first by **calcining** <term>reducing a mineral to powder through heat</term> it, if it has unequal parts; but by melting it thoroughly if its parts are equal. Therefore, **crystals** solidified over a long time in the **Alps** and northern regions are formed by great cold, whereas **diamonds** are mostly formed under the tropics and the equator. Although **Alpine crystal** <note>original: *crystallum alpestre*, or rock crystal</note> has its origin from liquefying heat, and thus from crystallization—from which it thrives and grows into cubic and five-sided shapes—it is nevertheless packed together by external cold. This does not happen to precious stones, unless perhaps they harden by both opposites <note>heat and cold</note> acting in turn.

Stones of the third type, therefore, are generated from similar fluids <note>original: *liquoribus*</note> disposed in a like manner, hardening by heat, cold, or both. However, they become red, green, or saffron-yellow because some other fluid, imbued with a particular color, is mixed into them. Indeed, a small amount of blackness poured into a white fluid often produces, to a greater or lesser degree, various colors from itself and the white fluid—colors that are more or less distant from whiteness or blackness, just as we were saying regarding the **rainbow** <note>original: *Iride*</note>.

For this reason, one can see a vessel full of white wine being stained by a small amount of dark wine because of the latter's material thickness (for blackness is the "face" or outward appearance of matter). Depending on whether the wine is more or less black, or whether more or less of it is added, it stains the white wine to a greater or lesser degree and produces many different colors. Since everything black is thick, it is penetrated and dissolved by the white, which is thin. Therefore, the white substance is everywhere clouded and stained by the black that enters it, just as the sweet is by the salty, which is also thick. 

This is why the **pyrope** <term>pyropus; a fiery red gemstone, likely a variety of garnet</term> is sometimes seen to be partly red and partly white at the same time, because the white fluid had not been entirely overspread by the red. Nevertheless, transparency remains in this type of stone because the red fluid (or whichever other is mixed in) is not entirely opaque. For if every fluid is produced by heat, it necessarily possesses some transparency; and when it is thinned out <note>original: *rarefcat*</note> by the white fluid, it must lose what little opacity it may have had.

The second type of stones is formed from a slippery or viscous consistency <note>original: *lubricofitate*</note> and white fluids that are thick and therefore not transparent. These were generated by a long-lasting, mild heat, which, by remaining inside, naturally turns the matter white. But because this heat cannot thin the matter out, it leaves it opaque. Then, when external heat, cold, or both act upon it, the stones harden. 

For this reason, one must conclude that **animal teeth**, **eggshells**, **marble** <term>marmor</term>, **alabaster** <term>alabaſtrum</term>, and all woods and metals—which do not arise from perfected fluids, but from a slippery consistency and an origin lacking a balanced temperature, and which were first generated by a uniform heat—have had their origin in and are composed of earth that is not uniform, but rather soft, slow, and dense. Therefore, since stones of this kind [harden] <note>The sentence breaks here; the catchword indicates the next page begins with the completion of the word "indurescant" (they harden)</note> by heat, or cold, or both acting in turn...

# On Metals.

## ARTICLE V.

<margin>The material difference between a stone, a plant, and a metal.</margin>
Furthermore, the darker, thicker, and harder to break they are, the more they have arisen from a bulkier mass and from earth that has been less "conquered" <note>original: *superata*; Campanella uses this to describe how heat masters and transforms raw matter</note>, and from a joining together condensed over a long time by the work of both opposites <note>The "opposites" likely refer to heat and cold, or the active and passive principles in nature</note>. Therefore, quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*; literally "living silver," known to us as mercury</note> seems to be generated from earth that is well-conquered and more uniform than any other metal, produced by a most powerful and uniform heat. For this reason, the whole substance is mobile; if it is placed in fire and one portion of it evaporates, they all evaporate together, because they are so similar. The force of the heat's action induces the same effect in all parts because they are of the same nature.

Lead and tin, however, are made from somewhat thicker parts that are less conquered; these are condensed as the heat evaporates, yet they do not possess total thinness. For this reason, they are flexible, just like plants, in which smokiness and viscosity are the causes of their flexibility. From this it becomes clear that stones consist of a denser matter than metals and are more deprived of thinner portions, since stones break while metals bend. Yet those things that are more flexible have a more lingering and viscous matter, as lead and tin—made from soft matter without dryness—testify. 

Nevertheless, lead has more parts that are softer, impure, and thin at the same time; therefore, when melted often, it is turned into tin, which is a purer and harder being, because in the melting process the dross <term>scoria; the waste matter separated from metals during smelting</term> is separated and the thinness is drawn out. Tin, when melted more frequently, is turned into silver, which is a purer and harder being for the same reasons. Then, from silver that has been heated in the fire, the purest parts melt into gold, the thinnest parts into smoke, and the more impure parts are turned into copper <note>original: *æs*; can refer to copper, bronze, or brass, but here indicates the less pure residue of the refining process</note>, a thing which is indeed arid, porous, and dry for the same reason. But if tin is added to copper and they are melted together, they produce the metal commonly called bronze <note>original: *brontium*</note>, which we shall call *Aeramentum* <term>Æramentum; a Latin term for copper-work or bronze, which Campanella adopts as a formal name for the alloy</term>, a thing more robust than either; for

From this, the bronze gains a filling for its pores, while the tin gains a sinewy stability <note>original: *neruosam stabilitatem*; a term used to describe structural strength or "toughness"</note> from the bronze. For this reason, they create a certain solid that is more compact, more tenacious, and more robust. 

Iron also arises from melted impure earth and a variation of matter turned almost into stone, which is then dissolved into a liquid and soon hardens into a flexible thing because its sandy and dry solidity has been separated out. If it is melted many times and immersed in water—especially water sprinkled with marble dust—it is turned into steel <term>chalybs</term> <note>Steel was historically viewed as a purified or "tempered" form of iron, often involving additives like bone or stone dust during the heating process</note>, a substance that is harder and less flexible but more brittle than iron. This occurs because in the melting process, it loses its thinness <note>original: *tenuitatem*; referring to the subtle, fluid parts of the matter</note> and receives rigidity from the reactive cold. Simultaneously, it gains brittleness and rigor from the marble atoms, just as it does from glassy ones. 

From this it shines forth that stone consists of a denser matter deprived of subtle elements; metal, however, consists of a viscous matter not entirely stripped of them; and wood consists of a slippery, smoky, and less hardened matter. Nevertheless, in each of these three named categories, there exists density, viscosity, softness, slipperiness, liquid, and smoke—but in some, there is more of one of these dispositions, and in others, there is less.

<margin>Response to the problems of St. Augustine in *The City of God*.</margin> 
Returning then, we see that silver contains within itself portions of tin, and indeed portions that are more hardened by the departure of subtle matter, just as tin is hardened by frequent melting. Yet, whatever remains is hot and has a certain thinness mixed uniformly into the consolidated and compact material. Therefore, silver is white and, as it were, lucid. Nonetheless, it leaves a black mark on a white page <note>Campanella is addressing a classic paradox: why a bright, white metal like silver creates a dark grey or black line when used as a stylus on paper</note>. This is because the matter that exists in all beings is inherently black, but metals stain with blackness more because they are more flexible, and thus they communicate more of themselves and are more easily impressed. The silver itself does not stain the paper with whiteness because white does not act upon white, its own likeness; indeed, if they were combined, they would be confounded and could not be distinguished. However, on a touchstone <term>lapis probatorius</term> <note>A dark, hard stone like basanite used to test the purity of precious metals by observing the color of the streak they leave</note>, which is black, the brightness of silver and the paleness of gold are discerned, but their blackness is not seen at all, because it is confounded with the black...

### F. TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

...[the black]ness of stone. Since black horn is composed of great opacity and very little transparency, its compact parts display blackness; yet its ground-up shavings and small fragments display whiteness. This occurs because their penetrable surface is bathed in the light of day, and being overcome equally, they show whiteness—that is, the light reflected from them combined with their native whiteness. This whiteness was previously mixed into the whole, but it did not appear because the compact blackness prevailed. The same thing happens with black glass: when it is crushed into small fragments, it immediately turns white for the same reason.

Gold, finally, is composed of parts that are purer and more uniform than those of all other metals. These parts are hardened as heat evaporates, and they are rendered tawny <note>original: *fulvis*; a deep yellow or reddish-gold color</note> by the heat remaining in a degree that is not entirely overcome by the mass. For this reason, gold is more flexible than silver due to the similar softness of its parts; it is also the heaviest of metals because its parts are most united and lack any porosity <note>original: *porositatem*; small gaps or holes within the material</note> through which air might enter and provide lightness. When gold is melted, it loses none of its weight because its parts are equal; it possesses no thinner elements which, by evaporating, would leave the remainder diminished, as happens to other metals composed of unequal parts. Nor does it spit out or suffer from rust <note>original: *rubiginem*; used here to mean oxidation or any corrosive "dross"</note>, because its parts are pure and similar. Thus, the hidden heat <term>calor occultus</term> <note>Campanella refers to the "innate heat," a vital force believed by Renaissance philosophers to reside in all matter and drive its development</note> acting within all things, even when it increases and emerges, does not extract any impure parts (which gold lacks) such as the rust found in iron. Iron, of course, is formed from red earth that has not been well conquered in the furnace and melted. Consequently, iron is composed of waste <note>original: *excrementis*; literally "excrements," referring to the slag or dross of the metal</note>, thin elements, liquids, and moderate stickiness. Because of the dissimilarity of these parts, iron is more easily melted, and its thinness and rust are separated. Indeed, things that are very similar do not easily permit themselves to be sequestered due to an ingrained "mutual friendship" <note>Campanella uses "amicitia" (friendship) as a physical principle where like substances attract and hold onto one another</note>. For this reason, horns and wood soften more easily in fire, because a certain thinness remained in them when they emerged from the "common mother" <note>Nature or the Earth</note> and were bound into solidity by cold and heat—a solidity that soon yields to fire. The liquids from which so many Beings have been born from the beginning of the world until now were generated by the Sun and purified in countless ways. Therefore, Art <note>Referring to "Ars," the human skill of alchemy or chemistry</note> finds it difficult in a short time...

# *On the Growth of Stones and Metals.*
## ARTICLE VI.

Stones increase into various shapes by growing larger—namely cubic, pyramidal, five-sided, and six-sided—just as plants grow into their own specific forms. For even the greatest mountains, such as the Alps and the Apennines, the Riphaean mountains <note>a legendary mountain range in the far north of Eurasia</note>, and the Taurus, could not have extended into such great mass and height all at once. Rather, it must be believed that they grow, just as we experience both internally and externally in the Aufidus <note>the modern Ofanto river in Italy</note> and Sarno rivers. Sea-shells and oysters have stony shells which clearly grow, as do those of snails. Hence, we see that the marbles in the mines of Spain and the salts in Calabria are restored and increased over a period of time, even if they are continually extracted and consumed.

A stone does not grow when it is in a wall, because things only grow in this manner when they remain born from and connected to their mother <note>referring to the earth as the "mother" of minerals</note>; but when they are separated from her, the veins through which they draw the juice <note>original: *succum*; the nourishing liquid believed to feed minerals</note> that nourishes them are destroyed. For this reason, a tooth that has been pulled does not grow, nor does a bone, nor even trees themselves; but while they are bound to the mother earth, they are nourished and increased. Stones do not merely grow from the outside by the addition of layers, but from within by nutrition. For simple addition creates a different kind of consistency, whereas stones are uniform and of the greatest size; where they are born, they become such things and of such size because their own native heat gradually sucks up a liquid similar to themselves, from which they are born, produced right alongside them. In this same way, the veins and mines of metals "vegetate" <note>meaning they grow like plants</note> and convert the earth attached to them—which is already disposed toward such a change—into their own likeness.

And in the mountains of Stilo <note>Campanella’s hometown in Calabria, Italy</note> stones grow clearly into an oblong square shape, divided from one another at the peak like the branches of trees. Therefore, it must be believed that their deepest roots are not entirely hard, but flexible <note>original: *lentas*; meaning supple or pliant like a living stem</note>. For both corals and newborn bones are flexible and soft; but once separated from the mother <note>referring to the earth or the living body</note>, they attain hardness. The Magnet <note>original: *Magnes*; lodestone</note> is nourished by iron filings and atoms near which it is born, and without this kind of food, it is consumed. There is also within stones and metals sense, friendship, and enmity <note>Campanella believed all things in nature possessed a degree of "sense" or "feeling," known as panpsychism</note>, as the magnet and iron declare, or quicksilver <note>mercury</note> with gold: as do the Star-stone <term>Astroites; a star-shaped fossil coral</term> and the Wheel-stone <term>Trochites; wheel-like segments of fossilized crinoids</term> and many others.

# On Plants.
## CHAPTER IX.
### ARTICLE I.

Then Wisdom <note>referring to the divine "Primalities" of being in Campanella's philosophy</note> decreed that, for the beauty of the World, for the nutrition and habitats of animals, and to provide substance for the arts of both land and sea, plants should be born for many other uses. These were born from that gentle heat which had made the earth soft, slippery, and smoky at the same time (wherefore they are produced neither in mud nor in dry sand). Within this slipperiness, a certain airy thinness—in which heat itself prefers to dwell—was generated and began to emerge above the earth and seek the heights. 

But because this thinness was held back by the thick moisture and outer stickiness, it could not be separated from it; therefore, it pulled the moisture out with itself. Suddenly, as it came out onto the surface, the thickness was condensed by the surrounding cold wandering through the air, while the thinness remained within it. Consequently, falling by fatal necessity into a desire for living there—because the cold and heat from the outside, being unlike itself, were harassing it—lest its existence fail, as the invisible thinness exhaled and the more solid portion remained diminished, it began to draw toward itself from the same places where it had emerged, and to be nourished by nearby juices, rendering them similar to its own thinness and thickness by [heat]...

<margin>*a God, Nature, and Art, by providing the desire for an end, provide the means and the manner of reaching it within and beyond their duty; they neither fail nor superabound.*</margin>

<margin>*On Putrefaction.*</margin>
<margin>*b The cause of Putrefaction is not the drawing out of native heat by an external one, as Aristotle believes; but the increase of heat surpassing its own mass beyond the usual order, whence it loosens, breaks, and turns it partly into thick vapors, which stink to us because they weigh down the thinness of our spirit with their thickness, and overcome our heat with great heat: and this is stench. Likewise, it generates worms from the loosened mass, within which the spirit newly generated makes an onset, and unable to exit, organizes it: wherefore a great fire burns and does not produce worms, because it brings forth thin vapors, and not stinking ones, since stench is a thick vapor.*</margin>
*b* Therefore, things rot because the native heat—increased by itself or by the heat of the air—softens, relaxes, and soaks the parts of the matter in which it resides. It turns them into thick vapors, which by their thickness weigh down the thinness of our own spirit, and by their excessive heat overcome the power of that same spirit: and this is stench <note>original: *foetor*</note>. For this reason salt, which causes heat to slip away and hardens matter, and likewise cold itself, which kills heat...

...preserve them from putrefaction. Therefore, the rotting earth is converted into plants and worms by the heat retained within its thickness and viscosity. And since all our beings are hot, they possess channels and invisible pores everywhere, through which the heat itself, along with its thinness <note>original: "tenuitate." In Campanella’s physics, this refers to the subtle, rarefied state of matter—like air or spirit—that allows it to move through denser bodies.</note>, continually escapes into the air—never forgetting its own origin. Some do so more, others less. 

Plants, however, have very many pores, which is why they float on water, with a few very dense exceptions—namely, the holm-oak and ebony, and others of that kind. Certain plants are generated from well-softened and sticky earth, such that a great deal of thinness is found in the middle of their thick mass, which expands the earth by lifting it; hence it happens that their stalks are hollowed out and marked by certain closed nodes placed at intervals, until the internal spirit, making an impulse, pushes them to grow with forces and efforts often repeated at intervals. We see this happen to many herbs which, because they are fragile, do not have a life longer than a year. This is because excessive summer heat accelerates the exit of their native spirit <note>The "native spirit" (spiritus natiuus) is the vital, warm vapor that Campanella believes animates all living things and directs their growth.</note> and dries out the sticky parts, weakening the path of their life-force. Consequently, herbs of this kind do not grow much, nor do they live beyond half a year or a full year, and they speed up their seeding because they sense their approaching death—such as wheat, oats, reeds, and the like.

Indeed, all are generated by a mild heat; therefore in Spring, when the Sun affects the earth with a mild heat and makes it pregnant, they are accustomed to emerge, and similarly in Autumn. But spring plants grow because the succeeding summer nurtures them and forces them to grow and ripen their seed. Autumnal plants, however, do so very little, because the winter cold follows, forcing the heat down into the roots and killing the upper growth. Nevertheless, some plants have dense and robust roots which—even if the stalk is scorched by the summer Sun—are preserved in the roots and afterwards sprout in Spring, such as fennel and thistle. Other plants are perforated but filled with pith, such as the Elderberry and the Bramble-bush. And these kinds live for three or four years; nor do they bear seed suddenly, because they are born from a somewhat dense and more abundant matter, and from a more abundant spirit. ...[the spirit] does not completely penetrate or dry them out, but only causes growth to cease by drawing out the softer parts that have turned into vapor—parts that were being transformed into the plant’s own substance. This is why plants stop growing when they are not born near water. Nevertheless, in Autumn they lose their leaves because the cold diffused in the air finds them, so to speak, empty, since a large part of their spirits <note>The "spirit" (spiritus) refers to the vital, warm vapor that Campanella believes animates all living things.</note> has been drawn out. Therefore, by the counsel of God’s Wisdom, they must recall their heat to the roots, where the seed for the coming new year is formed. Since this heat no longer draws nourishment to the furthest parts, the leaves, lacking sustenance, wither and turn pale, because they are "cooked" <note>original: "coquuntur." In early natural philosophy, "concoction" or cooking was the process by which internal heat transformed nutrients into living tissue.</note> by both their own and external heat. The moisture <note>original: "humor."</note> that once masked the presence of heat and created the green color is so consumed that the leaves, now stripped of their resources, must fall.

Other plants live for many years—perhaps twenty, thirty, a hundred, or even three hundred—depending on whether the parts that compose them are more or less balanced, and whether they are dense enough to resist excessive heat and cold. To these extremes, all moderate temperatures are enemies <note>The author suggests that moderate heat acts as a defensive "enemy" against the destructive power of extreme cold or heat.</note>, as it is from moderation that plants receive life. These plants are slower to produce seeds, as they rely on the long duration of their own lives.

Of this kind are the Orange <note>original: "Arancius seu malus citrea." This refers to the citrus family, including oranges and citrons.</note>, the oak, the mountain ash, the fir, the cypress, the olive, and the pine, for the reasons mentioned. Consequently, they do not lose their leaves because they are able to resist harm. Nevertheless, the oak *does* lose its leaves, while the Orange does not. This is because the Orange tree possesses a thick, sticky, and uniform substance that extends even to the tips of its branches. Therefore, the internal heat protected by its own mass does not fear the cold or external heat, but remains throughout the tree, nourishing and giving life to both the trunk and the leaves. For this reason, it does not thrive in cold northern regions, because a great deal of heat—enough to overcome the heavy Earthly mass—is required to refine its matter into nourishment and life. This can only be achieved by a plentiful and uniform heat in strength and action, which cannot be found in colder regions. In such places, vines are not produced either, as they consist of a spongy and loose mass which cannot protect their native heat, especially during the winter. But

### FRIAR TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

Oaks, although they have acquired a vast and hard substance suited to resist the evils <note>In this context, "evils" refers to environmental stressors like wind, storm, or decay.</note> surrounding them, nonetheless do not possess a viscous and tenacious substance equally throughout their form. Instead, the ends of their branches are tender; for this reason, they are always growing upwards, because this spongy tenderness possesses more open passages <term>meatus: the internal channels or pores within a plant’s structure through which heat and moisture circulate</term> from which they are more fully nourished. These open passages are not present in lemon and orange trees. Furthermore, the leaves of oaks fall because they cling to these extremities, from which the heat flees into the dense trunk when the cold arrives. 

Likewise, when the trees are loosened by excessive heat, it draws out a portion of their native heat <term>native heat: the innate vital warmth that Campanella believed drove growth and life in all organisms</term> and leaves it diminished. This does not happen to the olive tree, even though it is more fragile than the oak, because its parts are somewhat thick, oily, and viscous in equal measure. Consequently, it possesses heat abundantly infused throughout its whole body—heat that is entangled and defended, and which does not fear the cold. The same is true for the orange and the mastic tree <note>The mastic tree (*Pistacia lentiscus*) is an evergreen shrub known for its resin.</note>, which nevertheless do not grow so large as to equal the oak, because their internal heat is diminished by external factors and restrained by their own internal viscosity. 

This same principle applies to human beings: those from the south are dark and small because their native heat exhales, being drawn out by the Sun; however, those from the North are large and fair-skinned because the vital juices and heat remain within them, compressed by the external cold, which whitens them and increases their growth.

The Fir and the Cypress grow tall because they have straight passages full of a dewy oiliness by which they are packed together. They never shed their leaves, nor do they spread their branches out in a wide circle, because their gummy material is easily condensed; it cannot be stretched out to the sides but is instead pushed upward by a robust heat. Nor do the leaves at their tips fall, as they do in oaks, because that viscous oiliness preserves the heat even in the tenderest parts. Their foliage remains small on account of this robust heat and because their substance is less expandable and less fluid.

# PHYSIOLOGY, CHAPTER IX.

## That Plants are Animals.

### ARTICLE II.

<margin>
a We say that plants are immobile animals, possessing external local motion only through outside forces, but not lacking the motions of alteration, growth, decay, generation, and corruption. These changes all occur through local motion as parts move toward other parts during growth, depart during decay, and are transposed during alteration. <note>Campanella refers to the Aristotelian categories of motion, arguing that even internal biological changes are technically "local motion" on a microscopic scale.</note>
</margin>
Plants are *a* immobile animals, because (as Wisdom has said) those things are moved which find it necessary to procure food and to avoid harms. But plants have a body so thick that it protects them from injuries, as well as a somewhat thick spirit <note>original: "spiritum"; in this context, a subtle material substance that carries life force</note>, and dull humors <note>original: "humores"; the vital fluids of the body</note> which are able to be nourished by earthly liquid. For this reason, they remain fixed in order to suck that liquid through their roots where they are born. Indeed, they find a greater supply there, continuously generated by the Sun, just as the Sun also generated that initial moisture from which the plants were first constituted. 

Within plants there are roots which serve as mouths, the trunk which acts as a belly, branches like arms, foliage <note>original: "frontes"</note> like hair, and bark like skin. Inside, there are fibers and many nerves *b* full of spirit, as well as veins full of sap—which is their blood—and then further inside, a hard bone full of marrow by which the plant is nourished. Therefore, if the bark is cut all the way around the circumference, the entire tree withers; however, this does not happen if the trunk is cut up to or even beyond the halfway point. An exception is the cork tree, which consists of many layers of bark; to kill it, one must cut through to the innermost bark, beneath which lie the veins and nerves full of spirit, which is their very soul <note>original: "anima"</note>.

Truly, certain small plants love nothing but their seed, such as wheat and barley with their <margin>with awns</margin> awns <term>awns: the hair-like or bristle-like appendages on the spikelets of grasses like barley or wheat</term>.

It remains like a sailor in a ship, within its body as if in its own home and instrument. # *On Fructification.*

### ARTICLE III.

All plants bear fruit in the Spring, because then, by the approaching Sun, their dormant heat—which had been cast down as if into a deep lethargy—is awakened and cherished. They are nourished by warm rains; for this reason, at that time or even earlier, the ground around them is plowed and dug, so that the solar rays can more easily penetrate to their roots, vivifying their power, opening the earth, and generating the fluids from which they may be richly nourished. Then, the heat poured out to the extremities with the Sun's help extracts vapor and liquid—well-processed through the veins—which is soon converted into soft flowers. These are clearly a more perfect and more refined <note>original: "decocta"; referring to the biological 'cooking' or distillation of nutrients within the plant</note> part of the tree itself. Therefore, these all have a scent, since a scent is a vapor well-refined by innate heat, similar to our own spirit. Thus the almond tree <term>amygdalus</term> sends out flowers first, and then leaves to cover the flowers so that they are not harmed by excessive heat or frost. But other, more prudent plants do not flower suddenly, but first send out thorns for the sake of defense, then leaves from the thick humor, and then, under the leaves, flowers from a more refined and thinned "sweat" [exudation]; and since these are composed of a very delicate mass,

## On Fruits.

### ARTICLE IV.

**F**ruit contains the best portion of itself at its very center, where the "native heat," the Entity, and the "Idea" of the plant are preserved in a pure, balanced state <term>temperie</term> <note>This refers to the Aristotelian and Galenic concept of "temperament," or the perfect balance of qualities—hot, cold, moist, dry—required for life</note>. An adjacent hardness protects this core from harm; this hard layer corresponds to the **bone** of the plant, just as the kernel corresponds to the **marrow** and to substantial purity. Surrounding this hardness is the pulp, which corresponds to the **flesh** of the plant itself; it is placed there to defend and nourish the seed so that even when it is cut from the tree, it is not dried out by the injury of the external air. On the other hand, larger and more solid seeds do not require so much pulp, but only a "bony" bark or shell, such as acorns and chestnuts, which also put on a thorny garment <note>the prickly husk</note> as a defense against dormice and mice. Most trees of longer life and more solid wood produce seeds without pulp, which animals also use for food.

<margin>a. Less perfect beings exist for the sake of the more perfect. Therefore, plants exist for animals, animals for humans, humans for Angels, etc.</margin> 
For **Wisdom** <note>Campanella refers to "Sapientia," the divine intelligence that organizes nature</note> provided not only for the propagation of plants, but also for the nutrition of animals—that is, for the more perfect beings. However, fruits that contain many small seeds and are born from fragile material—such as the grape, the fig, the pumpkin <term>pepo</term>, and the like—require more pulp for their defense, and it is this pulp that we humans eat.

Fragile plants ripen their seed in the summer because the Sun, by penetrating them, assists in the "cooking" <term>concoctionem</term> <note>In ancient science, ripening was viewed as a process of internal heat "cooking" the raw juices of a plant</note> and completion of the seed; soon after, the Sun opens the plant, causes its thin moisture to vanish, and accelerates its death. More robust plants, however, ripen their fruit in the winter, such as Olives, Oranges <term>Arancij</term>, Cypresses, Mastic trees <term>Lentisci</term>, and Chestnuts. In these cases, the summer heat was only strong enough to stir the plant's vital power and its dense moisture toward fruiting and nourishing the fruit, but not enough to ripen it. But when the winter cold arrives, the heat of the fruit and the tree is "united" <note>The theory here is *antiperistasis*: external cold forces the internal heat to concentrate and intensify</note>; thus, this increased heat cooks and more fully ripens the fruits, though sooner in some and later in others. lemons and oranges do not ripen until the return of spring's heat, because their substance is abundant, dense, acidic, and difficult to "cook" <note>original: "coctibilis"; in Aristotelian biology, ripening was viewed as a process of "coction" or "concoction"—a metabolic "cooking" driven by heat</note>.

Once the seed’s native heat is finished and the summer heat assists, the moisture—which was distilled through the stalks of the fruits to nourish fragile plants—is dried up. Thus, the seed falls to the ground, just as the leaves do. Once covered by rain, the movements of the earth, and fallen foliage, the seed's internal heat is concentrated and strengthened throughout the winter. This occurs because snow and ice force the heat inward to the depths, causing the plant to fix its roots deep and soon bear better fruit. This is provided, however, that the cold is not so extreme that it kills them, as often happens in Germany and in Muscovy <note>Russia</note>; in those places, they sow in the month of April and harvest at the same time we do, for the great length of the days there compensates for the shorter duration of the growing season in our region. In our lands, when Spring approaches, the native heat of the seed, stirred by the Sun, pours outward. It draws with it the sticky portion in which it was trapped and, emerging with it, *b* begins to form the plant.

<margin>
*b Aristotle denies the existence of Ideas because he denies that the World was made by a Craftsman according to the likeness of His own Mind. But he is clearly in error, as all of Nature cries out against him. For "like" does not produce "like" unless it spreads the Idea of its own likeness, nor would an offspring generate something similar to its parent unless it preserved the Idea of the parent. Likewise, while he denies Ideas, he affirms them by asserting that a "like" thing is sufficient to generate another "like" thing. Furthermore, he is proven wrong by worms born from decay; they are not born from something similar in species, but from the Idea of the species which is preserved in the First Being. For the Elements themselves do not possess the Ideas of the things composed from them.*
</margin>

In the beginning, the plant is nourished by the pulp that was rotting next to it, as if from a substance most similar to itself and more beneficial to its tenderness (for the pulp serves exactly this purpose). Then, by the power of the sun, it draws, sucks, is nourished, and grows from the earth, which has been turned into a liquid similar to itself by this very decay. And just as the seed worked within its mother tree to produce trunks, branches, bark, foliage, and flowers, and by nourishing them, so it works now by converting its own mass and the adjacent earth into a plant. For it preserves the **Idea** and likeness of its mother, which took its origin from the **Idea of the First Wisdom**. Thus, it learns how to act and how to exist in its own way, and how to generate its like, just as the mother acted and gave birth by Divine command and counsel, through the Author of Nature—the **Internal Art** of all things. A skilled lyre-player <note>original: "Citharoedus"</note> does not pause to think or deliberate...

# On animals, and first on their origin and structure.

## CHAPTER X.

### ARTICLE I.

<margin>a The animal spirit, since it is more free, moves itself as the pulse and the movement of the chest demonstrate. Therefore, it is able to separate itself from the mass in which it is born and move it, which the spirit of a plant cannot do, being frustrated by its own density.</margin>
<margin>b Breathing <note>original: "inspiratio"</note> brings the animal to life in the beginning, and thereafter preserves it. The occasion of nutrition: why and how it happens.</note></margin>
So that, because these immobile living things <note>referring to plants</note> were unable to exercise all the feelings and operations of sense due to their lack of movement, other "mobile plants" <note>Campanella often views animals as "mobile plants" that carry their soil (nutrients) inside them.</note> were created. Since motion is the work of heat, and heat cannot move except within a thin and agile subject, (at the command of Divine Wisdom) certain thin substances called **Spirits** <term>Spiritus: A physical, warm, and subtle vapor that Campanella believed was the primary instrument of life, sensation, and movement.</term> were generated within the liquid, sticky, slow, and hard earth. These were more freed from the earth than the spirits found in trees. Soon, these spirits were stirred up within the mass, and being unable or afraid to leave, they were held back by the air blowing in through the very passages <note>original: "meatus"</note> they were trying to escape through; thus, they remained trapped inside.

Because the spirits were pushed back inside the mass where they were born by this **b** breathing, they began to consume themselves with their own heat, thinning out their mass until the whole structure began to collapse. To prevent this, they began to move around, stretching themselves out and shaping the surrounding mass—which they had separated from the earth or other material they were born in through their agitation. At the same time, they formed certain organs and openings. Through these, not only could the spirits nourish and restore themselves from air (which is similar to their own nature), but the "workshop" called the body could also be nourished and restored by similar materials. Heat is always in motion, warming every mass it lives in and turning it into a thin vapor, which is then lost through exhalation. Therefore, the foresightful spirit takes other bodies into itself, warms them, and transforms them into its own substance, just as it built its own body. It makes these materials like itself and generates new parts; then, through hidden passages, it sends them to the places where the old particles had evaporated, so they can take their place. When a greater amount of substance is poured into the body to restore its substance than is lost through evaporation, **growth** <note>original: "augmentum"</note> occurs:

<margin>The origin of the sense organs.</margin>

Because of its subtle nature, it is easily moved and sensitive. When it touched things, it was troubled if they were hostile, but preserved if they were friendly. Wisdom—which taught the spirit the art of building a body out of necessity—also instructed it to build eyes and ears. Through these, it could perceive not the things themselves, but the light and air affected by things moving from a distance, and thus know which things were useful and which would be harmful.

## On the Levels of Animals, and their logic as perceived from their motion and structure.

### ARTICLE II.

<margin>The multiple levels of Animals.</margin>
Certain animals move only through expansion and contraction, such as sponges, oysters, and shellfish—which some mistakenly believe are born from moisture within sea-stones. For salt, with its sharp quality combined with light, has generated a spirit within the thick, rheumy slime of the rocks; this spirit then formed a soft body from the surrounding moisture using a sticky bond. Its thicker parts, which were pressed against the rocks, were separated from them by the moving spirit and became encrusted and hardened by the constricting cold and the heat that draws out the subtle parts. In some cases, the creature is not separated, which is why sponges remain bound to the hard rock like "animated plants" <note>original: "animatæ plantæ," referring to zoophytes, organisms that appear to be midway between plants and animals</note>. The spirit of such flesh could be satisfied with that simple motion; for **Wisdom** <note>original: "Sapientia," the divine intelligence that Campanella believes guides the "Spirit" to build suitable bodies</note> dictated that it should be nourished by the moisture of the sea, which would never be lacking in the place where the creature is born. 

But snails <term>limaces: in 17th-century Latin, this could refer to both snails and slugs</term> had their origin from a spirit within terrestrial moisture, surrounded by a viscous softness that is prone to hardening. For the spirit itself, being moved in a circle and unwilling to go out to meet an enemy, creates many spirals out of that moisture and soft matter. ...us, who also perform those operations which their substantial forms <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "substantial form" is the essential nature or "soul" of a thing that makes it what it is</note> are able to produce while they sense. <gloss>e</gloss> Likewise, they would not obey the Angels nor know them, unless they sensed the command. Furthermore, it would not be fitting to take away the power of acting from things, nor for me to work without them, since it is appropriate for the work to be modified by them. Therefore, it is entirely fitting that all things have sense—some clearer, such as the heavens, the winds, and animals; others more obscure, like the earth, plants, stones, and bones. Yet their friendship <note>original: "amicitia"; Campanella uses "friendship" and "enmity" to describe the natural attraction or repulsion between physical substances</note> and enmity, arising from the recognition of similarity or difference between them, will reveal this.

<margin>
f A human sustains himself on one foot while moving his own body; a horse on two, because it is of a heavier mass. A gnat stands on three, because it has six legs; for since it is slender and light, it would be disturbed by any little wind wherever it might stop for the sake of sleeping or eating. A spider has many for the same reasons, and so that it might handle the threads of its web. A centipede has very many, because its body is long and flexible, and it only crawls and suffers friction.
</margin>

Nor will all things require organs for sensing, since these are only required to carry a sensible object from a distance to the sensing part. Yet liquids and vapors sense by touching; likewise, they easily turn away from what is harmful. Plants also, and stones, are endowed with a faint sense; therefore, they feel little pain. Likewise, they have their nourishment right next to them and do not need to seek it from afar; they do not, therefore, need to sense from afar, and consequently have no need for organs of sight, hearing, and the like. Furthermore, they do not need feet for movement. For feet are required for the use of the spirit <term>Spirit; original: "spiritus". In this context, a thin, subtle material substance that acts as the instrument of the soul</term> enclosed within a heavy machine <note>Campanella refers to the physical body as a "heavy machine"</note>, whose half <gloss>f</gloss> by bracing it upon one or more bases, moves the other half, upon which it soon clings in turn to move the other. But air and other similar Beings move without the resistance of gravity and without the need for support. Fish and birds are supported in turn upon wings that press upon the air. Therefore, sense does not belong to the ears or other organs, but to the spirit itself, and to the principles of the things themselves. Animals, therefore, are within the belly of the world—which is a great animal—just as worms are in the belly of a human being.

Those who do not understand the human soul do not even think that man <gloss>g</gloss> senses. Nevertheless, let the Angels be assigned as governors of the animals—

# On the Origin of Man.

## ARTICLE IV.

<margin>Genesis 1.</margin>
<margin>a Natural instinct is the same as impulse. Nature, however, does not drive things toward an end unknown to it: just as an arrow does not go toward a target unless it is shot by a force that knows the goal.</margin>
When God, praising how timely sensation was for things—which are urged and driven to their operations and actions by that sense which they obtained from Nature or birth—He added that, for the completion of the whole Work <term>Opificium; refers to the universe as a crafted "Great Work"</term>, a certain Being should be made in His own likeness and image, in which would be contained whatever is found in all the things that make up the "great statue" <note>Campanella frequently uses the "great statue" (magna statua) as a metaphor for the physical universe as a divine masterpiece</note>. Therefore, He commanded that from the earth should be made an animal composed of a body most absolute and harmonious, and of a spirit most perfect and outstanding above all other animals, distinguished by more delicate organs and fashioned with the most excellent skill. This being would surely have its face turned upward toward the heavens to contemplate the great divine statue and its wondrous maker. For this reason, He turned its front feet <note>original: "pedes anteriores"; here referring to the evolution or design of hands/arms in the upright human posture</note> [into a different orientation].

*Since all Nature is Art, or an essential form placed within things, and every natural agent acts for a pre-known end, it is necessary that every Being senses and knows: and that instinct is the impulse of a sensing power. Likewise, things do not tend toward an end only in the way an arrow does; for in these things there is also a desire for the end: therefore, there is also a knowledge of it. Nor should we posit a World-Intelligence or World-Soul that knows the end while the desire remains in the operating thing itself: for the same Being must both desire and know the same end; otherwise they would be like you and I, where one cannot desire while the other knows the same end simultaneously and always. See what we have written in the Metaphysics against Avicenna, Alexander of Aphrodisias, and the Arabs <note>Campanella is arguing against the medieval Arabic Aristotelian view that a single "Active Intellect" thinks for all humanity, insisting instead that individual things must have their own internal knowledge and desire</note> on this matter.*

<summary>Campanella argues that the universe is a hierarchy of sensing souls, comparing the internal organs of a human to the various parts of the "World-Animal." He introduces the creation of Man as a microcosm designed to contemplate the divine "statue" of the universe through an upright posture and superior spirit.</summary>
