He turned [part of the body] into an instrument of wonderful craftsmanship called the **Hand**, so that man, wishing to use it for things as complex as composing a statue, could handle physical bodies at his pleasure. And He was so delighted by this kind of craftsmanship that, beyond the common Spirit <note>Campanella distinguishes between the "Spiritus"—a subtle, material vapor that animates all animals—and the immortal "Mens" or "Animus."</note> shared by this and other living creatures, He willed to infuse a **Mind** created immediately by Himself through a simple emanation without Matter. This Mind depends on Him just as the Angels were created, so that it might be immortal.

For all beings generated by mortal agents like Heat and Cold die amidst the conflict of physical opposites. However, the divinely established **Mind** is exempt from this: because it is simple, because it comes from God, and because it is not a composite of parts. Instead, it is given essence out of indissoluble power, wisdom, and love, which are unified in a real identity devoid of opposites and share a mutual essential coexistence. Therefore, it *is* life itself, rather than merely a participation in life like the corporeal Spirit, which only participates in these primalities <note>original: "primalitates"; in Campanella’s philosophy, these are the three fundamental principles of Being: Power (Potentia), Wisdom (Sapientia), and Love (Amor).</note>. <margin>From St. Bernard.</margin> This Animal, called Man, was soon distinguished into two sexes by God so that he could reproduce, just as other animals had been distinguished for this very purpose.

## *On the origin of perfect animals, the manner of their multiplication, and the difference of others.*

### ARTICLE V.

<margin>a Avicenna, Epicurus, Diodorus, Democritus, and others assert that the Sun can produce a human: But our reasoning teaches the contrary. Furthermore, at least some...</margin>
The **Sun** (said Wisdom) a will not be able to generate a human by itself, nor an elephant, nor any other perfect <note>In this context, "perfect" refers to complex organisms with specialized organs and higher functions, as opposed to "imperfect" animals like insects or worms.</note> animal. For a moderate heat—acting according to the measure of the human **Idea** and other things pre-existing in me—is required. This heat must be steady, long-lasting, and must work through many cycles and parts endowed with various temperaments to architect the craftsmanship of a perfect animal. 

If the Sun had to stop its motion for this purpose, it would suffer violence [to its nature]. Likewise, where it remained stationary, it would burn everything; but where it was absent, a destroying cold would prevail over all things. Therefore, let the Sun be permitted to continue its course just as it began. For in this way, it will generate only those animals whose constitution requires only a single day, or weeks, or a month to form.

*Therefore, man cannot be propagated except through intercourse, as Averroes <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), a medieval Andalusian philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to university life.</note> affirms, who also honors Noah’s Ark in this regard. ## On the propagation of living offspring, the miraculous formation of the Fetus, and the use of the parts.

### ARTICLE VI.

**W**herefore, just as the Sun by its heat makes the earth pregnant and fruitful, so the male would impregnate the female. And since the male was not as powerfully diffusive of his own virtue as the Sun, he received a fleshy member similar to the Sun's rays, through which he might pour out seed while entering the womb of the female. And so that the seed might be stirred to exit, it required some commotion, by which it is poured into the female womb. The womb, situated within and driven like a pouch, contracts and wrinkles with a greed for enjoying the soothing seminal heat; and it is so tightly closed that not even the thinnest stylus can enter: such is the pleasure placed there by Wisdom. For these two portions of the animal would not have wanted to be brought together for this kind of coupling—in which they lose a part of their Spirit <note>The material, airy substance that fuels life in the body.</note> and substance and become weaker, because they lack pure virtue,

<margin>
a. An animal possesses a diminished heat, which is hindered by the density of its own mass. Thus, when the heat wishes to pour itself out, it cannot be freed from that mass; therefore, it "cooks" <note>Campanella uses the term "decoquit," referring to the internal "cooking" or refining process of digestion and maturation in Renaissance medicine.</note> the mass more as it is poured out with it, and then organizes it, creating another animal. The Sun, however, being most copious and robust in its innate heat, does not emit a part of its own matter when it pours itself out. For the Sun’s heat is not hindered by matter, since that matter is entirely overcome and animated by the Sun's strength. Therefore, since the Sun pours itself out without matter, it does not suffer the diminution that an animal does, but only multiplication—which we see also happens to an animal when that which was poured out by diminution is, in turn, poured out again.
</margin>

[heat that is] simple and robust, from which the Sun overflows. Therefore, by pouring itself out, the Sun is not diminished because it does not emit its own bodily substance. For this reason, so that creatures might be enticed [to reproduce], a pleasure was instilled in such a union. This pleasure arises from the mutual, similar heat of both parts, each one cherishing the other, and from the passage of a sharp, stimulating heat <note>original: "caloris mordacis" — literally a "biting" or "stinging" heat that triggers a physical response.</note> through the nervous substance, which is less warm. Therefore, when the seed abounds, and the Spirit <note>term: "Spirit" (Spiritus); in 17th-century physiology, this refers to a subtle, vapor-like substance that flows through the nerves and vessels to facilitate life, movement, and sensation.</note> in the genital vessels is stimulated by an excessive and gathered heat trapped within, a titillation arises and a desire to escape that stinging sensation. Hence, through the rubbing of its like, the stronger part is delighted, desiring to extinguish the "itch" at the same time, and through a certain agitation, it emits the seed. For this reason, the cooler female also emits seed within her own vessel—where indeed there was a need for it—and the male emits into the same place. Then the uterus itself is closed and grows warm inside, so that the seed may liquefy. 

But since the seed consists of dissimilar parts—namely, fatty, viscous, liquid, and spiritual parts—while the Spirit enclosed within it is agitated, preparing an exit, it creates a rather large and shapeless bubble. From this bubble, by making an impetus, the Spirit spreads the seed further into many threads drawn out from the viscous parts; these are perforated and held together without the risk of breaking. Among these threads, those through which the Spirit (which was forming them) ran most copiously remained perforated—some more, some less; these are the veins and arteries. Those, however, into which "windiness" <note>original: "ventositas" — often referring to gas or air-like movements within the body's cavities.</note> flowed together with the inspiring Spirit from their very beginning, are dilated more and become the intestines and the vocal artery <note>term: "arteria vocalis"; an old anatomical term for the trachea or larynx.</note>. But the portions that were collected more and more tenaciously, composed of many threads, turned into nerves. The fatty parts are more easily extended, but in certain places they are broken and distinguished, and they harden somewhat more due to the agitation made by the Spirit retained in the tenacious parts stretched over the fatty ones. From this, bones are made, so bound together by nerves that they do not fly apart from their composition. On account of this, moreover, by a certain viscosity...

<margin>
**b** We have argued elsewhere in my *Anthropology* that all parts arise from the head: and that the head itself is first formed from the seed swollen by the **spirit** <term>spiritus: a subtle, vaporous substance believed to carry life and motion through the body</term>. Hence **Aristotle** is mistaken in claiming that an animal is not made from seed except by an active cause. Our response to Aristotle is found below.

That first mass **b**, however, from which channels of this kind began to be extended, and where the nerves, bones, arteries, and membranes took their origin (which are also made from the same viscous liquid spread out flat, just as the skin stretched over them is made from thickened viscosity), was made the head of the entire work. It is the first and universal part for this reason: the spirit entangled in the mass of the seed is stirred and increased by the heat of the womb—just as the seminal heat of plants is made fertile by the heat of the earth—and it desired to go out. Because it could not escape, it created certain cavities and ventricles by lifting up the surrounding mass.

<margin>**bb**</margin>

> ...it is not that the female has the same part acting as both active and passive, for heat acts, while the physical bulk is acted upon. The spirit acts, and the body undergoes transformation into organs. Nor is the heart made first, as they think, because it is the principle of motion or the mind, or because it dies last, it must live first. The heart dies last only because it is woven with fibers and tunics full of spirit that cannot easily escape. But men have been seen to die even after their hearts had withered. Nor is a lizard's tail, which dies last, the part born first: this happens to the tail because it has narrow nerves from which the spirit—since it is corporeal <note>Campanella emphasizes that the "spirit" is a physical, bodily substance, not an abstract soul</note>—cannot exit as quickly as it can from other, wider passages. Thus, chicks move even when their heads are cut off until the spirit exits, which would not happen if the spirit were incorporeal, as they say—or "one in potential and many in act," as Aristotle speaks when he does not know what else to answer. **bb** Because some women are said to conceive even before they emit seed, the entire "work" can be constructed from the male seed if there is enough of it, as we stated in the *Second Dispute against the Peripatetics* <note>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle</note>. **c** While the spirit tries to exit, it raises up bubbles <note>original: "ampullas"</note>, but it does not do this while it desires to be hidden, as **Galen** <note>A famous Greek physician whose works dominated medieval medicine</note> thinks. It is the nature of spirit to exhale out of narrow spaces; thus the brain consists of little mounds and spheres made by the elevation of the seed, driven by the impulse of the spirit as it tries to exit.

From there, having gained momentum, it began to pour out and stretch the mass into bones, arteries, nerves, veins, membranes, fibers, and skin. Truly, these parts arise from similar parts of the head itself: namely, the bones from the bone called the **skull** <note>original: "calvaria"</note>, which was the hardened exterior part; the **spinal cord** <note>original: "medulla spinalis"</note> from the soft brain itself; and from this the nerves, which are indeed the spinal cord extended lengthwise and further dried out. And finally, like a swollen organ, the intestine and the **vocal artery** <note>likely referring to the trachea or windpipe</note> were extended. Likewise, other threads, channels, coverings, thin membranes, and openings were created by the spirit while it prepared an exit downward, since it was unable to find one upward. For this reason, it could never fully escape; thus, forced to spend its life there, it often returned into the head and rested there, which is the origin of **Sleep**. It also frequently ran out through the channels, giving life to and moving the exterior parts; hence **Wakefulness**. Soon, the increased spirit began to feed on its own body and consume it; this is because its heat always exhales as a very thin and invisible vapor, never forgetting to do what it first did in its struggle—and always does—which is to be lifted upward toward kindred bodies.

### ON PHYSIOLOGY, CHAPTER 10.

...[they] are, than in the head, their source, once the blood was drawn out. This source, hardening a little while deprived of the thinness drawn from the veins, became the **liver** <note>original: "iecur"</note>, which is exactly like clotted blood. While the blood was being cooked in the liver, from the burnt foam and scrapings, the **gallbladder** <note>original: "vesica fellea"</note> was formed; for that reason, it draws and is nourished by that kind of liquid called **bile**. But the dregs of the blood, having slipped further to the left of the stomach, clotted there and became the **spleen** <note>original: "lien"</note>. The purer part of the blood flows through the wide vein, which they call the **portal vein** <note>original: "porta"</note>, scattered into many branches toward the lower belly and intestines, only to nourish the lower organs. But before these organs were formed, blood flowed upward through a very large vein, which they call the **vena cava**; and in the middle of the chest—where many fibers and little nerves are extended from the head along with the **great artery** <note>the aorta</note>, and with that same vein adhering to the junction of the ribs with the vertebrae—that blood, I say, was poured into their midst. It was compressed and bound together by the membranes seen within it, after which it became the **heart** from solid, dense flesh, rendered so by the agitation of heat.

<margin>
*f* The blood flowing into the **venous artery** <note>the pulmonary vein</note> forms the **lung**. It is called an artery because it is composed of three layers just like arteries; but it is called **venous** <note>original: "venalis"</note> because it contains blood without a noticeable pulse, like a vein.
</margin>

The heart, just as in the beginning, draws blood from the vena cava immersed in its left source, while it dilates by contracting the straight fibers and extending the transverse ones from which it is woven. Thus, while the heart dilates, so that the source is not left empty, blood enters through an opening to which a hanging membrane <note>a valve</note> is attached; and soon, while it is constricted, it sends the blood upward through the *f* **venous artery**; and the opening that was open during dilation is closed by the aforementioned membrane. Another opening is opened, over which another membrane stands; it is forced to yield by the compressed blood, which therefore leaps upward. By the same reasoning, blood exiting from the left ventricle through hidden openings enters into the right ventricle during the heart's dilation; but during constriction, it enters from the right into the great artery inserted there; and at the same time, it is spread through the whole body, because that artery is also scattered throughout, just like the vena cava.

Blood, oozing out from the veins and arteries, adhered to the nerves, bones, and other vessels; as its thin parts departed, it solidified into flesh, which clothes all portions of the human statue <note>Campanella often refers to the body as a "statue" or "fabrica" to emphasize its design by a divine architect</note>. It serves as a cushion and a defense against cold and heat, lest the body dry out or break; it also fills the ligaments in many divided bands so they are held together as one and do not fly apart when the "statue" is bent and extended. This kind of flesh with its ligaments takes on the *i* shape of a fish or a mouse; for this reason, it is commonly called a "little fish" <note>original: "pisciculus"</note> or a "muscle" <note>original: "musculus," which literally means "little mouse" in Latin</note>. The entire statue is clothed in these, destined for various uses of motion.

But because the gentle, living heat of the heart was being dulled by the thickness of its mass, **GOD** commanded that from that same florid arterial blood, the lung—by whose work the heart might be vivified and nourished—should be made. This lung, inflated by the great artery in which the voice is made, and which is branched and spread through the lung itself, would stir up the heart's heat and vivify it like bellows. Just as bellows push back a freely exhaling flame and force it to enter the pores of the wood to kindle it further, the lungs do for the heart. Therefore, by squeezing the veins, it thins the blood, expels soot and waste, as well as bloody sweat, and draws forth the venous blood for vivification; in dilation, however, it receives blood, and consequently its own increase.

# OF TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

<margin>
**n** Hence, a response is given to Galen, who thinks the pulse is not a voluntary motion <note>original: *arbitrarium motum*; motion governed by the will or "arbitrium"</note> because it is not stopped at the whim of the animal. A reason is provided for why it cannot be stopped: because it serves the immediate use of restoration, etc. Likewise, an animal cannot choose not to feel, not to imagine, and not to desire, and yet these acts are still considered voluntary.
</margin>

Likewise, the animal cannot command the pulse to cease, <gloss>n</gloss> for it would be commanding its own destruction. Indeed, when decay or soot <note>original: *fuligo*; in medieval physiology, this referred to the "smoky" waste products of the heart's internal fire</note> is generated within the body, or when there is undigested matter, the spirit itself makes the pulse larger, faster, and more frequent, so that it might expel the troublesome humor by thinning it, or remove some other harmful thing. This is what happens in a fever, which is surely an ignition of heat; it is the spirit fighting against an evil. For that reason, a fever is good in the same way that a war [for a good cause] is good. Finally, respiration, <gloss>o</gloss> because it is necessary for maintaining the fire of the heart (a function which water performs <gloss>p</gloss> for fish) and for kindling that same fire for the sake of generating spirit, never fails.

But because its use does not have as much absolute necessity as the pulse does, an animal can, by its own will, refrain from breathing for a little while. Thus, one who is intently thinking of something very desirable, or something very terrifying, does not breathe. But soon, desiring to restore the interrupted use, they draw in a great deal of air and emit a great deal in a single moment: and this is called a <gloss>q</gloss> **sigh** <note>original: *suspirium*</note>.

When the blood is too hot and there is a great deal of spirit in the heart, the breathing becomes large, prolonged, and slow: just as we are accustomed to blow for the sake of kindling a fire when it is large and great. But truly, when the heat is faint, diminished, and vanishing—as in summer, or after labor, or after running—

***

**n** Therefore, Galen's reasoning is empty. Likewise, even a fever is for the sake of something better, since it is a war against disease; and when this war is not undertaken by the spirit, it yields to the disease and the animal dies, etc. **o** Respiration does not occur for the sake of cooling the heart's heat, as pleases Aristotle and Galen, but for the sake of exciting and increasing it, etc. Nor would most wise Nature have foolishly placed so much heat in the heart that it required perpetual cooling. Likewise, we would not breathe in air to cool ourselves inside baths where the air is hot; nor would we do so in "cold" diseases. Likewise, in winter, when the heart is hotter, we would use more frequent breathing, which does not happen; rather, we use larger breaths for the sake of movement and fire, etc. Nevertheless, from the inhaled air, the heat becomes more abundant and less parching. (For heat is increased in soft matter, but in hard matter it is strengthened and burns); but it is not diminished, as Aristotle writes, but increased. Add also other uses. Nor should the Soul be seen (as Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman scholar</note> thought) as air breathed in by the lungs, warmed by the heart, and spread through the viscera—even though it *becomes* the Soul, that is, the spirit, and is the quickener of vital heat, as Lactantius Firmianus <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325) often called the "Christian Cicero"</note> well said. **p** Fish do not need inhalation to carry in native heat to vivify the body and generate spirits. For their spirit is retained by the water and pushed back so that it does not exhale. Nor are they endowed with such robust heat that it generates soot, and therefore they have no necessity for respiration. **q** A consumptive <note>original: *phthisicus*; someone suffering from a wasting disease like tuberculosis</note> sighs so that they may compensate for many interrupted movements with a single motion.

...[if it is] impetuous, respiration becomes small, short, and frequent, lest a great breath scatter and extinguish the heat. Indeed, it is frequent so that it may suddenly restore what has been gradually stirred up but not shaken out—just as we are accustomed to blow lightly on a fire when skillfully lighting it, taking away its time to fade by the frequency of our breaths, but avoiding the chance of it scattering by the smallness of the breaths. Yet indeed, the animal can take up or pause the movement of the nerves of the entire machine at its own will. For that movement is not for the sake of restoring the **spirit** <note>In this context, "spirit" refers to the "pneuma" or vital heat—a subtle, gas-like substance that Campanella believed animated the body and mediated between the soul and the flesh.</note> so immediately that the body would fail without it; but for the sake of carrying the body wherever there is a need to flee or pursue inconvenient or convenient things, and to accommodate the use of the animal life: which, once done, it requires rest.

For (as **Active Wisdom** <note>Campanella often uses "Active Wisdom" (*Sapientia activa*) to refer to the divine or natural intelligence that designed the functional structures of living beings.</note> used to say), since an animal is composed of a spirit that is perpetually mobile and celestial, and of a body that is inert to movement and terrestrial, it must necessarily now move and now stop its movement, for the benefit of both. For by continual rest the spirit would wither; but by continual movement the body—composed of various parts, some thin and some blunt—would be dissolved.

<margin>
**r** Movement does not come from the soul unless the soul itself is mobile. For it does not give what it does not have, nor (as **Aristotle** thinks) does imagination alone produce heat and cold, and from these, dilation and constriction occur.
</margin>

Therefore, the **spirit** <gloss>r</gloss> is carried through the internal ligaments of the muscles and nerves (which are composed of many threads, packed together and full of spirit, so that if they had only one wide pore, the spirit would be disconnected by a bend and cause pain); wherever it gives an impulse, it also gives movement and drives the body.

And since it needed to be moved in various ways for various uses, it was granted (at the command of **Wisdom**) a mass supported upon bones: which, originating from the head, are divided into 34 spiny **vertebrae**, <term>vertebrae</term> <note>The individual bones of the spine.</note> embracing <gloss>f</gloss> and embraced by mutual hollows, recesses, protrusions, and processes; and continued by a surrounding membrane [to the] **marrow** <note>original: *medulla*; here referring to the spinal cord.</note> infused within them, led down from the brain through a hole common to them; and joined by certain intermediate cartilaginous appendages, by which the animal might more easily bend forward and backward.

*For it cannot be that imagination itself, being neither hot nor cold, produces heat and cold, especially at the same time—as when someone dances in choruses and simultaneously bends and unfolds the joints. <gloss>f</gloss> But the middle vertebra among all is received on both sides, but does not receive those contiguous to it. The vertebrae are also bound together by the membrane surrounding the marrow infused in them, and by cartilaginous appendages grown between them, both so the animal may better bend and turn without dislocation of the bones and without interruption.*

<margin>† An animal does not need an immobile part to move, like a fixed center, as Aristotle <note>Campanella frequently debates Aristotle’s "Physics," specifically the idea that for anything to move, something else must remain perfectly still.</note> writes; since the heart, in which he himself founds all motions, moves more than all other parts. It does, however, need a support upon which to rest its heavy mass. Therefore, it firms one foot on the ground to support the mass while it moves the other. But the spirit <note>The vital heat or "pneuma" that acts as the driver of the body.</note> moves outside the body by itself without the service of an immobile part; such a part is necessary now not to produce motion, but to sustain the weight, which the spirit cannot move all at once.</margin>

Seven pairs of nerves originate from the head, along with the spinal medulla <note>The spinal cord.</note>, which, produced from each individual vertebra, creates a pair of nerves in each for the sake of binding the body together and moving it. From the end of each joint where they are immersed, ligaments emerge through openings prepared for them by the counsel of Wisdom <note>Campanella attributes the perfection of anatomy to "Active Wisdom" (*Sapientia*), his term for the divine architectural intelligence of nature.</note>. These ligaments are filled with flesh so they do not dry out, and with veins so they may be nourished, and arteries so they may be vivified, and fibers and nerves so they may be moved; when they are tightened, they extend the portion of the joint into which they are inserted. But when they are dilated, they bend that same joint, and thus the movement of the animal occurs. †

*He [Aristotle] is also wrong in thinking that winds rely on immobile mountains to move. For they blow also from the sea and plains. A man, however, cannot move a boat unless he rests upon the earth—not because the immobile earth gives motion, as Aristotle says (referring even to the sailor and the heavens), but because while he pushes the boat forward, he must have his heavy body rest elsewhere. If he rests on that same boat, then it happens that he moves it forward with his hands but backward with his feet; thus, since the force pushing forward is equal to that pushing backward, no motion occurs. But if a dove clinging to the air, and not a boat, were able to pull it, then a boat tied by a rope to the mast would move it, not leaning on an immobile thing—which is also what the winds do when swelling the sails, and so on. Therefore, etc.*

This occurs after the exit of the fetus from the womb.

But before that time, it emits urine through another opening into a channel running to the navel, from which the exiting urine creates a pool between the first and second membranes by which the entire statue <note>original: *statua*; Campanella’s term for the physical structure of the human body</note> is contained and surrounded. Wisdom <note>original: *Sapientia*; referring to Divine Providence or the intelligent design of Nature</note> provided for this so that the salty humor <note>Urine</note> exiting from the genitals would not burn or ulcerate the tender flesh. For this same reason, Wisdom provided that the fetus be nourished without producing stool. Therefore, the maternal blood <note>original: *sanguis foemineus*</note> does not pass through the stomach and the intestines, where feces to be expelled would remain, but runs immediately through the navel into the liver. There, being "cooked" <note>Refined by heat</note>, it is distinguished from the wastes—which are yellow bile, black bile <note>original: *melancholia*</note>, ashy waste, and whey—from which the aforementioned vessels are made and nourished. The purer part of the liver serves the constitution of the heart and the flesh; indeed, it is purified more by the mild heat of the fetus than it was in the mother.

Therefore, the useful part is then spread from the liver through the veins to nourish the whole body. Furthermore, in the heart there are two fountains <note>The ventricles</note> perpetually full of blood; if food were lacking, these would remain as a sort of granary for the nourishment of the spirits of the head. These spirits are never the same, for some exhale away, while others are made to replace those exhaling. They are like the flames of lamps: they always appear to be the same, even though some parts disappear, driven into invisible thinness, while others are continually generated from the oil supplied through the activity of their own heat. The same happens to the portions of the body, though more slowly: some parts exhale away, while others succeed them from food. While the new parts are more numerous than those lost, growth occurs; when they are fewer, decrease; and when they are equal, a state of stability.

# F. TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

Therefore, the Spirit, foreseeing through Wisdom <note>original: *Sapientia*; referring to the intelligent design of Nature or God</note> that its nourishment from the umbilical cord would fail, prepared for itself a mouth, intestines, an esophagus, a stomach, and other internal organs attached to these vessels for the purpose of processing <note>original: *distillandi*; literally "distilling," here referring to the breakdown of food</note> future solid foods, transmitting them where needed, and cleansing them. For this reason, 

<margin>
α The powers of attraction and expulsion are not different faculties, as Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD) was the most influential physician of antiquity; Campanella often critiques his theories</note> believes, but are the actions of the same spirit performed in different ways or with different instruments for the sake of self-preservation, as is evident.
</margin>

α the veins, arteries, intestines, and all the bladders are woven with transverse, straight, and oblique fibers for the purposes of transmitting, attracting, and retaining. The **arteries**, however, were made more solid, composed of three layers <note>original: *tunicis*; literally "tunics" or coats of tissue</note>, because they were to hold the more refined blood. The **veins**, in turn, were made of two layers, as they contain the thicker blood. The **nerves**, however, were granted great density so that they might resist motion and contain the thin spirit <note>The "vital spirit" or *pneuma* was believed to be a subtle, heat-like substance that traveled through the nerves to animate the body</note> so it does not escape; they consist of many threads, in each of which the spirit is held, rather than in one broad pore; for in such a pore, the spirit would not have been able to exert much force for movement—which would be necessary for seeking food—easily and without harm. 

So that it might be stimulated to seek food after exiting from the womb, Wisdom prepared a channel from the spleen into the stomach. When the stomach is empty, a melancholic <note>original: *liquor melancholicus*; Black Bile, one of the four bodily humors, thought to be acidic and cold</note>, acidic, and somewhat bitter fluid flows into it. When the stomach is stung <note>original: *mordicaretur*; literally "bitten"</note> by this, it is constricted and affected by a feeling of discomfort; to remove this, it desires to be filled. Likewise, when blood is lacking, the veins themselves suck from the stomach and wrinkle it further. This type of troublesome sensation creates the appetite for food and is called **hunger**:

<margin>
β Hunger is the appetite for solid things for the sake of filling, while thirst <note>inferred from context of heat/dilation</note> is for the sake of dilating, since the sensation of constriction is one of cold. Nevertheless, cold foods are often desired after hot ones have been consumed, which have already dilated the stomach.
</margin>

β This is a passion of constriction, and a desire for solid things that may fill, and usually for warm things that may dilate. When the stomach is full, such a great abundance of spirits runs to it as is sufficient for industriously heating the food. But as all the spirits rush together to be refreshed, the stomach is greatly heated and dried out because of the new ignition occurring within the food. Therefore, when it seems to the spirit that it is not gaining anything but rather being harmed if it expels the burning food—since it feels itself being increased and helped by it—it desires only to quickly extinguish the heat; nevertheless, cold foods are often desired after hot things are taken, which have already dilated the stomach. Likewise after fever, and labors, etc. And thus drinking is required, which nevertheless ought to be warm of its own accord for the sake of cooking <note>original: *coquendi*; in early modern medicine, "cooking" or "concoction" refers to the heat-driven process of digestion</note> and transmitting the food, and strengthening nature, as my excellent and most learned friend **Antonio Persius** <note>Antonio Persius (1542–1612) was an Italian scholar and follower of the philosopher Bernardino Telesio, whose naturalistic views deeply influenced Campanella</note> has rightly written. See our *Apology* for him.

For moisture easily receives heat and carries it into the solid parts of the food, softens it, melts it, and then easily transports the cooked material through the vessels to where it must be directed for the sake of nutrition. This desire is called **thirst**; and therefore, the appetite for moisture is satisfied by water, wine, or another liquid, whether hot or somewhat cool. This liquid removes the accidental burning of added heat and makes the heat itself more abundant. For this reason, food is better digested <note>original: *coquitur*; literally "cooked," but used here for the physiological process of digestion</note> and is more easily transferred when incorporated into that same liquid, having been made capable of spreading due to the slipperiness arising from the drink and food. However, if there is no accidental burning, a hot drink is more useful and contributes more to all functions. Nevertheless, after eating, a slightly cool drink is beneficial for the sake of gathering the heat and compressing the vapors so they do not rise upward into the head.

<margin>
Thirst is not always a desire for cold, as Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) whose theories dominated medieval science</note> thinks, but is always a desire for moisture, which certainly quenches thirst more effectively. This is true unless roasted meats and foods seasoned with excessive pepper and salt are eaten, which cause a burning sensation; in that case, there is a need for something cold to extinguish the accidental heat, and something moist at the same time to increase the spiritual heat. For moisture is easily heated and easily turned into spirit, as is evident in water thrown onto lime <note>Quicklime reacts violently with water, releasing heat; Campanella uses this as an analogy for how moisture fuels internal "fire"</note>; thus, it increases the abundance of heat and diminishes the strength—that is, the burning—of the fire. Telesio <note>Bernardino Telesio (1509–1588), a philosopher who emphasized sensory experience and heat/cold as primary forces; Campanella was a follower but often corrected him</note> also erred against his own doctrines by saying that thirst cannot be quenched except by a cold liquid. This is true regarding accidental thirst caused by pepper and salty things, but not regarding natural thirst. For nature would not have placed such heat in the stomach, nor superfluous heat in the heart (as he says regarding the use of breathing), if it required constant cooling. Likewise, the Lapps <note>original: *Laponenses*; the Sami people of northern Scandinavia</note> use hot drinks by the fire, and they quench their thirst and live longer than we do; the ancient Greeks and Romans did the same. See Antonio Persio <note>A contemporary philosopher and friend of Campanella</note>, and our *Apology* for him, and the *Questions*.
</margin>

It also saw to it that a small piece of flesh <note>the uvula</note>, like a little column, hangs from the throat to distinguish voices. These voices are produced when, with the lid open, the inhaled air exits during the constriction of the lungs and the windpipe to purge the heart and form the voice. ## Recapitulation concerning the Organs in detail.
### CHAPTER XI.

<margin>
The older philosophers spoke only of the organs of the sensing Soul: they said nothing about the organs of the Power-principle and the Appetite-principle, but merely assigned the heart as the seat for Power and the liver for Appetite, and wrongly created three souls, whereas the soul is essentialized <note>constituted in its very essence</note> from these primalities <note>The "Primalities" are Campanella’s core metaphysical concept: Power, Knowledge, and Love/Will</note>. Their doctrine has been hidden until now. See *Metaphysics* and *Questions*.
</margin>

From what has been said, it is clear that the entire body is the dwelling and organ of the Soul. But since the Mind is essentialized from the Power-principle, the Intellect-principle, and the Will-principle, and the spirit serving it participates in these primalities, their organs will be threefold. Some are formally **Potestatory** <note>related to power, action, or physical capability</note>, others **Sensory**, and others **Appetitory**; for materially, these three are present in every organ, because the Primalities are the same in reality and exist mutually within one another. Therefore, just as cognition is generally in the spirit and has special ways of knowing which it exercises in special organs toward special objects—as it sees through the eye and hears through the ears—so too are Power and Appetite in the spirit; and it exercises special ways of Powering and Appetizing in special organs toward special objects.

# ON PHYSIOLOGY, CHAPTER XI.

...senses and sense organs, as many as there are sensible things. First, the Animal Power <note>original: *Potentiæ animali*; the power of the "anima" or soul that governs movement and sensation</note> is opposed by the weight of its own body, which pushes it downward against its own effort; it is able to conquer this through the organic erection of the bones. Next is the pouring out and dissolution of the body's composition, and of the humors and spirit <term>spirit: a subtle, vaporous substance that was believed to flow through the nerves and vessels to animate the body</term> contained within it; against this, the Power-principle <note>original: *Potentatus*; Campanella's term for the soul's governing capacity</note> uses the organic structure of the vessels. Also, the loss of life within the vessels: for fire, when enclosed, is extinguished; when left out, it escapes. Just as containment stands against the fire escaping, so Ignition <note>original: *Accensio*; the "lighting" or maintenance of the vital heat</note> through breathing stands against its extinction. Also, the rawness of things that must be turned into the substance of the body attacks the animal; it overcomes this by cooking <note>original: *coctione*; "coction" is the traditional medical term for digestion, viewed as a heat-based process like cooking</note>. Also, the smallness of the forces and the body; which it overcomes by the augmentative power <note>the power of growth</note>. Also, injury from external objects; to which the Power-principle of fortification is opposed. And finally, it wastes away through idleness; the motive force <note>the power of movement</note> counters this. Lastly, it is killed by enemies, against which it is aided by the fighting power. Finally, there is Death, which the Generative power remedies <note>Campanella views reproduction as the soul's way of overcoming individual mortality</note>.

## *On the Supporting Power.*

### ARTICLE II.

**T**he mass of the flesh and the rest of the solid matter pulls downward continuously. The manner of being able to support this machine is achieved through the bones, without which the upright body does not stand. For the softer parts are not so united and condensed together that they can avoid bending. Bones, however, are hard because of the union and coherence of their parts. Neither do the bones support the body unless the spirit is within. For a corpse collapses; and even if the bones were not distinct <note>referring to the joints or individual segments of the skeleton</note>, it would still collapse when pushed by any force.

The power of supporting, therefore, is in the spirit dwelling in the nervous system—by which the bones are bound together—and in the spinal cord <note>original: *spinalem medullam*</note>; this spirit, with the help of the bones applied to it, holds up the "statue" <note>the body</note> and bends it against things pushing it, so that it is aided by its own weight against opposing weight. Likewise, tightrope walkers <note>original: *funambuli*</note> are balanced on both sides by weight so they cannot fall; and where a fall is imminent, they throw their weight to the opposite side. Thus weight, which is the cause of falling, becomes the cause of standing through the ingenuity of the soul, which opposes that weight to the part that is being pushed or falling.

# F. THOMAS CAMPANELLA

The object of this Power-principle is weight <note>original: *pondus*; in Campanella’s philosophy, weight is a "sense" or "appetite" of bodies to seek their natural home</note>. Weight, moreover, is the weighing-down of any thing away from what destroys it toward what preserves it. And for that reason, all bodies betake themselves toward the center of their own system, where they are simultaneously preserved and united, just as all parts of an animal contribute to the union and commonality of their own animal, and they abhor a divided vacuum. Thus, Lunar bodies strive toward the Moon, Saturnian bodies toward Saturn, and so on, just as Earthly bodies <term>Telluria: objects belonging to the Earth</term> strive toward the Earth with a like conspiracy <note>original: *conspiratione*; literally "breathing together," a Stoic term for the harmony of the universe</note>.

Those things, however, which on earth "weigh" upward—such as wood rising from the bottom of water, or even more forcefully an inflated wineskin, which cannot be held back from weighing upward to reach the air—and fires from any place, and winds moving obliquely to the sides, all tend toward their like, and are driven away by what is unlike them, or flee from it. For although all our local bodies, insofar as they are bodies, seek the center of common union, nevertheless those which are more massive and more unified weigh downward more, since they have a greater right to union; such as gold, lead, and earth. The natural appetite of these is stronger and less subject to injury. Fine <note>original: *tenuia*; thin or less dense substances</note> things, however, have less "body," and therefore yield to the stronger. For if you throw earth into water, you see the water rise upward, having been expelled. So it is with other things, insofar as they are corporeal.

But since they additionally have various forms, and various appetites and modes of sensing, for that reason they also have other movements. Fire, therefore, tends upward because it is hot. Heat, moreover, comes from the Sun, and it snatches away the "corpulence" it has conquered toward the Sun, as is indicated by the vapors flying around that were recently detected on the solar disk <note>a reference to the telescopic discovery of sunspots, which Campanella interprets as matter being drawn into the sun</note>; for it is not right to think that they emerge from the Sun, which is most pure. Nor is it right to think that fire overturns the earth and buildings with such force simply because it is being pushed out by stronger things; since even within cavernous places, where it is not being squeezed, it destroys everything, nor can it be held by any machines to keep it from flying out.

Furthermore, any amount of water, no matter how small, is not heavier than a piece of wood, and yet the wood moves upward in it; because it has air united within it, which weighs more toward its own totality <note>the atmosphere</note> than the thickness of the wood weighs toward the earthly affinity. If, however, the wood becomes ash, you would see the ash sink step by step to the bottom of the water; so too with coals and pumice stones, which float because of the air in their pores...

### ON PHYSIOLOGY, CHAPTER 11.

contained within them; for if they are broken into tiny pieces, they are submerged. This is the reason why both snow and ice float. We also see that chaff, once you have pressed the air out of it and made it thoroughly wet, as well as rotting wood in water from which the air is being separated, seek the bottom. This is also why old ships are heavier <note>Because the wood has become waterlogged, displacing the air that previously provided buoyancy.</note>. Therefore, every body that is denser and more **unified**, even if it is of the smallest quantity and does not weigh as much as a millet seed, is submerged in something less unified, unless it is held up by something more abundant and far less unified. For even thin plates of gold, ebony, and lead float if they are concave and full of air; likewise if, on their flat surface, they are held by **hooked air** <note>original: *aëre hamato*; a reference to the contemporary theory that air particles had tiny hooks or shapes that allowed them to "grip" surfaces</note> within their own tiny pores. However, if drops of water are oiled, they fall, because they are separated from the air that was holding them.

In its own **kindred element** <note>original: *cognato*; referring to a substance's natural environment, like water for water</note>, nothing feels heavy, because it does not weigh against the medium in which it exists. For this reason, wood is heavy in the air, but in water it loses its weight because of the included air, which prevails. In the wood of the holm-oak and ebony, however, this air does not prevail <note>These woods are denser than water and therefore sink.</note>. A corpse floats when its humors begin to turn into air; a living person sinks, unless they prevent it by spreading their hands and using motion to stop the submersion, in the manner of fish and birds. A man swimming at the bottom of the water does not suffer from the weight of the water’s mass—a weight he could not sustain in the air—because the parts of the water are held together by their own kinship, and they have nothing to weigh against.

<margin>※ Thus also the parts of the body do not weigh against other parts, but the whole weighs downward against the air; and it is sustained upright by the **spirit**.</margin>

But where this downward inclination is absent, every tiny force sustains and moves any body in any direction; as perhaps happens in a vacuum outside of the planetary systems. You could likewise move a ship in the sea with a single hair, if it were shaped so as not to be stuck in the "holding" water, and if no wind were present. Is it any wonder, then, if beyond the limits of the world, **blessed bodies** <note>original: *beata corpora*; likely referring to celestial or glorified bodies in a state of grace, which were thought to be weightless</note> are not heavy?

An animal also sustains not only its own **machine** <term>machinam: the physical structure of the body</term> with its bones, but other weights as well upon its head, hands, and shoulders; this it could not do without the support of bones. Fish called "soft" <note>Campanella refers here to cartilaginous fish or perhaps cephalopods.</note> use cartilage in place of bones. Crabs have these in a more crust-like form on the outside; snails likewise have them on the exterior. Eels and serpents use only a spine and the small bones of the head, since they have prone and crawling bodies, not tall and large ones that would require harder supports. Sardines sustain their weight with their fins and the water.

FRIAR THOMAS CAMPANELLA

### On the Power of Containment.
#### ARTICLE III.

The substances and the structure of the body are contained in vessels not by sense and appetite alone, but also by the power of the vessels and ligaments. Every harder and more unified thing contains within itself that which is less unified, lest it burst apart. Thus the nerves contain the **spirit** <note>original: *spiritum*; in 17th-century physiology, "spirit" or *spiritus* was a subtle, vaporous substance that traveled through the nerves to facilitate movement and sensation</note>, having been drawn and dried out from the brain, which is the seat of the spirit. For the thinner a thing is, the sharper it is for penetrating and the swifter it is for escaping. Thinner things are therefore held by tougher and more unified vessels. Blood and the other humors are held by veins and organs that are less dense, because they are less prone to escape and less thin than would be required to leak through cracks. But the arteries are denser, because arterial blood is more "spirited" <note>original: *spiritalior*; arterial blood was believed to contain more of the vital "spiritus" than venous blood</note>. 

The previous discourse taught the construction of these parts. The whole **statue** <note>original: *statua*; Campanella uses this term to describe the physical body as a structural shell or framework</note> contains the organs within; and it is itself contained by the framework of the bones, the binding of the nerves, the filling of the flesh, the tightening of the membranes, and the enclosure of the skin. 

But how is the spirit contained? For if it shut itself in the nerves of its own accord, like we do in a house, the nervous structure would be a protective vessel, not a containing one. If it is there by some fate or from God, it will be a fortification and a prison, contrary to the power of the inhabitant, and not the organ of its own strengths. This must be debated in the **Metaphysics**. But God said: this is the nature of the Living Being from the beginning, which, without containing parts, dissolves. Therefore, the power of the spirit is unified and strengthened in these vessels, and is defended; for this reason, we attribute a particular use to its power through these organs. The true containing power of the spirit is that by which it holds all vessels to their uses, and itself within them. The object is the thing contained, but the spirit is not "the thing contained," except insofar as it is the servant of the Mind or of God: in all other things, it is the spirit that contains [the body].

# On the Vital Power.

## ARTICLE IV.

The power of heating, transforming, and moving exists in every limb where the **spirit** <note>original: *spiritus*; in this context, the subtle, vaporous substance believed to animate the body</note> is found; it does not have a specific organ of its own, just as the cognitive power lacks one in its second primality <note>A term in Campanella’s philosophy referring to the primary principles of being: Power, Wisdom, and Love</note>—and in these things lies **vitality**. 

But because life is the preservation of all parts in their duties and mutual uses—all of which are performed through spirit and heat—and because the spirit is constantly breathing out, and heat likewise is extinguished if it does not breathe out, the spirit required an organ to kindle and enclose that heat. Through that retained heat, the spirit could perpetually generate itself, since it is perpetually exhaling. The spirit accomplishes this with the **lung**, through which it breathes air into the **heart** as if through **bellows** <note>original: *folles*; a common metaphor for the lungs in early modern medicine</note>. It generates spirit from the blood and retains the heat so it does not slip away, thrusting it into the heart and the arteries; and, to prevent it from being extinguished, it kindles the heat that is held within. 

For life is fundamentally the persistence of the **innate heat** <note>original: *caloris nativi*; the internal warmth considered the source of life and movement</note> at its root, although the total life consists of the preservation of all parts in their existence. This power of the spirit resides in the fibers of the lung; the organ is the lung. Its method of use is inflation—drawing air in by means of a **vacuum** <note>original: *ratione vacui*; the belief that air rushes in to fill empty space to prevent a void in nature</note>—and exhaling by means of opposition. Its work is kindling, ventilating, retaining, and the generation of spirit. Its object is the vital heat in the heart.

# On the Power of Concoction.

## ARTICLE V.

For conservation, it is necessary to apply those things which may be converted into the substance of the animal; this is achieved through **concoction** <note>original: *concoctione*; the process we now call digestion, which ancient and medieval doctors compared to "cooking" food in the stomach</note>. Concoction occurs through heating. Heating is a property of the whole spirit, which has the power to pour itself out even where its own substance does not flow. For heat is capable of amplifying and multiplying itself, since it is the first of the physical powers and a principle derived from **Divine Power**.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "Vital Power," specifically focusing on the process of concoction (digestion and transformation) and how heat acts upon the body's substances. It transitions from the general nature of heat to the specific physiological processes of the stomach and liver.</meta>

...so it is created. Although simple heating does not require a specific organ, **concoction** <note>original: *coctio*; in early modern medicine, this refers to the "cooking" or transformation of substances by the body's internal heat, most notably during digestion</note> does, since it only occurs within an organ suited for that specific type of heating. For concoction is the heating of a solid body until it reaches a new state of existence, pre-defined by art or nature for a specific use. For example, dough is cooked in an oven until it reaches the state of bread, which is useful for human nutrition. However, if it is cooked more, it becomes "burning" rather than concoction, because it exceeds its utility; if it is cooked less, it remains "rawness." Concoction is divided into **Roasting**, **Boiling**, and **Frying**.

<margin>What concoction is.</margin>

<margin>Roasting and Boiling.</margin>
**Roasting** <note>original: *affatio*</note> occurs at a certain useful degree in the air. **Boiling** <note>original: *elixatio*</note> occurs in water, though also caused by fire. Water, aided by heat, penetrates the solid and incorporates its fatty and less-dense parts into itself; this is why the substance of meat or herbs is found in the broth. If they are boiled excessively, only the dregs remain.

<margin>Frying. See the "Questions against Aristotle."</margin>
**Frying** <note>original: *frixio*</note> occurs in a fatty liquid, which penetrates more deeply and lubricates the thick parts, but consumes the thin and watery parts as if they were enemies. Wine consolidates the firmer parts and dissolves the thin ones, yet it does not "fatten" the parts as much as vinegar does.

<margin>What the concoction of ripening is.</margin>
Therefore, when the fruits of trees ripen, they are "cooked" by the Sun through roasting, and by their own internal heat within their moisture through boiling. For the thick parts are softened and expanded, and this is what it means to lose "rawness." In the same way, an abscess "cooks," and so does food within the body. There is a triple concoction of food:

The **first** is **chylification** <note>original: *chylificatio*; the process of turning food into "chyle," a milky fluid</note> in the stomach, by which the thick parts are softened and incorporated into liquids. The liquids do not evaporate but remain to prepare the solid parts to become fluid; simultaneously, they become similar to the intestines in color and consistency.

The **second** is **sanguification** <note>original: *sanguificatio*; the process of turning chyle into blood</note> in the liver, which draws the softer parts of the chyle through the **mesenteric veins** <note>original: *mesaraicas*; the veins connecting the intestines to the liver</note>. From these, the liver draws out the thin parts and separates the dregs into the **spleen**, and the "foams" into the **gallbladder**. Those parts which are suited to the nature of blood become blood and turn red, just like the liver; for the liver retains those things which are most like itself and which it is able to assimilate into its own nature.

<margin>Aristotle errs in thinking that every animal adopts what is sweet to itself from food. See the "Questions."</margin>
Hence, from the same food, a dog emits one kind of waste and a pig another, because the liver of a dog retains certain parts for itself, while the liver of a pig retains others. Indeed, a pig eats human feces because there are still parts within them useful to its own nature, though no longer useful for human blood. Similarly, every limb has the power of turning the portion of blood distributed to it into itself, and gifting it with its own color and consistency, since the heat has been established at the specific degree of that limb’s life, and so—

...just as it established that thing, it changes the added parts into its own nature. It does not attract anything except what is suitable, just as the veins of metals do in the earth. This continues as long as that heat remains in its proper proportion <note>original: *symmetria*; referring to the balanced ratio of heat required for health</note>, and provided that what is applied to it can be converted without being the converter itself, as will be explained in [the book on] Medicine. Whatever turns into dregs or thinness is not suited for that specific body part, but perhaps for others in the same animal or for other things entirely. For nothing in nature is useless, as its Creator has said.

In the heart, there is a **spirit-making power** <note>original: *vis spiritificativa*; the capacity to transform physical blood into the "spirit" or pneuma that carries vital life through the body</note> derived from the thinner blood, and a power to thin the thicker blood that is to be sent into the arteries. Even bones know how to turn marrow into their own substance through their own **internal boiling** <note>original: *elixatio*; a metabolic process where nutrients are "stewed" into solid tissue</note>, as do nerves and every other part. Therefore, this conversion does not happen through heat alone—like simple cooking—but through **consensus** <note>original: *consensione*; a harmonious agreement or "sympathy" between the parts of the body that allows them to work together</note>. Otherwise, the same parts would be separated out in everyone. For heat always draws out the thinner parts. **Suppuration** <note>original: *suppuratio*; the formation of pus in a wound</note> is also a form of concoction, which draws superfluous or damaged moisture toward the nature of separable waste, just as some waste transforms into worms because of a **Symbol** <note>original: *symbolum*; a shared likeness or correspondence between substances in early modern science</note> of separation. Therefore, the goal of concoction is conversion—not just through evaporation, but through a substantial change in existence. The organs involved have been described elsewhere.

## *On the Augmentative Power.*

### ARTICLE VI.

It was necessary for the animal to increase in body and strength. This is achieved by heat, which is capable of multiplying itself and thinning the things taken into the body into spirit. This is the power of a limb or organ that does not give out more than it attracts and generates; and this cannot happen except through an organ. Indeed, **weak heat** increases growth more than **strong heat** does; for weak heat is more suited to the organs and changes the ingested food into the proper **temperament** <note>original: *temperiem*; the specific balance of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness unique to an individual part</note> of its member. Strong heat, however, is so powerful that it converts even the limb itself into a thinness that evaporates away; thus, the more such heat is increased, the more destructive it becomes. For the decline seen in old age does not arise from a mild, governing power, but from a robust heat that draws the body toward an external nature and diminishes it as a side effect. Therefore, although the **augmentative power** <note>original: *vis auctiva*</note> is weaker according to general nature, it is not so in this specific case. Its own growth is, by accident, the destruction of its own subject [the body]. For by its innate power, it desires this growth, even if the animal—once the power was placed within the body—might desire something else. It is a wonder how...

## Concerning the Motive Power.

### ARTICLE VII.

The motive force resides in the spirit <note>original: *spiritus*; the subtle, vaporous substance that Campanella believed carried life and sensation through the body</note>, in which it is hot; it resides in the spirit's thinness, by which it is obedient to motion. For thick, heavy things weigh downward, which is why even a hot coal cannot be moved as easily [as the spirit]. This force is found in the appetite, insofar as motion is directed toward specific objects. It is found in the cognitive faculty, insofar as it is performed with skill and method, rather than recklessly like the shaking of other objects. It is found in the "potestative" <note>original: *potestatiuo*; relating to *Potentia* (Power), one of the three fundamental principles—Power, Wisdom, and Love—that Campanella believed governed all being</note> faculty, insofar as it flows from the power of God. And this principle comes from God as the first creator; from the brain as the seat of the spirit and the origin of the organs; and from the organs—namely the muscles and joints—insofar as they were adapted for the movers so that movements could occur in this manner. And since motion, insofar as it is an execution, pertains to "operation" <note>the actual performance of a task</note>, its full declaration awaits us at the end. <margin>Against Epicurus</margin> Wisdom laughed at those who claim motion arises from a spirit full of void <note>original: *vacuitas*; a reference to the Epicurean view that movement requires a vacuum or empty space between atoms</note>, since void cannot be admitted within a spirit that loves and knows itself; nor can such motion occur except recklessly and without a purpose.

<margin>Note on Putrefaction and wasting against Aristotle and Galen; see [my books] *Questions* and *Medicine*.</margin>
The object of motion is that which can be achieved through actions; but in the strengthening of the body, its object is the ventilation of the spirit, the increase of heat, and the separation of dregs <note>original: *fecum*; the metabolic waste products left over after digestion</note>. Other benefits will be discussed elsewhere. For now, it is clear that movement alone brings vivification <note>the process of making something alive and vigorous</note>, and this is health. For the body wastes away in idleness. Wasting <term>original: *marcor*; a medical term for the shriveling or "withering" of the body's solid parts</term> is the dissolution of solid matter caused by heat retained in dregs that have not been expelled, which then acts against its own subject through them. For those parts that the heat does not separate, the dregs pull the other parts toward themselves; and while the heat acts upon them, it simultaneously relaxes the useful parts, and thus "tabes" <note>a progressive wasting away</note> and putrefaction occur. These are discussed elsewhere. Another type of wasting is "incineration" <note>literally "turning to ash"</note> resulting from excessive heat that even consumes the solid matter, and from labor. This is provided for during sleep by the restoration and resting <note>original: *feriatione*; a "holiday" or cessation of activity for the spirits</note> of the spirits.

# *On the Protective Power.*

## ARTICLE VIII.

The organs with which the spirit <note>original: *spiritus*; in Campanella’s philosophy, this is a subtle, warm vapor that acts as the primary instrument of the soul, flowing through the nerves and arteries</note> fortifies itself and all its parts so they are not harmed by the external things they encounter, are the skin, the flesh, and the hair—as was said previously when we explained their use and essence. In animals <note>original: *brutis*; literally "brutes" or non-human animals</note>, one must add scales, feathers, and shells <note>original: *cortices*; can refer to bark, husks, or hard outer coverings</note>. In place of these, Man prepares for himself armor, clothing, and shields through the power of the mind. This protective power resides in the spirit, both in its capacity to manufacture [defenses] and to resist. Hence, the art of building houses and cities emerged after the art of clothing. The object [of this power] is that which is harmful, just as light is the object of sight. For everything harmful is intercepted and avoided by the aforementioned organs.

Every injury is either a **perforation**, by which the continuity of the blood and spirit is broken; or an **incision**, by which even more of that continuity is dissolved; or a **contusion**, by which the structure and its material are shaken; or an **intemperance** <note>original: *intemperies*; a technical medical term referring to a disruption of the balanced "temperament" or qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) of an organ</note>, by which the symmetry, form, and degree of existence are destroyed; or a **fracture**, by which the supporting structure is affected.

Perforation is caused by a body that is harder and sharper acting upon one that is less hard and less sharp. This cannot be countered except by something harder. Hardness arises from the union of matter and the density of a solid. Things that are less hard have their parts less united. Therefore, they suffer a "disaggregation" <note>a breaking apart of their unified pieces</note> from the harder object. For this reason, every more-solid thing breaks apart that which is less solid: thus, falling water breaks the air, and a small stone, or earth, or wood pierces through water. Harder earth pierces soft earth, because it has more parts united together. "For a plurality is stronger, and more powerful when united," said the eternal Omnipotence <note>a reference to the divine principle that unity grants power</note>.

When, however, something thin and less hard penetrates a solid, it does not do this by [raw] power, but because it finds holes—even invisible ones—within that solid, and by its own slenderness it can be thrust into them. Thus, air penetrates walls and wood through cracks; Fire, however, penetrates everything, because it is thinner. But fire does not break things down unless it is increased by the particles of the thing being broken (as happens in wood), or by an abundance of heat, the nature of which is to increase itself. And so, fire liquefies gold and all the hardest things—not insofar as fire is a "body," but insofar as it is hot, and capable of converting thickness into absolute or partial thinness. Against a sharp body, the sharpness of fire does not prevail, but rather another harder sharpness; indeed, any hardness [prevails], provided it is...

...angled shapes even more so, because the blow slips off and is supported by two sides. Roundness follows this, which is almost entirely composed of obtuse angles. It opposes many parts against a few; for when a round shape is opposed to a sharp striking object, it leans upon other parts placed behind and to the sides at the same time, all resisting with a unified force. Therefore, an egg compressed at its ends <note>original: *fastigiis*; the tips or apexes of the egg</note> within the hollows of the hands cannot be broken, but it can be broken on its sides. For this reason, Omnipotence <note>A common Renaissance term for God as the supreme architect</note> gave a round shape to the bodies of plants and animals for the most part. He added sharp points to the offensive parts, and to those which must pierce air or water, such as the keel of a ship; this is evident in the beaks and breasts of birds, and in horns. All bones are round unless they have a need to receive one another <note>i.e., at the joints</note> or to protect something else. The walls of cities, if round, resist blows more effectively because of many parts coming together, and they can be defended by fewer men, because the inner circle is smaller.

A flat surface is less suitable for avoiding perforation, because the part that is struck is aided by fewer surrounding parts. But a concave surface <note>original: *curua*; in this context, Campanella refers to inward-curving or "hollow" shapes</note> is the worst, because more parts are shaken by fewer forces, and they are prone to yield, collapsing under their own weight due to such a shape. Nature abhors this shape in animals, and where it exists, she has fortified it with hair, such as under the armpits, the buttocks, and so on. From this it is clear why a large body, if it is sharp, pierces more even when pushed with less force, and if it is blunt, bruises more than a small body—unless it is moved against its natural inclination. For a large body is aided by its weight if moving downward; likewise if moving obliquely, because the striking front is driven forward by the mass of many parts. And when it is impelled from a distance, its forces are increased by the motion and by its inclination, even when moving obliquely; for the outer parts of a wheel move more than the inner parts when both are pushed by the same force at the same time.

An incision is similar to a perforation, but wider. The hardness of the hide <note>original: *corij*; referring to skin or leather</note> and a tenacity joined to it are opposed to both, so that the body is not broken. For friable <note>brittle or easily crumbled</note> things are the worst of all for protection, since they lack tenacity, like a dry-stone wall. Tenacious things that are slightly soft yield to a blow and are not cut, unless a long sharp point, such as a sword that has pierced the surface, is drawn across in the manner of a saw <note>original: *ferræ*; likely a transcription error for *serræ* (saw)</note>. For then the blade enters the opposing small furrows with its tiny teeth and tears them. Hair helps in this regard, because the blow and the intrusion of those tiny teeth slip past it; therefore, Wisdom <note>God</note> [protected] the pores with soot from...

# PHYSIOLOGY, CHAPTER XI.

...made from transpiring heat, Nature coated the body with hair to guard against external heat and cold, and likewise against cutting, piercing, and bruising blows. A contusion <note>original: *contusio*; a bruise or internal injury caused by impact</note> occurs when a non-sharp body strikes another non-sharp body. The thicker it is and the more parts it has, the more parts of the structure it shatters—especially the hard parts, because one part holds onto another strongly, and while it is shaken, it shakes those it embraces. Stones are weak against concussion; wood and wool are better, as are metals. Yet, every harder metal cuts and strikes a less hard one. Although gold is heavier than iron, because it is more unified and does not allow for pores, it is nevertheless not harder. For iron, when its pores are excluded, is more unified, just as a pumice stone is more solid than water if you do not account for its pores being full of air. Therefore, just as a pumice stone pierces water, so iron pierces gold. The power to resist a contusion opposes hardness mixed with viscosity. Union happens through the similarity of parts, as in gold, or from conformity; it is not merely due to hooked shapes in the atoms <note>Campanella is critiquing the ancient Epicurean theory that atoms were held together by physical hooks</note>. For they would dissolve suddenly if they were not held together by consent and love—and therefore by power.

Nature gave shells <note>original: *crustas*; carapaces</note> to crabs; but so that they might move, she added joints. To man she did not give them, so that he might be bent and raised in any direction, and so that his senses would not be hindered. She gave spines to hedgehogs, but these are held at the base by nerves for the sake of movement. She gave scales to fish to guard against strikes, so that the body might be flexible and protected at the same time. We have made the breastplate <term>lorica: a piece of body armor, such as a cuirass</term> in imitation of these.

Traction or distension tears the body, like an incisive blow; compression bruises it, like a contusive blow.

An unhealthy imbalance <term>intemperies: a medical state where the primary qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) are out of proportion</term> occurs when heat is increased or diminished. The form of its existence in matter changes through robust heat, which dissolves the parts, draws out the thin elements, and dries the rest. Alternatively, it occurs through freezing cold, which extinguishes the moisture and heat, rendering the remaining parts as if scorched and dried. Flight <note>original: *fuga*; moving away from the source of the imbalance</note> resists both of these, as do warm clothes that defend our innate heat against the cold, and smooth, thick garments made of leather against the heat. For heat does not pierce with a single sting, but with innumerable ones at once—not as physical bodies, but in a physical manner. For those things which exist incorporeally and are mobile penetrate the body without injury or occupying space, such as an Angel; but those things which are immobile...

From these facts, it is established that the whole of Nature consists of four parts: the craftsman <note>original: *opifex*; referring to the Divine Artisan or Creator</note>, the base, Matter, and the active instruments.

## On the Fighting Power.

### ARTICLE IX.

The fighting power <note>original: *Pugnatiua vis*; the defensive or aggressive instinct</note> does not take just any harmful thing as its formal object, but specifically hostility, which we endure from living beings, and especially from rational ones. For an enemy is properly defined as one who, out of intentional hatred, or contempt, or for their own advantage, prepares to kill or afflict us. Hunters are "enemies" to wild beasts—though the beasts are not "enemies" to them, except in a backward sense—simply so that the hunters may be nourished by their flesh. Against an enemy, the irascible power <note>the "spirited" part of the soul associated with anger and self-defense</note> of the Power-principle <note>original: *Potestatiui*; one of Campanella's three "Primalities" of being: Power, Wisdom, and Love</note> arms us. Weapons, therefore, are the organs of this power given to almost all animals: to some, horns; to others, sharp claws and long spines; protruding teeth; stingers; or a beak. 

To man, however, these are denied. For human nails, which merely cap the extremities so they do not split or get injured, are useful to him only for that purpose. And while the Almighty has gifted those creatures deprived of weapons with agility, like hares, or wings, like doves, for their safety, He denied even these to man. Instead, He committed man to Wisdom. By his brilliant participation in Wisdom, man was so endowed that he might surpass fish in swimming, birds in flight, elephants in strength, lions in violence, and hedgehogs and shellfish in their armor. For this reason, God added the hand as the organ of weapons and of all instruments. 

And so that men would not fight against one another except with reasons, He denied them innate weapons. They will instead prepare for themselves a staff for support; houses and vessels for containment; spices for the vital spirit; pots and fires for the digestive power <note>original: *concoctiuo*</note>; friends and servants for the power of growth <note>original: *augmentatiuo*</note>; horses and ships for movement; and clothes and breastplates for protection. Finally, they will craft spears, swords, and cannons <note>original: *bombardas*; early firearms or artillery</note> for offense.

All these same instruments are given to plants, with the exception of the lung. The sense organs—which we will discuss shortly—are denied to them, except for a proportional sense of taste. Desiring faculties <note>original: *Appetitoria*</note> are present in plants proportionally. The reproductive faculty is present in both plants and animals. But concerning its specific power, we shall speak in the section on Desires.

<summary>Campanella argues that while animals are born with physical weapons like claws and horns, humans are born "naked" so that they must rely on Wisdom and the use of their hands to create tools and technology. He categorizes various human inventions—from houses to cannons—as extensions of natural biological powers.</summary>
