->*On the external senses in general.*<-

->CHAPTER XII.<-

->ARTICLE I.<-

Since an animal is an indeterminate Spirit <note>original: *Spiritus*; for Campanella, this is a thin, warm, and mobile physical substance that inhabits the body and serves as the seat of sensation and movement.</note> enclosed within a thick, organized mass that is shaped and arranged by the spirit itself in various ways, and divided into continuous and connected parts as was necessary for the primary preservation of the spirit and its secondary home <note>the physical body</note>: it must be able to move. It moves to acquire the things by which it is preserved and to flee from the things by which it is destroyed. Because this movement cannot happen without a great deal of sensing, the spirit indeed feels and knows things by touching them, while it is changed by them, to such an extent that it can discern the powers of the things that are changing it.

<margin>a Sensation does not occur through "information" <note>The Scholastic idea that the mind takes on the "form" or essence of an object without its matter.</note> as Aristotle thinks.</margin>
<margin>Nor is the sensing power a "pure potentiality," but a being in act, which is not affected by a being similar to itself; hence our spirit neither sees the air nor hears its sound. etc. Therefore, sensation happens through physical change.</margin>
However, because the spirit within the animal does not sense every single thing that acts upon it, but only those things that reach the point of actually transforming the spirit itself—which acts as the Judge of these transforming things—a we therefore say that sensation is the **perception of an impression** <note>original: *perceptionem passionis*; "passion" here refers to the act of being physically affected or "suffering" an impact from an external object.</note>. Nor does it happen through "information," as if the spirit had to be transformed into the very substance of the object and take on the object's form. If that were so, the spirit would literally become the Sun when it senses the Sun, or the Earth when it senses the Earth, or a table, a stone, cold, and so on. In truth, it is enough that the spirit be changed not in its entirety, but in some part of itself, since it is a physical entity; and even then, not totally, but only slightly. Thus, ordinary sensation is not to be totally transformed—which would mean to die—but to be affected just a little bit, and then to discern, from the judgment of that small impression, the remaining powers of the object acting upon it. For this reason, when one feels a little of the fire's heat and moves closer to it, the spirit is transformed more by it and soon judges its overwhelming power. And so, sensing seems to be mixed with the **judgment** of the thing being sensed. This sensing is diffused throughout the whole body, but it is located especially in the "nervous skin" <note>likely referring to the membranes or the nervous system</note> originating from the skin of the head, which is full of the sensing spirit in different ways in different parts. For this reason, the sense of hunger and thirst is in the stomach; the sense of Venus <note>sexual desire or sensation</note> is in the genitals; and in other parts, the senses of other objects.

<summary>Campanella defines sensation as a physical "impression" where the internal spirit is slightly altered by external objects, allowing it to judge their properties. He rejects the Aristotelian view of "information," arguing that sensing is a physical interaction rather than a purely formal or abstract one.</summary>

# FRIAR THOMAS CAMPANELLA On Touch.

### ARTICLE II.

<margin>a Since hair and bones draw nourishment to themselves and desire it, they must necessarily feel—some more, like the teeth, others less, like hair; but the blood is entirely overflowing with sensing spirit. Hence Aristotle is mistaken in denying sensation to these parts.</margin>
The sense of the spirit is one, diffused throughout the whole body along with the spirit <note>original: *spiritus*; the warm, thin, mobile substance that mediates between the soul and the physical body</note> within the nervous and fibrous substance, and it is entirely called **Touch**, because sensation does not occur unless the sensible object touches the sensing portion. But *a* hair, nails, and bones seem not to feel because, on account of their solid dullness, they do not communicate their sensation to the spirit reigning in the head. Yet teeth show themselves to be gifted with sense. Likewise, if parts of this kind are nourished, secrete nourishment, rejoice, and desire, they must necessarily feel. So too, if blood leaping from a vein is touched, it does not communicate that touch to the internal spirit; for since it is fluid, it is separated from the spirit and does not return. This, however, was fitting, so that the animal might be spared many unhappy sufferings <note>original: *passionibus*; in this context, "passions" refers to things the body passively experiences or undergoes, such as pain from injury.</note>. Therefore, if the spirit is preserved in its being by the thing it touches and is increased—since the thing is similar to it and beneficial to its bodily organ—it is delighted, just as it is affected by gentle warmth or tasty food. But if *b* it is changed into a thing dissimilar to itself, it feels pain. Thus **Pleasure** and **Pain** are found in all sensing things that either benefit or hinder their own preservation: the former as the sense of a preservative good, the latter as the sense of a destructive evil.

<margin>b To be suddenly and not gradually transmuted into a dissimilar Being is pain. To be transmuted into a similar being while being simultaneously increased is pleasure.</margin>
Heat and cold are the objects of touch *per se* <note>original: *per se*; in their own right, or essentially</note>: for they pour themselves out forward, backward, upward, downward, and everywhere in every direction to act upon the sense by themselves. But *c* material properties <note>original: *passiones*; qualities inherent to matter</note> such as weight, hardness, largeness, smallness, a stone, a table, and other beings shaped diversely out of matter and constituted by heat, do not act except through heat itself; therefore, they act *per accidens* <note>original: *per accidens*; accidentally or indirectly, rather than through their own active essence</note>. Indeed, a heavy thing does not pour out its heaviness as heat pours out heat, but it weighs down when placed upon the sense. We feel the coldness of a stone *per se*; but we feel its hardness *per accidens*—that is, by squeezing it and experiencing it resisting and not giving way; from which we then argue that it is a stone, if we are not made certain by our eyes.

<margin>c Wetness and dryness are not sensed *per se*, since they are passive rather than active qualities, except by the intervention of other active ones; rather, their fluidity or stability is sensed through pressure, and a judgment is made about them; for even motion itself is sensed *per accidens*.</margin>

<meta>catchword: Likewise</meta>

<summary>Campanella defines touch as the universal sense of the spirit and identifies pleasure and pain as the spirit's perception of its own preservation or destruction. He distinguishes between active qualities like heat, which are sensed directly, and passive qualities like hardness, which are sensed only through resistance.</summary>

I say the same regarding other sensible things, which do not change the forces of the spirit—which is heat <note>Campanella views "spirit" as a warm, material substance that flows through the nerves; therefore, its primary "force" is heat.</note>—but rather change its disposition, which is the thinness and refinement of its particles within its whole. These are sensed not by a simple sense, but by a discursive sense <note>original: *discurrente*; a sense that "runs through" or processes information rather than just receiving it passively</note> at the same time, because they are mixed with objects that are perceptible in themselves, rather than acting on their own. The spirit does not perceive all degrees of heat, but only those exceeding its own; it does not feel those equal to it, since like does not act upon like, given that every action occurs for the sake of assimilation <note>The Aristotelian principle that a thing is changed by something different from it until it becomes "like" the thing that changed it.</note>. In this case, it is already assimilated.

->On Taste.<-

->ARTICLE III.<-

<margin>
a. Taste is not a form, as Aristotle thinks—an image—but an active force with its own proper mass; if this force is in the elements, it must also be in the compounded things. Aristotle is therefore mistaken in producing tastes from elements that have no flavor. Nor is taste born from the dry and the moist as he thinks—that is, bitter from the dry and sweet from the moist—and then the other intermediate vapors being composed from those two extremes. For very moist liquids, such as wine, oil, and others that are salty and bitter, would not be found, which is entirely false. Likewise, there are dry beings that are sweet, such as Sugar. Taste therefore follows the native heat, not the mixture of dry and moist. Since, moreover, taste is an active quality, while dryness and moisture are passive qualities; and bitter and sweet are neighboring tastes, not extremes.
</margin>
The discerning Spirit, realizing that in the outer parts of its instrument <note>The "instrument" refers to the physical body.</note> that are touched, it could not experience sensation (on account of their being solid) except from the strongest things; and because the spirit itself is not preserved by those parts alone; Likewise, many things do not appear to be what they actually are. For Water and wine, and many other things, are hot with native heat <note>term: *calor nativus*; the "native heat" is the internal, life-giving energy of a substance, as opposed to external temperature.</note>, yet they seem cold to the touch because they are occupied by external cold, which binds and dulls the native heat. Therefore, the spirit prepared for itself an entrance reaching all the way to its own self in the tongue, where it senses not only the external and dominant nature of the thing to be eaten or handled, but also its internal faculties with which it was endowed at its birth. And this happens through taste, *a* which is surely a moderated and tempered heat implanted in things, together with its own mass and not merely poured out alone (as the heat of a fierce fire is poured out) to act. Penetrating with this mass into the cavities of the spongy tongue, it not only changes the heat of the inhabiting spirit, as strong heat is accustomed to do, but also the disposition—that is, the thinness—of the spirit. Therefore, the spirit itself senses whether the food within is beneficial...

<margin>b *Like does not experience an increase in strength from its like, but only an increase in quantity; although strength soon follows. Furthermore, it suffers no destruction except by accident, as it draws its like to itself from the subject in which it was entangled.*</margin>
That which is insipid <note>tasteless</note> is similar to our own natural heat *b*, and therefore it does not act upon us; for like does not suffer transformation from its true like, but only an increase in its quantity. All sensation, however, consists in transformation. When a fruit is first born, it is suddenly insipid, such as a plum; soon, having been slightly "cooked" <note>original: *decoctus*; referring to the ripening process driven by heat</note> by its own heat and the heat of the sun, it becomes styptic <note>astringent or mouth-puckering</note>. When applied to the tongue, this flavor constricts it by filling and closing the pores with its abundant, undigested mass, changing the tongue very little with its own heat. Then, being cooked further, it becomes acid; for a great part of it has been thinned by heat, which, by penetrating sharply, as if tears the spirit apart. To avoid suffering this, the spirit gathers and draws itself together. Therefore, because of this flight of the spirit—and because where it reaches with its sharpness, it causes heat to exhale and what remains to be united—this flavor is well-suited for preserving what remains constricted from corruption. After this, being cooked even more, it becomes piquant <note>original: *puncticus*; a "stinging" or sharp flavor</note>; which is surely an acid that is becoming somewhat sweet, because the thick parts are now more digested, while the thinnest and sharpest parts have exhaled; the remaining parts have been rendered equal, their sharpness having been lost. Then follows the sweet flavor, when its parts have been heated more until they are reduced to a rich equality; therefore, it greatly delights our taste, since we flourish with a most tempered spirit. Sweetness has the power of liquefying the dry parts of the tongue, drying the softer parts, and wiping away the viscous parts, bringing them all to a balance.

<margin>c *Therefore, the bitter flavor is closest to the sweet, contrary to the opinion of Aristotle. For this reason, Doctors also forbid sweets to those with tertian fevers, because they are suddenly turned into bitter and choleric humor.*</margin>

If the sweetness of the thing exhales copiously and is turned into a liquid or fatty consistency, it becomes an **unctuous** <note>original: *unctuosus*; meaning oily, greasy, or rich</note> flavor. This is most suitable for nourishing fire; when placed upon the tongue, it dilates it with its mild power and thins it out, rarefying it so much that it brings on nausea. For this reason, an unctuous liquid mixed with vinegar creates a temperament that is very pleasing to the spirit: while one dilates, the other constricts. In this way, the dregs of oil are bitter because their sediment is bulky, which constricts the passages of the tongue, burdens the spirit, and saddens its thin nature by binding it; oil, however, is sweet, unctuous, and light due to the thinness and uniformity of its parts. Finally, if the matter is cooked further and reduced to a sharp temperament—all its portions being unfolded by the force of a heat that conquers uniformly—it turns into a burning or **acrid** flavor, such as pepper. But if it is then burned further and consumed, the remains become a salty temperament, ignited, which penetrates quickly by thinning and then immediately by constricting. Truly, because heat penetrates everywhere and carries its own substance with it, **Salt** is suitable for all dishes and foods; by its heat, it thins and disperses the thicker and poisonous parts, warms all the small particles, and consequently makes them flavorful. Salt is drawn out from all ashes by the force of fire and from burned earths.

There are also other nearly infinite flavors; but these are the better-known ones, which expand into the more or less salty, sour, sweet, and so on. Every species of thing is endowed with its own flavor, the best messenger of its essence, and a thing greatly necessary in Medicine. Moreover, the greater agreements and oppositions of things themselves are recognized from the similarity and difference of the flavors presented to **taste**, which is the most exquisite of the forms of touch.

<margin>d Because the Definition is the Epilogue <note>original: *Epilogus*; a concluding summary</note> of a science, we place it here after the matter has been investigated.</margin>
Flavor is therefore *d* the action of the **innate heat** <term>calor nativus: the internal heat believed to drive all biological functions</term> entering into the tongue with its own mass, changing not only the faculty but also the disposition of the **spirit** <term>spiritus: the subtle, vaporous substance that carries sensation and life through the nerves</term> within the tiny nerves of the tongue, its sensory organ of discernment. For this reason, things that are too hot or too cold have no flavor, because the excessive heat or excessive cold hides the action of the tempered innate heat in the flavorful matter; it forestalls it, just as the light of the Sun hides the light of the stars. Likewise, it transforms the powers of the **spirit**—

*e* The use of saliva is not to provide flavor to dry things, as Aristotle thinks, for things do not have flavor unless the dry is mixed with the moist at the same time. For it would have been necessary for the tongue to be given a dry solidity at the same time, by which even moist things might acquire flavor. He erred, therefore, in judging flavor to be a composition of the dry and the moist together, since flavor is found in purely dry things and purely in moist things. And since flavor is an active property, it cannot be composed of the moist and the dry, which are passive entities.

In the same way, the **pericardium** <note>the sac surrounding the heart</note> is a membrane encircling the heart, perpetually full of water made from the vapors exhaling from it, so that the heart does not dry out from its own constant movement.

...before the disposition; for this reason, frozen wine and excessively hot cakes do not reveal their flavor in the mouth. Likewise, unless dry food is broken into tiny bits, it does not reveal its flavor, because a blunt thickness cannot penetrate the "sponge" of the sense. Therefore, *e* nature sagacitously uses **saliva** <note>original: *sputum*</note> to soften dry food. This saliva arises from vapors exhaling upward from the stomach, which are prevented from proceeding further by the cavities of the throat, and are therefore condensed into water. This water, by its own heat and the air exhaled from the artery, is filled with thinness and becomes bubbly, as is visible. It keeps the tongue moist so that it is not shriveled or dried out by its movements, and so that food may be received and swallowed easily by its slipperiness. This was the first precept of the **Holy Monotriad** <note>Campanella’s term for the Divine Trinity of Power, Wisdom, and Love</note>, *f* that every superfluity and every evil should be turned to good use, just as has been said regarding foam, ash, dregs, and the serum of the blood.

# On Smell.

## ARTICLE IV.

Wisdom understood that while things to be tasted are admitted to the tongue, wicked and poisonous things could have brought about death or great evil; and that foods beginning to rot do not immediately lose their flavor, and therefore could deceive an animal into devouring them, and consequently falling ill. Furthermore, beneficial things at a distance or those hidden were not sensed, and the tongue—if drenched in bitter or other foul humors—would have infected the softened food with bitterness, and thus even a good thing could have appeared foul. For these reasons, Wisdom willed that there be another way of sensing things before they were admitted to the tongue. To this end, she fashioned the nose with two...

...with the nostrils, which through two passages sends air to the heart, and through a certain "spongy" opening <note>original: *os quoddam spongiosum*; likely referring to the ethmoid bone at the roof of the nasal cavity</note> would distribute the air and admit it into the brain for the sake of ventilation and for nourishing the **spirit** <term>spiritus: in early modern physiology, a subtle, vaporous substance that carries life and sensation through the body</term>. And together with the air, a thin and vaporous substance of things would enter, through which Nature judges the things themselves even before the judgment of taste. Therefore (Nature said), let there be a *sensorium* <note>an organ of sensation</note> of this kind looking downward, for the reason that from the earthly things by which an animal is nourished, a thin part continually exhales toward the *b* heavens along with heat. When this exhalation enters the nose, where the air of the native spirit is contained—if it increases and strengthens the spirit by being added to it and converted into it—the animal will understand that those beings from which such an exhalation is drawn are useful, and it will seek them out. But if it burdens and harms the spirit by overpowering it with an abundance of heat and weighing it down with a heavy thickness, the animal will turn away from it as something heavy and harmful. And so it was done. Therefore, smell is a certain more "spiritual" taste, because it does not admit a thick mass of food and other things, as the tongue is accustomed to do, but only a thin substance. Likewise, smell does not have its spirit enclosed in a nervous thickness like the tongue, but perceives from a distance, having its spirit free in the cavities in which it moves and is affected by odor and air.

*...and let it meet the nose looking downward, as Democritus said. b Aristotle wants odors to be made from non-odorous elements—meaning they would come from nothing—for he grants no being to that which he does not have. Likewise, many bitter beings have a sweet odor, such as incense, the lily, and many other flowers. Therefore, odor does not correspond to flavors, but is a thinner substance than flavors. Odor, therefore, arises from heat exhaling in a thin substance. <meta>This page continues the physiological investigation into the sense of smell. # FRIAR TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

Odors themselves are thin substances, namely vapors; for this reason, if the mass from which they are drawn out is rotten <note>original: *putrida*; referring to the state of decay or putrefaction</note>—since putrefaction occurs through an increase in the native heat, which then thins the solid parts of its own matter and, being made abundant, forces them to evaporate along with it—these odors are heavy, thick, and troublesome. This is because they overcome the heat of our own **spirit** <term>spiritus: the "vital spirit," a subtle substance believed to carry life, heat, and sensation through the body</term> with their own abundant and excessive heat, and by their thick mass, they weigh down the thin mass of the spirit itself. 

But if the matter from which they are drawn is lively and similar to us, the odors are useful and pleasant; and because they are turned into our own spirit, they strengthen and increase it. If very thin vapors are drawn from an excessively hot thing, they are displeasing, because they move the spirit too much and inflame it, and sometimes overcome it in heat and strength—especially when the spirit is faint and small. For this reason, the sharp odor of frankincense and pepper is bothersome in summer, when the spirit is diminished and small and easily overcome; but it is pleasant in winter, when the spirit is plentiful and victorious. 

The spirit is nourished by odors, but the other parts of the body are not, because those parts are thick and are nourished by thicker things. Thin things, such as odors, cannot become thick and pass into the substance of the body's limbs, just as they can be thinned out into the substance of the spirit, which is even thinner than they are. Therefore, when we sense an odor after labor and exhaustion, we are immediately revived <note>original: *refocillamur*; literally "warmed again" or "refreshed"</note>, because the thin odor is similar to our spirit and is suddenly convertible into it. We say that the portion of the spirit lost through labor is restored and created anew from the odor—what is commonly and quite aptly called "recreation" <note>original: *recreari*; Campanella is playing on the literal meaning: to be "created again"</note>. Clearly, a drink of noble wine immediately restores an afflicted person by its "spirituality" <note>the vaporous, alcoholic essence of the wine</note> and recreates the lost spirits.

The odor of some things is good and pleasant, but the taste <note>original: *sapor*</note> is actually bad, as is the case with lilies. Therefore, Nature does not rely enough on the nose alone, but resorts to taste at the same time. Taste discerns not only the thin matter of things (which can almost always seem pleasant and good) but also the thick matter. Likewise, in judging whether things are rotten, Nature does not trust taste, but recurs to smell. Thus, the knowledge of food is, by a wonderful reasoning, entrusted to two "witnesses" <note>smell and taste acting together to verify safety</note>.

Odors arise from things with a stronger heat than the spir-

### PHYSIOLOGY CHAPTER XII.

...our body, our **spirit** <term>spiritus: the "vital spirit," a subtle, vaporous substance believed to carry life, heat, and sensation through the body</term> standing above the nostrils, with the senses bestowed. Therefore, water emits a vapor, but not an odor to us, and just as it is tasteless to the sense of taste, it is the same to the sense of smell. There are also styptic <note>original: *stiptici*; astringent or contracting</note> odors, which as it were veil the spirit; and pungent ones, which penetrate slightly; and acidic ones, which prick; and sweet ones, which balance the spirit; and salty and bitter ones, which constrict; and finally, they induce effects similar to flavors, and therefore borrow their nomenclature from them. 

Yet not every odor corresponds to its own flavor: for a thin substance is often better than a thick one, as in things resulting from moderate heat and from matter well-overcome from a soft state, just as many flowers are. Likewise, in things composed of great heat and from dense matter well-overcome, such as frankincense and cypress, the vapor comforts and strengthens, but the flavor disturbs and afflicts because the burnt matter binds the tongue.

<margin>c Meats beginning to rot, such as those eaten by the Lombards <note>A reference to North Italian culinary habits of the time, which sometimes involved aging meat until it was "high" or slightly gamey</note>, emit a heavy and copious vapor.</margin>
However, for certain things composed of soft matter, the flavor is more useful and pleasant than the odor; for the odor exhales too copiously and consequently weighs down the spirit, as happens with meats <gloss>c</gloss> starting to rot.

The spirit is therefore nourished not only by the arterial vapor of the blood, and from the vapors of food raised up from the stomach through the internal nostrils, but also from the air entering the brain through the nose. Wherefore healthy, thin, and well-ventilated air keeps animals healthy, robust, and clever; but thick, impure, and sluggish air renders them stupid, heavy, somnolent, and sick. From this it follows that odors rising into the head from dried or soaked earth can kill; for the spirit is not able to convert them into its own substance, since they are very dissimilar to it and heavy; and when they are copious, they suffocate the animal spirit, or shut off the passages in which it moves, and fill the cavities where it resides, as happens at the cave of Acherusia <note>original: *antrum Acherusiæ*; a legendary cave in Bithynia thought to be an entrance to the Underworld, known for emitting toxic vapors</note>, and in locked houses, in which lamps are lit...

Nature is accustomed to purge the lower belly, the chest, and the head—the principal parts of the living composite—through these parts because they are porous, slender, and warm. This happens when the disease is strengthened internally and the spirit is not able to expel it.

By this same reasoning, the Venereal disease <note>original: *morbus Venereus*; likely referring to syphilis, which was often attributed to "foul vapors" in this period</note> arises from a foul vapor infecting the spirit, and consequently the blood, then pouring itself through the whole body and reducing it to a different condition and a foreign temperament. Therefore, so that such a plague is not nourished, it is appropriate to feed the patient with dry foods; for moist foods easily pass into the nourishment of a thick vapor, which winds its way through the body like a serpent. But dry food is turned into thin vapors, by which the harmful vapor is also thinned out. 

Likewise, in order to drive it outward, labor <note>physical exercise</note> is useful, by which the vapors of the spirit are thinned and exhaled, and the humors are thinned and forced to sweat out. For this reason, baths are also beneficial, especially those sprinkled with virtuous scents; for thus, as the vapors and bad humors depart, the body remains thinned and affected by a new temperament. However, since the body is then weak and diminished, it needs to be strengthened in the meantime by new spiritual vapors which may bolster the spirit and lead it back to its former state, fit for nourishing the body as it was before it fell ill. 

Therefore, from a single pestilential change in the spirit, the temperament of the entire body can be changed for the worse. To restore it, it is necessary to change the whole being—that is, the thin, moist, and solid parts of the animal. This is shown by fever: when it begins in the spirits, it is a one-day fever <term>diaria: a fever lasting only twenty-four hours</term>; it then passes into the humors and becomes a putrid fever; and from these it passes into the solid parts and becomes a **hectic** fever <term>hectica: a deep-seated fever affecting the actual tissues of the organs</term>. If you wish to cure this, you must change the entire temperament. Therefore, one must first look to scents and the air.

*in an anatomical dissection a man who had separate optic nerves, and yet did not see two things from one. For this reason, I assert that the nerves of the eyes are intersected so that they may come together as one, whereby the eyes cannot easily be separated to look at different positions of a thing without use, and with the detriment of knowledge. That man of Vesalius, however, held his eyes together by another means and by other restraints.*

* **d** *There is no common sense in the back of the head, as Aristotle thinks, bringing together the objects of the other senses so that knowledge may occur. From this it also follows that the sensory organ does not have a power of sensing that is its "form"; since he who thinks attentively, or sleeps with open eyes, sees nothing. Therefore, it is the same spirit performing all functions in all the sensory organs; those organs are not "informed" with sensing faculties, but rather that spirit is exercising various sensations. Aristotle, by positing an incorporeal sense, could never give an account of how it perceives two contraries at the same time. But at last, he said there is one "common sense," just as one center is the terminus of many lines. From this it follows that there are different paths of sensing, but one sense, as we say. But truly, how heat and cold, or white and black, can be received at the same time in this one indivisible center, he could never declare. Others say that such objects are diverse in the judgment, just as flavor and color are in an apple, but this is a lie. For they are not known by the sensing soul as being merely "diverse," but as "contraries"; otherwise the soul would never know they were opposites, nor would it judge them. Whence Alexander of Aphrodisias foolishly asserts that these contraries exist in nature, but not in the judgment of the one who knows; for in that way they would never be judged to be contraries. Likewise, each of us clearly feels himself being made cold by cold, and made hot by heat; therefore, the contraries are also in the sense; for thus in the sense, whiteness scatters the vision, and blackness gathers it. And therefore, Alexander of Aphrodisias soon contradicts himself and Aristotle. But these absurdities do not press upon us, as we posit a corporeal sensing spirit—not because it is simultaneously "informed" by the forms of heat and cold, or white and black, as they say. Nor indeed does our entire spirit become cold so that it may feel cold, but because a particle of it is changed by the cold part, and from that it immediately judges the power of the whole cold. Sense, therefore, is not a "pure potentiality" that receives all forms, but an "act"—a thin, mobile being in every way. And Alexander of Aphrodisias confesses that the sense of touch is not a pure potentiality, but a middle-point of tangible qualities—that is, of heat and colds, etc. Therefore it does not feel similar heats and colds and other qualities, but those that are stronger or weaker than its own. But he ought to have pronounced the same concerning the other senses. For the sense does not see air, nor does it hear, nor taste it, because it itself is*

The inner part of the cornea remained black because of the abundance of the many spirits <term>spiritus: vital spirits, a subtle "gas" or heat believed to carry life and sensation through the body</term> which went out to form the eyes. These spirits, making a forceful push as if to exhale, formed the cells of the brain, and at the same time rushed out to these types of globes, resembling pouches, as if burning them. Therefore, people with blacker eyes have thinner spirits resulting from their original heat, and they see nearby objects well, but distant ones with difficulty. Consequently, their eyes are not black but blue, even though the humors and the more or less cleansed and polished layers <note>original: *tunicæ*; the membranes of the eye</note> add much variety. These certainly serve the purpose of multiplying the light, which is the sole object of sight. The cornea is polished and translucent for the sake of admitting light. But because it is necessary to see in all directions, it was made round. It is hard, however, so that nothing can penetrate and harm the delicate craftsmanship; for this reason, the eyelids are stretched over it, made of a spirit-filled membrane and capable of sudden movement, by which the primary surface of the "mirror" might be protected at night, and when dust flies about or other things that might stain or infest it. From this, we ourselves have been taught to cover our mirrors with cloth. For whatever nature does within us, art—having arisen from nature—later imitates. Therefore, just as the spirit has fashioned its body from within like a lodging—much like a city whose citadel is the head, or like a palace whose highest chamber is the head—the membrane is the tapestry <note>original: *peripetasma*; decorative wall hangings</note>; the brain is a soft bed, so that the most delicate spirit, the lord of the house, would not be harmed by striking against the skull and the membrane. And there are two halls in the back of the head <note>original: *occiput*</note> where the spirit walks and conducts external business, and a posterior chamber in the back of the head surrounded by more solid bone, where it withdraws to think, distant from the senses; and there is a dining room, as it were, which is the lower chamber of the brain, where it consumes blood...

...feeds, which there in the net-like network <term>plexu retiformi: the *rete mirabile*, a complex of blood vessels at the base of the brain once thought to refine vital spirits into animal spirits</term>, as if upon a table, is transformed into the spirit itself. In this same way, the Spirit has built for itself a house and a city from the outside, constructing windows corresponding to the eyes, a bed for the brain, and chambers for the ventricles <note>the cavities of the brain</note>—one for taking counsel, one for walking about, and one for eating. 

The rest of the body was also the original model for things invented for human use. For a chimney corresponds to the mouth and esophagus, a cooking pot to the stomach, distillation stills <note>original: *alambicca*</note> to the intestines, a granary to the liver, a kitchen to the heart, and a sewer to the anus. In architecture, stones correspond to the bones, and lime or glue to the ligaments by which they are bound together. The inner mound of a fortification corresponds to the flesh, and the outer wall to the skin. Weapons are mirrored by claws and horns, pack-horses by the feet, and ropes by the nerves. Even ships were modeled after the chests of birds, and oars after their wings. Thus, one by one, all external things are very similar to internal ones; the Arts follow Nature, and Nature is traceble back to the Divine Intellect, from which it learns.

Returning then to our subject, we say that the eyelids were also made for the sake of concentrating the light. The hairs hanging from them <note>eyelashes</note> serve to join the upper and lower lids together and to provide warning if anything approaches, since they are easily moved by the slightest stir of air. The eyebrows exist to gather whatever enters through the "windows" <note>the eyes</note> so that it may be better perceived. The skin on the forehead was made muscular so that it could contract and expand, raising the eyebrows to better open the eyes, or weighing them down to better close them. The head was made without much flesh so as not to hinder the senses or weigh down the spirit; it is planted with hair to provide a light covering suited for sensitivity. These hairs are born from sooty vapors drawn out from the interior of the head and from other viscous wastes that harden as they exit the pores. Ultimately, whatever is made by necessity is also made for the sake of the "better."

<margin>e This excludes the opinion of Plato and the Mathematicians, who say that rays go out from the eyes to produce vision; and Galen, who says spirits are emitted; and Aristotle, who asserts that an "intentional species" <gloss>a mental likeness or image of an object</gloss> or the forms of things come into the eyes, and that light only serves the function of activating and preparing the air to receive such forms. But Aristotle's view is lacking, for it does not teach what power is so effective in a stone that it could transmit the "form" of the stone all the way into the eye: for neither light itself does this, nor the stone by its own power...</margin>

[Against] Epicurus, it is not a cone, because the spirit [does not go out] to alter the air <margin>to produce or send these images, nor does he teach how one might experience it</margin> so that it would issue from the eyes and seek an external meeting <note>original: *synodum*, a "coming together"</note> with the light itself; nor that it would fly up into the sky as far as the stars that we see; for if it were attracted by similar bodies, it would have flown into the sky and not returned, or it would be disturbed by the force of winds and rains.

He <note>Epicurus</note> strips the stone of its images <note>original: *simulacra*</note>, yet he does not explain what these images are, nor how they are made. Democritus erred less, saying that there are atoms <note>original: *atomos*</note> exhaling from every side of the stone in a specific configuration. For he at least provides some reasoning, though it falls short: for if vision were to diminish the surface of visible things, then an apple seen by many at once would lose its skin, and the winds would drive the atoms elsewhere, and thus the apple would not be seen. For this reason, other Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> invented an "active sense" as the cause of those species <note>original: *specierum* - the mental or visual forms of objects</note>, but they do not declare, nor do they know, what this "active sense" is. Nor do they say whether it remains within us (for then it would be the spirit described by Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon, the famous Greek physician</note>), nor whether it is outside us. Nor do they say how the species penetrate the eyes. Likewise, since these species are not real things, how can they announce things realistically? And since sensation for them is a being-acted-upon <note>original: *passio*</note> and a taking-on-form <note>original: *informatio*</note>, they do not say how the sense is formed by them. Nor do they say how this drawing-out sense <note>original: *sensus alitiuus*, likely meaning a sense that elicits or draws out information</note> can strip the stone of its image and bring it to us, nor why, if it is so powerful, it can only lead the image to the eye in a straight line, and not if it deviates slightly from straightness. But to us it is clear by what means light carries the faces of things, as has been shown by many examples, and how light, clothed in those faces, can enter through the cornea as far as the crystalline lens <note>the lens of the eye</note>, just as it leaps through other transparent things.

Nor is it possible for the visible thing itself to reach the eye. For all things would be thrown into confusion if all animals were rolling their eyes. Nor could they be contained within the eye, being of such great mass; nor could they be stripped of their own forms or colors, which they are not strong enough to emit into the eyes. Nor is there any power that can appropriately undertake the task of stripping them and carrying their faces into the eye. Therefore, it is better, he says, that light be the object <margin>f. Eyes possess a lucid spirit, but it is not its own light that produces vision, although—</margin> of the eyes, and that no thing be seen except light itself. For while light is seen, all visible things are seen, because light is most mobile, incorporeal, and multiplicative of itself, since it is apparent heat itself, a diffusive principle; and wherever it leaps, it leaps back in lines...

> *—although cats are thought to see at night by their own light, which can happen by their own abundant light going out, as we see, and illuminating the visible thing just as if it were poured out from a lucid spirit. Dark nocturnal animals have a thin spirit and an eye proportioned to the light of the nocturnal air. Tiberius Caesar used to see for a short time at night by his own light; I also see this way for the most part. But internal light does not therefore become the cause of vision, except insofar as it illuminates the visible thing, just as the light of the Sun does. The Sun can be seen by its own light, not directly, but reflected from things to the one seeing the things. For thus vision happens not through internal illumination, but that of the object.*

We perceive things outside of ourselves where they actually are; not because something flows out from us into them (for not even the swiftest light could stretch from us all the way to the stars; and if it stopped in the middle of the way, we would see things closer than they are), but because light comes from afar when it is weak, and from nearby when it is strong; it is this that provides a judgment of distance. A flat painting composed of various colors also appears to emit light to us in such a way that it seems not flat, but protruding and prominent like a statue. This happens because a weak reflection is cast from colors closer to black, and consequently, their position appears distant. But from colors closer to white (which is **dying light** <note>Campanella views white not as a primary color, but as light that has lost its vigor by becoming trapped in the "thickness" or density of matter.</note> held within density), the reflection is more vivid and not fully tinted; thus, their position appears close. For this reason, a painting perceived through these nearby and distant lights appears as a three-dimensional statue.

It was said previously that colors are created from light and darkness mixed within matter. Whiteness is the "dead" light itself, which is soon followed by a whitish color; then follow yellow, green, purple, blue, pale yellow, and finally dark brown. Therefore, very deep seas <note>original: "Maria profundissima"</note>, even though they are white, appear black because the light is diminished and fails within such a vast mass; consequently, the "face" of the matter appears more clearly. Less deep waters appear blue; the shallowest waters appear yellow, or are shown to be affected by the color of the ground beneath them. In the same way, mountains are seen as blue from a distance because the light rebounding from them toward us is sullied <note>original: "foedatur," suggesting the light loses its purity or strength.</note> and turns yellow across the great distance of the intervening mass of air. The sky also, although it is most white, since it is material and light is expanded by the Sun into its immense depth, eventually turns yellow and is sullied to the degree of blueness.

Not only is the distance of objects represented in the "mirror" of the eyes just as in other mirrors, but also the space of the air positioned between the sight and the visible object. For since air is a transparent mass, pyramids expand and rebound from every point and atom of it...

<meta>This page continues Tommaso Campanella’s exploration of optics, specifically moving from the internal anatomy of the eye to the geometric behavior of light rays as they form images in mirrors and define perspective. He uses the concept of the "visual pyramid" to explain why objects change size and orientation based on distance and the shape of the reflective surface.</meta>

### ON PHYSIOLOGY, CHAPTER XII. ###

...pyramids of rays <note>In Renaissance optics, the "visual pyramid" is the cone-shaped volume of light stretching from the object being viewed (the base) to the observer's eye (the point or apex).</note> multiplied by the multiplicity of light. Therefore, the parts of the air closest to the eye appear near, the distant parts appear distant, and the middle parts are represented in the middle. Thus, within a mirror, we see our own image on the surface if we approach it; but if we move back, we see our image as if it were deep inside, remote in the depths beyond the mirror, just as far as we ourselves are distant from it. As we move away or approach, we observe the image itself receding or approaching from the inner depth toward the outer surface, because not only is our face received in the mirror, but also the entire space positioned between us and the mirror. However, in **concave mirrors**, the upper part is seen as the lower, and the right as the left. This occurs because from the cone of the pyramid (whose base is our face and whose point is in the mirror), the rays are projected further and intersected <note>original: "intersecati"</note>, so that in the opposite part within, they form another base of a second, simultaneously created **inverted pyramid**. This second pyramid has the upper rays of the first as its own lower rays, and the right rays of the first as its own left, just as is clearly seen in a closed room when the sun enters through a narrow glass opening and the ray falls upon an opposite mirror.

Things that are large are seen as large because the light springing back from them, as if from a base, forms a large **angle at the eye**; conversely, small things are seen as small because they form a small angle, reflecting a narrow light that always converges toward the eye in the manner of a pyramid. For this reason, even large things are seen as small from a distance—not only those seen by reflected light, but even luminous things which are visible by their own power. Thus the **Sun**, the father of the Spirit <note>Campanella refers here to the "Vital Spirit," a thin, warm substance he believed was generated by the sun and animated all living things.</note>, the font of light, and the majesty of all bodily things, does not appear as large as it truly is:

*kk* Two different examples showing that the same appearance is produced by the motion of the sight and by the visible object. Therefore, he who is carried in a boat perceives the earth to be moving.

Indeed, [the Sun] is not seen, for the reason that its overwhelming light dissolves the humors <note>In ancient and Renaissance medicine, "humors" were the vital fluids of the body; here, it refers to the fluids within the eyeball.</note> of the eyes, and thins and consumes the spirits. A single mountain and the sky do not enter all at once into the very narrow eye, although they appear to be seen in a single vision. This is because the eye—and the visual spirit <note>Campanella refers to "spiritus visivus," a subtle substance then believed to travel from the brain to the eyes to enable sight.</note>—revolves with such speed that as soon as it gazes upon one part *k* of the mountain, it revolves to another, and suddenly to another, and revolves through the whole. The mind does not perceive that the eye has changed its own position, for it does not pay attention to its own native motion, but rather to the visible thing. Thus, when a lit stick *k* is moved in a circle, a circle of fire appears to the eye, even though the stick is in only one point of the circle at a time, and not in the whole circle continuously. From these things, it is clear that the same appearances are produced whether the object is moved or the eye is moved.

<margin>
*l* For those having thin and meager spirits, or a liquefied crystalline lens, spectacles are necessary, which make small things visible by compressing the light in place of a thickened crystalline lens. Sparse lenses <note>original: "specilla rara," likely referring to concave or specialized lenses used to disperse light.</note> that expand the light are suitable for those having many spirits and liquid humors; the former see better at night and from a distance, because a small amount of light is proportioned to them; but a great amount of light is suited to the latter, who have few and dense humors, and they see better by day and up close.
</margin>

Some things are seen by direct vision, like a lamp; others by reflected vision, as all things carried by tinted light. Others indeed are seen by refraction, like an apple inside a vessel full of water, which truly appears larger because the water multiplies its light—much like the spectacles *l* we acknowledge. The same occurs at the upper surface of the vessel, that is, where the light is refracted as it exits the water and enters the air—passing from a thick medium into a thin one. For this reason, an oar appears broken inside the water, because its distant part appears nearer due to the light being doubled in the water. Likewise, an apple inside a vessel full of water is seen at the surface by those looking from a distance, though if the water were poured out, it would no longer be visible to them.

Different light is proportioned to different animals: for some see in strong light, others in moderate, and others in weak light, such as nocturnal creatures, which perform long journeys by the light of the air and sky. Perhaps cats see at night by their own emitted light—not as it is emitted, but as it is reflected—unless perhaps they see just as the Sun does, which beholds all things by its emitted light.

### *On Hearing.*

### ARTICLE VI.

Then she added: Since the eye is not sufficient for knowing things—except those that reflect direct light to it, and not those that come from behind or from elsewhere—and likewise it senses nothing in the darkness, it is therefore necessary to craft other organs of sensation for the knowledge of things. And so she said: Air is so mobile that it suddenly expands from everywhere and in every direction into a sphere; therefore, when things are moved and strike the air, the impulse must be carried all the way to the animal itself. Let there be made, then, two organs in the temples to receive it, and let them carry its sound to the spirit dwelling within the head. 

And behold! The head is pierced at the temples, and from the tender bone it sends out dry cartilage, like a bone, shaped into several channels, spirals, and windings. It is expanded outward into the air, but gathered at its beginning into a certain cavity, where it could easily be moved and suddenly collect sound into itself, and through those passages take it inside and admit it to the center of the spirals. There, a small drum <term>Tympanum: The eardrum; Campanella describes it as a membrane filled with "spirit."</term> remains, upon which stands a small piece of flesh like a hammer <term>Malleus: One of the tiny bones of the middle ear; Campanella uses the Latin term for "hammer" to describe its function in striking the eardrum.</term>. When this is struck, it simultaneously beats the drum more or less, according to whether it is struck more or less by the external air. Thus, the spirit coming here through the auditory nerves—which are made from the brain, extended and hardened, and expanded into the drum—[perceives]...

<meta>This page continues Campanella’s discussion on the mechanics of sensation. Having previously established the "spirit" as the active agent of the soul that perceives through the organs, he now shifts from the eye to the ear, explaining how the spirit interprets the motion of air as sound.</meta>

[The spirit] perceives sound—that is, the motion of the air—and discerns the magnitude, smallness, slenderness, and thickness of the objects striking the air, according to how it is more or less beaten. By the diversity of the shapes of this motion, it recognizes the quality and force of the mover; and through multiplied experience, it learns what and of what kind each mover is. It avoids very loud sounds, because they drive it violently into the hollow of the head and condense it, and therefore harm it, since the spirit is itself rare <term>Rare: In Renaissance physics, "rare" means thin, subtle, or expanded—the opposite of dense. The vital spirit was thought to be a very thin, vapor-like substance.</term>. It also avoids very sharp sounds, because it is penetrated by their edge, torn, and divided; a thing very troublesome to its continuity. But it delights in sounds similar to its own native motion; for the nature of the spirit is mobile—it is always moved, and if deprived of motion, it perishes. Therefore, it delights in motion as its own proper operation, by which it is preserved in its being. And because sound invites it to motion (since sound itself is motion perceived by this sense), and consequently to its own preservation—because it helps it to act and move itself according to its nature—it therefore greatly delights in Music proportioned to itself.

<margin>Pythagoras correctly wrote that the celestial motions produce Harmony. It is not heard by us because it is ordinary and supernatural. But we feel unusual sounds, yet not those smaller than the motion of our spirit, but rather those exceeding our ordinary state. The noise of inferior things innate to us, and the thickness of the air, hinder us, etc.</margin>

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 41. <note>original: "Eccl. 41." This likely refers to the order of the world or the names of things as described in the Book of Sirach.</note></margin>

There should seem to be no doubt that the whole World is a Harmony. For everywhere in things there is motion, and all motion, while it occurs, is called sound. It seems reasonable that the Heaven also moves harmoniously, and that all things reverently agree with their Maker—whom all also adore in their own way—and that it delights His most divine ministers. But we perceive the heavenly sounds not at all, because we do not sense those sounds in which we were born (since they have become similar to us, and "like is not affected by like" <note>original: "simile a simili non patitur." This was a standard philosophical principle: sensation requires a contrast or a change. Constant stimuli become "invisible" or "inaudible" to the senses.</note>). For this reason, pharmacists do not sense smells well <note>They are desensitized by constant exposure to herbs and chemicals.</note>, nor do cooks sufficiently crave feasts, by whose smell they are nourished. Nor do those dwelling where the Nile, falling from on high, produces a great noise, perceive our accustomed voices, since they are used to other louder or innate sounds. So also millers are somewhat deaf. Nor do we perceive the perpetual motion of the air as we are carried in a circle, except when we place a hand to the ear; for then the air, by striking the hollowed hand (which is unusual to us), moves the spirit itself in an unaccustomed rhythm. We also sense less the humors contained within our body, nor the digestions and separations of food...

<summary>Campanella explains that hearing is the spirit's perception of moving air and argues that the entire universe exists in a state of "Harmony." He justifies why we cannot hear the "Music of the Spheres" by explaining that we are so accustomed to the constant motions of nature from birth that they become imperceptible.</summary>

### ON PHYSIOLOGY, CHAPTER 12.

...their similarity with the parts in which they lie, and because of habitual contact. However, when water enters, or food, it is felt. And if the humors <term>Humors: The bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) whose balance was thought to determine health and temperament.</term> are alienated from their own usual temperament, they produce unusual passions and sensations in us. Just as, therefore, those who are under water perceive the sounds of the air less, and those who have their own sounds do not perceive foreign ones, so too we, accustomed to our own disturbances under this thick air, can hardly see the celestial motions, and much less can we hear them. <note>Campanella is referring to the "Music of the Spheres," the ancient Pythagorean idea that the planets produced a divine harmony as they moved, which humans cannot hear because it is constant and we are accustomed to it.</note> Let us acknowledge, therefore, that it did not please Eternal Wisdom for there to be any discord of sounds in the universe. The whole is therefore Music, composed of all the consonant tones and semitones. 

But for us, not all voices make Music, because we are particular <note>meaning: finite or limited</note> beings, and we are endowed with a warm spirit that does not rejoice in every violent motion as the Sun does, nor in a sluggish one, as water rejoices only in slow motion; rather, a tempered motion is proper to us. We rejoice in those motions which are not very dissimilar to our own internal motion, but slightly more vigorous, so that we may be stirred toward strength and fullness. From these gentle motions, therefore, the human spirit devised a gentle Music, using the magnitude of our pulse <note>The author suggests that the human heartbeat is the natural foundation for musical tempo or "tactus."</note> as the measure that regulates the quantity of musical sounds.

<margin>b Aristotle, overcome by the truth, does not deny that sound is a real entity by which the auditory power is moved; for this reason, he is forced to set aside intentional species and the incorporeality of sense. <note>original: "species intentionales". In Scholastic philosophy, these were non-physical "forms" or images that traveled from an object to the mind. Campanella rejects this, arguing sensation is a physical "touch" or impact on the spirit.</note></margin>

Sharp sounds penetrate the spirit and strike it with sharp angles; <insert>b</insert> therefore, when they are violent and shrill, like little bells or the cutting of cork, they disturb us too much. Deep sounds, however, strike the spirit with blunt angles and a great deal of air, as if driving it through a flat surface inside the head. And if they are too strenuous and powerful, they disturb the spirit too much by condensing and disrupting it, like the sound of cannons and massive bells. 

Therefore, it is neither the overly deep nor the overly sharp sounds that create human Music, but the moderate ones. When these are composed together, some strike the spirit with a straight edge, while others strike it with a flat face, as it were; they fan, amplify, cleanse, and strengthen it. Therefore, the spirit is flooded with pleasure, since pleasure is the sensation of what is good. Now, "good" is that which preserves; conversely, Pain is the sensation of what is bad; and "bad" is that which destroys the thing for which it is bad—for it is not bad for everyone. Thoroughly taught by such natural instinct, the spirit discovered the use of sounds in battles and in temples.

Because of this, the spirit, having gathered entirely in the head to enjoy the Music that preserves it, grows drowsy; and this is what sleep is.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of how sound—and thus music—interacts with the "vital spirit" of the listener. ### ON PHYSIOLOGY, CHAPTER XII.

...like a bell or a great oak beam. Hard and thin objects produce high-pitched sounds because their parts, when struck, are bent backward slightly by the blow and then suddenly snap back to their original position. Or, they expand and stretch out, striking the air again as if with a point, just like a glass cup. If such a cup is touched while vibrating—even if it is not hanging freely—it does not give off a sharp sound, because it cannot stretch out during its reflection from the initial bending into the air; instead, the sphere of its returning motion is terminated and hindered by the object touching it. Thick objects, because their parts do not bend independently of one another, strike the air evenly as if through a flat plane. One part does not return to strike the air without the others, since they possess a solid continuity. For this reason, thick <term>strings|the Latin "chordae" refers to the strings of musical instruments</term> among the <term>lyres|the Latin "fides" is a general term for stringed instruments like the lute or lyre</term> produce a deep sound; when one part of the string is touched, all parts of that same string follow the same motion because they are well-compacted together. Since these parts are quite large, they move a great deal of air simultaneously. In contrast, slender strings move very little air and do not strike all parts of it at once, because one part of the string bends easily without the other, as they are not held together with such solid density. Dry things produce more sound than soft things; therefore, strings made of bronze drawn into wire produce a louder sound than those made from the intestines of animals <note>original: "intestinis animalium" — This refers to "gut strings," the standard material for musical instruments like the violin or lute before the common use of steel.</note>, because a dry thing does not yield to the air in any of its parts, whereas a soft thing does yield.

<margin>On the Echo.</margin>
<margin>The last words of an Echo are heard, not the first, because the first words do not return, as they run into the sounds coming toward them.</margin>
Air moves in a sphere, just as water shows us when a drop is cast into a vessel. From hollow objects, the voice is reflected and returns, because the circulations of the air returning backward restore the voice. It is just like the circulations of water poured from the center of a shell: when they reach the edge, they soon return to the center of their motion, driven back by the falling drop. In this way, an Echo is created by the reverberated air from valleys, caves, and hollow buildings, where the impulse of the sound strikes and then returns. However, it does not return from flat surfaces, because the sound is diffused to the sides rather than back toward where it was first pushed.

For indeed, when a voice approaches from a distance, the air...

<meta>This page continues Campanella’s physical investigation of acoustics, moving from the properties of vibrating materials to the way sound waves propagate through the air and how this physical process serves as the foundation for human speech and the "vital spirit's" expression.</meta>

...it moves significantly, for it first moves the part of the air adjacent to the object emitting the sound; that part, in turn, moves the next part closest to it, which moves the following, and another and another, until it finally reaches the part touching the ear. For this reason, because the ear is preceded by a great quantity of air (since it first feels the motion of the part of the air touching it, then the next, then that which the moving object emitting the sound touched), it consequently judges that the moving object itself is distant.

Indeed, it is clear that before a very powerful noise from a distance reaches us, not only the ear, but the whole body is affected and trembles from the blow of the preceding air. But when a moving thing is close to the ear, we recognize it immediately, because we perceive every particle at the same time without the precedence of a dull sound, and every point of the air reflects the sound everywhere and in every direction to every other point. For this reason, all of us standing around catch the same sound. The wind can also carry it away or bring it elsewhere, because sound is a motion of the air; the wind can push this air and the sound elsewhere, since sound depends on the air. But light, which is also reflected everywhere in every direction from any point of air, does not depend on the air, but on the luminous body, which remains bright constantly and uniformly. However, when a sounding body has emitted one part of a sound, it loses it immediately, because the sound does not remain with the body to be constantly derived from it. Therefore, light cannot be carried away by the winds and is swifter than sound. Thus, we see the light of a distant <term>cannon|the original "bombarda" refers to early artillery or mortars</term> being fired a little before we hear the sound.

<meta>This page continues Tommaso Campanella’s physical and linguistic analysis of sound. ### CHAPTER 12 OF PHYSIOLOGY

...wanting to signify the various external positions from which it experiences other multiple motions, it shaped many strikes with the tongue, the palate, the teeth, and the lips; from this, the consonant letters have their origin, so much so that their motions were similar to those motions it received from things. Therefore, from the sound *Tup. Tup.* which one piece of wood makes when striking another, the Greeks have the word *Typto* <note>original Greek: *τύπτω*, meaning "I strike"</note>, and we in the common tongue say *Batto* <note>Italian: *battere*, to beat or strike</note>; and from the vibration of a leather strap, *verbero* <note>Latin: *verberare*, to lash or whip</note>. Wanting to signify the height of some thing, we say *Altum* <note>Latin: "High"</note>, touching the tip of the tongue to the highest part of the palate, and so on. Therefore, strikes of this kind by the vocal organs shape the air in a manner similar to the things themselves. For this reason, the characters on a page expressing sounds of this kind are called **consonants**, because they "sound along with" <note>Campanella is using the etymology of *con-sonant* (sounding with)</note> the air as they strike upon the air sounding from the windpipe <term>arteria: here referring to the *arteria aspera* or trachea</term>. Indeed, since that windpipe is composed of cartilaginous rings that are not complete circles but are interrupted—yet held together by a lighter and softer membrane facing the esophagus, so that it is not damaged by hardness there—it can be contracted and dilated. This allows it to simultaneously sharpen and expand the voice by squeezing or dilating more or less air, in greater or smaller amounts, pushed against the lid of the windpipe itself. There, it has two perfect rings for the sake of more conveniently receiving air and expelling it outward, where sounds are shaped in the mouth by the work of the "little reed" <note>likely referring to the glottis or epiglottis</note> and other organs.

<margin>Audible motion. Voice is sound emitted for the purpose of signifying. Therefore, animals have voices and speak to one another. But we do not perceive their speech because they imitate in a different way and with different instruments. Yet they call each other, respond, and move. Bees, ants, cranes, etc., live in a "Republic"; indeed, no society can be gathered or persist without speech. Fish understand each other by motion.</margin>

*b* When Wisdom <note>Referring to Divine Wisdom or God in Genesis</note> told man to impose names on existing things, and on actions and passions—that is, motions lacking physical substance—man himself, according to the property of those very things by which he was moved (and through which he recognized them), immediately formed similar motions in his mouth and expressed them just as they are. For that reason, sounds signify naturally. But because there are different ways of imitating in different regions (for Northern peoples, fearing the cold, constrict their breath and reverberate a great deal of air with many consonant characters, as the Germans understand, etc.). Indeed, it is no wonder if we do not understand the voices of "brutes" <note>animals</note>, since we do not even understand those of the Scythians <note>An ancient nomadic people of Central Asia, used here as a classic example of a "barbarian" or unintelligible language</note>, although we hear them, and so on. How all the vowel letters and all the consonants are formed in the mouth, and what each is naturally suited for, has already been written in our *Poetics*. *b* Motions noting **Beings** (Entities) are called **Nouns** (Names), while those noting the **motions** themselves are called **Verbs**.

<summary>Campanella argues that human language is not arbitrary but "natural," formed by the vocal organs imitating the physical sounds and shapes of the world. He also observes that animals possess their own forms of speech necessary for their social structures (Republics).</summary>

# F. THOMAS CAMPANELLA

...Germans and Poles, etc. But Southerners, being too relaxed and open because of the heat of their region, emit longer sounds full of vowels, just like the Arabs. For this reason, the Spaniards also have broad and long words, and they commonly pronounce *Adelante* <note>Spanish: "Forward"</note>, *Primiero* <note>Spanish: "First"</note>, and *Notario* <note>Spanish: "Notary"</note>, rather than *Avante*, *Primo*, and *Notaio*, as the Italians pronounce them in a less hot climate. Indeed, even the soil itself creates a specific difference. For the Venetians, born on liquid soil <note>referring to the lagoons of Venice</note>, pronounce almost without consonants: *Frio* <note>Venetian dialect for "cold"</note>, not *freddo*; *peccao* <note>"sin"</note>, and not *peccato*; *cauai* <note>"horses"</note>, and not *cavalli*. The Lombards, who border them, pronounce with a truncated voice fuller of consonants because of the hardness of the soil; and because the breath going out into the cold and hostile air—as if afraid—returns inside and does not complete the whole pronunciation. Therefore they say *pan* <note>Lombard dialect for "bread"</note> and *vin* <note>"wine"</note>, not *pane* and *vino* like the Neapolitans. One can also observe this in the softness of children’s tongues, the solidity of men’s, and the weak dryness of the elderly—namely, that pronunciation varies; but among Nations, it varies far more. From this it happens that while nations are mixed together, words are varied; and those things which signify by nature <note>original: *natura*</note> seem to signify by convention <term>ex placito: a philosophical term meaning by human choice or agreement rather than natural necessity</term>. This is even more so because men mostly signify things from which they experience no motion by means of those things from which they do. For we call God "Spirit," borrowing the word from the wind and from the Soul. We also call a certain fish a "dog" <note>original: *piscem canem*, likely referring to a dogfish or shark</note>, because it is similar to a dog. Sometimes the thing from which a word is naturally assigned is confused with the thing to which it is assigned by convention.

# On the unity and variety of the human body, on the Mind sent by God, on the Spirit, etc., and again on the use of the parts.

## CHAPTER XIII.

### ARTICLE I.

<margin>
From the *Clementines* <note>original: "Ex Clement." — referring to the *Clementinae*, a collection of Roman Catholic canon law promulgated by Pope Clement V</note>, title "On the Supreme Trinity and the Catholic Faith."
</margin>

<margin>
a. The formation of the male is completed in about 30 days, but the female in about 60, because she is granted less heat for refining the bodily organs. At these times, the bodies are made ready to receive the Soul sent by God, just as a mirror, when it has been highly polished, is ready to receive a clear image.
</margin>

a. Once the body has been shaped by the work of the Spirit <note>the "spiritus" or "spirit" here refers to a subtle, warm vapor that acts as the tool of nature, not the immortal soul</note>, and divided into its parts, organs, and pathways of sensation, God looks upon this beautiful craftsmanship, which is far superior to the dwellings of the spirits of brute animals. Therefore, delighting in it as His own work, He sends into it an immortal and divine Soul, which perfects the entire building, as well as its duties, uses, and operations. And since this Soul does not have an operation of its own <note>i.e., it does not act independently of the body while alive</note>, like a sailor in a ship, it becomes the "form" <term>forma: the organizing principle or essence that makes a thing what it is</term> of the whole man. Before receiving such a soul, the man was composed of spirit, moisture, and solid matter, duly crafted. The **solid** b parts exist for the sake of containing, the **moist** parts for the sake of nourishing and binding, but the **spirit** is for the sake of moving, sensing, and knowing. This spirit is indeed one, continued through the head and the limbs, and it produces all movements, changes, and sensations. For it is not itself the "form" of the composite whole, nor of any specific part, but moves itself through the whole and performs its duties, like a sailor in a ship. For this reason, when we listen to something with intense focus, we can hardly see at the same time; and when we are deep in thought, we do not digest our food; and while occupied with the acts of Venus <note>sexual intercourse</note>, we almost lose our senses; and when angry, we lose our ability to reason and our sense of touch. From this it is clear that there is a single Spirit performing all these operations; therefore, while it is busy with one task, it can hardly perform another. For this reason, even our pulse and breathing are altered by fear, joy, attention, contemplation, and all our other actions.

---

a. From this discourse it becomes clear, against Aristotle, that the soul of brutes and the human soul—which he nevertheless recognized and described—is not the "form" of the body, and that the sense organs are not "informed" by their own particular powers. And against Galen <note>a Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries</note>, it shows that there is one single spirit—animal, vital, and rational—and that this same spirit is the soul...
