<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous chapter regarding the nature of the soul. The text begins mid-word ("mam"), completing the phrase "animam rationalem" (the rational soul) from the preceding page. Campanella is arguing against Galen's view that the different "parts" of the soul (reason, anger, and desire) are located in different organs (brain, heart, and liver) as mere physical temperaments. Instead, he argues they are functions of a single, unified "spirit."</meta>

->THOMAS CAMPANELLA<-

...the rational, irascible, and concupiscible soul <note>These are the three classic divisions of the soul in Greek philosophy: Reason, the "spirited" part (anger/will), and the "appetitive" part (desire).</note> resides in the head in its entirety. These are not merely the temperaments of the brain, heart, and liver, since temperaments of this kind are coarse, stupid, and blunt, feeling nothing. Likewise, if the heart and liver feel nothing, as Galen admits, they would not obey the brain—an idea he proposes which actually contradicts his own position. Plato, observing this, attributed sensation to these parts so that they might obey the head. Likewise, we have shown that the pulse, respiration, and other motions are voluntary <term>arbitrarias: movements performed by choice or will, rather than by mechanical necessity</term>. 

Likewise, anger and appetite are produced by both reason and sense. For it is clear that we do not become angry at an offender, but rather at the contempt and disparagement shown to us; for we do not consider the lashes of a magistrate to be worthy of vengeance, nor those things inflicted by chance or by someone who did not intend them. Nor do we desire just any food, unless it is good, nor just any woman, but those who are beautiful and fit for quickening the seed. 

Now, although anger often opposes reason, and sometimes desire does as well (as seen in a person with a fever), this does not indicate that the power which judges is different from the power that feels anger or desire. For even the same reason fights with itself by creating contrary arguments, as is evident when the mind disputes with itself and with others regarding doubtful matters. Yet, for all that, the rational soul is not "double," as it seems to Galen. Thus, I say that anger and desire are affections of the cognizing spirit. 

But because the spirit sometimes does not pause to consider whether it becomes angry rightly or wrongly, it is moved to anger; and as it fluctuates between one reason decreeing vengeance and another denying it out of fear for its own life, it wavers, since it is a single thing performing contrary operations. One should not think that because of this diversity of arguments, the "irascible" <note>the faculty of anger</note> part is distinct from the "cognizing" part. Similarly, while a person simultaneously desires to extinguish feverish heat but fears that water might be harmful, it may seem that the rational faculty is distinct from the desiring faculty, even though they are one. For when reason decrees that something must absolutely be done, anger does not proceed, nor does desire go where it was being carried. But if these souls were of a different kind, opposed to the rational soul and lacking cognition (as Galen affirms), they would never permit themselves to be persuaded, nor could they be induced by persuasion to set aside their own perceived good to follow that of another—namely, the rational soul—whose persuasions they would not even be able to comprehend. 

Therefore, it is a single spirit operating in this way. The heart is truly the instrument of the nutritive faculty, as are the liver and the stomach; however, when any of these suffer, nutrition is not carried out properly because the spirit itself is suffering with them. And since in anger the eyes enlarge and become troubled because the spirits rush toward them, and the nerves swell, etc., it follows that anger belongs to the spirit dwelling within them, and not to the physical temperament of the heart. Likewise, in the act of love, the eyes shine, etc. Therefore, the same principle applies. 

Galen correctly said that the optic nerves and the spinal cord are perforated so that the spirit may run through them; but he then wrongly denies pores <note>microscopic passages or channels</note> to other nerves on the grounds that they cannot be seen, even though the pores of the optic nerves or the spinal cord are not clearly visible either. For this reason, Vesalius <note>Andreas Vesalius (1514–1564), the father of modern human anatomy</note> also denies pores to them; he believes that an incorporeal faculty runs through the whole body to produce voluntary motions <term>motus sectares: purposeful or willed movements</term>. For he argues that this incorporeal faculty cannot arise from the four elements from which they describe the animal as being composed. Therefore, they are mistaken, as they fail to consider the subtlety of the spirit, which travels even through the visible openings in the legs of flies.

Because the spirit is corporeal and is carried through the nerves, we are able to hear, see, and walk at the same time, with the spirit being distributed to various functions. But we can only perform a second task with difficulty when we are very focused on one. Indeed, when we listen attentively to a voice that affects us strongly, we cannot hear another—at least not its meaning—even though it moves the spirit in another portion of itself. It is evident that when the spirit collects itself in the head for the sake of sleep, or in another part for the sake of meeting...

### CHAPTER XIII OF THE PHYSIOLOGY

...the necessities of living, just as occurs in women suffering from **uterine suffocation** <note>original: *uteri suffocatio*; a historical medical term for "hysteria," which at the time was believed to be caused by the womb moving or being "smothered" by vapors</note>, the body remains deprived of sense and motion. Likewise, when a nerve is filled with some **humor** <term>humor: one of the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—believed to determine health and personality</term>, the spirit cannot run through it to produce any motion because the spirit is **corporeal** <note>Campanella argues that the "spirit" is a very thin, vapor-like physical substance, rather than a purely ghostly or non-physical entity</note>. For this reason, the limb over which that nerve is extended remains tense and motionless, as we experience in **spasms** and **paralysis**. This could not happen if the spirit were an incorporeal thing; nor would a person die from infected vapors filling the head, which do not weigh down and suffocate the brain itself, but rather the spirit. 

Indeed, so many diverse functions and actions would not occur in an animal if it were informed by a single sensing and moving form at the same time. For since a form is the condition of a **temperament** <term>temperament: the specific balance of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness in a body part</term>, it necessarily depends on matter that has been conquered and arranged in its particles according to a certain measure, which nature, acting as one with the matter, requires. This measure—of the matter itself and of the acting forces, as well as the "temperature" of those things joined with it—is called "form." 

Therefore, if there were only one form in the whole body, it would necessarily have only one function; as in a stone, in iron, in wind, or in water. In those things, a single form has a single function. But in an animal, at one and the same time, the hand moves, the feet stand, the stomach digests, the heart dilates, and the **spleen rumbles** <note>original: *stertit lien*; literally "the spleen snores," a reference to the internal gurgling or noises of organs thought to indicate activity</note>. Therefore, we must think that several spirits, depending on a single whole, rule the composite body through a continuous connection; just as many men rule a single ship, depending on one captain through a continuity of command and obedience, even though they have separate bodies. This is not exactly the same as the spirits that provide impulse, sensation, and change in the human body.

# BROTHER TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

<margin>a Diverse and disagreeing things cannot combine to form a single entity unless one of them does not depend on the other.</margin>
...depends on matter alone. But indeed, the **Mind** <note>original: *Mens*; Campanella distinguishes between the "spirit" (a physical vapor) and the "Mind" (the immortal, divine intellect)</note>, which God sends into the human composite, can be the **shaper** <term>shaper: translating *informatrix*, the principle that gives a specific form and essence to a thing</term> of a thing that possesses many diverse and partial forms; this is because the Mind itself does not depend on matter, but on God, from whom it is produced by a simple emanation. In the same way, light—which depends on the Sun—at the same moment shapes water that is moving, water that remains still, the air, crystal, and fire-stone <note>original: *pyropum*; likely referring to a bright red gemstone or bronze alloy</note>, and so on. These are all beings diverse in color, consistency, and form, and this is possible because the light does not depend on their matter, but on the Sun.

<margin>d When God sends in the Mind, the workmanship already created is not destroyed by being broken down into "prime matter," as some followers of Aristotle believe; for that workmanship would have been made in vain. Nor could the soul destroy one workmanship and build another in a single instant. Rather, it perfects what has already been made, as Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major medieval philosopher</note> rightly says. Furthermore, it will now repair any fractures much more effectively and suddenly, since it holds more mastery over the composite than it did when it was first suddenly sent in to invisibly build the new structure.</margin>
The human Mind, therefore, gives life to the composite and perfects its functions. However, if the Mind were to perform all operations by itself, the body would easily suffer dissolution. For since the Mind itself is a *e* **contemplator** of its own creator, the one God, and of infinite being (which is why it is never satisfied in its knowledge or its appetite, but extends its understanding infinitely above the heavens, showing that it does not originate from the Sun or the elements, and is therefore not subject to them), it follows that no effect is raised higher than its primary cause. Since the Mind is never satisfied by the finite goods of the world (because it depends on an infinite cause), it would consequently only contemplate divine things, and it would despise the body and fail to nourish it. This is what happens to those caught up in divine **ecstasy**, or in some intense study where the Mind draws an action out of itself, yet performs that same action in cooperation with the spirit. For this reason, God willed that the Mind should perform no natural function by itself without the body; otherwise, it would be like an Angel in a body, and not like a soul. Indeed, He did not even want it to learn anything...

For indeed, other animals do not inquire into what God is, or what Angels are, or what the more beautiful parts of the World are, nor do they take delight in the contemplation of them. Therefore, by bonds of necessity, God tempered this composite of solid matter, liquid, spirit, and the *f* immortal, incorporeal **Mind**. This Mind is the **shaper** <term>shaper: translating *informatrix*, the principle that gives a thing its specific form and essence</term> first of the frail spirit, second of the blood, and then of the body and all its distinct parts. He did this by a law where each individual part loves the preservation of the whole for the sake of its own good, and its own good for the sake of the good of the whole. This is just like what happens in a Republic when it is well-governed for the common preservation, as the history of Rome once showed, and Venice shows now. From this, one can see how the Mind rules the spirit and the body, while simultaneously needing to be taught through them the "divine art" that is implanted in physical, sensible things.

<margin>*f The divine Soul cannot be joined to a crude body without the intermediary Spirit which is very similar to it, nor can the Spirit exist without blood that is suitable to itself and the body,*</margin>

The spirit, truly, moves, cooks <note>original: *coquit*; referring to "concoction," the early modern biological theory that heat "ripens" or digests food and blood</note>, nourishes, and separates the pure from the impure, so that it may restore itself and the body which is its house. Flesh is similar, serving as nourishment and as a defense for the bony and nervous parts; there is much of it in the rear parts so that a human may rest upon soft bedding: for hardness harms the very delicate spirit and its vessels. 

The bones are distinct and separate so that they may serve for bending, yet they are hard so that they may support the machine <note>original: *machinam*; a common 17th-century metaphor for the mechanical structure of the human body</note>: for if all parts were soft or flexible, the body would collapse under its own weight. Nerves are present for contracting and expanding the limbs. The feet exist for walking for the benefit of the whole, so that the person may obtain useful things and avoid harmful ones. The hand is equipped with fingers set against a stronger and more solid finger <note>the thumb</note>, so that it might grasp useful things and take up arms against enemies. To these, nails are attached to serve as the hardened ends of the nerves, veins, and arteries; they act as armor and simultaneously support the "pulp" <note>original: *carunculam*; the soft flesh of the fingertip</note> from behind, so that while handling and grasping objects, the flesh does not slip backward or give way to the thing being held. # *On Sleep, Wakefulness, and the Pulse.*
## CHAPTER XIV.
### ARTICLE I.

<margin>a. Sleep arises from Labor, or from vapor occupying the brain. Aristotle says that frozen fumes in the head fall upon the heart and stupefy it, thus causing sleep, but he is greatly mistaken. For the heart never sleeps, but in sleep it moves more. Nor is there a path by which vapors descend into it; rather, the path leads to the mouth and lung. Nor is the heart the principle of motion and sensation, but the head, as we have shown, and as the Apostle <note>St. Paul</note> teaches in the Epistle to the Ephesians and St. Thomas [Aquinas] in the third part [of the *Summa Theologiae*], asking whether Christ is the head of the Church. Likewise, Aristotle does not give the cause of sleep that happens after labor without smoky food. Galen, however, says sleep occurs in the head when the primary sensory organ—that is, the brain—is cooled, not the heart. But he too is mistaken, both because he does not account for sleep caused by labor, and because cold northern winds do not induce sleep like hot southern winds, which even Hippocrates admits. Likewise, the vapors of hot wine induce more and deeper sleep than the vapors of snow. Therefore, the thickness of the vapor causes sleep, not coldness.</margin>

When <insert>a</insert> the spirit <note>original: *Spiritus*; for Campanella, this is a thin, warm, vaporous substance that flows through the nerves to enable movement and sensation</note> has worked by sensing, moving, and carrying the body, it becomes exhausted, because that part of it thinned by movement and increased heat exhales [is breathed out], and the spirit itself is diminished; wherefore, with the Mind's permission, it is gathered into the head to be restored. And this is said to happen, by God's decree, preferably at night, when light is absent—in which light the spirit would otherwise learn and conduct more business. Sleep also happens when fumes from food ascend into the head, to which the spirit then runs to convert them into its own nature; and so it leaves the nerves and the outer limbs, which appear deprived of the motion and sensation they had from the spirit. And so, one sleeps. It contin-

PHYSIOLOGICAL WORKS, CHAPTER XV.

The motion of respiration remains, however, so that it may vivify the blood and create spirits <note>original: *spiritus*; the "vital spirit," a subtle, airy substance thought to circulate through the body to provide life and heat</note>, by which the entirety of the body's parts is restored. And this respiration becomes more prolonged and greater than during wakefulness, because much fire <note>internal heat</note> is then collected from the periphery toward the interior, or needs to be, requiring this kind of ventilation.

The pulse likewise persists to generate spirits, which must never cease. But at the beginning of sleep, the pulse has a more frequent and greater contraction as the spirits return from the extremities to the center. In the middle of sleep, however, the pulse is small, indistinct, and slow; this is because the spirits are occupied in the head, battling against fumes <note>vapors arising from the stomach during digestion</note> and thinning the blood; they cannot enlarge the pulse and can barely produce it. But at the end of sleep, the now-refreshed spirit returns outward for waking. Then, the dilation of the pulses is more frequent and larger, and its motion is strong and wavy, since it is now abundant from restoration. For this reason, sleep is more suitable for the concoction <note>original: *concoctioni*; the "cooking" or digestion of food by internal heat</note> of food, while wakefulness is better for its distribution and the purging of waste. 

The spirit converts the thin, refined part of nourishment into itself, but excretes the thick dregs through the nose, ears, and eyes—which serve as natural outlets <note>original: *cauteria*; literally "cauteries," used here to mean drainage points for excess humors</note> and not only as windows for sensing. Thick waste is led out through the sutures of the bone and the pores into the skin, where it hardens like grass into hairs. These hairs remain for both the protection and the beauty of the statue <note>Campanella frequently refers to the human body as a "statue" or "vessel" shaped by the spirit</note>.

Insofar as the body cannot convert [nourishment] into its own substance—either because its strength is weak or the nourishment is too excessive—the physical form is altered as tubercles, tumors, fleshy growths, and abscesses are formed. This transformation of life is usually completed in the fated numbers of seven and nine <note>referring to "climacteric years," ancient beliefs about critical 7 and 9-year cycles in a person's life</note>. Almost all celestial and terrestrial things seem to attain a renewal in these cycles, although different things have different periods according to celestial measurements.

# **On Childhood**
## ARTICLE III

<margin>
The Age of Mercury <note>In the "Ages of Man" tradition, Mercury (the messenger god) governs childhood, the time when speech and basic reasoning develop.</note>
</margin>

Next, the heat of the liver and other parts increases, drawing out certain thin fluids. Because of this, the body is dried out somewhat, the hair turns dark (losing its pale thinness), the face becomes less swollen, and the limbs appear more distinct. The bones become quite hard. Teeth are born because the body now requires food more solid than milk—food suited to the acquired solidity of the frame and the strength of its heat. The whole body becomes more solid and grows less rapidly. Nevertheless, as long as the heat is not yet so robust that it expels more parts than it generates within, the animal continues to grow, so long as it enjoys this mild heat and possesses soft, spongy parts. For this reason, <margin>Ecclesiastes 4 <note>Likely a reference to biblical observations on the vanity or transition of youth.</note></margin> much fluid is generated, and much of it runs through the channels of nutrition. During this time, once the spirit is briefly unburdened from the weight of its own restoration and the clearing of vapors, the child begins to learn passions—and the things by which they are affected—and to signify them through the voice.

# **On Adolescence**
## ARTICLE IV

<margin>
The Age of Venus <note>Venus, the goddess of love, governs the transition to sexual maturity.</note>
</margin>

<margin>
a. Aristotle says the testicles sit above only for use, so that they might keep the channels open.
</margin>

Around the age of 14, however, a miraculous change occurs in a human being. For the heat, well-increased by its own action and the ingestion of food, thoroughly warms the entire blood supply, especially that which is more protected within the seminal veins. It renders this blood white and full of spirits. This blood, flowing into the testicles, nourishes them abundantly; furthermore, by the immense heat of the testicles themselves, the blood is cooked far more, becoming whiter and fuller of spirits. These spirits, surely...

*...by their weight [hold open] the spermatic channels, and [Aristotle claims they are] not for the purpose of elaborating the seed; he claims that the seed is instead made from the agitation of intercourse. O, what ignorance! There are winged animals <note>birds</note> that do not have hanging testicles, but have them inside. Likewise, many emit seed while dreaming without any agitation; therefore, it is already completed and is not made by the movement of the venereal act. For even by touching them, the testicles appear filled with seed during abstinence from intercourse. Many also emit seed with their urine. And Eunuchs <note>men who have been castrated</note> lose their strength, and do not grow a beard, nor does their voice change; therefore, the testicles are destined for greater uses.*

<summary>Campanella describes the physiological transitions from childhood (the Age of Mercury) to adolescence (the Age of Venus), emphasizing the role of internal heat and the development of the reproductive system. He specifically critiques Aristotle’s mechanical view of the testicles, arguing they are vital organs for "cooking" seed rather than mere weights for the spermatic ducts.</summary>

## On Virility
### ARTICLE V

<margin>The Age of the Sun</margin> Humans continue to grow as long as their internal heat is not yet so strengthened that it converts into bodily substance all the parts it has thinned and set in motion. When that peak is reached, it is called the state of "human virtue" or excellence. In all the warm parts of the body, hair is produced shortly before this stage; the skin becomes harder and somewhat darker; and strength is maximized by the abundance of vital spirits <note>Subtle vapors believed to carry life through the body.</note> and the consolidation of the limbs. However, after the 40th year, the heat burns more intensely upon the body's nourishment, and the body hardens because it can no longer be properly nourished. The heat itself evaporates in greater volume than can be gathered from food. Thus, the cheeks become furrowed and all the flesh wrinkles as the moisture fails, and old age stands ready.

## On Old Age
### ARTICLE VI

<margin>Of the Old Man</margin> Therefore, in old age, a biting and scorching heat reigns because it is concentrated within dryness; it is no longer gentle like the heat of a child, which is abundant in moisture. The hair also turns white because, as a great deal of heat exhales outward, only a thin, weak heat remains shut deep inside the dry density of the body. Since this remaining heat is feeble and lacks the softness in the now-dried body through which it might exhale once thinned, it remains inside and turns the hair white—for whiteness is a form <note>original: "species"</note> of heat. This is also why the hides of donkeys and horses...

He explains physiological markers like voice changes, facial hair, and the whitening of hair through the lens of early modern thermal physics.</summary>

# PHYSIOLOGICAL TOPICS. CHAPTER XV.

...of wounds, where a part has been gashed or struck, it turns white because the heat there has become weakened and can no longer escape, which in turn makes the hair white. For this reason, those living in the North are large, white, and soft, because they are more nourished by their heat being held inside, and by a thinness of fluids produced by the rigor of the cold—much like the condition found in children due to their natural temperament. The Ethiopians <note>original: "Æthiopes"; a historical term used here to describe people of sub-Saharan Africa.</note> are black, small, and hard, because excessive external heat draws out the innate internal heat; it burns away much of the body’s "thinness" <note>Referring to subtle fluids or vapors.</note> and, as a side effect, hardens and scorches the skin. Those who live in the middle climates have attained a moderate stature, color, and disposition, due to the balance of their internal and external heat. But those who live under the poles are small and blackish, because the cold there is so powerful that it does not merely constrict the heat to prevent it from evaporating, but actually extinguishes it in part. This makes the heat unfit for "metabolic cooking" <note>The "decoction" or processing of nutrients into body tissue.</note>. By taking a firm hold of the skin, the cold also turns it black because it extinguishes the "white" heat, just as we see happen to our own hands when a fierce frost rages. Those who are a short distance from the poles are greenish; those further away are red; those much further are pale, until you reach the white Poles <note>The Polish people.</note>. One may judge the physical consistency and stature of nations in the same way as their color. Nevertheless, colonies <note>Settlements or migrant populations.</note> tend to vary the temperament proper to any climate, as do an abundance of lakes or the height and frequency of mountains. For these reasons, people are not everywhere or always black within the Tropics.

<margin>From one’s age, the temperament can be recognized as being more or less inflamed.</margin>

Therefore, a person's temperament <term>temperies</term> <note>The specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which determined health and personality.</note> varies at different ages, and the life-stages of animals differ in various climates—that is, they are either longer or shorter. Old age does not happen to everyone at the same time. For the "red" or sanguine people grow old late; the phlegmatic <term>flegmatici</term> grow old quickly, as do women; the choleric <term>cholerici</term> and melancholic <term>melancholicique</term> grow old in a moderate amount of time. <header>FRIAR TOMMASO CAMPANELLA On Decrepit Old Age and Death.</header>

### ARTICLE VII.

<margin>
a. Doctors do not realize that the heat of an old man is more robust than that of a child, because they think "natural heat" is composed of the hot, the cold, the moist, and the dry, and that natural moisture is accidentally dry. But this is impossible, because heat is...
</margin>
<margin>
Of Saturn. <note>Saturn was traditionally associated with old age, coldness, and melancholy in astrology and medicine.</note>
</margin>

Finally, decrepit old age arrives, when the vital spirit <note>term: vital spirit (spiritus vitalis); in Renaissance medicine, this was a subtle, vapor-like substance that circulated through the body to sustain life and movement.</note> is at its weakest, because too much of it has exhaled due to the scorching heat. What remains is thin and meager, easily escaping through the pores of the dried-out solid parts of the body. The flesh is very hard, so that it can hardly be nourished; the bones indeed are so dry that the cartilaginous appendages of the vertebrae become bony; and thus the person becomes bent over. Vision grows dim and hearing is dulled as the sense organs harden and the spirit, weakened, gradually exhales. That which remains is unable to perform the duties of all the "instruments" <note>Campanella refers to the organs and limbs as instruments used by the spirit.</note>; therefore the limbs tremble, pulled downward by their own weight and upward by the meager spirit. The liver hardens, turns bitter, and becomes like stone, and consequently cannot "cook" <note>term: cooking (coquere); the process of digestion and metabolic transformation of food into blood and tissue.</note> nutrients; for this reason, an old man needs food in small amounts and frequently. For his heat is extinguished by a large amount of food, just as a tiny flame is put out when too much oil is poured on it. However, as long as it can, the spirit is nourished while the body is nourished at the same time, but only slightly due to the body's hardness. It gradually exhales until no portion of it remains, like the glowing heat of a lamp when the oil fails. Therefore, in old age, the human spirit vanishes into the air without affliction and with great **b** pleasure.

<meta>catchword: Then</meta>

---

<margin>
*...corporeal. Both moisture and dryness are passive, not active things. Nor can a being be composed of four contraries such that they become one. But one would have to say "natural cold" just as "natural heat," otherwise we would overcome these contraries not with heat but with cold. These contraries can be reconciled, because they would no longer be contraries but another being. And it would be a process of generation, not a mere mixture. Nor can we say that in a child there is more natural heat because of moisture, and in an old man less because of dryness, since both dry and moist—according to Galen <note>Galen of Pergamum (129–216 AD), the Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note>—are equal parts of natural heat. Therefore we say: in the child there is a greater quantity of heat, but in the old man, it has more strength. 

b. Natural death is sweet, but death from disease and by force is painful. A "hectic" state <note>original: "Hectica"; a wasting condition or fever.</note>, which mimics the natural end, is not so bitter, even though it is a continuous wasting away little by little. From this we know that extreme old age is a kind of "hectic" condition—that is, the drying out of the dewy, fleshy, and membranous moisture, as is clear in the example of the lamp given in Part 2, in the chapter on Exercise. 

When the spirit departs, the body remains whole. Therefore, the spirit is not its "form" <note>A critique of the Aristotelian idea that the soul is the "form" or organizing principle of the body; if it were, the body would instantly dissolve into elements once the soul left.</note>. For wood, by losing its form, is dissolved, and so is every other being. Therefore, the soul which God bestows is not a form dependent on the body, otherwise the body itself would not remain. From this it appears that the dissolution of the body does not happen into the four elements, but into other intermediate substances. And when the compound is dissolved into water and air, it is not the ultimate dissolution, which clearly occurs into fire and earth. Nor is an animal nourished, as Aristotle thinks, from the raw elements, but from things composed of elements <note>original: "elementatis"; substances already processed by nature into a complex state.</note> similar to itself; for otherwise, the body would be destroyed by the unmitigated powers of a pure element, which only has diminished powers when in the conflict of the elements from which it arises.*
</margin>

<summary>Campanella describes the physical mechanics of extreme old age as a process of desiccation where the body hardens and the vital spirit gradually evaporates like a lamp running out of oil. He argues that natural death is painless and uses the preservation of the corpse as evidence that the soul is a divine gift rather than a biological "form" dependent on the body's structure.</summary>

Then indeed the Soul, having been breathed in by God, is no longer able to rule the **corporeal machine** <note>original: "corpoream machinam." Indeed, God did not insert the will for eternity within us in vain.

## *On the Manner of Sensing based on Knowledge.*

### ARTICLE II.

<margin>St. Augustine, *On the Divination of Demons*.</margin>
**T**he spirit does not feel heat unless it is itself heated, nor cold unless it is cooled, nor motion unless it is moved; therefore, to sense is to be changed <note>original: "per immutari." Campanella follows the idea that sensation is a physical "mutation" or alteration of the perceiving spirit by an external object.</note>. Since the change is received in the power-faculty from which it immediately senses the changing object as something to be known; and the appetitive <term>appetitituum: the faculty of desire or "reaching out" for what is good</term> is affected by pleasure or pain from the changing sense, because of their real identity <note>He means that the power to know and the power to feel are essentially the same thing within the spirit.</note>. Change happens with pleasure when it is toward the better, but with pain when it is toward the worse, and suddenly. However, if it happens gradually—as in hunger, when the particles of the body fail insensibly and bit by bit, from which the desire for replenishment arises—pain is not felt. Nor is pleasure felt when health is restored gradually, as is evident in the healing of wounds. But it is felt when the restoration of health occurs instantly, as when the hand is affected by a soothing heat, or the tongue by tasty food. Conversely, a sudden wound affects the flesh with pain. For the animal consists of a moderate temperament and soothing heat, and a soothing melody is preserved, or it is disposed toward preservation. But it is destroyed by excessive heat or sound, or disposed toward destruction, since it is alienated from its own proper temperament.

## *On the Fallacy of Particular Senses and Their Correction.*

<margin>a Sensation is the principle of knowledge and certainty:</margin>
*<gloss>a That which appears to the sense is not always such by nature, but this is proven either by another sense or by its own; as when the noise of a drum is displeasing and the spirit recognizes its own deception through another sense. For example, the sight is taught by touch that an oar in the water is not broken; and by another vision from above the water. From this, the mind is moved to ask why it appeared so. Therefore, the first certainty is from the senses: for whatever we imagine, think, reason, and understand we hold as uncertain until we are made certain by the experience of the senses. Thus, the New World was uncertain until the experience of Columbus. Nor is it true that no science can exist because the sense is sometimes deceived, as Sextus Empiricus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and proponent of Skepticism who argued that because senses can be fooled, true knowledge is impossible.</note> says: for the sense even knows this—that it is being deceived—and it corrects itself from other sensations, or sense organs, or from the senses of other men. But concerning this, see the first part of my Metaphysics.</gloss>*

<summary>Campanella explains that sensation is a physical alteration of the spirit and argues that while individual senses can be deceived, sensory experience remains the ultimate foundation of all certain knowledge.</summary>

...[is unpleasant] to a sick person because their thin spirit is agitated too much by it; but the same thing pleases healthy people, because they are invited to action and the spirit is refined, provided the stimulus is not so great as to cause fatigue. Furthermore, sweet and bitter, harmony and dissonance, stench and scent do not exist in the world except in relation to our sense, which is tempered in a certain way; any mode unlike this is hostile to it. Look, what stinks to us smells good to a dog or a pig; and broom <note>original: "genistam," a type of flowering shrub</note> is bitter to our taste but sweet to a goat; and whatever pleased us when healthy displeases us when ill. The sense corrects all these errors by using past or present sensations, whether its own or those of others, through reasoning <note>original: "discurrendo," referring to the spirit moving back and forth between different impressions to compare them</note>. When all sensations—present and past, our own and others'—agree, certain knowledge <term>scientia: certain, demonstrated knowledge, as opposed to mere belief</term> is formed; but when many [agree, but not all], it is opinion.

### On Memory and Remembrance.

#### ARTICLE III.

<margin>St. Augustine, *On the Divination of Demons*.</margin>
<margin>a. Sense is not only a "perfecting passion" <note>An "active" or "improving" experience</note>, as Aristotle thinks; for pain is also a destructive sense. But the sense rejoices in pains after they have passed, because it emerges wiser, not because it desired them.</margin>
Since the spirit is highly mobile and corporeal, and most suited for sensing and receiving different things, it simultaneously rejoices **a** in sensing because it becomes wise concerning those things by which it is preserved and those by which it is destroyed; likewise, it is often invited toward its own preservation while it is moved; and it is preserved by motion, which is its own proper operation. Motions of this kind remain within it, just as they seem to persist in highly mobile air. But as other infinite motions from the things it senses come upon it, it seems no longer to distinguish those earlier motions, because they remain dormant within the spirit itself. And therefore, a great battle, a savage blow, or a solemn feast is never handed over to oblivion, even if it happened only once. **b** In those in whom the spirit is very hot, because...

# FRATER TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

Those who possess excessive heat in their heart and in their liver are the most ready to perceive sensations. For a spirit of this kind, because it is extremely refined <gloss>c</gloss>, is affected by even the smallest thing, both near and far. The air itself, in which all things occur, is affected by them; as it easily enters through the nostrils into the brain, it communicates to the spirit not only present things, but those that follow from the present, just as effects follow causes. Such men excel in **natural prophecy** <note>This refers to the ability to predict the future through sharp observation of natural signs rather than divine revelation.</note> because of the thinness of a spirit that is easily moved and sagacious, sensing causes suddenly and immediately foreseeing the effects within those causes, as it runs through similar motions and pieces of information at the same time. Nevertheless, they do not retain a memory of the things they have sensed, because the sensing spirit, being very hot, exhales before it can communicate its experiences <note>original: "passiones," meaning things the spirit has undergone or "felt."</note> to the succeeding spirit that is converted into it from the blood.

<margin>
c Speculation <note>The act of deep intellectual contemplation.</note> arises from the agility of the spirit passing from motion to motion, even if it is barely perceived.
A thick spirit is only affected by larger experiences, such as a blow, or by continuous ones, such as a man one always looks at among many individuals; but it is not affected by the <unclear>nasicuritate</unclear> <note>Perhaps "uniqueness" or "novelty." The Latin transcription is likely a corruption of "nativitate" (birth/nature) or "raritate" (rarity).</note> it sees in one or a few.
</margin>

However, those who are endowed with a **thick spirit**, because their internal organs are not hot enough to refine it, sense things with difficulty. This is because their spirit does not move well, and it is not affected except by violent and great things. They do not retain anything in memory except common things which they sense continuously, or particular things that make a powerful impression. They are unfit for the speculative sciences. In this way, water receives and retains motion with more difficulty than air.

Those who are gifted with a successful <gloss>d</gloss> memory are those endowed with moderate heat and a spirit that is not so thin that it exhales suddenly before retention, nor so thick that it does not immediately grasp moving objects. Such are the people inhabiting temperate climates, possessed of a moderated heart and a liver of gentle heat, which digests food evenly. Therefore, the treasure of memory is a spirit of moderate purity, thinness, and mobility. 

Motions <gloss>e</gloss> truly remain in the spirit, yet not as shapes or figures are painted on a tablet; for some impressions would overturn or reject others—

<column-break/>

<gloss>d</gloss> A pure spirit, not composed of mixed thin and thick parts, retains distinct motions without confusion. Its thinness makes it able to be stirred by any present motion similar to a past one; and the lack of "soot" <note>Impurities or vapors resulting from poor digestion/heat.</note> allows it to grasp the whole, so that the movement of remembrance is not interrupted.

<gloss>e</gloss> A thing that has undergone an experience <note>original: "Res passa."</note> is predisposed to that same experience again; just as a sickness warns of a relapse. This applies even more to the spirit, as it is more susceptible. Therefore, the cure for a desire <note>or "appetite"</note> resulting from a spider's bite <note>A reference to tarantism, where victims were said to dance to cure the bite.</note>: when they see others who have been bitten, the spirit is affected by the old experience excited by the new one, to the point that it is communicated to the body. Just as a pestilential fever passes from the air to the spirit, from the spirit to the blood, and from <gloss>f</gloss> the blood to the body, so too does the madness of diseases pass from dogs.

## *On Assenting and Dissenting Faith.*

### ARTICLE IV.

<margin>a Faith is the mind’s assent to its own senses, or to the testimony of others regarding what they have certainly experienced. Trustworthy witnesses are those who love us, who know the truth, and who are not afraid to speak it. Therefore, since all men are liars—some out of ignorance, some out of malice, and some out of fear—only God is a truthful, most excellent, and most wise Father, worthy of undoubting faith. Others are to be believed only insofar as they are His witnesses, either through revelation or through experience gained in the World, which is His "book," as was stated in the *Metaphysics*.</margin>
Sensation and memory were not sufficient for knowledge, for not all things can be perceived by one's own senses. Therefore, we require **faith**, **a** by which one assents to those who have sensed and experienced things themselves. Thus, so that we might know that Rome exists, that Caesar once lived, that Adam existed, and that there is a New World, it was necessary for the <term>animal spirit</term> <note>The "animal spirit" (spiritus animalis) is the physiological medium of thought and movement in the body.</note> to place faith in those who saw these things and reported them to us by voice or in writing. To believe, therefore, is to sense through another's sense rather than one's own. In this same way, regarding divine matters, it was necessary to believe Moses, the Prophets, and the Apostles. But because the Mind only assents to the spirit when it is testifying truly and not merely guessing—and because human testimony is often deceitful—miracles were necessary to confirm faith in divine matters, for such acts can only be performed by God. This allows reason to judge that faith, as well as its own disbelief, by comparing it to other things held in the memory or recently perceived. Thus, a human believes Rome exists by comparing it to other cities or to his own fatherland.

<margin>Theology does not use sense, but faith, as its starting principle.</margin>
We believe in those things which are presented as certain to our own sense or to the senses of others, provided that experience does not contradict them, nor any prior perception, whether in itself or in something similar. On the other hand, we hold as "opinion" those things which are contradicted by some sense or reason. We judge as "true" that which is supported by many senses and reasons. Therefore, it is clear what constitutes opinion, judgment, and Faith.

<meta>catchword: On</meta>

<summary>Campanella defines faith as an epistemological necessity for knowledge beyond personal experience, distinguishing it from opinion and judgment. He argues that while human testimony can be flawed, faith in God and divinely sanctioned witnesses (confirmed by miracles) provides certain knowledge.</summary>

## On Reasoning.

### ARTICLE V.

**A**long with faith, a third type of knowledge is born, called **Discourse** or **Reason**. It is so named because it "runs" <note>Campanella derives *Discursus* (Reasoning/Discourse) from the Latin *discurrere*, meaning "to run to and fro."</note> from known facts to the knowledge of unknown things, guided by the similarity found between them. In this way, we know that if one <term>drachma</term> <note>A small unit of weight, roughly 1/8th of an ounce.</note> contains 12 grains of wheat, then one **Ounce**, being made of eight drachmas, will contain 96 grains—that is, eight times twelve. Likewise, if a forearm contains two palms, an <term>ell</term> <note>A traditional unit of length (Latin: *ulna*), often the length of a man’s arm.</note> will contain eight. This is because every drachma is similar to every other drachma, and every palm to every other palm. We are guided by experience, which is the confirmed knowledge resulting from many sensations and memories. It is innate within us to proceed from the better-known to the unknown. Therefore, by doubling the grain as many times as necessary, we measure <margin>a To measure and to count is to investigate an unknown quantity by comparing it to another quantity that is known to us and very similar to it.</margin> *a* weights; and by the finger and the palm, we measure sizes, because the palm and the grain are things very well known to us. Furthermore, because the motion of the sun is the most well-known of all motions to us, it measures for us all the movements of the heavenly bodies; yet, by the motion of a clock—which is even better known to us—we distinguish the motion of the sun itself. So too, in the nature of things, I understand how a plant is made based on how I see hair grow; and I distinguish stone from bone, or Lycurgus from Solon, through affirmative reasoning <margin>b Through continuous reasoning I come to know any existing being. Look into the <term>Predicaments</term> <note>Also known as the "Categories" of Aristotle; the fundamental ways in which things can be classified (e.g., Quality, Quantity, Place).</note>, that is:</margin> *b* Indeed, however many similarities there are, that is how many types of reasoning and <term>syllogisms</term> <note>A form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note> must be recognized. There is similarity of Origin; of Time; of Place; of Matter; of Action; of Passion <note>In this context, "passion" refers to the way a thing is acted upon or "undergoes" an effect.</note>; of Operation; of Disposition; of Form; and of Accident (that is, something that happens to a thing outside of its essence, its intention, or its

<sig>Z 3</sig>
<meta>Catchword: will)</meta>

*or Nature,*

*wherein you should consider: 1. The Principles from which it arises, its powers, place, time, and the force of that which is being born. 2. Its particular Matter, which includes its own Quantity, number, and dispositions (whether it is dense or rare, soft or hard). 3. Its Operation (whether it moves itself, whether it breathes in part, or in some way, or entirely). 4. Its outward Figure, which is the messenger of its internal arrangement of parts within the whole, combined with the temperament of the cause that acts and rules within it. 5. Its Action (whether it is strong or weak, whether it involves matter or is without matter), and its flavor. 6. Its Passion (whether it is easily acted upon, by what, when, and how). 7. Its Color (white, black, or mixed). 8. What happens to it after it is fully formed, and whether it acts, is acted upon, is shaped, colored, or born by chance or by art. 9. What things it is opposed to in its operation, action, principles, shape, and so on. 10. What things it is similar to in nature, operation, and passion. I have written about this in the pages of the Metaphysics—against Aristotle—and in the Logic.*

<meta>This page continues Campanella’s exploration of the mechanics of thought. Having previously discussed how physical conditions like heat and "sooty vapors" affect the vital spirit, he now moves into "Article VI" to define the act of understanding (intellection) itself. # FRIAR TOMMASO CAMPANELLA On the Intellect and Intellection.

### ARTICLE VI.

<margin>
a. <note>original: "Arist. vt Vniuersale sequestret..."</note> Aristotle, in order to isolate the Universal, makes the intellect and the senses into different entities. He claims the intellect is a passive power <term>passive power: the capacity to receive impressions, like wax receiving a seal</term> for all things, perceiving only the universal. However, in the second book of the *Posterior Analytics*, he also grants this ability to the senses. He further claims there is an "active intellect" which strips universal species <term>species: the mental images or forms of things</term> of their individual traits, separating them and making them fit to be perceived by the passive intellect. This passive intellect, once activated by the species, understands—just as wood, which is potentially hot, is made actually hot by fire and then provides heat itself. This is a fiction. For the "universal" is simply the similar particulars themselves, apprehended as one because of their similarity, and therefore labeled with a single name. Therefore, if the sense perceives particulars, it perceives the universal even more, since it sees the universal in all the particulars, but not the particulars themselves [at a distance]. Even from a distance, the sense recognizes the universal and not the particulars. Likewise, I say the intellect is an "actual being," and not pure potential like matter; it is able to understand because it is mobile and capable of being affected. For it does not understand through "information" <term>information: the Scholastic theory that the mind takes on the literal "form" of the object it contemplates</term>; otherwise, once one thing were understood, others...
</margin>

**Understanding** <sup>a</sup> occurs when the spirit senses within itself common traits without their specific individualities: such as when one understands "human" without thinking of John, Martin, or others. This happens because, in a multitude of similar things, there are entities common to all of them by virtue of their being similar; for example, in humans, the physical shape, the capacity to sense, to speak, and to reason are common to everyone. There are also particular entities within that same community of things: for instance, the shape of Peter is formed one way, Paul’s another, and Socrates’ yet another. Likewise, they sense, speak, work, and conduct business in different ways, and they are endowed with different levels of heat and passion—even though they all share these things in common. This is because they are made from the same material and active principles, but are divided into different parts, existing in different times and places, and differing in their abundance and strength. Therefore, these types of common entities (in which things agree) and particular entities (in which they differ) are represented in the spirit through the senses. But commonalities are retained more strongly in the memory because they are sensed more frequently and in a greater number of objects, and thus they "move" <note>Campanella views cognition as a physical movement or "passion" (affection) of the vital spirit.</note> the spirit more. Indeed, in Peter, Paul, and Socrates, we observe the human traits of sensing, speaking, shape, and having a nose; but we do not see in all of them *that* specific man, or sensing acutely, or speaking with a deep or thin voice, or a tall or short stature, or a snub nose, or those specific eyes, or that specific action.

And so, universals are held in the memory more than particulars, which are not the same in everyone and therefore do not move the spirit as often or as much, and consequently are not known as well.

<meta>catchwords: Truly-; not</meta>

<summary>Campanella defines "understanding" as the spirit's ability to recognize common traits (universals) across many individuals. He rejects Aristotle's complex theory of the "active intellect," arguing instead that we remember general concepts better simply because we encounter them more frequently than specific individual details.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Campanella's critique of the Aristotelian (Peripatetic) model of the mind. On the previous page, he argued that the "universal" is not a separate abstract entity but a recognition of similarities. Here, he attacks the concept of the "active" and "passive" intellects by highlighting the logical contradictions of the Peripatetic school and their failure to account for human experience like forgetting or individual differences.</meta>

### CHAPTER XVI OF NATURAL PHILOSOPHY. 185

The intellect would not understand a thing unless it were destroyed by it—just as wood that has been set on fire cannot simultaneously be cool or remain something else. Likewise, once it has understood something, it could not forget it once it has become "actualized" <term>actualized: moving from a state of potential (could be) to reality (is)</term>; just as wood, once it has become fire, always provides heat and is never "deceived" into cooling instead of heating. Yet the intellect forgets and is deceived. This would not happen if the intellect were joined to the "intelligible" object more closely than wood is to heat, or matter to form, as all the **Peripatetics** <note>original: "Peripatetici," the followers of Aristotle</note> claim.

Furthermore, if the **active intellect** is so powerful that it "strips" the universal of its particular traits, why can it not do this in all cases, and from the very moment of birth? If it only arrives later, why do forgetfulness and deception remain within us despite the presence of such a powerful force? Also, what is a "universal species" <term>species: the mental image or "form" of a concept</term>? For if it is not the actual form of the object being perceived, it is merely a fiction of the intellect and will not provide true knowledge of the understood thing. And from where do these "species" arise? Are they created out of nothing, or out of something else? Furthermore, what kind of "species" can exist for heat and cold? Since these are contraries, how can they exist together in the same indivisible and incorporeal intellect? And why is there such great labor in investigation, and such failures of "digestion" <note>Campanella often compares the mental processing of information to the physical digestion of food</note>? If the active and passive intellects come from the outside and are one and the same in all human beings—as **Averroes** <note>Averroes was a 12th-century Islamic philosopher who argued that all humans share a single "Active Intellect"</note> believes—by what fate is it forced to be confined? And why in man more than in wild beasts? And why do we not remember what the intellect knew in other people in times past? If the body causes it to forget, how is that possible, since the intellect itself is "impassible" <term>impassible: incapable of suffering or being changed by external forces</term>, not mixed with matter, and not tied to any physical organ? Furthermore, if it suffers this, why does it enter into bodies where it falls into ignorance of itself and into misery? To this logic, the Peripatetic can respond nothing without invoking **Christianity** and the plurality of souls.

Likewise, if the intellect is one, why do you and I understand different things? Why do I remain ignorant of what you know? This is especially problematic since the imagination <note>original: "phantasia"</note> is its object, and not a power of the intellect itself. But if the same stone is seen by many people at once through a single light (which Aristotle uses as a metaphor for the active intellect), and if the passive intellect is also one, the argument cannot be avoided. **Avicenna** says that memory resides in the senses, and that is why we forget. But his master **Aristotle** says that "species" are imprinted on the passive intellect while it is active. Therefore, memory is within the intellect; why then do we forget? **Alexander** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous commentator on Aristotle</note> posits one Active intellect but many passive ones, yet he suffers the same difficulties regarding how a universal is formed. **Averroes**, however, takes away man’s own unique form. The **Latins** <note>The Scholastic theologians of Western Europe</note> say there are two powers of the same soul: active and passive. But Aristotle posits one as mortal and the other as immortal, one as actual and the other as potential. Therefore, they must be two distinct things.

Furthermore, if individual men have immortal souls, one must either posit the **transmigration of souls** <note>The passing of a soul into a new body after death</note> in the manner of the **Pythagoreans**, or posit an infinite number of souls (since the world is eternal), which Aristotle denies. **Christian followers** admit that souls come from God, but some err when they attribute the operations of the physical spirit to the "infused mind." They thus make the mind itself suspect of mortality, as they follow Aristotle before following reason and the **Holy Fathers**. **Scotus** <note>John Duns Scotus, a medieval theologian</note> rightly says that Aristotle’s view on the soul is doubtful; and **Durandus** <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain</note> says that the "active intellect" is fictitious and superfluous.

Nevertheless, the same spirit that sees **Peter** sees "man," and "such a man"; that is, it sees both the universal and the particular. This means it sees what Peter has in common with others, and what he possesses as his own, which is unlike them. Thus, the spirit bestows names upon things—whatever moves the spirit—by noting them for itself and signaling them to others. So, it notes rational animals with the common name, **"Man."** It notes particularities, however, by using proper names, like **Peter**,

</margin>
**Crassus**, **Agrippa**, **Naso**, etc., based on individual differences.
<margin>
...properties, such as from the nose, or the foot, etc., and not by chance as we do, living by personal affection rather than wisdom.

Instead, he distinguishes waters by the vessel or the spring they come from, and by those names. Furthermore, because he sees that a human agrees with a horse and other beasts in movement, sensation, sensory organs, and the soul operating in a similar way, he labels all these with a more common name and says **Animal**. Every smaller community contained under this, he labels with less common names, saying **horse**, **lion**, **dog**, and so on. Then, grasping as a single thing that in which animals and plants agree—which is "to live"—he grants it a single name, saying **Living Being**. But that which he recognizes as similar in animals, plants, and stones, he grants a more universal name and says **Body**. And because all things "are," he says **Being** <term>Being: original Latin *Ens*, the most basic and universal category for anything that exists</term>, the most common name of all. Furthermore, he calls the community of individuals a **Species**, but the community of communities a **Genus**, such as "animal," etc.

<margin>
d Aristotle and Porphyry <note>original: "Porphyrius," a 3rd-century scholar whose "Isagoge" was the standard textbook on logic in the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note> did not know how to define what a species or genus is in itself, but only what they are in the use of speech, when they say: "a genus is that which is said of many things," etc. I, however, say: a **Genus** is a community of communities, or a similarity of common things perceived as one, because of the similarity noted by the spirit—which knows and is moved by them—under a single name. A **Species**, however, is a community not of communities, but of individuals, etc.
</margin>
d **Species**, therefore, is the similarity of many individuals perceived as a single thing; for insofar as they are similar, they are one, even though they are many similar things. **Genus**, however, is the similarity of many species perceived as a single thing, in that they are similar, even though there are many things labeled with a single general name, because they are one insofar as they are similar.

There are also similarities of names and things which are not essential, and these produce **equivocation**, **analogy**, and **metaphor**, according to whether the similarity is greater or lesser.

Although unities of this kind among many similar things are formed in the **corporeal spirit** <term>corporeal spirit: in Campanella’s philosophy, a subtle, physical substance in the nerves that perceives the world by being physically moved or "shaped" by external objects</term>—because it is moved by them and affected in a like manner by one and the same kind of motion—to all of which the spirit afterward imposes one common name, imitating with a single voice through the vocal organs the motion it received from them; nonetheless, this kind of community corresponds to a single **Divine Idea**:

<summary>Campanella argues that general categories like "Genus" and "Species" are simply names we give to groups of things that look or act similarly, rather than being mystical abstract realities. He explains that our physical "spirit" creates these names by imitating the way similar objects physically affect our senses.</summary>

...of the divine Mind, from which every community <note>original: *communitas*; here meaning "shared nature" or "commonality"</note> of things emanates in its own degree of participation. Therefore, since brute animals possess a corporeal spirit, they also have this knowledge of similar things and of the "universal"; yet it is not as perfect as it is in the human spirit. For not only is the human spirit perfected by the immortal Mind, but in itself it is also gentler and purer—neither too thin nor too thick. It resides in a more spacious brain and in cavities <note>original: *cellis*; referring to the ventricles or chambers of the brain.</note> that are much better formed in the human head, where it can move and reason <note>original: *discurrere*; to run through a sequence of thoughts.</note> better than in beasts. Beasts do have a sensory reasoning, but not a mental one. 

As is evident, **Bees** and **ants** work for the future based on their memory of the past. **Monkeys** and long-tailed apes are capable of being taught because they retain in their memory the movements and instructions to which they grow accustomed; just as children become knowledgeable through habituation. Even before children fully recognize individual traits, they assign a common name to all men, saying "**Father**," and they call all women "**Mothers**." Then they grow accustomed to distinguishing individuals, and step by step they learn the knowledge and the words that signify specific individuals. 

So too, we see that a dog brought from Poland to Italy does not understand the unfamiliar Italian language, unless someone had spoken to him in Polish. And although beasts do not speak as we do—because they do not have a mouth formed in a way very similar to the human, unlike the parrot which, having a concave palate like a human, is able to form human voices—nevertheless they all speak in their own idiom: they reason, and they understand. For **Horses** recognize the universal and the similar, since they do not only know this or that specific grain of barley, but *all* barley—otherwise they would only eat this one grain. BROTHER TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

<margin>f. It is appropriate for even brute animals to understand universals. And although David <note>The Psalmist; see Psalm 32:9: "Be ye not as the horse, or as the mule, which have no understanding."</note> says there is no understanding in them, he then took "Intellect" to mean the **Mind** instilled by God, but not the universal, faint <note>original: *languida*; suggesting a weak or diluted form of knowledge.</note> cognitive power, since even Job says that the cock has intelligence. And St. Augustine grants understanding to the "estimative" and "cogitative" power which is in brutes, as St. Thomas Aquinas witnesses. And Solomon attributes thinking to the sense, saying "the body weighs down the thinking sense" <note>Wisdom of Solomon 9:15</note>, where he takes "sense" for the **Mind**, or for the **spirit** <term>Spirit: the subtle, vaporous substance that carries sensory information through the body.</term> that serves it. And St. Thomas says that animals possessing memory have **prudence**. In his *Summa*, he says the cogitative is part of the particular deliberative power (in the section "whether intellect is a part of prudence") and he also calls the cogitative power "intellect." But he who is so mad as to say that the particular instances—from which a general conclusion is made—belong to one power, while the general conclusion itself belongs to another, is mistaken. For example, when I say, "this man moves, and that one, and this one, etc., therefore all men move," it is clear that the conclusion belongs to the same knowing power as the premises. Therefore, etc. A horse knows that all barley is good, but it does not know that barley is similar to an **eternal Idea**, as we do; for Aristotle, by removing the Craftsman from the World, foolishly removes the understanding of **Ideas**, as Eusebius, St. Dionysius, St. Justin, and St. Thomas argue well against him.</margin>

...but when it <note>referring to a dog or similar animal</note> approaches and recognizes its master, a particular man, it fawns upon him; therefore, etc. Although this kind of understanding, reasoning, and **prudence**, and every sensory power of brute animals is merely physical, not mental—even though the **Soul**, which is the **Mind** recently instilled in humans by God, is also called **Intellect** and **Spirit**—it happens just as when we learn and name the unknown from a known similarity. And we often make specific to one what is common to many; thus, we call humans "intellectual" and "rational," but not brutes, although *f* they understand and feel by reasoning in a certainly obscure way. Since all knowledge comes from the **First Wisdom**, it is therefore similar in both us and them.

The understanding of an **Idea**, as if of a seal, is therefore proper to the **Mind**. But the understanding of an Idea as the *thing sealed* <note>the impression left by the seal</note> belongs to the internal sense. This must be seen as a "faint knowledge," because it grasps and retains what is common, but cannot hold onto specific details. This is because common things are found in many similar objects and thus move the spirit many times; but specific details are in few things and thus move it rarely. For this reason, details are less easily retained by the memory.

He is truly wise who does not merely know that Peter is a man, but who thoroughly knows Peter's particular properties of temperament, appearance, virtues, vices, actions, and his smallest, most peculiar passions. **God is the wisest**, because He knows all the smallest singularities completely by looking into Himself, from whom they are derived, just as a craft derives from the craftsman. But man, acquiring knowledge from things, cannot retain anything except the common element which he finds in them, by which he is therefore more often moved to be imprinte—

### ON PHYSIOLOGY, CHAPTER XVI.

...is impressed by the object, but does not grasp the minute and intrinsic properties that are distant from the senses, which it instead investigates through similarity; for the sense is not the creator of these properties, but only their observer. This kind of universal knowledge <note>General concepts, like the idea of "a tree" rather than "this specific oak."</note> concerns an object that is not immediately present, and this applies to the internal sense just as it does to the external. For when the sense sees a man from a great distance, it judges: "It is a living creature." Then, as he approaches further, it says: "It is a man." As he draws even closer, it says: "It is a monk." Finally, when he is at the closest range, the sense says: "It is Peter."

<margin>g. A response to Aristotle, who says the power of sensing is one thing and the power of understanding is another, because a powerful object destroys the former but strengthens the latter.</margin>
From this g it becomes clear why a powerful sensible object destroys the sense—just as the Sun blinds the eyes or fire burns the hand—whereas a powerful "intelligible" object strengthens the intellect. This is because the intelligible is simply an object that is absent or viewed from a distance. Indeed, he who can see a distant thing can see a nearby thing even better, but the reverse is not true, because a distant thing moves and affects the observer less. For someone who easily receives a small impression can even more easily receive a large one that affects them more strongly. However, a nearby sensible object moves the sense more intensely; thus, one who is feeling a massive sensation cannot simultaneously feel a small one. Children, on the other hand, learn the "common" <note>General categories.</note> before they learn the "particular" <note>Specific individuals.</note>; yet they do not know how to apply this knowledge because they do not yet discern specific details from universality. This is why they call all men "Father."

<margin>h. Universal propositions are a summary of particulars, and definitions are a compendium of the knowledge of particulars; hence they are suitable for teaching those who believe. But to learn...</margin>
h Therefore, many memories of the same thing perceived by the sense create **experience**, which is the "universal" itself and the starting point of the doctrine we pass on to others. But "particulars" are the starting point of science <note>In this context, *scientia* refers to systematic, investigated knowledge.</note>, which is learned through investigation. This is the proper work of the pure and agile **spirit** <term>Spirit: In 17th-century physiology, this refers to a subtle, vaporous substance that flows through the nerves, carrying sensations and thoughts.</term>, which is capable of every movement and runs readily toward all similarities. It is enough for this spirit to have glimpsed a thing once to retain it, compare it to another, and produce science by investigating the essence from the actions, or the actions and passions from the essence. It moves from one action to other actions and passions, depending on whether this thing or that condition presents itself first. Therefore, to "discourse" <note>To reason through a series of steps.</note> is simply to sense in other things; to understand...

***

*...the universals themselves, it is necessary to look at the particulars and perform an induction <note>Drawing a general conclusion from specific examples.</note>; and when someone is uncertain of the universal, they return to the experience of particulars. One who understands also investigates; or if they forget, they return to the sense for certainty. Therefore, the whole of human science resides in the sense—not in the physical organ itself, but in the sensing **spirit** within it, which is fit to retain and compare the things apprehended by the organs.*

# On Judgment.

## ARTICLE VII.

After the act of understanding <note>original: "intellectionem"</note> comes Judgment in the Soul, provided that knowledge of the thing is now complete through those qualities which the intellect "reads" within the essence of the thing. The intellect penetrates the object through the sense organs, as well as through preceding sensations, memories, beliefs, and discourse <note>term: discourse <gloss>the step-by-step process of the mind moving from one premise to another to reach a conclusion</gloss></note>. For the intellect is like the "dart" of discourse—either sensory discourse, in which case it draws out a **partial judgment** and gives the thing a name conforming to the knowledge it has; or mental discourse, in which case it draws out a **total judgment**. This total judgment is called a *definition*, a *description*, an *axiom*, a *declaration*, or a *proof*. These are the goals of investigation and the principles of teaching or the theoretical sciences. For a Name is an imperfect definition, but a definition is a perfect name.

However, when an investigation concerns the Will <note>original: "volitiuum"</note>—the goodness or badness of a thing in relation to a goal—that discourse is called an **Examination**, just as in the investigation of truth and falsehood it was called **Reasoning**. An Examination is not made solely from the notions of the senses, faith, and reason; it also involves the "affections" (feelings) of the appetitive organs. These include the stomach and the tongue, as they serve in the approval of food and drink; the genitals, as the appetites for procreation; the bladder and the anus, as the appetites for expulsion; and other things that stimulate these same parts. Physicians even examine the liver and all the vessels of nutrition. Finally, there is the **Will**, which relates to these appetites in the same way that **Reason** relates to the senses. It also considers the faith and memory of others. 

A **partial judgment** follows when only the appetites are consulted; but when the Will is also involved, it is a **total judgment**. For we do not immediately approve of whatever the stomach or the genitals <note>original: "mentula"</note> desire. From these factors, Judgment draws out praise, blame, approvals, and rejections. It forms propositions corresponding to definitions and axioms, which are called **decrees**, the goals of investigation, and the principles of the moral sciences, as well as persuasions and choices.

But when a thing is investigated pertaining to the power of the soul <note>original: "potestatiuum"</note>—such as whether it is possible or impossible, easy or difficult, great or powerful...

<meta>catchword: pon- (likely "ponderatio" or "weighing")</meta>

<summary>Campanella defines judgment as the final step of mental processing, distinguishing between "theoretical" judgment (which seeks truth and definitions) and "moral" judgment (which evaluates goodness based on bodily appetites and the higher Will).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the cognitive process.
