### CHAPTER XVI. PHYSIOLOGY. 191

...weighing whether a thing is small, weak, or light. This mental movement is called **consideration** <note>original: "perpensio"</note> and **commensuration**, by which the **power organs** <term>power organs <gloss>the physical parts of the body used to perform actions or sustain life</gloss></term> are questioned to see what they are capable of and which tasks should be undertaken. These power organs exist either to sustain the machine of our body, such as the bones; or to contain humors and spirits, such as the veins, arteries, spleen, gall, bladder, and intestines; and also the brain and the nerves. In these, the extent of the expulsive, attractive, and retentive powers is weighed. 

The soul also weighs the force of the objects contained within these organs, or the organs used for transformation—such as the liver, heart, stomach, and the "net-like" structure <note>original: "retiforme," likely referring to the *rete mirabile*, a network of blood vessels at the base of the brain once thought to refine vital spirits</note>. Or it considers the organs used for carrying the body; thus the feet are questioned, as is the terrain upon which they must walk. Birds and fish likewise weigh the capacity of their wings and fins. Or the organs are for fighting; and so the mental discourse weighs the strength of the arms, the claws, and the sturdiness of the spine—both one's own and the enemy's alike. 

Indeed, animals <note>original: "bruta"</note> weigh whether their bared teeth, horns, and claws are effective against enemies; if they find them lacking, they flee. Or there are organs for defense, and thus the soul questions the skin, flesh, and hair. Animals also consider their scales, spines, fur, or feathers. 

Man, however, does not only question his natural instruments in these matters, but also those which Art <note>meaning technology or skill</note> has added: such as clothing and armor for defense; the spear and sword for offense; the horse and chariot for transport; and the staff for support. Regarding the organs of internal containment <note>such as the bladder or veins</note>, he has no artificial equivalent; nor does he have them for all the sense organs. For although he has eyeglasses for the eyes and hearing aids for the ears, he has no such "nose-aids" or "genital-aids," etc. 

From this weighing of parts follows a **partial judgment**. But when the soul also questions the powers of the master-faculty <note>the will or the central governing power of the soul</note>, then a **total judgment** emerges, which is called **determination**. This is because it sets the "terminus" or limit of its own powers and those of the object, and it is the end-point of investigation. From this come the concepts of **appreciation** <note>valuing</note>, **under-weighing**, **over-weighing**, and **equal-weighing**. 

These are the principles for the study of economic, military, political, and physical operations. Hence the saying: *One must not fight a lion while unarmed, for the powers are unequal.* Also: *One who fights an equal man cannot be certain of victory; one should only fight a lesser man.* Or: *A weight of a thousand sesterces <note>a Roman unit of value/weight</note> is not to be tackled.* Both the Mechanical and Mathematical arts derive their principles from these determinations, just as the moral arts derive theirs from maxims and decrees, and the theoretical sciences from definitions and theses.

<summary>Campanella explains how the soul performs a "determination"—a final judgment of its own physical and technological capabilities—before acting, serving as the foundation for practical sciences like mechanics and politics.</summary>
<keywords>determination, power organs, consideration, commensuration, self-preservation, technology, partial judgment, total judgment</keywords>

<meta>Continuing from page 191, Campanella concludes his discussion on how the soul "questions" the physical organs (like the feet or arms) and now transitions into the mental process of deciding whether to act based on those physical capacities.</meta>

# F. THOMAS CAMPANELLA

But when it must be decided whether something is to be done or not, the discourse that comes before is called **Counsel** <note>original: "Consilium"</note>. In this process, it is not only the specific organs destined for the execution of the task that are questioned—such as the hands used for crafts, the parts of the body used for pushing or pulling, and the muscles and joints (which are the organs of motion needed by all other organs to carry out their work)—but also the common faculties. Specifically, the sensory, appetitive <note>referring to desires and drives</note>, and power-based faculties are consulted in a partial judgment. Then, in a total judgment, the "notions" of the **cognitive faculty**, the "sentences" of the **volitional faculty** <note>the faculty of the will</note>, and the "determinations" of the **power faculty** <term>power faculty <gloss>original: "potestatiuum"; the mental capacity to exert force or realize an action</gloss></term> are questioned, both regarding themselves and the object at hand. 

From this counsel emerges the judgment called **choice** and **deliberation**. It is called this because it is done freely <note>original: "liberè"</note>, and because it "delivers" or frees the person from the doubt they were investigating. For a human can also rush into action based solely on the passions of the power faculty, the notions of the cognitive faculty, or the feelings of the sensory faculty, just as animals <note>original: "bruta"</note> do; in such a case, one might achieve a good end by mere chance. However, such an operation is called **precipitation**, which is the opposite of consultation, and its deliberation is called a **rash judgment**. 

Therefore, animals do not possess a perfect judgment in all these matters because they lack **Mind** <note>original: "Mente"</note> and **intelligence**. Instead, they have what is called the **estimative power** <term>estimative power <gloss>original: "æstimatiua"; in medieval philosophy, the instinctual ability of animals to perceive "intentions" like danger or utility without reasoning</gloss></term>, which serves them in place of intellect, judgment, and measurement. 

We, however, have used the term "judgment" for that which emerges from reasoning, though it ought to be called **intellect**; and for that which emerges from weighing <note>original: "perpentione"</note>, it should be called **comparison** or **measurement**. For judgment belongs solely to the **volitional faculty**. Indeed, **Justice** is a virtue of the community, judging what good or evil is owed to each person according to their merits. But since "just" is the same as a "due equation" <note>original: "æquatio debita," meaning a proper balance or matching</note>, the term is extended even to the true and the false, and to the possible and the impossible. 

Indeed, our truth is the **equation of the intellect to the thing**, and of the thing to the divine Idea in the divine intellect <note>Campanella is using the classic Scholastic definition of truth as a matching between the mind and reality</note>. Hence, in the Holy Scriptures, justice is also called truth. Similarly, when we measure our own strengths and the nature of things, it is decided whether an attack is "just" or "unjust"—that is, whether it is balanced <note>original: "æquata"</note> against the object. Therefore, our "possibility" is the equation of our power faculty to what is possible, and of what is possible to the divine power. For whatever we are able to do without God is attributed to **impotence**, such as sin in the mind. And when we judge concerning evil and good, we consider whether it is balanced with its "end" <note>its goal or purpose</note> or not, or whether it is contrary to it. We call this thing "evil" and that thing "good" based on whether it serves our own end or the end of the **Commonwealth** <note>original: "Respublica"</note>; to which, in turn, we "adjudge"—that is, we equate—either a punishment or...

### ARTICLE VIII.

<margin>a Images are not physical shapes, but motions of things which are then fashioned by the spirit <term>spirit <gloss>original: "spiritus"; in early modern science, this refers to a subtle, flowing substance in the body that carries sensory information and thoughts</gloss></term> into likenesses of other things. Therefore, those things that lack a likeness cannot be perceived by the imagination unless they are actually seen.</margin>
This cognition is followed by **Imagination**, which is another act of the same spirit. By this act, when the imagination is correct <gloss>a</gloss>, we fashion unknown things from known things—just as we might imagine what England is like by contemplating Sicily. Therefore, the Imaginative faculty is a form of discourse, although it mostly uses a thing as an image rather than the thing itself as perceived by the senses; it is known through discourse, or by the intellect through other things known to it. For example, I fashion a **Centaur** by thinking of how a horse and an armed knight are joined as one. Since things known by thought are more effective when they are more sensible and more corporeal <note>meaning more physical or tangible</note>, the Imaginative faculty usually represents things through bodily shapes. Hence, poets represent the virtues as images of women; and to signify something, they use the imagination to compose and divide things perceived by the senses. This faculty should be given less trust than the other types of cognition, even though it too is an act of the same spirit. Thus, because motions remain in the sensing soul, they are often stirred up in either a mangled or mixed form; this is why we dream of a headless man or a golden mountain. Thus, if the "motion" of a **hen** is stirred within him, he will think he *is* a hen, and will then stubbornly affirm it to be so. This affection is so intense that it does not allow him to recognize other differences or contradictions, which might otherwise allow his reasoning to realize the falsity of such an act. This also happens to the external senses: for a tongue that is bitter because it is flooded with **bile** <note>One of the four "humors" or bodily fluids believed to govern health and temperament</note> perceives everything as bitter. 

As long as he remains in this vain thought, he will assert its truth for as long as the **spirit** persists in that excessive passion. For this reason, men are known to go mad from excessive anger or excessive love. Sometimes, indeed, the **spirit** heats up too much from excessive study, while it is agitated by so many motions while investigating the "uncertain" within the "certain" and "semi-certain." From this, the person is too greatly affected and goes mad; for wanting to return to himself, he cannot, since the **spirit** is now greatly thinned and over-strained. 

Furthermore, if the thin and faint **spirit** is not sufficiently held by a specific motion (due to the heat by which it is thinned and drawn outward), whatever is offered to the senses agitates it. The person passes from one motion to another without stability. All his **discourse** <term>discourse <gloss>the process of logical reasoning or moving from one thought to another</gloss></term> is interrupted for this reason, and because of "sooty vapors" <note>original: "fuligines"; these were thought to be smoky byproducts of bodily heat that clouded the mind</note>, as well as the rapid exhalation and new generation of the **spirit**, as has been said. 

Therefore, such a person is said to be insane and to rage. Indeed, since the **spirit** shrinks in fear from the blackness of these humors, the person seems to see monstrous and terrible things. ## On Dreams.
### ARTICLE IX.

<margin>
a. Aristotle says the **imagination** was given to man so that it might rule him while the other powers of the soul are sleeping. Would it not have been better to give this rule to the **intellect**, which never sleeps? Indeed, reasoning and syllogisms occur while sleeping, which to Aristotle do not seem to belong to the **imagination**, etc. **Dreams** occur in the head, not in the heart, as Aristotle thinks.
</margin>

The **imagination** prevails with great activity, but even more so while sleeping, because whatever humor is exuberant in the head moves the **animal spirit** in various ways. Thus, one troubled by a **choleric humor** <note>associated with yellow bile, heat, and anger</note> dreams that he is fighting. One troubled by heat dreams of being thirsty and consequently remembers fountains. One troubled by **black bile** <note>original: "atrabili" – melancholy</note> sees demons and monsters in his dreams. When vapors have ascended into the head, upon which the **spirit** floats, one dreams of flying and swimming; and if they are divided, with the spirit rushing downward between them, one dreams of falling. Moreover, things we are accustomed to feeling remain in the **memory**, and are excited in a sleeping animal by even the smallest similarity. For this reason, a soldier dreams of waging war, a farmer of plowing, a philosopher of debating, and a lover of the things he loves. Because they are always thinking of these things, they dream of them at the slightest movement of a similar nature, just as a person with a faint sense of sight seems to see an animal in any small sketch on a wall. 

Nor is the **spirit** of the sleeper able to discern whether the things he sees are true, because it resides in the innermost parts of the head; it is not accustomed to knowing things except through the external senses. Therefore, in dreaming, it seems to itself to feel things not inside the head, but outside, where it is accustomed to sensing them. From this it becomes clear that **sensation** occurs by receiving impressions inward <note>original: "intramittendo"</note> and not by sending them outward. Sometimes, however, the dreaming **spirit** simultaneously dreams that it is not dreaming, because of the memory of past dreams excited within it; and it says:

For this reason, many animals foresee rains and battles: because the beginnings of these things occur in the air, which, being moved by them, consequently moves the animal spirit. And just as the air carries voices to us, so too it carries other impressions. Yet humans, intent on other cares, do not perceive these impressions, and therefore they do not sense future effects beforehand. **Melancholics**, however, being endowed with a very thin and capable **spirit**, for which reason they avoid the company of others, [perceive these things more] easily...

For when it is hot, it affects us with anger; when clear and bright, with joy; when cloudy, with sadness; when agitated, with fury; when thick, with sleep; and it often forces us to seek out and consult the inner rooms of houses, etc. Impressions of this kind penetrate even to the immortal **mind** <note>original: "mentem" – for Campanella, the "Mens" is the highest, immortal part of the soul, distinct from the "spiritus," which is a subtle physical vapor</note> which is free from corruption, in which resides **free will** <term>liberum arbitrium: the capacity to choose or refuse an action, which Campanella argues remains free even from celestial influences</term> of willing and not willing, and of resisting or believing such impressions flowing from the heavens. And in this mind occurs **supernatural prophecy** through the communication of the **First Wisdom** <note>original: "Primæ Sapientiæ" – a reference to God as the source of all knowledge</note>, which is more intimate to the mind than the air is to the corporeal spirit, which is the seat of **natural prophecy**,

OF PHYSIOLOGY. CHAPTER 17.

# *On the Special and Organic Faculties of Appetite.*

## C H A P T E R XVII.

From what has been said, it is clear that the whole **spirit** <term>spirit: a thin, warm substance that Campanella believed acted as the primary instrument of the soul, flowing through the body to enable movement and sensation</term> desires, but it does so through the **appetitive** [faculty] <note>original: "appetitiuo" — the faculty of "appetite" or innate drive</note>; just as it perceives through the **cognitive** [faculty], and acts through the **potent** [faculty]. But it exercises special modes of desiring through special **Appetitive organs** <note>original: "Appetitoriis organis"</note>, for the eternal will has ordained it so, in order that the Mind, the spirit, and the **material body** <note>original: "organica moles" — literally, the organic mass</note> might live together. Although wherever there is **attraction**, **retention**, and **expulsion**, appetitive powers are present; for they indicate by attraction a love for things necessary and useful, by expulsion a hatred for things superfluous and harmful, and by retention an enjoyment of things selected; and these are present in every limb, just as sense is: however, we do not locate special appetitive modes everywhere, except where special objects and organs indicate them. And since an Animal either desires that by which what is continuously lost may be restored—as if a medicine for mortality; or selects the profitable from the useless, once it has satisfied the first appetite; or hates the useless and expels it; or, conscious of its failing nature, intends to preserve it in another through propagation; therefore, since these must be exercised through organs, it was necessary to fashion as many **appetitive systems**. First, therefore, is the appetitive system of **ingestion**, such as the stomach. Second, of **digestion**, such as the belly, liver, and heart. Third, of **egestion** <note>egestion: the process of discharging undigested food or waste</note>, such as the anus and bladder. Fourth, of **generation**, such as the genitals.

### *On the appetite for ingestion, or hunger and thirst.*

### A R T I C L E I.

The first mode of desiring is **Hunger**. It is exercised through the stomach as its proper organ. It arises from the sense of suction and the power of sucking and eating. For we have said that every **appetite** <term>appetite: in this context, any innate impulse to seek life-sustaining things or avoid harm</term> arises from sense and power; but sense arises from power alone. For the cognitive faculty does not sense anything except what it can or

From this, the **spirit** <term>spirit: the vital, subtle substance that Campanella believes mediates between the soul and the physical body</term> residing in the fibers and nerves of the stomach feels discomfort; therefore, to remove this pain, it desires to fill the vessel. This appetite is hunger. If such a sensation of discomfort, and the faculty for fleeing [pain] and seeking nourishment, did not precede it, hunger would not occur.

The object [of hunger] is not everything that fills, but that which fills and can be transformed into the things that are fleeting <note>original: "res fugentes" — the substances of the body that are constantly being used up or "fleeing" through heat and movement</note>. For we do not hunger for earth nor metal, but for the parts of living things similar to ourselves—for plants, too, are living things—and not just any parts, but those usefully convertible. Soon the ingested thing that was desired grows warm and hardens by the approach of the spirit and the union of the stomach for its **cooking** <term>cooking: "coctio," the standard term for digestion, which was viewed as a process of ripening or boiling food using the body's internal heat</term>; and then thirst follows. Thirst is the appetite for liquid nourishment, arising from a sensation of acidity and heat, and from the power of boiling down solid food and distributing it through a penetrating and liquefying liquid, as was said before. Therefore, a warm drink is beneficial for digestion, separation, and distribution, provided the heat of the food has not become excessive by accident, thus bringing about a balanced temperament. How the stomach draws in, sends away, and retains food by means of straight, transverse, and oblique fibers has been said before; since appetite consists of love, hatred, and enjoyment, three types of fibers and faculties are enumerated for that reason.

### *On the Types of Subsequent Hunger.*

The second hunger and thirst together, like that of a nursing infant, is in the liver; arising from a sense of its own emptiness and its **blood-making power** <term>blood-making power: "potentia sanguificativa," the liver's specific function in Galenic physiology to turn "chyle" from the stomach into blood</term>. The object is not the whole of the nourishment from the first digestion, but the part more suited for blood-making. This is carried out through the attraction of the **mesenteric veins** <note>original: "mesaraicarum" — the veins that carry nutrients from the intestines to the liver</note>. Soon, when the digestion is finished and the liver has taken what it desired, it transmits the rest through the vena cava to other hungry parts; the waste, however, it sends into the vessels that hunger for waste. The heart does the same from a hunger for blood arising in it from a sense of emptiness and dryness,

->*On the Digestive Appetite.*<-

->ARTICLE II.<-

Digestion occurs through **cooking** <term>cooking: "coctio," the standard Renaissance term for digestion, viewed as a process of refining substances through heat</term>. Insofar as this process is transformative, it belongs to the faculty of "power"; insofar as it does not transform all things indiscriminately, it belongs to "appetite." For every limb incorporates into itself only that which it desires as being "like" itself; then, through a kind of "hatred," it expels what is superfluous and dissimilar, rejecting it toward other limbs that might desire it because it is "like" them. Therefore, the sequestration <note>original: "sequestratio" — the separation of nutrients from waste</note> in every cooking is performed by the "love" and "hate" of the members—moving toward what is desired and away from what is not. Retention is caused by pleasure, for there is a sense of a present and preserving good. 

Conservation is either a remaining "whole and entire," as seen in the Mind and the angels, or a "continual restoration," as seen in the spirit and the body. Attraction is achieved by suction and the constriction of fibers inward; repulsion is achieved by constriction outward. It is just as when we squeeze our fingers: we expel cherry pits if we squeeze outward, and we draw them in if we squeeze inward. All heat, produced from the very substance of its own limb, assimilates the nourishment to the nourished part through cooking; this is done by a specific faculty of appetite and sense, through a process of selection. Indeed, if there were no dissimilarity in the food, no selection would take place.

Since all love is simultaneously a hatred of the opposite object, every part expels through hatred just as it attracts through love. But the primary organ of the expulsive appetite is the Anus <note>original: "Anus"</note>, just as the stomach is the organ for attracting. For feces are gathered in the rectum once every useful part has been sucked out by the veins. These feces, by their bitterness and weight, burden and embitter the spirit residing in the fibers,

The heart is also celebrated in this duty, as it expels sooty vapors and the blood. The brain emits its own excrements through the sensory organs. Even sneezing, anger, and fever are commanded by the expulsive appetite and are carried out by the power of the spirit, just like any other work of the body.

## On beauty, in passing.

### ARTICLE 5.

<margin>a Therefore, beautiful things please us because they represent preservation, while deformed things represent destruction. Thus, the lame, the sick, and the elderly frighten us because they remind us of our own mortality. A man hardly loves a beautiful woman more for any other reason than that the seed is preserved more safely and better in her than in an ugly woman, and the offspring is rendered more excellent. A young man is loved for the same reason. Beauty in art consists in imitation, which preserves us by imitating nature; therefore, an old woman painted by an excellent painter is more beautiful than a young girl painted by an unskilled one, because the former is a sign of superior art. Thus, Dante’s *Inferno*, which he imitates more excellently, is more beautiful than his *Paradiso*, which he describes with less mastery. In the same way, nature makes things beautiful when it successfully imitates the Divine Idea. Therefore, beauty is the "flower of the Good," whether natural or artificial.</margin>
**F**or every good thing, *a* whether for itself or for others, is beautiful to those for whom it is good; since beauty is the outward appearance of goodness. Goodness consists in the power and Wisdom innate to things. Therefore, beauty signifies that the power implanted in the body was well able and knew how to build it; thus, beauty consists in the stature of the body, in strength, agility, proportion of parts, and vividness of colors. Therefore, neither a Pygmy can ever be called beautiful, nor a woman <note>Campanella is reflecting a common Aristotelian view of his time, which defined the "perfect" human form by male proportions; he views anything departing from that ideal as a lack of "strength"</note>, nor one with a missing hand, nor one with a twisted or oversized nose, nor the filthy, nor the old, nor the sick: because in all these, something is missing—a sign of strength, or of their own Wisdom, or of the formative cause <term>formative cause: "causa formatrix," the internal natural force or "blueprint" that shapes a living being according to its type</term>.

<summary>Campanella argues that reproduction is driven by a love for immortality rather than a need to expel waste, and defines beauty as a physical sign of "goodness" and biological strength. <meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter 17, where Campanella argues that beauty is not merely a superficial quality, but a biological signifier that guides the "generative appetite" toward the best partners for the preservation of the species.</meta>

F. THOMAS CAMPANELLA

Charm, then, is the outward appearance of beauty, which consists in movement, in speech, and in the visual prospect of the beautiful; it is, as it were, the flower of beauty, just as beauty itself is the flower of goodness. We have been speaking of relative human beauty, according to which even a donkey is beautiful to a donkey, a snake to a snake, and the wound of an enemy is "beautiful" to his foe. Likewise, gray hair is beautiful as a sign of wisdom, but as a sign of decay, it is deformed. We are not, however, speaking of true and absolute beauty, which is mostly simple, like light—the evidence of solar power—and like divine beauty. The beauties of all things are certain translucent flowers of the divine goodness shining through the mass of their physical forms; and of this goodness, man is the most sacred compendium. For this reason, the beauty of things made by human art consists in the imitation of the thing itself, just as the beauty of a natural thing consists in the imitation of the Idea <note>original: "Idea"; referring to the Platonic "Forms," the perfect spiritual blueprints of things in the mind of God</note>. Therefore, the painting of a little old woman by an excellent painter is more beautiful than a painting of Diana <note>The Roman goddess of the hunt, typically depicted as the pinnacle of youthful female beauty</note> by an unskilled one, because the former is a sign of more excellent art. Moreover, we are preserved by art. And Preservation is the highest Good, in respect to which all other things are called "good." The signs and appearances of these goods are "beauties." They are lovable for this reason: because they display preservation or things that preserve. In the same way, ugliness is hateful because it is an indication of destruction, or of things that are in some way destructive.

*f* Aristotle’s opinion is foolish: that the seed is not the substance of the fetus but only the active agent. This is proven by placing ten eggs under a brooding hen and breaking one each day to observe. Having exited the womb, the infant is not suddenly nourished by just any food, but by that which is most similar to itself—that is, food that is tender and soft. Since, indeed, **f** the bones, nerves, membranes, and all the white and bloodless parts were formed from the white seed, while the bloody and red parts—such as the liver, heart, and flesh—were formed from pure female blood (not the menstrual kind), the infant is therefore nourished by things similar to its own parts from its very origin. This substance is the mother’s milk; it is made from the pure blood that previously nourished the fetus, which is then drawn into the breasts by divine skill, as the breasts correspond to the womb. There, once it has been "cooked" <note>In Renaissance medicine, "concoction" or "cooking" was the process by which the body refined nutrients into higher substances like blood or milk</note> by the work of the arteries, veins, and many fibers, it is taken into the mammary glands, refined, and turns white. From here it is sucked out by the fetus, prompted by the ancient counsel of the **First Idea** <note>Campanella uses the term "First Idea" to refer to the primordial divine intelligence that provides the "program" or "blueprint" for all natural instincts</note>. Every **g** newborn animal likewise turns to suckle something from its mother, just as plants turn toward their mother, the Earth. However, animals born from eggs, which are already sequestered from the mother, do not turn back to her, but rather to the "common mother" [the environment] for the sake of drawing nourishment.

Those animals which are **Egg-layers** <note>original: *Ovipara*</note>, by divine command, must produce and nourish many offspring at once, and they cannot mature them all inside their internal organs; for this reason, they emit them surrounded by membranes—first one, then a second—which soon harden. Afterward, however, they **h** bring them to life with their own heat (just like the seeds of plants) or by external heat, and they rouse the spirit within. *f* Aristotle’s opinion is foolish: that the seed is not the substance of the fetus, but only the agent; since the seed of a plant turns into the plant, and the white parts of a chick are made from the white of the egg. Matter does not have a soul hidden within itself; nor can the seed act if it is not alive. Nor would it preserve the "motion" of the parent; for a stick that has been moved (the example Aristotle uses) loses its motion once it is let go, but the motion of the seed is always growing stronger, prevailing in its movement and in the skillful shaping of the fetus. # *On the passions of the soul arising from the volitional and the powerful.*
## CHAPTER XIX.
### ARTICLE I.

<margin>a Since appetite is born from cognition, pleasure and pain—which are the attendants of appetite—are also senses. See Metaphysics, part 2. But they are senses causally, not formally; for in this way they are affects <note>original: "affectus" - the "feelings" or "dispositions" that move the soul</note>.</margin>

Since all cognitions of Living Beings are motions imprinted by objects—whether those objects are present or absent, acting either through themselves or through their likenesses—and since these are given for the preservation of the composed living workmanship; and since preservation does not happen by itself, but is acquired by the pursuit of good and the flight from evil; it follows that, just as memories, reasoning, acts of intellect, and imaginations are born from sense, so too do certain affections toward good and evil arise in the spirit <note>original: "spiritus" - for Campanella, this is a thin, warm, vaporous substance that carries life and sensation throughout the body</note> from pleasure (which is an affect following the principle of Appetite upon sensing a present good) and from pain (which is an affection of the sense when a present, joined evil is felt), whether these are present, absent, or mixed.

Pleasure and Pain are indeed instilled in the Animal like two stimuli, and like two scouts of Evil and Good; without them, the animal would suddenly perish. For it would not eat without pleasure; nor without hunger, which is a pain,

[...so it] is, it would seek food; nor would it flee fire, or serpents, or other harmful things, unless there were pain: nor would it pursue sexual union <note>original: "Venerem" - Venus, used here to mean procreation or sexual desire</note>, nor food, nor other goods that preserve it, unless it were drawn by pleasure. Therefore, Pleasure and Pain are the primary scouts and the final causes <term>final cause: the ultimate purpose or goal for which something exists or is done</term> of the Wisdom and Love involved in the preservation of every being. Pleasure is thus called the Feeling <note>original: "Affectus" - the "feelings" or "dispositions" that move the soul</note> following the sensation of a good joined to the sensing power, which is followed simultaneously by enjoyment <note>original: "fruitio"</note>, an internal knowledge that preserves and expands the being who enjoys it.

<margin>St. Thomas [Aquinas], part 2, question 5. St. Irenaeus, book 3.</margin>
So too the Mind, when deeply immersed in God, enjoys the pleasure arising simultaneously from the union of the known good and the knower, since enjoyment is a sense—or the offspring of a sense—that tastes the good joined to itself. Desire, however, is causally (by way of final causality) a certain pleasure for an absent good, and a tendency toward it. <margin>b Since sight and hearing receive objects from a distance, with respect to them things are called beautiful. But to smell, taste, and touch—because they have the object within themselves—it is called "good" and not "beautiful." Thus the beloved good of procreation <note>original: "Veneris"</note>, when it is granted to be enjoyed, is called a pleasant good; but when it is desired, it is called beautiful. And when it is said that a "joined good" is loved, this is only said insofar as that which is not present is loved; that is, the persistence of future enjoyment, not present enjoyment as something already present.</margin> The same *b* seems to be true of Love, even if it includes more. Therefore its object is beauty, which is the appearance of the good. And because Love is the desire of the soul leaning toward the beloved thing, and a thing is loved insofar as it is known to be good (whether truly or falsely)—and goodness is known by its appearance, which is beauty itself—for this reason we are said to Love the beautiful, but to Enjoy the good. This Love is called Appetite in the spirit <note>original: "spiritu" - the thin, warm physiological vapor that Campanella believed mediated between the body and the soul</note>, but in the Mind it is called Will. Properly, it is a desire for immortality: for this is preservation, eternity. We love food so that we may be preserved in ourselves; but we love sexual union and fame as remedies against mortality, which cannot be avoided by food alone forever.

When the good is absent, and the spirit—trusting in some argument—thinks it will acquire it: then this pleasure of an absent good, tasted beforehand in its sensation, is called Hope, the offspring of power <note>original: "potestatiui proles" - referring to the soul's power to act and achieve its goals</note>. It is also implanted in the Mind, which hopes for the truly good, which it infers from mortal goods.

Confidence is usually the precursor to hope. For in its own strengths or those of others, it senses beforehand the good to be acquired.

### CHAPTER XIX OF THE PHYSIOLOGICS.
<sig>Dd</sig>

When one doubts this, either through a lack of one's own strength or the lack of others', it is called **Distrust** <note>original: "Diffidentia"</note>; and **Fear** <note>original: "Timor"</note> follows it. This is born from **Pain** and **Impotence**, when the Spirit <term>spirit: for Campanella, "spiritus" is a thin, warm, vaporous substance that acts as the primary instrument of the soul, moving through the nerves to produce sensation and action</term> considers itself unfit to attain a goal, or perceives a difficulty on the part of the beloved good. This fear is called **Jealousy** <note>original: "Zelotypia"</note> when one fears that another might acquire for themselves the good that we love; it is an argument for one's own inferiority in virtue, or a distrust toward the object, or the instability of the object in returning love, or its smallness and insufficiency to satisfy many lovers. For this reason, **Divine Love**, whose object is most sufficient and not partial, lacks the pain of jealousy; it joins lovers together rather than dissolving their bond.

**Pain** is therefore the other source of the passions, and it is the feeling <note>original: "affectus"</note> arising from the sense of a present evil joined to the one suffering; **Hatred** <note>original: "odium"</note> depends on this, being the abomination of an absent evil and the flight from it. Its object is **Deformity** <note>original: "Turpitudo"</note>, the appearance of evil, just as **Beauty** <note>original: "Pulchritudo"</note> is the appearance of Good.

But when an evil is imminent, this kind of pain is called **Dread** <note>original: "Pauor"</note>: for **Fear** is pain due to the lack of a good, but **Dread** is caused by the evil itself. Hence, when we dread, the spirit flees into the internal parts; the eyes remain small, and the nerves tremble because only a small amount of spirit remains to move them; the face turns pale and the hair stands on end. This happens because, as the warm spirit departs inward, the skin is constricted and the hairs are raised, just as a fleece is when pressed at its edge. A sense of cold arises there because of the lack of heat from which the spirit has fled.

Furthermore, if the spirit does not yield to the evil, but girds itself to repel it, this feeling is called **Anger** <note>original: "Ira"</note>: which occurs by the spirit gathering itself against the evil. Hence the eyes burn, the nerves are stretched, and the blood boils as the spirit is impetuously agitated toward vengeance.

Pain and pleasure arising in us from the evils and goods of others are derived from these same principles; so too are laughter and weeping.

<margin>c Joy occurs with the expansion and increase of the spirit; Pain with its constriction and decrease. For in the former, the expanded spirit grows toward the good, while in the latter it decreases, fleeing from evil and forcing itself together, etc.</margin>
**Joy** *c* and **Sadness** are also derivatives of pleasure and pain...

<summary>Campanella defines the negative passions—distrust, fear, jealousy, and anger—as physical reactions of the "spirit" (spiritus) to perceived evil or the lack of good. He provides a proto-scientific explanation for physical symptoms like trembling, paleness, and goosebumps as the body's internal spirit fleeing from external threats.</summary>

...great displays <note>original: "ostensiones grandes"</note>. When the Spirit is breathed out, it moves entirely outward, flowing to the eyes as if to its windows, where it may show itself as blessed; it makes the eyes bright and clear with its own light, and the skin serene, transparent, and plump—full of itself—by increasing, dilating, and amplifying itself. And often it flows out with such great force when an unexpected good arrives that the Spirit, becoming too abundant and impetuous in a narrow space, is suffocated and dies <note>Campanella refers to the classical medical belief that sudden, intense joy could cause fatal syncope by over-expanding the vital spirits</note>. Those in sorrow, on the other hand, gather their spirits into their internal parts, being averse to being seen in their unhappiness; therefore their eyes appear small, their skin wrinkled and dark, their nerves limp, and their limbs and voice low, for the spirit is indeed departing and turning away from view.

### *On Laughter*

### ARTICLE II.

When the Spirit <term>spirit: the subtle, vaporous substance that mediates between the soul and the body</term> perceives something good, it spreads out and laughs. Thus, **Laughter** can be called the dilation of the spirits, manifest in the lips, which are pulled toward the jaws by the abundance of spirits rushing to dilate themselves within the muscles and nerves proceeding from the **fourth pair** <term>fourth pair: in early anatomy, this referred to the nerves controlling facial expression and sensation, though modern numbering differs</term>. 

Sometimes one laughs unwillingly, even when no good has arrived to cause dilation; but rather when one is poked in the more exposed and thinner parts, such as under the sole of the foot or in the sides, where there is much spirit and where much harm could be suffered because one is more exposed to injury there. While the spirit tries to flee inward and cannot, it rushes outward; it dilates into laughter, rejoicing that it is not being as badly affected by that rubbing <note>original: "confricatione"</note> as it could be, but also resisting the evils there at the same time. **Pleasure**, moreover, consists largely in not feeling detriment from a present evil. But when one is rubbed in those parts by one's own hand, the spirit does not flee, nor does one laugh; for it perceives no fear from itself, and therefore does not rejoice in not suffering harm, since no threat from itself is imminent there.

Beholding the shipwrecks and battles of others without danger to ourselves, we rejoice and laugh <note>This is a reference to a famous passage by the Roman poet Lucretius on the nature of "Schadenfreude" or the relief of the spectator</note>, not because they are suffering, unless they are...

<summary>Campanella explains the physiological mechanics of joy, sorrow, and laughter, defining laughter as the physical "dilation" of the vital spirits in response to perceived good or the absence of expected harm.</summary>

...enemies, in whose misfortune our own good reflects; but this is because we are free from those evils through our own virtue or divine fortune, or because we learn to be cautious. Knowledge, moreover, is sweet, because it preserves us. But to see armed knights and to read the deeds of heroes delights us even to the point of laughter, because they show a strength and virtue that surpasses our own nature—just as contrary things cause us distress. Sometimes a person laughs while another weeps at something which deserves little weeping. Hence the Spirit, which is forced to grieve inwardly by another’s wailing—as if its own evil were being presented in someone similar to itself—eventually notices that the thing for which the other person grieves (and which invites it to grieve) does not truly cause harm. After it has been contracted <note>original: "post ubi contrahitur"; the spirit pulls inward during fear or sadness</note>, it breaks out into laughter by expanding itself and refusing to be drawn inward by another’s contraction; it rejoices in its own virtue, not knowing how to fear what others fear and weep for. Thus also sometimes, after it has grieved and simultaneously considered that there is no cause for grief, it suddenly expands into laughter. At other times, even when it sees that a situation cannot be countered by any skill, in what it merely observes, a noble spirit laughs.

### *On Wonder and Laughter Together.*

<margin>a Laughter is not an effect of wonder, as the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: the followers of Aristotle, who defined humans as "the only animals that laugh"</term> believe, but its opposite. Those who wonder more, see less. Nor is it a passion of reason; for the foolish laugh more, and children laugh before they have use of reason.</margin>
Laughter sometimes occurs after wonder <term>admiratio: in this period, this refers to a state of being startled or struck by the novelty of a thing</term>, which is its <insert>a</insert> opposite. For wonder is a gathering together of spirits united to behold a new and great thing. For this reason, the eyebrows are arched and the eyelids are opened wide, so that the thing perceived might enter the contemplating Soul as something worthy of consideration. But when the Spirit has understood it well and recognized it, it then rejoices that it knows the thing, expands, and laughs—doing so to compensate for its previous constriction and to refresh itself after the labor of consideration. But if it ever recognizes that the thing was not worthy of the attention previously given to it, it blames its own ignorance and sluggishness and becomes sad. Nevertheless, if it suddenly realizes that the thing is not worthy of wonder, it laughs, as if despising both the thing and those who wonder at it, rejoicing that it knew better and did not succumb to it. And expansion <note>original: "dilatatio"</note> is the life of subtle things <note>referring to the spiritus, which is a subtle, vaporous substance</note>; therefore, laughter is greatly sought after.

<summary>Campanella explains laughter as a physical expansion of the vital spirits that occurs when the mind realizes it is safe from a perceived threat or has successfully understood a complex object of wonder. He argues against the Aristotelian view, suggesting that laughter is a release of tension following the "constriction" of focused study or empathy.</summary>

<margin>b Comedy is pleasing and beautiful because it is a sign of human art consisting in imitation; in this, every human rejoices in what is similar to themselves, because our common nature senses what is good. Unless, of course, an impure person grieves out of envy: for a pure person rejoices in the goods of others as if they were their own—unless the possessor is wicked, unworthy, etc.</margin>
Thus in b **Comedies**, when we see or hear something presented as wonderful—which later does not result in the outcome that was proposed, but turns into an industrious wit—we are accustomed to laugh for that very reason, and because of the Artifice, which is a sign of the knowledge that preserves us, and is therefore greatly pleasing. Alternatively, if it results in a foolish end due to laziness, we laugh—not because another is lazy, but because we recognize and experience that we are more skillful in that matter and can perform better. Or, we laugh because we wisely detect the follies of those who are considered industrious. We also laugh whenever wonder ceases at any monstrous thing, or because we emerge more learned.

# On Weeping.
## ARTICLE III.

Weeping arises from contrary causes. It is a gathering of the spirits <note>In early modern physiology, "spirits" (spiritus) were thin, subtle vapors produced by the blood that acted as the medium between the soul and the body</note> which flee inward so that they do not appear miserable on the outside if any evil occurs. By contracting themselves, they discharge moisture into the eyes; this moisture is formed outside the membrane of the brain from vapors that cannot be drawn out through the skull. Therefore, these vapors are squeezed into water which—being compressed and stirred by the spirit that has contracted (and which therefore lifts the brain and its tunics)—rushes out through the membrane into the sockets of the eyes.

<margin>a In the misfortunes of others, there is mercy; in our own, there is sadness.</margin>
Sudden joy also triggers weeping, as the spirits, moved to fly outward, are simultaneously pulled back inward so they are not suffocated <note>Campanella suggests that extreme joy can be so overwhelming that the body’s "spirit" retreats for self-preservation, causing a physical reaction similar to grief</note>. Also, by observing and thinking about a our own or others' hardships, a very similar contraction produces a similar weeping. Many people are gifted with an excessively moist brain and a powerful, easily imaginative spirit; by drawing themselves inward, such a person produces weeping whenever they wish by perceiving and imagining sorrowful things.

## *On Execution, or Organic Works.*

### CHAPTER 20.

After the Affections follows Execution, which is the extension of the Affections toward their objects, just as an Affection is an extension of a faculty; a Faculty, however, is the extension or relation of the essence toward external things.

It is also called Operation, a term which signifies the internal emanations of the <term>Primalities</term> <note>Campanella’s term for the three fundamental principles of being: Power, Wisdom, and Love.</note>; it also signifies the Acts arising immediately from the affected primalities, as well as the external Actions which the Animal puts forth through certain organs.

Therefore, just as the most holy <term>Monotriad</term> <note>A term for God, representing Unity in Trinity, who endows living things with three basic capacities: the ability to act, to sense, and to desire.</note> adorned the animal with organs for Power, Sensation, and Appetite, so too did it provide organs of Execution, which serve all the aforementioned capacities. For we execute what we are able to do, what we know, and what we will, in order to attain their objects.

Therefore, since we execute everything through motion, the organs of motion are also generally the organs of execution: namely, the Muscles and the joints of the bones. For through the muscles, dilation and constriction occur, with the spirit carrying its own mass into the belly of the muscle or into its extremities; through the joints, flexion, extension, and rotation occur, as was stated in the description of their structure. The internal sensory and appetitive organs use the muscles to draw in and expel; the organs of power and the external parts of the body's frame use the joints, as is clear from what has been said. Hence, however many joints of the bones there are—which act as centers of motion—and however many vertebrae, there are just as many partial...

<summary>Campanella defines "Execution" as the physical fulfillment of internal emotions and desires, explaining how the body's "spirit" uses muscles and joints to act upon the world. He links these biological functions to his philosophical system of the three "Primalities": Power, Wisdom, and Love.</summary>

...are the executory organs. But neither does bending occur without a dilating muscle, nor does the extension of joined parts occur without that same muscle. The spirit <note>In Campanella’s philosophy, the "spirit" is a subtle, physical vapor that acts as the intermediary between the soul and the body.</note> performs this action because it possesses a underlying thinness that is swiftly obedient to any impulse—whether for making a union, for inflating, or for withdrawing. For nothing else moves another thing physically if it does not move itself, nor does it know another thing if it is ignorant of itself.

Heat, however, moves this thinness <note>The airy substance of the spirit.</note> both formally and effectively. It moves toward a specific object because it desires it; it desires it because it senses it; it senses it because it is capable of acting and suffering <note>In the philosophical sense, "suffering" (*pati*) refers to being acted upon or receiving an impression from the outside world.</note>. It suffers because it is of a finite nature; it acts because it is a participant in divine power. Therefore, all motion is from God. For both the first volition, the first knowledge, and the first essential power <note>Campanella refers here to his "Primalities": Power, Wisdom, and Love.</note>—from which these accidental versions arise—come from God, the founder of essence. <margin>a. Aristotle also recognized new motions from a divine cause in his books *On Forms* <note>original: *de For.*</note>, which he wrongly denies in the *Metaphysics* because he denies the origin of things.</margin> From Him, many things are sent anew.

# On the Means of Conveyance.
## ARTICLE I.

There are only two specific executory organs in Man: the Foot and the Hand; in beasts, the same organs exist, or something analogous to them. For all execution looks either toward the flight from evil or the pursuit of good (among things known to be possible), and this is performed organically by the foot; or it looks toward the handling of external things, applying them to our uses, and this is done by the hand.

Regarding the structure of the feet and the use of its parts, we spoke when we celebrated the structure of the Animal. We also discussed how it is possible for there to be a single eye in Cyclopes, but not a single foot; this is because while an animal moves one foot, it must simultaneously support its posture <note>original: *statuam*</note> with the other so that it does not fall. Indeed, not even a wingless locust <note>original: *bruchus*, which can also mean a caterpillar.</note> could jump with only one foot, unless its weight were awkwardly tilted toward the other side. ...instead of feet, many fish are given fins; birds are given wings; and even if some are footless, they expand the circle of their wings in the air even while sleeping. For Sea Stars <note>original: *Stellæ Marinæ*</note> rotate by their rays, sea urchins by their spines, sponges remain motionless, and others are content with only dilation and constriction. The object of feet <note>Meaning the purpose or goal of locomotion.</note> seems to be the advantageous and the disadvantageous. For whatever we pursue is either a comfortable place, or food, or something knowable, or something conquerable, or something delightful. For indeed, we also pursue an enemy to destroy them, so that our lives may be in safety and our comforts preserved. All these things are declared by the word "advantageous." Regarding the "disadvantageous," there is the useless or harmful place, and things that are hostile, injurious, and vain—that is, those devoid of utility. Therefore, every external thing that is possible, knowable, and desirable is an object of **execution** <note>Campanella uses "execution" (*executio*) to describe the physical fulfillment of a desire or impulse.</note>, which is advantageous either through itself or by accident, and either common or private. Even the disadvantageous "pleases" in a sense, as it is the standard by which the advantageous is measured.

Opposites also belong to the same execution of avoidance, just as the sight of white and black belongs to the same faculty of vision. In pursuit <note>original: *adsecutiva*</note>, we turn the face and the sense organs toward the object as if toward something good and preservative; in avoidance <note>original: *declinativa*</note>, they turn their backs, as if toward something evil, lest the face and the "spirit" of the sense organs be harmed.

**Execution** is sometimes natural, sometimes moral, and sometimes supernatural. **Natural [execution]** occurs as soon as the **Power** <note>original: *Potestas*. One of Campanella’s three "Primalities" (Power, Wisdom, Love) that constitute all being.</note> is acted upon by an object, the cognitive faculty judges the nature of the object from that impression, and the appetitive faculty is affected well or poorly. Then immediately the faculty of Power begins the execution of pursuit or flight. **Moral [execution]** occurs when, after the impression, the notion, and the affection, deliberation is applied based on experiences already had—because not everything that affects us poorly or [well...]

## *On the Tactile Faculty*
<note>original: *De Contrectatiuo*. This refers to the ability to handle, grasp, and manipulate physical objects.</note>

### ARTICLE II.

It is of no help to have reached a comfortable or uncomfortable thing unless you are able to use them for preservation. Therefore, the most holy **Active Mind** <note>In Campanella's philosophy, this refers to God as the ultimate artisan of nature.</note> added the **Hand** as the organ of handling, by which man adapts all things to his own use: stones, metals, plants, the air, the sea, liquids, animals, their parts, flesh, bones, hides, and hair, with admirable skill. Concerning its construction, it was spoken of in its proper place. The double hand corresponds to the two active principles of Nature <note>Campanella often identifies these as "Heat" and "Cold," or more broadly as the principles of Power and Wisdom.</note>; for matter would not be worked by one alone. The exercise of the hands, impressing comfortable forms upon bodies and erasing uncomfortable ones, is called ***Art***: which pours the ideas of the human Mind through the spirit into the hand, and through the hand into matter, in a certain divine manner.

Of these arts, some serve the principle of power, such as **Blacksmithing** <note>original: *Ferraria*</note>; others the principle of knowledge, such as **Printing** <note>original: *Typographia*</note>; others the principle of appetite, such as **Cooking** <note>original: *coquinaria*</note>. Concerning these, a discussion awaits us in the *Ethics* <note>original: *Moralibus*</note>. In certain arts, the foot takes up the work of the hand and serves the hand, as a disciple serves a teacher, eager to become a hand, whenever this...

### CHAPTER XX. OF PHYSIOLOGY

...it will be, even when its use ceases in the next life; for it also possesses its own form. Other exercises that are not strictly "arts" we undertake by the hand: offenses, defenses, expulsions, and applications. For hands attract, retain, and expel on behalf of the **appetitive faculty** <note>The part of the soul responsible for desires and aversions.</note>; they fight and fortify on behalf of the **power faculty**; they mark, erase, speak, weigh, number, measure, and reveal on behalf of the **cognitive faculty**.

The entire Nature of things admires the Hand of man, which brings all things to its own use: taming animals, the winds, and the sea; handling even the unmanageable fire; making day out of night by means of the lamp; and placing the stars beneath his own genius with the **Astrolabe** <note>An ancient astronomical instrument used to map the positions of celestial bodies.</note>.

And **Wisdom** <note>original: *Sapientia*. Campanella often personifies Wisdom as a divine attribute through which God creates.</note> said: "From this, let my bright participation in man be recognized. For I did not give the hand to those who lack knowledge. The Ape has only an imitative use of it, and only for the sake of its belly; so too the Spider and the Crab. Let it be proper to **Man**."

In other beasts, the mouth serves in place of a hand, so that you may understand that only the care of the belly and bodily preservation has been entrusted to them. To Man, however, is entrusted the care of all things which he touches by his hand and through the instruments his hand has fabricated. He does this so that through them he may preserve the contemplation of me, and the memory of his own dignity and dominion over all things—as a Prince for whose sake they exist—in every one of his works. Thus, he may read in his own **workshop** <note>original: *operatorio*</note>, as if in a book, the accusation of his own fault if he should abandon me—who am made so manifest to him in every manual act and inspection—as if I were unknown.

For neither by chance, nor while sleeping, did I decorate the hands with so many rhythms and advantages, nor did I mark anything in vain; just as you yourselves would be indignant if someone said you had drawn even a tiny point or a small letter in your writing without reason or purpose.

Unhappy is he who takes the occasion for failing and erring from the very source where he ought to find progress.

...through participation [in the primalities], and composed it of a very thin, bright, and mobile substance <note>Campanella uses "spirit" here in the Renaissance medical sense: a subtle, vaporous matter that carries life and sensation throughout the body, acting as a bridge between the immaterial soul and the flesh.</note>, and therefore it is dissoluble. 3. Considered inwardly, the Primalities are the essence of the mind; but when considered outwardly, they regard objects and are called faculties or powers. Indeed, as they are directed toward objects through the beginning of actions, they emit passions. These, insofar as they arise from the "power-aspect," are properly called passions; insofar as from the "cognitive-aspect" or wisdom, they are called notions; and insofar as from love, they are called affections. This occurs both in the mind and in the spirit. From these follow outward actions or omissions, which arise from the primalities of "Nothingness" <note>Campanella’s metaphysics posits that all created things are a mixture of Being (from God) and Non-Being (Nothingness). Our limitations—like ignorance or weakness—come from the "Nothingness" part of our composition.</note>—namely, from impotence, ignorance, and a lack of love. But in the spirit, these are called force, sense, and appetite; or the irascible, the cognitive, and the concupiscible <note>The "irascible" faculty deals with anger and defense; the "concupiscible" with desire and pleasure.</note>. In the physical body, they appear as impetus or weight, apprehension, and propensity.

<margin>They are in error who, following Galen <note>Galen was a 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries. For these differ only as partial species, just as mind, spirit, and body do; yet they compose a single individual, just as blood, bone, and flesh do. Likewise, the body, because it is the instrument of the mind and spirit, has other organs serving the operations and affects of the appetite: such as the stomach, liver, and heart for hunger and thirst; the genitals for lust; and the anus, spleen, gall, and bladder for hatred and expulsion. For the cognitive aspect, it has the eyes, ears, nostrils, and tongue (which also serve expulsions). For the power-aspect, it has the solid vessels, but properly the muscles and joints of the bones for execution, as we shall discuss in our *Medicine*.

4. The objects of the power-aspect and its passions are the possible and the impossible. Of the cognitive, the true and the false. Of the appetitive, the good and the evil. This is because a finite being is constituted of Being and Nothingness; and therefore of power and impotence, wisdom and ignorance, love and a lack of love. Thus, there is a double source for passions, notions, and affections, and consequently for action.

# CHAPTER 1 OF MORAL PHILOSOPHY.

<margin>Ec 3</margin>

...it retreats from things not solely through the **power-faculty** <term>potestativo; the soul's innate capacity to act or be acted upon</term>, simply because it can or cannot; nor solely through the **knowledge-faculty** <term>cognoscitivo; the faculty of sense and intellect</term>, because it knows or does not; nor solely through the **will-faculty** <term>volitivo; the faculty of desire</term>, because it loves or hates. Rather, it acts from all of these together, since they are one in their root and essence through an essential identity, even if they appear to vary when directed toward different objects because of some accidental or added quality. It is necessary that all our actions proceed from love and hate regarding what is already known and possible. For we do not love anything unless we first know it to be good; nor do we know anything unless it is necessary or possible for us to do so.

<margin>See on this my *Metaphysics*, part 2, book 1, chapter 11, article 1 and following.</margin>

**6.** And just as love is understood in metaphysics to emanate from wisdom and power, and wisdom from power, so too the **passion** <note>In this context, "passion" refers to an "affect" or a state of being moved or changed by an external object.</note> of love arises from the passion of wisdom and power, and the passion of wisdom from the passion of power; and every action follows this same order.

**7.** Indeed, after we know through the knowledge-faculty that something received in the power-faculty is a "possible good," then the love of such a good follows. But even after we know something is good and we love it, we do not immediately set out to obtain it unless the command of the power-faculty is added. For many people know that observing the law is good, and they love it as something good, yet they do not obey it; "seeing and approving the better path, they follow the worse" <note>original: "videntesque meliora probantesque, deteriora sequuntur." This is a famous classical adage from Ovid, often used by theologians to describe the struggle of the human will.</note>. However, after that command is given, action begins through the forces of the power-faculty, the spirit, the body, and the mind. Thus, just as power is primary in all things, so it is primary in our actions, just as it is in our feelings and our very being.

**8.** Every **action** <term>operatio; the outward exercise of a faculty</term> is either a way to seize a foreknown possible good, or a flight from a foreknown possible evil. Thus, **feeling** <term>affectio; the internal movement of the soul</term> is an action already begun, or rather its origin, as follows from what has been said. Feeling is divided into a beginning, a middle, and an end, during which the emotion usually changes. Hence, love at its root is called *desire*; in the middle of the action, it is called *exaltation*; and at the end, it is called *pleasure* <note>original: "voluptas"</note>. The same applies to other emotions. Regarding evil, at the beginning there is *hatred*; in the middle, *horror*; and at the end, *pain*—this occurs when the object is joined to the faculty that hates it.

**9.** Therefore, the passions of the power-faculty before an attempt is made are: ferocity and weakness, rigidity and flexibility, promptness and sluggishness. In the pursuit of a goal, however, they are: speed and slowness, obstinacy and instability, spiritual sloth <note>original: "acedia"</note> and swiftness, distrust and disregard.

...presumption and despair. In the grasping or obtaining of a good: impulse (or attack) and retreat. In fleeing from or destroying an evil: anger and dread, boldness and fear, cruelty and mercy. For "to imitate" is a mixture of the operations of the power-faculty and the knowledge-faculty.

**11.** The affections of the **appetitive faculty** <term>appetitiui; the faculty of desire and will</term> are called, at their root, love toward the good and hatred toward evil. But because goods are of different kinds, the Appetite receives many names and affections. For we do not love our children and a dog in the same way. Therefore, love toward God is holiness; toward parents and country, charity <note>original: *caritas*; social or familial love</note>; toward wives and women, concupiscence; toward children, affection <note>original: *dilectio*</note>; toward external goods, greed; toward honors, ambition; toward food, hunger...

<meta>This page continues Campanella's exploration of ethics, specifically refining the definition of Virtue. Having previously categorized the passions, he now systematically distinguishes virtue from common philosophical definitions—denying that it is merely a habit, a middle ground (mediocrity), a natural faculty, or simple purity.</meta>

-># FRIAR TOMMASO CAMPANELLA<-

<margin>He denies that men are brave by habit; [the rest is] forgotten.</margin> [A habit] adds ease, brilliance, and manifestation, but it does not give the essence <note>original: *essentiam*</note> to virtue. Similarly, brute animals act virtuously through habituation, yet they are not truly virtuous because they do not derive rules from within themselves. Nor are soldiers called brave because they act bravely out of a custom of winning, but because they act from a rule of choice. Neither God nor the state rewards habits, but rather acts, even those performed before a habit has been established. Likewise,
<margin>Nor is it mediocrity.</margin>
virtue is not a passion placed in mediocrity <note>A critique of the Aristotelian "Golden Mean," which suggests virtue is always the middle path between two extremes</note>. For mediocrity is not of the essence of virtue, since it is necessary sometimes to be affected more, sometimes less, and differently toward different people; and to act accordingly; and sometimes even to cross over into the extreme in many virtues, especially the heroic ones. Rather, virtue is the **rule** of the passions. Indeed, moderate anger is not virtue, but the rule imposed upon anger is virtue. This rule is imposed by its relation to the goal, as we shall soon discuss. Likewise, virtue is not a
<margin>Nor a faculty, as Galen holds.</margin>
faculty <term>facultas; a natural power or ability</term>, although it is more like this than a passion or a habit. Otherwise, all men would be virtuous by nature without a rule, which is nevertheless false in the case of the fearful, the wrathful, and the lustful, to whom the law—which is the virtue of the state—gives rules for acting. And they often fight against themselves and conquer their vices. For even the lustful whip themselves and withhold food. And although they may not acquire the habit of acting virtuously with joy in every respect, they nevertheless act joyfully in the mind alone. For Attilius <note>Marcus Atilius Regulus, the Roman general who famously returned to Carthage to face certain torture and death rather than break his oath</note> while being tortured by the Carthaginians, and Francis <note>St. Francis of Assisi</note> while burying his private parts in the snow <note>An act of extreme asceticism to conquer lust</note>, rejoice in their pains because they act virtuously as conquerors of pain.
<margin>Nor purity, as Telesio holds.</margin>
Nor is virtue purity, except fundamentally. For it makes the possessor good. Just as the purity of gold is the "virtue" of gold, because it consists of such a type and degree of heat, material disposition, weight, and warmth as are required for the constitution of gold in relation to its **Idea**;
<margin>If there were no Idea, one would not know what purity is.</margin>
vice, however, is the lack of such a degree, or the impurity that comes from the mixing of another metal or earth or degree. In this same way, the purity of the **primalities** <term>primalitatum; the fundamental principles of Power, Wisdom, and Love</term> in the mind, spirit, and body—which produces good, that is, preserves the being of a human—appears to be called virtue. And this is true fundamentally. For there are some who are virtuous by nature, so that without any effort they are immediately affected and act according to the rule regarding sexual matters, friends, and property; others, however, are impure by temperament, and do not do these things unless frequently warned, whipped, and compelled, and

<meta>This page continues Campanella’s systematic definition of ethics. Having previously argued that virtue is not merely a habit, a middle ground (the "Golden Mean"), or a natural faculty, he now establishes that virtue requires the active participation of the mind and will, rather than just natural temperament. He transitions from defining what virtue is not to providing formal definitions for virtue, vice, and sin.</meta>

->## CHAPTER I. ON MORALS<-

Purity and impurity exist by nature, as do regularity and deviation in their raw material; however, virtue and vice do not formally exist unless they are exercised through knowledge, choice, and the command of the **primalities** <term>primalitates; Campanella’s core metaphysical concept that all being consists of three "primalities": Power, Wisdom, and Love</term>. Indeed, a lustful man who acts against his lust earns more merit than one who is chaste by nature. Furthermore, a person who is naturally chaste often falls into sin through bad company in matters of physical desire. Therefore, since virtue cannot be placed where there is total impurity—as in the case of the "furious" <note>original: *furiosis*; those suffering from total insanity or madness</note> who are immune from blame for this very reason—virtue must be purity, either in whole or in part, but only as a foundation. Those who possess this measure in their own purity sin if they do not use it. But those who do not possess it, because they are partially impure, sin if they do not adopt the precepts of others and of the commonwealth as their own rule.
<margin>From St. Leo.</margin>
For they dominate both the stars and their own temperament with greater merit than those for whom being virtuous is easy. Indeed, in all things there is love and fear, obedience and disobedience, according to nature: and these things are sufficient even for the impure to achieve virtues, as the Lord said, who denies his help to no one; rather,
<margin>Virtue is not knowledge, as it seems to the Stoics.</margin>
because He runs ahead with help, His precepts are justly urgent. Yet virtue is not the "science" <note>original: *scientia*; the Stoic view that virtue is a form of knowledge or a teachable craft</note> of being affected and of acting. For almost all of us know what ought to be done and how, yet we do not act on it, but instead allow passion to overwhelm our knowledge.
<margin>Nor is it the will, as it seems to Justinian.</margin>
Nor is it simply the will: since many wish for and know the better things, yet follow the worse. Rather, virtue is a **rule** and a **decree** discovered by the **intellectual power** within oneself or externally in others, accepted by the **volitional power**, commanded by the **potent power**, and—as far as is permitted—entrusted to execution and declared and illuminated through action.
<margin>Conclusion: What virtue is.</margin>

<margin>What vice is.</margin>
**Vice**, on the other hand, is a deviation <note>original: *enormitas*; literally a "falling outside the norm or rule"</note> of the affections and actions, directed toward evil as if it were being carried toward a good. Indeed, in every vicious action there is ignorance or inadvertence, and—by interpretation—a hatred of the good and of God. For although I may not want to displease God, the most upright Creator, I nevertheless do that which I know displeases Him, or I refuse to examine whether it might displease Him. If I were to cling to this awareness, I would not sin; just as I would not sin if I looked back at the evils that follow from that forbidden "good." It is also a lack of power toward the better, but a voluntary one. If it were involuntary, it would not be vicious.
<margin>What sin is.</margin>
For **sin** is the placing of a lesser good before a better one, and the voluntary and foreknown abuse of a good,

<sig>Ff</sig>
<meta>catchword: tus,</meta>

<summary>Campanella defines virtue as a deliberate "rule" created by the intellect and commanded by the will, rejecting the Stoic idea that it is merely knowledge. He further defines vice as a deviation toward evil and sin as the conscious choice of a lesser good over a greater one.</summary>
<keywords>virtue, vice, sin, primalities, free will, Stoicism, moral law, St. Leo, intellect, merit</keywords>

--- Page 270 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding the transition from "natural" states (like innate temperament or ignorance) to "moral" states (virtue and vice). Campanella is establishing that moral responsibility requires the active involvement of the will and knowledge, rather than just natural disposition.</meta>

...for ignorance that precedes or accompanies an action excuses an evil act from being a fault. Similarly, inability and the involuntary excuse a person when they are understood negatively <note>meaning a simple absence, such as a stone not being able to speak</note>, but not when they are understood privatively <note>meaning the lack of a quality that should be there, like a human who cannot speak</note> or as a contrary. For example, if someone does not wish to know so that they are not held responsible for acting well, or if they attack what is good as if it were evil because they choose to do so, or because they "cannot" do otherwise, they do not act well; in such a case, the cause of their inability was their own voluntary choice.

Therefore, virtue is perfected through the voluntary, and vice is perfected morally. For before a passion or an operation reaches the will, there are natural states of goodness or badness that lack merit or punishment. However, when they arrive at the voluntary state, they become moral, and they are no longer without merit or blame. This is even more the case if the will is the cause of the subsequent ignorance and inability through its own action rather than by accident; for the will cannot be the cause of ignorance that precedes it. Thus, the operation of the **primalities** <term>primalitates; Campanella’s metaphysical theory that all beings consist of Power, Wisdom, and Love</term> is circular, such that they both precede and follow one another, as has been said elsewhere. Therefore, just as the process of essentialization is perfected by the "willing" power, so too are passion, operation, virtue, and vice, since nature fundamentally requires and ordains it so. Thus, the mind is the cause and the subject of virtue by its essence; the spirit <note>original: *spiritus*; in Campanella's thought, the "spirit" is the subtle material substance that acts as the intermediary between the soul and the body</note> possesses it by participation; the body possesses it through execution; and passion and operation are the "matter" around which virtue is concerned. The same is true for vices.
