## *On Human Liberty and Morality, etc.*

### ARTICLE II.

1. The question is asked: if being able to do something and knowing good and evil is neither vice nor moral virtue, but rather a natural quality, why then is *willing* good or evil considered virtue and vice, or an act of these? For the will originates from power and knowledge, and the act of willing comes from the act of being able and knowing—and it is not possible to will otherwise. Likewise, if we are moved toward being able, knowing, and willing by external objects, and the will is also moved by the things preceding it in origin—namely power and wisdom—in what way is the will free? And if the will is free, why is "power" not even more free, since it is moved by the object alone, and not by any other preceding **primality**, but by God alone, as is every being? And what is the difference between the "natural" and the "moral"?

2. A work or an agent is called "moral" because it generates in us a "custom" <note>original: *morem*; the root of the word "moral"</note> of living, that is, a method and a reason based on habit...

<summary>Campanella argues that moral responsibility only exists when the will is involved, distinguishing between natural traits and moral virtues. He raises the problem of free will, questioning how the will can be free if it is dependent on the "primalities" of Power and Wisdom.</summary>

### CHAPTER I ON MORALS ###
Ff 2

<meta>catchword: pec-</meta>

...[to be] maintained by us within ourselves, and with our fellows, and with the **state** <note>original: "respublica"; referring to the political community or commonwealth</note>, and with God, and with the things we require. For no man is born for himself alone, but for God and the state, and for parents, and for children, and for friends; otherwise, he would have no need for external things, nor God, nor the world, nor his peers—which is impossible. It is also called **morals** <note>original: "morale"</note> because we are not able to be affected or to act as we ought toward ourselves and the things already mentioned as soon as we are born; rather, this happens after much habituation with external things, and then truly when the **mind** <note>original: "mens"</note> begins to be unburdened from the business of the bodily framework, and is able to rule the **spirit** <note>original: "spiritum"; in Campanella’s philosophy, the subtle material substance that connects the soul to the body</note> in which it is wrapped, and to discern between a true good and what is not true. This is said to happen generally in the **seventh year** <note>The "age of reason," a threshold in legal and theological tradition</note>; for some earlier, for others later. 

Whatever deed occurs before this emergence of the mind is considered **natural**; as is whatever happens in us suddenly, without the application of the mind's consideration. For this reason, infants—whom we see to be somewhat envious, angry, and lying even at three years old, and especially at five—and those who, though grown, deviate from the rule of living by a first, ungovernable impulse of the will, do not transgress **morally**, but in a certain natural way. This is just as when fire burns grain, or a madman strips himself naked, or a dog breaks a pot, or a mouse gnaws a sacred book; they do not know what evil lies hidden in these acts, but are following their own impulse and first pleasure. 

For nature is determined toward one thing, nor is it turned from it by any persuasion, except by the impulse of God. Therefore, not only do **power** and **intellect** <note>referring to two of Campanella's "Primalities"</note> sin naturally and work well [naturally], but the **will** does so as well when it is carried along in the manner of nature. In the same way, we say that moral sin does not exist in the first volition—when the act of the will flows from power and wisdom—but in the second, and in 그 at time when a person has already learned that evil is mixed with good, and that one should not immediately seize whatever good or pleasure is offered, but must examine whether evil lies hidden within it. 

Hence, the infant **Moses** <note>A reference to a Midrashic legend where the infant Moses chooses a glowing coal over a crown to prove his lack of seditious intent to Pharaoh</note>, delighted by the light of the fire, put coals to his mouth; but once he experienced that the burning was repeatedly destructive, he did not handle fire in that way again. 

<margin>morally</margin>

If, however, having been actually warned, he had handled it again, then he who at first [sinned] naturally...

<summary>Campanella defines morality as a developmental state reached when the mind begins to govern natural impulses, typically around age seven. He distinguishes between "natural" faults—committed by children, animals, or the mad without knowledge of evil—and "moral" sins, which involve a deliberate choice by the will after the mind has learned to discern hidden evils.</summary>

<header>FR. TOMMASO CAMPANELLA</header>

...[has] sinned naturally. For this reason, in the faculty of **power** <note>original: "potestatiuo"</note> and in the **intellect** <note>original: "intellectiuo"</note>, as well as in the **will** <note>original: "volitiuo"</note>, an action is a moral sin or a moral justice when the cause of our powerlessness and ignorance is a choice not to examine what we are capable of, or a fleeing from that which gives us the ability to do good. Therefore, we say that the powerlessness and ignorance that follow a deliberate choice <note>original: "voluntatem secundam"; a secondary act of will following the initial impulse</note>—and are thus willed, at least in an interpretive sense <note>original: "interpretatiuè"; meaning that even if not directly intended, the responsibility is implied by one's actions</note>—do not excuse a crime but aggravate it. Conversely, their opposites increase the merit of a good work. 

Indeed, he who gets drunk for the purpose of doing evil, or who knows that evil deeds usually happen because of drunkenness (even if he does not get drunk specifically to commit them), still sins and increases his sin; but he sins even more who does it specifically for that purpose. This is how all those sin who allow themselves to be weighed down by the passions of fear, love, anger, and so on, and do not immediately resist the temptation. Thus, we are warned to **resist the beginnings** <note>original: "principiis obstare"; a classical maxim from Ovid, advising to stop an impulse before it gains momentum</note> and to turn our eyes away from another's maiden, lest the growing affection carry the mind away with it. For this reason, only a "preceding" ignorance and powerlessness—that is, those not caused by our own will—provide an excuse; for in these cases, the fault is natural, just as it is in the preceding will. But this excuse does not apply to the "following" powerlessness, ignorance, and choices that we ourselves have caused.

3. We also say that essential **power**, **wisdom**, and **love** cannot be moved to their own act by external objects. Instead, they possess that act naturally within themselves and outside of time, such that wisdom proceeds from power, and love from both of them, following the imitation of the first holy **Monotriad** <note>original: "Monotriadis"; Campanella’s core metaphysical concept that Being is composed of three "primalities": Power, Wisdom, and Love</note>. I have recently expressed this secret in my *Metaphysics*. 

To perform external acts, however, they go forth together as one thing adorned with three aspects. Therefore, **faculties** are the outward flows and aspects of the essence. **Passions**, **notions**, and **affections** are the extensions of these faculties toward external objects. Finally, **operations** are the extensions of the passions toward either the grasping or the shunning of those objects. For this reason, objects do not move our faculties "objectively" <note>meaning the object is not the primary cause of the faculty's existence</note>. We are not capable simply because we are moved by what is possible, nor do we know simply because we are moved by what is knowable, nor do we will simply because we are moved by what is desirable. Rather, these propensities emanate from our innermost essentials. Nevertheless, they are specified and made particular by objects, so that we choose this and not...

<summary>Campanella argues that ignorance and weakness only excuse a sin if they are not self-imposed, using drunkenness as a primary example. He then explains his "Monotriad" theory, stating that Power, Wisdom, and Love are internal essentials that move outward toward objects rather than being created by them.</summary>

# MORAL PHILOSOPHY, CHAPTER 1

...let us approach that capacity to be able, to know, and to will <note>original: "posse, scire, & velle"; these are Campanella's three "Primalities"—the fundamental principles of all being: Power, Knowledge, and Love/Will</note>. For a stone does not produce the knowledge of a stone within us, since the stone itself is senseless, neither teaching anything nor intending to teach; nor does a shadow create fear in us, since the shadow itself does not intend it, nor is it able to think. Rather, the object offers us an occasion for turning and particularizing our innate knowledge and fear toward those things. Similarly, a teacher teaches by proposing objects to the mind, but not by infusing knowledge itself. 

Therefore, we live free from the control of external objects, since we are not moved by them to the exercise of our faculties, but rather to the **specification** of the acts of our **primalities** <note>Meaning external things don't give us the *power* to act, but they provide the *specific direction* for our innate power, knowledge, and will</note>; and we are able to recall our actions and turn them toward other objects. <margin>The error of the Stoics.</margin> Those who say that the **affections** <note>original: "affectiones"; the passions or emotions</note> are sicknesses are in error. For if hunger were a sickness, or the love of children and friends, it would follow that all sciences, and joys concerning God and things that are good and true, and even our powers themselves, would be sicknesses. Yet these things were given by nature for our preservation, so much so that we cannot live without them. They only become sicknesses when they "exorbitate" or wander out of their proper bounds. For vice is a sickness of the soul, whereas virtue is its health. 

Freedom, therefore, does not reside in the will alone, but in the intellect, and also in power, once the first impulses have passed. For it is within my power to will to go to Rome, to learn how to go to Rome, and to be able to go by making use of a horse. For this reason, it is called the **free choice of power** <note>original: "liberum potestatis arbitrium"</note>. And although the mind is specified and invited by external objects, it remains within the mind's power to follow them or not to follow them, to believe or not to believe. Likewise, when many good things are proposed, the mind pursues that which is better and greater. But when things are equally good, it weighs within itself which one inclines toward the better; and then, without hesitation, it approaches that one. It can also pursue a lesser good because it considers that thing as "greater" in that it is obtained with less labor, or more quickly, or is joined to a more powerful immediate pleasure. 

From this, we know that man is free in willing and nilling, in the good, and in the knowledge and power of the good, but not always in the execution or in the suffering of things. For there are as many opposing things as can overcome him and turn him away from execution; and there are as many more powerful things as can disturb and hinder him. Indeed, even weaker things can do this: for a single flea can take away the good of sleep and of health.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of human agency. Having previously established that external objects provide the "specification" for our innate powers rather than controlling them, Campanella now categorizes the different types of natural and voluntary actions to define exactly what constitutes "free will" compared to the behavior of animals, children, or enslaved people.</meta>

# [FRIAR TOMMASO CAMPANELLA]

<margin>
Remarkable
distinctions.
165.
</margin>

4. Furthermore, the **natural** <term>naturale; that which follows the ordinary course or laws of the world</term> is distinguished from the **preternatural** <term>præternaturale; something that happens outside the usual course of nature, though not necessarily a miracle—such as a medical anomaly or a physical rarity</term>. This distinction is twofold: one arises from the **intrinsic essence** <note>original: "intrinseca essentia"; the internal "what-ness" of a thing</note>, such as fire having the power to heat; the other arises from the **natural order of things**, such as a man being burned when he is in a fire. The preternatural is divided in the same two ways. Again, the natural is divided into the **necessary** and the **contingent** <term>contingens; something that could happen or not happen, depending on circumstances</term>. Both of these are similarly divided into those that come from within and those that come from the order of things. For instance, it is necessary "from within" for a triangle to have three angles, but it is contingent "from within" for a thing to be made of wood. According to the order of things, it is necessary for water to fall out of a flask that is turned upside down; yet it may happen <note>original: "contingit"; it is contingent</note> that it does not fall when it is held back by the force of a vacuum.

Furthermore, of the necessary and the contingent, one type is **spontaneous** and the other is **coerced**. The spontaneous arises from within and is always an internal leaning, such as a stone sinking or a dog going toward a hare—even though they are invited by the object. The coerced comes from without, such as a man or wood being burned, or a stone being thrown upward. Again, the spontaneous is divided into the **free** and the **servile**. The free is led by itself, and for its own sake; the servile is led by another, and for the sake of that other. For this reason, slaves <note>original: "serui"</note> lack **free will** <term>libero arbitrio; the capacity to choose between different courses of action</term> in part, because they are led by a master to deliberate in one specific way and not another. In natural matters, however, they are free from servitude, though not from necessity. He is truly free from both who is able to deliberate about himself, and to will or not will by his own guidance rather than another’s, and to draw out an act of willing and of knowing by himself, even when not invited by external objects. For this reason, dogs and infants are not free in this way, even if they are spontaneous; they are moved by objects toward passions and acts, and they do not refrain from following or fleeing these things unless they are invited by other, stronger objects or driven by active causes. Man, however, draws out for himself **syllogistic reasons** <note>original: "syllogisticè rationes"; logical arguments consisting of premises and a conclusion</note> for pursuing or desisting. And although he is led by God going before him in good acts, and by God accompanying him in bad acts (insofar as they are acts of being), he is not for that reason a slave. He is able not to follow, and he often strives against even **supernatural grace**, rejecting it even when he possesses it, let alone when it is offered. For God does not desert us unless He is first deserted—matters which are discussed in **theology**. Nor is a son a slave for following the guidance of his father. Indeed, we are moved by God as sons. Therefore, to depart from the rule of virtue within us comes from our power when it is in excess, and from our weakness when it is in defect.

<summary>Campanella categorizes natural actions into necessary, contingent, spontaneous, and coerced, eventually defining human freedom as the logical ability to deliberate and act for one's own sake, distinct from the impulse-driven behavior of animals.</summary>

...destroyed, physically. He who commits a sin becomes a slave to passion, such as greed or anger. And yet he is free, because he wills it. Even when people throw cargo into the sea against their initial preference <note>original: "non sponte"; a classic ethical example of a "mixed" action where one chooses a lesser evil under pressure</note>, they throw it freely so they do not drown. They could also choose not to throw it, but that would be to no purpose. Thus the greedy man could choose not to seize wealth, and usefully so, yet he does not wish it, giving more weight to his appetite than to his will. In supernatural matters, however, one cannot cease [sinning] meritoriously <term>meritorie; in a way that earns spiritual merit or God's favor</term> except by the special help of God. But for natural merit, God’s general influence is sufficient. It is more important, however, to stop demeriting <note>original: "demereri"; to lose favor or act wrongly</note> further.

## *On happiness and the highest good, the distinction of human goods, and the operation of virtue and vice.*

### ARTICLE III.

1. All beings seek their own **happiness**. It is certain that happiness is the goal for the sake of which all affections and operations are performed. These are done for the **preservation of their own being** <note>original: "sui ipsorum esse conseruationem"; a central tenet in Campanella’s philosophy that everything strives to persist in existence</note>. Therefore, one’s own being or life is happiness for each individual, which consists in the possession of the highest good possible for them. For this reason, things tend toward their natural places where they may be preserved in the company of what is similar and related to them: earthy things toward the earth, waters to the sea, and fires toward the sun <note>Campanella follows the ancient view that elements have "natural places" they seek to return to for their own safety</note>; and they fight against things destructive to their being, while seeking out those things that preserve it. It is clear that happiness is held within oneself and not in another. Otherwise, if it were in something else better, then all things would desire to be destroyed and converted into that better thing. Thus earth and water and trees and stones would strive to turn themselves into fire and the sun—as a more noble being—by killing themselves, if they could. But in truth, it is not so: instead, they fight against fire and hate everything destructive, even if it is better than themselves. Moreover, they consider themselves blessed when they have been placed in a safe location, far from opposites and full of friendly things. For all being is a **participation in the Divine**; for that reason, it is most lovable...

<meta>catchword: to itself [sibi]</meta>

<summary>Campanella argues that the fundamental drive of all beings—from humans to inanimate elements—is self-preservation, which he equates with happiness. He further discusses the nature of the will, explaining that even when acting under pressure, a human remains "free" because they choose the action to preserve their own life.</summary>

...for itself; so that everything may be content and happy. And just as God is eternal, so all things desire to be made eternal. And since they cannot achieve this in themselves, they seek remedies in offspring, which are a second version of themselves.

And finally, because things do not exist for their own sake, they preserve themselves for the sake of that for which they do exist. For although trees bear fruit for themselves, so that they may be made eternal through successive generations, they nevertheless benefit the animals that feed on them. Other animals, in turn, serve as food for others. But all things exist for the sake of man. If, however, man exists for the sake of other higher beings, he will not be made eternal in himself for his own sake, but for theirs; or he will die completely. Just as a flock is sold, killed, or shorn for the sake of the shepherd.

<margin>+</margin> 2. Human preservation seems to be threefold: in oneself, in one's children, and in one's fame. And a fourth is believed to exist after death in God. Whether this state is evidently believable or only believable as a matter of opinion, the human race wavers. But truth cries out on behalf of man. For if stones are preserved in themselves, since they resist harm through their hardness; and plants are preserved in themselves and in their offspring because, being more fragile, they have provided for themselves through succession by the nature of God <note>original: "natu Dei"; this refers to the divinely established natural order of reproduction and growth</note>; and animals even in honor—for lions and elephants, when deprived of honor, have been known to kill themselves, and horses seem to be desirous of glory—it remains that for man, a far more divine preservation in God is appropriate. It is man, after all, who subdues animals far more powerful than himself by the aid of his mind, and has subjected the sea, the winds, the compass <term>pyxides; literally "boxes," here referring to the nautical compass used for navigation</term>, and the heavens to his own ingenuity. <margin><unclear>mark</unclear></margin>

For although, while we look upon the mortal body and all its organs made for physical preservation (as we taught in the previous sections), it may seem devoid of a better hope; nevertheless, if you look at the mind, it raises itself infinitely above all physical things through understanding and desire. It subjects all things of the heavens, earth, and sea to its own ingenuity, and climbs toward God, and glories in His fellowship and friendship. This is demonstrated through miracles above nature, through teachings, through the prophecy of future events, and through martyrdom—by which man scorns physical life, trusting in a more divine one. This is not like the beasts, which kill themselves out of despair of living well when they are deprived of certain things they love. Then you will clearly understand that man can attain another eternal life, one not swarming with disturbances and miseries like the present one. Just as when seeing a long piece of wood, rather...

In the same way, in the highest part of man, if you look at his immortal mind, you will certainly understand that an immortal preservation is owed to him, which God—who does not lie—calls **eternal life**. To deny this history is more impudent and insane than to deny the histories of **Caesar**, **Livy**, and **Sallust**, or **Columbus’s** announcement concerning the discovery of the other hemisphere. <note>Campanella argues that the evidence for the soul's immortality and the historical record of divine revelation is as factually certain as the Roman histories or the recent voyages of Christopher Columbus.</note> However, how this mind will also bless the body when it is clothed in immortality is not the place for discussion here. 3. The **highest good** and **happiness** <note>original: "Summum bonum & beatitudinem"</note> must be the same in God. Since the preservation, eternity, and tranquility of His being is not from another being but from Himself, therefore, for Him, "to be" is the same as "to be happy." Indeed, for all other things, even if the preservation of their own being is their happiness, nevertheless, since they do not preserve themselves, their highest good is not the same as themselves. Rather, it is that by which they are made happy—that is, the source in which they are preserved in a state of tranquil being. For this reason, seeking again what the **highest good of man** is, we find it to be God, who gives and preserves being in all things. But He is not known among mortal things except by man, who alone is a **religious animal**. No other creature inquires into what God and the angels are; nor does any other boast of their patronage and fellowship as man does, who proves this even by his own deification, ecstasy, prophecy, and miracles. Indeed, no being seeks or finds a good that does not suit it; and if it finds it, it does not recognize it—just as a chicken neglects a gemstone. Therefore, just as other beings direct their affections toward that good by which they are immediately preserved—as the donkey toward the meadow and the she-ass, water toward the sea, the bee toward flowers—so man, by directing his own affections and operations toward God, will be best preserved. For this reason, we have said that **virtue** is the rule that directs the passions and operations toward the acquisition of the good.

4. If, therefore, the **highest good** is that which has no evil mixed into it, is perfect in itself, lacks nothing, and is the end-point of all desires and actions—so that those who possess it desire nothing more, as everyone says—and if all things are called "good" by analogy to it, because they are its effects, signs, preparations, or pathways: it follows that God is the **highest good**. Our own existence is not the highest good, for we lack so many things and are mixed with so many evils; possessing ourselves does not make us blessed unless we cling to the **highest good** from which our existence flows. Just as fire, therefore, does not consider itself blessed unless it returns to the sun, its origin; so too a human being is not blessed except in God. Therefore, a person should not love God for their own sake, but rather love themselves for God’s sake, just as a part exists for the sake of the whole. For when a person desires to be always and everywhere and to be all things, to be able to know all things, and to enjoy all things, they are actually desiring to be God. Since this cannot happen through our own essence, it is right that we should be <term>deified</term> <note>original: "deificetur"; the process of becoming god-like through union with the Divine.</note> through participation and fellowship with God. <margin>Aristotle in the *Ethics*.</margin> Unhappy are those who think that friendship cannot be forged between man and God. For since they deny that things are created by God, they do not understand that just as He created us without needing us, so He stoops down to us in friendship and raises us to Himself out of His own goodness.

5. All beings are **metaphysically** good; only non-being is evil. For things are good to themselves, to the world, and to God, from whom they share in goodness. **Physically**, however, not all things are good for everyone, but rather those things are good for an individual which preserve them, while those things that destroy them are evil. For this reason, the "goods" of a human being in a physical sense are three-fold:

*   **Goods of the Mind:** Such as power, intellect, and will, and the virtues and affections arising from these by which the mind is preserved. These are called <term>honorable goods</term> <note>original: "bona honesta"</note> because of the honor owed to them and because they preserve our reputation. The "evils" of the mind are weakness, foolishness, hatred, and vice.
*   **Goods of the Body:** Such as health, beauty, strength, and the organic life of the body. The opposites are evils, such as sickness, deformity, weakness, and death.
*   **External Goods:** Those things that serve the mind and body, which are called **useful** because of their use. These include wealth, servants, positions of power, children, and a wife. We use some of these for ourselves, some for our reputation, and some for our legacy to achieve bodily happiness. The corresponding evils are poverty, slavery, and bereavement.

As for **pleasurable goods**, none are good in themselves unless they are also useful or honorable. Fol-

For the feeling of delight follows the perception of a possessed good. Hence, we find delight even in a prostitute, insofar as there is a utility for procreation in her. In a sin against nature, however, others find pleasure insofar as they hold an image of a useful good, even if it is mixed with dishonorable evils. And the depraved sense of a sick person even finds delight in his own evils, just as those suffering from <term>pica</term> <note>original: "cittam"; a medical condition where a person craves non-nutritive substances like coal or clay</note> delight in coals. However, that which is "pleasant" in and of itself is not found apart from the "useful" and the "honorable." Even in play, the <term>expansion of the spirits</term> <note>original: "spiritus dilatatio"; a contemporary medical-philosophical idea that joy physically expands the vital "spirits" within the body</note> and joy is useful, and therefore pleasant, even though it is mixed with uselessness and loss. It is the role of virtue to choose those goods which are pure, or at least less impure—that is, less mixed with evils. For in a moral sense, nothing is "good" or "evil" except by its use or abuse, as we shall soon discuss.

6. <margin>Wealth is not the highest good, as Bias claims.</margin> From these points, it is clear that blessedness is not drawn from external goods. For these things are outside of us and are teeming with miseries; and he who abounds in gold and slaves, if he is ignorant or sick, either does not know how to use them or is unable to do so. It is also foolish to think that a human being, endowed with the highest intellect and sublimity of will, could be made blessed by things inferior to himself—things lacking sense, reason, or a more divine power. For every single thing is preserved in happiness by things better than itself, <margin>Nor honor, as the Romans thought.</margin> not by those that are worse. Nor is honor a good that makes one blessed, since it does not reside within us, but in those who honor us, and it stands in need of them (whereas a blessed person does not stand in need of inferior things). Furthermore, honor is often given to the unworthy; it is a testimony of blessedness that follows it like an effect, rather than preceding it as a goal—but sometimes this testimony is false, and it is never blessedness itself. <margin>Nor domination, as the Machiavellians think.</margin> Nor is domination the highest good, as others think, since it requires many things, depends on others, can fail, and does not become "good" except through virtue. <margin>Nor the goods of the body.</margin> Nor does blessedness lie in the goods of the body, though it is found in these more than in external things. For it is better to be healthy and robust than to be wealthy and sick. But even these bodily goods require the wisdom of the soul to be useful, and they require external goods to be preserved. Moreover, being beautiful or strong has often been a hindrance to people. Therefore, the body is not the highest good, nor the source of blessedness. <margin>Nor virtue, as the Stoics claim.</margin> Those, however, who think we are made blessed by the goods of the mind are closer to the mark. For virtue makes good use of all the goods of the body and mind; and by its use, things become good, just as by vice they become evil. Nevertheless, because virtue does not possess eternal life within itself, but hopes for it from elsewhere, it is clear 

<summary>Campanella argues that true happiness (blessedness) cannot be found in external wealth, social honor, political power, or physical health, as these are all inferior to the human soul or dependent on others. Even virtue, while the highest earthly good, is not the ultimate end because it points toward an eternal life beyond itself.</summary>

# BROTHER TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

<margin>Boethus</margin>
...is not to make us blessed, but to lead us to the Good that makes us blessed. Those who say that happiness is a state perfected by the gathering of all goods of the body, soul, and fortune, speak most correctly—provided they are speaking of preservation in ourselves, in our children, in our reputation, and in God simultaneously. 
<margin>Where the highest good is found.</margin>
But since all forms of preservation fail except in God, all must be directed toward God. Thus, a person should not live for himself, but for God; he should not beget children except for God; nor should he cultivate friends and honors except in God, nor sciences and virtues, except to obtain God as much as possible. In God, there exists, in an eminent way, a state perfected by the gathering of all goods.

<margin>Aristotle does not correctly define "activity" as blessedness.</margin>
7. Therefore, those who say that blessedness consists in activity—just as a lyre-player’s excellence consists in playing the lyre well, so a human’s consists in contemplating—are mistaken. <note>Campanella is critiquing Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics*, which argues that happiness is "activity in accordance with virtue."</note> For a human being does not exist for the sake of the activity, as if he were a lyre or a tool; rather, the activity exists for the sake of preserving the human being in God. Thus, blessedness is eternal life itself, and not the activity, except as a consequence of that life. 
<margin>How the highest good makes us blessed.</margin>
We receive this life communicated to us through the grasping of the highest good. This occurs through the <term>power-principle</term> <note>original: "potestativum"; Campanella believes all being is composed of three "primalities": Power, Wisdom, and Love. Here, Power is the capacity to reach or "touch" the divine object.</note>; for unless you first reach the object, you cannot know it. It also occurs through knowledge via the <term>intellect-principle</term>, and through enjoyment via the <term>will-principle</term>. In this state, pleasure does not disturb the soul, nor is it merely a fleeting taste as it is in this life, but it calms and perfects. Nor can there be blessedness unless all the <term>primalities</term> are equally poured out into the supremely good object, so that they may live a higher life; we have discussed this matter in our *Theology*. 

At present, it is enough to know that the blessed person is one who possesses all things, knows all things, and enjoys all things simultaneously. This cannot occur except in God, known through His essence and joined to us. This happens supernaturally in heavenly blessedness; but in a natural sense, it will occur in a transformed world that represents God and all things without any mixture of evils. Expel evil from the world, and we will all be naturally blessed. Likewise, even if we were not destined to obtain any other blessedness, God must be held as the highest good and the giver of all goods.

<margin>From St. Chrysostom and all the Church Fathers, who—like the Stoics, but in a moral sense—regard nothing as good or evil [except virtue/vice]. This is overlooked by those who treat "goods" physically alongside the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note>, and who oppose St. Augustine.</margin>
8. Finally, it is necessary to know that, speaking morally, no thing is good or bad for us in itself: but only virtue is good, along with its works...

...nature, vice alone is evil, along with its works. All other things are indifferent <note>original: "indifferentia"; a Stoic term for things that are neither inherently good nor bad, like wealth or health</note>, depending on whether we use them well and virtuously, or poorly and viciously. We cannot use virtue badly, nor can we use vice well, since these are good or bad in their very use. Therefore, honor can be evil for those who use it poorly, and children can be an evil, and riches can be gathered to the ruin of their master. Even life, health, and beauty are bad if we use them viciously. On the other hand, poverty, infamy, death, and infirmity can become good things if they are handled and embraced virtuously. Is not Regulus <note>Marcus Atilius Regulus, a Roman general who chose to return to Carthage to face certain torture and death rather than break his word</note> better in his torture than Sardanapalus <note>An Assyrian king legendary for his decadent and self-indulgent lifestyle</note> at his sumptuous table? 

<margin>Against Epicurus and Muhammad.</margin> Is not the burning of Scaevola <note>Mucius Scaevola, a Roman hero who famously burned his own right hand to prove his resolve</note> more blessed than the pleasures of Thais <note>A famous Athenian courtesan often used in literature as a symbol of worldly lust</note>? It is indeed shameful to argue with those who place human happiness—which they share with the beasts—in the pleasure of the body, and view the virtues merely as paths to reach that pleasure. As if we eat so that we might take pleasure, and not rather so that we might live! As if wars, martyrdoms, and sciences were held in price and honor only for the sake of obtaining the titillation of the belly and the genitals.

Pleasure is the sensing of a good affection; and the highest, true, and stable pleasure is in the Highest Good which makes us blessed. But the pleasure found in the belly and the genitals does not belong to a "blessing" good, but to a "medicating" good <note>Campanella views physical pleasure as a temporary relief or "medicine" for the "sickness" of hunger or the need for procreation</note> for the individual and the species. For this reason, it often ends suddenly in sadness. If happiness ends, and ends badly, it is not true happiness. Who would not consider Lawrence <note>Saint Lawrence, a martyr who was famously roasted alive on a gridiron</note> more blessed in his torments—and indeed even Alexander in battle—than Nero in the embrace of Poppaea? We can even abuse pleasure. But a "Good" is that which we cannot use badly, and which renders all things good by its application. And thus, virtue alone is good, because it is the good use of things; and vice is evil, because it is the bad use. 

Even God, if we were to abuse Him externally (for we cannot do so internally), would become an evil to us. For as His Prophet said to Him: 
<margin>David, Psalm 18.</margin> *With the holy you will be holy, and with the perverse you will be perverted.* <note>original Latin: "Cum sanctis sanctus eris, & cum peruerso peruerteris."</note> 
<margin>Bernard in "On Consideration."</margin> And another divine man said: *God is no less the glory of the good than He is the punishment of the wicked.* For His divine righteousness, when it runs up against our malice, does not endure it without punishing it. Yet not all punishment is evil. For that which is medicinal is good. That which is a perpetual punishment is evil.

<margin>
The Marcionites <note>A 2nd-century sect that believed the God of the Old Testament was an evil or inferior creator, distinct from the benevolent God of the New Testament.</note> who make God out to be evil.

...[He] cannot be morally evil toward us because He is just, as certain unhappy men have claimed; rather, He is good. For justice is a good thing and a virtue, as will soon be made clear. Virtue is virtue because it comes from Him and directs us toward Him. Therefore, it is good because it originates from Him. It is a shameful thing to suggest that the rule is better than the Regulator <note>original: "Regulatore"; here meaning God as the source of all laws and order</note>.

9. But if virtue is the rule, how does the mind come to know it? It is known from God, who regulates us from within, and from the goal <note>original: "fine"; the 'end' or purpose of an action</note>, which shows itself from without. For when you perform actions and experience passions that are consistent with your goal, you act virtuously. For example, in our own self-preservation, when you eat the types and amounts of food that are sufficient for a healthy appetite to maintain life, you are **sober**. If you eat more, you are **gluttonous**; then nature punishes you with indigestion, sleepiness, laziness, and the other evils born of gluttony. When you eat less, you are punished with wasting away, fever, and the torment of hunger. Therefore, since nature provides punishments for vicious operations and rewards for virtuous ones, we must conclude that God, as the author of nature, does the same when He gives us laws and rules.

10. A good action and a good affection is called <term>Justice</term> <note>meaning "Equity" or "Rightness" in this context</note>, because it is made equal to its goal. In common speech, we call "just" whatever is equal to the thing for the sake of which it is applied. A bad action, however, is called a **sin** or an **error**, because it stretches outside the rule. For an act to be virtuous—whether it is an internal affection or an external operation—it requires all the causes of its essence and existence to be present. These are the <term>agent cause</term> <note>the person doing the act</note>, the <term>patient cause</term> <note>the person or thing receiving the act</note>, the <term>final cause</term> <note>the purpose</note>, the <term>formal cause</term> <note>the manner of the act</note>, and the <term>ideal cause</term> <note>the mental model or standard</note>; likewise, the proper time and place are required. This harmony we call **decorum** <note>propriety or fitness</note>.

As an example, sexual intercourse fails in the **agent** when it is with someone other than a husband; it fails in the **patient** when with someone other than a wife; it fails in the **goal** when it is not for the sake of procreation (for which the Maker of things established it); it fails in the **form** of the act when it is done "outside the vessel" <note>original: "extra vas"; a common scholastic euphemism for non-procreative sexual acts</note>; it fails in its **ideal** likeness when done in the manner of beasts; the **place** is condemned when it is done in the street; and the **time** when it is done immediately after a meal. Judge all other matters in the same way. Therefore, an act is vicious from the defect of just one cause. For a thing to be good, all its parts must be good; for it to be evil, a single defect is enough.

<margin>
Note well.
</margin>
You will recognize the malice of these five causes in the essence of an act, and two more in its existence: namely, when it goes against the reason of that same virtue, or when it hinders another virtue or its goal, or twists it into a vice. For example, sexual intercourse in the street is against...

### ***On the distinction and number of virtues.***

## ARTICLE IV.

1. <margin>| +</margin> Virtues are distinguished first by their sources. For some are drawn from the **Power** <note>original: "potestativo"; referring to the faculty of the soul associated with power, will, and the "irascible" appetites</note> as rules for its passions and operations. For example, **fortitude** is the rule for fear and audacity, and for the actions that flow from them. **Strenuousness** <note>Vigor or active energy</note> is the rule for weakness and ferocity. **Constancy** is the rule for rigidity and flexibility. **Alacrity** <note>Cheerfulness or readiness</note> is the rule for promptness and sluggishness. **Opportunity** is the rule for speed and slowness. **Perseverance** is the rule for obstinacy and instability. **Longanimity** <note>Patience or long-suffering</note> is the rule for sloth and rashness. **Confidence** (or trust) is the rule for diffidence and low self-esteem. **Hope** is the rule for presumption and despair. **Comprehension** is the rule for exultant outbursts and withdrawal. **Imperiousness** <note>The ability to command</note> is the rule for anger and dread. **Clemency** is the rule for cruelty and mercy <note>meaning excessive or misplaced pity</note>. **Tolerance** is the rule for impatience and insensibility. **Meekness** is the rule for wrath and excessive attachment <note>original: "afinitas"; likely referring to an unhealthy proximity or lack of proper boundaries</note>. **Modesty** <note>original: "verecundia"</note> is the rule for impudence and blushing. **High-mindedness** <note>original: "celsitudo"</note> is the rule for pomposity and contempt. **Diligence** is the rule for negligence and suspicion. **Equability** is the rule for arrogance and self-abasement.

Others are derived from the **Intellect** <note>original: "intellectivo"</note> as rules for its concepts and operations. For instance, **prudence** is the rule for knowledge and ignorance; through **real philosophy** <note>The study of the actual nature of things, rather than just abstract logic</note> it ensures that one does not err regarding the means to an end; through **divine philosophy** <note>Theology or metaphysics</note> it guards the end itself; through **common philosophy**, it guides investigation; through **medicine**, it provides for the preservation of oneself; through **economics**, for the family; and through **politics**, for the republic. **Faith** (or credibility) is the rule for unbelief and gullibility. The **art of memory** is the rule for memory and forgetfulness. **Counsel** and **logic** are the rules for perplexity and rashness. **Grammar**, **Rhetoric**, and **Poetry** are the rules for concealment and...

2. Second, virtues are divided according to the modes of preservation, which is their goal. For some preserve us in ourselves, such as fortitude, exercise, skillfulness, prudence, integrity, liberality, and so on. Others preserve us through our children, such as chastity. Others in our friends, such as **beneficence** (doing good), **benedicence** (speaking well of others), and **good-speaking**. Others in the State, such as justice. Others in God, such as **sublimity** <note>original: "sublimitas"; a highness of spirit or reaching toward the divine</note>, and so on.

3. Third, they are distinguished by their objects when they require a special way of feeling and acting. For the feeling toward sexual matters is one thing, regulated by chastity; that toward food is another, regulated by sobriety. Therefore, it is not proper to combine both into a single virtue of temperance—especially when they happen to be distinguished by the specific people involved. For example, drunkenness is perhaps found among the Germans, and gluttony among the Calabrians <note>Campanella, a native of Calabria, uses these common ethnic stereotypes of the 17th century—German drinking and Italian eating—to illustrate how different vices require different specific virtues</note>; the former concerns drink, the latter food. 4. They are also distinguished by their primacy. For from fortitude, prudence, and holiness, all other virtues simply arise.

MORAL MATTERS, CHAPTER II.

# On holiness and its opposite vice.
## CHAPTER II.
### ARTICLE I.

1. Just as among the physical virtues <note>The author uses "physical" to refer to the natural, innate capacities of a being before the exercise of choice.</note> the first is power, strength, or fortitude—since it preserves the subject first, before the use of free will, and is the offspring of the first principle by its very origin—so, conversely, among moral virtues, the first is that which strengthens the **volitional faculty** <note>original: "volitiuum"; the power of the Will.</note>. In this faculty, the "essentialization" <note>The process by which an action gains its specific character or essence.</note> and the beginning of operations are perfected; it is from here that a return to the prior primary principles reveals morality. For it is not a **moral evil** to mistake the false for the true in the intellect—that is a physical defect—unless it is voluntary. The object of the will is the good, which organizes the "possible" and the "true" toward itself for its own preservation. Nor is the will morally evil except where the intellect is able to distinguish between choices; and the intellect cannot distinguish unless it has the capacity to do so. Therefore, morality exists in three things <note>likely referring to Power, Intellect, and Will</note>, and it is received in the volitional faculty following the physical operations.

<margin>
Plato posited holiness as a virtue, but Aristotle did not; yet Plato did not place it in the first rank as we do, nor did he understand it in the true sense.
</margin>

2. And since virtue makes good things out of "indifferent" things <note>A reference to the Stoic concept of "adiaphora"—things that are neither good nor bad in themselves until directed by the will.</note> insofar as it adapts them to the true and highest end, that virtue is first which establishes for us the **end** <note>original: "finis"; the ultimate goal or purpose.</note> we must follow. All other ends are merely means to this one, and are good only insofar as they serve as means to it; otherwise, I say, they are morally evil. **Holiness**, therefore, is the primary virtue; it ordains <note>original: "sancit"</note> that God is our end, and directs everything back to Him from whom everything comes. Nature itself teaches that all things return to their principles so that they may be preserved by them: waters return to the sea, fires to the sun, and so forth, as one may observe in other natural systems. Since there are so many different opinions regarding the "highest good" and the ultimate end, it must be decreed for man what he is to follow. After long reasoning, we have found nothing else that we might worthily establish as the best end except God, from whom and toward whom all things exist, and by analogy to whom all things are called "good," as we mentioned a little earlier. It is called **holiness** <note>original: "sanctitas"</note> because it *ordains* <note>original: "sancit"</note> the end and "sanctifies" us—that is, it makes us pure and clean from the contamination of wicked ends, their impulses, and wicked works. For every man acts according to his disposition: he who is moved by philosophy acts philosophically; he who is moved by women acts womanly—

<meta>Catchword: —ly (from the Latin "muliebriter")</meta>

<summary>This page establishes holiness as the foundational moral virtue because it defines God as the ultimate goal (end) of human life, mirroring the natural law where all things return to their source.</summary>
<keywords>holiness, moral virtue, ultimate end, God, will, intellect, Plato, Aristotle, ethics</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous section where Campanella established that holiness is the primary moral virtue. He is now explaining how holiness functions as the "ultimate end" that organizes all other human activities, contrasting a life lived for worldly ends (play, wealth, power) with a life lived for God.</meta>

F. TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

...ably <note>The text begins with a word fragment, likely "wholesomely" or "famously."</note>: he who [acts] for games, leads a life of play; he who acts for riches, acts greedily; he who acts for dominion, acts proudly. However, he who acts for God leads a divine life and performs divine operations—and far more so. For the love of the **true good** surpasses the love and affections for false things, if He is loved with the whole heart, the whole mind, and all one's strength, as is required. For we have these faculties from Him; therefore, they exist for His sake. And although a saint performs many actions for his own preservation—in himself, in his species, in the commonwealth, and in his reputation—he nevertheless directs all these things toward God. Thus, he lives his life for God; he procreates children for God, the Father of all; he administers the commonwealth for God, the King of Kings; and he acquires his honors for the most glorious God, from whom he holds the gifts, virtues, opportunities, and fortune for such acquisition. 

In this way, he **sanctifies** the <term>intermediate ends</term> <note>Secondary goals, such as eating or working, that serve as steps toward a final purpose.</note> by relating them to the <term>ultimate end</term> <note>The final, supreme goal of human existence: God.</note>. Without this, unstable things are most vainly established and "sanctified" by others as if they were the final ends themselves. Furthermore, our own fragility reminds us of this. When something good happens to us, it is natural to stretch our hands toward heaven in thanksgiving; when something evil happens, we stretch them to implore help. And since we have nothing from ourselves—not even our very selves—we ought to acknowledge that we have received everything from Him from whom we have our being. 

Therefore, as soon as a man is in control of his mind <margin>St. Thomas Aquinas, part 2</margin> and has received the use of freedom, he is bound to establish a "sanctification" regarding the **end** toward which he directs all his affections and operations, much more so than he is bound to learn the art by which he sustains his life. And even if a man were born in the woods and knew nothing of God, if he were to consider himself and other animals—by whom they were formed, and from where they draw their senses and strength—and the sun and the heavens, from which so many goods come, he would immediately understand his Creator as if from a **public writing** <note>original: "publica scriptura"; Campanella refers to the "Book of Nature," the idea that God’s existence and laws are readable in the physical world without needing a Bible.</note>. To Him, he would dedicate and commend himself. 

<margin>+</margin> For if God builds animals with such great art and deigns to show such great goodness, it is necessary that He not be lacking in that same art and goodness in their governance. For a deed that we do not want to exist <note>original: "esse nolumus"; implying a creation intended to function and fulfill a purpose.</note> is done in vain. Wherefore, He gave to bees the power to recognize flowers from a distance, to make honey, and to build cells, but not to us; to ants, He gave the foresight of gathering; to lions, the hunting by which they live. Indeed, a kid <note>A young goat.</note> recently cut from the womb of its mother knows how to walk alone immediately; and out of many vessels filled with liquids, it knows to taste only the one full of milk, despising and not tasting the others—as witnessed by experience...

<summary>Campanella argues that holiness is the redirection of all human actions toward God, the ultimate end. He uses natural theology to show that even a person in the wild can recognize a Creator through the "Book of Nature" and the specialized instincts given to animals.</summary>

How much more, then, has He bestowed upon man the power to know those things which suit his purpose, and to know that purpose itself, since the human mind comes immediately from God. Thus, the holy man will walk within the world as if within the palace of God; he will honor the Author in all things, and acknowledge that his protection and the goods of his mind, body, and external life come from Him; and he will praise God in His works: he will trust God, believe that God exists, and believe into God.

This is why it is called a **mortal crime**. <note>Commonly known as "mortal sin," a grave turning away from God.</note> Nor do certain people correctly claim that all sins are equal, for the objects, actions, affections, and sources of these sins are unequal. Therefore, just as a traveler who keeps a tower or a light in view at the harbor where he is headed—even if he wanders from the path, yet always keeps his eyes on the tower—eventually reaches it through whatever road, though with much labor; but he who loses sight of the tower fluctuates, is blinded, wanders, and knows not where he goes, arriving only by chance and failing to reach the desired destination: so it is with him who keeps God before his eyes. Although he may err, he does not err unto death, but comes to his senses; realizing that all his deeds, actions, and feelings are in the presence of God, he feels shame and corrects himself. Just like one who stands before a king, he does not sin except in the smallest things, and immediately corrects himself so as not to offend the king's gaze. But he who denies that God exists, or thinks He does not care for human affairs, entangles himself in every crime and falls into countless evils. For this reason alone, believing God and in God is a most useful virtue.

## On Probity, its Opposites, and its Branches.

### ARTICLE II.

1. Having established the rule of affection toward the [ultimate] end, the second rule follows concerning our affection toward ourselves. For although self-love comes before the love of God in terms of acquired and physical knowledge—since the mind, when first placed into the body, does not know God but instead cares for the body's physical structure—nevertheless, innate love for God is prior in the order of nature and time. In reflective thought also, once the use of free will begins and one separates good from evil and the greater from the lesser, the love of God is morally prior. Self-love, therefore, follows after. The rule for this, which was unnamed by the ancient philosophers, may be called **Probity**, or **Goodness**, or **Rectitude**. <note original: "Probitas, vel Bonitas, vel Rectitudo"> For it directly makes a person good to themselves and to others. Indeed, from a right or a perverse love of oneself, there follows a right or perverse love regarding all other things. For to whom will he be good, who is wicked to himself? Probity establishes an order: that a person should love God more than himself, just as one loves the whole and the best more than the part and the inferior. If, however, man were not man by participating in the divine being, but from some other source (which is impossible), he would not be bound to love God more than himself, but at least to value Him as better. Just as if a hand were not a part of the body, but had whatever it possessed from somewhere other than its own "whole," it would not then expose itself to death for the sake of the head and the body as it does. But since the hand's own preservation consists in the preservation of the whole, it rightly prefers the whole to itself. Thus, Rectitude directs man toward God—from whom, in whom, and for whose sake he exists—more than a part belongs to the whole and exists within the whole. Secondly, he will love his soul more than his body, and the goods of the mind more than those of the body; then the body more than external goods. Among external goods, he will even prefer friends—viewing them as parts of his own species—as well as parents, wife, and children, who are even parts of himself. However, he does not prefer the material goods of friends over his own, unless he subordinates his own small gain to a gain ten times greater (or at least five times greater) for his friends. For I would allow myself to lose one unit if a friend gains five, whether in goods of the body, of fortune, or even of the mind. For I gain in <term>charity</term> <note>original: "caritas"; in this context, it refers to a selfless, divinely-inspired love for others</note> and holiness toward God, if I act in this way out of respect for Him...

A person never loses anything if they gain in virtue. However, if they lose their virtue, they never truly gain, even if they were to become the master of the world.

2. **Probity** is divided into several virtues. Since it is a form of self-love, it branches out toward one’s parents (who are the source of one’s being), toward a wife (who is one’s partner), toward children (who are one’s own image), and toward the fatherland (which is the "whole" to which one belongs). From this arise **piety**, **charity**, and **affection**. <note>original: "pietas, caritas, dilectioque"</note> Piety is directed toward parents and the fatherland because both are the origin of our existence; we actually lack specific words to describe this fully. Piety offers reverence and obedience, as well as a more sacred form of devotion because of the dignity of our origins.

<margin>+</margin> We are also bound to stand ready in the times of need of our parents and our country, and to fight for them even unto death. When they commit some injustice, we should admonish them privately out of reverence. We must strive to ensure they live worthily and honor them even after death. We should plant virtues within the fatherland and feel shame for its vices. We must treat the temples, squares, bridges, and all useful parts of the fatherland as if they were our own home, and endeavor to leave the country better than we found it. We should prefer the fatherland over our parents—just as one prefers the whole over a part—when the lives or honor of both are at risk; however, in small matters of utility, we prefer our parents.

<margin>+</margin> 3. **Affection** <note>original: "Dilectio"</note> toward a wife should be as if toward a part of yourself. Therefore, you shall not beat her like a slave, nor shall you insult her, but you shall honor her in all things. Where she errs, you shall correct her mildly—unless she becomes brutish and internalizes dishonor so that she requires the rod. You shall not be unfaithful in marriage. You shall entrust the care of the home to her, commending its preservation to her while taking the acquisition of goods upon yourself. We have discussed the rest of these matters in our writings on household management. <note>original: "æconomicis"</note>

<margin>+</margin> 4. Similarly, the love of children is perhaps called **charity** <note>original: "caritas"</note>—because God’s love toward us, His children, is also called charity. This requires us to provide them with protection and discipline, and to care for their minds, bodies, and fortunes in the same order that we care for our own. This is the same order used for the fatherland and the wife. We have discussed their education in our writings on politics and household management.

5. The opposite of probity is **Wickedness**, <note>original: "Improbitas"</note> which exceeds the proper limit and order of love for oneself and one's own. It occurs when a person loves himself more than God. Consequently, being deprived of God's help, he falls into many evils.

### CHAPTER II. ON MORALS

Sometimes a person even makes himself a god and wishes to be worshipped—just as Alexander <note>Alexander the Great, who demanded the Greek ritual of proskynesis (prostration) and claimed to be the son of Zeus-Ammon.</note>, Nebuchadnezzar, and Solomon <note>original: "Salmon". This likely refers to King Solomon, who fell into idolatry and pride in his later years, or possibly Salmoneus, a mythological king punished for imitating the lightning of Zeus.</note>, having forgotten their own fragility and having been rebuked by punishment, finally restore divinity to God, just as the wicked Antiochus did. <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes, the Seleucid king who notoriously desecrated the Temple in Jerusalem and died a miserable death, which contemporary writers interpreted as divine punishment for his pride.</note> Those who exalt God above themselves with words, saying to Him, "Thy will be done," yet place their own will before the divine will—blinded by a wicked self-love—are also dishonest. Likewise, those who love the body more than the soul become ignorant and weak; while they spare the body from labor, they fail to acquire knowledge and virtue. Others, devoted to beauty and health and industrious in caring for their skin, become a burden to themselves and a laughingstock to others. While they fatten the body, they are impoverished and bury the mind, so that it tastes nothing of the heavenly or the honorable. Also dishonest are those who treat external goods—which are the body's servants—as masters; while they spare those goods, they destroy the body itself. Similarly, there are those who prefer these goods over friends, parents, and the fatherland, as well as over their children and wife. It is clear how many evils spring from this: for they oppress the fatherland with tyranny, stain it with thefts, afflict their parents with poverty, their wife with unchastity, and their children with disgrace.

6. **Impiety** <note>original: "Impietas"</note> arises from this, for it either denies reverence, obedience, and worship, or offers insult, oppression, and injury in their place. We do not have specific terms for the opposites of charity and love, except for the general term "hatred." But their malice is manifest, since such a person treats his wife like a slave or a harlot, and often sells her or divorces her without cause; he "adorns" his children with vices, prostitutes them, or abandons them—from which so many evils fall upon himself and the commonwealth. <note>original: "rempublicam"</note>

7. However, those who love their children, wife, and fatherland more than is fitting—so that they throw away their lives for any trivial cause, observing neither time, place, nor measure—sin less; their vice can be called **zeal**. <note>original: "zelus". Here used in the sense of an over-intense or misguided passion.</note> They err more, however, if they do not desire to acquire true goods for their loved ones, but only pleasures and appearances; this stems from ignorance.

## On obtaining the knowledge needed to acquire the means toward the ultimate goal.

After we have established man in his best goal and have regulated his self-love toward that goal, it is right that we acquire those things that relate to that goal. ## On Studiousness and its Opposites.

### ARTICLE I.

<margin>Those who categorize studiousness as a part of temperance <note>original: "temperantia." Many medieval thinkers, following Thomas Aquinas, placed studiousness under the virtue of temperance as it restrains the "hunger" for knowledge.</note> fail to see that it is elicited from the intellect, not from the appetite, except occasionally in an imperative sense.</margin>

1. Let the rule of this inquiry be called **Studiousness**: which teaches us not to investigate just any things from the very beginning, but those which pertain to our salvation. This includes realizing that God is the author of all good things and the judge of rewards and punishments; that He has given us a law; and that where we are unable to know these things by ourselves, we should consult the learned and our parents. Furthermore, it teaches us what foods, what clothes, and what air are useful for the life of the body; what imitations and actions are necessary for living in the republic; and what we owe to ourselves, our parents, and our friends, and other things of this kind. Only after these should we seek hidden things, or those which are far distant and relate to us only indirectly.

2. Opposed to this virtue is the vice called **curiosity**; namely, when we investigate those things that pertain less to us while abandoning those that do. Examples include wondering how fish walk under the water, what God did before the creation of the world, how a spider weaves its webs, or how flies are caught with birdlime <note>A sticky substance used to trap birds; Campanella is referencing a famous anecdote about the Roman Emperor Domitian, who supposedly spent his hours catching flies with a sharp stylus.</note>—as Domitian used to do. It also applies to those who, having neglected their own duty and art, turn their attention toward the affairs of others, or those who wonder what goats, lizards, monks, and innkeepers do at night, and other such things; they thus pass from actual knowledge into sophisms. And although it is the role of the philosopher to investigate everything—since we cannot understand the whole without understanding all its parts, and such investigation results in praise for the Creator—nevertheless, he should not do this until he has first mastered the useful, nearby, and necessary things. *Wonder* is the beginning of investigation, but it must be ruled by studiousness.

3. He who does not even seek out useful things, as if the knowledge of nothing pertained to him, falls into the vice of **neglect** <note>original: "incuriae"</note>. This is the sign of a base and idle mind, and of a thick and obscure spirit; just as curiosity is the spirit of one who is too thin, vain, unstable, mobile in every direction, and sophistic. He who thinks he has easily found what can scarcely be reached with infinite labor is a fool: such as those who boast that they see God and know angels in their very essence <term>quidditatively: from the Latin "quidditas," meaning to know the "what-ness" or essential nature of a being</term>. Others promise to create gold from quicksilver <term>hydrargyro: mercury</term>, while others promise wonders through necromancy and "curious" opinions as if they were true sciences. Vanity...

BROTHER TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

...their vice becomes an adjunct to curiosity. Some wish to know just so that they may know; these are the **curious**. Others wish to be known; these are the **ambitious**. Others wish to make a profit; these are the **greedy**. Others wish to improve themselves; and these are the **studious**.

# On Prudence and its Opposing Vices.
## ARTICLE II.

<margin>
Prudence is the **right reason of things to be done** <note>original: "recta ratio agibilium." This is the classic Aristotelian and Scholastic definition of prudence as practical wisdom.</note>; therefore it is the use of the sciences, as it also seemed to Ambrose. Aristotle and others distinguish between science and wisdom, because they consider science and wisdom to be virtues that are only effects—the first regarding letters <note>academic learning</note>, the second regarding objects.
</margin>

I. **P**rudence follows next, which weighs the use of the sciences—discovered through studiousness and curiosity—toward utility. Having tested who is fit for which science, it assigns each person to their own study and provides a remedy for their difficulties. For indeed, dullness or sharpness of the senses and the mind are not moral virtues or vices, but natural ones; likewise forgetfulness and memory, confusion and quick-wittedness, or madness and delirium. 

However, those who have <term>spirits</term> <note>In Renaissance medicine, "spirits" were subtle vapors that carried signals between the soul and the body.</note> that are dull due to "thickness" are not fit for the sciences, nor are those with a confused way of reasoning caused by "intervening soot" <note>Campanella uses "soot" or "fumes" to describe metabolic byproducts that cloud the mind's clarity.</note>; nor those who are headstrong due to excessive "thinness" of spirit, nor the unstable in reasoning, nor the forgetful due to excessive "fluidity." 

Therefore, Prudence will apply to the sciences those who have been granted a spirit that is bright, pure, and moderate in heat and thinness. This is easily recognized from <term>physiognomy</term> <note>The practice of judging a person's character or abilities from their physical appearance, especially the face.</note>, movement, speech, the light in the eyes, and from their manners and actions. 

To the **mechanical arts**, Prudence assigns those who abound in a spirit that is thick and plentiful. 

The **care of the republic** it assigns to those who fall in the middle between these types. For neither those with the "thinnest" spirits nor those with "thick" spirits are fit for administration: the former because they change everything in an attempt to "improve" it, and their practical actions do not match their theories; the latter because they are incapable of the oversight required for many different things. 

Furthermore, Prudence assists the forgetful through the **art of memory**; it helps those who reason poorly through **logic** and **mathematics**; and it aids the dull through practice and the use of summaries of the sciences. It heals the mad through physical medicine. It benefits everyone, however, through written books, **printing**, natural history, and politics, so that from past events they may know how to act in the future. 

For this reason, even "prudent" animals gather food in the summer for the winter, and they foresee imminent rain in the clouds and the cold; therefore they eat more and more greedily to provide for their bellies when they will not be able to go out to pasture.

<summary>Campanella defines Prudence as the practical application of knowledge and explains how different physical temperaments (the quality of one's "spirits") determine whether a person is best suited for science, manual labor, or government.</summary>

### CHAPTER II. OF MORALS.

<margin>He uses prophecy and all the sciences</margin>
Furthermore, man, having been granted a more divine prudence in his mind, foreknows future events through <term>syllogism</term> <note>Logical reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two premises.</note>, both from the changes in the air and from celestial causes. He does not act from mere impulse alone, as the brute animals do; and where reason fails, he turns back to the Author of things to receive prophecy. Since man is born between heaven and earth—contrary entities—and can suffer something of evil or good from all things, Prudence has decreed that he should experience everything through the senses, either in themselves or in similar things, and he has fulfilled this through studiousness. For there is nothing that man does not use. Therefore, he gathered **natural philosophy** <note>original: "physiologia." In the 17th century, this referred to the study of the entire natural world, not just bodily functions.</note> so that he might know the powers of herbs—those useful to him and those hostile—and the natures of waters, winds, stones, and metals; the influences and movements of the stars; the seasons of the year; the elements; their differences and successions; and climates, animals, and temperaments. He does this so that he may provide for his health, meet the challenges of infirmities, and increase his comforts. Next, he discovered **mathematics** so that he might construct dwellings and cities with art and ease, organize an army, measure celestial movements, distinguish times and know whatever happens within them, and so that he might count, weigh, and measure. Brute animals participate very little in these sciences because they lack a mind. Yet, by a participation in the <term>primalities</term> <note>Campanella’s metaphysical term for the three basic principles of all being: Power, Wisdom, and Love.</note> and by instinct, bees build their cells and organize an army with the highest art; and in medicine, the hippopotamus performs **bloodletting** <note>Naturalists like Pliny the Elder claimed hippos would press against sharp reeds to bleed themselves when sick.</note>, the ibex uses an enema, the dog purges itself by vomiting, and the snake and swallow use medicine for the eyes. Nevertheless, we know how to use their discoveries, but they do not know ours. Likewise, Prudence has applied studiousness to **divine things**, for the sake of which the body, strength, health, and life itself are held of little account; this is so that we may understand what God is, pursue the attainment and worship of Him, and place all things in God as the highest end. This is proper to man—a creature endowed with mind and a religious animal—and is denied to the others; therefore, it is the true "difference" in his definition <note>In logic, a "difference" is the specific characteristic that distinguishes one species from others in the same category.</note>. Although all created beings are granted the instinct to revere their Creator—some more, some less—it is because He Himself can do the most, knows the most, and wills the most to do us good, and from Him and in Him we exist. Prudence added **moral science** to man, by which he might know himself and how he ought to act...

<header>F. TOMMASO CAMPANELLA</header>

<margin>+</margin>...but toward the attainment of the end: and he <note>Referring to man or the personification of Prudence.</note> joined this <note>The science of Morals</note> to physics, because moral principles are founded in natural ones. Likewise, he joined **politics**, by which the multitude is ruled; this governance shines forth in bees, ants, and cranes in such a way that we would be ashamed of our own, had God not adorned us with a divine legislature. Prudence does not reject this as false arrogance, as shrewd politicians claim <note>Campanella likely refers here to "Machiavellian" politicians who separate politics from divine or natural law.</note>. For it cannot be denied that God cares for the entire universe of things. All things are governed by art and work wisely toward an end—even more so the governance of animals, and most of all that of men. If it is fitting for the parts to be ruled by reason, it must be even more fitting for the whole; and all wisdom does not take its origin from nothing, but from the **First Wisdom** <note>original: "prima sapientia." A reference to God as the ultimate source of all knowledge and order.</note>, which towers over the world, yet is set apart so that it can rule.

Wisdom herself, therefore, brought forth a law, not only implanted in all natural things <note>A reference to "Natural Law."</note>, but given to men in a human manner; indeed, those who boast of this law have proven its embassy through signs, miracles, prophecy, and the martyrdom of blood. For He <note>God/Wisdom</note> is most intimate to us, although through our alienation from ourselves we seem most distant from Him: for even the soul itself, after many disputes, does not well understand what the soul is.

And so that men might communicate their knowledge to one another, Prudence invented **Grammar**, the art of speaking, which through use joins the harmony of words and their connection; **Rhetoric**, which persuades toward the good and skillfully dissuades from evil, things to be done and not done; and **Poetry**, which shapes words with metaphors, meanings with fables, and speech with sonorous rhythm, so that it might persuade hiddenly and sweetly.

It is clear that an imperfect speech exists in brute animals, suited to their needs, since they sharpen, dampen, and vary their voices just as we do, though not with organs like ours; for this reason, we do not understand them, just as we do not understand the voices of the **Scythians** <note>A nomadic people from antiquity, used here as a classic example of a foreign or "barbarous" language that sounds like noise to the uninitiated.</note>.

Prudence accepts other sciences for recognizing human inclinations, such as **physiognomy** <term>The practice of assessing a person's character or fortune from their outer appearance, especially the face.</term>, and our correspondence with celestial bodies, and all those sciences which reveal something from either general or specific causes, or from emotions and their shared effects, or from signs placed by God and nature. But those sciences which arise from signs placed or imagined by man, she refutes as being invented by curiosity and full of deceptions,

He further describes how Prudence employs the arts of language (Grammar, Rhetoric, Poetry) and observational sciences like physiognomy to govern human life.</summary>
