<header>CHAPTER III OF MORALS</header>
<sig>Li 3</sig>

<margin>Aristotle unlearnedly makes the sciences into virtues.</margin>
...divine things, though often full of superstition. Finally, Prudence—if any wisdom is found for the governing of the family, the military, and the state—praises this, but it does not praise the sophistical and Machiavellian arts <note>Campanella frequently critiques Niccolò Machiavelli, viewing his political theories as "cunning" divorced from morality and divine law.</note>. For Prudence itself is the good use of the sciences, or rather the rule for using sciences to acquire true goods, to flee evils, and to detect sophistry. For science is not a virtue, but the work of one of its principles; and we are able to use it badly—as a doctor might use medicine for the destruction of the sick—but one cannot use Prudence badly. For Prudence itself requires counsel, science, and practice, so that a choice of rule can be reached for rejecting evils, choosing goods, and refuting sophistry. This Prudence illuminates all our affections through the sciences, and it applies a proper end to our actions through true means. It is called "wisdom" because of its primacy, yet it is only so in a moral and analogous sense: Metaphysics corresponds most closely to it in the realm of speculative thought. Indeed, it is the "prudence of the sciences," just as Prudence is the "Metaphysics of affections, operations, and notions." <note>Campanella argues that Prudence is the highest practical faculty, organizing all human action just as Metaphysics organizes all abstract knowledge.</note>

2. Imprudence and Cunning are opposed to Prudence. The former is a defect, since it does not know the use of the sciences, nor does it select true goods from those that merely appear so, nor does it look around at the connected goods and evils, and thus it lies open to deception; it does not foresee the future through science nor through the patterns of the past. This is a sign of a thick and smoky spirit. <note>original: "spiritus crassi fuliginosique." In the physiology of the time, "spirits" were thin vapors that carried thought; if they were "smoky" or "thick," the mind was considered dull or clouded.</note>

3. Cunning, however, thinks that it measures everything by its own wit. It does not believe divine men—as if it were more divine than they—nor does it allow itself to be "deceived." It is ignorant of its own ignorance, which is the thing Prudence knows most of all. It thinks it can deceive everyone in practical affairs. It scrutinizes sophistical and occult sciences that lack a foundation and applies them to its own glory. This is the sign of a vain spirit—thin, smoky, looking around at the smallest things, but not grasping or else neglecting the great ones.

4. Counsel is the companion of Prudence; rashness is the companion of Imprudence; and suspiciousness is the companion of Cunning. To judge and deliberate based on science and skill belongs to the prudent man; to do so rashly belongs to Cunning; while irresolution belongs to Imprudence and stupidity.

<header>FRIAR THOMAS CAMPANELLA</header>

## On Vigilance.
### ARTICLE III.

1. **Vigilance** in our actions looks around at everything, lest something creep in to disturb them or frustrate their purpose, and to ensure that passion is not mistaken for reason. **Inadvertence** <note>original: *inadvertentia*; the state of being inattentive or distracted</note>, on the other hand, being led by passion and emotion, chooses what it has previously experienced as good; it does not consider hidden factors, but only those that are immediately apparent. **Attentiveness** is vigilance itself. These qualities are linked to Prudence and are found in the active pursuit of business.

---

## On Teachability.
### ARTICLE IV.

1. **Teachability** <note>original: *disciplinabilitas*; the capacity or willingness to be a student and to be led by instruction</note> belongs to those who wish to learn well what must be done, so that they may carry it out properly; the same applies to what must be known. **Lack of instruction** <note>original: *ruditas*; a state of being unrefined or raw</note> is a physical inability to learn, but in a moral sense, it is the choice to flee from the knowledge of what should be done and known. There is a vice among **smatterers** <note>original: *scioli*; those who possess superficial, "little" knowledge but act as if they are experts</note>: when they have had a mere greeting's acquaintance with the sciences, they think they know everything. They do not fear to correct the most learned—not out of malice, but because they truly believe they are knowledgeable. These were the ones who opposed **Socrates** <note>Socrates was famous for claiming he knew nothing, which Campanella contrasts here with the arrogance of the "scioli."</note>. This is also a vice of certain teachers, and of those who, while learning only one science, believe they can judge all things through it—or judge all books based on a single book. They rely on the "authority of being right" rather than on reason and experience. Regarding the things they are ignorant of, they boast that if they had only studied them, they could have excelled beyond all other mortals. They admire whatever they themselves say and wish to be admired by others; when they are mocked, they accept the mockery as true praise, being overwhelmed by their own folly.

The **Teachable person**, however, the more they know and the more they learn, the more they understand how much they do not know. Such a person will not stop at logical tricks <note>original: *sophismata*; arguments that seem plausible but are fallacious</note> nor cease from inquiry, nor will they be deceived by a mocker, for they are a just judge of themselves and others.

<summary>Campanella defines vigilance as the active oversight of one's actions against passion and describes teachability as an intellectual humility that stands in opposition to the arrogance of superficial "smatterers."</summary>
<keywords>vigilance, teachability, prudence, Socrates, intellectual humility, folly, smatterers, attention, reason vs passion</keywords>

<header>MORAL PHILOSOPHY, CHAPTER II.</header>

# *On Ingenuity and its Opposites, Likewise on Art and Nature.*

## ARTICLE V.

1. Since man is not preserved nor made happy by himself alone—as God is—without any attack from external opposition or from pleasures luring him outside of himself, it was necessary for us to be preserved by other things. We do this by adapting those things for food, drink, clothing, and other uses; and whatever we discover through the sciences, we must accommodate to our necessities through work and labor. We must always be acquiring new things, lest, while those already acquired are being consumed, we lack the things that keep us alive. This, however, we achieve through the mechanical arts. The faculty that invents these and the virtue that uses them well is called **Ingenuity** <note>original: *Solertia*; a combination of skill, resourcefulness, and cleverness in practical matters</note>. It is the sign of a spirit that is thick yet pure, suited to handling and imitating corporeal nature well; without it, the human race would live in great discomfort. For brute animals are less delicate; nature gave them horns, protruding teeth, claws, and beaks as weapons against hostile beings; she gave them hides, hair, wool, feathers, or scales against cold and heat, hardness and stings; and she gave them thick spirits and warm internal organs so that they might be nourished by raw things growing from the ground and by raw flesh. Thus, they required very few or no arts. But man—naked and unarmed with either defensive or offensive tools, and delicate, for whom uncleaned and uncooked food is difficult to digest—stood in need of innumerable arts. These he skillfully invented by imitating nature, which is Divine Art. <margin>What art is.</margin> For **Art** is an external nature impressing upon matter those ideas which the human mind thinks up by inspecting the natural things designed by God, so that Art can be seen as the daughter of nature and the granddaughter of the Creator. **Nature**, however, is an intrinsic art expressing divine ideas, which she receives through the service of the forming principles <note>original: *ideantium*; the active powers or "ideas" that shape physical matter</note> and has held since the beginning of the world, as we have said in the *Metaphysics*. Every natural being practices only one art: as in the fig tree there is the art of making figs, and not pears; in the chestnut tree, chestnuts, and so on. But a single human being learns and practices many arts,

<summary>Campanella defines Ingenuity (Solertia) as the human capacity to invent and use mechanical arts to compensate for biological vulnerability. He distinguishes Art as a "grandchild of God" that imitates Nature, noting that while animals are born with natural defenses, humans must use their intellect to create them.</summary>

...because the human mind was created in the image of the founder of all natures.

2. Some arts are derived more closely from the mind's **power** <note>original: *potestatiuo*; referring to Power, one of Campanella’s three "Primalities" of being</note> and serve it; others from its **cognitive** faculty; and others from the **appetitive** <note>desiring or emotional</note> faculty. To the power-based faculty belongs the **military art**, which imitates wild beasts in their battles. This is served by the art of making swords and spears, which imitate horns and teeth; and breastplates, which are like scales. There is also the **equestrian art**, in which the soul imitates its own governance of the body by governing a horse—adding spurs to simulate anger and desire, and the bridle to simulate fear. 

Likewise, the **art of navigation** imitates fish and birds. It is served by **shipbuilding**, which imitates a bird: the oars are like wings, the rudder like a tail, and the prow like a beak. Likewise, the **art of metallurgy** exists so that there may be a material "element" for all the arts; for almost no art can be practiced without metal. This art resembles the lungs with its bellows, which act like the "workshop of spirits" found in the heart. **Blacksmithing** serves all the arts: it gives the plowman a plowshare like a pig’s snout; it gives the digger a mattock like a tooth; it gives the reaper a sickle, which imitates a whole set of teeth; it gives the carpenter a saw like the teeth of a fish; and it provides the chisel and the ax in the likeness of other animal parts. Indeed, the smith himself, using fire and iron just as an angel uses the sun and the earth, fabricates all the weapons and instruments of the arts. This is a marvelous thing.

Likewise, the **art of construction** <note>original: *fabrefactoria*</note> builds a house in the likeness of a small human body, and a city in the likeness of a giant body: with a citadel for its head and windows for its sensory organs—matters we discuss elsewhere. Likewise, the **art of cannons** <note>original: *bombardarum*</note>, by which we imitate thunder more effectively than a tightrope walker imitates flight. There is the **quarrying of stone**, which is like nature preparing bones for the building of the body; and the **potter**, who makes vessels like human internal organs. To these are added the glassmaker and similar craftsmen.

3. Belonging to the cognitive and manifestative faculties are **writing**, which imitates the world by expressing all divine ideas from a few elements <note>referring to the alphabet as the fundamental "elements" of language, just as physical elements compose the world</note>, just as God himself is a writer. **Typography** <note>printing</note> does the same thing through a kind of "angelic" imitation. Likewise, **painting** imitates all the shapes and colors of physical natures. **Sculpture** and **casting** produce masses shaped by God; because of their durability, they preserve the knowledge of things for future generations and for those who are absent. Likewise, the **art of clock-making** imitates the heavens and indicates the hours, simulating fate through a certain divine logic. Likewise—

He categorizes various trades—from blacksmithing to clock-making—as extensions of biological functions or celestial patterns.</summary>

...the art of bell-making, which calls people to the temple and serves many purposes, imitates the voice of an animal. Likewise, the art of the trumpeter produces a noisy blare that rouses men to arms, and the drum acts as a sort of wake-up call. Musical sounds imitate the harmony of the spirit, as well as the song of the Sirens <note>mythical creatures whose song was irresistibly beautiful</note> and birds; they delight and move the spirit toward an action that preserves itself. Other sounds imitate and represent the harmony of the heavens. Likewise, through words that signify our thoughts, we reveal known things that have been imitated in this way. The art of the spectacle-maker <note>original: *ocularium*</note> serves the eyes and adds power to them, imitating the eyes themselves. There is an art of "hearing-aids" <note>original: *auricularium*; likely referring to ear trumpets</note> fashioned in the likeness of ears. Mirrors <note>original: *specularia*</note> were invented in the likeness of water bounded by earth, in which we see ourselves; or perhaps they represent the crystalline lens of the eye.

4. The **arts of the appetitive faculty** <note>related to desire and physical needs</note> are: **agriculture**, which prepares the material for food, imitating God as He inserts seminal virtues <note>the creative powers of life</note> into the elements; and the art of the gardener planting vegetables. **Milling** imitates the mouth of an animal chewing food with its molars. **Cooking** imitates the stomach <note>original: *ventriculum*</note> as it "cooks" or digests food, and pots are similar to it; the liver stands by like a fire and a distributor of heat. **Butchery** emulates wolves as they divide portions for their young. The **pastoral art** <note>shepherding</note> imitates the guardian angels. **Dairy-making** imitates the mother providing milk. The art of **distillation** <note>original: *alembiccatoria*</note> reflects the use of the intestines and the head, into which vapors ascend and are condensed. **Pharmacy** imitates the sun as it matures herbs into medicines for mortals. The **physician** imitates God by commanding what must be done and teaching applications. In many things, the physician emulates the brute animals, as we said a little earlier. There are many arts serving the palate <note>original: *gulae*; literally "the throat" or gluttony</note> which certainly imitate the internal organs, transforming food in various ways so that it may become nourishment for the body. The **art of clothing** provides shirts, doublets, full-length robes, and cloaks in the likeness of the bark of plants, where the innermost layer is the thin shirt and the others, thicker in their order, correspond to the aforementioned garments. The **bed and pillow** are made in the likeness of the brain. The **table** is in the likeness of the "network" <note>original: *retiformis*; likely referring to the *rete mirabile*, a vascular network in the body which Campanella discusses in his *Physiologia*</note>: see the *Physiology*. **Acting** <note>original: *histrionia*</note> imitates the behaviors of men. But this is wonderful: that with the **lamp** we imitate the sun, making day out of night—which makes one wonder whether the sun itself is "nourished," as the recently discovered spots of the small clouds surrounding it <note>a reference to the discovery of sunspots, which Campanella interprets here as "clouds"</note> show. To review all the other arts would be a laborious task.

5. But which is the more noble, and which the more ignoble? The **purgative arts** <note>cleansing arts</note> are more ignoble because they deal with filth, such as the art of the **fuller** <note>someone who cleans and thickens cloth</note>...

...art, and that which scrapes hides <note>the art of tanning</note>. Likewise, the **hangman’s art**, which purges the city of foul and vicious citizens at the judge's command. The **military art** is therefore not similar to it, as it fights against external enemies. The art of the **lictors** <note>officers who executed the sentences of magistrates</note> is also preparatory in this kind of purging, and for that reason it is considered base, because it is exercised against the foul, decaying members of the commonwealth. **Mercenary military service** is not dissimilar to these base arts, since it fights against enemies for a price; **auxiliary service** is nobler; but one’s **own citizen military** is noblest of all, because it acts for the defense of the state and not for money.

Arts that dirty the body are considered baser by some, such as tanning; but this is a deceptive judgment. For **painting** also dirties the artist in part, and yet it excels many arts that do not dirty the person. Those arts that foul the soul are the basest of all: such as money-changing, trading, tax-gathering, pimping, and prostitution—if indeed they even deserve to be called "arts." For not every occupation by which we live is an art; properly speaking, an art is that which impresses some form onto matter by imitating nature. 

By this definition, the **trader** only imitates nature when he buys in order to resell items he has improved, just as the liver "buys" chyle <note>original: *chylum*; the milky fluid of digested food</note> and turns it into blood, which it then "resells" <note>distributes throughout the body</note>. 

However, the **art of dance** <note>original: *chorearum*</note> does not impress its form on matter. It does indeed impress upon us rhythmic movements that imitate the celestial choir <note>the harmonious motion of the stars and planets</note>, though it does not do so in solid matter (much as sounds exist in the air), but rather as transient forms, like the colors of a rainbow or the boom of thunder. For these arts have their use in the *doing* of them, not in a permanent result, except perhaps within the animal spirit <note>the subtle fluid believed to transmit sensation and motion through the nerves</note>. 

Likewise, arts seem nobler when there is more **intellect** <note>original: *ingenii*</note> than labor involved. Yet the military art involves more labor and less intellect, and it does not yield in status to painting (where intellect is highly praised) or to the lyre-player. This assertion is true for the most part, but not always. 

Furthermore, the more useful art might seem to be the nobler. But the most useful of all are **herding, agriculture, and medicine**; yet the first two are held as base within the commonwealth. Or is an art better if it imitates a nobler craftsmanship of nature? But **blacksmithing**, which imitates the "angelic craftsmen," is not considered nobler than **shipbuilding**, which imitates the birds. 

Finally, for an art to be considered noble, it seems that the nobility of the material and the form, the ingenuity required, and its utility must all coincide; where more of these are present, the nobility is greater. Add to this the **hierarchy of command**. For shipbuilding is nobler than the hewing of wood, and hewing is nobler than the cutting of timber; and **navigation** is nobler than shipbuilding. In the same way, **horsemanship** is better than the craft of bridle-making, because to this...

[the higher art] commands this one to make a bridle in such a way, and this one serves. However, this is only true when the art being served is noble; otherwise, the preparatory art is the better one. For the **farmer** producing grain for the **miller** is not inferior to him. And the **miller** producing flour for the **baker** is not better than the baker. Nor is the **blacksmith** inferior to the **ditch-digger**, for whom he prepares the shovel. Enough has been said of these. Animals also serve our various faculties: some serve the *power-giving* faculty <note>original: *potestatiuo*; the part of the soul responsible for movement and physical strength</note>, such as the horse; others the *intellective* faculty, such as the rooster and the crow; and others the *appetitive* faculty <note>the part of the soul driven by desires and needs</note>, such as the lamb.

6. The contrary vices [of industry] are **Anxiety** and **Laziness**. The latter <note>original: *Inertia*</note> cares nothing for acquiring goods or the arts by which one lives; nor is such a person fit for discovering what exercise is good for them. This is surely a sign of a "thick" spirit—smoky, cramped in dense vessels, or meager and easily affected—yet applicable to many industries; the mind can make little use of such a spirit in either internal or external works. **Anxiety** <note>here meaning a restless, obsessive drive for profit rather than modern "worry"</note>, however, belongs to a base, distrustful, but abundant spirit, dwelling in loose vessels from which it frequently exhales. For this reason, the anxious person sweats more in their industries than is profitable, searching everywhere, working much, and consuming themselves. They are always devising means to acquire things from anywhere and at any time, hardly distinguishing between holidays, feasts, locations, or methods, unless forced to do so. This man is bad; but the **lazy** man is worse, because he is either a slave or the "excrement" of the state—an idle member who, even if he has the means to live, hinders others; such are those who are falsely called "nobles." I have not touched upon the **art of command**, nor that of **judges** or **priests**, because they belong to a higher rank than the mechanical arts. See the following, point 3.

<margin>Aristotle wrongly thinks that virtues and sciences are "habits" <note>stable dispositions or learned qualities</note> simply because arts are habits.</margin>

7. The **mechanical arts** require aptitude and practice. For they are acquired when one handles objects, testing the objects and oneself through them. **Sciences**, however, are inherent by nature; they are specified by the things that can be known, and the mind is called back to the consideration of these knowable things, rather than acquiring knowledge from external and "ignorant" things, as was said before. Nor does this apply to art, insofar as art is a science. For the **theory** of an art is perceived suddenly, but its **practice** <note>original: *praxis*</note> is gained through habit and time.

---

<summary>Campanella argues that the status of a trade depends on its purpose, not its messiness, and identifies "anxiety" and "laziness" as the two psychological extremes that ruin productivity. He distinguishes between mechanical arts, which require physical practice, and sciences, which he believes are innate and merely "recalled" by the mind.</summary>

<page-num>260</page-num>
<header>BROTHER TOMMASO CAMPANELLA On Moderation or Sufficiency.</header>
<meta>Catchword: 2. When</meta>

#### ARTICLE VI.

Closely related to the vice of **Anxiety** <note>as defined on the previous page: a restless, obsessive drive for profit</note> is **Greed** <note>original: *cupiditas*</note>, which similarly concerns the act of acquiring things. It is an excessive appetite—often attributed to women <note>Campanella here reflects a common 17th-century stereotype regarding domestic consumption and status</note>—that is never satisfied by any amount of riches, plunder, or prey. It is not the same thing as **Avarice**, although the two are often confused. **Avarice** is a vice regarding the *possession* and *spending* of things already acquired, and it stands as the opposite of **Prodigality** <note>reckless wastefulness</note>; yet an avaricious person is also typically greedy in acquisition and prone to grasping.

The virtue opposed to **Greed** is **Moderation** of mind, which is content with a few things. For this reason, it is also called **Sufficiency** by those who know how to live in both abundance and in want. Others call it **Voluntary Poverty**, though that is a more extreme term. This is truly a noble virtue, characteristic of philosophers who, being content with their own integrity, do not place their happiness in external things but in themselves before God. The vice of "deficiency" <note>having too little desire for what is necessary</note> is unnamed, but it could be called **Scantiness**, for it hardly desires even necessities. This leads to many evils, as it accompanies those who are sluggish or idle.

---

## *On Frugality, Magnificence, and Refinement, and their opposites.*

### CHAPTER IV.

#### ARTICLE I.

<margin>11.</margin> Next is **Frugality** <note>original: *Parsimonia*</note>, which uses skill to set a limit on the use of things already acquired, doing so not out of greed but out of utility. For there are those who exceed the proper limit in every matter of preservation: they want clothes with long trails, they consume more wine and oil than is fitting, and they waste resources even as they use them. They use pots larger than required for their meals, keep more servants than needed for their service, and they double their comforts and consume them, treating them as if they will never run out. The vice of these people is **Luxury** and **Overabundance**, which occurs through a lack of consideration.

<summary>Campanella distinguishes between Greed (the drive to get) and Avarice (the drive to keep), championing 'Sufficiency' as the philosophical ideal. He introduces Frugality as a practical virtue of consumption, opposing it to the wastefulness of luxury.</summary>
<keywords>Greed, Avarice, Moderation, Sufficiency, Voluntary Poverty, Frugality, Luxury, Tommaso Campanella, Ethics</keywords>

--- Page 305 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of moral virtues from page 260, specifically transitioning from the concept of "Frugality" into "Magnificence" and "Liberality." It explores how we manage the appearance of our lives and the distribution of our wealth.</meta>

<page-num>261</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER IV ON MORALS.</header>

2. When, however, spending arises from ostentation, it is **boasting** and **vanity** <note>original: *ventositas*, literally "windiness" or "puffiness"</note>, for which **magnificence** is the cure. You may see vain and ambitious people of the world who are sumptuous in their clothing, food, and homes, so that they might appear elegant, ornate, and luxurious; yet they are often sordid in their excesses, poorly prepared, and use things that are burdensome rather than truly delightful. **Frugality** <note>original: *parsimonia*</note> cures these evils by being provident, ensuring that nothing is lacking; it does not allow even a single penny <note>original: *obulum*</note> or the smallest drop of vinegar to go to waste—not out of avarice, but out of a hatred for superfluity, which nature avoids in all things, just as nature does not fail in what is necessary. Nevertheless, it overlooks the smallest details for the sake of great matters. **Meagerness** <note>original: *modicitas*</note> is a vice of "deficiency," in that it fails to follow a rule; it is not the same as avarice, but it is described as using things in a meager and insufficient way. It is a friend to **meanness** <note>original: *paruificentiæ*, literally "small-doing"</note>, which, out of a smallness of spirit, results in tiny expenses, small houses, short clothes, and a cramped theater. **Magnificence**, however, belongs to a great spirit; it makes all things great, provided they are useful. If they are useless—such as pyramids, grand tombs, and things that serve little purpose—it is merely vanity.

3. An excessive affectation of **cleanliness** <note>original: *munditia*, implying elegance and order</note> in clothing—not just the external kind born of boasting, but in any form—is a vice that is tiresome to oneself and others; it neglects better things for the sake of the lesser. The same applies to having too many ceremonies regarding dishes and other objects; this has no specific name, but it belongs to a servile mind. **Squalor** belongs to the impure and provokes nausea. True **cleanliness** is the virtue of the pure, delightful to oneself and to others.

---

## On liberality and its opposites,

### ARTICLE II.

For the sake of our own preservation, another virtue follows, called **Liberality**. This is because it is the sign of a **free spirit** <note>Campanella makes a linguistic connection between *liberalitas* (liberality) and *liber* (free)</note> dwelling in a spacious, pure, abundant, and confident house. This virtue spends the goods that skill has acquired. It uses them generously for its own benefit and for the benefit of the friends with whom one lives, so that life may be preserved. For it is of no use to know how to acquire things unless you also know how to use what has been acquired. This, therefore, is a portion of wisdom (since every virtue is itself a form of wisdom): knowing how to rightly use external human things.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of moral virtues from page 261. While the previous page contrasted Frugality with Meanness and Magnificence, this section moves into the specific vices of wealth management—Avarice and Prodigality—before transitioning to the physical virtues of Sobriety.</meta>

<page-num>262</page-num>
<header>OF FRATER TOMMASO CAMPANELLA</header>

2. When, however, a person focuses only on acquiring goods and fears to use them for their own benefit—worried that they might perhaps run out—and consumes their own mind and body by increasing the family estate through any business, whether honest or dishonest, which profits neither themselves nor their friends enough, and preserves the wealth but not themselves: such a person possesses the vice they call **Avarice** or **Illiberality** <note>original: *illiberalitatem*, a lack of the "liberality" or generosity expected of a free person</note>. This is a sign of a base, distrustful, gloomy <note>original: *fuliginosi*, literally "sooty," referring to a spirit clouded by dark or melancholic vapors</note>, and tiny spirit, conscious of its own cowardice; as we see in the elderly, who have little confidence and are prone to avarice. Truly, avarice defiles the acquisition, the conservation, and the spending of wealth; **Illiberality** properly concerns the spending.

3. He, however, who recklessly spends and squanders whatever he acquires at the vain whim of himself or his friends—whether they are deserving or undeserving—beyond necessity and discretion, suffers from **Prodigality**. Such a person is ignorant, not knowing how to consider that what he squanders will eventually be lacking for his own needs and those of his friends, and that this deficiency will be a cause of evil. This is a great vice, but less so than avarice. For at least the prodigal person gains friends, even if they are of little use. Since the upright and the wicked alike know they are being treated the same by him, they do not remain grateful to him. Those who are born as princes suffer more harm from prodigality; for once reduced to need, they soon become rapacious, just like **Caligula** and **Nero**. But for those seeking to gain a principality, it is more beneficial—as it was for **Caesar** and **Cyrus**—to win over soldiers to themselves, upon whom the entire future of their rule depends.

---

## *On sobriety and the opposing vices.*

### ARTICLE III.

<margin>1.</margin>Since human life depends first upon food and drink, acting as natural medicines against death, and since the medicinal enjoyment of things acquired is essential; yet he who eats too much suffers from countless diseases arising from indigestion <note>original: *cruditate*, literally "rawness," referring to undigested food in the stomach</note>; while he who eats too little and is afflicted by perpetual fasting suffers from weakness and wasting away, and is greatly harmed by any cold, heat, or injury: [there is] that science <note>Moral philosophy or Ethics</note> which prescribes food and drink by the command of the will...

<meta>...drink.</meta>

<summary>Campanella defines Avarice as a sign of a cowardly spirit and Prodigality as a reckless but slightly less harmful vice, then introduces Sobriety as the essential balance for maintaining physical health.</summary>

<page-num>263</page-num>
# CHAPTER IV ON MORALS
<meta>Catchword: tus, (likely the end of a word like 'separatus')</meta>

<margin>
Sobriety and chastity are categorized by Aristotle as a single virtue, called temperance. But this is done erroneously. For they are separate things.
</margin>
...and drink only as much as is sufficient for necessity, is a virtue called **Sobriety**: it is a great part of the science of medicine. This virtue teaches the proper time for eating—which is when hunger is present in a healthy body—and it is practiced for the sake of preservation, not for pleasure (for pleasure should invite us toward preservation, not be an end in itself). In a sick person, however, it teaches eating only when the <term>native heat</term> <note>original: *vis nativa*, the internal vital force or "fire" believed to govern digestion and health</note> is not occupied fighting the disease. For the same reason, it prescribes more solid foods for those who exercise the body and lighter foods for those who exercise the mind. It always allows for slightly more food to be taken in than what is lost through daily activity. In summer, in infancy, and in old age, it commands that food be sparse, frequent, and soft; in winter and in youth, it allows for more food, solid in nature and taken less often; in moderate seasons and ages, it advises moderation.

*For these virtues are found to be separate; for example, Northern peoples struggle with drunkenness but not with lust, while the opposite is true for Southern peoples. Likewise, there are different paths to acquiring what is good: one path preserves us through our children <note>referring to the virtue of chastity</note>, while the other preserves us within ourselves <note>referring to sobriety</note>.*

2. The opposite vice in excess is **Gluttony** and greed regarding food, and **Drunkenness** regarding drink. These provide an excess of food or drink, ignoring the proper timing and the necessary goal of living, acting instead as if we live only to eat. From this follows <term>indigestion</term> <note>original: *cruditas*, literally "rawness," referring to food that has not been properly "cooked" or transformed by the stomach's heat</note> of the nourishment. This happens because the <term>native heat</term> is too weak to separate the waste from the good juices when they are too abundant. Nor is that heat strong enough to strip away the foam, ash, soot, and dregs from those juices once they are turned into blood. Consequently, when this blood is carried to the parts of the body that need nourishment, it fills their passages with waste and suffocates their own native heat. This, in turn, feeds all the diseases that take root in the joints and the weaker parts of the body. From this vice of gluttony arose <term>cannibalism</term> <note>original: *anthropophagia*</note> and the indiscriminate eating of things; for nature never acts upon its own kind (just as heat does not act upon heat), nor is a thing nourished by what is entirely dissimilar to it. Therefore, the better parts of both mobile and immobile animals are food for us, but human flesh—being of our own species—is not; nor is earth or dung; nor are plants and beasts of an entirely opposite nature, which affect us either as poison or through difficulty of digestion and the corruption of our health, as we shall teach in our works on Medicine. Drunkenness brings about no less an evil. Through the immoderate use of wine, the body is rendered "vinous" or saturated with wine. Just as <term>pica</term> <note>original: *citta* or *pica*, a medical disorder involving a craving for non-food items</note> arises from dregs and filth sticking to the stomach walls, this creates a foul appetite for similar things...

<meta>This page continues Campanella's exploration of the physical and moral virtues, specifically focusing on the vice of drunkenness as an excess of food and drink, the vice of starvation (inedia) as a deficiency, and the spiritual virtue of fasting.</meta>

<page-num>264</page-num>
<header>FRIAR THOMAS CAMPANELLA</header>

...excessive use breeds a dire greed for wine. What was given by God for the strength of the stomach and the intellect, to make the body’s powers fruitful, and to bring cheerfulness to the sorrowful when taken in moderation, is turned to a completely contrary use by drunkards. For it clouds the <term>animal spirits</term> <note>original: *spiritus animales*, the subtle fluids believed to carry sensory information and motor commands through the nerves</note> even more, dulls the intellect, and overwhelms the body’s strength with heaviness and heat, so that they think and act like different people. It adds sleepiness, quarrels, <term>phantoms</term> <note>original: *laruas*, referring to hallucinations or ghostly apparitions</note>, paralysis, immobility, vomiting, spasms, and other evils; it makes a man like not only a beast but a corpse. As for which wine should be used, by whom, and at what age, we have discussed this in Book 2 of our *Medicine*. There, we occasionally permit a "vomiting drunkenness" in the manner of <term>antimony</term> <note>a chemical element used historically as an emetic to induce vomiting and "purge" the system</note>.

3. The opposite vice of deficiency—not eating as is necessary and beneficial—is called starvation <note>original: *inedia*</note>. This gradually consumes the spirits and the nutritional moisture, whereby the body becomes <term>hectic</term> <note>original: *hecticum*, a state of feverish wasting or consumption</note>, and the spirit becomes empty, seeing many phantasms because its thinness makes it prone to be affected by any appearance as if it were a reality. Often the nerves are dried out and contracted, and a spasm occurs; this must be treated with sweet baths and plenty of moist food.

4. However, those who abstain from meat and fast out of veneration for God are not acting out of vice but are filled with Holiness. This indeed is derived from Religion, from which every virtue flows into the higher Soul. And whatever the soul wisely commands in "rational service" to God becomes a virtue. For virtue is Reason and counsel. Moreover, the highest Reason is God, upon whom all reasons depend. For through fasting, the disturbances of vapors in the mind cease, and it becomes more fit for contemplation; it stops the "ticklings" in the flesh <note>referring to physical lust or agitation</note>, the undigested matter in the bowels, the diseases of body and mind, and the urge toward evil. He who fasts for any other reason or cause commits a sin.

<summary>Campanella discusses the physical and mental ruin caused by drunkenness and starvation, while distinguishing religious fasting as a holy virtue that clears the mind for divine contemplation.</summary>

# *On the virtues accompanying the acts and affections of operation.*

## CHAPTER V.

<margin>1.</margin>
After we have corrected the internal affections <note>original: *affectiones*, referring to the soul's inclinations</note> and notions, we must now move on to the passions that occur during difficult executions, for it is in these that virtue shines most clearly. For although virtue exercises itself in all things—even easy ones, provided they are not done indifferently, or by one who is unwilling, or by one who is inattentive and ignorant, or in omissions by one who is unable—it is in arduous matters that it truly glows. Now, some executions are for the sake of attaining good, such as learning the arts, concluding a marriage, or sailing for the sake of wealth, etc. Others are for the sake of repelling evil, such as military expeditions, duels, the repelling of robbers, etc. Therefore, let us first speak of those which are acquisitive <note>directed toward obtaining something good</note>.

### *On Manliness.*

->ARTICLE I.<-

<margin>1.</margin>
Generally speaking, in all things, the primary virtue is <term>manliness</term> <note>original: *virilitas*, a term derived from *vir* (man), signifying strength, vigor, and courageous excellence</note>. This is the middle ground between the ferocity of beasts and the weakness of women. For a true man turns away from both extremes. The <term>Scythians</term> <note>an ancient nomadic people of Central Eurasia, often used by classical authors as symbols of raw, unrefined ferocity</note> are ferocious; the <term>Lydians</term> <note>an Anatolian people known in antiquity for their supposed luxury and softness</note> are effeminate. The latter [the Lydians] are open to the prey of the strong, while the former [the Scythians] are open to the prey of sophists and heretics. Weakness and ferocity, when innate, are natural vices, as we experience in many people. However, those which are found through one’s way of life and choice are moral vices. For the ferocious man is carried away impulsively toward what he wants, and immediately and recklessly toward what displeases him. Weakness, on the other hand, moves sluggishly toward either. These are cured by manliness, by exercise, and by the company of great men. However, the ferocious are better cured by religion, while the effeminate are better cured by military exercise.

<page-num>266</page-num>
<header>FRIAR TOMMASO CAMPANELLA On Hope and Confidence.</header>
<meta>catchword: Concerning</meta>

## ARTICLE II.

1. **AT** the start of carrying out any task, the hope of attaining the goal must come first. Hope does not fix itself upon a good that is impossible, but upon one that is possible, whether it be difficult or easy. We also hope for victory and the escape from evil, insofar as it is a "good" to be free from harms. However, the struggle against evil is properly the domain of <term>fortitude</term> <note>original: *fortitudo*, the virtue of courage and inner strength</note>, which governs both our daring and our fear. Hope is found in a noble and confident spirit that is full of life. This is why the young and the strong are full of hope, while the elderly and the suffering fall into despair. Hope is, therefore, the mind's journey within a lofty spirit toward a difficult goal. The mind first weighs whether it is able to begin the attack, considers the difficulties that might occur, and calculates what its "shoulders" refuse to carry and what they can bear; from this point, the spirit moves itself, even if it only vaguely understands at first what it is trusting in. But when it becomes clear that the goal can be achieved—whether through one's own strength, the help of friends, or through God (when the work is a holy one)—then a companion virtue is born called <term>confidence</term> <note>original: *confidentia*</note>. It is so named because it possesses "faith" (*fides*) alongside the action. This is a truly good thing; for we do not truly trust in God unless we love Him, possess His promises, and see the examples of the "friends of God" <note>a common term for the saints or those who lived in divine favor</note> who reached their desired goal. These noble virtues do not abandon a person even in prison, nor in the depths of the sea, nor in death itself; yet it is said that hope is like the "dream of a waking man," while confidence—or trust—is the vision of one who is fully awake.

2. The opposing vices are despair and presumption. Despair belongs to a base soul that has little faith in God. However, if a task is wicked, it is a virtue to "despair" of it, and a vice to "hope" for it. Sometimes, as the saying goes, "the only safety is to hope for no safety" <note>original: *salus nullam sperare salutem*; an allusion to Virgil's *Aeneid*, suggesting that in desperate situations, the realization that there is no escape can provide the desperate courage needed to actually survive</note>; this occurs when you realize you cannot escape an evil, and so you rush in to avenge yourself and die. In such a state, it often happens that one actually escapes, whereas a hesitant person would perish. <term>Presumption</term> <note>original: *praesumtio*</note> belongs to a spirit that is too "hot" and fails to weigh dangers, trusting instead in its own ferocity; or it belongs to a vain and shallow spirit that treats any minor assistance as if it were sufficient. <term>Distrust</term> <note>original: *diffidentia*</note> is related to despair, while <term>rashness</term> <note>original: *temeritas*</note> is related to presumption. These bring about many evils, they "tempt God" <note>an expression meaning to demand a miracle from God to cover for one's own lack of preparation or wisdom</note>, and they bring certain ruin in the face of danger.

<vocab>Campanella, Hope, Confidence, Despair, Presumption, Virtue, Fortitude, Ethics</vocab>

<summary>Campanella defines hope and confidence as the necessary drivers for any difficult undertaking, distinguishing them from the vices of despair (too little spirit) and presumption (too much unthinking heat). He argues that true confidence arises when one realizes a goal is possible through personal strength, friends, or divine aid.</summary>

<meta>catchword: ties,</meta>

## *On Eagerness.*

### ARTICLE III.

1. **IN** the pursuit of a work, there occurs immediately either a state of preparation or one of sluggishness and slow-moving apathy. <term>Eagerness</term> <note>original: *alacritas*, a lively readiness to act</note> cures these passions, which arise from either rashness or a lack of confidence; it is the force of a mind that trusts, and not in vain. For some people are over-hasty, such as the French; others are slow from the very start, such as the Spaniards. Both of these tendencies are flawed, unless the specific matter and the timing demand otherwise.

---

## *On Strenuousness.*

### ARTICLE IV.

**TO** this virtue succeed Rigidity and Flexibility. Both of these extremes are unrefined. For to yield ground where it is necessary, and to stand unshaken where it is necessary for the pursuit of an action, is the virtue of <term>Strenuousness</term> <note>original: *strenuitas*, a disciplined vigor that knows when to push and when to pivot</note>, a quality worthy of great men.

---

## *On Longanimity.*

### ARTICLE V.

**NEXT** follows <term>longanimity</term> <note>original: *longanimitas*, literally "long-mindedness" or patient endurance over a long duration</note>. This virtue aids those already engaged in a task when they fail to make progress due to boredom, or when they ruin the work through excessive haste and render themselves unfit for the consequences. To fail to progress in what is good is, in fact, to fall behind; and to leap over steps is sometimes to destroy the work entirely. Therefore, there is a need for longanimity, so that a useful delay does not displease the worker—as is proven in the example of <term>Fabius Maximus</term> <note>Quintus Fabius Maximus, the Roman general nicknamed "Cunctator" (the Delayer), who defeated Hannibal by refusing to be rushed into a direct battle</note>. It ensures that a long pursuit does not weary the man, but rather that he stretches out his spirit alongside the operation itself.

---

## *On Deliberation.*

### ARTICLE VI.

**DELIBERATION** <note>original: *cunctatio*, a calculated hesitation or "lingering" to find the right moment</note> seems to be nearly the same virtue, standing midway between acceleration and slowness, insofar as these are qualities of time...

<summary>Campanella defines the virtues of active pursuit: eagerness (balancing haste and sluggishness), strenuousness (balancing rigidity and flexibility), and longanimitas (the patience to endure long tasks without rushing or quitting).</summary>

...qualities, not insofar as they are individuals; for in that way they belong to the circumstances of actions. In all things, however, the logic of the end will measure the work. For <term>virtue</term> <note>original: *virtus*</note> is not a middle ground <note>Campanella here critiques the Aristotelian "Golden Mean," suggesting virtue is an exact "measure" (*mensura*) rather than just a midpoint.</note>, but a measure that matches the action to the achievement of the thing toward which we strive.

->*On perseverance,*<-

### ARTICLE VII.

Perseverance in a work is opposed to instability and obstinacy. It might better be called constancy. For every virtue perseveres in its own work; but perseverance in the works of all virtues successively, until the end of life, without an interval of vice, is a <term>gift of God</term>. For who is able never to err, even slightly, although one might be able to avoid erring in any single individual moment? Constancy differs little or not at all from <term>longanimity</term> <note>original: *longanimitas*, patient endurance over a long duration</note>.

->*On diligence,*<-

### ARTICLE VIII.

There is also a need for diligence and sedulity, to which negligence and suspiciousness are opposed; this ensures that nothing happens to overturn and frustrate the entire labor. If we neglect the smallest things, we will gradually waste away. If we fear everything with suspicion, we shall neither sow nor reap. Yet, there is a "diligent negligence"—neglecting the smallest details so that we do not lose the greater and more necessary things.

->*On attainment.*<-

**WHEN**, however, you have arrived at the desired thing <note>original: *comprehensio*, literally "grasping" or "attainment" of the goal</note>, beware lest you pour yourself out for joy as if you have reached the "supreme good," and do not draw back as if in awe or as if you will labor no longer, like <term>Hannibal</term> <note>Campanella refers to the Carthaginian general Hannibal, who was famously criticized for not marching on Rome after his victory at Cannae, choosing instead to rest his troops at Capua.</note>. I have seen a dog, just as it was reaching a hare in the chase, turn back, and another jump over it out of sheer over-excitement; and so the hare escaped. But <term>attainment</term> <note>original: *comprehensio*; in this context, it refers to the successful grasping or reaching of a desired goal or the "finish line" of a virtuous act</note> belongs to the one who has power over their own happiness, as was said before. Those who exult too much in the acquisition of things show that their happiness depends on those objects, not on themselves. And this is a form of unhappiness.

## *On zeal and security.*

### ARTICLE X.

After acquisition, or near to it, <term>zeal</term> <note>original: *zelus*; this term encompasses both "fervor" and "jealousy"—the intense desire to protect what one loves</note> follows, lest the beloved thing be lost. It is an unhappy passion, the daughter of fear impregnated by love; in matters of lust, it is a second hell. Fear occurs because that good is more bound to another, or a rival is better than you, or you are unworthy of it, or the thing itself is flawed and insufficient for both; hence the love of God, who is most sufficient in all things, is without such jealousy. However, one who is zealous for the honor of God or a friend, so that it is not lost within us, is virtuous. For he loves the good of God and his friend, and hates evil. Likewise, he who is zealous lest he lose property, health, or virtue, is good. But he who is zealous lest he lose a questionable pleasure is evil. To be zealous for one's wife is also good—but not excessively, nor not at all. <term>Security</term> <note>original: *securitas*; here meaning a state of internal peace and freedom from anxiety</note> and the love of the true good may cure this disease. See the *Economics* <note>Referring to Campanella's writings on household and social management</note>.

<margin>
Aristotle errs in placing fortitude in the irrational part of the soul, since knowing what to despise and handling commands are acts of reason.

In the actions that, on the contrary, repel or flee from evil, great virtue is frequently required. # MORALS, CHAPTER V.

*...irrationally, we even grow angry at a physician. This only happens when the spirit <note>original: spiritus; in Campanella’s philosophy, this is a subtle, warm physical substance that acts as the instrument of the soul, flowing through the nerves</note>, ignoring any new and specific circumstances, follows a universal logic which states that one must rise up against every evil and the servants of pain. In this way, reason itself struggles within, as when it is drawn by two equally good things and must decide which to pursue first; often, by following a universal rule, it is deceived in specific instances. Likewise, desire <note>original: concupiscentia; the biological drive for self-preservation and pleasure</note> is formed by reason: its purpose is to restore what the body has lost and to generate offspring like ourselves so that we might be preserved. Thus, it does not seek out all foods, but only the useful ones, nor all women, but only those who are beautiful; it engages in procreation with skill, digests food, and separates the blood. It resists reason by following an old decree before it can weigh an imminent evil, and wanting to assist two needs at once, it loves and hates at the same time. Hence, a person with a fever desires water to remove dryness, yet hates it so as not to increase the disease. Finally, the wise person allows himself to be persuaded by a higher reason and no longer struggles. But how would the desiring part allow itself to be healed by something contrary to it if it were not itself capable of reason? Galen <note>original: Galinus</note> errs along with Plato in asserting three souls—the desiring, the angry, and the rational—which we have argued against in our "Questions" and in our "Defense of Telesio" <note>Bernardino Telesio (1509–1588) was a natural philosopher who heavily influenced Campanella's physicalist views</note>. Aristotle, moreover, should not have placed "irrational" virtues in the angry or desiring parts, but should have made all virtues rational, since he posits a single soul. Yet, because he did not know how to solve the arguments of Plato—from whom he borrowed the virtues—he contradicts himself, positing a threefold soul in his Ethics alongside Plato, despite having rejected this in his own "On the Soul." Duns Scotus, being more learned, makes all virtues rational.*

[The] rule <note>The Latin text "gula" is the continuation of "Regula" (Rule) from a missing section or intended heading</note> which teaches how much, in what manner, and against which library of evils one must resist—what labors must be overcome and what pleasures must be restrained—is called **Fortitude**. It borrows its name from physical strength <note>original: robore</note>, which exists in brute animals as well (and to a greater degree) in a physical sense, though not in a moral sense. In soldiers, this strength comes from the habit of winning, not from the rule of reason. This virtue handles weapons, subdues enemies, builds empires, and avenges insults born of contempt, but not those resulting from chance or intended for correction. It is **Clement** <note>merciful or mild</note> toward subjects and debases the proud; for it, having conquered is enough. Indeed, it hates nothing more than being held in contempt—that is, being seen as unworthy of honor, fear, or love. Contempt <note>original: despicientia</note> occurs when the spirit expands, especially into laughter (hence the term "derision"), because it refuses to pull itself together to consider or admire a thing, as if neither good nor evil could be expected from it; thus, the object appears unworthy of being loved or feared. Reputation and esteem, on the contrary, occur when the spirit contracts to admire something offered to the sight or the mind as something powerful enough to do good or ill. Therefore, this virtue is acutely cognitive and resides in the **animal spirit**. This is shown by the movement of the nerves and the fire in the eyes when someone carries [something] out—

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 271 regarding the motivations of the "spirit" (the subtle, warm substance that Campanella believes mediates between the soul and the body). It transitions from the psychological causes of movement to the specific moral definition of Fortitude and its opposing vices.</meta>

-># F. THOMAS CAMPANELLA<-

[...the spirit] is moved by anger, which is an impulse toward vengeance; likewise by the appetite for ruling, so that one might be held in high esteem. For this reason, it fights even unto death for liberty, for honor, and for God, the author of all good things. It does so partly lest it become base by performing base tasks in servitude—which for a noble spirit <note>original: generoso; refers to a person of high character or a spirit that is well-constituted</note> is to die, while existing and living like cattle—and partly because it exchanges a few years of a physical and lowly life for many glorious years in the minds of future men, or for eternal years in God. 

However, it does not succumb to labors for external goods and dangers, but bravely overcomes them. Yet, it flees those labors and those dangers in which fleeing does not diminish virtue nor bear a true mark of baseness. For it will not resist many people just to appear fearless unless all ways of escape have been closed; nor will it fight to the death for trivial causes. It is knowledgeable in both fearing and daring; in these matters, it will seem not as if it is fearing, but as if it is preserving life; and not as if it is daring, but as if it is repelling evil.

2. But that force which opposes every danger, for any trivial cause and against many people at once, attacking impossible things not by compulsion but by choice—not indeed out of a contempt for danger where one’s baseness cannot be proven (for example, when provoked by children, by insulting drunks, by a kicking donkey, or by the unlearned and the foolish), but which fights out of pain or pride and boasting—is called Rashness <note>original: Temeritas</note> and Audacity. 

It is a destructive vice, a sign of a base spirit—one that is plentiful and impure, wishing to appear noble. From this follows a wild cruelty called Barbarity <note>original: Immanitas</note>, which, when victorious, does not spare others and even destroys those reaching out their hands in supplication. From this it is clear that neither a city nor an individual man provoked to a duel is bound by the rule of Fortitude to go out to fight merely to show off who is stronger. The consciousness of one’s own virtue is sufficient. 

If, however, one is attacked, he will defend himself with the moderation of blameless defense <term>moderamine inculpatæ tutelæ; a legal and moral principle meaning one uses only the force necessary to repel an attack without seeking to cause unnecessary harm</term>, repelling force with force. Yet he will not kill unless he is unable to escape death, and even then, he should not intend to inflict death. This is the same way we conduct ourselves when fighting with beasts. For there is no virtue in displaying strength without cause. Indeed, one must even flee when many men attack you, just as when many beasts do. For they are not using virtue, but bestial strength. Not even Hercules [fights] against two, as [the proverb goes]...

<summary>Campanella defines Fortitude as a noble pursuit of liberty and honor rather than a reckless search for danger. He condemns unnecessary dueling and "barbarous" cruelty, arguing that true bravery includes knowing when to retreat from overwhelming or trivial threats.</summary>

### CHAPTER V ON MORALS

...is a proverb. <note>The text likely completes a phrase such as "to fight with many is a proverb," or a similar sentiment regarding the folly of uneven odds.</note> But if you cannot escape without dying unless you fight, then you must fight even against a thousand, and use clever stratagems; however, you should not do so against a single opponent if they are not fighting deceitfully. Having suffered an injury, refer those injuries to a judge; for a human being does not take their own revenge fairly without exceeding limits, and for this very reason there are courts in the republic. While an injury is being inflicted, you shall either fight or flee; but you shall not take up arms again *after* it has been inflicted, and especially not by calling in defenders. 

But, you say, "I will be held in contempt." Certainly, if you were struck justly because of a crime you committed against the one who struck you, if you then wish to take revenge, you will double your guilt and your shame. If you were struck unjustly, call upon the law. But, you say, "I will be despised." Truly, you will be if you act this way out of fear, but not if you do so out of virtue. Let the one who did the injury feel shame, for he has declared himself a wrongdoer. Let the one who suffered it declare himself patient and brave; and it will be a glory to him, just as it was for Paul <note>The Apostle Paul, who recounted his sufferings—including being stoned and beaten—as badges of his service to God.</note> when he was struck with fists and stones. 

Work bravely in war for your country and in other just deeds: provoke the enemy for this reason, so that everyone may learn that you forgave not out of fear but out of virtue—especially toward one seeking pardon or one declaring that they did wrong not out of contempt, but because they lacked self-control due to a defect of character. 

The city indeed should prohibit <term>duels</term> <note>original: duella; Campanella was writing at a time when private dueling was a major social issue among the nobility.</note> and decree shame upon the one who does the injury, not the one who suffers it. And when the city itself is provoked by another city, let it do the same. If it is attacked justly, let it satisfy the cause of the war. If unjustly, let it resist with as many forces as are more than enough to achieve victory. For justice must not be exposed to the danger of insufficient strength, but must be defended with more than enough force. But if this cannot be done and public safety is endangered, a duel will not be out of place, so that forces may be equalized and the blood of citizens spared, if the dispute cannot be ended in any other way; just as the three <term>Horatii</term> and the three <term>Curiatii</term> <note>A legendary battle from early Roman history where two sets of triplets fought to decide the outcome of a war between Rome and Alba Longa, avoiding a full-scale battle.</note> decided the empire between Rome and Alba. 

Perhaps a brave man will punish a perverse wrongdoer after injuries have been inflicted, not as an avenger, but as a physician and teacher, so that at least through fear the wrongdoer may stop doing evil; just as we are accustomed to correcting horses, madmen, and children.

3. But that disposition which opposes nothing—not because of a lack of strength, but by choice, because one fears for their life or property—is a vice called **Cowardice** <note>original: Timiditas</note>: most humble toward superiors, most cruel toward subordinates,

<meta>This page continues the discourse on the virtue of Fortitude and its relationship to fear, specifically addressing how fear leads to cruelty in rulers. It then transitions into Article VI, which begins an investigation into the philosophical origins of power and dominion.</meta>

# FRA TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

...never believing itself safe: for this reason, fear is most destructive in the minds of princes. They do not spare the conquered, but instead destroy even those who beg for mercy because they continue to fear them. Likewise, they diminish the number of their subjects and kill off the best men through traps and false accusations, for they fear these men rather than the common people. Courage <note>Latin: *Fortitudo*. In this context, Campanella defines it as a balanced virtue that knows what to fear and what to brave.</note> does indeed feel fear, since it serves as the standard for both daring and fearing; it neglects nothing out of recklessness—as Audacity does—but considers where it might suffer harm. Therefore, it fears vice, not virtue; it fears the devil, not God, whom it loves and worships. This worship is sometimes called "fear," but it is "filial fear" <note>A theological term for the fear a child has of offending a beloved parent, contrasted with "servile fear," which is the fear a slave has of punishment.</note>. Servile fear belongs to sinners who fear punishment, and in this way, they too "fear" God. Similar to this is the fear of losing small external goods, the favor of princes, or vain honors, rather than fearing the loss of virtue and God. 

It is beautifully said, *No one is harmed except by himself* <note>original: "Nemo læditur, nisi à seipso." This is a famous Stoic and Christian maxim, most notably the title of an essay by St. John Chrysostom, arguing that external circumstances cannot harm the soul unless the individual allows their virtue to be corrupted.</note>, as long as one does not prize fear or pleasure above virtue. For other "evils" are not morally evil, nor do they harm anything but the "outer man"; meanwhile, we double the gain of the "inner man" through virtue. From these points, it is clear what the Clemency of the strong is, what the clemency of the timid is, and what the cruelty of the bold and the fearful is: the former is a kind of madness, while the latter is treacherous.

## On dominion and law.

### ARTICLE VI.

<margin>1.</margin> Since powerful men believe they can rule over anyone they wish, it is necessary to carve out the nature of dominion, law, and their governance from the secrets of wisdom rather than from the mere sayings of men. Dominion is the outpouring of an active power over a thing subjected to it, whether by some right or by injury <note>Campanella is distinguishing between "rightful" rule and rule gained through "injury" or injustice.</note>. For the passive faculty of matter cannot rule; it can only receive the dominant "active forms," such as cold and heat. Nor does heat "rule" except in a thing into which it pours its power. Hence we say that where its rays do not penetrate, the sun does not rule at all, even though it is more powerful [than the object]. It only rules over a subject thing—that is, something inferior in strength and force. For the moon, though it is active, does not rule over the sun or over Jupiter; rather, the sun rules over the moon. Nor does an equal rule over an equal: heat...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of power, specifically defining the differences between the faculty of power, the faculty of intellect, and the faculty of will, while introducing the crucial distinction between "Right" (law) and "Dominion" (power).</meta>

### CHAPTER VI ON MORALITY

...For just as a heat measured at three units does not dominate another heat of three units—for they are equal—it does, however, dominate a heat of one unit because of its superior abundance. Yet, it dominates while nurturing that heat with love and incorporating it into itself rather than destroying it; for in nature, like does not suffer from its like. I spoke of the <term>powerful faculty</term> <note>original: *potestatiui*. This refers to the soul's capacity to act or exert influence, as opposed to its capacity to know or to desire.</note> because the intellectual faculty does not dominate, but rather knows; the volitional faculty desires; but both pour themselves out toward their objects through passions and operations. Therefore, the pouring out of the powerful faculty alone constitutes "dominion," and for this reason, it happens either by right or by injury. It is by right when it is directed toward some useful end—as when a lion kills a goat so that it may eat. It is an injury when it is done according to one's whim, for no useful purpose.

<margin>Note Well +</margin> 2. For "Right" <note>original: *Ius*. This word means both "Right" and "Law" in a legal and moral sense.</note> is the same as the just. The "just" equates an inclination or an operation to its proper end, which has been established by God, by nature, or by human choice. <margin>1</margin> Because of this, Right is threefold: divine, natural, and human. Regarding **divine law**, the Jews of old abstained from pork because that abstinence was equated to the end of saving themselves from leprosy—which God intended in this law—or perhaps to signify something else. <margin>2</margin> Regarding **natural law**, the sun rises and man eats; for the rising of the sun is equated to the end of nature (which is the illumination and generation of things), and man’s eating is equated to his own end (the preservation of the individual). <margin>3</margin> Sexual intercourse likewise belongs to natural law, because it is equated to the end of preservation. Regarding **human law**, there is the division of fields so that peace may be maintained; this includes the **law of nations** <note>original: *ius gentium*. The traditional legal concept of laws common to all "civilized" peoples, such as treaties and the protection of ambassadors.</note> pertaining to the whole species, and **civil law** pertaining to each city-state for its own specific ends. Therefore, Dominion and Right are not the same thing. For "Dominion" is the relationship of a superior to an inferior, whether it be just or unjust. But "Right" exists in every proper equation or balance. <margin>+</margin> For a servant has a "right" to seek food from a master, and a hare has a "right" to flee from a dog; they do not have "dominion," since they are inferior, but they equate their actions—the former his petition, the latter his flight—to the end of their own safety.

<margin>3</margin> 3. Finally, there is another kind of dominion that is **spontaneous**, such as that of the moon over the waters, which it illuminates and nurtures; it is called "spontaneous" on the part of the one receiving the influence. The other kind is **coerced**, as when a lion kills a donkey, which is forced to undergo that dominion.

4. I say, therefore, that dominion is fourfold: one is divine, another natural, another animal, and another human (or arbitrary).

<meta>catchword: ...bitrary.</meta>

<summary>Campanella distinguishes between "Right" (the proper alignment of an action to an end) and "Dominion" (the power of a superior over an inferior). He categorizes laws into divine, natural, and human, arguing that even animals possess a "right" to survive through actions suited to their preservation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the classification of "dominion" (authority or power) established by Tommaso Campanella, moving from the definition of "Right" to the specific categories of authority: Divine, Natural, Animal, and Arbitrary.</meta>

# FRIAR TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

<margin>1</margin>
...trary. **Divine dominion** embraces all forms of authority; it extends the power of God over all beings—specifically over their substance, their quality, and their use. This is because all things are subject to Him by the right of creation. For every creator has power over their own work and that which is subject to them, but not over what belongs to another or what is not subject to them. Therefore, God is able to annihilate, to transform, to kill, to bring to life, and to employ things for any use whatsoever, just as He does. He does this neither by whim nor by necessity, but in a **super-eminent** way <note>original: *super-eminentiori modo*. In Scholastic philosophy, this describes a way of possessing a quality that far exceeds the way created things possess it—God doesn't just "have" power; He is the source of power itself.</note> that exceeds both. 

<margin>2</margin>
We call **Natural dominion** that by which any superior being acts upon an inferior through its power—as the sun acts upon the moon, the moon upon the waters, fire upon wood, or a higher angel upon a lower one. This is divided into "spontaneous" and "forced" actions, as previously stated. It is always exercised "by right" when it is done for an end established by God or by nature, even if it involves force. For example, wood is consumed by fire through force, yet this serves the "multiplication" <note>Campanella refers to the Aristotelian idea that elements "multiply" their own nature; fire seeks to turn other things into fire.</note> intended by the Author of nature.

5. **Animal dominion**, furthermore, is the extension of the power of a stronger animal over an inferior one, whether by right or by injury. Examples include the hawk over the doves (which it eats) and the dog over the grass (which it does not eat, but tramples upon as the more powerful creature). For indeed, **plants are immobile animals.** <note>This is a characteristic belief of Campanella: that plants possess a level of sensation and soul, differing from animals only by their lack of movement.</note> There is also a "spontaneous" animal dominion, such as that of the king bee <note>Early modern writers often referred to the "Queen Bee" as a king.</note> over the bees, and a "forced" dominion, such as that of the lion over other beasts. Spontaneous dominion always occurs within the same species. For like is subject to its like by choice, because it experiences this authority as something that perfects it rather than destroys it.

<margin>4</margin>
6. **Arbitrary dominion** <note>original: *Dominium arbitrarium*. This refers to authority based on the "arbitrium" or "will/choice" of an intelligent agent, rather than fixed natural laws.</note> is that of the angels called "Dominations" over the Archangels and others; this is spontaneous. Over the demons, however, their dominion is forced. In this same way, one human rules over another by arbitrary dominion, whether spontaneously or by force; and either may be by right or by injury. This dominion is subdivided into **moral**, **domestic** (economic), and **political**. 

**Moral dominion** is that by which a human being—through moral virtues, which are essentially private laws—rules over their own passions and actions. Indeed, the mind commands the spirit <note>original: *spiritui*. In the medicine of this era, the "spirit" was a subtle vapor that carried the soul's commands to the muscles.</note> and the body in moral acts. However, in "natural" acts, it commands by natural dominion. For before a child learns to use morality, the child's soul moves the body wherever it wishes; it extends its power into the body, and through the body into food, drink, and external objects, over which it rules naturally. But

## MORAL CHAPTER VI.

...afterward, he adds moral dominion to natural dominion. **Household dominion** <term>original: *Dominium oeconomicum*; derived from the Greek *oikos* (house) and *nomos* (law), referring to the management of a private estate</term> is threefold: marital, paternal, and masterly—that is, over a wife, children, and rational servants. For over irrational beings, such as dogs, he possesses animal and masterly dominion; over inanimate things, such as a field or a house, he possesses natural, masterly, and animal dominion. To these is added civil dominion. All these forms of power are evident in the very composition of our own human nature. For the mind rules the animal spirit <note>In Renaissance physiology, the "animal spirit" was a fine fluid that carried signals from the brain to the muscles.</note> as a partner, to govern and nourish the body, and for the sake of knowledge and other matters; it treats the spirit as a companion, just as a husband rules a wife who is lower than himself. With **masterly dominion**, both mind and spirit rule the body, using it as their instrument for their own needs. With **paternal dominion**, they rule the passions and actions as if they were children born from them; they regulate these toward the good as one does with children, rather than extinguishing them. For neither the pleasures of Venus <note>original: *Veneris*; the Roman goddess of love, representing sexual desire.</note> nor Bacchus <note>original: *Bacchi*; the Roman god of wine, representing intoxication or revelry.</note> are destroyed by chastity and sobriety <margin>|| +</margin>—instead, they are perfected. Origen <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 184 – c. 253 AD) who explored the soul's internal governance.</note> had an inkling of these truths.

7. **Political dominion** does not come from nature, except in a secondary sense, and only when applied to a large number of people. Since men, overcome by passion, were not able to properly discipline their children, their wives, or even themselves, and could not judge fairly between themselves and others, they placed over themselves a single person who would use reason alone. It was to this person that they transferred their own power. Therefore, such a ruler does not possess superiority from his own nature, but from his subjects. He is not a "lord" <note>Campanella distinguishes between a *dominus* (an owner or master of property/slaves) and a *princeps* (a first citizen or leader).</note>, but a prince who leads, like a head among the members of his own kin, acting according to laws, which are the virtues of the community. 

However, when a ruler is provoked by a just war and captures a hostile city, he treats it as a servant because of its fault. This is not according to nature, but because the city deserved it. In this way, a king punishes the wicked as slaves, because they have made themselves slaves to sin. Nor can he assume for himself a power greater than that which he received through civil agreement. Truly, slaves captured in a just war are driven into servitude by right, because it is better for them to be preserved in this state than to be killed; the law equates servitude to this end. Otherwise, it is unjust. 

A person can also sell themselves into the galleys <note>original: *remigandum*; literally "to rowing," referring to the common punishment or desperate employment of rowing in galley ships.</note> or into service to flee greater evils. However, if they do so to escape minor evils, they act unjustly in a moral sense, though not in a natural one. For a person is able to kill themselves or violate their mother through "violent physical power" <note>original: *potestate physica*. Campanella refers to the raw physical capability to perform an act, which is distinct from the moral right to do so.</note>, but not through spontaneous or moral power. Those who are sent by God to a kingdom, however, can do only what God has permitted them. There-
