->F. TOMMASO CAMPANELLA<-

...civil power can be taken away and transferred; natural power, however, can never be removed by civil power. For you cannot command a servant, by the right of a master’s dominion, not to urinate or not to drink for an entire week, since in nature he is your equal, not a servant. However, through violent physical force, you can even kill him; indeed, if he is physically stronger, he can kill you. Therefore, when we struggle to make people good, we use civil dominion; when we struggle to punish, we use masterly dominion <term>original: *dominio herili*; the power a master holds over a servant or slave</term>. Civil dominion differs from paternal dominion as a whole differs from its part. We will provide the rules regarding all these matters in the following books on *Politics* and *Economics*. Furthermore, commanding and obeying are the actions of a superior and an inferior, to be moderated by these same rules.

8. In civil matters, there is dominion over the substance and the use of a house or an estate; there is also dominion over the use alone—as when someone leases the fruits but not the substance of the estate, they grant "dominion of use." In things consumed by use, both types of dominion are granted, for they cannot be separated. For example, if I give bread for use, I also give its substance. The "use of natural law" always accompanies this, though the "use of civil law" does not necessarily, as it can be separated—for instance, at a banquet <note>Campanella likely means that at a banquet, you have the natural right to eat the food provided, but you do not "own" the silver service or the room in a civil sense.</note>. All these things depend on human judgment.

## *On Exercise and its Opposites.*

### CHAPTER VII.

#### ARTICLE I.

<margin>
The wonderful benefits of exercise, which is a virtue, not because it is an action, but because it is performed wisely for such purposes. I wonder why Aristotle, Telesio <note>Bernardino Telesio (1509–1588), an Italian philosopher who heavily influenced Campanella with his emphasis on sensory experience and nature.</note>, and Plato and others passed over this virtue.
</margin>

1. For the health of the body and the perfection and illumination of the virtues, as well as the well-being of both, it is necessary to speak of the regulation of the operations and omissions of the moving power <term>original: *vis motiua*; the faculty of the soul or body responsible for physical motion</term>. For these are commanded by the will, put into execution by power, and ordered by wisdom. This order itself is a virtue. For indeed, if the body is moved too much, its composition is distressed and destroyed; if it is moved not at all, it withers and is lost. Therefore, the measure in the operation of the moving power is a virtue. It is granted for the sake of ventilating the spirit <note>original: *spiritus*; in Renaissance medicine, these were subtle fluids that carried life and thought through the nerves.</note> and thinning it, so that it might be more fit for movement and knowledge, and for thinning the blood, from which the spirit is nourished and increased, and for cleans- <note>The Latin text cuts off at *expur-*; the catchword "gandi" indicates the word is *expurgandi*, meaning "cleansing" or "purging" the body's wastes.</note>

**CHAPTER VII OF ETHICS**

...purging the soot of the spirits <note>original: *spirituum fuligines*; in early modern medicine, "spirits" were subtle fluids carrying life force, and "soot" referred to the smoky waste produced by the body's internal heat.</note>; likewise for cleansing the blood and distributing food more easily to every part of the body; for purging it of all superfluities by turning them into sweat, hair, and vapors; for easing the paths of nutrition and keeping open all the "outlets" <note>original: *cauteria*; here meaning the natural excretory channels of the body</note> by which the living being is purged—such as the anus, nostrils, ears, mouth, and the pores with which the whole body is sprinkled, through which a continuous heat exhales, carrying out smoke and oily wastes that cling to clothing. Furthermore, it serves the grace of making the body beautiful, healthy, agile, tall, well-colored, robust, and capable of labors—fit for vengeance and victory, so that it may not be the prey of those more powerful.

Therefore, wisdom says that the whole must be exercised equally. For one who exercises only the legs, such as runners, strengthens only those parts, while the rest of the body becomes flabby or less robust, and he loses confidence in himself, which is not without danger. He who exercises only the arms errs in a similar way. For a limb that is not exercised attracts bad humors <term>humors: the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—which were believed to determine health and temperament</term> to itself, and it is unable to properly digest or purge them; the disease of the other parts flows toward it, causing spasms, abscesses <term>apostemata: swellings or gatherings of inflammatory matter</term>, and joint pains. However, one who exercises the whole body equally at once—such as the legs, arms, neck, and spine—is strengthened far more effectively. For this reason, gymnastics <term>gymnastica: the ancient art of physical training and athletics</term> was invented, as were ball games and the use of weapons. Nor should the body alone be exercised through movements, but also the intellect through the study of wisdom, so that we are not the prey of sophists and false prophets; just as the intellect should not be exercised without the body, lest we be the prey of men-at-arms. For this reason, the poets decorate Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the Greek goddess of both wisdom and strategic warfare.</note> with both a book and a spear.

2. The vice in excess is called affliction; it is destructive because it causes a great many of the spirits to exhale, leaving the body dry, feverish, and trembling. It dries out the vessels of nutrition and the nerves so that they contract; it often breaks the spine, dislocates bones, bruises the flesh, and ruptures the membranes of the lower belly, leading to a hernia through the escape of wind, or even at times the prolapse of the intestines. Therefore, it is necessary to grant frequent rest to the corporeal part so that it is not dissolved.

## Universal causes of all diseases, and their history: and first, concerning Inflation.

### ARTICLE II.

1. **I**dleness generates excessive appetites, removes natural ones, and induces various diseases. For almost all of these tend to arise from distillation <term>distillation: in early medicine, the downward flow of "excessive" fluids or catarrh from the head to other organs</term>, from inflation, from rot, from crudity <term>crudity: undigested food remaining in the stomach</term>, from obstruction, and from inflammation.

<margin>Women who use makeup and not exercise—by which true beauty is gained—are a ruin to themselves, their offspring, and the commonwealth.</margin>

2. Inflation <note>original: *inflatio*; refers to the buildup of "windy" or "flatulent" vapors within the body's cavities and vessels</note> arises from a thick and abundant vapor, generated within some of the vessels or in all of them; and since it cannot exhale, because it is not thinned by exercise, nor are the pores opened through which it might exit, it brings various torments. Inside the intestines, it causes griping and colicky pains, by compressing the spirits <note>In Campanella's philosophy, "spirits" are subtle, warm fluids that act as the primary instrument of the soul to move the body.</note> remaining between the fibers as it rises, and by blocking their passage. In the heart, it causes palpitations; in the stomach, hiccups; in the head, vertigo, as the vapor—prevented from moving forward—is carried in a circle and seizes the spirit. Finally, it makes the whole body lazy, swollen—showing a false fatness—and pale. This paleness women correct with makeup <note>original: *fuco*; a red algae-based dye used as rouge</note>, to the ruin of themselves and their offspring. Often it also produces tumors in the lower belly, and dropsy <term>dropsy: an old medical term (hydrops) for swelling caused by excess fluid in body tissues</term>. Although dropsy can occur from excessive heat of the liver, which liquefies food into water before it can be turned into blood. Therefore, its remedy is solid food, which cannot easily be melted. It is also useful to strike fear into the liver by the dripping of water, so that it may soften and cool. Inflation is cured by the use of warm drink, and dry meat dishes seasoned with cinnamon and garlic; and by various substances and clysters <note>enemas</note>.

<margin>The liver, upon which water is dripped drop by drop from a high channel at alternating intervals, softens and expands so that the flame may exhale. For the fear of cold thrusts the exhaling heat inward in its thinness—heat which was causing hardness—and consequently relaxes the hard parts and disposes them toward softness. For this reason, quails killed by hawks are more tender due to fear.</margin>

## *On diseases caused by distillation.*

### ARTICLE III.

Distillation <term>distillation: the "dripping" or downward flow of excess fluids (catarrh) from the brain into the rest of the body</term> occurs from thick vapors raised into the brain, where they are condensed and multiplied. When these fluids cannot be expelled through the usual openings because of their great volume, they slip downward through the nerves, or between the skin and the muscles. If they flow down and remain in the feet, they produce gout of the foot <note>original: *podagram*</note>; if in the knees, gout of the knee <note>original: *gonagram*</note>; if in the great joints of the hips, sciatica; if in the hands, gout of the hand <note>original: *chiragram*</note>; and in any joints whatsoever, they cause arthritis.

If these fluids flow in great abundance through the spine, they cause paralysis, because the "spirits" <note>In this era, "spirits" were viewed as a subtle fluid or heat that carried commands from the soul to the muscles.</note> cannot be distributed through the nerves originating from the spine. If the fluid slips into the nerves from the skull, it fills the path of the spirits and takes away both motion and sensation. This leaves the parts stiff and upright, while the nerves themselves are contracted—much like how a rope, when soaked, is pulled tight, shortened, and hardened. Thus, a nerve is contracted and a spasm <note>original: *spasmus*</note> occurs, either from extreme dryness or from a thick dampness.

Furthermore, the thinner and sharper these flows are, the more acute is the pain they bring, though it lasts for a shorter time. Thick and "sweet" <note>Early physicians categorized humors by "taste" (sweet, bitter, salty, sharp) to diagnose their nature.</note> flows cause longer-lasting pain, but are less sharp. 

If the distillation falls into the throat, it causes catarrh; in the uvula <note>original: *columnula*</note> and the glands, it often causes quinsy <note>original: *anginam*; a severe swelling of the throat</note>. Below the chest, between the membrane and the muscles of the ribs, if it causes ulceration by its sharpness, it produces pleurisy <note>original: *pleuritidem*</note> and abscesses. However, if a great quantity simply drenches the intercostal muscles, it creates difficulty of movement in the thorax <note>chest</note>. 

If this heavy matter falls into the lungs, it produces difficulty in breathing; and if it is salty and sharp due to heat in the head, it ulcerates the lungs. From this follows a cough and the spitting of frothy blood, which is expelled by the breath as the body tries to cast out the troubling fluid. If these flows are retained in the head by occupying the ventricles <note>cavities</note> of the brain, they [induce] <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword *indu-* suggests the word *inducit*, "they induce."</note> various...

->*On diseases from decay and fevers.*<-

### ARTICLE IV.

Decay <note>original: *putredo*; the corruption or "spoiling" of bodily fluids</note> can occur from any humor, inside or outside the veins. And wherever it occurs, it produces a putrid fever. Indeed, the spirit seethes when disturbed by any event: such as from anger—in which the spirit runs impetuously through the body and excites the humors and is set on fire—or from excessive labor, or from lack of food, or from much wakefulness, in which vapors are not digested. Therefore, the spirit prepares itself with greater motion and heat (which is called a fever) in order to digest them. Or it may arise from a foul vapor in the air infecting and weighing it down by entering the head, or through the pores between the flesh and skin (as happens in the disease commonly called *Castron* <note>original: *Castron*; likely referring to *febris castrensis* or "camp fever," a term often used for typhus</note>), which the spirit soon [attempts] to remove with its own heat...

For this reason, in "putrid" fevers, constriction is more frequent, because it is more necessary.

## *On the continuous putrid fever.*

### ARTICLE V.

When the humors <term>humores: the four primary bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—whose balance determined health</term> truly decay <note>original: *putreſcunt*; meaning they become corrupt or "putrid"</note>, if this occurs within the vessels and especially near the heart, a continuous fever arises, regardless of which humor is decaying. For the spirit does not stop moving and generating heat until it has expelled the corrupt humor from the vessels. Therefore, the pulse becomes larger, faster, and more frequent than usual, especially during contraction, so that the humor may be compressed, thinned, and driven out. 

The body struggles with such heat until either the spirit is defeated and dissolved by the motion—at which point it loses its heat and dies—or it emerges victorious, yet remains weak, thin (because a large portion of its substance has evaporated), and weary. Therefore, death usually occurs at the height of the conflict, rather than at the beginning. Victory...

<margin>
Expansion becomes greater because, once the humor is expelled, the spirit seeks enlargement and growth.

...indeed, in the decline of the fever's heat, it is recognized when the expansion <note>dilation of the pulse</note> becomes more frequent than the constriction. For once freed from labor, the spirit is now amplified; it seeks to be increased and fed. This ignition, called a "fever," is useful and necessary to life, just as war is to animals. Otherwise, a corrupt humor would attack the heart and occupy the vital parts, and death would follow immediately from that humor, just as it follows those unwilling to do battle with an enemy. Malignant fevers occur within the capillary veins of the chest, where the spirit cannot fight easily with its full strength and expel the disease due to the narrowness; likewise, they occur in the deeper parts. Therefore, the extremities of the body are seen to grow cold while the internal parts burn, because the spirit is gathered from the exterior to the interior to do battle. If the spirit is overcome by the suffocation of those narrow places and by its own reduction from the heat, the person dies; if not, it soon returns to the outer parts, victorious and surging, as the pulse indicates. But then it is necessary to feed it. This should be done in all the declines of the fever, but not at the beginning or at its peak, because the spirit would abandon the war for the sake of food. It would be conquered while unprepared, both by the disease and by the labor of "cooking" <note>original: *coquendi*; the metabolic process of digestion and processing illness</note> the food simultaneously, by which the disease would also be nourished. However, where danger is imminent from weakness, it is appropriate at any time to give easily digestible food, and to purge the humors that are swelling greatly before the complete "cooking" <note>original: *coctionem*; the process where the body 'cooks' or matures the illness to expel it</note> occurs.

<margin>
A fever can occur, and perhaps perpetually does occur, before the heart is affected, because anger, grief, or the vapor of the air present in the spirits <note>original: *pnt.*, likely *presentes*</note> do not only induce a feeling. A putrid fever begins in the blood, and often in abscesses of the groin, not in the heart. Galen is therefore mistaken.
</margin>

### On the cycles and number of fevers of this kind.
#### ARTICLE VI.

<margin>
Plato thought there were four elements and four humors in the human body; therefore, from their ignitions, he makes four fevers: assigning the continuous fever to fire, the daily to air, the tertian to water, and the quartan to earth—quite according to his decrees.
</margin>
When, indeed, rottenness <note>original: *putredines*</note> occurs from bad humors drawn outside the vessels through an abundance of heat in the wasting moisture, various kinds of fevers arise: that is, Daily, Tertian, Quartan, Sextan, Septan, Octan, etc. <note>These terms refer to the frequency of the fever's return—e.g., a "Tertian" fever returns every third day</note>. For if the humor was thick...

### CHAPTER VII OF MORAL PHILOSOPHY.

...its own, but not in accordance with nature. For a "continual" fever is not always caused by bile, but by every kind of humor within the innermost parts of the body. Nor does a **tertian** <note>A fever that returns every third day by the Roman inclusive counting—meaning every other day</note> fever always arise from phlegm, but rather from bile, as Galen proves; nor is a **quartan** fever <note>A fever recurring every four days—meaning every three days</note> always caused by melancholy <note>black bile</note> alone. Likewise, there are **quintan** and **sextan** fevers, etc. And to which humor will they attribute the **hectic** <note>a persistent, wasting fever</note> and **ephemeral** <note>a fever lasting only one day</note> fevers? Galen, recognizing this, rejected Plato's views on fevers, but he foolishly followed him regarding the "elements," attempting to reduce all fevers to the four humors and four elements—a futile effort. For blood does not produce a fever for him; from which he ought to have understood that blood alone is the constitutive humor <note>the building block of the body</note>, while the others are actually excrement <note>waste products</note>, as Aristotle rightly noted—though Aristotle spoke against himself when these things did not match the rational rules of Plato. Hippocrates also contradicts himself in this by affirming the existence of "quintan" fevers, etc. Yet he teaches well that the body is composed of spirit, liquid, and solid. But how is it that only the liquid part corresponds to the four elements, while the spirit and the solid parts do not? Likewise, every humor is generated by heat, which performs various actions on different parts of matter. Therefore, all humors are "hot," some more and some less; they correspond to the four seasons of the year produced by the sun's heat according to its distance, not to the four elements.

If a spirit has become "phlegmatic" and ignited for the purpose of expelling that phlegm, it leads the consumed matter outward; but it does not do so so completely that no remnants of it remain. While the spirit exits, the humor is turned into a thick vapor within the cracks of the flesh and fibers. Likewise, in the principal place where it has its origin and its "mine," as it were, and within the veins themselves, the thicker portions remain, while the thinner parts have been breathed out from the previous ignition. Consequently, from the juices of the body and food, a portion is then turned into the remains of this type of "sinning" <note>original: *peccantis*; a medical term for a diseased or excessive humor</note> humor. Therefore, the spirit must return again to "cook" <note>original: *coquendum*; the metabolic process of refining or breaking down disease</note> and drive it out. And it returns daily, until it has consumed the whole. Furthermore, when the periods of the fever appear shorter and the ignition happens later than usual, they give a sign of victory. But if those periods are longer and the fever anticipates its usual time <note>starts earlier than expected</note>, they indicate a loss, because the harmful humor has increased, signals a fight, and is slower to soften.

2. When, however, the humor is thinner, so that the whole of it is breathed out in the first ignition and cannot be retained in the cracks of the flesh, a **tertian** fever occurs. For in order for this kind of thin humor to be regenerated, more time is required, since more of it has evaporated. For this reason, tertian fevers usually arise from the "choleric" humor <note>yellow bile</note>, from the "foam" of the blood, or from somewhat thick matter. And when they end in sweat, with a complete decline of the heat, and a complete "sequestration" <note>original: *sequestratio*; the separation and settling of waste</note> or something near it appears in the urine, a sign of victory is given: because etc.

3. **Quartan** fevers <note>A fever that recurs every seventy-two hours; named by the Roman inclusive counting as occurring every "fourth" day</note> arise from a more corporeal <note>thicker or more solid</note> humor, and for that reason, they delay their ignition until the fourth day. Indeed, thick substances are not easily moved or set ablaze; therefore, they also do less harm and are mostly nourished by **black bile** <note>traditionally associated with melancholy and earthiness</note>. **Quintan** fevers <note>occurring every five days</note> occur in a humor that is even more corporeal and dreg-filled, the restoration of which requires more time. Understand the same regarding **sextans** [every six days], **octans** [every eight days], etc. These are certainly seen very rarely, because before the "mine" <term>minera: the source or reservoir in the body where a humor is produced</term> of thick humors can be replenished, the innate power of the body—having gained a long period of truce—is nourished, increased, and strengthened to such an extent that it does not allow the rot to be rebuilt, to grow strong, or to rebel.

4. All kinds of fevers can occur in every type of humor, but they are slower in the thicker ones, though not invariably, as has been clearly shown. It also often happens that the same kind of humor arises in two different parts of the body; one of these is moved first and brings more suffering today, because it exists in a more abundant and harmful humor. The other part, however, moves later and causes less affliction, such as tomorrow. For both the **tertian**, the **daily**, and the **double quartan** are found <note>fevers that overlap or occur in multiple cycles</note>. Thus, it happens that one may be removed by the purging of a medicine while the other remains. Sometimes, indeed, the same humor in the same part is ignited once or twice a day and provokes a battle; this is because a large part of what was ignited today was converted into smoke by the heat of the **spirit** <note>the vital energy or "pneuma" that Campanella believes regulates the body</note> and exhaled. Tomorrow, however, other parts are generated by similarity from its remains, or are added and ignited from the thick "mine" having been slightly dissolved. Therefore, the fever does not return as quickly, nor with such equal affliction as today, nor with the spirit laboring in the same way over the thick source. It can also happen that today’s remains, staying outside the vessels and not being well consumed, are reignited tomorrow; while on the day after tomorrow, the battle is reserved to be repeated against the primary humor, or perhaps they are reignited on the same day.

<margin>The cold and shivering of fevers do not happen from the coldness of any humor, or from an excess of **phlegm** <note>pituita</note>, as Hippocrates thinks in his book *On Spirit*;</margin>

5. All fevers of this kind begin with shivering and trembling, because the spirit, fearing the wickedness, the sharpness, the heaviness, or the foul appearance of the agitated humor, [retreats] backward...

### CHAPTER VII. ON MORAL MATTERS <note>original: MORALIVM. While the header says "Moral Matters," the content continues the medical discussion of fevers and the body's spirit.</note>

*For a **tertian fever** <note>a fever that recurs every three days</note> driven by burning conditions does the same thing: but it arises from the "bite" <note>irritation or stinging sensation</note> of a muscle or vein, and from the flight of the **spirits** <note>the "spiritus" or vital heat that carries life through the body</note>, and from a puncture which causes a contraction, and consequently a sensation of cold. This is just as happens in fear, when the spirit flees inward, and the external parts of the body, deprived of that heat, are compressed and feel cold, as it were. **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the famous Persian physician and philosopher</note> recognized this, but caught by the deceptions of the Greeks, he clung to the theory of the four elements.*

[Inwardly] <note>original: "trorſum," likely the end of "introrsum"</note> it is gathered toward the heart and the internal organs, as if fleeing an enemy; and the exterior parts grow cold and tremble, because they lack the spirit that warms and sustains them—not because some internal cold is gaining strength. For these reasons, the pulses produce a slow <term>dilatatio: the expansion or opening of the artery</term>, but a dense <term>constrictio: the contraction or closing of the artery</term>. Furthermore, when muscles, veins, and nerves are pricked by sharp and bitter **humors** or vapors, they desire to cast off the evil they contain; but being unable to do so, they are lifted up and twisted by the suffering spirit. They shake and agitate the whole body, especially in the deeper spinal muscles, which are unable to remove the trouble for that reason, as is clearly seen in **quartan fever** <note>a fever recurring every four days</note>, where the acidic dregs affect them in this way.

Soon the gathered spirit decides to engage in battle and begins to pour out heat to the exterior along with itself. Then the pricking sensation ceases—from which blunt or sharp injury the thickness or thinness of the humor is usually recognized—and the expansion of the pulse gradually increases. This reaches a point where, in the heat of the "battle," the expansion and contraction are equal; but in the end, the expansion is greater, just as the contraction was dominant in the beginning. 

In these cases where the blood is putrefying, it is appropriate to let blood along with the troubling humor, and to purge **phlegmatic humors** with sharp and salty medicines, "cutting" and thinning them so they may be easily separated. For **choleric humors**, one should use bitter and sharp medicines, drawing them outward by the power of similarity <note>the principle of "like cures like" in traditional medicine</note>. In summer, thin humors should be removed through vomiting; in winter, thick ones should be moved through the lower bowels. The thickest humors, however, should be smoothed, warmed, and gradually dissolved with warm wines, noble juices, and by inducing sweat.

->remedy, however, is exercise, which prevails<-
->in prevention.<-

### ARTICLE VII.

**H**ectic fevers <note>From the Greek *hektikos*, meaning "habitual" or "settled." In pre-modern medicine, this referred to a chronic fever that had "settled" into the solid parts of the body, often linked to tuberculosis.</note> arise from the aforementioned fevers, acting as their remains. For after the **humor** <note>The body's vital fluids</note> has been consumed and the **spirit** <note>The vital heat or "spiritus" that carries life through the body</note> and heat have been drawn out by preceding inflammations, the solid parts remain dry with a meager amount of heat; however, this heat is great in its intensity, since it is sharp and burning within such dryness. For this reason, the pulse of those suffering from **phthisis** <note>Pulmonary consumption or tuberculosis</note> and hectic fevers is small and thin because of the meager spirit, yet it is swift and frequent due to the body’s desire to increase itself: just as we are accustomed to nurture a tiny flame with frequent, small, and swift blowing. It is also hard because of the dryness of the contracted artery.
<margin>The touch is cold at the beginning because of the meager heat; it soon becomes "biting" to the hand that continues to touch it. But in **diary fevers** <note>Fevers lasting only one day</note> the touch is mild, pleasant, and moist. In **putrid fevers** it is biting, and all the more so from a **bilious humor** <note>Yellow bile</note> in which a sharp pulsation is felt; in an **acid melancholic humor** <note>Black bile</note> it feels rough, like a hot file pricking with many points; in a **phlegmatic humor** the touch is blunt and the heat is not felt as biting.</margin>
It is difficult to recognize, since the touch appears cold at first because of the meagerness of the heat; yet, it soon becomes biting to the hand that remains in contact. However, the proper sign of a hectic fever is when the pulse is ignited after a meal, because the moisture thrown onto the dryness causes the heat to evaporate, just as happens when water is poured over **lime** <note>Calcium oxide, which reacts violently and generates heat when wetted</note>. The urine is also thin, produced by dry vessels, and oily due to the liquefaction of the body's solid substance. It is not even certain that this is truly a "fever" in the normal sense. For when the lung is ulcerated, it can neither cool the heart with a little breeze, nor purge and refine the blood to create spirit; then, as these functions fail, there remains the unventilated heat of the solid parts. These parts soon decay and lose their balance, increasing in their own humor and "sooty" vapors, which the weak heat was previously unable to purge; thus, they have constricted the skin, and subsequently caught fire, conceiving the hectic fever. And so, while the spirit boils to remove the evil, it harms itself and the solid structure—an action that would have been beneficial in putrid fevers.

*A hectic fever is not a heat created for a beneficial purpose, as other heats are, but a remnant of them made by nature for a harmful purpose. For even if it brings help to itself through the pulse, while it tries to do good for itself, it does harm by accident: because etc.*

Just as in a lamp, the oil is consumed first; then the oil soaked into the wick; and finally the native moisture of the wick itself. The remedy is to moisten the solid parts with sweet and warm baths of the first degree <note>In Galenic medicine, "degrees" measured the intensity of a quality like heat or moisture on a scale of one to four.</note>, to open the pores of the skin, and to nourish the body with milk that is not too hot (the source of natural moisture and solids), and to revitalize the **spirit** <note>The "spiritus" or vital breath that carries life through the body</note> with gentle exercise in air that is somewhat cool, purified, and thin, but not excessively so.

### *On diseases caused by obstruction.*

## ARTICLE VIII.

Obstructions caused by thick and raw **humors** <note>The body's vital fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>, when they block the **spleen** <note>Traditionally viewed as the seat of melancholy</note>, produce **black jaundice** <note>A darkening of the skin associated with an excess of black bile</note>; for the melancholic humor must necessarily expand through the body, infecting and weakening it. However, those humors blocking the gallbladder produce yellow jaundice for the same reason. Those blocking the **liver** cause inflammations. In the **intestines**, they cause **volvulus** <note>A painful twisting or blockage of the bowels</note>. Finally, in the head, they cause other diseases (as has been mentioned), especially if there is a **distillation** <note>A "dripping" or discharge of excess fluid, like a chronic runny nose or catarrh</note>. Therefore, exercise is a miraculous virtue (as God says), by which we both acquire our bread and protect our health.

### *On diseases caused by crudity.*

## ARTICLE IX.

**Crudity** <note>Undigested or poorly "cooked" food and fluids within the stomach and veins</note> is the workshop and the mine of all the aforementioned evils. For from it, thick vapors are drawn out which cause bloating; when these are condensed in the head, they cause distillation. As these crudities run through the internal organs, they bring about obstructions of the liver, the spleen, the gall, the capillary veins, the nerves, or the fibers, from which pains and inflammations follow—

For this reason, women fall into these depraved cravings due to retained menses. 

From the foul and excessive evaporation of these humors, the spirit is terrified, giving rise to **lycanthropy** <note>A delusion where a person believes they have turned into a wolf</note> and other forms of insanity. It often leads to **demon-seizure** <note>original: "dæmonoplexiam"; a condition where the body is struck or possessed by malevolent spirits</note>, because the site becomes a seat for evil spirits, which can then only be expelled through religion. The cure for this rawness is a violent purging, strengthening the stomach from the outside, and good exercise. One should use wines and foods that are artificially heated, cleansing, purifying, and somewhat harsh, such as <term>Pythacusium</term> <note>A medicinal or sharp wine mentioned in classical texts, used for its cleansing properties</note>. One should eat cooked, slightly acidic things that are "cutting" to the thick humor, so that it may be more easily expelled.

### ARTICLE X.

**I**nflammation arises either from excessive exercise—which is termed <term>Afflictio</term> <note>Physical strain or exhaustion</note>—or from a great passion, such as wrath, deep thought, sleeplessness, or fasting; or it is driven by an obstruction in one or more parts or organs. If it arises from physical strain, it can occur in the spirits alone; in that case, it is an **ephemeral fever** <note>original: "ephemera"; a fever that typically lasts only one day</note>. This is cured by drinking cold water and seeking cold air, unless some other disease or cause is present which this might harm. If it arises from a great passion, it is still ephemeral and is cured by procuring the opposite emotions. If, however, the inflammation is in the blood alone...

These herbs are indeed called "cold" because of their effect, or in relation to the warmer internal organs. Applying cold things topically is harmful because they constrict the passages, causing the heat to concentrate and increase, which further hardens the organ; no differently than intense heat, it increases the inflammation. Therefore, a gentle heat transmitted through moisture is the proper remedy. 

Furthermore, when the liver is extremely hot, it draws the heat of the stomach to itself, just as a large fire draws a small flame, thereby weakening the stomach. It liquefies the food with such violence that it turns into water or wind <note>gas</note> before it can become blood. In such cases, thick food that is difficult to dissolve into water is useful. It is also beneficial to have water drip from a height at intervals onto the region of the liver. softens. <note>original: "mollificat"; likely the conclusion of a sentence describing the effect of a remedy on the liver from the previous page</note> Likewise, it soon passes out more easily toward moist nourishment; and it more readily receives the juice of the food. Wine is harmful, especially red wine because of its thickness; white wine is helpful, being slightly acidic, diluted with water, easily penetrating, and dulling the heat for the reasons mentioned. The care for other internal organs follows the same logic, but for the kidneys, one specifically uses parsley, melon seeds, watermelons, and cooked onions, so that they may purge and break up any stone <note>original: "calculum"; a kidney stone</note> that might have formed there. For the spleen, fennel and coriander are used to thin the waste products, etc. For abscesses and inflamed swellings, one applies cold milk, animal fat, cooked onion, turpentine resin, and egg yolk, so that the heat may move out toward the moisture, and what remains may be spread out and reduced, and the site may be softened and relaxed. For this reason, lukewarm water, not freezing cold, is suitable for a burn, so that by opening the pores it gives the "flame" a way out; wine, however, is not suitable because it adds heat. Therefore, every inflammation is a fever, at least a partial one of that specific limb or organ in which it occurs; and it is treated with the care given to a fever: by expelling the excess and putrid humor, and by reducing the heat kindled within it. However, in the liver, it does not seem to be a fever, because its inflammation happens gradually and not all at once. Thus, a fever does not begin from the heart, but in the affected place where the heat boils, so that it may expel the suffering from the inflamed part.

## Chastity, and its opposites.

<margin>||</margin> The second kind of preservation, which we obtain in our children—who live as our images—is provided for through chastity. These people study virginity and restraint not because procreation is bad, but because they have exchanged this kind of fleshly generation for a spiritual one; and, being devoted to the service of the mind, they renounce the flesh and despise human goods so that they may possess eternal ones. It is natural for men who are not occupied with great affairs and are physically vigorous to procreate; but priests and philosophers, who prevail in intellect, grow weak in contemplation and are therefore not suited for Venus <note>the goddess of love, here meaning sexual activity</note>; and frequently, if they do procreate, they father children who are ignorant and unrefined. Therefore, it is better for them to give birth in the souls of beautiful youth to their own virtues, which that youth may propagate and amplify for longer times than sons are accustomed to do, who often degenerate from their fathers.

# MORALS CHAPTER IX.

...for those living in reputation. Therefore, understanding that they exist for him and he was born for others, he expressed three virtues, derived from the three primalities <term>primalities: Campanella’s core philosophical principles of Power, Wisdom, and Love</term>, by which friendships are forged and maintained after other families began to multiply from the sons of the first man. These are **Benevolence**, **Good Speech**, and **Good Deeds**. These have their summary and model in a proper and upright love of oneself, found in these precepts: *What you rightly wish for yourself, you should wish for and do to others. What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another.* <note>original: "Quod tibi recte vis, velis, faciasque aliis. Quod tibi non vis, alteri ne feceris." A variation of the Golden Rule.</note>

## On benevolence, its parts, and its opposites.

### ARTICLE I.

<margin>An example misunderstood by Aristotle.</margin>
**Benevolence** is the rule of wishing good for others, not primarily insofar as it benefits you, but insofar as it is good for them. For this is what makes a friend. If you love someone for your own sake, you do not distinguish them from a slave, a horse, or an ox; we wish for the good of their health so that they may be of use to us. We even wish for good color and flavor in wine, but for our own sake. It is true that all love begins from self-love <note>original: "amore proprio"</note>. Just as the soul knows other things because it knows itself to be changed by them, so it loves other things because it loves itself as it is well-affected by them. I love a gentle warmth because I feel myself well-affected by that gentleness; I hate a harsh heat because I feel myself ill-affected and burned by it. 

Yet, not everyone understands how someone can be loved for their own sake. For although they may cite the example of a mother who loves an illegitimate son who has been exposed <note>original: "adulterinum filium expositum." Exposure was the historical practice of abandoning unwanted infants in public places</note> and wishes him well even though she never expects any good from him, they do not see that the mother loves in him her own image and substance—which is not present in others. Therefore, it must be said that since we are all parts of the human species and children of one God, we ought to wish well to one another, even if we expect nothing in return. Hence, we feel an aversion to seeing the sick and the lame because they represent to us a wretched—and therefore our own—state of our species. That man is impious and ungrateful to his own kind who wishes ill upon another.

<summary>Campanella defines the three social virtues—Benevolence, Good Speech, and Good Deeds—arguing that true benevolence involves wishing good for others for their own sake, rooted in our shared identity as humans and children of God.</summary>

...to a man, even if harmed by him. Hate the vice, not the man. Therefore, benevolence makes all men friends.

<margin>On friendship.</margin>
2. **Friendship** is a mutual love, confirmed by reciprocal duties, for the sake of the utility, honor, and pleasure of both parties. Hence, the immodest love of a woman is not friendship, because you desire pleasure from her for yourself, and not her other goods; nor do you offer your goods to her, except by way of purchase. Although a person might pour out much upon women while deceived by pleasure—just as a person with a fever, overcome by his own passion, destroys himself—this is not friendship. **A friend is another self.** <note>original: "Amicus alter ego." A classical Pythagorean and Aristotelian definition.</note> He who cannot be "myself" to me will not be a friend. Therefore, God deifies us <note>Campanella refers to "theosis" or "divinization," the idea that God raises humans to a divine state of grace so they can participate in a relationship with Him.</note> so that He may make us His friends. We wish for a friend the goods of the soul first, then of the body, and finally of fortune, just as we do for ourselves and our children. We wish away the opposite evils in the same order. For this reason, friendship is divided into **Benignity**, **Mercy**, and **Indignation**.

3. **Benignity** <term>Benignitas: here meaning "active goodwill"</term> does not merely consider that—since we are members of one family or commonwealth—the goods of others benefit us directly or indirectly through exchange, example, and imitation. It also considers that those who lack their own goods stand in need of ours, and whether by theft or by our free will, our goods must be shared with them. Furthermore, those who lack goods of the body and soul cannot be of help to others but only a burden, just as a withered hand is a weight to the rest of the body rather than an aid. Beyond this, benignity recognizes that the human race is cheapened when others suffer, and we are cheapened within them; therefore, it rejoices in the goods of others.

4. And this same virtue, when it grieves with the miseries of others with a desire to help, is called **Mercy**.

5. When it bears with annoyance the success of the wicked—which they use to the destruction of the virtuous—it is called **Indignation**.

6. **Malevolence**, the opposite vice, makes enemies by wishing ill upon others; it also distresses and annihilates the self. It is called **Malignity** insofar as it is saddened by the goods of others, regarding them as witnesses of its own cowardice, ignorance, or weakness, which it fears. It does not grieve for the misfortunes of friends or fellow men, and then it is called **Lack of Mercy**. And when it rejoices in the success of the wicked, it is called **Wickedness**.

7. On the other hand, he who grieves too much over even the slightest misfortunes of others, and...

## On Emulation and its Opposites.

### ARTICLE II.

Since **Envy** is close to malice, it reminds us that we should now discuss **Emulation**. Therefore, so that we might invite one another through mutual competition to acquire all good things, a virtue was sown in the soul which men call **Emulation**. This virtue, when seeing the wealth, health, and virtues of others, notices that these goods are also suitable for oneself; not merely because they are useful, but because one sees oneself reflected in those who are like us. Just as they possess good things, so too should one possess them. Thus, one imitates the methods by which they became enriched, so that he may become so himself. Indeed, when a man sees himself surpassed in good things, he is saddened, tormented, and diminished; and unless he imitates those who are more powerful and wiser, he is not preserved. This virtue was necessary to moderate such passions, so that he does not desire the destruction of those more excellent than himself, but rather strives to become just like them. It is, therefore, the sign of a vigorous and noble spirit, which is tormented by nothing except its own fault—not the fault of others or of fortune—that it is not such a person as those it admires (the honest, the wealthy, and the virtuous). Such a spirit honors these people as those from whose example it learns to excel, and whom it desires and hopes to resemble.

2. But **Envy**, the opposite vice, belongs to a swollen, boastful, and impure spirit, which desires to see those it knows to be more excellent than itself extinguished; this is so they do not stand as witnesses to its own boastful, timid, and cruel laziness.

3. However, he who does not recognize that the goods of others ought to belong to him <note>Meaning he does not see the success of others as a standard he should also reach.</note>, and does not emulate them, suffers from the vice of **Meanness** and **Abjection** <term>Abiectio: a total lack of self-worth or "low-spiritedness" that refuses to strive for greatness.</term>.

<header>FRAY TOMMASO CAMPANELLA On Good Speech and its parts.</header>

## CHAPTER X.

### ARTICLE I.

**G**ood Speech <term>Beneloquentia: a term coined by Campanella to describe the moral virtue of speaking well, distinct from mere rhetorical skill</term> is the virtue that regulates our discourse so that it is profitable to ourselves and others, preserves friendships, and communicates the goods of our minds. It spreads love, greets others, offers praise, prays for good things, makes knowledge common to all, persuades toward the good, and rebukes vice. It is divided into four parts: namely, **Affability** on the part of the speaker; **Eloquence** regarding the manner of speaking; **Benevolent Speech** <term>Benedicentia: literally "well-speaking," referring here to the kindness shown toward the audience</term> regarding those to whom we speak; and **Truthfulness** regarding the object of the speech.

<margin>On affability.</margin>
2. **Affability** is the rule for presenting oneself for conversation with others. For if you do not respond or do not speak easily, you are despised as a boor <note>original: "rusticus," suggesting a lack of refinement or social grace</note>, and people pull away from you. If you speak always and to everyone everywhere, you will be seen as a burden and a person of low value. Therefore, affability requires that we be ready to respond, using humane words that entice the listeners, condescending with cheerfulness even to stable-boys and laundry-workers <note>original: "agasonibus & fullonibus." Campanella emphasizes that true virtue reaches across social classes</note>, showing ourselves to be loving, offering greetings, and praying for their well-being. In this way, mutual benevolence and virtue are maintained.

3. **Sullen Silence** <term>Obmutescentia: a vice of excessive or prideful silence</term> is a certain austerity and abstinence from speech, such that a person barely deigns to give an answer to even their closest friends, or to greet them, or to perform the social duties of conversation. This is a natural vice of those with "smoky" melancholy <note>In the medical theory of the time, "smoky" or "sooty" melancholy referred to dark vapors from the bile that clouded the spirit</note>, who struggle internally with their own darkness and do not deign to pour out their spirit to others because it is occupied within. This happens to many who are sick. But when it is done by choice, it is a great vice, especially among nobles and princes: either because they do not deign to mix with other men (as if they themselves were gods and others were beasts), or because they are ignorant and simulate wisdom through silence. They take care to avoid having witnesses to their unlearned speech, and they restrain themselves from laughter even when they most desire to laugh, so that they may appear "grave" or serious. And indeed they are grave—but like lead, not like gold.

<meta>catchword: 4. He who</meta>

# *On Eloquence.*

## ARTICLE II.

1. Eloquence is the rule for the manner of speaking. Speech becomes clear and in accordance with the custom of those with whom you speak if you are fluent in the language. You should not use foreign or pedantic jargon <note>original: "grammaticales voces," referring to overly technical or bookish language used by grammarians</note>. Let your speech also be brief, and only as long as is sufficient to express what you desire, just as we have explained in our writings on Rhetoric.
2. To Eloquence are opposed Boorishness <term>Rusticitas: a lack of social refinement or clarity</term> and Mockery <term>Dicacitas: a biting or overly-clever wit</term>. The former, being the way of boors, does not know how to speak and weaves a tangled discourse; it never expresses what it wants well; and it brings forth strange and rural words, even though it knows they are less understood. Therefore, such people do not obtain what they want; they satisfy neither themselves nor others; and they are hated in gatherings and held in derision.
3. Truly loquacious people are those who affect a roundabout way of speaking, and when they do not have a choice word, they stitch in foreign and pedantic terms: they always cite authors so that they may appear learned. This is the vice of schoolmasters <term>pædagogorum</term> and unlearned men who wish to seem wise. And these people are held to be ridiculous and boastful; for this reason, they obtain what they desire neither in the senate nor in other assemblies, and they are ranked lower than boors—just as Metellus was compared to Marius <note>Quintus Caecilius Metellus was a refined aristocrat, while Gaius Marius was a "new man" of rural origin; despite his lack of polish, Marius’s directness was often more effective in Roman politics</note>. <page-num>300</page-num>
->FRIAR THOMAS CAMPANELLA on Good Speech.<-

### ARTICLE III.

**G**ood Speech <note>original: "Benedicentia," which combines "bene" (well) and "dicere" (to speak). It is the virtue of speaking well of and to others</note>, or Blessing, is the rule of words regarding the listeners and their understanding, insofar as it produces certain emotions in their souls. Accordingly, it produces several effects: it greets, it prays, it praises virtues, it rebukes vices, it corrects those who sin, it softens anger, it consoles the sad, it honors those present and absent, and it covers the sins of others when revealing them would not serve the individuals or the common good; it provides a good example, and it spreads doctrine and profitable things.

<margin>Imprecation. Foul Language. Vain Speech. Contumely. Insult. Detraction. Whispering. Murmuring. Slander. False Testimony. Blasphemy.</margin>
2. Therefore, the vice of Evil Speech <note>original: "Maledicentia," the opposite of "Benedicentia"</note> is opposed to this virtue. It is divided into: **Imprecation**, when we ask God for evil to befall our listeners or others; **Foul Language**, when obscene matters are discussed; **Vain Speech**, when the talk is neither serious nor relevant to the matter at hand; **Contumely**, when we commit injury with arrogant lips; **Insult**, when we wound someone by reproachfully throwing their sins in their face; **Detraction**, when we secretly diminish the reputation of others; **Whispering**, which causes discord between friends by introducing mutual offenses and faults; **Murmuring**, when we speak against the deeds and words of others with a perverse interpretation, as if they were harmful or less than good, and when we bear nothing from them patiently without grumbling; and **Slander**, which brings charges to a judge that it cannot prove, or which are entirely false; likewise **False Testimony**. The evil tongue produces other evils as well, being hateful even to God when it blasphemes His divinity, and when, instead of giving thanks, it murmurs against the providence and governance of God, attributing to God what He does not have and taking away what He does. All these things, insofar as they produce wicked emotions and make men evil or hostile to us, belong to Evil Speech. For by their very object, they are acts of impiety and malice against one's neighbor. Judge responses in the same way: soft ones break anger, while harsh ones stir up fury. Both death and life are in the power of the tongue <note>A reference to Proverbs 18:21</note>. How many kingdoms and families have collapsed because of it? It is also the instrument of empire, religion, and wisdom; it plucks up and it plants.

<term>Benedicentia: The virtue of well-speaking, characterized by kindness and constructive intent.</term>
<term>Maledicentia: The vice of ill-speaking, encompassing everything from gossip to blasphemy.</term>
<term>Suſurratio: Whispering or tale-bearing specifically intended to break up friendships.</term>
<term>Contumelia: A public or direct verbal injury fueled by pride.</term>

plants, destroys, and builds up. Therefore, this virtue must be cultivated with the highest effort, and its opposite must be utterly rooted out.

3. To this is opposed, by way of deficiency, **Flattery** <term>original: "Adulatio"; the act of giving excessive or false praise to gain favor</term>: which praises whatever others say and do, especially the deeds of the powerful, whether they are good or bad. It makes those who are upright become ignorant and wicked, and it confirms the depraved in their depravity; it blinds the minds of men who are immensely greedy for praise; and it transforms them into beasts, just as **Circe** <note>In Greek mythology, the enchantress Circe famously turned Odysseus's crew into swine</note> did. This is the vice of harlots, of jesters, and of **false prophets** <note>A reference to Biblical passages like Jeremiah 6:14 and Isaiah 5:20</note>, who say "peace" where there is no peace, and call good "evil," and evil "good," so that they may extort money and honors from the people and from princes. I do not know whether flattery is worse than slander, if it were possible for flattery to rage against God as slander does. For you cannot praise God in such a way as to exceed the truth, because He is greater than all praise. And those who preach His false miracles, thinking they are hunting for His favor, are worse than devils, since they make God resemble beastly men.

## *On Truthfulness and its parts and opposites.*

### ARTICLE IV.

The **truth of a thing** is its being <term>original: "entitas"; the essential nature or reality of an object</term> insofar as it corresponds to the idea of its maker; just as a **true sword** is one that corresponds to the idea of the one who manufactured the sword. However, man does not know things as they are in themselves, because he did not make them—except partially and confusedly. Therefore, no one is entirely "true" except God, who is Truth itself and the measure of all things. Nevertheless, a man is **truthful** by saying things as he knows and believes them to be, and by doing what he promises he will do, and by denying things as he does not know them, and by not doing what he promises he will not do. For a man can be "truthful" while saying something false that he believed to be true, and he can be a "liar" <term>original: "mendax"</term> while saying something true that he believes to be false. The sense-organs first enjoy the duty of testifying by announcing to the spirit <note>original: "spiritus"; in Campanella's philosophy, this is the subtle, material vapor that acts as the bridge between the physical body and the higher mind</note> how they are affected: then the spirit returns this testimony to the mind. And they can deceive without a loss of truth <term>original: "veritas"; objective reality</term>, by saying a thing is not as it is, but not without **truthfulness** <term>original: "veracitas"; the speaker's internal honesty</term>: since they testify to the thing exactly as they are affected by it. And this was sufficient for individual men living apart from one another.

<summary>Campanella defines the vice of flattery as a transformative evil that blinds the powerful and contrasts the objective "truth of things" (known only to God) with human "truthfulness," which is a matter of internal honesty.</summary>

<header>FRIAR THOMAS CAMPANELLA</header>

But among themselves and others, and in the body of the community, it is necessary for men to tell the truth to one another; otherwise, a son would not believe his father, nor a wife her husband, nor a merchant the farmer, nor a student his teacher, nor a general his soldiers. Thus, commerce, friendship, and the **political order** <term>original: "politia"; the organized structure of a self-governing community</term> would be destroyed.

<margin>What truthfulness is in word and deed.</margin>
2. Truthfulness is divided into several virtues. For it is called **Truthfulness** <note>original: "veracitas"</note> in assertions, when a person expresses in words what lies hidden in the mind. It is called **Faith** in promises, when what is said is actually done, as the very word suggests <note>The Latin "Fides" was often etymologically linked in the Renaissance to "fiat quod dicitur" (let what is said be done)</note>. It is called **Faithfulness** in commissions—for example, when someone entrusts themselves to me to be kept safe, or trusts me with a secret that must not be told without causing ruin; even if he is my enemy and I do not explicitly promise to protect him, I am bound by the fact that, holding me to be faithful, he trusted himself to me. It is called **Simplicity** in outward appearances: for a man ought to show himself as he truly is; or if he hides his own vices, he must not sell himself as a saintly or virtuous man through words or deeds. It is called **Clarity** in contentions: for when a man is bound to fight with equal weapons, and when a display of prowess is made, he must not attack from a hidden place nor with unseen weapons; for victory is the proper fruit of **fortitude**, not of prudence or cunning. It is called **Sincerity** in contracts and commerce, and **Ingenuity** <term>original: "Ingenuitas"; here meaning the quality of being open, honest, and high-minded in social interaction</term> in conversation.

3. The vices opposed to these are: **Lying**, which is the opposite of truthfulness, whereby one goes against the mind by saying what is not in the soul and denying what is. To do this knowingly and willingly is the sign of a most unhappy spirit—impure and **smoky** <note>original: "fuliginosi"; a metaphor for a mind clouded or darkened by deception</note>—which neither tastes things as they are, nor speaks as it tastes them. Such a spirit does not look toward the truth of its own being, nor toward the Divine truth (to whose model it ought to be conformed), but rather toward a brief and false utility that is foreign to it. In this, the liar annihilates himself by saying what is not in his mind, and thus reduces his own **being** to **non-being**. **Perfidy** is opposed to Faith; it deceives the hope of another and breaks one's own entity, ruining commerce and dissolving the human race. This is a lethal crime when the promise was just, and made by one who was of sound mind and not reduced to impossibility—alas, the plague of our age! **Treachery** <note>original: "Proditio"</note> is opposed to Faithfulness: for we call him a betrayer and a traitor who delivers a friend or a committed matter to enemies, or who gives them up when they fall into misfortune. This is a vice of an ignoble soul, which [seeks] an opportunity even [to show] itself as noble...

<header>ON MORALS, CHAPTER X.</header>

...of showing off turns to his own disgrace. Others betray secrets, others their fatherland to enemies, and others sell and publish the writings and doctrines of friends entrusted to them as if they were their own; this is worse than if you were to sacrifice a son in the presence of his father. Those who are simple in mind are magnets for traitors.

*Hypocrisy* is opposed to **Simplicity**; it feigns holiness in dress or words with the intent to deceive. However, this does not apply if the holy dress is simply the required uniform of one's profession: for no one is bound to reveal their own private vices and misfortunes unless it is absolutely necessary. Those who, through *irony* <note>original: "ironiam"; here used in the classical sense of "dissimulation," or pretending to be less than one is, often associated with Socrates</note>, pretend to be bad when they are actually good, also commit a sin if they cause a scandal to others or do so out of empty pride. However, they do not sin if they humble themselves by acknowledging their own real imperfections. For good things come from God, and we must not boast of them as if they were our own, just as we must accuse ourselves of our own evils. Those who falsely praise themselves with the mark of *boasting* <note>original: "iactantiæ"</note>—which is arrogance in words, just as arrogance is boasting in deeds, and both are lies—these are proud scoundrels, and they find no trust anywhere.

**Insidiousness** <note>original: "insidia"</note> is opposed to *Clarity* (a virtue which lacks a specific name). Deceit is permitted against enemies of the state and where they deserve to be deceived; these are counted among military *stratagems*. But where men compete on equal terms by agreement, such snares are shameful. Those who disparage another’s reputation in secret are treacherous, yet they are less evil than those who do so openly and add the act of mockery. **Circumvention** and **Fraud** are opposed to *Sincerity*; this involves cheating in prices, deceiving in business, and pushing labor onto a partner while keeping the profits for oneself. **Duplicity**, **Guile**, and **Deception** are opposed to *Ingenuousness* <note>original: "ingenuitati"</note>; these involve deceiving one's companions in word and deed for one's own benefit. The falsified height and beauty of women also pertain to both guile and fraud; we reveal the evils of these things in our work on *Economics* <note>original: "Oeconomicis"; Campanella refers here to his treatise on the management of the household and social roles</note>.

4. On the other hand, the person who, conversely, insists on telling the truth about everything immediately and wants to be completely open—even if evils follow—just so he himself is not a liar, suffers from a vice with an unknown name. It could be called **Truth-killing** <term>original: "Vericidium"; a coinage by Campanella combining the Latin for truth ("veritas") and killing ("-cidium"), modeled on "homicide"</term>, for he slays and betrays the truth. For why, when questioned by anyone at all about his own enormous sin, should he confess it? Let him confess to GOD and the minister of GOD as is proper. If David, Solon, and Brutus <note>Campanella refers to historical and biblical figures who feigned insanity ("insaniam," the catchword for the next page) to survive or achieve a greater good: King David before the Philistines, Solon to incite the Athenians to war, and Brutus to survive the tyrant Tarquin.</note>

<header>OF BROTHER TOMMASO CAMPANELLA</header>

...if they had not feigned insanity, they would have lacked the praise of wonderful prudence. This, however, is lying by deed rather than by voice, when the situation demands it. Likewise, why would a doctor sin if, while offering bitter medicine to a boy, he were to say it was sweet? <margin>+</margin> For this reason, others allow the <term>dutiful lie</term> <note>original: "mendacium officiosum"; a lie told for a helpful purpose or out of duty, rather than to harm</note>, since it is not done with the intent of deceiving but of helping—indeed, even if it involves deceiving one who deserves to be deceived. Examples include Judith deceiving Holofernes; the mother of the Maccabees likewise mocked Antiochus; and Elisha said to Ben-Hadad, "You shall not die," even though he knew he was going to die. Furthermore, Jacob <margin>+</margin> lied to the detriment of his brother in the presence of his father; and although his speech was the truth in a figurative sense, in a historical sense it was a lie. History provides the foundation for dogma. For it is not as if the adultery of David was not adultery just because it signifies wonderful things, as St. Gregory testifies. Indeed, fables and parables are not lies, nor are they evil, unless they are destructive. For they possess meaning not in what the words sound like, but in what the things signified by the words signify in turn. Yet, what we are discussing here is history, not a comedy. Therefore, without prejudice to the judgment of those better than myself, the "dutiful falsehood" is permitted along with Chrysostom and Jerome, because it is not counted as a lie, but as a stratagem. <margin>+</margin> For if it is permitted to kill a night intruder so that he does not kill me, why, when asked for my name by someone who seeks me for my death, could I not say, "I am not Thomas," thus looking out for my own life and his at the same time? Do not some think it a lesser evil—indeed, a good thing—<margin>+</margin> to kill the intruder? Outside the order of law, no one is bound to confess the truth. Regarding a "jocose lie" <note>a lie told in jest or for fun</note>, there is only slight doubt.

5. **The Oath** is added to this virtue as a divine testimony; it requires judgment, justice, and truth, just as a promise or a vow does. If these conditions are not met, or if the oath turns toward an evil outcome, it must not be kept. In such cases, the sin was in making the oath, and it is a crime to observe what you swore, as was the case with Herod and Agamemnon. For God is not a witness to evil things. Promises, assertions, oaths, and other demonstrations are to be understood according to the sense of the speaker when he speaks obscurely, ambiguously, or with double meaning—specifically in cases where he is not bound to speak the truth and keep his word. Where he is bound, they must be understood according to the sense of the listener.

# Concerning credibility and its opposites.

## ARTICLE V.

<margin>A marvelous rule of believing, from philosophy.</margin>
**T**ruthfulness stands for little in the state and among friends unless it is believed. Nor, indeed, should one believe everything said by all men, nor should one believe nothing, since we have experienced so many lies and falsehoods. Therefore, let the rule of believing be called Credibility, the object of which is trust in those who promise, truthfulness in those who assert, and so on; and for this reason, it is sometimes taken for credibility itself. Those whom we believe should be neither deceived nor deceivers. Therefore, a person ought to know what they are saying, and they must be able and willing to speak without fear. Wherefore, one should believe the upright, the wise, and those who are not afraid when they speak as witnesses; however, when they speak merely as those suspecting something, you should likewise only form an opinion. For this reason, I would believe Columbus more when he testifies affirmatively about the other hemisphere than St. Augustine when he holds a negative opinion <note>original: "S. Augustino opinanti negative"; St. Augustine famously argued against the existence of the Antipodes—people living on the other side of the Earth—reasoning that they could not be descended from Adam. Campanella uses the discovery of the Americas to show that empirical evidence outweighs even the highest theological authority in physical matters.</note>. Let us believe the words of God so that we may understand. To the words of men, let us apply intellect and experience so that we may believe, at least where there are no eyewitnesses. In common conversation, it is a matter of politeness to believe; and it is voluntary where it does not matter whether one believes or not; but where it does matter, weigh the evidence carefully.

2. Credulity and Incredulity are opposed to Credibility. The former belongs to a fickle mind, giving faith to anyone expressing an opinion. For a weak spirit is easily moved by every wind of doctrine and talkativeness. Fools are they who believe new <term>heresiarchs</term> <note>original: "haeresiarchis"; the founders or leaders of a heretical sect or movement</note> without the evidence of miracles, the shedding of blood, or divine status: because they do not want to examine the accusations these leaders make against the old religion. This is a vice of children, of old women, and of those who profit from the credulity of others.

3. Incredulity is stiff-necked; it does not know how to examine truth and testimony. Whatever it has once drunk in, it holds onto obstinately. Whatever you <term>logically demonstrate</term> <note>original: "syllogizas"; to use a syllogism or formal logic to prove a point</note>, it considers false. Those infected by this vice sometimes do not believe the prophets, yet they believe in empty sciences. They need the rod, for they wish to be deceived. Yet it is not thus in the marketplace, where buyers and sellers deal with so many lies, which they are well aware of. But let the winner thrive through credulity and incredulity. Good God, who [would have thought] so many...

## *Concerning requesting and its opposites.*
### ARTICLE VI.

Furthermore, since no one is so self-sufficient that they do not require the help of others—not even if you were a king; indeed, the greater one is in political life, the more needy they become—hence arises the abundance of soldiers, attendants, and servants who assist and minister. For Wisdom willed that everyone should mutually require the labor of others, so that one might become a benefactor to another, and so that no one should be idle, isolated, or devoid of duties. And indeed, since not everyone knows or perceives our needs—which, if we keep silent about them, would lead to our ruin or to a most uncomfortable life—and since there are those who, though they know our needs, will not help unless asked; yet if we were to beg for every single thing from anyone at all, seeking help, food, clothing, defense, and other necessities, then we would become hateful, like lazy drones <note>original: "fuci inertes"; Campanella uses the classic metaphor of drones in a beehive to describe those who consume the resources of the community without contributing labor.</note> living off the labor of others. Moreover, the state would perish if everyone were to beg while no one worked, for there would be no one to give us external goods of the body or the mind if everyone were a beggar and no one possessed anything.

Hence, there is a need for a rule of petitioning—of what is proper, when it is proper, and from whom we might obtain it. This virtue was unnamed by the ancient philosophers, but Wisdom has commended it, saying: "Ask, and you shall receive; knock, and it will be opened to you even in the middle of the night" <note>Campanella refers to the words of Jesus in Matthew 7:7 and the parable of the persistent friend in Luke 11:5-8.</note>; for they will give to you at least because of your persistence. This virtue is a species of **Good-Speaking** <term>Beneloquentia: literally 'speaking well,' here used as a technical term for the art of using speech to achieve a good or necessary end</term>, insofar as it benefits oneself, rather than others (unlike the types of speaking already mentioned). Let it therefore be called **Requesting** (*Rogatio*): which advises us on what we should ask for, from whom, how, where, and when.

Certainly, since a petition declares a need—which happens to us either through our own fault or by fate—it is a matter of modesty and shame. For anyone shudders to declare their own misfortunes and faults, except where necessity compels them, or where an excuse for the fault (even if feigned) is present. For this reason, we should not ask for just anything, nor at just any time, but only for what is needed and when it is needed. For an impudent person will ask for bread in May for a future need that will not arise until the month of August; and when...

...[when] he who wishes to give does not have the means. Likewise, when he is occupied in a more urgent business than your own necessity requires, would you rightly ask him to tell you Roman history, or to walk a long road with you? Nor shall you ask for bread from a starving man; nor ask a king to lift your donkey out of the mud; nor ask a doctor for shoes, but for medicine—asking from each person that in which they abound. 

But when no one [with an obvious surplus] is available, ask from anyone; for perhaps someone has what you need, whether they are known or unknown to you; although we feel less shame asking those who know us and are aware of our necessity. Regarding superfluous things, however, one should ask less from strangers. 

But you shall ask for the goods of the soul <note>Bona animi: refers to intellectual and spiritual benefits like wisdom, advice, or religious instruction.</note> more boldly, yet never without humility—such as seeking advice, teaching, or an explanation of the law. Do not be afraid to do so even if you are an old man, for it is worse and more shameful to remain ignorant than to learn. You shall also ask for the goods of the body boldly when you are sick or have fallen, so that you may be healed or lifted up. 

Likewise, you may ask for external goods in times of poverty, such as food and clothing, provided you are in need not out of laziness or idleness, but because you were robbed by bandits, or afflicted in prison, and so on. From those who owe you something, you may ask more freely, but do not demand it as a formal debt lest they be put to shame; rather, ask as if for a favor, so that they may give more generously and cheerfully. 

You may even be persistent where the benefactor is harsh yet capable, and your necessity is urgent—especially if he has a duty to help. For instance, a friend, by reason of friendship; a judge, because he is paid to administer justice; or a teacher, because he knows how to teach and has a duty to do so. For every human being owes love and kindness to every other human being: but especially those who are more closely connected, those who are chosen for a specific duty, those who have previously received from you, and those who promise help of their own accord. 

Indeed, such people are not only wrongdoers if they do not provide what you ask, but they are moreover ungrateful, and betrayers of faith and hope—especially those who have received the goods of the soul from you. "For if we sow spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal benefits?" <note>original: "Si n. vobis seminamus spiritualia, quid magnũ est, si vestra beneficia carnalia metamus?" This is a quote from the Apostle Paul in 1 Corinthians 9:11, justifying the material support of those who provide spiritual leadership.</note> 

Therefore, it is also permitted for monks to ask for necessities from the people, on whose behalf they labor in spiritual matters; just as the priests of all nations have always done. Nor are they idle when, through wisdom, prayers, and good example, they build up and refine the human race, if one considers it rightly. For this reason, they bind themselves to minister spiritual things even to those who do not ask; to mix these spiritual duties with the "mechanical arts" <note>Campanella refers to manual labor or trade crafts, arguing that scholars and clerics should focus on intellectual labor rather than manual work to avoid diminishing their spiritual service.</note> is to diminish them. You shall not, however, ask for superfluities, but only for necessities, and for things which do not conflict
