...conflict. <note>The text likely concludes a thought from the previous page regarding requests that clash with moral law.</note> For one should not ask for sexual immorality from a woman, even if she is willing; nor should one ask a thief to steal so that he may give an offering to the altar. In short, whatever can be refused by any law—whether divine, natural, or human (provided that law is not yet defunct <note>original: "cadaveroso," literally "corpse-like" or "decayed," referring to laws that have lost their force or moral relevance</note>)—must not be requested even from someone who is ready to give it. This type of seeking is called a **Petition** <term>Rogatio: In Campanella’s ethics, this is the specific virtue of knowing how to ask others for help correctly</term>, because it involves prayers, reverence, and submission. For he who needs another’s help submits himself to that person in the matter of his need.

But a prince and a lord requests from his servants as a debt, without prayers, that which is owed to him as the public head or as a master; just as the head immediately commands the limbs, but not without cause. However, in those matters where the master is equal to the servant, he shall not request imperiously, but humbly. For he shall not ask a fisherman for a fish except for a coin <note>original: "denario"</note>; and when he does not have one, he shall ask for it as a favor. Nor should he ask the people for new and superfluous taxes; for this is unworthy and against virtue—just as if the head should ask the hand to strike a muddy plate or a horn against the forehead, by which both the head and the hand are defiled.

In making a request, beware of persistence <term>importunitatem: an inappropriate or annoying level of social pressure</term> and arrogance. Admit that you suffer necessity just like other men, and that for this reason you have the right of asking and obtaining. And you may press your case if the one who has the means refuses you, perhaps to test your patience, or to see if you truly are in need, or if you wish to use what is given badly; or perhaps because you do not acknowledge a mutual obligation. 

If he gives quickly, and you ignore the greatness of the benefit and hold it as nothing; for these reasons it is permissible for a giver to delay his generosity, especially when what you ask for is more convenient for him to keep than for you to receive. Your own merits, the other's debt to you, your necessity, and the honesty of the cause can and should add urgency to your requests—especially if the request results in *his* own good. In such a case, it will be permissible to argue, beseech, and rebuke, whether the time is right or wrong <note>original: "oportune importune," a reference to 2 Timothy 4:2, meaning "in season and out of season"</note>. If they still do not give, they are moreover ungrateful, because prayers are themselves a kind of payment; having received these, and yet they do not give. Therefore, we should feel pity for them rather than for ourselves.

From God, however, we ought to ask for things worthy of God and things that are good for us. And since we do not know whether children, a wife, possessions, wealth, health, and other goods of the body and fortune—or even knowledge of the mind—will be profitable to us; for this reason, **Socrates** <note>The Greek philosopher, whom Campanella frequently cites as a model of natural virtue</note> thought that we should ask God for nothing except that He give us good things as it pleases Him; not so that our will might obtain what it seeks, but so that our will might desire what is truly good. Indeed. But yet, it is permissible to ask for both virtues and physical goods, as well as external things—since without Him nothing was made—insofar as they are directed toward virtue and eternal life, which is the only thing we worthily seek from such a great Giver. We should also ask that He not grant them if they should turn toward a bad outcome, or that He might turn even these things to good. And if He does not give, we shall be healthily insistent; for we do not "wear him down" <note>original: "caput obtundimus," literally "to beat his head," a Latin idiom for annoying or pestering someone through repetition</note> when we ask. On the contrary, He considers us to be troublesome only when we are *not* insistent. Just as a father considers us to be falling away from our character if we do not constantly and always ask him for those things which contribute to virtue. For He rejoices more in our love for the good because of this asking, than He grieves over the evil. No craftsman does not hate a flaw in his own work, as the fault of the effect seems to reflect back upon the cause. Furthermore, in this way He binds us to Himself and accustoms us to His love and fellowship. God also delays for this very reason: because He *wants* to give, and for the reasons mentioned shortly before.

Furthermore, when we ask God for temporal goods <term>temporal goods: material or worldly things like food, health, or money, which exist only within "time" as opposed to eternity</term>, we recognize Him as the author of both visible and invisible things. This stands against the heresy which believes that only invisible things come from the good God <note>This likely refers to Manichaeism or Gnosticism, which viewed the material world as evil and created by a lesser or wicked deity</note>. However, this must be done such that when we seek what we can acquire through our own efforts, we should labor and pray at the same time.

For he who expects God to send him his necessities while being idle himself—not by God’s command as Elijah was <note>Refers to the prophet Elijah being fed by ravens or by a widow during a famine by divine decree (1 Kings 17)</note>—is testing God. He might be testing God’s power, to see if He "can prepare a table in the desert" <note>A reference to Psalm 78:19, regarding the Israelites doubting God in the wilderness</note>; or His wisdom, when he asks for knowledge that he could obtain on his own; or regarding the future, when those things do not concern him; or regarding His love for us, when he demands a sign of salvation from God while neglecting the available medicine. Such things must not be done. Instead, one must assume that God is all-powerful, all-knowing, and all-willing. When we cannot achieve something through human means, we must ask Him to help miraculously; but when we can, we should work, asking that He aid our labor, since without Him we can do nothing. We may, however, test human beings—to see if they love us, if they know something, or if they are capable—whenever it is in our interest or the public’s interest to experience their character.

2. Moreover, he who refuses to ask for the things he lacks, lest he appear contemptible, suffers from the vice of pride and boastfulness. In this way, the Giants <note>In classical mythology and biblical tradition (the Nephilim), the Giants were often used as symbols of "superbia" or overweening pride that challenges Heaven</note> did not petition God, trusting instead in their own strength. If...

Truly, because he considers himself unworthy, he will make himself worthy by this very fact, because he confesses his own miseries. If, however, he does not ask because he does not understand the way of living, this "littleness of spirit" <term>littleness of spirit: Campanella uses the term *exiguitas*, implying a lack of the magnanimity required to sustain one's life</term> is his vice, the sister of sloth. Since no one is self-sufficient, one dedicates oneself to the arts and practical exercises so that by doing good for others, one may receive benefits in return. When a person is unable to do this, he asks and receives. Indeed, he will even steal, since all things are common by nature before the institution of a polity <term>polity: a structured government or civil society</term>, and they become common again in a time of necessity <note>Campanella refers to the legal and theological principle that in cases of extreme, life-threatening need, private property ceases to exist and all things return to their "natural" state of being shared.</note>.

3. However, he who asks everyone for everything while living in idleness is gripped by the vice of petulance; this is born from laziness and a lack of shame. For such a man does not wish to work, yet he is not ashamed to declare himself unworthy of those very things which he admires in abundance even among the lowliest craftsmen. Furthermore, the man who asks from those he should not (such as those who have nothing), or asks at the wrong time or place, or asks for things that benefit him little or serve his vices, is worse than a drone <note>original: "fuco," the male bee that does not gather honey; a common classical metaphor for a social parasite</note>, which we expel from the "republic" of the bees. For this reason, those scoundrels who pretend to be sick, or even fake scabs and ulcers and sometimes mutilate their own arms to extort alms, must not be tolerated. Neither should we tolerate those who trifle and act as parasites in the courts of princes, so accustomed to gaping for favors that they make those who do not give feel ashamed, as if they were illiberal <term>illiberal: in this context, meaning "stingy" or "un-gentlemanly," the opposite of the virtue of Liberality</term>. And indeed, the givers would be truly liberal if, having warned these parasites of their vice, they sent them away empty-handed to face their shame. What shall I say of prison-keepers—or rather of prefects and magistrates—who seek and extort gifts from the poor through secret force? If they ever "ask," their request is a command to the miserable.

# *On Beneficence and its Opposites.*

## CHAPTER XI.

### ARTICLE I.

Beneficence is a noble virtue. It does not act from the compulsion of a legal command, as justice does, nor from the hope of profit. Instead, it considers doing good to be a divine and excellent thing. It directs its own goods toward the benefit of others, not as bait on a hook, but as the fruit of an exuberant nature...

<meta>This page continues the ethical discussion on the nature of asking and receiving, transitioning from the individual's need to the virtue of the giver. It focuses on "Beneficentia" (beneficence or doing good) as a rational and divine-like extension of one's own abundance to others.</meta>

# MORAL PHILOSOPHY CHAPTER XI.

...[of a noble soul], confident in its own excellence, and being sufficient both to itself and to others, it shares itself. It does good to those who deserve it, often to its own detriment, when the good of the recipient outweighs the giver's loss. Therefore, reason <term>reason: for Campanella, reason (*ratio*) is the fundamental ordering principle of the universe and the soul; all virtue must be a manifestation of this order</term> forbids doing good to those who do not need it, or taking from the needy. Every virtue is, in fact, reason. Dying for an inferior or a baser person is not an act of beneficence. But to die for one's country, and for the many—especially for the good—is the highest act. As a rule, the man who prefers the whole to the part, the community to individuals, those more closely related to those less related, and the noble to the base, is not mistaken. For he imitates God, who cares for the parts for the sake of the whole, creating plants for the beasts, beasts for man, and the lower for the sake of the higher. Sometimes a beneficent man, in dying for those who seem lower, does not believe he is dying for them specifically, but for the sake of virtue and the love of God, whose creations they are. Likewise, he is preserved in those he has saved; though dying, he lives on in honor—which is to exchange a brief and narrow life for one that is long and wide.

Therefore, one must do good even to those from whom we expect no benefits and fear no harm; indeed, even to those who do us harm. In this way, we manifest the actions of a noble, pure, and confident spirit, who does good simply because he is better and more divine than others through virtue. Thus God does good to all because He is the Best; He **makes His sun rise upon the good and the evil** <note>original: "solemq; suu oriri facit super bonos & malos" — a reference to Matthew 5:45</note>, not because He desires anything from us (since He lacks nothing), but because He rejoices in the overflowing abundance of His own goodness. This is why Monarchs and Kings are especially bound to this virtue. You shall measure your benefits by the needs of the recipients: by providing defense to the oppressed, food to the hungry, hospitality to strangers, clothing to the naked, consolation to the sorrowful, counsel to the perplexed, knowledge to the ignorant, correction to the sinful (even through the force of justice), and liberation to captives. **You shall be eyes to the blind and a foot to the lame** <note>original: "Oculis eris cœco, & pes claud" — a reference to Job 29:15</note>; but do not be an eye to the lame or a foot to the blind. Do not give everything to one person, nor too much or too little; but as you are able, be merciful—that is, beneficent in action. For mercy in action is what we call beneficence.

2. This virtue is the **touchstone** <term>touchstone: original Latin *lapis Lydius* (Lydian stone), a dark stone used since antiquity to test the purity of gold and silver by the color of the streak left behind</term> upon which a man tests his own and another's benevolence and fine-sounding words. Oh, how many have said, and intended to act, and believed they were ready to go with me even to prison and to death—yet when it came to deeds, they retreated,

FRIAR TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

<gloss>8th</gloss> ...or they did the opposite. Thus, they finally understood that they loved only in word, not with a stable will, but with a mere passing affection stirred up by present circumstances. This love was not supported by the command of power or a foresight of the future, but only by "scent" <note>original: *odoratione*; likely meaning a superficial attraction or a mere 'whiff' of virtue rather than a deep-rooted commitment</note>. It is easy to speak well and wish well for friends; but when we come to actually doing good, as is proper, *this is the task, this is the toil* <note>original: *hic opus hic labor*, a famous quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid* regarding the difficulty of returning from the underworld; here used to describe the difficulty of turning words into action</note>. Hesitation, the fear of losing wealth, life, reputation, pleasures, or comforts—these things throw everything into confusion. When you demand deeds, they offer only words and deliberations; they refer you to the help of others as if it were more convenient, claiming they are ready to do everything for you except the very thing you ask. In this, they lie, and they are **Maleficent** <note>original: *Malefici*; literally evildoers or those who act with ill intent</note>.

3. Indeed, **Maleficence** <term>maleficence: from the Latin *maleficentia*, the active practice of doing harm or the wicked neglect of one's duty to do good</term> is the opposing vice, wicked both in what it omits and what it commits. Indeed, failing to help a person in need when you are able—and failing to strive by every means to become able when you are currently unable—is the mark of a perversely malicious soul. Nor are they excused by the claim that they "wished to help but could not," for if one applies true diligence, it is often possible to find a way. This is why God judges those who did not feed the hungry or free the captive to eternal punishment, as if they had committed a crime against Him personally <note>A reference to the Biblical Last Judgment in Matthew 25</note>; they acted as if these people were nothing to them, or as if they were powerless. How much more, then, will He punish those who [harass] those visiting captives, and those who hinder works of beneficence?

But even more malefic are those friends who promise to be there for us when the need arises, but when finally called upon, they make excuses and frustrate our hope; they show themselves worthy of the punishment meted out to traitors. Perhaps those who actively do harm are even worse—certainly so, if they harm friends or even strangers. But those who delight in maleficence are dreadful—a plague and a scourge to the human race. These people often converse with devils to learn their wicked arts; they dare to do anything, even if they are often just timid women or low-born men. For baseness is the mother of cruelty wherever the spirit is impure. They often wish to see good men destroyed because they feel a natural antipathy toward them.

**Tyrants**, however, are the most malefic of all. They betray the justice entrusted to them. Because they are base and wicked themselves, they kill philosophers, prophets, and the friends of God. They keep abject men around them while banishing the noble from their court, for they are conscious of their own unworthiness to rule...

<summary>Campanella defines maleficence not just as doing evil, but as the failure to do good and the hypocrisy of false friends. He concludes by condemning tyrants who surround themselves with the base and persecute the wise and the holy.</summary>

# MORAL MATTERS, CHAPTER 11.

...they fear those superior to themselves, or those instances where wiser witnesses are present—witnesses who are enemies to their own wickedness or ignorance. They certainly ought not to expel or kill these witnesses, but rather yield authority to them, or invite their counsel into a share of the government, just as Pharaoh did with Joseph <note>referring to the biblical account in Genesis, where Pharaoh elevated Joseph to high office because of his wisdom</note>.

4. On the other hand, the person who confers benefits without any discretion or selection—giving to everyone, even the base and the unworthy, and to those who have no need of them, or doing so when the time and place are improper—takes away from himself the ability to do good to those who are truly deserving and truly in need. Such a person is not "evil-doing" <note>original: *maleficus*</note>, but rather ignorant or faint-hearted, attempting to buy security and empty, vain glory from everyone. His vice has no specific name; it could be called **Inconvenience** <note>original: *Incommodatio*; here meaning a lack of suitability or social disruption</note>. For he is an inconvenience both to himself and to others. However, the person who gives gifts, and the person who receives them for the purpose of perverting justice or doing harm, are both "evil-doers" in the direct sense <term>elicitive: in Scholastic philosophy, an "elicited" act is one produced directly by the power of the will itself</term>; whereas the greedy man and the liar, etc., are so by command <term>imperative: an "imperated" act is a behavior performed by another faculty (like the hands or the tongue) at the command of the will</term>.

5. Here a problem arises: who loves more, the benefactor or the one who receives the benefit? Indeed, it is the benefactor, because he loves his own goodness as it is spread into others. The receiver, however, spreads nothing of himself, but remains obligated. Hence, it is more blessed to give than to receive <note>Acts 20:35</note>, since the former belongs to the one who overflows, and the latter to the one in need, as Wisdom has taught. For this reason, a holy man <note>likely referring to a Church Father such as John Chrysostom</note> once stated a paradox: that the benefactor even owes more to the receiver than the other way around. For the benefactor gains a good reputation, the love of men, and a reward from God. The beneficiary, on the other hand, gains only that small thing he received, in exchange for which he is now obligated. Therefore, I ask: does a father then owe more than a son? This problem is true regarding the circumstances, but not regarding the essence of the act.

...therefore <note>the text begins mid-sentence; "pterea" is likely "propterea"</note> [Nature] added **Gratitude** to that virtue as a daughter. This virtue returns a favor to benefactors whenever it can, and whenever it is useful to them. Indeed, it returns more than it received whenever possible and beneficial to do so. At the very least, by giving thanks in words, the grateful person shows themselves to be both bound and mindful; this is, as it were, the first fruit of the act, not a final reward or "interest" <note>original: *usuræ*</note>. However, one should not exceed moderation in the desire to pay someone back; for it would be a meanness <note>original: *vilitas*</note> to try to "buy" favors with favors, as if one did not trust in their own virtue to be worthy of benefits without a direct trade. Similarly, it is a fault to return a favor to someone who has no need of it when the giver themselves is in need, or to do so too suddenly and at an improper time.

### 2. The unnamed vice of this virtue.

This vice can be called **Ingratitude** <note>original: *Exgratitudo*; literally "out of gratitude," a term Campanella uses to describe the deviation from the virtue</note>, because it is carried outside the bounds of gratitude. It is said that we cannot truly repay God, our parents, or the teachers of those sciences that are not sold for money (as is the custom of unlearned sophists <term>sophists: here referring to "wisdom-sellers" who charge for teaching without possessing true knowledge</term>). But this is only strictly true regarding God. For if, having been made better and more learned, you save your father from death or your teacher from ignorance, you return to the one the life he gave, and to the other the doctrine. Indeed, you may sometimes return even more than what was equal. Regarding God, however, thanks must be given not only for prosperity but also for misfortunes—far more than the thanks we owe to parents, doctors, and teachers for their "blows" <note>meaning discipline or painful treatments</note>, let alone for their flatteries. Our failure in these matters is what must be blamed.

Truly, the person who returns a favor immediately—as if unwilling to remain obligated to repay it later when the other person might actually have a need—or the person who is indignant at being "in debt," is ungrateful. This is just like the "benefactor" who confers certain favors only so that he can demand greater ones, or to keep the receiver obligated to him; and when the time comes to give more, he refuses, thinking that he holds his friend on a hook <note>original: *hamo*</note> because of the previous favors and owes him nothing more (as a certain student of ours once did). Such a person is not a doer of good, but an evil-doer and a **Usurer**.

(For **Usury** exists in any exchange of a benefit, not just in money; indeed, it is harsher in many other things. It is the specific trait of illiberal, cunning, and greedy men, who do not do good because a benefit is a good and divine work, but who spread it out like a net to catch fish.)

Equally ungrateful is the man who repays a favor only so that he may receive more in return. Likewise, he who waits for a person to beg for help before he compensates a favor doubles the "price." For a truly honest man, there is no greater cost than having to beg; and that which is obtained by begging is bought at the highest price. # MORAL ETHICS CHAPTER XI.

For we should not grieve if someone surpasses us in wealth and the capacity for doing good, but rather in purity and will—which we ought to emulate, not envy.

->*On equability, and its contraries*<-

### CHAPTER XII.

#### ARTICLE I.

**Equability** <term>Equability: from the Latin *aequabilitas*, referring to a steady fairness and the quality of treating others with a sense of shared humanity regardless of rank</term> was given so that he who is honored may, in turn, honor those who honor him. Such a person is glorious because of his own excellence and virtue, not because of the honors themselves, which are merely signs of his virtue. 

He who is elected king or pope will conduct himself as if he were one of his subjects. He will cherish them as younger brothers who have placed him over themselves as an elder, so that he may care for the goods of their minds, bodies, and fortunes. He should teach everyone to live well by his own example, doctrine, and law; he should nourish them by providing necessities, defend them by force of arms from enemies, and settle disputes and wrongs through justice. In these duties, he maintains the power of command, not the humility of a subject. For he does not exercise authority out of arrogance, but for the benefit of his people. Just as the head orders and commands for the benefit of the limbs, it does so not out of pride, but as one of the members of the body. He will cut away superfluities, luxuries, and things that distract him from this purpose. 

If, however, you are a subject, you will obey those in authority, not out of fear or flattery, but because it is fitting for a member of the community to live for the good of the whole. Nor should you consider yourself lesser for this reason, but rather the best in your own place, if you maintain that place through virtue.

### 2. **Arrogance** is the contrary vice. 

It does not return answers or greetings. It seeks out unusual things so that everyone might marvel at it as if it knew what no one else knows; it usurps all glory for itself. It desires to stand out in its clothing, in public gatherings, and in social life...

...he despises others as if they were not even human once he has risen to a position of dignity. He does not feed the people, but only himself; he turns the care of others toward himself, rather than turning his own care toward others. He deigns neither to speak to them nor even to be seen by them; he appears like a statue of God or a hollow idol. This is a sign of a proud and base soul—one who, conscious of his own lack of true excellence, desires at least to appear excellent through seized honors, of which he considers others unworthy. While he lacks such honors, he is anxious and considers himself unhappy, for he does not know how to obey except out of fear or the hunting for petty glory. For when such men wring some cheap service or a flattering word from their king, they boast as if they had attained heavenly eminence. They gild the tools of their service as if they were the keys of paradise, and they treat the badges of their guards as if they were the rods of imperial power <note>original: *imperii fasces*, referring to the bundles of rods that symbolized the authority of Roman magistrates</note>.

3. But he who gives more honor than he receives, and flatters those who honor him, bestowing upon them more glory than they deserve, can be called a **Flatterer**. This behavior stems from a dejected, timid, and cowardly soul, which begs for the excellence it lacks by bestowing it on others who also lack it, in the hopes that they might return and restore it to him more abundantly, or at least not harm him. Truly, this flattery is born rather from a weak arrogance. The "Abject" person is therefore one who subjects himself to everyone, not from the virtue of humility, but from a consciousness of his own worthlessness.

## On Witnessing, and its types: praise, honoring, worship, fame, glory, etc., and their opposites.

**Witnessing** <term>Witnessing: from the Latin *protestatio*, meaning a public declaration or testimony of the value and character of a person or thing</term>, as the name suggests, is a voluntary testimony regarding the goodness and badness of things, done fittingly as they relate to their purpose. Whatever indicates something in any way is a testimony of it: just as smoke declares a fire from afar, and every effect bears witness to its cause, and vice-versa; indeed, the whole nature of things is a testimony of its author. --- Page 361 ---
<meta>This page continues Tommaso Campanella’s discussion on Moral Philosophy, specifically focusing on Chapter XI regarding the nature of honor and "protestation" (public testimony). He is distinguishing between intellectual knowledge of God and the moral act of praising or honoring Him, emphasizing that true virtue requires "decorum"—the fittingness or appropriateness of an action to its context.</meta>

### CHAPTER XI ON MORALS

...when we wisely discuss God—stating that He is the highest good <note>original: *summum bonum*</note> and the primary being—this is a testimony of wisdom, not of the will; it pertains to the explanation of His essence <note>original: *quiditatis enucleationem*, literally the un-shelling of the "what-ness"</note>, not to a moral intention. This testimony is said to concern goodness and malice, whether metaphysical or moral; this is to distinguish it from a testimony of truth and falsehood, which does not consider things insofar as they are good or evil. Likewise, this moral testimony is regulated by a public declaration <note>original: *protestatio*</note>, whereas the other is regulated by wisdom, which perceives things as they truly are. Therefore, it is added: *insofar as they relate to their end.* For as a moralist, you do not praise beauty or wine based on how they are formed and outlined by nature, but based on how they relate to their purpose: beauty for delight, and wine for drinking. The "end" of things is their perfection and their use, and those things which are acquired as "goods" from that use, whether for the thing itself or for us; for a moral declaration respects both of these ends. Thus, we praise God as the highest good to Himself, and we praise, honor, and worship Him as a good to us.

We said that this must be done **becomingly** <note>original: *decenter*, meaning with propriety or decorum</note>, so that we might establish the rational basis for virtue. For since we have not called this the *rule* of testimony, but the testimony itself, it would have no claim to being a virtue unless we had added the element of "the becoming." This was done deliberately: for although decorum is necessary in every virtue—so that all the causes of a virtuous act are present as they should be, in both essence and existence—it is known more expressly and clearly in the act of public testimony. 

For a very fat man does not commend fasting becomingly without it being an accusation against himself. Nor is the beauty of Venus <note>the goddess of love, representing sexual beauty</note> censured in itself, but rather its immodest abuse is what is unbecoming. Nor do the Peruvians <note>original: *Peruuini*; Campanella refers here to early colonial accounts of indigenous religious practices</note> becomingly show their buttocks to their idol-god out of reverence; for it is nothing but a dishonor to offer up one's shameful parts. Such people sin in both the matter and the manner of the act. 

Ajax <note>the Greek hero of the Trojan War</note> becomingly receives the horns of an ox from Agamemnon as a testimony of his strength; he would have received the feet unbecomingly, as those would be more fitting for a runner—and even then, not the feet of a sluggish ox, but the feet of a tiger or the wings of an eagle. Thus, in family coats of arms <note>original: *insignibus gentilitiis*</note>, which are declarations of one's profession or of deeds rightly performed, the decorum of the symbol must be strictly observed. Nor does Diogenes <note>Diogenes the Cynic, who famously defied social conventions</note> becomingly consort with his wife in the open street; for while the likeness of a beast in the act of healing the mortality of the species <note>i.e., procreation</note> is a matter of shame <note>original: *verecunda*</note>, it should furthermore be performed in a place where it is not hindered by, nor offends, the sight of others. But in that which he thinks he hon—

...to disregard nature is to profane it. The end of such an act was to testify that nature is honorable in all things. So it is with other things. For whatever is repugnant to the goal of virtue, or to truth, or to the rational basis of other virtues, is unbecoming <note>original: *indecens*; refers to a lack of "decorum" or appropriateness to the situation</note>.

2. Public Declaration <note>original: *Protestatio*; in this context, it refers to a formal witnessing or outward testimony of one's internal judgment</note> is divided into Praise, Honor, Worship, Fame, and Glory, and into their opposites.

<margin>On praise and blame.</margin>
3. Praise <note>original: *Laus*</note> has the widest scope. It is the becoming testimony of any good—whether metaphysical, physical, or moral—accompanied by commendation. Therefore, the world, the stars, the earth, heat, a geometric line, and all existing things can be praised. This is because there is no being that is not "good," either for itself, for its own kind, for the whole world, or for God; nothing is devoid of utility, as was proven in the *Metaphysics*. Indeed, even death, lameness, defects, and faults—insofar as they are directed by God toward a good use or are permitted for a happy outcome—are praiseworthy for some reason, at least for their final cause <note>the ultimate purpose for which a thing exists</note>, whether proximate or remote. They may also be praised because the Author of their making and ordering is commended in them, for He is the supreme Author and end of all things. For there is no being, nor any use of a non-being, that does not manifest God's omnipotence, wisdom, and goodness, either together or separately—just as every workmanship declares its craftsman. 

We used the word "becomingly" <note>original: *decentem*</note>, as in the previous definition: for we do not praise the substance of death, but its use; we praise it because of freedom, or because it allows for the generation of another, or because it is endured with fortitude; and we praise it with appropriate signs, as we have discussed in the *Rhetoric* and *Poetics*. Furthermore, all praise is pleasant, since the memory of any good thing mixes a certain delight even among tears. I find that only "Nothingness" is blameworthy, if it is devoid of any use. 

Physically, however, not all things are good to us, but only those which are good for our preservation and use. This is because such a consideration is not referred simply to the whole of being and all its uses, but only according to our own perspective and our own needs. In this way, the strength of a horse is praised for war, a donkey for carrying loads, bread for food, wine for drink, and beauty for delight. The same thing can be praised as "good" and condemned as "bad" in relation to us: for example, the mild sun in May is praised, but the burning sun in July is condemned; likewise, a horse may be praised for being fierce or gentle depending on the need. Therefore, blame <note>original: *vituperium*</note>, which is the testimony of an evil against us accompanied by condemnation, is directed toward death,

4. Honor, however, is a becoming and truthful declaration of

praising. I said "truthful": for false testimony is mockery. Wherefore to be 
praised by liars, the wicked, and the impure is not honor but reproach, 
reputed as such either because of a likeness to them, or because of the lie itself. 
Honor from illustrious men, however, is sought after: hence those who are 
honored by kings are held in high value, as if kings do not lie about those 
who are worthy of honor—which is true as a matter of duty <note>original: *ex debito*; the ideal expectation of the royal office</note>.

# BROTHER THOMAS CAMPANELLA

### MORAL WRITINGS

...philosophers and divine poets. But since it happens that even these men are deceived, and sometimes stoop to flattery—especially the poets, who are truly worthy of the fork <note>original: *furca*; an ancient Roman instrument of punishment resembling a yoke or gallows, used here to suggest that corrupt poets deserve criminal punishment</note> rather than merely exile, as they are perverters of their own duty and harmful to virtue—therefore, better men remain content with their own integrity. They glory in the testimony of their own conscience and their continuous good works, even if they appear otherwise to the common people. They wait for the testimony of God alone, who alone is truthful; and because they possess true honor within themselves, they do not beg for it from other men. 

Nevertheless, they rejoice when honor is offered freely and without falsehood, insofar as they are thus rendered useful and worthy of imitation by others. However, to be a slave to honor "begged" from elsewhere is a dire servitude; it is a murderous hag <note>original: *saga necatrix*; a vivid metaphor suggesting that the desperate need for external validation "kills" one's inner peace like a predatory witch</note> of all joy and tranquility. 

Indeed, such men do not praise themselves—even if they are certain of their own standing by the testimony of their conscience, both humanly and divinely—except when the utility or necessity of others compels it. We see this, for instance, when Paul spoke before his disciples, and occasionally in the writings of Bernard <note>Refers to St. Paul the Apostle and St. Bernard of Clairvaux, who both wrote of their spiritual experiences to instruct their followers</note>. There are also times when defending oneself before a judge, when suffering under slander, demands this. Likewise, it is necessary among princes and strangers, lest they despise an unknown virtue hidden under a ragged habit <note>original: *pannoso habitu*; referring to the humble or poor clothing often worn by traveling scholars or monks</note>. Even then, this must be done modestly, and only where the man is ready to immediately demonstrate those things he boasts of, which must be known and proven to others. 

An eminent man, who knows nothing of falsehood and is not deceived by self-love (the fear of which prevents most men from daring to praise themselves or beg for honor), will narrate his own illustrious deeds; just as Moses and Julius Caesar wrote their own histories. In the mouths of mediocre men, however, self-praise becomes foul. Therefore, the more ambitious men, wishing to be praised in a backwards manner, actually defile themselves. They act as if they are the most just, humble, and truthful, while they are actually swollen with a wretched desire for empty honor, acting against themselves, their parents, and their wives; thus they stain themselves with the disgrace of duplicity. Outside of cases of necessity and the highest utility, these self-testimonies are scandalous and entirely indecent. A philosopher, however, differs from the common crowd in this: that even if he is tickled by such emotions <note>original: *affectibus*; the "affects" or passions of the soul</note>, he is not, like the commoners, overcome by them.

5. Praise is indeed owed to all men, not only because they are useful to one another and to the commonwealth—which is why we praise women and lictors <note>original: *lictores*; Roman civil servants who carried out the orders of magistrates</note> when they perform their duties well. We condemn them if they perform poorly, but we do not condemn them simply because they cannot write well <note>Campanella argues that people should only be judged based on the specific duties of their station in life</note>. But...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 319 (and the missing page 320) regarding the nature of honor. Having previously established that truly virtuous men do not "beg" for honor, Campanella now expands the scope to argue that every person possesses a spark of virtue and deserves honor when performing their specific vocation.</meta>

### MORAL WRITINGS, CH. XII.

...there is even a small portion of honor [due to everyone]: for no one is entirely devoid of virtue. Indeed, one who was totally evil could not live even for a moment without being destroyed by himself or others; for it is by virtue that we are preserved and live. Therefore, by a certain right, men are honored with praise, greetings, social fellowship, and participation in sacred rites—but especially when they are performing their own specific work <note>original: *proprio exercitio*; referring to one's craft, vocation, or professional practice</note>.

For at that moment, every man is a king: he is served and obeyed even by those of higher rank, because the purpose of his art <note>original: *in fine gratia cuius est ars*; the author suggests that the ultimate goal or benefit that a skill provides grants the practitioner authority during the act</note> takes precedence. When a barber shaves others, or even a king, he commands them—and the king himself—to turn their head this way, to bring warm water, to hold the mirror, and so on. A physician does so even more. A builder <term>Fabricator: a skilled craftsman, architect, or master-builder</term> becomes prominent through the labor of his work-gangs carrying stones and lime, and through the watchful eye of his master while he builds. Even a cook is praised and requested by his master, and is served by boys and attendants, especially if he has a natural fitness for his duty. 

For when the hand is about to grasp something, it is moved there by the service of the feet and aided by the eyes; all the limbs serve it, as it were. And when the eye looks at something intently, all the limbs rest, offering their strength to it. Indeed, even when the anus purges the bowels, the feet support the body, the hands wipe, and the eye watches the place.

It is rightly said, therefore, that honor is owed to every man just as it is to every limb. This is most clearly proven during the performance of one’s duty, where skill or some other virtue is displayed. When kings play at dice or occupy themselves with hunting, they are less distinguished and receive less honor; but upon the throne, where they dispense justice, they appear as gods—especially if they are fit for the task. 

In the same way, every man "dispenses justice" <note>original: *ius dicit*; a legal term for a judge’s ruling, here applied metaphorically to a craftsman's authority over his work</note> and acts within his own workshop <term>opificio: a place of work, trade, or the act of making something</term>. We see everyone—tailors, stonecutters, dealers in delicacies <note>original: *cupidinarios*; those who sell luxury foods or specialized goods</note>, rowers, and the rest—speaking of and striving for their own honor. Truly, this profession of honor must be fostered toward everyone within the commonwealth <note>original: *republ.* / *republica*</note>. For it is a testimony of the divine participation hidden within us, and at the same time a bridle that restrains us from unworthy passions and wicked deeds, as well as a most watchful guardian of the laws. Yet honor should not be granted to the unworthy, lest those who are worthy grow cold in doing good. 

Woe to those who are void of honor and do not even claim to possess it! They defile themselves and the commonwealth with every crime, obscenity, lie, and act of plunder.

# THE MORAL WRITINGS OF FRIAR TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

6. On the contrary, every king and every man, if caught in the practice of vice or in a crime, is a slave <note>original: *mancipium*; referring to a person held as property or one who has lost their moral agency</note>, and is reviled by all. For this reason, contempt and **Disgrace** are the opposites of honor. The former [contempt] is a testimony to the absence of virtue: for we despise those who abound in laziness, imprudence, cowardice, and other vices that indicate a failure to follow the rule <note>Campanella often uses "the rule" to mean the rational or natural order that governs healthy behavior</note>; and we brand them with the titles of their own vices. In assemblies, social circles, and public gatherings, we assign them the last places and the most base functions; we dedicate them to the service of their betters, so that they may follow the rule in others which they do not possess within themselves. If they do not act like the insane and the foolish, they are nourished through mercy, though by justice they ought to be cast out from the community. For a part that has no function in the body, as if it were not a limb, is rightly severed. 

**Disgrace**, truly, is the standard for dishonoring those who are vicious in excess, such as the cunning, the fraudulent, the wicked, the slanderous, and so on. And if they are marked for the sake of a cure <note>original: *ad medelam*; suggesting that social shame is intended to rehabilitate the offender</note>, it is called **Reprimand** and **Detestation**. They take their name from their primary crime; hence they are called robbers, adulterers, heretics, or traitors. In public gatherings, they are corrected, held in contempt, and filled with ignominy so that they might come to their senses <note>original: *resipiscant*; to return to a state of wisdom or sanity</note>. This degree of shame is opposed to "magnification" [exaltation], just as the previous degree [contempt] was opposed to simple commendation. The final degree is accusation and punishment; and this is disgrace in the proper sense: for this, men are mutilated, imprisoned at the oars <note>Sentenced to be galley slaves</note>, and are forcibly disgraced by vile garments and tasks, so that they are made wonderfully abject.

<margin>
What 
scandal 
is.
</margin>
Disgrace is fruitful when it ensures that others—"scandalized" by the example of the wicked (that is, moved away from the right path by a stumbling block <note>original: *offendiculum*; Campanella provides a literal etymology of the word "scandal" as a physical trip-wire or obstacle</note>)—do not sin in a similar way, and that the offenders themselves do not "return to their vomit" <note>A common biblical proverb for returning to one's previous sins</note>. But indeed, not only are those who do evil to be disgraced, but also those who omit to do good when they are able, or those who do not strive to become capable of doing good. For it is a greater evil to fail to help a friend than it is to harm them in trivial matters. In great matters, this failure is even worse. Just as a foot is considered bad and dishonorable not only if it walks poorly, but also if it does not walk at all, or if it does not expose itself to extreme dangers for the sake of the head (which is more excellent than the foot). Indeed, all things are full of capacities which, when they are either corrupted or left idle, defraud both the whole and its parts of their prescribed end; such things show themselves to be worthy of blame and destruction.

7. From these points it becomes clear that the honor and disgrace which we offer to the virtuous and the vicious are not merely testimonies of virtue and vice from the perspective...

<summary>Campanella defines disgrace and contempt as the natural social consequences of vice and idleness, arguing that a person who fails to fulfill their social function is like a useless limb that must be corrected or severed. He emphasizes that failing to do good is as punishable as actively doing evil, using the organic metaphor of the body to justify social hierarchy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the social manifestations of honor. Having established that honor is a testimony to virtue, Campanella now explores "ornaments"—the external symbols of status—and distinguishes between general honor and the specific "veneration" (cultus) owed to superior natures.</meta>

### CHAPTER XII OF THE MORAL WRITINGS

...there would have been testimonies, approvals, and disapprovals on our part. For good and bad actions are testimonies of virtue and vice according to their own essence; but according to our arbitrary morality <note>Campanella refers to "arbitrary morality" as the social customs and laws established by human agreement, as opposed to natural law</note>, they are the testimonies that we provide. In respect to the virtues themselves, these are called ornaments, but in respect to us, they are called testimonies. For when we grant men titles or the professor's chair, we are said to "decorate" them. To decorate, moreover, is to give an ornament that is fitting <note>original: *quod decet*; playing on the etymological link between *decor* (beauty/fitness) and *decet* (it is fitting)</note>. 

<margin>What beauty and ornament are.</margin> 
An ornament is something notable added to what is already good and beautiful so that it may shine more brightly. Hence, just as we decorate a good house with paintings, we decorate those who are shining with virtue with the office of magistrate, the throne, the purple robe, the professor's chair, and titles. To the unworthy, these things are a mockery—like a mask wearing a crown in a comedy, or golden and embroidered garments on an old woman, or when the Goths forced the Danes to worship a dog on a throne as their king.

<margin>Why and how evil princes are to be tolerated and worshipped.</margin> 
This mockery exists on the part of the recipients, but not on our part. Indeed, they are usefully worshipped for the sake of observing the laws; for in them, it is not the individual person that is commended, but that which *ought* to be, as well as the dignity of the office. For we assume that no one is honored with a magistracy, a doctorate, and so on, unless they surpass others in virtue sufficient for themselves and for the utility of others, as required for such functions. Sometimes the mockery is on our part and not theirs—as when the Jews, mocking the Lord Jesus (who was a true king, not a masked one), decorated him with purple, a scepter, and a crown; they did not actually mock him <note>Campanella implies that because Jesus truly possessed the royal virtue they were satirizing, the "ornaments" were actually fitting, making the mockers the fools</note>. Similarly, in a game of dice, small stones are used by us as if they were gold shields, while real gold shields might be used as mere pebbles by chickens.

<margin>On worship, or observance, or manifold reverence; and on their opposites.</margin> 
8. From this, it becomes clear what **Veneration** <note>original: *cultus*; often translated as "cult" or "worship," here meaning the specialized reverence given to superiors</note> and **Observance** are. It is a rule of testifying not just to virtue, but to a more excellent virtue and nature. Hence it differs from honor: for honor is exhibited by anyone, and even by a superior toward inferiors; veneration, however, is only shown by inferiors toward those who are more excellent. And just as custom exists within nature <note>original: *phyſi* (Greek: φύσει); meaning the natural order</note>, and law exists within custom, so honor is commanded within praise, and veneration and glory are commanded within honor; the former are not separated from the latter, though the latter may be from the former. 

Indeed, a more eminent nature ought to be venerated by an inferior by right—as the heliotrope <note>The "sun-turning" flower</note> venerates the sun, and the elephant the moon. However, one is not venerated *morally* unless they can also be honored—that is, if they possess excellent virtue joined to an excellent nature. For this reason, even though the devil could be praised and venerated as a wise... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; Campanella likely intended to say the devil has a superior "nature" as an angel, but lacks the "virtue" to be morally honored</note>

<summary>Campanella defines social ornaments as external testimonies of internal virtue and explains that even unworthy leaders are honored to maintain legal order. He distinguishes between general honor and "veneration," which is the specific reverence an inferior owes to a naturally superior being.</summary>

<keywords>ornaments, decoration, magistracy, political authority, Jesus, Veneration (cultus), honor, natural hierarchy, social order</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the distinction between honor and outward show. Campanella is arguing that true honor belongs only to virtue. Even when we appear to honor objects (like statues) or animals (like Alexander's horse), we are actually honoring the virtue or the divine order they represent.</meta>

...endowed with great wisdom and power; nevertheless, because he does not use these well through virtue, but poorly through vice, he can be praised—since praise is referred back to the Creator <note>original: *autorem*; Campanella argues that if someone is naturally talented but wicked, we praise God for the talent but do not honor the person</note>—but he cannot be worshipped <term>veneration (cultus)</term>, for he cannot be truly honored. For honor belongs to virtue alone. Moreover, Alexander honored his horse Bucephalus with the title of the city Bucephala <note>Alexander the Great named the city of Bucephala in modern-day Pakistan after his beloved horse</note>, whom he could only praise as being good for war; yet he honors not the horse, but himself in the honor of the horse, as if decorated by God with such a good animate instrument for his virtuous actions. The statues of Caesar are also honored, because it is not the object, but the Caesar represented in the object who is distinguished. I have even seen those who honor and kiss the walls and the Roman theater and the ruins of trophies, as if they were venerable memories of Roman virtue. Some venerate the relics of dead parents, others of heroes, and others the image of a mistress. All these things are done rightly, however, if they are directed toward the honor of virtue and its author <note>God, as the source of all excellence</note>. For virtue is so great a thing that it graces even the very limits of its connections with its own honor; it turns evils into good, and makes lower natures better than those higher ones that should be revered, making the lower ones worthy of reverence instead. Thus, virtuous angels of a lower hierarchy are preferred to the wicked ones of a higher hierarchy.

There are many degrees of reverence and observance. For the wealthy are revered as being excellently clever—for wealth is often acquired through cleverness <term>cleverness (solertia)</term>—and not simply as being wealthy, except by fools. Otherwise, a donkey laden with gold would be more worthy of reverence than many rich men. Riches are gathered by accident, sometimes through other virtues, and sometimes even through vices. Kings are revered as being eminently just and beneficent, and therefore sharers in God’s governance: not simply because they are most powerful and stand above many. If power alone mattered, then the lion would be more worthy of reverence, or even the devil, who is "king over all the children of pride" <note>A reference to Job 41:34, describing Leviathan/the Devil</note>, and there is no power among us that compares to his. Even "Queen Avarice" would have to be worshipped, who commands countless people and sets laws for the greedy. Hence the lustful adored lust as a god, whom they called Cupid; others worshipped Fever, others Paleness in temples. They were fools because they separated outward worship from true honor. Elders are revered as being wiser, and as people who instruct our lives by their example, not merely because they are old: for in that way...

<summary>Campanella argues that honor and reverence (cultus) must be rooted in virtue rather than power, wealth, or age. He explains that even when we honor symbols or animals, we are actually paying homage to the underlying human or divine excellence they represent.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Campanella's investigation into why we honor certain people or things. He previously argued that honor is reserved for virtue alone, even when it appears we are honoring animals or inanimate objects. Here, he examines the specific roles of parents, friends, and the learned, while cautioning against the abuse of devotion.</meta>

### OF MORALS, CHAPTER 12.

...if everything that preceded us in time were to be worshipped, even stones would be. Parents are honored with the devotion of **piety** <note>original: *pietatis*; the Roman concept of *pietas* refers to a sense of duty and religious devotion to gods, country, and family</note>, as those who are benevolent and beneficent toward us, our very origins, and God’s vicars for the production and nourishment of our being. Hence, they are not so honored by those who are not their children, to whom they were not exceptionally beneficial; nor are they honored by their own children when they wander from their role as God's vicars by teaching things contrary to God—except in matters of natural physical needs.

Friends seem worthy of <term>veneration (cultus)</term> for this reason, but only to their own friends, as being exceptionally benevolent to them. And this form of devotion is dangerous, since it is often transferred to anyone who is greatly loved or who loves greatly in return; as a result, we often see the vicious, those worse than ourselves, or even prostitutes being honored by those far more excellent than they. Hence it is said that the Chinese often worship their friends as if they were gods. Likewise, Alexander the Great commanded that Hephaestion be worshipped as a god because he had been his dearest friend; and the Emperor Hadrian even placed his favorite, Antinous, among the stars.

The abuse of love produces such an abuse in devotion. Therefore, I believe that friends should be *honored*, but not *venerated*, unless they excel in virtue—and this must be according to the judgment of others, not just one's own. For the rule of love is not love itself, but virtue. Philosophers and the learned are more reasonably respected as being eminently studious, prudent, and capable of being taught, acting as God's vicary principles in teaching and governing us. Yet they are not honored simply because they are wise; otherwise the devil, being wiser, would be more worthy of worship. Wisdom is praised, but not venerated, unless it is joined to moral virtue, which is its proper and good use.

Nevertheless, Power, Wisdom, and Love approach the status of veneration because they are the <term>Primalities (primalitates)</term> <note>In Campanella's philosophy, Power, Wisdom, and Love are the three fundamental "primalities" or essential principles of all being</note> of the virtues. He who possesses these perfectly is better suited for virtue than a virtuous person who lacks perfection and must follow another's rule. For, as Hesiod says: *He is the best who knows all things by himself; next to him is he who believes the one giving right advice.* <note>Campanella is quoting Hesiod's *Works and Days*</note>

But God created these good principles in vain unless they progress toward the best possible end. Above all others, we praise men who are bravest in war, those most wise in the invention of things and the revealing of secrets, and those most loving as faithful friends; but they are not venerated unless they are made honorable by virtue. **Integrity** <note>original: *Honestas*; refers to moral rectitude or being "honorable"</note> is therefore virtue itself, so named because it is worthy of honor. Hence, when we command that something be done virtuously—in a way that suits the proper end—we command it to be done with integrity.

<meta>This page continues Campanella's discussion on the objects of veneration. Having previously discussed parents and friends, he now turns to religious figures, the criteria for losing honor, and the distinction between worshipping God and his creatures.</meta>

->F. TOMMASO CAMPANELLA<-

...we venerate. Finally, the **Religious** <note>original: *Religiosi*; those in holy orders, such as monks or priests</note> are worshipped as being eminently holy, and therefore as mediators between us and God, and as "deifiers" of the human race. But if kings, fathers, elders, the wealthy, philosophers, friends, and the religious wander away from their profession in their actions toward us, we shall certainly still observe whatever they say; however, if they also wander in their speech, teaching things contrary to virtue and God, then they fall away from honor, and consequently from <term>veneration (cultus)</term>. Like salt that has lost its flavor, they are to be trodden underfoot. For they are like counters in a game, which are neither gold coins <note>original: *scutati*; a reference to the scudo or gold crown coin</note> nor do they even represent gold coins.

For this reason, a greater indignation is inflamed against heresies, sophisms, and the criminal principles of our life than against common sinners. From this also stems the detestable ignorance of the **Chinese** and other nations, who worship devils whom they know to be evil and enemies of virtue, simply so they might not suffer evils from them; and for that very reason, they suffer worse things. For he who is bad to himself is even worse to others. Nature teaches that contraries are to be expelled by contraries; therefore, one should repel evil spirits by means of good ones. From this you may see that those who worship power, wisdom, and love when these are not joined to virtue err beyond all measure.

Finally, God is observed with the **supreme worship**, as the most super-eminent in nature and virtue, and the author of all natures, virtues, and things. He is praised in every creature, honored in the virtuous, glorified in the heroic, and worshipped in himself through a devotion that cannot be shared with any creatures—for being and goodness do not flow from them as they do from him.

Next are **divine men**; those who, being like God by nature, have striven through virtue to turn all evils into good. They have known how to wonderfully draw pleasure from painful things, and not just from pleasurable ones (as beasts and the common people do); rejoicing in oppression, in death, and in torture, and treading upon all evils with the loftiness of a divine mind. They have propagated to us the goodness they shared from God; and we hold this to be true when we have God's own testimony for them.

If God were the soul of the world—as **Varro**, the leader of the pagan theologians, rightly concluded—then all creatures could safely be adored by the Romans as if they were members of God's body. But since God is "abstract" <note>Campanella means God is transcendent and distinct from the physical world</note>, so that, being free from the passions of the world, he can rule and judge most rightly and precede all as the Creator, people are miserably deceived when they share his worship with beasts, elements, stars, and devils; nor do they know his images...

<summary>Campanella argues that honor is conditional on virtue and that religious or political leaders who teach against God lose their right to veneration. He distinguishes between the supreme worship of a transcendent God and the secondary honor given to "divine men" (saints/heroes) who transcend suffering.</summary>

### MORALS CH. XII.

...either they are traces <note>original: *vestigia*; in Scholastic philosophy, a "trace" is a faint mark of God in non-rational nature, whereas humans are an "image"</note>; though in devils this image is disfigured, and in angels, although it is highly polished, it gives rise to idolatry <note>when angels are worshipped as gods instead of messengers</note>; even though Socrates would rather adore God in a good man than in an idol. Yet the soul is not the image itself, but is made **according to the image** <note>original: *ad imaginem*; a distinction based on Genesis 1:26 suggesting the soul is a likeness, not the essence of God</note>. Concerning these matters, see my works on **Theology** and **Metaphysics**.

9. Now, the manner of worship is twofold: one is **internal**, <margin>Concerning the visible ways of worshipping.</margin> by which we subject our soul to a more excellent nature and virtue. Nature and utility teach us this, for every inferior thing that subjects itself to a superior is improved by it; for if it were made worse, that thing would not be superior in virtue and nature. The other is **external**, such as through titles, higher thrones, offerings, obedience, bowing, imitation, and other things that declare their superiority over us. For they are called **Nobles** as if they were "Notable": hence they are named "Most Holy," "Most Reverend," "Most Illustrious," "Most Serene," "Most Bright," "Fathers of the Fatherland," "Most Observant," and so on.

These titles do not always arise from the nature of the thing, but according to custom. For **"Most Illustrious"** <note>original: *Illustrissimus*</note>, which is like the sun, is a higher concept than **"Most Serene"** <note>original: *Serenissimus*</note>, which is like clear air; and yet the latter is a title for kings, while the former is for petty rulers. Likewise in reverence: some uncover their heads, like **Christians**; others their feet, like the **Muslims** <note>original: *Machometani*</note>; some bow, others kneel; some touch the beard, others kiss the hands or feet. Before **God**, we also prostrate ourselves and offer sacrifice, which can be done for no creature; and this worship must be internal and external at the same time. <margin>u1 +</margin> <margin>l</margin> For such bowings and offerings are a mockery unless the soul is also bowed and offered to Him. External worship is therefore a public declaration of the internal, which often carries the soul away into such an ecstasy of admiration and love that it even snatches the body with it into the air. <margin>r</margin> He who denies this denies the senses, countless histories, and experience. <margin>+</margin>

But indeed, there is no better worship than **obedience** and **imitation**; for this reason, it is also called **observance** <note>original: *obseruantia*; literally "watching over" or "paying heed to"</note>. If you truly profess that the one you worship is better than you, you surely desire to be improved by him. You do this if you obey his precepts and imitate his deeds. Therefore, it is not those who say, "Lord, Lord," etc.; titles and bowings and kneelings are empty before God, who looks at the heart, unless the attentive soul is humbled to receive grace and **divine influence** <term>influxum (divine influence)</term> <note>the flow of grace or power from God into the human soul, often compared to the influence of stars in medieval thought</note> from Him to whom it humbles itself. In this way, philosophers, and kings, and parents...

He notes that external devotion can lead to mystical ecstasies, including levitation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Campanella's discussion on the relationship between internal disposition and external ritual. He argues that physical gestures—like kissing or touching—are not just social customs but outward expressions of the soul's alignment with superior or inferior powers.</meta>

-> F. THOMAS CAMPANELLA <-

...then they believe they are sufficiently worshipped when their commands are followed; because through this, the intent of the mind is revealed to them. Ceremonial acts are useful for preparing the mind and showing through the body what resides within the soul—not only as an example to others, but for your own benefit. For when the soul is changed, the body is changed in like manner, and wherever the soul is carried, the body follows. For this reason, the science of **physiognomy** <term>physiognomica: the historical practice of assessing a person's character or personality from their outer appearance, especially the face</term> examines the condition of the soul through the state of the body. Therefore, when the body does not follow, the soul did not lead; or, if the body follows but with no true feeling—driven only by pretense—it serves its purpose in vain.

10. It would be a heavy task to explain how touching the beard, a kiss, and other signs declare the inferiority of those who perform them. Those who touch [another] profess to receive a good influence from the superior person they have touched. Those who kiss profess delight. Indeed, we "pre-taste" pleasurable things with a kiss, as if extracting and drawing out something fruitful that blesses the spirit. This is why **adoration** <note>original: *adoratio*</note> is so named, as if from "bringing the hand to the mouth" <note>Campanella uses a traditional etymology of *ad* (to) and *os* (mouth)</note> to be kissed; and what we cannot reach with our mouth, we touch with our hand, then draw the hand back to our mouth to kiss it, professing the same reverence. Yet in these times, even when someone hands something to a friend or their master, they kiss the object; this shows an analogy to worship, though it is not used very appropriately.

11. Opposed to worship are **execration**, **excommunication**, **blasphemy**, and similar acts; and finally punishment and destruction, which we inflict upon or wish for the most enormous wickedness. For there is a rule of protesting against the massive vice and perverse nature of others when they behave badly toward their own end and ours. And just as we said that we should honor—on account of their excellent virtue—the wealthy, kings, parents, friends, philosophers, religious figures, and God; so on the contrary, we detest, curse, and abominate the extremely poor—not those who are so by chance or choice, but those made so by vice through gambling, prostitutes, taverns, and notorious crimes. We loathe even more those **tyrants** who, being addicted to vice in their kingdom, are like wolves among the flock or fornicators in a brothel; we would wish them entirely removed, unless a certain hope of their improvement shines through. This is not the case with parents; they must be supported, yet not listened to <note>in the sense of obeying their commands when those commands are sinful</note>. For nature cannot be denied, but their behavior can be rejected when it stands against God. Ene-

# ON MORALS, CHAPTER 12.

[...enemies of] friends also, if they are even enemies of virtue, must be equally detested and accused, especially enemies of the fatherland and of a good King. The most foolish as well, and those who teach wicked doctrines, are to be despised along with the devil and sent away. Woe to those who do not hold in low regard <note>original: *floccipendunt*, literally "to value at a tuft of wool"</note> the malicious, the perverse, and the sophists. False prophets, charlatans <note>original: *circulatores*, itinerant peddlers or performers</note>, soothsayers, leaders of heresy, and men of this sort <note>original: *huiusmodi farinæ*, literally "of this kind of flour"</note>, you shall dishonor according to the law; do not even say "Greetings" to them. Finally, you shall exterminate and annihilate, if you can, those false gods and evil spirits who crave divine worship, as a protest against their supreme malice.

<margin>
**Honor,**
**praise, and**
**worship are**
**not**
**rewards, but**

**what are they?**

12. From these things, nature clearly shows that honor is sought not as a reward for virtue—for virtue is better than honor, and is therefore its own reward, expecting nothing except from the most righteous judge. For honor is not the goal <term>finis: the ultimate purpose or end-point of an action</term> of virtue, but rather that for which virtue exists. Just as praise is not the goal of a horse's excellence, but rather war, in which that excellence is proven; and the good results that follow from war. Therefore, some foolishly make honor the reward of virtue, when it is nothing but a witness to what virtue is worth, produced by one's superiors and inferiors. 

Worship is even less of a reward, since it comes only from inferiors, however much more majestic it may be. What is more foolish than to say that God is made happy by our religion? For it is the ultimate goal that makes one happy <note>Campanella argues that since God is already the ultimate goal/end, He cannot be "made" happy by external acts; He is happiness itself</note>. Therefore, offices and public duties are conferred upon those outstanding in virtue as ornaments—partially resembling a reward, but not in truth or fullness; and they are granted more for our benefit than for theirs. 

Conversely, the goods that wicked people possessed are taken away, likewise partially resembling a punishment. For prison, exile, loss of property, mutilation, excommunication, beatings, and the death of the body do not equal what the soul deserves for defiling itself—the image of God—and subjecting itself to vile passions. This is especially true since these are evils of the sinning "organ" <note>the physical body</note> rather than the sinning soul; and a greater punishment is the soul's own malice. 

Just as power is not what virtue deserves, these things are merely testimonies and decorations of merit. For Socrates said, in his own way, that the bad man is "adorned" with punishment just as the good man is with a reward; and that he who suffers just things, suffers beautiful things.

--- Page 374 ---
<meta>This page continues Tommaso Campanella’s discussion on the nature of rewards, specifically addressing the afterlife and the definitions of reputation and glory.</meta>

...we are very often deceived [if we think otherwise], that after death true and full rewards and punishments remain. We have previews and testimonies of these now; and that curable sins are purged, as Plato, Pythagoras, Socrates, and the most excellent philosophers—not to mention the lawgivers—taught. Those sins that are incurable, however, are detained for long ages; for it is only Faith that reveals they are held even for eternity.

<margin>
**On reputation.**
</margin>
13. **Reputation** <note>original: *Fama*</note> is a widespread, clear recognition or public testimony of any remarkable goodness, accompanied by praise. **Infamy** is that same recognition, but accompanied by the condemnation of some evil. Here the discussion concerns physical and moral matters. For there is no such thing as "infamy" within the study of Metaphysics <term>Metaphysics: the branch of philosophy dealing with the fundamental nature of reality and being</term>; otherwise, such a flaw would reflect back upon the very source of being itself. We are speaking here of the spreading of news by human choice, not the "natural" kind (such as how the sun is known everywhere), nor the "angelic" kind (by which many things hidden from us are made known). For reputation is threefold, just like praise. And sometimes the word is used figuratively to mean infamy.

<margin>
**On glory.**
</margin>
14. Finally, we define **glory** as reputation and honor combined, built up through most brilliant and well-executed deeds, which demands a kind of devotion. Furthermore, although a person may take pride in any of their own goods, whether natural or moral, and everyone possesses some small measure of honor—with the more outstanding individuals receiving even greater marks of respect—one does not arrive at true glory except through the most magnificent deeds and wonderful labors endured to prove one's internal worth.

Hence, not everyone—such as infants or simply "good" men—is admitted equally to glory in the eyes of God, even if they are admitted to honor. Or to put it another way, God judges glory differently than we do. He places more value on the victory of virtue over vice than on the conquest of the whole world, the slaying of monsters <note>A likely reference to the labors of Hercules</note>, or the subjugation of barbarians.

And indeed, how great a thing it is to conquer excessive, rash, and depraved thoughts, the itchy craving <note>original: *titillantes*, literally "tickling"</note> for praise, the lures of the flesh, and the fear of losing external goods—even life itself. And once these are conquered, if it is even possible, there arises a new and many-headed monster of twisted pride <note>original: *superbiæ præposteræ*, "preposterous" or "backwards" pride</note> that stains all previous victories, always rising up at the end or lurking in secret. No one understands the weight of this except for the one who has declared a truly serious war against vices and has continued to fight well. Woe is me! I find nothing more difficult—indeed, nothing more impossible—without the help of God. Who, nonetheless...

<summary>Tommaso Campanella distinguishes between reputation, infamy, and true glory, arguing that while humans celebrate outward conquests, God values the internal victory over vice and the "monster" of pride above all else.</summary>
