### CHAPTER XII ON MORALS
<sig>Tt 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: lem</meta>

...justly insists upon His command, because He runs ahead with help. No one knows this inner glory and wondrous pleasure except the one who has fought lawfully against themselves. Fools, who only look at the outer shell of things, admire *Alexander*, *Caesar*, and *Orlando* <note>Referring to the legendary knight Roland, a symbol of military might</note>—men who were victors over other men but were often conquered by their own vices and by wine. They could kill a thousand men in a single hour, but in a thousand years they could not raise one person from the dead, nor could they command a fever to depart or a hair to change its color by their order. This is because their victory is by no means valued before God in the same way as the victory of those who have conquered themselves. For this reason, God—who alone is truthful—has honored and glorified these virtuous ones with miracles as a testimony of their virtue, not of homicide. 

Therefore, we hold this peak of honor in this life, through which we are not only commended and magnified, but moreover made wondrous. As for the reward following from this—rooted in divine providence and almighty love toward us—we shall boldly and securely declare that it remains after death, despite the foolish Peripatetic School <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle, whom Campanella often critiques for their views on the soul and nature</term> which considers things proven by reason and experience to be mere fables. This has also been made clear by the preceding arguments. Conversely, a shield is called "Inglorious White" <note>original: *Inglorius alba*</note> when someone has not yet performed any noble deed worth depicting upon it, as was said of the young soldier *Euryalus*; or, in the opposite sense, it applies to those who are most wicked, even to the point of ultimate punishment, like *Cacus* <note>a mythological giant killed by Hercules</note>, *Nero*, or the traitor *Judas*.

15. **Derision** <note>original: *Derisio*; here meaning mockery or a failure to properly represent someone's worth</note> is opposed to moral expression <note>original: *protestatio*</note> by way of excess. It is named after the way we laugh at fictional characters in comedies; in this same way, we mock false honors and insults. It is of two types. First, it exceeds the truth by offering more praise, worship, honor, fame, and glory—or conversely more vituperation, disgrace, cursing, infamy, and character assassination—than the recipients deserve. Second, it attributes baseness to the good and beauty to the evil, calling good evil and evil good. 

The first degree of this derision occurs when we bestow titles and other honorable or shameful ornaments upon people we do not know. For example, treating the sons of the rich as "most excellent" and those of the poor as "most vile," or receiving guests and strangers with unearned honor or ignominy. For honor is our testimony, but it should only be attached to the testimony of those who are actually honorable, like a decoration. He who does not first show himself to be honorable...

<summary>Campanella argues that internal self-mastery is superior to the military conquests of figures like Caesar and Alexander, as evidenced by the power of miracles versus mere killing. He then defines derision as a moral failing where honor or shame is distributed based on false pretenses or social status rather than actual merit.</summary>

<keywords>inner glory, self-mastery, miracles, afterlife, Peripatetics, Derisio, social status, moral protestation</keywords>

<page-num>332</page-num>
# FRIAR TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

...[worthy of respect] <note>The word "venerabilem" is completed from the previous page's catchword</note> by showing it through good works, or blameworthy through evil ones, he ought not to be decorated by us. For a painter does not apply gilding or filth to an unknown form. The Romans gave titles based on deeds; for instance, they called a man "Africanus" <note>A reference to Scipio Africanus, who received the title after defeating Hannibal in Africa</note> after he conquered Africa, and so on. However, people are often excused from proving their own merit by the testimony of their lineage, though this is often a false witness. This is not quite the case among the Chinese, where children can only take up the craft and training of their parents; yet this is also not right, since virtue is not something inherited by birth.

Second, we err when we magnify that which is merely commendable, and treat the "magnifiable" as if it were "wondrous" in matters of honor and dishonor. For example, if you were to call a diligent mule-driver "illustrious," or a magistrate "most serene," or a beautiful woman "the sun" and a "goddess"; or if you place a good man in the office of the "distinguished," and the "distinguished" on the throne of heroes. Such hyperboles <note>Exaggerated claims or titles</note> are certainly tolerable, unless they produce harm immediately or gradually. Indeed, idolatry arose from this very thing: because people used to call excellent men "Gods," and thus power, wisdom, and friendship are worshipped in place of true virtue.

Likewise, teachers, doctors, and philosophers are made "wondrous" by fools—especially ancient writers, as if they never erred. Defended "tooth and nail" <note>original: *mordicus*</note> by their followers, they ruin human safety and subject free minds to a dreadful slavery. And while it is true that in the pursuit of wisdom—especially regarding divine things—anyone who thinks he has already reached what he seeks has not actually found the truth, but has merely given up on the search; these people, on the contrary, boast that they have ascended to the very heights of divinity once they have swallowed the doctrine and brief summaries of their own philosophical sect.

Conversely, they are not to be tolerated when they mock the teachings of other wise men as if they were the words of a "fuller" <term>Fuller: a cloth-worker; used here as a derogatory term for a common, unlearned laborer</term>, and they condemn whatever we investigate anew. They went so far as to hold Columbus to be a heretic for professing that he was sailing to the Antipodes <note>The "Antipodes" refers to the regions on the opposite side of the earth; many theologians of the time argued they did not exist or were unreachable</note>, which were denied by certain theologians based on mere opinion.

From this, one moves into the second and more dangerous form of **Derision**. This is the kind that has cursed, condemned, and dishonored holy men, most learned philosophers, and divine prophets as if they were wretches, or hypocrites, fools, fanatics, and rebels against divine and human majesty. This is done so that hypocrites, sophists, false prophets, and tyrants can be placed on thrones, in magistracies, and in academic chairs—or so that those already in power might remain there safely. Through this most destructive Derision, the devil is worshipped in place of God among many nations.

<meta>catchword: nations</meta>

<summary>Campanella argues that titles and honors should be based on merit rather than lineage, criticizing both the Roman system and the Chinese caste-like structure. He warns that exaggerated praise leads to idolatry, while the "Derision" of new discoveries—like those of Columbus—protects the status of false leaders and stifles intellectual freedom.</summary>

# MORALS CHAPTER XII.

...nations; while they foolishly wonder at any power and wisdom they possess, without regard for virtue. Others bow themselves to things inferior to themselves, which are neither wise nor powerful, such as idols, rivers, snakes, and the like. What is more ridiculous than to take those acts by which we testify to God’s dominion over all things—such as sacrifice and adoration; or his power—such as vows and petitions; or his all-knowing wisdom—such as oaths, the consultation of future events, divine mysteries, and the secrets of the heart known only to God; or his goodness and love toward our race—such as thanksgiving and praise; and to use these to worship a lizard, a monkey, or a calf? In this comedy, the angels watch as spectators and laugh with indignation; and so do good men.

Sometimes this mockery stems from the nature of both the worshiper and the object of worship. For instance, when *Diogenes* <note>The Cynic philosopher known for mocking social conventions</note> sacrifices to false gods in whom he does not believe; or when one calls the deformed *Gabrina* <note>A character from Ariosto’s *Orlando Furioso* personifying an ugly, treacherous old woman</note> by the name of the most beautiful *Marcia* <note>Original: "Marsia." Likely referring to Marcia, the wife of Cato, a symbol of female nobility and beauty</note>. Sometimes it stems from the worshiper: as when the Jews ironically adorned Jesus with purple and a crown, as if he were a king. Sometimes it stems from the object of worship: as when we place an unwise man in a government office, believing him to be wise and worthy. Sometimes it stems from the manner of worshiping and praising: for example, if you were to give an iron crown to a poet, or a laurel or priesthood to a soldier; or if you called the pope "Most Serene" <note>original: "serenissimum" — a title usually reserved for princes or the Doge of Venice</note> and a king "Most Reverend" <note>original: "reuerendissimum" — a title for high-ranking clergy</note>.

One also errs in the use of emblems <note>original: "insignibus"</note> if you assign a lily to a martyr or a rose to a virgin. <note>In traditional iconography, the lily represents the purity of a virgin, while the rose or palm represents the blood and victory of a martyr; the author suggests reversing these is an error</note> In worship, sacrifices, and ceremonies, one must carefully observe whether they truly express what they claim to testify. In the law of *Moses*, this propriety is preserved most wonderfully in the garments, the sanctuary, the sacrifices, gestures, rites, and other ceremonies.

16. Opposed to this, as a vice of deficiency, is another unnamed vice which might be called <term>Lack of Testimony</term> <note>original: "Intestatio"</note>, because it fails to praise, fails to honor, and so on. This is ruinous to us in our relationship with both God and upright men. For we do not obtain their grace, help, or guidance if we do not acknowledge them. Indeed, all honor and worship benefits the giver more than the receiver. From this arises the imitation of the good and obedience to their instructions, than which nothing is more useful. For us, even the fountains of grace are dried up if they are not honored. Hence the earth, from which we receive fruit, must be cultivated <note>The Latin *coli* means both "to be worshiped" and "to be tilled/cultivated." Campanella is making a pun on the necessity of "cult" (worship) for spiritual fruit and "culture" (farming) for physical fruit</note>; and without this analogous "cultivation," it does not bear fruit. There is another form of testimony where we testify less than the reality, as if you were to call the best wine merely

...a good man, or calling a "reverend" bishop merely "reverend" <note>Campanella is arguing that misapplying titles—either by under-honoring the great or over-honoring the mediocre—is a form of social falsehood</note>. This likewise is harmful; it provokes indignation and leads to duels. Princes sin greatly when they do not honor the best men with important duties, but choose the mediocre instead; the same is true in elections. In this way, character and nature are everywhere degraded. Great talents scorn small honors. The third type of mockery is when we testify outwardly but not inwardly: as when we say to God and the prince, "Thy will be done," while intending to do our own. Such people are mockers and false witnesses. They put on a greater show than true worshippers, much like mourners hired for pay <note>Original: "conducti mercede." Professional mourners in antiquity were paid to wail loudly at funerals to simulate high status for the deceased</note> to weep for the dead; they show more grief by their wailing than the wife and children who truly mourn. In these vices are wrapped up lying, flattery, and cursing in a material sense; but they are formally distinct, as is clear from what has been said, differing in manner, object, purpose, and utility. This vice—when it fails to testify against the wicked when they do harm even in a court of law—causes immense damage. Thus, the philosophers did not cry out against the falsity of the gods, even though they knew the truth; and against the ruling sophists and false prophets, the "guardians of men" <note>A reference to leaders or intellectuals who should act as watchdogs for society</note> do not bark. Woe to them: rather than suffer some personal inconvenience, they allow the republic <term>republic: from the Latin "res publica," meaning the common good or the state</term> to fall into ruin. Others fail to accuse the wicked; this should always be done when they plot against the state and honest citizens. In other cases, depravity that does not harm others should be overlooked and corrected in secret, as the other virtues teach.

## *Of Gentleness, and its opposites.*

### ARTICLE III.

Gentleness <note>Original: "Mansuetudo." Often translated as "meekness," it refers to the virtue of remaining calm and composed under provocation</note> follows next. It is not twisted or disturbed by the errors of others directed against itself, since its own purity cannot be stained by their spots. It rejoices in itself and forgives freely, especially when it understands the impurity, the miserable nature, and the temperament of those who sin. Out of justice, it rebukes sins committed against God and neighbor, but always with a tranquil mind. Regarding offenses against itself, it is lenient, unless they result in damage to the state or to divine honor. Moses and David were renowned for this virtue.

2. The vice of one who does not spare others is called **Wrath** <note>Original: *iracundia*</note>. It belongs to an impure spirit that seeks a purity and displays a nobility it lacks, in that it takes revenge against those who "sin" against its own false sense of nobility.

3. He is afflicted by the vice of **Stupidity** who spares all errors indiscriminately. This happens not because he is merely happy with himself, but because he neither considers nor feels the sins committed against him or against his own nobility—precisely because he lacks true nobility himself. For **Nobility** is the light of innate virtue, leading a person toward moral actions through which it may reveal itself.

->*On cheerfulness, and its opposites.*<-

## CHAPTER XIII.

A sad spirit, when driven inward, dries up the bodily humors <note>referring to the four fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—which early modern medicine believed governed health and temperament</note>, dissipates life, and cannot live with others toward whom it does not pour itself out; it delights in lamentation and solitude. Friendship and social life are the opposites of this state; they seek joy, pleasantness, and games or pastimes by which the spirit is dilated, amplified, increased, and preserved. For this reason, the virtue of **Cheerfulness** <note>Original: *hilaritas*</note> tempers both joys and laughter, as well as sadness and mourning. It is content with present goods and the hope of future ones, being anxious for nothing beyond that. In times of adversity, it foresees better things through the natural changing of affairs and the goodness of the One who governs all things. It is the sign of a bright and pure spirit that does not despair because of evils, but pours itself out and plays with its own light. From this, such a person becomes lovely to himself and to others, whom he soothes with his appearance, example, and play, inviting them to hope for better things. He turns away from vulgar or ungentlemanly games, but embraces those that nourish strength and talent.

2. The opposite vice is **Sadness**, or **Severity** <note>Original: *Tristitia, siue Austeritas*</note>, which is not content with the present and is overly anxious about the future. It is always weighing its own troubles and is therefore a burden to itself and others; it does not smile upon pleasant gatherings. This is the sign of an impure, "sooty" spirit <note>Original: *fuliginosi*. Campanella uses the image of soot or smoke to describe a spirit clouded by the "black bile" of melancholy</note>, perpetually fighting with its own inner darkness. For this reason, it frequently draws itself inward and turns away from the festive outpourings of others; consequently, it becomes hateful to everyone. It always brings bad news. It breaks apart

2. This is a sign of a spirit that is very thin and soft, as well as "sooty" and impure. Because this spirit despairs of being able to fight its own internal "smoke" <note>The author uses *fuligines* (soot/smoke) to refer to the dark, heavy vapors that early modern thinkers believed clouded the mind and spirit</note>, it fears to retreat into itself; instead, it pours itself outward in its own thinnness toward external delights because it lacks internal ones. Such men do not know how to live in solitude. Many princes are similar to them; not daring or knowing how to sustain the weight of serious business, they pour themselves into jokes and love parasites, with whom they share a natural kinship. For the eye is not delighted by light unless it is itself luminous within, nor does the ear easily perceive sounds in the air unless it has air implanted within it <note>referring to the ancient theory that "like is perceived by like"—that our sense organs must contain a portion of the element they perceive</note>. Philosophical minds loathe such people.

### *Whether there are other virtues. And on Modesty.*

### CHAPTER XIV.

A person acts virtuously when they make proper use of opportunity in speaking, in dressing, in business, and in responding. This also applies to one’s manner of movement, gait, posture, clearing the throat, gestures, and physical carriage, ensuring that others are not offended but rather find joy in them; even though these are not virtues in themselves, but rather the *acts* of virtue.

2. Opposed to these are **Rudeness** <note>original: *Importunitas*</note> and **Immodesty** <note>original: *Immodestia*</note>. These show a disregard for the needs of others and are hostile to serious study, producing scandal, envy, ill-will, and a sense of "nausea" or disgust; they are displeasing to the sight.

3. Indeed, virtue is every faculty established by reason that preserves ourselves and others. Vice, however, is that which destroys. There appear to be as many virtues and virtuous acts as there are angels in heaven; and as many vices and vicious acts as there are demons in hell. Therefore, the former were wisely marked with the names of virtues by the ancient saints, and the latter with the names of vices...

<summary>Campanella distinguishes between healthy cheerfulness and the vice of buffoonery, while defining virtue and modesty as rational behaviors that preserve social harmony and personal well-being.</summary>

## *On Correction or Modesty, and their*
## *Opposites.*

# CHAPTER XV.

### ARTICLE I.

If indeed man had persevered in the original purity of the animal spirit <term>spiritus animalis: in early modern science, this was a subtle, vaporous substance believed to carry messages from the brain to the muscles and senses</term>—a purity which was suited to the human mind for a few virtues that nonetheless contained many others in an eminent way—there would be no virtue for correcting and punishing errors. We see, however, that in every age men have strayed from the rules of virtue—some from all of them, some from certain ones—nor can anyone persevere forever without offense. Therefore, it was necessary (as the Wisdom of God used to say) that there be some virtue to serve as the reformer and punisher of sins. For a man is not truly reformed simply because he stops the act of sin and returns to the virtue he had cast out, unless he is also chastised and "bent" in the other direction so that he remembers not to offend again; just as we bend a twisted branch in the opposite direction (even with pain, if the branch could feel) so that it remains straight in the middle. For this reason, he who has committed illicit acts ought to abstain even from those that are licit. The mind, conscious of its crime and full of guilt, also feels within itself a certain stain of irregularity; it fears itself, and even when it is safe, it is by no means secure. Nature also punishes the drunkard with frenzy and **gout** <note>original: *podagra*</note>, the lustful with jealousy and weakness, the greedy with anxiety, and the angry with inner turmoil. Therefore, the punishment of guilt is natural; and

<page-num>338</page-num>

...they understand <note>This completes the word *intelligunt* from the previous page's catchword.</note> indeed, when a virtue already defeated does not inflict that punishment. For where there is chastity in a brothel, or gentleness in one driven by the furies of anger, it follows that some virtue must be the regulator of punishment and lack of repentance. And those who deny this virtue deny that a virtuous man can sin, which is foolish, since constant perseverance in acts of virtue has been seen to be impossible in every age without the special help and privilege of God. 

But the passion of modesty <note>original: *verecundia*; this term encompasses both shame and a modest sense of propriety</note>, which is not the specific property of chastity, nor health, nor any other virtue, offers us penance itself. For it is not fear, as some claim, or a mixture of fear and boldness; but it is properly anger punishing not others, but oneself. For a man, whatever evil he does, especially in the presence of others, immediately blushes and feels shame; but in fear, he grows pale, as the spirit <term>spiritus: the "animal spirits" or subtle fluids believed to drive bodily functions</term> flees inward with the blood away from the thing that causes harm. 

However, we blush when we are angry at someone. For the spirit stretches the nerves as it moves outward, and carries the blood out with it toward the power of the one who harms. In this way, in the state of modesty, the spirit works toward its own vengeance. But immediately moved against itself, it spares itself out of self-love, so that others may not perceive the punishment. Indeed, by nature we all fear to show ourselves worthy of punishment. And while we are being corrected by a teacher or a father, we flee the gaze of others. 

From this it is clear why women and children are immediately shamed when appearing in the sight of others. It is because they surely realize they lack virtue, or that they could commit something that might harm others and offer poor hope for their future life. Now, to lack virtue and to commit that which causes harm is a fault, which they would wish to punish immediately. Prostitutes, however, who regard faults as if they were not faults, lack shame. Old men—because they have learned through long habit that a fault is not punishable, and because they have already lived out their lives—are shameless. 

But virgins are very modesty fearful <note>original: *verecunde timentes*</note> lest there be anything bad in them which would make them unpleasing to men and future husbands. Likewise, when they notice they are loved by those looking at them, they feel shame and punish themselves as if they were the cause of that love and offense—especially if they have cast their eyes upon those watching, so that rays are opposed to rays. For then a real mutual injury <note>Campanella refers to his theory of vision, where rays of the spirit literally exit the eye; when gazes meet, these rays collide physically.</note> occurs, as we have taught elsewhere, and they realize they are responsible for this injury and commotion.

<summary>Campanella defines modesty (verecundia) not as fear, but as a form of "self-punishing anger" that manifests physically as blushing. He argues that this trait is essential for self-correction and explains its presence or absence in different social groups like virgins, the elderly, and children.</summary>

...they understand. We feel shame regarding poverty and low birth, as if they were the appearance of some fault. For these reasons, if modesty <note>original: *verecundia*; here meaning a sense of shame or propriety</note> is a partial punishment and anger directed at ourselves, it follows that it is natural for a man to punish himself, just as he punishes others who sin against him. For even when we say a wicked word in the presence of great men, we immediately bite our offending lips, and we never blush more than when we are deprived of honor because of a fault. From this, it is clear that modesty is both an acknowledgment and a punishment of a fault; for without a fault, it would not be so. Therefore, modesty is an imperfect penance, or correction and vengeance; and penance is perfected modesty. Moreover, fasts, disciplines <note>referring to ascetic practices or physical acts of penance</note>, and abstaining from lawful things were not introduced into religion in vain—as the shameless and impudent chatter—but were established with the Creator of things and nature as the guide.

2. Modesty, therefore, which is **Honorableness** <note>original: *Honestas*</note>, is the rule between bashfulness and impudence in the process of imperfect correction. I speak not of that which occurs naturally, but that which comes through choice, guided by conscience, even if the face does not blush. The rule of this virtue is not to be so ashamed that you lose heart <term>spiritum despondeas: literally "to despond the spirit," meaning to lose one's vital energy or fall into despair</term> and, overwhelmed by confusion, become unable to speak. Rather, it is to determine a fitting penalty, to resolve not to sin in the future, and to embrace the virtues for whose lack we feel shame.

3. Shamelessness and impudence are the hallmarks of harlots, who, through constant disgrace and wicked acts, have unlearned how to feel shame. This is why God calls peoples who are stubborn in sin "harlots" and "brazen-faced" <note>original: *perfrictæ frontis*, an idiom for someone who has "rubbed their forehead" smooth so they can no longer blush</note>. It is a great crime: for they have proclaimed their sin like Sodom and did not blush with repentance. Instead, holding the rule that "whatever pleases is permitted," they boast when they have done evil, and they no longer sin in secret, but openly. The princes of the earth, impudent in the sight of the whole world, rage against the human race, and for the sake of the smallest greed, they stir up wars; they slaughter and are slaughtered by the thousands. They are the most impudent of all.

4. Opposed to this is the excessive bashfulness and blushing of some, who have even killed themselves because of it. A certain Spartan, overwhelmed by shame...

So great is the force of false loftiness that even the devil is ashamed to ask God for mercy, and chooses rather to live in death than to be subject to the Author of Life, even though he himself thoroughly understands this evil. From this, consider how divine the human mind is, and the loftiness of its essence. Even the elephant of Antiochus <note>Referring to a story from antiquity where a prized war elephant allegedly committed suicide after losing a mark of honor</note> killed itself when deprived of its honor during the crossing of the Nile; for it too is a participant in the primalities <term>primalitatum: Campanella’s metaphysical concept that all being consists of three "primalities": Power, Wisdom, and Love</term>, although it does not possess them essentially as a human does. Nor is its soul life itself, but a participation in life, and therefore it is mortal.

->*On perfect penance, or correction.*<-

### ARTICLE II.

In perfect penance, the virtue is called Emendation or Correction, which establishes a rule similar to nature: you should correct yourself through the very things by which you sin. If you have burdened yourself by eating too much, weaken yourself with fasting. If, seized by lust, you have squandered your goods with harlots, abstain from women and chastise your limbs with snow and thorns—as the saints did—or withdraw Bacchus and Ceres <note>original: *Bacchum & Cererem*; Roman deities of wine and grain, used here as metaphors for alcohol and food</note>, without whom Venus <note>the goddess of love, representing sexual desire</note> grows cold; stay far away from women. If you have harmed a friend by robbery or theft, restore as much as you stole, and moreover, pay fourfold as a penalty so that you do not repeat the evil. But if you have killed or mutilated someone, shall you kill yourself? Indeed, legal justice would kill you;

### CHAPTER 15 OF MORAL PHILOSOPHY

...virtue, however, desires that you undergo punishment willingly and not by force, and that you accuse yourself before a judge without being accused by others, just as it seemed right to Socrates. It was for this reason that Torquatus <note>Titus Manlius Torquatus, a Roman consul famous for his strictness, who executed his own son for a breach of military discipline</note> killed his son, and Brutus <note>Lucius Junius Brutus, founder of the Roman Republic, who executed his sons for conspiring to bring back the monarchy</note> killed his own, and Oedipus blinded himself; and Zaleucus <note>A 7th-century BCE lawgiver of the Epizephyrian Locrians; when his son was sentenced to blinding for adultery, Zaleucus gave up one of his own eyes so his son could retain one</note> plucked out one of his own eyes and one for his son, for whom the law had decreed the loss of two; and a certain man, discovering that his wife—whom he had killed as if she were guilty—was actually innocent, killed himself. I would certainly waver in my judgment, were it not that divinely revealed Religion warned me: man is not the master of himself, but belongs to his Creator, whose sheep we all are. From this it follows that he does not have such power over himself that he may kill himself; such power is granted by God only to the state. The state puts a man to death because it cannot know if he is truly reformed in his soul so that he will not sin again, or so that others might not sin by his example—not simply because of past sins, which cannot be undone. Therefore, if a man determines in his heart to sin no more and makes restitution to those he has harmed in their physical well-being or other goods, he will be able to persevere by mortifying himself without seeking death. For the innate love of life refuses to act against one's own life, even if it allows the spirit to suffer. Indeed, this worst crime of self-murder finds hardly any recompense, just as the damaging of one's reputation or property. Yet, when a state sins, it does not kill its entire self; likewise, a man should not kill his whole self. Let him submit himself to the judgment of a wise man for punishment. Hence Religion, in harmony with nature, has established the secret tribunal of priests <note>The Sacrament of Penance or Confession</note> to whom you may confess (which would have wonderfully pleased Socrates), and from whom you may learn your punishment and counsel, and through whom you may make satisfaction.

2. Regarding others, however, we shall exercise correction and vengeance according to the law. Before the law existed, nature dictated the **Law of Retaliation** <note>original: "Talionis pœnam" — the principle of "an eye for an eye"</note>, where the harmer and the harmed meet on equal terms. But modesty <note>a sense of shame or propriety</note> advises that you spare a portion of the penalty, which is a rule of nature: treat others as you would yourself; and do the same for your children and wife, who are a part of you. See the section on *Household Management* <note>original: "Oeconomica"</note>. Correction, not destruction, nor lawlessness, is the goal of this virtue. But when someone attacks you, what punishment should you demand? Defend yourself and employ defenders with modesty, without excess. Yet after a quarrel is finished, you shall not seek ven-

<meta>This page follows the discussion of how man belongs to God and not himself. It continues the exploration of "verecundia" (shame or modesty) as a social and internal corrective, now pivoting to how this sense of shame gives rise to the specific Christian virtue of Humility.</meta>

-># FRIAR THOMAS CAMPANELLA: On Humility and Obedience.<-

### ARTICLE III.

From shame arises another virtue, known only to Christian philosophers, namely **Humility**. It is not immediately the opposite of *pride*, but of *elation* <note>original: "elationi"; here meaning a swelling or loftiness of the soul</note>, which is the path toward pride. It begins from the love of one's own being—not insofar as that being is given its essence by <term>Power, Wisdom, and Love</term> <note>These are Campanella’s "Primalities," the three basic principles he believes constitute all Being</note>, but insofar as it also stems from the "primalities" of **Nothingness**. These are **impotence, ignorance, and lack of love**. Because of these, a man loves himself not for the sake of God—from whom he exists and by whose grace he exists—but for his own sake, even though by himself he is nothing. 

While he loves himself for his own sake, he subjects himself to lust, avarice, vainglory, and other vices that spring from the primalities of **Nothingness** and drag us toward nothingness. He does not subject himself to God through the virtues that arise from the primalities of **Being**, which flow from God, the First Being. Thus, he does whatever avarice and lust command, and not what God commands. 

**Humility**, therefore, is most wise; it subjects a man to God so that he loves himself only for God's sake, lest he be reduced to nothing, but instead be preserved for eternal life. And in this sense, *to serve is to reign*. 

For this reason, the humble man subjects himself not only to God but to every human creature for God’s sake, even to those lower than himself. He does not do this by subjecting his own great "goods" to the lesser "goods" of those beneath him—for that would be against nature—but rather he subjects his own "evils" (which he possesses from nothingness and vanity) to the "goods" of others (which they possess from God). 

In this way, he conquers vain desires and, through the shame that rebukes us in all things, he has learned to be humbled. He does this so that he does not fall into death, annihilation, and eternal punishments (where he would suffer because he cannot be fully annihilated), which happens when a man wishes to be exalted—not by God or toward God as his final end—but by doing whatever he pleases, as if he existed of himself and not because God commands it. This elation causes a turning away from the **Highest Good** toward "deficient goods"—that is, things viewed in their deficiency and as products of nothingness, rather than as beings established by God, the Supreme Being. For it is permitted to use all things for the sake of God, from whom and for whom they exist. The humble man, bearing this in his mind, cannot be lifted up in spirit above the precepts of God, nor above God's creatures,

<meta>catchword: because (qua-)</meta>

<summary>Campanella defines Humility as a uniquely Christian virtue that counters "elation" by recognizing that human failings come from "Nothingness" while human strengths come from God. He argues that true humility involves subjecting one's own faults to the divine gifts found in others.</summary>

<keywords>Humility, Primalities, Power Wisdom and Love, Nothingness, Elation, Pride, Christian Philosophy, Metaphysics of Being</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Humility from the previous page, where it was established that Humility subjects man to God to avoid the pull of "Nothingness." It now explores the practical applications of humility in knowledge and social hierarchy.</meta>

# MORAL MATTERS, CHAPTER XV.

...of which he is ignorant of the end foreknown by God and the conscience, but shamed by his own defects, he forgives all, sympathizes, and humbles himself. Whence the Holy Doctor <note>likely St. Augustine; the sentiment appears in his writings regarding the danger of spiritual pride in virgins</note> said that for virgins who do not acknowledge their own defects, but boastfully trust in their virginity, it is expedient that they fall, so that being shamed by this fault, they might also acknowledge their other defects and be humbled. Furthermore, **Humility** is the magnet of virtues. A man does not presume that he knows, but he learns; and the more and the greater the things he learns, the more he understands how much he does not know, as has been proven in the *Metaphysics* <note>Aristotle's *Metaphysics*, which Campanella often cites regarding the limits of human knowledge</note>; and thus he realizes he knows nothing perfectly. But by understanding a few things and doing so imperfectly, he subjects himself more to God, from whom he may know; and by humbling himself to all, he gains knowledge. He considers it more profitable to be defeated than to win in disputations: and this is a reality that the "know-it-alls" <note>original: "scioli"; those with superficial or prideful knowledge</note> do not notice. Likewise, in the way of the virtues, while he humbles himself as if he has made little progress, he is always progressing, and he seeks and finds. But he who thinks himself learned and holy does not progress, and thus he fails on the path and does not reach God. In this way, he who says he is full does not accept food, while he who is fasting does. Therefore, God gives grace to the humble and resists the proud, as if they think they have less need of Him. Likewise, because you have nothing that you have not received, you should be ashamed to boast as if you had not received it, which would be a lie. But if you did receive it, and you did not persist in the purity of what was received, you should be even more ashamed. From ourselves, there is only <term>Nothingness</term> <note>original: "Nihilitas"; in Campanella’s philosophy, the void or "non-being" from which all things are drawn and to which they tend without God's sustaining power</note> and fault: therefore humility is necessary to acknowledge this.

2. From this is born **Obedience**. For the humble man wishes to be subject; since it is difficult to rule oneself, while it is easier to rule others—unless they are something of your own, like children. For affection deceives you regarding your own; toward others, you exercise reason alone. Therefore, the Republic <note>original: "respub."</note>, having been advised of this, transfers dominion over children and over oneself to a King, and often to an external Magistrate <note>original: "Prætorem"; a reference to the medieval Italian practice of hiring a foreign official (the *podestà*) to ensure impartial justice</note>, as was the custom of the Florentines; and the most learned religious men obey brothers who are less learned. To humble oneself before inferiors, therefore, is to subject one's own passions to the reason of others. For this reason, it is neither humility nor obedience to subject your rationality to the passions of others; rather, it is a greater bestiality than subjecting it to your own passions. Therefore, when they command evil, they must not be obeyed; but if they command good things, or indifferent things ordered toward the good, one must obey.

3. The opposite of humility is **elation**, arising from a lack of shame and from love...

...born from being impregnated with the mask of deficiency and falsehood. From this boastful pride, arrogance, sophistry, hypocrisy, and other related vices sprout.

4. Regarding **Obedience**, its opposite is **Disobedience** in good things and in those neutral things ordered toward the good. However, in matters of evil and those ordered toward wrongdoing, it is a mark of fortitude and sublimity <note>original: "sublimitatis"; a loftiness of spirit that refuses to comply with immoral commands</note> not to obey.

5. **Command** <note>original: "Imperium"; the power to rule or the office of the ruler</note> does not arise from humility, except by occasion. Yet, in the act of governing, it stands in absolute need of humility. For the ruler will consider those whom he commands to be better than himself, and in this way, he will not be puffed up with pride. He will correct sins mercifully, with love for the people and hatred for their vices, always considering lest he himself also be tempted. He also requires **Fortitude** to defend his subjects from internal and external evils, and all the virtues—which **Justice** employs—so that he may teach, nourish, justify, and defend them. He must possess these in a "heroic degree," since virtues in a prince must be more excellent than in others; he must not merely be a good citizen, but simply good in the highest degree. He should excel like the head excels in a body, making others good by his example. Therefore, the specific virtue of a ruler is **Magnanimity** <note>original: "Magnanimitas"; literally "great-souledness," the virtue of being worthy of great things and knowing it</note>, which is the summit and summary of all virtues; we shall speak of this shortly. Regarding dominion over servants, beasts, and slaves, we have spoken in our writings on *Economics*; regarding the commonwealth, we have spoken in our *Politics*.

## *On Political Preservation, and Justice,*
## *as its Virtue.*

# CHAPTER XVI.

If men had remained in that natural purity in which they were created by the Supreme Craftsman <note>original: "opifice summo"; a common philosophical term for God as the Great Architect or Creator</note>, they would not have needed any virtues beyond those already declared. Through those previous virtues, they would be sufficiently preserved in themselves, in their children, and in their reputation, directed through holiness toward eternal life in God. For no other preservation is granted. Therefore, **Justice**, of which we are about to speak, would be superfluous. For justice was not established for the just and the pure, but for the unjust—that is, for those transgressing the moral laws already mentioned. For every virtue is a form of justice, because it establishes what is right and equal among the passions and actions directed toward an object...

The good act of the fourfold preservation <note>original: "conseruationis quadruplicis"; refers to Campanella's theory that all beings seek to preserve themselves in four ways: in their own being, in their species, in the world, and in God</note>, of which we have spoken. Those things which deviate from this are injustices—that is to say, they are vices. Hence, in all of God's scripture <sup>a</sup>, the "virtuous man" is synonymous with the "just man," and the "vicious man" is the same as the "unjust man." However, those who believe there is a "special justice" <note>original: "iustitiam specialem"; a reference to the Aristotelian distinction between general virtue and the specific virtue of fairness in distribution and exchange</note>, distinct from the other virtues, which "gives to each their due," are misled by the multiple meanings of words. For to give what is due to a benefactor is a work of **Gratitude** and **Benevolence**; to give to one whose property we hold is a work of **Fidelity**; to punish a sin is a work of beneficence and shame; to harm no one is a work of **Benevolence**. In short, whatever legal justice <term>legal justice: "iustitia legalis," the system of laws and courts established by the state to maintain order</term>, of which we are about to speak, commands, was already observed by the natural virtues. For legal justice commands those things belonging to temperance, fortitude, fairness, and the other virtues. Now, the power to command and the duty to obey flow from the "first primality" <note>original: "primalitate prima"; in Campanella's metaphysics, this refers to the three primal "pro-principals" of Being: Power, Wisdom, and Love</note> through the passions into our actions, and this is first reflected in the relationship between a father and his sons. This is where legal justice takes its root. It merely added a new coercive force, which it also borrowed from shame <note>original: "verecundia"; modesty or the healthy capacity to feel shame</note>. For when men began to leap over the rules already given and no longer felt shame, they had to be compelled to pay penalties so that they might learn to feel shame once more.

2. Therefore, [Wisdom said,] many children will be born, and they will not agree with one another through **Benevolence**. For a great variety of spirits will be created from the varying degrees of heat and the different materials from which they originate. Not everyone will obey the Mind, which I place within them as a leader; indeed, the Mind itself will become a servant to the passions once it has fallen away from obedience to God. Animals, too, will revolt against humans, just as people revolt against tyrants. Humans will no longer be able to provide food and other necessities for themselves on their own, but one will seize the labors of another through malice. **Ingratitude** will also destroy beneficence, so that no one will do good for another, and thus no one will be grateful. Many will be ignorant of the purpose for which they were born, and what the proper measure of passion and action ought to be to acquire the good. For some will be born strong in body but not in soul; these are well-suited for tilling the earth and guarding animals. Those who are robust and spirited are suited for defense and military service. Those who are virile in both mind and body will be fit to rule. Others...

...[those who are] weak in body but powerful in spirit, suited for investigating the sciences and handling religion. Others are weak in both, suited for serving. Therefore, it is necessary to gather them into one, as if into a single body, in which they come together like limbs, so that they may help each other through mutual duties and protect themselves from hunger, cold, heat, wild beasts, and mutual injuries; and so they may resume, at least in part, the lost dominion over the animals. In this way, each person may be occupied in the exercise for which they were born most fit. For thus it will happen that the lost virtues may be recovered—either through force in those who are not led by love, or at least in their actions, even if not in their souls.

This governing rule shall be called *Justice*, because it is a common virtue; for this reason, it bears the name of all the virtues, for it is the restorer of them all. It will first care to bring modesty <note>original: "verecundiam"; a sense of shame or moral restraint that prevents wrongdoing</note> back to life, as the guardian of the virtues. If modesty is not enough, Justice will perfect it, even to the point of punishment. And just as every virtue establishes a penalty for those who wander from it and a reward for those who observe it—not unlike the nature of the body [of which the polity and the common body will be the image], which punishes the limbs with disease when they withdraw from their duty and rewards them with health when they remain in it, using the stings of pain and pleasure for this very purpose—so too will *Justice* act in the Republic, the common body. 

And so that it may call them back from vile and fleeting goods, for which they fight to the death, it will call the eternal good back to memory through *Religion*, the seed and guardian of holiness. But if even *Justice* does not make men good, I have appointed a Great Day, on which I myself will judge deeds both good and evil; and I will call back the heaven and the earth, and I will complete the way I began from the start. I will return those who escaped the great battle of evils and were purged—those not pulled away from my friendship to the very end—to a state as pure as they were at creation, and better, and glorious. Furthermore, he added this speech, sounding perpetually in the secret ears of the soul:

**3. The head does not dominate all, but leads, commands, and helps, not only for its own sake but also for their benefit, acting as one of them. It provides them with movement and wisdom, in which it excels them as much as a shepherd excels his flock.

To be joined together like head and limbs, you must embrace Religion—born of holiness toward me, the One and Most Unified—which shall gather you into one. It distinguishes you in your duties so that each person, by doing what benefits himself, also benefits others by a single consensus, content with a common life. Woe, however, where there are diverse consensuses arising from diverse religions and gods. Religion must be the mind of the "mystical body" <note>original: "corporis mystici"; a traditional metaphor comparing a society or church to a living organism</note>, which couples you to my unity; the law of justice shall be the spirit; and the people shall be the body.

...wisdom, but fortune will govern, which knows nothing of harmony and is inexorable, since fortune is not "being" itself, but rather disorder. They cause harm to the laboring members of the community and deal with one another through trickery, having neglected the truthfulness and love by which they were meant to live bound together.

4. These transgressors of justice are called the "Unjust." They defraud individual men of the goods of the soul, the body, or external things, and they defraud the commonwealth by acting wickedly or by omitting good deeds. However, those who observe temporal laws too strictly—such as the Hebrews keeping the Sabbath even when they are attacked in war, or Torquatus <note>Refers to Titus Manlius Torquatus, a Roman consul who executed his own son for winning a battle against orders; he represents "Rigidity"—choosing the letter of the law over its spirit.</note> killing his victorious son because of a perceived fault—are not called Unjust, but rather Rigid. This Rigidity is born from the fact that they are ignorant of the "reason" of the law and its source: the Eternal Law. This Eternal Law is the First Reason and the First Wisdom, a teacher of utility and preservation, not of ruin. Laws are not established for all time regardless of circumstances, but for the evils of the moment; once those circumstances have passed, the "reason" (which is the soul of the law) ceases to exist. Therefore, the law is then merely a corpse. And those into whom God has infused His light have the power to change laws by persuasion; and when they have also obtained public authority, they may do so even by restraint. All justice is equity: the balancing of passions and actions toward a good end. He who possesses the knowledge of what is good and equitable—he alone should establish, abolish, or invalidate laws inter-

<meta>This page continues the discourse on governance and the nature of law. ->### MORAL PHILOSOPHY CHAPTER XVI.<-

...knows how to interpret and distribute things usefully. <term>Natural Equity</term><note>Latin: *Aequitas naturalis*. In Renaissance philosophy, this refers to a sense of fairness inherent in human nature and reason, which serves as the foundation for all written laws.</note> is natural law, from which moral law arises. The rule of equity, which is the eternal law, is the wisdom of God, and it endures without change. However, <term>positive law</term><note>Latin: *posita lex*. These are "man-made" laws decreed by a legislator to address specific, temporary circumstances, as opposed to eternal divine laws.</note> is established for present, not lasting, causes. He who established a law can change it: God can change divine laws, a King his royal laws, and a Pope his pontifical laws—but only in those areas where the laws are neither natural nor divine, for no one has power over a superior.

5. From what has already been said, one may understand that <term>legal justice</term> is the virtue of the community. It regulates the passions, ideas, affections, and actions of both the community and individuals for their preservation—in themselves, in their children, in their reputation, and in God. It is inspired by the Author of all things so that those things we do not wish to perform (or are ignorant of) through natural virtues, we may perform by being led and directed by legal justice. Therefore, legal justice is nothing other than those same virtues brought into the service of the community. Indeed, it commands nothing else; even when it makes rulings on "indifferent" matters <note>In legal philosophy, "indifferent matters" (adiaphora) are actions that are neither inherently good nor evil, but are regulated for the sake of public order.</note>—such as forbidding someone from riding a mule, or wearing silk, or requiring the streets to be cleaned—it is directing us toward the exercise of some virtue. It provides an advantage to the virtues and takes it away from vice and wrongdoing. 

For instance, where mules are necessary for the transport of grain (which <term>Moderation</term><note>original: "Sobrietas"</note> uses), the law forbids them from being employed in other services. Where silk draws the heart toward luxury and wastefulness, it is forbidden so that <term>frugality</term><note>original: "parsimonia"</note> and <term>generosity</term><note>original: "liberalitas"</note> may be preserved. All laws, therefore, are rules of virtue intended to preserve the common body. Laws that are not so are actually the excesses of vice. 

And indeed, the <term>divine positive law</term> commands all virtues and all acts where appropriate, and forbids all vices and all vicious acts. But <term>human law</term> commands only those things that hold the body of the republic together as one, and forbids those that destroy it; it treats other matters as indifferent. For this reason, it permits brothels and prostitutes, and lies that harm no one; however, it does not permit adultery or lies in sales and contracts confirmed by agreement, because these lead to the injury of others and to discord. But in well-ordered republics, more vices are forbidden, while in others, fewer are. And nowhere is every form of ingratitude forbidden, except that which arises from a contract. For the law intended that, since people often pretend not to know how much they should repay for a benefit received, after the loss of shame...

He justifies mundane regulations, such as clothing laws, as tools to encourage frugality and curb luxury.</summary>

The law does not grant fathers the highest power over their sons because they are often overcome by passion; instead, it brings all judgments before one judge and father <note>The "one judge and father" refers to the state or the sovereign, who is expected to act with the impartiality that a biological father might lose due to personal emotion.</note>.

6. Therefore, some laws concern holiness toward God; others concern the relationship of parents to children and children to parents, and marriages, looking toward integrity and chastity; others concern the social life of citizens and peace among themselves, looking toward **Goodwill**, **Good Speech**, and **Good Deeds** <note>Latin: *Benevolentia, Beneloquentia, & Beneficentia*. This triad was a common rhetorical device used to describe the ideal social cycle: thinking well of others, speaking well of them, and doing good for them.</note>, and their associated affections; others concern equal fairness, as well as unequal fairness (that is, concerning command and obedience); others concern punishments and rewards, looking toward shame, correction, and honor; others concern the defense of the Republic, looking toward fortitude. The rest follow from these.

7. And since all men are equal in their natural state, that part of Justice called <term>commutative justice</term><note>Latin: *Iustitia commutativa*. This is the branch of justice that regulates private exchanges and contracts, ensuring that the value given equals the value received.</note> ensures that you receive as much as you give in those matters that preserve a person in their own right; and yet, every person may still do good even if they receive nothing, following moral standards rather than legal ones. Therefore, justice devised these types of contracts: namely, **Gifts** and the **exchange of goods**; likewise **selling** and **buying** (which are essentially one thing); the **lending** of what is not returned as the exact same item <note>Latin: *mutuatio*. This refers to "fungible" goods like grain or money, where you return the same amount, but not the specific grains or coins you borrowed.</note>; the **lending** of things which are returned as the exact same item <note>Latin: *commodatio*. This refers to a specific object, like a tool or a book, which must be returned itself.</note>; to which you may add **deposits** [safekeeping] and **pledging**; likewise the **leasing** of things that yield fruit <note>Latin: *fructificantium rerum*. This refers to assets that generate income or products, such as livestock or orchards.</note> and the **hiring** of a person for their labor; likewise **currency exchanges**, **partnerships** in profits; **confederations**, **insurances**, **arbitrations**, and other agreements. All of these look toward Good Deeds, Gratitude, and Fairness simultaneously; they nourish Goodwill and Good Speech. In these dealings, you receive as much as you give, according to the agreement. Therefore, **usury** <note>The charging of interest on loans.</note> is abolished, as it is contrary to the spirit of doing good; except in cases where a loss has occurred for the benefactor, who nonetheless may choose not to demand payment out of his own generosity.

8. However, since men are unequal in their divine gifts and virtues—just as the different limbs of a body are suited for different functions—the law has decreed more honor for those who excel, for honor is a sign of respect given to virtue. And thus the law preserves our **reputation**, and converts...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of legal justice as the organizing principle of a community, specifically how it directs individual behavior toward the collective welfare. [justice] turns private virtues toward the common good. Therefore, it grants honor or reverence to the elderly as those excelling in **prudence**, and to men distinguished by their intellect and strength. It grants a certain honor to all members of society, simply as members, but a greater share to those who are superior; for when those of high character are honored, they are encouraged to do good for others. 

But to those excelling in virtue and dignity, such as **magistrates** <note>In Campanella's time, "magistrates" referred to any high-ranking civil officials or judges responsible for upholding the law.</note> (who, ideally, should only be men of virtue), both honor and obedience are given in those matters which they command for the public good; for in their private lives, they are equal to everyone else. To parents, however, one owes respect, obedience, and <term>piety</term><note>Latin: *pietas*. This refers to the Roman concept of dutiful devotion to family, country, and the gods.</note>, since they are the very source and the instruments of our existence. 

The same applies to the **homeland**, because it is the greater whole and the total source of which the father is but a single part. For this reason, in public or difficult matters, you must not prefer your father's interests where the common good is at stake. You should not entrust a public office to your father if there are better men suited for it, and you must save your country from ruin even if it means you cannot save your father. However, in private matters such as food and clothing, you should prefer your father’s needs over your own as a member of the country who is more venerable to you personally, even if he is not so to others. In matters of reverence, put the father first; in matters of comfort, put the children first; in matters of love, put the wife first, according to the laws. 

Finally, respect, obedience, and piety are owed to **God**, and above these, **Religion**, which is perfect service and worship. You shall serve no man as a master in the same way you serve God, since all men are your fellow members and fellow servants before Him—so much so that a pauper may be greater in the eyes of God than a king. Rulers, therefore, preside as the more vital members of a body; they do not dominate like a lion over beasts of another species, but rule within their own species, just as the head directs the limbs. 

They are sometimes called "Lords" and "Gods," but only by analogy and through a shared participation in divine authority. When a man sins, he makes himself like a beast and thus deserves a human master; yet a man who perseveres in virtue is commanded to serve God alone. For this reason, those who use force to subdue <term>cannibals</term><note>Latin: *anthropophagos*. Campanella is likely referring to the contemporary accounts of indigenous peoples in the Americas, which were often used in European legal theory to justify colonization as a form of "civilizing" mission.</note> and idolaters are doing a service, much like those who bind the insane to heal them—provided that healing is truly their goal.

9. Religion consists of **sacrifice** and **vows**, which are owed to God as a sign of His omnipotence; these can be shared with no created being. Oaths and the seeking of counsel regarding doubts or the future—which can be known by no one but Him—pertain to the same duty, as a sign of His wisdom and truth. Likewise, praise, thanksgiving, and petition, which are parts [of prayer]...

For this reason, **legal justice** chooses pure priests, acting as the "mind" of the <term>commonwealth</term><note>Latin: *respublica*. In Campanella’s organic theory of the state, the community functions like a living body, with the priesthood serving as the mental or spiritual faculty.</note>, to manage these aforementioned duties toward God; and it punishes the opposite behaviors most severely.

<margin>+</margin> The components of **superstition**, which are the opposite of religion, involve omitting these duties or applying them to created beings instead of the Creator; these include idolatry, the worship of demons, and the worship of the elements through sacrifices, divination, vows, oaths, and so on. **Irreligiosity**, however, is the vice by which all these things are attacked as if they were empty or "vain," even though they are ordained by God and all of nature cries out in their favor. No political system could ever be established without religion—not even by **Atheists** or **Epicureans** <note>Followers of the ancient philosopher Epicurus; in the early modern period, this term was often a slur for those perceived to deny the immortality of the soul or divine providence.</note>—since no human body can truly be human without a mind. Certain philosophers are fools to think these things were merely invented to trick the masses; in truth, they have been established by many miracles and by the very necessity of life derived from God and nature. Concerning these matters, we have already spoken in the *Theology* and the *Metaphysics*, and a little earlier in this work.

10. Whatever stands in opposition to <term>piety</term><note>Latin: *pietas*, the Roman-inspired virtue of dutiful love toward God, parents, and country.</note>, obedience, and respect falls under the categories of malice, ingratitude, and inequality or arrogance. Furthermore, all injuries to a person’s reputation, body, or wealth are components of **injustice**. Thus, you can see that in every case, justice is nothing other than the virtues performed as a duty and made public. From the practice of these duties comes **peace**, which is the result of a goodwill that binds the commonwealth together—uniting the higher and lower classes, and God and humanity. Those of higher rank return teaching, protection, and a good example. **Magistrates** provide the same, while also maintaining peace among the members of society. A **father** provides the same, as well as an inheritance and his own goods, beyond the simple acts of birth and education. The **homeland**, moreover, grants these things along with protection from internal and external threats, the correction of vices, rewards, dignity, and senatorial or other social rank. **God**, however, grants all of these and more: existence, life, virtue, protection from devils, help in doing good, and eternal life. The commonwealth establishes the legal way to honor God and men so that no one has an excuse and so we may be joined as one; it brings to light what was hidden within the virtues and adds further rules regarding <term>indifferent matters</term><note>Latin: *indifferentibus*. These are "adiaphora"—actions that are not inherently good or evil by nature but are made mandatory or prohibited by civil law for the sake of social order.</note>, as has been stated.

# ON MORALS, CHAPTER XVI.

11. Finally, the **Commonwealth** receives its military and the practice of war from the virtue of **fortitude**, directed both against external enemies and against corrupt members of the state; these members it cuts away when it despairs of them ever being useful again, and as an example to others. The state derives this from the <term>virtue of retribution</term><note>Latin: *virtus ultionis*. In classical and medieval philosophy, this is the moral habit of the state to restore justice through punishment, rather than personal revenge.</note>. Just as a man does not kill himself, but punishes himself and submits to the judgment of better men, so the Commonwealth does not destroy itself as a whole, but asks forgiveness from God; sometimes, due to its own crimes, it surrenders itself into the hands of others. There are even times when it must live in servitude, much like a man captured in war—for in all things, the whole and the part correspond. 

The state establishes schools, sciences, and public teachers so that it may use knowledge well, just as **eagerness for study** and **prudence** taught us earlier. It distributes the arts through **cleverness**, and provides all manner of training through the virtue of **exercise**. To convict those of vanity and ignorance who do not establish laws based on virtue, the state has adopted **moralized comedies** from **Cheerfulness**, along with other useful games. It has erected Tribunals of Justice with accusers and witnesses, mirroring the **inner conscience** which accuses, condemns, defends, and protects us—no theater is greater than this. Every disordered soul is its own punishment. Guilt may leave one safe <note>That is, safe from being caught by the law.</note>, but it leaves no one secure <note>original: *securum*. Referring to the internal peace of mind.</note>; nor does it leave the impudent at peace. Hence, at the end of the ages, **Wisdom** will condemn those who, neither restrained by the state nor by nature, never ceased to sin until the end. I believe this, and I understand it as such.

### *On Sublimity, the Apex of the Virtues, and the Epilogue.*

## CHAPTER XVII.

<margin>Theologians say that so many evils flow from **original sin**; this is why we feel shame.</margin>
We experience such great loftiness in the human soul that even if it does not possess virtue and goodness in itself, it still pretends to have them. It is as if the soul is teaching us that being deprived of virtue does not suit its nature; instead, this lack arises as if by accident or through some hidden fault, for which the soul feels **shame**. It hides its own depravities as much as possible, and when it cannot, it defends them as if they were virtues. It covers up the low birth of parents, homeland, friends, and kin whenever and wherever it can; and when it cannot, it excuses itself for this in wondrous ways. The soul finds being subjected to another as abominable as death. And when it serves, there is nothing it so greatly dreads—

...[the soul] knows how bitter it is to be called a servant or a slave. Even the most menial tasks, to which a man is driven by necessity, he praises and pretends are honorable as far as he is able; and when he cannot, he complains that he is weighed down by them unworthily—blaming his fortune, not his own fault. **Shame** <note>Latin: *verecundia*. This term encompasses both modesty and the fear of disgrace.</note> also clearly demonstrates this, as it so suddenly drenches the human face with a blush. This happens not only because of vices and wicked deeds, but also because of an unfitness for virtues, a lack of virtues or of external and divine goods, a lowliness of birth, and any appearance of evil—let alone its actual existence. Indeed, even the mere reputation among others for an evil <note>original: *q* (abbreviation for *quod*)</note> that is not even in us, or the suspicion that they might suspect us of it, is hateful to a man, as if he wished to punish himself for lacking [perfection]. It is an amazing thing. How many have even killed themselves because of this! For instance, when a black slave, seeing himself in a mirror looking so different <note>original: *deformem* (literally "unformed" or "misshapen" relative to the environment). Campanella is citing a contemporary anecdote about the psychological impact of perceived "otherness" or "deformity" in a foreign social context.</note> among white people, threw himself from a window. 

And those who have destroyed their children, their parents, and their fatherland for the sake of honor show how immense the desire for praise is, even in the wicked. Nor, after so many divine religions have persuaded us otherwise, can the human race believe that when it is provoked, despised, or harmed, it is not bound to drive the offender to death. It does not suffer even a word (which is but wind) or a spit (if it is a sign of contempt) without taking revenge if it can. 

A man is not ashamed of **pride** and **envy**, which are grave evils, because they possess a kind of false loftiness; yet he is ashamed of the venereal act, and of eating and excretion, which are lesser things. This is because these latter acts bear the mark of the contemptible, for they are the <term>medicines of mortality</term><note>A common philosophical concept of the era: we only eat and reproduce because we are mortal and must maintain our bodies or replace ourselves; therefore, these acts remind us of our animal nature.</note> and are common to us and the lowly beasts. 

What is so sublime that lies hidden within us, O men, that we consider it worthy of such great veneration? Why do we think it right that no evil—neither natural, nor accidental, nor moral, nor even inflicted by God—should touch it? Why do we find it impossible to believe that such evils befit us, even if the order of all nature and God Himself should decree it? Is there truly such a **treasure in earthen vessels**? <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 4:7: "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us."</note> Does even the Devil himself use this "treasure" as an excuse not to humble himself, lest he become vile by asking God for forgiveness like a subject? Is there, then, something in us higher than God? And why, I ask, have men wished to be called and believed to be gods, even though they knew themselves to be mortal and dying? Even in death, they claimed they were immortal gods and were now casting off their mortality. Thus Her-

...Hercules, Bacchus, Jupiter, Alexander <note>Campanella refers to historical and mythological figures who were either deified or claimed divine status, illustrating the human impulse toward the divine.</note>. Without doubt, the divine image in our mind suggests this to us, being conscious of its own divinity; yet it errs, since this divinity must be credited to the One from whom it is given. If He has bound the soul among so many storms and dangers of the elements and within the coverings and chains of the **animal spirit** <term>animal spirit: In the science of Campanella's time, these were subtle, vaporous fluids that acted as the bridge between the immaterial soul and the physical body.</term>, He has undoubtedly done so not without cause and the highest reason; and He will also grant that we may emerge. Meanwhile, the desire for false praise, fame, and glory must be reined in, until light arises in the darkness and leads us back to Himself, who by His own grace created us in exile. Neither rest outside the fatherland, nor deification outside of God, is to be sought.

2. Therefore, some men command and are honored because they abound in such goodness and virtue as is sufficient for their own preservation and that of others. Such goodness shines in the mind when it is possessed without disturbance by the spirit which the mind informs. Thus, a clear purity—an animal spirit very similar to the heavens—is the foundation of the lower moral virtues, while for the natural virtues it is their very essence. As the servant of the mind and higher things, this is true nobility and, consequently, intrinsic preservation. The works of this nobility are the virtues by which external goods are prepared—namely, wealth, honors, friendship, power, glory, health, and both private and public affairs. These exist for the sake of internal preservation, which we desire to make eternal; they are not the ends for whose sake internal goods exist. Therefore, since we value the indicator of this nobility—which is honor—so highly, we do not do so merely to live comfortably (since we often live better without it, and for its sake we might lose life, fatherland, and property), but because we wish to be held as gods, even if false ones. On the contrary, there are those who do not care for **fame** <note>original: *famā*</note>, the witness of such great hidden beauty, having stripped away their shame so that they may enjoy the objects of their passions. Hence, those who neglect the honor given by God are cursed. Others do not even know what nature intends by the feeling of shame. For this reason, there was a need for **heroic virtue** <note>original: *heroica virtute*</note>, which can be called Sublimity, Magnanimity, or Generosity; this virtue corrects and moderates such a great desire for glory or, conversely, the neglect of it. It teaches that one must not fight with those who deny us honors; for honors are not goods in themselves, but merely witnesses of internal goodness. Indeed, they are often false witnesses, since even vicious and unspeakable Kings and Emperors are adored. Nor does the sublime man grieve at a lack of riches, since these are often present even for the wicked, and are themselves false [witnesses] of virtue...

He therefore cares for and cultivates only his own excellence, rejoicing in that inner purity which he possesses; and he desires to see that excellence honored by others as a reflecting **image of God**. He considers that he would be accepting a law from them, and becoming like them, if he were to imitate their wrongdoing in word or deed by returning evil for evil. Instead, he returns good to all, even for evil; not because he is afraid, but because he wishes others to receive the law of doing good and of imitating him. He knows himself to be worthy of doing good to everyone, so that he might overcome beastly minds with **humanity** <term>humanity: *humanitas* in Latin, referring here to the refined kindness and rational conduct that separates humans from animals.</term> and make them truly human—which is a property of God Himself. If he is unable to do this, he asks God to make them righteous, not to punish them, except for the sake of their own salvation. Finally, he does not fear to die, except for his own fault. Thus, in private as in public, he fights against vices and misfortunes so as not to degenerate from his own nature; it is not, therefore, merely a matter of appearing not to degenerate. [He fears] himself more than he feared [others] previously, if ever he acts wrongly; for he considers it a sacrilege to commit a fault in his own presence as if before the most excellent witness. Therefore, he will not cheat even when playing "fingers" with himself in the dark <note>original: *in tenebris secum micantem*. 3. Yet he loves and honors all men as parts of his own kind; he believes he was born not for himself, but for the whole world. And this is the worship he offers to his own mind, which was created in the **image of the divinity**. Just as God, the creator of all, hates nothing He has made—for He created all things good and lovable to Himself not by compulsion but by love, not as things to be hated—so the noble man, a sharer in divinity through the mind (which the pure animal spirits do not disturb, but leave in its natural serenity), loves all things. He loves especially those that are more excellent and more closely joined to him; therefore, he loves men more, who excel all physical things. Thus, he respects the lowly and the least as parts of his own species, and he strives and takes care that they may become like him in virtue; he respects equals as those similar to himself; and he respects his superiors as those whom he hopes and cares to become like. He obeys holy laws as if they were issued by those like himself—or even more so if from God, whom he recognizes as the one to be worshipped above himself. He honors those who bestow honor and benefits upon him, even if they are inferior in virtue, because he honors in them that which he knows himself worthy to share, and sees them as witnesses and admirers of his virtue. He even does good to his enemies and prays for them, pitying their impurity as if they were distorted or diseased members of his own body, for whom he procures health. Likewise, because of such high-mindedness, he believes everything wonderful said about God—about His providence <term>prudence: here meaning God's divine foresight and care</term> toward us, His descent to humanity in the flesh, and the glorification of man after death—regarding all these things as even lesser than the credibility of His greatness suggests. He approves such great love and care as being worthy of God.

4. Furthermore, in order to imitate God, he desires to be able to do all things, to know all things, and to will all things, and that nothing should oppose him. Thus, being the best through the serenity of his natural talent, he easily learns every kind of **mechanical art** <note>original: *artium mechanicarum*. In this period, these included engineering, architecture, and skilled crafts, which Campanella believes a clear mind can master quickly.</note>...
