He cultivates Mathematics, so that he may experience the stars and the systems beyond the world by whatever means possible. He will devote himself to the Prophets, to confirm the divinity of the soul in the knowledge of future things and to distinguish [true] prophecy from that of brute animals. He will perfectly scrutinize the colors, motions, powers, and irregularities of the stars; full of admiration for God alone, who shows so many wonderful riches of His power and wisdom within them. He will not despise Medicine, so that he may provide for his own health and that of others, and not be subject to the ignorance of physicians. 

And in Ethics, for the sake of his own self-governance, and in Politics and Economics for the governance of others, he will make wonderful progress—surpassing all mortals—since he has reached the archetype of both Nature and God. He will be well-versed in Rational Philosophy—that is, Logic, Rhetoric, and Poetics; he will understand and illuminate their parables, fallacies, insights, and strategies. He will love Metaphysics, as it is the field in which all arts are contained, just as all poems are contained within the Art of Poetry. In Metaphysics, he will investigate things as they truly are, not as they appear in other sciences; therefore, he will found a new Metaphysics, neglecting the old version which does not savor of this [truth]. 

He will cultivate Theology above all, as the place where he finds things worthy of our minds. Indeed, he will search out the doctrines and sciences of all the ancients; yet he will not be content to know what has been written by others unless he himself experiences whether he finds the same things in the same way within the World—which alone he examines as if it were the **Book of God** <note>original: *Dei Codicem*. This is a central theme in Campanella’s philosophy: the idea that Nature is a primary "book" or "manuscript" written by God, which must be read directly rather than through the commentaries of ancient scholars like Aristotle.</note>, in which the Artisan of things has written and depicted all His secrets as living realities. 

As an emender of writings, examining all things by comparing the copies <note>i.e., human books and theories</note> to the Original <note>i.e., the universe itself</note>, he will cease to be a mere admirer [of authority]. Yet he will praise the intentions of the ancients; nor will he twist their words for his own minor glory. He will disdain to copy or steal anything from those who have written correctly. He will understand that the Divine Scriptures are worthy not of correction but of explanation; these cannot be fully known by anyone not inspired by the spirit of the Author, just as one cannot understand poems unless he is a poet. Therefore, he will desire as much as possible to be like holy and learned men, whom he will uniquely love and honor. Furthermore, whatever is found in the world that is stupendous and admirable, he [would desire] himself to be their inventor...

### CHAPTER XVII. ON MORALS

<page-num>359</page-num>

# ON MORALS, CHAPTER XVII.

...he would desire [these things]: yet he does not feel envy, but praises and admires those who willed so much; nor is this excessive, since he understands these same things to be possible for himself. Among all men, he will praise Columbus for the discovery of a new world, and Galileo for [the discovery] of new stars through wonderful ways; and Origen <note>original: *Originem*. Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD) was an early Christian scholar whose daring theological speculations were later controversial.</note> in Theology, because he dared to form opinions about wonders beyond revelation, even though he might have erred: for in this, the hunger of a lofty soul is praised, not the error. He admires Ambrose and Chrysostom for their zeal for virtue.

But Gregory Thaumaturgus <note>original: *Gregorium Thaumaturgum*, meaning "Gregory the Miracle-Worker," a 3rd-century bishop known for his missionary success and wonders.</note>, and Elijah, and Moses—the loftiest splendors of the human race—oh, how he thinks they are to be loved! He cries out that Peter and Paul, the victors over the World and the Empire, and John speaking of divinity, are above [ordinary] men. The Magnanimous man <note>A term from Aristotelian ethics meaning "great-souled," referring to a person of high virtue and ambition.</note> indeed praises his ancestors and does not envy them; yet he emulates them. 

And he wishes, if he were able, to penetrate above the heavens and know the beings hidden from him, to enter into the individual stars, and to learn beforehand what God does, represents, and preserves in so many systems, stages, and storehouses <note>original: *armariis*. Campanella uses the metaphor of cabinets or storehouses to describe the various regions or "compartments" of the universe.</note>. Therefore, he tries everything so that he might understand: and when exhausted, he seeks knowledge from God; asking for pardon because he does not delight more in His works, since he does not see more, but only catches a scent of them, as if from a distance. 

Furthermore, he will read through all histories from the beginning of the world until our time—natural and civil, and those of the whole human race—[for purity of spirit and serenity of mind carry a divine-like, almost sudden intelligence and memory] and in these histories, he takes delight as if he were present, praising good deeds and grieving when they acted wrongly. He will seem to himself to be not thirty years old, but to have as many myriads <note>A "myriad" is ten thousand.</note> of years as the world has, as if he had been present through so many ages and events; nor [were these years] spent in one region, but in the whole world; so that he can be called an inhabitant of the entire world from the beginning until our time. 

From this, he knows most things, compares and points them out, and teaches beyond others: and he investigates the celestial changes corresponding with terrestrial ones, physical matters with astronomical, astronomical with civil and moral, and moral with divine visitations <note>original: *visitationibus*. Refers to divine interventions or judgments in human history.</note> in any century; he conjectures about the future from the past, and seeks [answers] from the prophets. And when [he encounters] a new or an old opinion, wonder-

...[when he] hears a full explanation, even if it is considered impossible, he does not immediately condemn the author; rather, he is indignant toward those who do. Instead, he examines the idea in the Book of God—which is the World <note>original: *Dei, qui est Mundus*. Campanella famously viewed the physical universe as a living book written by God that must be read alongside scripture.</note>—and in divine revelations. He considers whether it proceeds from causes and effects, or from signs placed by God or by Nature, or whether it proceeds pointlessly from the author's own whims. Only then does he pass judgment with sobriety. He runs through all the occult sciences <note>technical vocabulary: *scientias occultas*. In the 17th century, this included fields like astrology, alchemy, and natural magic, which Campanella believed should be tested empirically.</note> and, having examined them, separates the true from the false. He will test all things, both good and evil, with humility, for the glory of the most wise Creator which shines in his own soul. He will love God, not out of fear of hell nor out of ambition for paradise, but because He is the supreme good and a parent worthy of all love—even if he knew himself to be destined by God for the pains of hell. However, he considers such a fate impossible, as he always perceives the goodness of God; thus, he considers those who believe in predestination to evil <note>A reference to the theological debates of the Reformation; Campanella strongly opposed the idea that God predestines anyone to damnation regardless of their actions.</note> to be wretched and willfully wicked destroyers of both Divine Providence and human freedom. Therefore, he will forge the sciences anew and will send out divine letters to all regions of the world concerning the care of their salvation and that of the human race, and for the restoration of religion, being most devoted to the zeal and study of Paul <note>Refers to the Apostle Paul’s missionary work and letters to various nations.</note>. Likewise, if he is able, he will travel through the whole world to put all things to the test.

5. He does not seek honors except to do good, being content with his own purity and nobility; he does not accept minor positions where he cannot be of use. He would desire, however, to be the Judge and legislator of all men, so that he might exterminate the many shames of false religions and gods, the worship of things lower than ourselves, and tyrants. He would seek to adorn his fatherland with the dominion of the universe, and he will take care to leave the world better to posterity than he received it. He will grieve over the world's evils and its servitude, and he will attempt many things to remedy this. Finally, he will commit all things to the providence of God after he has done everything in his power. In tribulations and in prison <note>original: *in carcere*. Campanella wrote much of his work while imprisoned for 27 years for his political and religious views.</note> he will rejoice, meditating on divine works and arts. He will consider himself more worthy of command at that time than when enjoying freedom; for when great virtue is hated and envied—virtue of which impure and masked princes and vicious men are afraid—then their persecution and his own patience provide a proof and a display of that virtue which was previously hidden.

scarcely did the World acknowledge him. God is also proven to be present to him even in his distresses. What, indeed, is more majestic than a divine visitation? In torments, he remains unconquered; he is not broken by the cruelty or the long duration of his suffering. He will not confess simply to satisfy his torturers; rather, he will mock them—for he is conquered by virtue alone. <note>Campanella is likely reflecting on his own experience; he survived the "Veglia" torture (being suspended for 40 hours) without confessing to the crimes the Inquisition accused him of.</note> Having experienced the envy of devils toward the human race, he will abhor their company; yet there is nothing he will not investigate. Indeed, he gladly hears the history of those who are carried through the air by the art of demons and perform wonders—not because he admires their crime or their apostasy, but because he admires the daring human power, a sign of extraordinary height. This shows that we can have commerce even with minds separated from the body, and that we shall have it with angels if we have it even with devils. <note>Campanella viewed even the dark reports of witchcraft or demonic magic as empirical evidence that the human soul is spiritual and capable of interacting with the supernatural realm.</note> From this, he strengthens his hope and his religion.

In evil things, he loves even a trace of the good; and in good things, he hates any trace of evil. Indeed, in all virtues—which is a wonderful thing—he selects the highest for himself: from Fortitude, he chooses martyrdom; from chastity, virginity; from liberality, magnificence. Regarding the arts of Daedalus <note>The mythical inventor of flight.</note>, he will gladly contemplate the act of flying and the machines of Archimedes <note>The Greek mathematician known for his war machines and engineering.</note>; for he seeks the "epilogue" or the ultimate sum of all virtues. He will not make himself a prey to pleasure or pain; he will hear the Sirens, but only while tied to the ship's mast, and he will stop up the ears of his own followers. <note>A reference to Odysseus in Homer’s *Odyssey*, who listened to the Sirens' song but remained restrained so as not to be lured to his death.</note>

If by chance he is made a slave, he will do nothing in a slavish manner; instead, he will minister to his fellow slaves as if he were their master, and by his virtue, he will emerge as the "master of his masters," to whom he will become most welcome. He would never have committed suicide <note>original: *Mortem sibi nunquam conscissett*</note> to reach the delights of God by fleeing his troubles; for he knows that God did not bind the mind to the body without cause, until He Himself wished to release it. He knows it is dictated by nature to everyone not to act against one's own composition, but to endure where necessary.

Where he can escape, he will not reluctantly imitate David feigning madness, or Solon, or Brutus; and he himself will mock his unjust persecutors. <note>These are three historical/biblical examples of "noble deception": King David feigned insanity to escape the King of Gath; Solon feigned madness to inspire the Athenians to war; and Lucius Junius Brutus feigned idiocy to survive the tyranny of Tarquin the Proud.</note> Yet nothing is more hateful to him than a lie, and especially betrayal. He will use only helpful strategies <term>stragegematis: tactical deceptions used for a good end</term> and ambiguities <note>original: *amphibologiis*. This refers to "mental reservation" or double-meanings used to protect the truth from those who would abuse it.</note> in word and deed against those with childish minds who persecute the very integrity that is most useful to them—not unlike a child who wants his doctor dead because he offers him bitter medicine. And, if it happens that he must handle wars, nothing is stronger than him, or more prudent in the military art. He touches the tillers of actions, not the hulls. <note>A nautical metaphor: he controls the direction and purpose of events (the tiller) rather than being weighed down by the bulk of the material (the hull).</note> For he knows the whole world is placed in a vacuum. <note>Campanella’s cosmology held that the physical world exists within a vast, pre-existing space or "vacuum" created by God.</note>

can be pulled by a single hair: just as a ship in the sea, where there is no resistance. He understands that all things are difficult to move because they stretch toward their own **natural wholes** <note>original: "vniuersitates"; Campanella refers to the natural spheres or systems to which things belong by nature.</note>—earthly things toward the earth, solar things toward the sun, and the parts of the moon toward the center of the moon within its own circuit. Yet outside of these, they move in whichever direction you wish; and according to their own inclinations, they move as you desire. From this, he becomes most wise in **Natural Magic**, <note>In the 17th century, "Natural Magic" referred to what we might now call experimental science or the study of the hidden properties of herbs, minerals, and the stars.</note> in the powers of herbs, and in the antipathies and sympathies of celestial things with earthly ones, and of men with other men and things. He considers nothing difficult if the proper means of operating is present. Nevertheless, such a great man will be humble, acknowledging all things as coming from God, in comparison to whom he himself is nothing. He will judge that he knows nothing, except when compared to others, whom he will honor according to their rank. This is especially true since he knows that one cannot perfectly know anything through <term>Metaphysics</term> <note>original: "Metaph."</note> unless he has already proven the reality of certain existences.

6. Opposed to Sublimity are **Vileness** (or <term>Pusillanimity</term> <note>Literally "smallness of soul." This is the vice of being timid or lacking the spirit to pursue great things.</note>) and **Pride** or **Ambition**. The former does not love honors and power, not because he scorns them as a noble man does, but because he does not understand their splendor; or he fears evils and dangers, and lacks the confidence to sustain them with the strength and talent he lacks. Serving his own pleasure, he neglects the care of others. He submissively honors the powerful and the wealthy, not as people who are superior or beneficial to the human race and himself, but as those who have the power to do harm. In trials, he collapses under the test without a word, and immediately thinks himself destroyed. When questioned under torture, he vomits up whatever the torturers want, whether it be true or false. He is affected by the shame of others rather than his own. He will not attempt great things. He will flee the sight of princes and wise men—not because he despises them, but because he fears them, knowing himself to be unworthy of their company.

7. **Pride**, an inordinate love of one’s own excellence, is the head of all vices. For we commit no crime except that by which we prefer our own will to the divine will. This is to be monstrously raised above God; just as a foot would not wish to walk above the head. Therefore, pride turns us away from the supreme good and turns us toward ourselves, so that we regard ourselves as the supreme good, worthy of all honor and worship, and self-sufficient as if from ourselves and existing for our own sake, being ashamed that we even depend upon God...

<page-num>363</page-num>
<header>OF MORALS, CHAPTER XVII.</header>
<sig>Zz 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: Ad- (Note: This is the start of the word "Admiration" or similar, appearing on the next page.)</meta>

How could a man not be arrogant, if God—providing such consolation—had not ensured that he required the earth, food, drink, sleep, and the most common of things? Unless a turning away <note>original: "aversio"</note> from God preceded this state, it would not be sinful; otherwise, that turning toward <note>original: "conversio"; here referring to the soul turning toward material things rather than the divine.</note> the material would not follow. Because of this turning, the soul—which once rose above God and the decrees of nature—finds itself insufficient and submits to the body. The body, in turn, is subjected to external, worthless goods. In these things, as if clinging to nothingness, the soul begs for a false honor, having disdained the true honor that flows from the **Primal Truth** <note>original: "prima veritate"; a common Scholastic term for God as the source of all reality and logic.</note>.

This love [of self] therefore seeks out honors for which it is not worthy through virtue. It does this not to grow wealthy—for that would be the vice of **Avarice**—but because it recognizes these honors as the "highest good." It does not value them as evidence of virtue or of the true and highest good, nor does it seek them to do good for others; rather, it seeks them so that the person may be seen on high. Such a person will even affect a likeness to the divine; he will greatly love those who admire him and his parasites. He undertakes grand tasks so that he might *appear* grand, rather than because he actually is, or to truly become so. Once deprived of honors, he no longer has the confidence to live, or barely so. He will use money and every kind of crime to redeem the status he craves.

When cast into prison and hardships, the proud man then considers himself unworthy of honors. This is the opposite of the **Magnanimous** man <note>The "high-souled" or "great-souled" person, a concept derived from Aristotle's *Megalopsychia*.</note>, who is always consistent with himself. In such trials, the Magnanimous man considers himself even more worthy; he will not ransom his life with money if he must die for the sake of virtue—especially when dying for the Republic he has served. Indeed, he becomes the master of those who persecute him, for while he is killed as an innocent for the sake of justice, he seals the defense of the Primal Truth and Wisdom with his death. In that moment, he declares himself to be a prince by nature, even though he is oppressed by those who are merely "princes" by fortune or by the masks they wear.

Thus, today, Peter and Paul are the masters of Nero, the man who killed them. Nero's laws, statues, and memory have been cast down into a curse; but the images of Peter and Paul have been raised in the temples and on the altars of the earth and heaven. Socrates is most highly praised, while his persecutors are most reviled. Through his life and death, Socrates established a law with holy words that will endure forever, such that anyone would desire to become as he was; but his persecutors are so hated and loathsome that no one wishes to be like them. He is the health of the world; they are its ruin.

<header>OF BROTHER TOMMASO CAMPANELLA</header>

## Admonition.

When eternal wisdom <note>original: "sapientia æterna"</note> was planting this virtue into the human spirit from the mind—the most beautiful summary of all virtues—it spoke to the immortal mind, in which it first cast the seeds of the virtues:

> You shall indeed be justly punished, unless you know how to use that spirit correctly, as a living organ of virtuous intelligence. I do not command you to tame stones and plants, but rather spirits that are celestial in origin, who share in your virtues and create a symphony and harmony with you. Do not excuse yourself by saying that they also share in vices; for the opportunity for the impurity of vices will not be present except when you sin; nor will they be carried away afterward unless you will it. Within you lies the freedom of willing and not willing according to my law, which I imprint as a living force upon your virtues, as the fulfillment of my likeness.
>
> The animal spirit <term>animal spirit<gloss>In Campanella’s time, this was not "spirit" in the religious sense, but a subtle, warm vapor (pneuma) that traveled through the nerves to facilitate movement and sensation.</gloss></term> is also more prone to good than to evil: for every being desires its own preservation, and therefore desires goodness. No being exists that would desire its own destruction; for my creation—always an imitator of my Being—will not be that same non-being. And because virtues are the paths to life, and vices the paths to death, the former are according to nature and are voluntary; the latter are against nature and are involuntary, unless someone mistakes evil for good. For no will is directed toward evil for its own sake.
>
> To prevent you from doing this, I grant you an infallible light. Indeed, I have poured out certain drops from the fountain of my delight—in which your ultimate happiness <note>original: "beatitudo"</note> will be fulfilled—into your labors. However, nothing is more laborious than the preservation of the individual and the species through food and sexual love <note>original: "venerem"</note>, managed against mortality. Therefore, pleasure in these things is a foretaste of a useful and medicinal good, not the final fulfillment of something to be enjoyed for its own sake. So it is in other things, but here it is felt more vehemently.
>
> Therefore, you must be careful not to place the "highest good" in the medicine and in the drop—which should be placed in the fountain—by enjoying what should only be used, and using what should be enjoyed. <note>original: "fruentes utendis & utentes fruendis"; this is a classic philosophical distinction: some things are "tools" (to be used) and only God is the "end" (to be enjoyed).</note>
>
> Therefore, look [it says] upon the love of me, and then of yourself for my sake. For this will be the leader of right actions in all things. Toward others, whatever you honestly wish for yourself, do also to them; and what you do not wish for yourself, do not wish or do to them. Love all things for my sake. But if you place the love of fragile goods after my love...

<meta>catchword: fragile [gilium]</meta>

It emphasizes the "Golden Rule" and the natural inclination of all beings toward self-preservation and goodness.</summary>

The previous text established that the "animal spirit" (the physical breath of life) is naturally inclined toward good, provided the soul governs it. Here, the text warns of the physiological and spiritual ruin that follows when the soul abandons divine love for fear and sensory appetite.</meta>

...and if you loosen your appetite from the bridle of the law of love <note>original: "legis amoris"</note>, you will put on the bridle of hateful fear; you will leap over the rule; nature will be perverted. The mind will become the handmaid of the body; an imbalance will arise in the body, as its heat rebels—shifting more or less away from its proper measure—and bringing about various sicknesses. The spirits <term>spirits<gloss>Specifically the "animal spirits" or pneuma—the subtle, warm vapors that early modern thinkers believed traveled through the nerves to carry out the soul's commands.</gloss></term> will become impure and sooty, or thick and stupid; and the organs, poorly fashioned by them, will become dysfunctional. From this, you will pass into ignorance of yourself and of the nature of those things; you will understand neither what you are, nor your origin, nor your immortality.

For it will rarely happen that these spirits remain pure and clear, balanced, and precisely like my own Ideas <term>Ideas<gloss>In the Platonic and Augustinian tradition used by Campanella, these are the eternal, perfect patterns in the mind of God from which all things are modeled.</gloss></term>. Then you will know by experience the virtues and the vices, good and evil, and the death of your body—which is rebellious to you. Because the body is deprived of my help, from which you will separate yourself, you will not be able to preserve it in its joined structure without it falling apart. The soul heard a speech of this kind; but what it did immediately afterward, history teaches.

### CHAPTER I.

The Mind <note>original: "Mens". Here, Campanella refers to the Divine Mind or Reason acting through nature.</note>, driven by the stings of primary necessity—since no one was sufficient unto themselves to protect their life from external and internal evils, nor to propagate the species—joined humans into what is essentially a single body. Within this body, some should rule and others be ruled: some should devote their efforts to the knowledge of things to be done <term>knowledge of things to be done<gloss>This refers to the "active" or "practical" sciences, like law, ethics, and governance, which guide human behavior.</gloss></term>, while others perform the actions themselves, all for the common good. Through countless mutual duties, arising from countless needs, they might help one another in life, directed toward that end for which God, the Lord of lords, created man in an ordered fashion.

<summary>This page introduces Campanella’s political theory, arguing that human society is not accidental but a necessary creation of the Divine Mind to ensure survival and the common good. He establishes the "social body" as a structure where different roles—rulers and workers—function together like organs in a living being.</summary>

2. Furthermore, since no one exercises political rule over themselves alone, and since one person can scarcely rule over another in isolation, it follows that Dominion <note>original: "Dominium". In this context, it refers to sovereignty or the rightful power to govern.</note> requires the unity of many together; this is what is called a Community, a Polity, and a City-State.

3. Natural dominion possesses a natural community; violent dominion possesses a violent one. In the former, the soul rules the body, its parts, and its emotions. In the latter, the emotions occasionally rule over reason.

4. All things that are joined by a mutual natural good are associated by nature. Therefore:
*   The first community or unity is that of male and female.
*   The second is of parents and children.
*   The third is of one family—that is, many parents and children, along with rational and irrational instruments, such as servants, oxen, and dogs. <note>Campanella follows the Aristotelian tradition here, classifying servants as "rational instruments" of the household.</note>
*   The fourth is of several families in one village.
*   The fifth is of several villages in one city.
*   The sixth is of several cities in one province.
*   The seventh is of several provinces in one kingdom.
*   The eighth is of several kingdoms under one Empire.
*   The ninth is of several Empires in various climates under one Monarchy.
*   The tenth is of all humans under the human species and the Papacy.

5. Community and dominion are more in accordance with nature when the "good" is shared among everyone. They are "violent" (unnatural) when the good is shared with only a few, or one, or none at all. This tends to happen more often when men perform duties for which they are naturally ill-suited, and when they act for their own sake rather than for the community.

6. The most powerful community is bound together by the good of souls; the second, by the good of bodies; the third, by the good of fortunes. A wise Religion creates and preserves the community of souls: it is the soul of the polity and the defense of natural justice, both toward God and toward men. The community of bodies is formed by living together. The community of fortunes is formed by trade.

7. The community of Religion holds the first and most tightly-bound place of unity, because it joins even the most diverse nations. By this bond, the Supreme Roman Pontiff <note>The Pope.</note> commands Asian, African, European, and American Christians.

8. The community of bodies holds the second place in binding people together. By this means, the King of the Turks <note>The Sultan of the Ottoman Empire.</note> rules over Muslims <note>original: "Machometanis".</note>, Jews, and Christians

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>1</margin>
By nature, the one who is superior in virtue <term>virtue: "virtus" in Latin implies not just moral goodness but also functional excellence, strength, and skill</term> commands; by nature, the one who is inferior or devoid of virtue serves. Where the opposite occurs, dominion is violent.

2. Excellence in political matters is based either on the virtue of the soul, or of the body, or of both.

3. He rules best who excels in both, like Caesar; second, he who excels by soul alone, like Ulysses; third, he who excels by body alone, like Ajax. <note>Campanella uses these classical figures as archetypes: Caesar for the complete leader, Ulysses for the cunning strategist, and Ajax for the physically powerful warrior.</note>

<note>Completing the sentence from the previous page:</note> ...power, soldiers are added; for wisdom, the law is added. In the aforementioned communities, either one man dominates, like the King in France; or several, like the patricians in Venice; or everyone, as among the Swiss and the Athenians; or one and many together, as in Rome formerly with the Senate and the Roman people; or one, many, and everyone together, as in Sparta <note>original: "Lacedæmone"</note> with the King, the Ephors <note>Ancient Spartan magistrates who shared power with the kings.</note>, and the people.

6. However, he is truly said to rule in whose hand the supreme power of the republic is held.

7. <term>Supreme power: "Summa potestas" or sovereignty.</term> is the power of the sword, of death, and of life. It resides in the person to whom the final appeal in capital cases is brought.

8. Therefore, the republic of the Romans belonged to all—that is, it was a "popular" government. For the final appeal belonged to the people, even though the senate and consuls presided. The Venetian republic belongs to the "many" <note>An aristocracy.</note>, although a Doge <note>The "Dux," the ceremonial head of Venice.</note> co-rules. The Church belongs to "one" <note>A monarchy.</note>, although the senate of Cardinals dominates together with the Pope.

9. Rule by one good person is called a **Kingdom and Monarchy**; rule by one bad person, a **Tyranny** etc. Rule by many good people is an **Aristocracy**; by bad people, an **Oligarchy**. Rule by all who are good is a **Polity**; by bad, a **Democracy**. <note>Campanella follows the classical Greek definitions where "Democracy" was often used to mean "mob rule," while "Polity" was the healthy version of rule by the people.</note>

10. The duties of those who rule are to teach, defend, nourish, and justify <note>To provide justice and legal order.</note> their subjects. Since a King cannot perform these alone, he does the first through priests and teachers and laws; the second through soldiers; the third through farmers, craftsmen, and merchants; the fourth through judges, who judge according to the law. These, then, are the parts of the republic. Conversely, the people owe the prince two things: namely, reverence and obedience, so long as he commands what is good or indifferent <note>original: "indifferentia" - matters of administrative rule that are neither inherently moral nor immoral.</note>.

11. *Whoever reaches the throne through virtue rules not for their own benefit, but for that of their subjects.* These are called Kings, because they place the public good before their private good. From this a tyrant is often born, as Cambyses was from Cyrus; a tyrant is one who places his own convenience before the public good. Against a tyrant, people conspire— <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page. The word is completed on the next page as "conspirant."</note>

12. Conflicts between the commoners and the nobles strengthen the republic if they arise from a rivalry for honor, and if the common people win in such a way that they can attain the honors of the nobles and share in their virtues; this turned out prosperously for Rome. But if the commoners win in a way that drags the nobles down to their own lower customs, the republic is greatly diminished; this happened unhappily in Florence. If the nobility wins, however, the state suddenly becomes tyrannical, as happened once in Genoa, and they collapse. Furthermore, conflicts regarding the changing of religion, or the redistribution of wealth <note>original: "fortunarum participio"</note>, always ruin republics, especially where only a few emerge as victors. However, in Flanders, Holland, and Friesland, because of the diversity of religion, they have not yet been consumed in the way that has happened to the French, Poles, and English; this is because they are forced to stand in harmony by the hostile arms of the Spaniards, and the common people won a useful victory, becoming participants in both religious doctrine and government. This covers internal changes.

13. As for external changes: occupation by foreign masters, plague, flood, and universal fire change republics so much that they begin a new age. This happens perhaps by the power of "fatal numbers"—namely, the numbers seven and nine <note>Campanella refers to a common Renaissance belief in "climacteric" years or periods based on numerology (7 and 9) that signaled major historical shifts.</note>—as one may observe in the deaths of republics and great monarchies; or when adverse constellations occur under these specific numbers...

### CHAPTER III.

**P**RINCES are set in authority either by election, or by lots, or by lot and election together, like the Doge <note>original: "Dux"</note> of the Venetians; or by wealth <note>original: "censu"</note> and succession, like the Carthaginian senators; or by election, lot, and succession, like the governors of the Grisons <note>The Grisons or Graubünden (in modern Switzerland) was known for its complex, communal system of governance involving various leagues.</note>; or by all these methods, as with the Ragusans <note>The Republic of Ragusa (modern-day Dubrovnik) utilized a highly complex system of drawing lots and voting to prevent any one family from seizing power.</note>, they are varied and mixed. Which of these methods is best?

2. The rule <note>original: "Dominium"</note> of one is better in time of war; in time of peace, the rule of many is better. For this reason, the Romans would appoint a dictator when dangerous wars pressed upon them, so that he might provide for needs suddenly and without the delay of many councils; but in peace, they had two consuls with the senate, and so on.

3. Nevertheless, the rule of one good man <note>original: "principatus"</note> is always better than that of many or all good men. But the rule of one bad man is worse than that of many or all bad men; however, it lasts for a shorter time. Therefore, I have taught in my book *The Monarchy of the Messiah* <note>Campanella’s work *De Monarchia Messiae*, which argues that a single world-leader (the Pope) should hold both spiritual and temporal power to ensure peace.</note> that the wickedness of one in power is to be preferred over the wickedness of many or all.

<page-num>373</page-num>
<header>OF POLITICS CHAPTER III.</header>
<sig>Aaa 3</sig>

4. God alone is the Lord in the absolute sense according to nature; for He possesses absolute power over both the substance and the use of all things. His will, being most wise, is a law unto itself, and it transcends the specific types and categories of things. Man, by contrast, is a Lord only in a relative sense <note>original: "secundum quid," a scholastic term meaning "in a certain respect" rather than absolutely.</note>; for his will cannot be a law unless it is regulated and modified by God's law, whether natural or positive <note>Natural law refers to moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature; positive law refers to specific statutes decreed by authorities.</note>. Therefore, man is not the lord of his own life, nor of his subjects, nor of his fortunes in terms of their core substance, but only in terms of their use, and for the purpose prescribed by God. Otherwise, he is bound to make restitution—at least to God—and to suffer punishment. Nature demonstrates this, as she rewards the sober with health and punishes the drunken with gout <note>original: "podagra." Campanella often uses physical health as a metaphor for moral and political order.</note>. And since a prince is of the same species as his subjects, he shall lead as a head among members, not rule as a master over slaves; as we have proven in our writings on ethics.

5. He cannot rightly rule the human species who does not know how to rightly rule a monarchy; nor a monarchy, unless he understands a kingdom; nor a kingdom, if he is ignorant of a province; nor a province, a city; nor a city, the villages; nor a village, a family. Furthermore, he will not rule a family well who does not know how to rule himself rightly; nor can he rule himself unless reason dominates and the will and appetites serve it. Nor can reason rule unless it is itself ruled by God, so that it obeys Him. Therefore, without a divine rule, no one is a prince truly according to nature, but should rather be called a "scourge of God" <note>original: "flagellum Dei," a title famously associated with Attila the Hun, implying a ruler sent by God to punish a people's sins.</note> and an executioner. But according to the divine rule, he is not an absolute lord, but a Leader and shepherd of the people, and a vicar of God the Lord, through whom kings reign.

6. A good prince, therefore, ought to excel his subjects in virtue as much as a shepherd excels his flock; for a shepherd is of a higher species than the sheep. However, one human does not surpass another in species unless he is divine and full of God, or an angel, or God made visible, such as Christ.

7. Of princes, one type is the **shepherd**, who labors for the good of the flock toward God; another is the **mercenary**, who does all things for his own convenience; and another is the **wolf**, who considers that everything must be done even to the detriment of the flock for his own sake.

8. Rightly, therefore, and according to nature, **wisdom** alone holds dominion;

...not sophistical, but philosophical; not eremitical <note>original: "eremitica," referring to the secluded life of a hermit or monk. Campanella argues for a "civil" or socially engaged philosophy.</note>, but civil; not opposed to God, but subordinate to Him.

9. Naturally, the male rules over the female, the father over his children, the elder over the youth, the strong over the weak, and the wise teacher over ignorant students. 10. Nature produces men who are powerful in intellect rather than in body, so that they may be priests, philosophers, and advisors to the republic <term>respublica: literally "the public thing," referring to the state or commonwealth.</term>; those who are agile and robust in body, and spirited, for military service; those dull in intellect but strong in hand, for agriculture; the heavy and robust for cavalry service; those industrious with their hands for weaving and crafts; those quick of tongue and learned for embassies and public assemblies; others skilled for trade; the just for the courts; those weak in both body and mind, that they might be servants and instruments of their betters; and those strong in both body and intellect, that they might be leaders, kings, and commanders of the military.

11. Therefore, the best republic is one where individuals devote themselves to those duties and crafts for which they were born naturally suited. For then, reason and wisdom return. But the worst is where individuals are occupied with functions contrary to their native aptitude; for then fortune and chance—that is, the power of ignorance—rule. A mixed state exists where some take up functions natural to them, and others do not.

12. Where, from an early age, people are selected for the functions and honors natural to them by wise and not fearsome <note>Campanella stresses that education should be guided by wisdom rather than intimidation.</note> public teachers, there the republic will be most powerful and flourishing. But where chance distributes functions—for instance, that one becomes king simply because he was born to a king, or a magistrate because they are the children of nobles, or because they are the children or friends of rulers, or because they are rich, or because they buy honors, etc., and not because they are good and wise, there the republic always falls into ruin, either suddenly or gradually.

13. It collapses even faster where a dowry and equality of wealth join a man and woman in marriage, rather than an equal value of bodies and minds from which the best offspring might be hoped, as the followers of Pythagoras <note>The Pythagoreans were ancient Greek philosophers who believed in social harmony and regulated living; Campanella often cites them when discussing "eugenics" or the scientific improvement of the human race.</note> advise.

14. Corruption also reigns more through the haphazard generation... <note>The text ends mid-sentence, leading into a discussion on how unplanned breeding leads to the physical and moral decay of society.</note>

However, those who act as mediators between God and men are to be esteemed as the more divine part of the republic, such as the wisest and most proven religious men.

## *On laws and customs, and Political Reason, which they call "Reason of State."*

### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>1</margin> So that the best people may be born and then applied to those functions for which they were born, and so that internal and external evils may be avoided—[since a prince, through impotence, ignorance, or willful neglect, is often distracted from what ought to be done; and there is no one who does not sin unless it is the Spirit of the Lord working all things through him]—the community always stands in need of law.

2. Just as virtue is the private law of the individual, so law is the public virtue of the community. Therefore, since virtue is the rule of the actions and affections <note>original: "affectionum," referring to the passions or emotions.</note> of the individual man, ordained by the decree of a powerful and willing reason for the sake of the highest private good: so law is the rule of the affections...

<summary>Campanella concludes his critique of social decay caused by idle nobility and poor education before defining Law as "public virtue." He argues that because even rulers are prone to error, a community must be guided by objective laws rather than individual whims.</summary>

...and of public actions, promulgated by the decree of the common reason of one who is powerful and willing, for the sake of the supreme common good.

3. The **highest good** <note>original: "summum bonum," the ultimate goal or purpose of human existence and society.</note> is preservation, whether private or common, which is sought as much as possible through things that preserve and by the expulsion of things that destroy. Simply put, to "preserve" is to make something eternal. Therefore, the supreme private and public good must be procured from the eternal **Supreme Being**; however, in a secondary sense, it is procured from others instrumentally and through the arrangements of the rules of reason.

4. For this reason, no one can make law except for the **Republic**, in which resides common reason and consensus; or the **wisest men**, to whom the common reason is entrusted by the republic—such as **Solon**, **Lycurgus**, and **Numa** <note>Solon of Athens, Lycurgus of Sparta, and Numa Pompilius of Rome were the legendary "founding" lawgivers of classical antiquity.</note>; or **God**, who cares for all and is the highest reason; or he to whom God delegates his authority, such as **Moses**; or those who are chosen by the republic through divine authority, such as the **Pope**. Elsewhere I have spoken of **Minos** and **Muhammad**, who, driven by their own actions or by a demon, pretended they were sent by God, acting as "apes" <note>original: "simii," meaning they were mere imitators or false mimes of the true prophets.</note> of His true messengers and of Moses.

5. The **eternal law** is the first law, by which God thought out, created, governed, and changes all things; through it, He leads even variable things to their ends in an invariable way. From this is derived the **natural law** <note>original: "lex naturalis," the moral order believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason.</note> inserted into the souls of men and into the entire nature of things, which is the "art" of God and its guiding principle. It cannot be violated except by God acting as Lord, not as a legislator. From the natural law is derived the **law of nations** <note>original: "lex gentium," the customary law shared by all civilized peoples, such as the sanctity of embassies or the right to self-defense.</note>, which is common to all human beings. From the law of nations, **civil positive law** <note>original: "lex positiva civilis," laws specifically enacted by human governments for a particular state.</note> is deduced: and insofar as it agrees with nature, it is invariable; but insofar as it is created for present necessities, it can and sometimes ought to be changed. God also gave a positive law when men were deriving law from nature in a wicked and erroneous way. This is invariable where it contains natural right, but changeable where it concerns our specific needs: just as the **Law of Moses** remains forever in the **Ten Commandments**, but not in the prohibition of pig’s meat, which was commanded to them so as not to encourage leprosy <note>In the 17th century, it was a common medical belief that pork consumption contributed to skin diseases like leprosy in hot climates.</note>. However, no one can change laws except the one who brought them, or the one who holds his place and authority for this purpose.

<meta>The catchword "tenet" indicates the next page begins with "tenet" (holds/occupies), finishing the sentence regarding who holds the authority to change laws.</meta>

<summary>Campanella defines the hierarchy of law, moving from the Eternal Law of God down to human Civil Law, and identifies who possesses the legitimate authority to act as a lawgiver.</summary>

# ON POLITICS, CH. IV.

...holds. For neither the Pope nor a king can grant exemptions from **divine law**—even positive divine law—but only from papal and royal laws, each from their own.

6. **Political reason**, which they call **Reason of State**, was in the past called **Equity** and <term>epieikeia <note>Greek: ἐπιείκεια. In legal philosophy, this refers to the "spirit" of the law. It allows a ruler or judge to deviate from the literal wording of a law to ensure justice in specific, unforeseen circumstances.</note></term>. It goes beyond the literal word of a law promulgated in writing or by voice, but it does not violate its spirit and purpose. This is because it only annuls, invalidates, interprets, or grants exemptions for the sake of a better and common good. An example of this is when the Roman Senate granted life to **Fabius Vibulianus**, who by law ought to have died, and to **Horatius**, who had killed the three **Curiatii** brothers <note>A reference to the legendary battle between the Roman Horatii and the Alban Curiatii; the surviving Horatius killed his sister for mourning the enemy, a capital crime for which he was pardoned due to his service to the state.</note> for the sake of the Roman Empire.

However, the modern **"Reason of State"** is an invention of tyrants designed to mimic equity. These rulers believe they can violate all laws—not only their own but even divine ones—just to acquire or preserve their own small territories. But there is a massive difference between **Reason of State** and **Equity**: the latter looks toward the true public good, while the former looks only toward the apparent, private good of the ruler. To hide this name—which has been recognized as impious ever since **Machiavelli** played the part of **Ahithophel** <note>original: "Achitophelizauit." Ahithophel was a biblical counselor who betrayed King David. Campanella frames Machiavelli not as a wise teacher, but as a treacherous advisor whose "wisdom" leads to ruin.</note>—princes now call it the "reason of good governance." These names can contain a good meaning, even if they were coined by the wicked.

For example: **Cleonymus** <note>A Spartan leader who attempted to reform the state by force.</note> killed the **Ephors** <note>The high-ranking overseers of the Spartan constitution.</note> in Lacedaemon by the **Right Reason of State**; but the King of the Turks does not act by right reason when he kills his brothers. For although the latter might seem to do so for the common good <note>A reference to the Ottoman practice of fratricide to prevent succession wars.</note>, it is done against the law of God, and since other ways could be found to prevent them from seizing the kingdom, he acts irrationally.

7. A **good prince** does not need this "Reason of State," because he protects himself through his own perpetual integrity. If anyone rises against him, he has all the people as his helpers, just as **David** did when he was deprived of his kingdom by his son. But not even a million Machiavellian arts can protect a **bad prince**, for he is hateful to the people and to God, the King of all. He who is out of harmony with the **First Cause** <note>A philosophical term for God, the ultimate source of all order and existence.</note> relies on a deceptive and fleeting success. In this same way, **Cesare Borgia** (Valentino) lost both his life and his state despite the most "provident" mastery of Machiavelli. Machiavellians are always caught in their own cunning, because they lack knowledge of divine and celestial things, and they think that...

# FRIAR TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

...[they believe] they can measure all things and foresee everything by their own prudence.

8. Laws are best if they are brief, easy to understand, few in number, and suited to the customs of the people and the public good. Tyrannical laws are numerous, obscure, and difficult—functioning like many snares—useful only to one person or a few; they are not adapted to public customs or benefits, but serve to ensure that the few who authored them are neither challenged nor removed.

9. Where laws are frequently changed, it indicates the imminent ruin of the state; as was once discovered in Florence <note>Campanella frequently cites the political instability of the Florentine Republic as a cautionary tale of "instability" in governance.</note>.

10. Where there are more punitive laws than instructive ones, they provide evidence of a depraved regime. The law of Jesus our God is the best, if one considers all its aspects.

11. The functions of law are: to command what is good, to forbid what is evil, and to permit what is indifferent <note>original: "indifferentia." In moral philosophy, these are actions that are neither inherently good nor bad, like choosing which clothes to wear.</note>.

12. The incentives of law are reward and punishment.

13. The guardians of the law are **honor** (that is, for those who observe it), **love** (that is, for the benefit that flows to everyone from its observance), and **fear** (that is, of the punishments to be inflicted on violators). He who applies these three guardians to the laws in the reverse order <note>Meaning a ruler who relies on fear first, rather than honor or love.</note> judges wickedly. Indeed, he who does not establish all the aforementioned guardians is a weak legislator, ignorant, a tyrant, or something similar.

14. Where something that was once good becomes harmful, it must be prohibited. Where an evil helps—provided it is a penalty and not a sin—it must be commanded. Where something naturally indifferent becomes bad or good for the state, it can still be commanded or prohibited. Classify the superfluous among the harmful.

15. **Divine law prohibits all vices and evils, whether internal or external, and commands all good things; it alone makes men <term>simply good <note>original: "optimos simpliciter." In Scholastic philosophy, "simpliciter" means "absolutely" or "without qualification," as opposed to being good only in one specific role, like a "good thief" or a "good soldier."</note></term>. Human law prohibits only external evils and commands at least those good things that benefit the state and communal life; it makes good citizens, not absolutely good men. Nevertheless, princes ought to be absolutely good, since they are the light and the law for others.**

16. The "light" <note>Referring to the Prince/Ruler mentioned in the previous point.</note> ought to establish equality, which is the nourisher of the state, and remove inequality, which consumes it. For the very poor are usually thieves, treacherous, perjurers, ignorant, and the instruments of wicked rich men—

[instru]ments: indeed, those who are very rich are proud, luxurious, unlearned, and insolent. Those who are very clever are the most fickle; those who are very dull-witted are slaves by choice. Those of moderate temperament are stable in a kingdom. The Florentine Republic was always the most unstable of all due to the subtlety of their intellects <note>Campanella argues that the Florentines were "too clever for their own good," leading to constant political maneuvering and instability.</note>. The Venetian Republic is the most stable of all, due to its moderate sturdiness <note>original: "crassitiem." In this context, it implies a lack of over-refined "subtlety," suggesting a more solid, reliable character.</note>.

**17.** Good custom is a second law, which preserves the republic more than the law itself. Five customs made Rome—the leader of republics—magnificent, as witnessed by Cato in the writings of Sallust <note>referring to the Roman historian Sallust’s account of the conspiracy of Catiline, where Cato the Younger lists these virtues.</note>:
1. Public wealth.
2. Private poverty <note>In the Roman ideal, individuals lived modestly while the state was rich.</note>.
3. Just rule abroad.
4. A free spirit in speaking at home.
5. Being subject to neither fear nor greed.

Venice observes all of these by law, except that it is subject to fear—not in its internal deliberations, but from external forces, because of the defect of having no military of its own. Furthermore, due to a defect in the first custom (public wealth), the Genoese are not masters of the sea or the New World, etc. Due to a defect in the fifth (greed/fear), they are almost like servants to foreign kings. Due to a defect in the third (just rule abroad), the French could never establish an empire outside of France. In this regard, the Spanish also err in part, ruling everywhere severely and with much ceremony, showing no respect for the customs of the local region. Because of a defect in the fourth (a free spirit in speaking), the Florentine Republic collapsed.

**18.** Good rulers introduce good customs; bad rulers introduce bad ones—and women do as well. But no custom prevails over divine, natural, or rational law. The "law of nations" is simply the custom of the entire human species.

**19.** For Northern people <note>original: "Borealibus."</note>, who are fierce by nature, a rigid rule is not suitable, but rather a permissive one, since they can hardly endure the order of a republic. For this reason, among them, anarchies, republics, and princedoms usually exist only through election; as the Tartars, Muscovites, Poles, Swedes, Germans, and Swiss have shown. And if a king is found there anywhere by succession, he has no more power than those who are chosen by election among us; demanding small taxes, with much liberty for the people, and with small power for himself; although, since Roman culture was introduced to them, they have begun to live a little more strictly. But for Southerners <note>original: "Australibus."</note>, especially those living under the tropics, only despotic rule and severe laws are suitable, since they are weak in physical strength but strong in cunning. For this reason, they have always been addicted to ceremonious superstitions. But under the equator, of princedoms...

### On Lawgivers.
### CHAPTER V.

A lawgiver <term>Legislator; one who establishes the fundamental legal and moral framework of a society.</term> is one who founds a new empire, usually under new laws, religion, arms, rites, and auspices <note>original: "auspiciisque." Ancient Roman ceremonial signs used to determine the will of the gods before an undertaking.</note>: such as the good Moses, and the perverse Muhammad <note>Campanella, writing from a 17th-century Catholic perspective, contrasts the Biblical prophet with the founder of Islam.</note>. Therefore, a lawgiver is either God, like Christ; or God’s messenger, like Moses; or a most shrewd politician who imitates these, such as Minos, Osiris, Jupiter, Muhammad, Zamolxis <note>A legendary social and religious reformer of the Getae (a Thracian people).</note>, and their like, who feigned that they were sent by God in order to capture the faith and love of the people. For a lawgiver ought to be most praised, most wise, most divine, and most revered.

**2.** Truly every craftsman, because he is wise, is a king within his own art. For even a doctor commands a sick king; and a sailor, during a storm, tells priests, leaders, and princes: "You sit here," "You stand there," etc. Therefore, he who is to give laws to many men of every rank must be skilled in the arts and functions of them all—or at least in their purposes—such as the benefits and harms they can bring to the republic. He must be able to expel the superfluous and the harmful, and retain and moderate the useful and necessary, lest they degenerate into wickedness. In this way, Plato expelled from his republic those lying and lustful poets who abuse the praise of good men to exalt the wicked; while Moses expelled false prophets, painters of divine images, tavern-keepers, and prostitutes, etc. He must also thoroughly know the customs and temperaments of regions based on the heavens <note>astrological influences</note> and the earth, as well as the fortunes and misfortunes that usually befall them,

<summary>Campanella defines the role of the lawgiver as a master craftsman of society who must understand all professions and the influence of geography on human character. He distinguishes between divinely inspired lawgivers like Christ and Moses and those who merely mimic divine authority to gain political power.</summary>

...[mitigated], such as floods, fires, leprosy, famine, etc.

<margin>||</margin> 3. Human lawgivers <term>Legislatores; those who establish the fundamental legal and moral framework of a society.</term> ought to possess wisdom hardly less than divine lawgivers, since they must have the power to change all things except religion, as did Lycurgus and Solon. However, they have the authority to reform or purify religion, but not to abolish it entirely; the Pope usually performs the former task when he drives out creeping abuses.

4. The founders of new orders within the Christian religion, such as Benedict, Augustine, Francis, etc., are also lawgivers. But these men receive their rules from God and His law, and not from us.

5. Among virtues, the first praise is owed to the lawgiver. The second to sacred rulers. The third to secular rulers. The fourth to counselors. The fifth to judges. The sixth to soldiers. The seventh to artisans. Among these, the most noble in mountainous states are the shepherds, as among the Swiss <note>original: "Heluetios"</note> and the Scythians; in the plains, the farmers, as in Egypt; and in maritime regions, the sailors and merchants. Because these latter provide the greatest utility, manage money, and gather knowledge from many nations, they have almost always held the primary roles. However, where other arts—especially superfluous ones—are prioritized over these, harm and ruin are imminent.

6. A divine lawgiver holds the Idea <term>Idea; in the Platonic sense, a perfect archetype or blueprint.</term> of his own republic in the celestial court. A human lawgiver finds it in the governance of the universe and the human body. Those who follow them as less wise successors take their Idea from the "idealized" republics of the best lawgivers, whether expressed in action, such as the Republic of Lycurgus; or in writing, as from the Republic of Moses—from whom everyone should learn.

7. Man and woman, the elements of the republic, consist of mind, body, and external goods. The Republic has wisdom and religion for <note>original: "p" (pro)</note> its soul; for its body, the senate, the council, and whoever performs a useful duty for the state; for external goods, it has soldiers, mercenaries, and auxiliaries, as well as foreign merchants and traveling artisans who come for the sake of the common service; for its spirits <note>In the medical and philosophical tradition of the time, "spirits" (spiritus) were subtle fluids that connected the soul to the body and enabled movement and sensation.</note>, it has the law; for its eyes, wise investigators of the sciences; for its ears, scouts and merchants; for its tongue, preachers, teachers, and ambassadors; for its hands, its own soldiers; for its feet...

# THE WORKS OF THOMAS CAMPANELLA

There are also "purgers" of the city appointed for the year; and for sustaining the goods of the body and soul (that is, virtues, sciences, health, strength, and beauty), the lawgiver possesses fortunes <term>Fortunae; external goods, including wealth, property, and social status.</term>, which is to say: servants, crops, estates, and money. A lawgiver should consider these things above all.

But the senate, the law, and religion command the soldiers, artisans, and the rest in their proper proportions.

9. The good of the soul must be desired and provided for in the first place; in the second, the good of the body; in the third, the good of fortunes. Likewise, a man ought to value the good of his own soul more than the soul of a friend or fellow citizen; and similarly, his own bodily health and fortune more than the body and fortune of a friend. However, the good of a friend's soul must be valued more than one's own external fortunes. For instance, when you would lose ten ducats in wealth, but a friend would gain a hundred, you ought to prefer his gain to your own loss: because he can compensate both you and the republic from that growing profit. For all the goods of others belong to us in some way. But when this order is not observed, all republics begin to fail; where it is observed more, a greater reason governs; where less, chance has more power. Therefore, you must be willing to lose a little of the good of your soul, body, or fortunes to gain much for your friends and the republic; as Gerard, the brother of Saint Bernard <note>Gerard of Clairvaux (d. 1138), brother of the famous Cistercian abbot Bernard; he was known for his practical management of the monastery which allowed his brother to focus on spiritual matters.</note>, used to observe. Otherwise, friendship would never reign, but only greed for oneself would rule in every individual. According to these rules, the law must be established.

### *On Colonies and the City.*
## CHAPTER VI.

1. He who rules over regions of different climates ought to give them different laws: or, he should give them the same laws only after an exchange of inhabitants has been made through mutual colonies and transmigrations. Thus, the Romans led colonies from their own people into Germany to keep the empire safe, and by the example of these colonies, they accustomed the Germans to their laws, to which they were previously unaccustomed.

<meta>This page transitions from the general hierarchy of goods (soul, body, and external fortune) discussed on the previous page to the practical application of these principles in state-building. Campanella here focuses on the establishment and physical placement of colonies and the classification of their inhabitants.</meta>

->ON POLITICS, CHAPTER 6.<-

2. Colonies are to be formed from the citizens of the empire's own mother city <note>original: "metropolis"</note>, or from neighboring people, such as the Romans and Latins. And they ought to be placed in as many cities as are sufficient to defend the province. These cities should be the capitals of the region itself, or others newly built, when the local inhabitants <note>original: "indigenae"</note> do not at all suit the customs or interests of the new colonies. Therefore, they are placed under new auspices <note>original: "auspiciis"; refers to the formal religious and political authority under which a city is founded</note>, laws, and religions. And the fields are distributed equally according to their merit through an agrarian law <term>lex agraria; a law regulating the distribution of public land, a frequent source of political conflict in ancient Rome.</term>.

3. If the colonists are sent by a **Republic**, new cities are more rightly located atop mountains for the defense of liberty. If by a **Monarchy**, they are better placed in a plain. If the capital of the monarchy is by the sea, like Venice, it is better on the shores. If on the continent, it is better in strategic locations through which the way for providing aid may be defended.

4. Cities should be placed on the banks of rivers, sea shores, and in plains so that they may grow large; there, the necessities of life are easily brought together, and foreign guests engage in trade. But on mountains and cliffs, they are more conveniently built for the sake of protecting liberty and law, and so that virtue is not weakened <note>original: "non eneruanda"; suggesting that easy living in the plains makes a population soft.</note>. Moreover, one must take into account healthy waters, the air, the winds, and the orientation toward the sunrise and other quarters of the heavens.

5. The number of inhabitants is to be divided into **Rectors** <note>original: "Rectores"</note> [that is, priests and judges], **Defenders** [that is, soldiers and leaders], **Artisans**, and the **Providers** of the republic <note>original: "nutritios"</note> [that is, farmers, shepherds, etc.]. And there should be as many as are sufficient for defense and as the land can nourish. Therefore, it is also necessary for the natives to migrate away from there if the land, because of them, is not sufficient to feed your defenders, or if they are a hindrance to defense.

6. Whether a larger or smaller number of defenders should be placed—just as with governors and artisans—the nature of the region will determine: whether it is flat or mountainous, near or distant, bordering enemies or remote, northern or southern, etc.

7. We might perhaps sufficiently prescribe for a colony as many shepherds and livestock as are required for wool for their clothing and milk for their sustenance...

**Vocabulary:** Colonies, Mother city, Agrarian law, Republic, Monarchy, Rectors, Defenders, Artisans, Providers, Natives.

## On the instruments for acquiring and preserving empires, and their use and comparison.

### CHAPTER VII.

1. There are three instruments for acquiring, preserving, and governing kingdoms: the **Tongue**, the **Sword**, and the **Treasury**. For the tongue is the instrument of religion and wisdom, that is, of the goods of the soul; the Sword is the instrument of the body and its goods. The Treasury pertains more to fortune, which serves the body and soul secondarily. However, the true instruments are the Tongue and the Sword.

2. Those who use the sword alone, basing their power upon it, quickly lose their empire: such as Tamerlane <note>The Turco-Mongol conqueror Timur (1336–1405)</note>, Attila <note>Leader of the Huns</note>, Brennus <note>The Gallic chieftain who famously sacked Rome in the 4th century BCE</note>, and generally the Northern peoples. Those, however, who use the tongue alone, quickly acquire power over souls; and afterwards, they gradually add political power. Yet they suffer the loss of their own lives for the truth they preach, and their successors establish political sovereignty. Thus the prophets and many holy preachers in the kingdoms of the infidels—and in modern times the Jesuits in the province of Japan—capture souls with the tongue. From there, once their princes have been converted to the faith, it will be easy to establish Spanish and Papal rule. Dominions of this kind are strong and durable, provided it is later proven that the preachers were truthful. Likewise, even when they deviate slightly from the truth, they still achieve something. Furthermore, those who [establish] a new sect in some...

...preaches it as founded on truth, the tongue acquires command by stirring up contentions between the old religion and a new sect, adapted to the taste of the people. However, this kind of command lasts little on its own. Nor do the founders willingly lay down their lives for their dogma. We have an example in the heresiarchs: who, although they acquire much at first, soon protect little, such as **John of Leiden** <note>Leader of the Anabaptist rebellion in Münster (1534–1535)</note>, and **Brother Dolcino** <note>A 13th-century Italian preacher who led a radical movement against the ecclesiastical hierarchy</note>, and **Theudas** <note>A Jewish rebel mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles who claimed to be a prophet</note>. Those, however, who preserved the dominion they gained, preserved it not by the strength of the tongue, but by the sword of those who believed in them; and they did so not so that they themselves might rule, but that the princes who were their followers in the faith might rule.

3. Those, however, who use both the **sword** and the **tongue**, found a long and durable empire. Therefore, if their tongues were truthful and they were just in both the sword and their acquisition, even if they should lose the political empire they gained, their laws nevertheless remain and pass into other nations, even those that conquered them. Thus **Moses**, equipped by God with a just sword and a truthful tongue, founded the Hebrew empire quickly and for a long duration. So much so that, although the Hebrews suffered the loss of their empire, the Mosaic religion nevertheless remained—with superstition among the Hebrews and the **Muhammadans** <note>original: "Machumetanis"</note>, and with a most excellent reformation <note>The author likely refers to the "perfection" or fulfillment of the Old Law by the New Law in Catholic theology</note> among the Christians. 

Those, however, who use the sword and a lying tongue, even if they establish a quick and long-lasting empire, nevertheless, once the empire is broken and overthrown, the law—which only the weapons of the empire protected—is abolished and extinguished. Thus **Muhammad** occupied many regions. But once his empire is destroyed, his law will be destroyed at the same time. Just as the law of **Cyrus** was destroyed, who made himself a commissioner of God to found new laws and empire; and that of **Alexander**, who for the same reason preached that he was the son of the god **Ammon**; and the laws of **Numa**, **Belus**, **Minos**, **Pythagoras**, and **Zamolxis** <note>A legendary social and religious reformer of the Getae people in Thrace</note> perished for the same reasons. The impious **Machiavelli** did not consider this.

4. He who does not know how to impose laws on the conquered quickly loses the kingdom he has gained; but he who imposes them, protects it. Thus **Charles V** lost **Tunis**, which he had occupied, and **Germany**, which he had defeated, because he did not know how to add laws and colonies. This also happened more than once to **Pyrrhus**; but not so to the **Romans**.

5. He who defends his own dominion with both the **sword** and the **tongue** preserves it better and more strongly than he who uses only a single instrument.

6. He who exercises only his intellect and his tongue will become the prey of those who exercise arms and the body. Therefore **Saturn** <note>In mythology, Saturn was associated with a peaceful Golden Age</note> and the ancient divine kings, although they were priests who protected their kingdoms solely through the fear and veneration of religion, by no means preserved their empire; instead, **Jupiter** defeated them with arms. **Perseus** the warrior took the kingdom away from **Atlas** the astrologer. **Pythagoras** <note>The Greek philosopher whose political influence in Southern Italy ended in a violent uprising against his followers</note> was also deprived of his status by others who were armed. And the **Roman Pontiffs** <note>The Popes</note>, whenever they lacked the use of arms, were frequently the prey of their enemies, and often even of their friends.

7. However, he who exercises only arms, and not the intellect and the tongue for the protection of the empire, rules weakly. For this reason, the **German Emperor** <note>The Holy Roman Emperor</note>, having populations that differ from him in religion, prevails in nothing over them. Rulers of this kind are usually the prey of those who exercise the intellect. For example, time and again Emperors have been granted or deprived of their dominion by the **Holy Pontiffs**; so too were the Hebrew kings by the **prophets**. For this reason, as **Sallust** <note>A Roman historian</note> says, the Romans never exercised the intellect without the body.

8. But he who exercises both certainly preserves his kingdom better and longer, such as the **King of the Turks** <note>The Ottoman Sultan</note>, the **King of the Abyssinians** <note>The Emperor of Ethiopia</note>, and the **Duke of the Muscovites** <note>The Tsar of Russia</note>. Mythological philosophy holds the same view, as it attributes both a book and a spear to **Pallas** <note>Athena</note>, the Goddess of Wisdom, so that she might be invincible; but to **Mars**, it attributes only arms, and the poets sing of how he was often defeated.

9. From this it has happened that the Northern peoples—because they abound in arms and in great numbers due to their ferocity and fertility—have always occupied the Southern kingdoms like swarming bees. Yet the Southern peoples, powerful in religion and intellect, have always imposed laws upon the Northerners, even when the Northerners were the victors. Thus the **Tartars** and the Northern **Turks** accepted religion and laws from the **Arabs** whom they had conquered; while the **Huns**, **Vandals**, **Lombards**, and **Goths** accepted them from the **Romans**, into whose kingdoms they had rushed.

<summary>Campanella argues that stable rule requires a balance of "the sword" (military power) and "the tongue" (intellectual and religious authority), noting that while Northern tribes often conquer through force, they are ultimately governed by the superior laws and religions of the Southern peoples they defeat.</summary>

10. Furthermore, God, as the shepherd of men, ensures that the southern peoples are fruitful in offspring and arms, while the northern peoples are fruitful in religion and science. He is accustomed to sending the former to the latter, and vice versa, grafting them into one another like trees so they may become more noble. In this way, He destroys what is ancient and punishes those populations that have begun to degenerate on both sides, rewarding each in turn based on where they excel or where they fail.

11. From the sons of **Japheth** <note>The son of Noah traditionally associated with Europeans and secular power</note> descend Empires. From **Shem** <note>The son of Noah associated with the Middle East and the origin of the Hebrew faith</note> come Priesthoods and Laws. From **Ham** <note>The son of Noah traditionally associated with Africa; in the political thought of this era, his lineage was often linked to servitude</note> come slaves and tyrants. This is evident from the division of the world into northern, middle, and southern regions, and from the prophecy of the most wise **Noah**.
