In the heat of battle, he who is first to scale the enemy walls receives, after the conflict, a **crown of grass** <note>original: "coronam gramineam"; the highest military honor in the Roman Republic, awarded to a soldier who saved an entire army or broke a siege.</note> as a mark of honor, amid military applause from the women and children. Each horseman carries one lance and two **pistols** <note>original: "piftolas"; Campanella incorporates 17th-century firearms into his utopian vision, emphasizing their power and design.</note> of strong temper hanging from the saddles; these are narrower at the mouth, by which they penetrate all iron armor. They also have a sword and a dagger. Others, the heavy cavalry, carry an **iron mace**. For if the enemy’s iron armor cannot be pierced by sword or pistol, they attack the foe with the mace, just as Achilles attacked Cygnus <note>In Greek mythology, Cygnus was invulnerable to weapons, so Achilles was forced to crush or strangle him; here the mace represents that blunt, overwhelming force.</note>; they shatter and strike them down. Two chains, six palms long, hang from the mace with iron balls at their ends; when thrown at the enemy, these wrap around the neck, pulling, striking, and throwing them to the ground.

<margin>The secret of governing a horse with the feet.</margin>
So that they may use the mace more easily, they do not hold the horse's reins with their hands, but with their feet. Specifically, the straps are crossed over the saddle blankets and the ends of the reins are tied with buckles to the stirrups, rather than to the feet. The stirrups have an iron sphere on the outside and a triangle on the inside. Therefore, by shifting the foot within the triangle and twisting it, the spheres are drawn in a circle as they hang by buckles from the stirrups. In this way, they tighten or loosen the bridle with miraculous speed, turning the horse to the left with the right foot, and to the right with the left foot. This **Secret** <note>original: "Arcanum"</note> is even unknown to the Tartars; for although they rule the reins with their feet, they do not know how to turn, pull back, and extend them through the **pulley of the stirrups**. They begin the battle with <term>arquebuses</term> <note>original: "Archibugiis"; early muzzle-loading firearms.</note>, then the phalanxes engage with spears. Next come the slingers, who are held in high esteem; they are accustomed to fighting by weaving between one another like threads in a fabric, with some advancing and others retreating in turn. They have units that strengthen the army with <term>sarissas</term> <note>original: "sarissis"; exceptionally long pikes used in ancient Macedonian-style formations.</note>, but the final danger is tested with swords.

After the war, they celebrate military triumphs in the Roman fashion, though even more beautiful. They offer prayers to God in thanksgiving, and then the General presents himself in the temple. There, the good and bad deeds of the campaign are recounted by a poet or historian who accompanied the expedition as is their custom. The **Great Prince** <note>The supreme ruler, also called 'The Sun'.</note> crowns the General with laurel, and small gifts and honors are bestowed upon each of the strenuous soldiers, who are then released from public labor for several days. However, this rest does not please them much, for they do not know how to be idle; thus, they spend their time helping their friends. Conversely, those who were defeated through their own fault or lost a victory are received with reproach. He who was the first to flee cannot escape death by any means, unless the entire army pleads for his life and each soldier takes a portion of the punishment upon himself. Yet this indulgence is rarely granted, and only when many reasons favor him. He who failed to bring timely aid to a comrade or friend is beaten with rods. He who was disobedient is handed over to be devoured by beasts within a certain <term>enclosure</term> <note>original: "vallum"; a fortified pit or arena.</note>; a staff is placed in his hand, and if he manages to overcome the lions and bears kept there—which is nearly impossible—he is received back into favor.

Conquered cities, or those that have surrendered voluntarily, immediately place all their goods into a common pool. They receive a garrison and Solar Magistrates, and gradually they become accustomed to the customs of the City of the Sun, the mistress of them all. They even send their children there to be taught, contributing nothing toward the expenses.

It would be laborious to speak of the scouts and their master, of the night watches, and of the orders and rituals both inside and outside the City; these things you can imagine for yourself. This is because all are chosen from childhood according to their inclination and the **astrological positions** <note>original: "constellationem"; the Solarians believe a person's character and destiny are heavily influenced by the stars at their birth.</note> observed in their horoscopes. For this reason, since each person works according to their own natural propensity, they perform their service well and with joy.

Guard duties <note>original: "Excubiæ"</note> are performed in the City both day and night at the four gates, and on the outermost walls of the seventh circle, upon the ramparts, towers, and internal embankments. During the day, these are manned by women; at night, however, they are manned by men. This is done so they do not grow lazy, and to be prepared for any chance occurrences. They divide their watches just as our own soldiers do, into three-hour shifts. At sunset, to the sound of drums and music <note>original: "symphoniæ"</note>, the armed guards are distributed. They use hunting as a mock war <note>original: "belli imagine"</note>, and practice games on foot and horseback in certain squares during festivals. Then follows music, and so on. They willingly forgive the faults and offenses of their enemies; and after victories, they treat them with kindness. If it has been decreed that walls must be destroyed or the leaders of the enemy executed, they carry out all these things on the very day of victory. Afterward, they never cease bestowing benefits upon them. They say that one should not fight except to make the defeated better, not to destroy them.

If a dispute arises among them concerning an injury or some other matter (for they hardly ever contend except over matters of honor), the Prince and his magistrates punish the guilty party secretly if he has broken out into harmful actions after his first impulse of anger. If the dispute was merely verbal, he awaits a decision until the time of battle, saying that anger should be vented against the enemy. He who displays more illustrious deeds in war is judged to have defended the better cause and the truth in the dispute, while the other yields. Regarding what is just, there are established punishments; nevertheless, they are never permitted to engage in a duel <term>monomachia</term> <note>From the Greek 'monomachia', meaning single combat or a duel to the death.</note>. He who claims to be the better man should prove it in public warfare.

...among them, [the more manual arts] are considered more praiseworthy, such as <term>ironworking <note>original: "Ferraria"</note></term>, architecture, and so on; and no one refuses to engage in them. Merchants from various regions of the world come to their City to buy the surplus goods of the Solarians. Indeed, the Solarian children break out in laughter when they see merchants giving away such a vast quantity of goods for a small amount of silver. But the elders do not laugh in this way. They do not wish the City to be corrupted by the foul morals of slaves and foreigners. For this reason, they conduct trade at the gates; and they sell those whom they capture in war, or they assign them to digging ditches or other laborious tasks outside the City.

<margin>Concerning the guarding of the fields.</margin>
Four columns of soldiers are perpetually sent out from the four gates to guard the fields, and with them go the laborers. The gates have roads constructed with paved sides leading all the way to the sea, so that goods may be easily transported and not hindered by <note>The OCR "luenæ" likely refers to "advenis" or "alienis," meaning strangers or travelers</note> travelers, to whom the Solarians are indeed pleasant and generous.

<margin>Concerning the showing of hospitality.</margin>
They maintain guests at public expense for three days, first washing their feet. They show them the City and its order, and deign to include them in their council and at the public table. There are men specifically appointed for the care and guarding of guests. If these guests wish to become citizens in the Republic of the Sun, they test them for a month in a rural villa and for another month in the City; afterward, they make a decision and receive them with certain ceremonies, oaths, and so forth.

Agriculture is held in the highest esteem; there is not a palm’s width of earth without fruit. They observe the winds and the propitious stars. By ingenious art, they use carts equipped with sails that are driven by the wind, even when the wind is blowing against them, through a marvelous mechanism of <term>geared wheels <note>original: "rotarum contra rotas"; likely referring to a system of counter-rotating gears that allow a vehicle to tack against the wind or utilize it more efficiently</note></term>. They do not use dung or mud to fertilize the fields, believing that the <term>seeds <note>original: "seminæ" (likely "semina")</note></term> would contract a kind of rot and, when eaten, would cause a short and weak life. Just as women who are beautiful through makeup rather than through exercise bear weak offspring, so they do not "paint" the earth with fertilizers, but instead exercise it well through labor. They also use secret remedies so that the seeds sprout quickly, multiply, and do not perish. They have a book for this work which they call the <term>Georgics <note>original: "Georgica"; a reference to Virgil’s classical poem on agriculture</note></term>. As much of the territory as is sufficient is plowed; the rest remains as pasture for the animals.

<margin>On the care of animals.</margin>
Furthermore, the noble art of breeding and raising horses, cattle, sheep, dogs, and every kind of domestic and tame animal is held in the highest esteem among them, just as it was in the time of Abraham. They are led to mate in such a way that they might breed well. Fine pictures of noble cattle, horses, and sheep are placed before them <note>This refers to the ancient theory of "maternal impression," the belief that what an animal sees at the moment of conception or during pregnancy influences the physical appearance of the offspring.</note>. They do not allow the stallions to remain with the mares in the pasture, but mate them at the opportune time in the courtyard of the country stables. They observe the sign of <term>Sagittarius <note>The Archer; traditionally associated with horses</note></term> in the horoscope, in a favorable aspect with <term>Mars and Jupiter</term>. For cattle, they look to <term>Taurus</term>; for sheep, <term>Aries</term>, and so on, according to their art. 

They keep flocks of chickens under the <term>Pleiades <note>A star cluster; the Solarians use astrology to govern the timing of all earthly activities</note></term>. Ducks and geese are led to pasture by the women near the City, which provides them with great delight. There are also specific places where the animals are penned, and where they produce cheese, butter, and other dairy products. They tend to capons and many castrated animals, as well as produce, etc. There exists a book on this matter which they call the <term>Bucolics <note>original: "Bucolica"; referring to pastoral poetry concerning the life of shepherds</note></term>. 

They abound in all things because everyone desires to be the first in labor, as work is brief and fruitful, and they are very teachable. Whoever among them is the leader of others in these various services is called "King." For they say this is the proper name for those who know, and not for the ignorant. It is wonderful to see how women and men walk together in groups, never acting outside the obedience of their King; nor do they feel any annoyance at this authority, as we do, because they recognize him as a father.

<margin>On navigation.</margin>
The art of navigation is held in very high esteem among them. They possess rafts and certain <term>triremes <note>Ancient galleys with three banks of oars, though here modified with advanced technology</note></term> that travel across the sea through a marvelous artifice without the need for oars or wind; others, however, are driven by wind and oars. They are well-acquainted with the stars and the ebb and flow of the tides. They sail for the sake of getting to know different peoples, regions, and things. They inflict injury on no one, nor do they allow it to be inflicted upon themselves. They do not go to war unless provoked. They say that the entire world will eventually come to live according to their customs; therefore, they are always examining whether there is another nation that lives a more upright or excellent life. They have treaties with the <term>Chinese <note>original: "Chinensibus"</note></term> and with many peoples of the islands and the continent—<term>Siam <note>Modern-day Thailand</note></term>, <term>Cochinchina <note>original: "Caucacinae"; a region in modern-day Vietnam</note></term>, and <term>Calicut <note>A major trading port in India</note></term>—through whom they are able to explore at will. They also possess "artificial fires" <note>Likely a reference to Greek fire or early incendiary weapons</note> for naval and land battles, as well as many secrets of strategy. For this reason, they are almost never anything but victorious.

<margin>On the life and diet of the whole Republic and its parts.</margin>
**Grandmaster:** It would be very pleasing now to hear what foods and drinks nourish them, and in what manner, and how long is their lifespan?

**Genoese Captain:** They teach that the well-being of the whole life must be consulted first, and then the well-being of its parts. Therefore, when they built the City, they placed fixed poles at the four corners of the world. In the <term>Horoscope <note>The Ascendant, or the sign rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of founding</note></term> they placed Leo, with Jupiter to the east of the Sun. They placed Mercury and Venus in Cancer, but close together, so that they might form a "satellite" <note>A group of planets accompanying the Sun</note>. They placed Mars in Sagittarius in the fifth house in a favorable aspect, strengthening the <term>Apheta <note>The "Giver of Life," a specific point in a birth chart used to determine the length of life</note></term> and the Horoscope. They placed the Moon in Taurus, which looked favorably upon Mercury and Venus, yet did not strike the Sun with a <term>quadrate <note>A 90-degree "square" aspect, traditionally considered stressful or difficult in astrology</note></term> aspect. Saturn was approaching the fourth house, yet doing no harm to the Sun or Moon, but rather stabilizing the foundations. The <term>Part of Fortune <note>A calculated mathematical point in a chart representing success and well-being</note></term> was with <term>Algol <note>A star in the constellation Perseus; though often considered unlucky, its placement in the 10th house here signifies power and authority</note></term> in the tenth house. From this, they prophesied for themselves the firmness and excellence of their dominion. Furthermore, Mercury being in a good aspect with Virgo and at its <term>apsis <note>The point in an orbit farthest from or nearest to the center</note></term>, illuminated by the Moon, cannot be evil. And since it is influenced by Jupiter, their knowledge is not "beggarly" <note>Meaning their science is robust, self-sufficient, and wealthy in truth</note>. They care little for waiting for it in Virgo or for the conjunction. They also observe these things for the sake of the strength and longevity of life...

<margin>On food.</margin>
Their food consists of meat, butter, honey, cheese, dates, and various kinds of vegetables. In the beginning, they were unwilling to slaughter animals, as it seemed cruel. However, after reflecting that it is also cruel to kill herbs—which they believe possess a degree of sensation—they realized that they would otherwise have to perish from hunger. They concluded that lower things are made for the sake of higher things, and therefore they now eat all kinds of food. Nevertheless, they do not gladly kill "fruitful" animals, such as oxen and horses. They observe a distinction between useful and harmful foods, using them according to the science of medicine. They rotate their diet in a perpetual three-part cycle: first they eat meat, second fish, and third vegetables; they then return to meat, so that nature is neither overburdened nor weakened. The elderly use more easily digestible foods and eat three times a day, but only a little. The general community eats twice a day, and children four times, as dispensed by the <term>Physician <note>original: "Physicus"; in this context, a supervisor of natural health and diet</note></term>. For the most part, they live to a hundred years, and many even to two hundred.

<margin>On drink.</margin>
In their drinking, they are most temperate. Wine is not allowed to youths until their nineteenth year, unless a medical necessity demands it. After this time, they use it diluted with water, as do the women. The elders, those in their fifties, usually do not add water. They eat whatever is most beneficial for the seasons of the year, following the advice of the <term>Chief Physician <note>original: "Protomedico"; the high official in charge of public health</note></term> who oversees this. They believe nothing is inherently harmful when it is produced by God, unless there is an abuse of excessive quantity.

<margin>Note.</margin>
For this reason, they eat fruits in the summer because they are moist, full of juice, and somewhat cool, acting against the heat and dryness of the season. In winter, they eat dry things; in autumn, they eat grapes, because they were given by God to counteract <term>black bile <note>original: "atram bilem"; in ancient medicine, the "humor" responsible for melancholy and sadness</note></term> and sorrow. They make great use of fragrances. Upon rising in the morning, everyone combs their hair and washes their face and hands in cold water. Then they chew mint, parsley, or fennel to clean their teeth, or rub them with their hands; the older men use <term>frankincense <note>original: "thus"</note></term>. They pray facing the East with a short prayer very similar to the prayer taught to us by **JESUS**. Afterward, some go out to serve the elders, others to the choir, and others to the duties of the Republic. Then they attend their first lessons, and then

<margin>On the diseases of the Solarians and their cure.</margin>
Among them, there is no <term>podagra <note>original: "podagra"; gout affecting the feet</note></term>, nor <term>chiragra <note>original: "chiragra"; gout affecting the hands</note></term>, nor <term>catarrhs <note>original: "catarrhi"; excessive buildup of mucus or "runny" symptoms</note></term>, nor sciatica, nor colic pains, nor swelling and flatulence. For these diseases arise from <term>distillation <note>original: "distillatione"; the ancient medical theory that "humors" or fluids flowed downward from the head to cause illness</note></term> and from swelling; they, however, through exercise, break up every humor and wind. Therefore, it is a great disgrace if anyone is seen spitting or clearing their throat; for they say this is a sign of either too little exercise, or of sluggish laziness, or of overindulgence and gluttony. Rather, they suffer from inflammations or dry spasms, which they treat with an abundance of juicy and wholesome food. <term>Hectic fevers <note>original: "Hecticas"; a fever associated with wasting diseases like tuberculosis</note></term>, indeed, they cure with sweet baths, and milk products, and pleasant living in country houses, and slow, joyful exercise. The "venereal plague" <note>original: "lues venerea"; syphilis</note> cannot prevail among them, because they frequently cleanse their bodies with a bath of wine and soothe them with aromatic oils, and through the sweat of exercise they break up the foul vapor from which the blood and marrow rot. They suffer less from <term>consumption <note>original: "Phthysim"; pulmonary tuberculosis</note></term> because they lack the "distillation" to the chest. They suffer least of all from asthma, for the development of which a thick humor is required. They cure burning fevers with a cold drink of water. <term>Ephemeral fevers <note>original: "Ephemeras"; fevers lasting only a single day</note></term>, however, they cure with scents, and rich broth, or sleep, or music, or exultation. <term>Tertian fevers <note>original: "Tertianas"; a fever that recurs every third day, typical of some forms of malaria</note></term> they treat with bloodletting and with <term>rhubarb <note>original: "Reubarbaro"; used historically as a powerful purgative</note></term>, or a similar drawing medicine, or with water boiled with the roots of purgative and acidic herbs; but they rarely drink purgative medicine. <term>Quartan fevers <note>original: "Quartanas"; a fever recurring every fourth day</note></term> they cure easily by striking a sudden, unexpected fear into the patient, and with herbs opposite to the humor of the quartan fever, or similar things; and they showed me secrets against these.

With more diligent work they treat continuous fevers, of which they are more afraid; and they fight against them with the observation of the stars, and herbs, and with prayers to God. You see almost no quintan, sextan, or octan fevers, etc., where thick humors are absent.

They use baths—and therefore they have hot springs <note>original: "thermas"</note> in the <term>Roman fashion <note>original: "ritu Romanorum"</note></term>—and oils; and they have discovered far more secret remedies for maintaining cleanliness, health, and strength. By these and other me...

F. TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

...for the confinement of rebellious enemies, etc., no formal indictment <note>original: "libellus causæ"; literally a 'little book of the cause'</note> is written, which we commonly call a trial record <note>original: "processum"</note>. Instead, the accusation and witnesses are brought before the Judge and the Power <note>the magistrate in charge of justice and defense</note>; and the defendant responds in his own defense. He is immediately acquitted or condemned by the Judge; and if he appeals to the Triumvir <note>one of the three high officials: Power, Wisdom, or Love</note>, he is acquitted or condemned on the following day. On the third day, however, he is either released for free through the mercy of the <term>Sun <note>original: "☉"; the symbol for the sun, representing the supreme ruler of the City</note></term>, or the sentence receives its unchangeable finality. Then, the defendant is reconciled to the accuser and the witnesses—as if to the doctors of his own sickness—with an embrace and a kiss, etc. 

No one is put to death unless he is killed or stoned by the hands of the people, though the accuser and witnesses must be the first to start the process. For they have no executioners or lictors <note>original: "lictores"; officials who carried out sentences in ancient Rome</note>, so that the Republic is not defiled. To others, however, a choice of death is granted: they surround themselves with bags of gunpowder <note>original: "puluerem bellicum"</note> and, with fire applied, they are burned, while exhorters stand by to encourage them to die well. 

The entire City weeps together, and they pray to God that His anger might be soothed; they grieve that they have reached such a point where a rotten member of the Republic must be cut away. Indeed, they convince the defendant himself with reasons and discourse until he himself accepts and desires the capital sentence; otherwise, he is not put to death. 

But if a crime is committed against the liberty of the Republic, or against God, or against the supreme magistrates, punishment is carried out immediately and without mercy. These crimes alone are punished by death. He who is about to die is compelled by his religion to state before the people the reasons why he should not die, as well as the sins of others who themselves ought to die, and even the faults of the magistrates—asserting that these others deserve a worse punishment, if it so seems to him in his conscience. And if he prevails with his reasons, he is sent into exile; and they purify the City with prayers, sacrifices, and amendments. They do not, however, harass those named by the defendant, but merely warn them. 

Sins of frailty <note>original: "Peccata fragilitatis"; common human weaknesses rather than malicious crimes</note> and ignorance are punished only with rebukes and by being compelled to practice the habit of self-restraint, or to study the discipline of those sciences or arts against which they sinned. Toward one another, they behave in such a way that they seem to be members of the very same body, each belonging to the other. ### OF THE CITY OF THE SUN
Lll 2

...[con]fessing himself and seeking amendment; he is freed from the punishment of a hidden crime, which is commuted to another, provided he had not already been accused. They take great care that no one frames another with a false accusation <note>original: "calumniam struat"</note>: for indeed, it is necessary that such a person fall under the law of retaliation <term>lex talionis; the principle of "an eye for an eye," where the punisher receives the same treatment they intended for the victim</term>. Because they always walk and work in groups, five witnesses are required to convict a sinner; otherwise, he is released with a warning after taking an oath. If, however, he is accused a second or third time, he pays a double penalty based on the testimony of two or three witnesses. Their laws are few, brief, and clear, all inscribed on a bronze tablet hanging at the gates of the Temple—that is, on the columns. On each individual column, the essences <note>original: "quidditates"; a scholastic term for the "whatness" or true nature of a thing</note> of things are inscribed in a metaphysical and very brief style. For example: what God is, what an Angel is, what the World, a Star, a Man, Fate, Virtue, and so on, are. These are written with great wit, and the definitions of all virtues are outlined there. The judges of each virtue have a seat—that is, a tribunal—each under the column where the definition of the virtue they judge is displayed. When judging, the official sits there and says: "My son, you have sinned against this sacred definition of beneficence, or magnanimity, or [another virtue]." Read it. After a discussion is held, he condemns the man to the punishment for the crime he is guilty of—whether it be malice, abjection, pride, ingratitude, laziness, or the like. These condemnations are certain and true medicines, and they possess a quality of sweetness rather than the sting of punishment.

<margin>Concerning the priests, Religion, sacrifice, and prayer.</margin>
**Guest:** Now you ought to speak of the priests, the sacrifices, the Religion, and their faith.

**Genoese:** The High Priest is the **Sun** <term>represented by the symbol ☉ in the original text, referring to the supreme ruler of the City</term> himself. All the Magistrates are priests as well, but only the primary ones. Their duty is to purge consciences. Thus, the entire City discloses its sins to the magistrates through secret confession—a practice we also use—so that they may simultaneously purify souls and learn which sins are spreading among the people. Then, these sacred magistrates confess their own sins to the three supreme princes; they also confess the sins of others—without naming individuals, but in general terms—especially those that are more serious or harmful to the Republic. Finally, those three men confess those same sins, along with their own, to the **Sun** himself, who then recognizes what kinds of sins...

### FRIAR THOMAS CAMPANELLA

...[calamities] spread through the City, he comes to the aid with appropriate remedies. Then he offers a sacrifice to God, and prayers: and first he confesses the sins of the whole people before God publicly in the Temple upon the altar, as often as correction is necessary, yet without declaring any sinner by name. Thus he absolves the People by warning them to beware of such crimes: then, he publicly confesses his own sins: then he offers sacrifice to God, that He may forgive the City, and absolve it from sins, and teach and defend it. Once a year also, the supreme Princes of the individual Cities of his subjects each confess their sins before Sol <note>original: "$\odot$"; the symbol for the sun and the title of the supreme ruler of the City</note>, whereby he remains aware of the evils of the province, and accordingly provides for all with both human and celestial remedies, etc.

The Sacrifice is of this kind: Sol asks the people, who among them wishes to give himself as a sacrifice to God for the sake of his fellow members: and he who is the holiest among them offers himself. Then, after the ceremonies and prayers have been performed, he is placed upon a square platform <note>original: "tabula"</note>, which is bound by four ropes through four clasps, hanging from four pulleys of the small dome <note>original: "testudinis paruæ"</note>. And they cry out to the God of mercies, that He might accept that voluntary human sacrifice (not an involuntary bestial one, such as the Pagans <note>original: "Gentiles"</note> perform); soon Sol orders the ropes to be pulled, and the sacrifice is raised upward to the center of the small dome. And there he dedicates himself with the most fervent prayers: and food is supplied to him through a window by the priests living around the dome, but sparingly, until the City has been expiated. And he himself, by prayer and fasting, beseeches the God of heaven to accept the spontaneous sacrifice of himself. And after twenty or thirty days, when the wrath of God is appeased, he becomes a priest, or (though very rarely) he returns below, but by the outer priestly way. And this man is treated thereafter with great honor and goodwill, because he offered himself unto death for his fatherland: but God does not desire death. Furthermore, twenty-four Priests dwell atop the temple, who at midnight, and at noon, and in the morning, and in the evening—four times a day—sing Psalms before God. And their duty is to observe the stars, and with astrolabes <term>astrolabe; an ancient astronomical instrument used to determine the position of celestial bodies</term> to note their movements and effects upon human affairs, and to know their powers thoroughly. ## CONCERNING THE CITY OF THE SUN.

...they know in what region of the world a change has occurred, or is about to occur, and at what time. They send out scouts to see if it is indeed so, and they record true and false predictions so that they can predict most accurately based on experience. These officials determine the hours of procreation <note>original: "generationis"; the Solarians believe the timing of conception must be astrologically aligned for the health of the offspring</note>, as well as the days for sowing, harvesting, and the vintage. They act as intermediaries, intercessors, and a link between God and humanity. It is from their ranks that the Sol <note>the supreme ruler of the City</note> is usually chosen. They write illustrious works and investigate the sciences. They do not descend from their heights except for lunch and dinner, just as spirits travel from the head to the stomach and liver <note>a reference to the medical theories of the time, where "animal spirits" moved from the brain to the rest of the body</note>. They do not consort with women except rarely for the sake of their physical health. Every day, Sol ascends to them and deliberates with them regarding the things they have newly discovered for the benefit of the City and all the nations of the world.

In the lower part of the temple, one of the people is perpetually present, praying before the altar, and another succeeds him every hour, just as we are accustomed to do in the solemn forty-hour prayer service <note>original: "supplicatione solemni quadraginta horarum"; a traditional Catholic devotion involving continuous prayer before the Blessed Sacrament</note>. They call this manner of praying the "perpetual sacrifice" <note>original: "iuge sacrificium"; a term traditionally used for the daily offerings in the Temple of Jerusalem</note>. After their meal, they return thanks to God with music. Then they sing of the deeds of Christian, Hebrew, and Gentile <note>non-Jewish or "pagan" heroes</note> heroes, and those of all nations; and this is a source of delight to them, for they envy no one. Hymns are sung concerning Love, Wisdom, and every virtue under the direction of their King. Each man takes the woman he loves most, and they perform honorable and beautiful dances under the peristyles <note>covered walkways lined with columns</note>. The women wear their hair long, gathered and bound together in a single crown-like arrangement at the top of the head, though with one lock drawn out into a braided curl. The men, however, have only a single curl, with the rest of the hair around it shaved; they wear a single veil and a single round hood above it, only slightly larger than the shape of the head. In the fields, they use hats; but at home, they wear white or red birettas <note>stiff, square caps</note>, or varied colors according to each man's craft and service. The magistrates, however, wear somewhat larger and more magnificent ones.

# F. THOMAS CAMPANELLA

...Capricorn and Aries, and they perform learned and beautiful acts, almost like plays. On every full moon and new moon, they celebrate a festival, as they also do on the days when they founded the City, or when they reported victories, and so forth. These are accompanied by music from female voices, and with trumpets, drums, and cannons.

<margin>On the use of Poets.</margin>
The Poets sing the praises of distinguished leaders and their victories. However, anyone who lies, even in praise of a hero, is punished. No one who creates deceitful fictions can hold the office of a poet. They judge such license to be the ruin of the human world, because it takes away the reward of virtue and often grants it to the vicious out of fear, flattery, ambition, or greed. No statue is erected to anyone’s glory except after their death. Yet, while living, anyone is inscribed in the "Book of Heroes" who has discovered new arts, or highly useful secrets, or has conferred a great benefit upon the Republic, whether at home or in military service. The bodies of the deceased are not buried, but cremated, so that no plague may arise and so that they may be converted into fire—a thing so noble and alive, which comes from the sun and returns to the sun. This is also done so that no occasion is given for idolatry <note>The author suggests that burying bodies might lead people to worship the graves or the physical remains of ancestors</note>. However, the statues and pictures of the Heroes remain; and these are gazed upon by the beautiful women who have been dedicated by the Republic for procreation <note>The Solarians believed that the visual environment and the thoughts of a mother could physically influence the appearance and character of her child</note>.

<margin>On the ritual of prayer.</margin>
Prayers are made toward the four horizontal corners of the world: first in the morning toward the East, then the West, then the South, and finally the North. In the evening, the order is reversed: first toward the West, then the East, then the North, and finally the South. They repeat only one hymn, in which they ask for a healthy body and a healthy mind <note>original: "mens sana in corpore sano," a classical Roman ideal</note> for themselves and for all nations, and for happiness. They conclude with: "as it seems best to God." Moreover, the formal prayer is long and poured out toward Heaven. For this reason, the altar is round and divided crosswise at right angles by paths through which the <term>Sol</term> <note>original: ☉; the symbol for the Sun and the title of the city's supreme priest-ruler</note> enters after four repetitions, and he prays while looking up to Heaven. This is observed by them as a great mystery. The priestly garments are of wondrous beauty and significance, like those of Aaron <note>referring to the elaborate vestments of the High Priest described in the biblical Book of Exodus</note>.

<margin>On sacred and civil time-keeping.</margin>
and for this reason, by traveling through narrower circles, it reaches the Tropics and Equinoxes sooner this year than in the previous one. Or, it appears to arrive earlier because the eye, seeing it from a lower and more oblique angle, perceives it to arrive and tilt sooner. They measure months by the lunar cycle, but the year by the solar cycle. Therefore, these two do not align until the 19th year <note>original: "19. annum". This refers to the Metonic cycle, the period after which the phases of the moon recur on the same days of the year.</note>, which is also when the "Head of the Dragon" <term>Head of the Dragon: The ascending lunar node, the point where the moon's orbit crosses the sun's path.</term> completes its own course. Because of this, they have established a new Astronomy. They praise *Ptolemy* and admire *Copernicus*, even though they value *Aristarchus* and *Philolaus* who lived before him. However, they say that one of these tracks the patterns of movement with calculations, and the other with "beans" <note>original: "fabis". A metaphor for using abstract counters or theories rather than physical reality.</note>; but no one has yet measured the things themselves in their real dimensions. They claim that [modern astronomers] satisfy the world with symbolic currency rather than real coin. For this reason, they investigate this matter with the greatest effort, for it is highly necessary to understand the construction and architecture of the World, and whether it is destined to perish or not, and when. They believe the prophecy of **JESUS CHRIST** regarding signs in the Sun, Moon, and Stars is absolutely true—signs which are not apparent to many of the fools among our own people, whom the destruction of the world will catch like a thief in the night. Thus, they await the renewal of the age, and perhaps its end. They say it is a matter full of doubt whether the World was made from nothing, or from the ruins of other Worlds, or from Chaos; but they consider it likely, indeed certain, that it was created and has not existed from eternity. For this reason, they strongly hate *Aristotle* in this and many other matters, whom they call a "Logician" rather than a "Philosopher." From astronomical anomalies, they draw many arguments against the eternity of the world. They honor the Sun and the Stars as living things and as statues of God, and as living celestial Temples and Altars, but they do not worship them. Above all, they venerate the Sun. Yet they deem no created thing worthy of the highest worship <term>latria: the supreme worship due to God alone</term>; they offer this to God alone. Therefore, they serve Him alone, lest they fall into tyranny and misery by serving creatures as a "punishment in kind" <term>lex talionis: the law of retaliation, or 'an eye for an eye'</term>. Under the sign of the Sun, they contemplate and recognize God, calling the Sun the emblem of God, His face, and His living statue through which light, heat, life, and the production of all things flow down to the lower realms, bringing all good things. Because of this, their altar is built in the likeness of the Sun. And the Priest—

# BROTHER TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

<meta>The text begins with the end of the word 'Sacerdotes' (Priests) from the previous page.</meta>

...priests worship God in the sun and in the stars, as if at altars, and in the Heavens as if in a Temple. They implore the good Angels as intercessors, who dwell in the stars—their living dwellings. For they acknowledge that God has displayed His beauties far more in the Heavens and in the Sun, which they consider His trophy and His statue. They reject the **eccentrics** and **epicycles** <note>original: "excentricos & epicyclos". These were complex geometric circles used by Ptolemy to explain why planets occasionally seem to move backward; the Solarians believe these are unnecessary mathematical fictions.</note> of both the Ptolemaic and Copernican systems. They assert instead that there is only one Heaven, and that the **Planets** <term>Planets: Literally 'wandering stars' from the Greek 'planētēs'.</term> move by their own power. They are raised higher when they approach and join with the sun; therefore, they move more slowly in a wider circle toward the leading parts of the sky, where they all strive to go. However, when they are positioned near the Sun, they gradually incline to receive light from it and take a shorter path because they are closer to the Earth. Thus, they are carried forward more quickly.

When they move at an equal speed with the fixed stars, they are called **stationary**; when they move faster, they are called **retrograde** <note>original: "retrogrados". This is the apparent backward motion of a planet as seen from Earth.</note> according to common Astronomers. When they move more slowly, they are called **direct** because of the greater light they receive as they are raised higher, and so on. For they are lowered during their quadratures <note>original: "quadraturis". An astronomical position where two celestial bodies are 90 degrees apart.</note> and in their oppositions, so that they do not wander too far from the Sun. 

The Moon, however, is raised up not only in opposition but even in conjunction, because it is located below the sun. Thus all the stars, although they are carried from East to West, appear to move in the opposite direction; this is because the Heaven of the stars rotates entirely and swiftly every 24 hours. The planets themselves do not move as quickly and are left behind on the journey; therefore, being overtaken by the Heaven, they seem to be moved backward. 

The Moon, however—which is closest to us—never appears to run backward in opposition or conjunction, but is instead carried forward just a little at those times when it is filled with much light, whether from above or below. For the first heaven <note>The outermost sphere of the universe in ancient cosmology.</note> moves with such great velocity compared to the moon that the moon cannot be seen to be carried forward in a way that exceeds the 13 degrees by which it falls short of that heaven. Therefore, it does not move backward, but only slows down or speeds up in its forward and backward appearance. 

From this, it is clear that they do not require **epicycles** or **eccentrics** to explain why planets rise, fall, move backward, or slow down. Indeed, they affirm that the wandering stars find a sympathy with supernatural things in certain parts of the world, and for that reason, they linger there longer; thus they are said to be raised into the **apsis** <term>apsis: The point in an orbit where a celestial body is at its maximum or minimum distance from the center of its system.</term>. Furthermore, as to why the Sun lingers longer in the Northern region

### ON THE CITY OF THE SUN.

...stays longer than in the South, they provide a physical cause: namely, that the sun is raised there to parch the earth where the earth had gained more strength during the sun's journey toward the south when it first rose along with the World. Therefore, they assert—along with the Chaldeans and more ancient Hebrews, and not as more recent thinkers believe—that the World began in our Autumn, which is the Spring of the Southern regions. Thus, having been raised up to restore what it had lost, the sun lingers for more days in the North than in the South, and it appears to climb into an **eccentric** orbit <note>original: "excentricum". This refers to an off-center circular path, which astronomers used to explain why the Sun seems to move at different speeds during different seasons.</note>. Despite this, they remain uncertain whether the sun is the center of the lower World, whether the fixed stars are the centers of other planetary systems, and whether those planets are surrounded by other moons, just as our earth is. But they remain vigilant in the investigation of this truth.

<margin>On Physics.</margin>
They assert two physical principles for lower things: namely, the **Sun** as the father and the **Earth** as the mother. They believe that the Air is an impure portion of the heavens, and that all fire is derived from the sun. The Sea, however, is the "sweat" of the Earth, or a fluid from the scorched and molten Earth within its bowels; it is the bond between air and Earth, just as blood is the bond between the spirits and the bodies of animals. They say the World is a massive animal, and that we live in its belly, just as worms live in our own bellies. For this reason, we do not belong to the providence of the Stars, the Sun, or the Earth, but to God’s alone. For in respect to those celestial bodies—which intend nothing but their own expansion—we are born and live by chance; but in respect to God, whose instruments they are, we were created with foreknowledge and order, and destined for a great end. Therefore, we are obligated to God alone as our Father, and we are bound to acknowledge all things as coming from Him. Without a doubt, they believe in the **immortality of souls**, and that after death, these are joined to good or evil Angels, depending on which ones they made themselves more like through their actions in this present life. For all things seek what is similar to themselves. Concerning the places of punishment and reward, they differ little from us. They are in doubt as to whether there are other worlds outside of our own; and they consider it madness to assert that "nothing" exists, for they say that nothingness exists neither inside nor outside the World. God, being an infinite **Being** <term>Being: "Ens" in Latin, referring to the fundamental essence or existence of God.</term>, does not allow for "nothingness" to exist alongside Him.

<margin>On Metaphysics.</margin>
They posit two metaphysical principles: namely, **Being**, which is God

<meta>This page continues the philosophical dialogue regarding the inhabitants of the City of the Sun (the Solarians). # F. THOMAS CAMPANELLA

[God] is supreme, and **Non-being**—which is a lack of existence and the "condition without which" nothing in Physics can happen—is its opposite. For that which already exists is not being made; therefore, that which is being made must not have existed previously. Likewise, they believe that evil and sin are born from a tendency toward non-being, and that sin has a **deficient cause** rather than an **efficient cause** <note>original: "causam deficientem, sed non efficientem". In Scholastic philosophy, an "efficient cause" is a positive force that creates an effect, while a "deficient cause" is a failure or lack in the agent (like a shadow caused by the absence of light) that explains how evil exists without God being its creator.</note>. By "deficient," they mean a lack of power, or of wisdom, or of will. They place the root of sin in this last one: for whoever knows what is right and has the power to do it, ought also to will it. For they believe the will is born from knowledge and power, and not the other way around. 

It is astounding that they also worship God as a **Trinity**, saying that God is supreme **Power**, and from this proceeds supreme **Wisdom** (which is simultaneously the same God), and from both of these proceeds **Love**, which is both Power and Wisdom; for that which proceeds cannot fail to possess the nature of that from which it comes. Nevertheless, they do not recognize the distinct Persons by name as we do in our Christian law, because they lack divine revelation. But they know that within God there is a "procession" and a relationship of Himself, toward Himself, in Himself, and from Himself. 

And so, all beings are given their essence metaphysically from **Power**, **Wisdom**, and **Love** insofar as they possess being; and from weakness, ignorance, and a lack of love insofar as they participate in non-being. Through the former qualities they earn merit; through the latter they sin. This may be a "sin of Nature" arising from the first two (weakness or ignorance), or a sin of character and skill involving all three or specifically the third (the will). Indeed, even a specific part of nature "sins" through weakness or ignorance when it produces a **monster** <note>original: "monstrum". In this historical context, a "monster" refers to any biological birth defect or anomaly where nature fails to achieve its intended perfect form.</note>. 

Furthermore, all these things are foreknown and ordered by God—who is entirely free from "nothingness"—as the most Powerful, most Wise, and most Good. Therefore, within God, no being sins; sin only occurs "outside" of God. Yet one cannot truly go "outside" of God, except from our perspective and in relation to ourselves, but not in relation to Him. For within us there is failure <note>original: "deficientia"</note>, but within Him there is only creative power <note>original: "efficientia"</note>. Therefore, a sinful act is an "act of God" only insofar as it possesses existence and power; but insofar as it possesses non-existence and failure—which constitutes the very **essence** <note>original: "quidditas"</note> of sin—it belongs to us and comes from us, who decline toward non-being through disorder.

**Guest:** Goodness, how clever they are!

<margin>On the cause of worldly evils.</margin>
**GENOESE CAPTAIN:** They plainly confess that much corruption spreads throughout the world; that humans are not ruled by true, higher reasons; that the upright are tormented and suffer a bad reputation, while the wicked dominate—although they call the lives of these [wicked] people "unhappiness" rather than a blessed life. For they see such status as a kind of annihilation, a mere show of being what they are not—namely Kings, Sages, Strong-willed, or Saints—when in truth they are nothing of the sort. From this, they argue that a great disturbance has arisen in human affairs from some "accident" <note>original: "ex quopiam accidenti". In this context, "accident" refers to a chance event or a catastrophic fall—specifically the Fall of Man—that was not part of the original divine design.</note>. At first, they were inclined to say, following Plato, that the celestial spheres in ancient ages revolved from the West toward what we now call the East, and afterward took up the contrary course <note>This refers to a myth in Plato's *Politicus* (The Statesman), where the universe occasionally reverses its rotation, leading to ages of chaos or decline.</note>. They also said it was possible that lower matters were ruled by some inferior deity, permitted by the First Deity; but they now repute this assertion as foolish. 

They think it even more foolish to claim that **Saturn** first ruled well, and then **Jupiter** less well, and then the other planets followed in succession—though they do admit that the ages of the World are ordered according to the series of the planets. They believe that due to the changes of the <term>apsides</term> <note>The points in a planet's orbit where it is nearest or farthest from the sun; Campanella believed these shifts signaled major historical changes.</note> after intervals of 1,000 or 1,600 years, things vary significantly.

This current age of ours seems to be assigned to **Mercury**, even if it is influenced by "great conjunctions" <note>A "great conjunction" is the meeting of Jupiter and Saturn, which astrologers of the time believed heralded the birth of new religions or empires.</note>; and they believe the return of <term>anomalies</term> <note>Irregularities in planetary motion.</note> possesses a fatal power. Finally, they affirm that the Christian person is happy, who is content to believe that such a great disturbance happened because of the sin of Adam. They also believe that evils are derived from fathers to sons as a punishment, rather than as guilt <note>original: "poenae, magis quam culpae". This reflects the Solarian view that children suffer the physical or social consequences of their parents' flaws, but do not inherit the moral "sin" itself.</note>.

However, they say the guilt returns from the sons back to the fathers: insofar as the fathers neglected <insert>the laws of</insert> generation [procreation], and celebrated it outside of the proper time, place, and choice of parents; or they neglected the education...

<meta>This page continues the dialogue regarding the social and legal structure of the City of the Sun. # BROTHER TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

450

...for the containment of rebellious enemies, etc., no written record of the case—which we commonly call a legal process <note>original: "processum"</note>—is composed. Instead, the accusation and the witnesses are produced in the presence of the Judge and the Magistrate <note>original: "Potestate," referring to a high-ranking official with executive power</note>; the defendant then offers his defense. He is immediately acquitted or condemned by the Judge. If he appeals to the Triumvir <note>One of the three high ministers who assist the supreme ruler</note>, he is acquitted or condemned on the following day. On the third day, however, he is either freely pardoned through the mercy of the Sun <note>The symbol ☉ represents "Sol" (the Sun), the supreme priest-king of the city</note> or the sentence attains an inviolable finality. 

The defendant is then reconciled with the accuser and the witnesses—viewing them as if they were doctors treating his illness—with an embrace and a kiss. No one is put to death unless it be by the hands of the people, who kill or stone the condemned, with the accuser and the witnesses being the first to strike. For they have no executioners or lictors <note>Professional state executioners</note>, lest the Republic be defiled. Others, however, are granted the choice of their own death; these individuals surround themselves with bags of gunpowder and, once fire is applied, they are consumed by the flames, while "encouragers" stand by to assist them in dying a good death. 

The entire City weeps together and they pray to God that His wrath may be appeased, grieving that they have come to such a point that a "rotten limb" of the Republic must be cut off. Indeed, they use reason to convince the defendant and discourse with him until he himself accepts and even desires the capital sentence; otherwise, he is not put to death. But if a crime is committed against the liberty of the Republic, or against God, or against the supreme magistrates, punishment is carried out immediately without mercy. Only these crimes are punished by death. 

The one about to die is compelled by religious duty to state publicly the reasons why he should not die, as well as the sins of others who also deserve death, and the faults of the magistrates—asserting that they would deserve a worse punishment, if his conscience dictates it so. If he prevails through these arguments, he is sent into exile instead. Then, they purify the City with prayers, sacrifices, and acts of amendment. They do not, however, harass those named by the condemned, but merely warn them. Sins of frailty and ignorance are punished only with rebukes and by a forced return to the habit of self-restraint, or to the study of those sciences or arts against which the person sinned. They behave toward one another in such a way that they appear to be members of the same body, each belonging to the other. # THE CITY OF THE SUN

...confessing of his own accord and seeking amendment; he is then freed from the punishment of a hidden crime, which is commuted to another penalty, provided he had not yet been formally accused. They take great care that no one constructs a false accusation against another: if someone does, they fall under the <term>law of retaliation</term> <note>original: "pœnam talionis"; a legal principle where the punishment corresponds exactly to the injury inflicted.</note>. Because the citizens always walk and work in groups, five witnesses are required to convict a sinner; otherwise, the accused is freed after taking a solemn oath, though with a stern warning. If, however, he is accused a second or third time, he pays a doubled penalty upon the testimony of two or three witnesses. Their laws are few, brief, and clear, all inscribed on a bronze tablet hanging at the doors of the Temple—that is, upon the columns. Indeed, on each individual column, one can see the <term>essences</term> <note>original: "quidditates"; a philosophical term for the "what-ness" or core nature of a thing.</note> of things inscribed in a very brief, metaphysical style: namely, what God is, what an Angel is, what the World, a Star, a Man, Fate, Virtue, etc., are. These definitions of all the virtues are drafted there with great wit and wisdom. 

The Judges of all the virtues have their seats there—that is, their tribunal—each one sitting under the column where the definition of the virtue they judge is displayed. When a Judge passes sentence, he sits there and says: "My son, you have sinned against this sacred definition of beneficence (or magnanimity, or another virtue); read it." Then, after a discussion has been held, he condemns him to the punishment for the crime of which he is guilty: namely, for malice, abjection, pride, ingratitude, or laziness, etc. These condemnations are certain and true medicines, and indeed they carry the scent of sweetness rather than the sting of punishment.

This allows the magistrates to simultaneously cleanse souls and learn which sins are becoming common among the people. They also confess the sins of others, though without naming any individual, speaking instead in general terms—especially regarding the more serious matters and those harmful to the Republic. ## BY FR. THOMAS CAMPANELLA

...evils rage in the City, and he assists with timely remedies. Then he offers a sacrifice to God, along with prayers: but first he confesses the sins of the whole people publicly before God in the Temple upon the altar, whenever correction is necessary, yet without declaring any sinner by name. Thus he absolves the People by warning them to beware of such crimes; then, he publicly confesses his own sins. After this, he offers a sacrifice to God, so that He may forgive the City, and absolve it from its sins, and teach and defend it. Once a year also, the supreme Princes of each city confess the sins of each of their subjects before the **Sun** <note>original: ☉; the symbol for the Sun, representing the supreme leader and high priest of the city, often called Hoh.</note>, so that he remains aware of the evils of the province, and accordingly provides for all with both human and celestial remedies, and so forth.

The sacrifice is of this kind: the **Sun** asks the people who among them wishes to give himself as a sacrifice to God for his members <note>That is, for the fellow members of the body politic.</note>; and he who is the holiest offers himself. Then, after the ceremonies and prayers have been performed, he is placed upon a square platform which is bound by buckles to four ropes hanging from four pulleys of the small **dome** <note>original: "testudinis"; literally "tortoise shell," an architectural term for a vaulted ceiling or dome.</note>. They cry out to the God of mercies, that He may accept that voluntary human sacrifice (not a wild, involuntary animal sacrifice, which the **Pagans** <note>original: "Gentiles"; referring to those outside the enlightened Solar faith.</note> perform). Soon the **Sun** orders the ropes to be pulled, and the sacrifice is raised upward to the center of the small dome. There he dedicates himself with the most fervent prayers; food is supplied to him through a window by the priests living around the top, but sparingly, until the City has been expiated. He himself, through prayer and fasting, prays to the God of heaven to accept the spontaneous sacrifice of his person. After twenty or thirty days, once the wrath of God is appeased, he becomes a priest, or (though very rarely) he returns downward, but by the outer priestly way. This man is henceforth treated with great honor and benevolence, because he offered himself up to death for his homeland—though God does not actually desire death. Furthermore, twenty-four Priests dwell atop the temple. At midnight, at noon, in the morning, and in the evening—namely four times a day—they sing Psalms before God. Their duty is to observe the stars, and with **astrolabes** <note>An ancient astronomical instrument used for measuring the altitude of stars and predicting the positions of celestial bodies.</note> to note their movements and their effects on human affairs, and to understand their powers thoroughly. 453

They know in which region of the world what change has been, or is to be, and at what time. They send out explorers to see if such is the case, and they note which predictions were true and which were false, so that they may predict most accurately from experience. These priests determine the hours for generation <note>The astrologically determined times for procreation, as the Solarians believe the stars influence the character of children.</note>, as well as the days for sowing, harvest, and the vintage; they are, as it were, the messengers and intercessors and the bond between God and men. Most of those chosen to be the **Sun** <note>The supreme leader and high priest.</note> are taken from their number. They write noble works and investigate the sciences. They do not descend from their heights except for lunch and dinner, moving like the spirits that travel from the head to the stomach and liver <note>A medical metaphor comparing the priests' seclusion in the temple to the "animal spirits" of contemporary physiology moving between the brain and the digestive organs.</note>. They do not mingle with women, except rarely for the sake of bodily health. Every day, the **Sun** ascends to them, and he reasons with them regarding the things they have newly discovered for the benefit of the City and all the nations of the world.

In the temple below, one of the people is perpetually present, praying before the altar, and another succeeds him every hour, just as we are accustomed to do in the solemn forty-hours' devotion. This manner of praying they call the perpetual sacrifice <note>original: "iuge sacrificium"</note>. After their refreshment, they give thanks to God with music. Then they sing of the deeds of the Christian heroes, and those of the Hebrews, the Gentiles, and of all nations; for indeed, they envy no one. They sing hymns of Love, of Wisdom, and of every virtue, under the guidance of their King. Each man takes the woman he loves most, and they perform honorable and beautiful dances under the porticos. The women wear their hair long, gathered and bound together into a single crown at the top of the head, though with one curl drawn out into a tress. The men, however, wear only one curl, with the rest of the hair around it shorn; they wear one veil, and one round hood above it that slightly exceeds the shape of the head. In the fields they use hats, but at home they wear white or red caps, or various colors according to each man's craft and office. The magistrates, however, wear caps that are somewhat larger and more ornate.

At every Full Moon and New Moon they celebrate a festival, as well as on the days when they founded the City, or won victories, and so on. These are accompanied by the music of female voices, and with trumpets, drums, and cannons. <margin>On the use of Poets.</margin> Also, Poets sing the praises of the most illustrious leaders and their victories. However, anyone who lies, even when praising a hero, is punished. No one who fabricates lies is permitted to exercise the office of a poet. They judge such poetic license to be the ruin of the human world, because it robs virtue of its true reward and often grants it to the wicked out of fear, flattery, ambition, or greed. No statue is erected to anyone's glory until after their death. Nevertheless, while still living, anyone is inscribed in the "Book of Heroes" who has discovered new arts or highly useful secrets, or who has conferred a great benefit upon the Republic either at home or in military service. The bodies of the deceased are not buried in the earth, but are cremated, so that no plague may arise from them, and so that the bodies themselves may be converted into fire—a thing so noble and living, which comes from the sun and returns to the sun. This is also done so that no occasion is given for idolatry. However, the statues and portraits of these Heroes remain; the beautiful women, who are dedicated to procreation by the Republic, gaze upon them <note>The Solarians believe that what a woman sees or thinks about during conception and pregnancy influences the physical and moral character of the child.</note>. Prayers are made toward the four horizontal corners of the world. <margin>On the ritual of praying.</margin> Indeed, they pray first in the morning toward the Sunrise, then toward the Sunset, then toward the South, and then toward the North. Conversely, in the evening, they pray first toward the Sunset, then toward the East, then toward the North, and finally toward the South. They repeat only one song, in which they ask for a healthy body and a sound mind <note>original: "corpus sanum & mentem sanam," a reference to the Roman ideal of 'mens sana in corpore sano.'</note> for themselves and for all Nations, and for happiness. They conclude by saying: "As it seems best to God." Otherwise, their focused prayer is lengthy and poured out toward Heaven. For this reason, the altar is round and divided crosswise at right angles by paths, through which the **Sun** <note>The "Sun" (Sol) is the title of their supreme leader and high priest.</note> enters after four repetitions, and he prays while looking up into Heaven. This is observed by them as a great mystery. <margin>Concerning sacred and civil times.</margin>
...understands this. They believe that the Sun is perpetually moving closer to the earth. Therefore, as it travels in ever-narrowing circles, it reaches the Tropics and the Equinoxes earlier each year than it did the last. Or, it seems to reach them sooner because the eye, being lower, sees the Sun at an angle and thus perceives it arriving and turning earlier. They measure their months by the lunar cycle and their year by the solar cycle. For this reason, the two do not align until the nineteenth year, when the <term>Head of the Dragon</term> <note>original: "caput Draconis"; a traditional astronomical term for the ascending lunar node, where the moon's orbit crosses the sun's path.</note> also completes its course. 

Because of this, they have established a new system of Astronomy. They praise Ptolemy and admire Copernicus, though they hold Aristarchus and Philolaus in even higher regard as precursors to Copernicus. However, they say that one of these astronomers marks the numbers of the movements with calculations, and the other with "beans" <note>original: "fabis"; likely a reference to using physical counters or an abacus rather than observing the celestial bodies themselves</note>, but no one measures the actual things and months themselves. They claim the world is satisfied with "currency"—mere symbols—rather than the reality. Consequently, they investigate this matter with the greatest effort, for they believe it is vital to understand the construction and architecture of the World: whether it is destined to perish or not, and if so, when. 

They believe the prophecy of **JESUS CHRIST** regarding the signs in the Sun, Moon, and Stars is absolutely true. These signs are not apparent to many of the fools among our own people, whom the destruction of the World will catch "like a thief in the night." Therefore, the people of the City look for a renewal of the age, and perhaps even its end. They say it is a matter full of doubt whether the World was made from nothing, from the ruins of previous Worlds, or from Chaos; but they consider it likely—indeed, certain—that it was created and has not existed from eternity. 

For this reason, they intensely dislike Aristotle (in this and many other matters), whom they call a "Logician" rather than a "Philosopher." From the anomalies of the heavens, they derive many arguments against the eternity of the universe. They honor the Sun and the Stars as living things, as the "statues" of God, and as living celestial Temples and Altars; however, they do not adore them as gods. Above all, they venerate the Sun. They do not deem any created thing worthy of <term>latria</term> <note>original: "latria"; the highest form of worship, which in Catholic theology is reserved for God alone, as opposed to "dulia," or veneration given to saints.</note>, which they offer to God alone. They serve Him only, so that they might not fall into tyranny and misery by serving creatures—a punishment of "an eye for an eye" <note>original: "poenam Talionis"</note> for those who worship the created over the Creator. Under the symbol of the Sun, they contemplate and recognize God, calling the Sun the emblem of God, His face, and His living statue, through which light, heat, life, and the creation of all things flow down to the lower realms, bringing all that is good. Because of this, their altar is built in the likeness of the Sun, and the Priests...

Priests adore God in the sun and in the stars, as if they were altars, and in Heaven as if in a Temple. They implore the good Angels as intercessors, who dwell in the stars, which are their living dwellings. For they acknowledge that God has displayed His beauties far more in Heaven and in the Sun, which is His trophy and statue. They deny the existence of <term>eccentrics</term> <note>An orbital path that is not centered on the Earth.</note> and <term>epicycles</term> <note>Small circles whose centers move around the circumference of larger circles; used in ancient astronomy to explain planetary motion.</note> used by the followers of Ptolemy and Copernicus. They assert that there is only one Heaven; and that the Planets are moved by their own accord, and are elevated when they approach and are joined to the sun. Therefore, they are carried forward more sluggishly in a wider circle, toward which all things strive to go; but when they are positioned near the Sun, they gradually incline themselves to receive light from it, and take up a shorter course because they are closer to the Earth. Thus, they are carried forward more quickly, and when they walk at an equal velocity with the fixed stars, they are called **stationary**; when moving faster, they are called **retrograde** according to common Astronomers; and when moving more sluggishly, they are called **direct** because of the greater light they receive and are elevated, and so on. For they are lowered from their <term>quadratures</term> <note>A position of a celestial body 90 degrees from another.</note> and in their oppositions so that they are not distanced further from the sun.

But the Moon is elevated even in opposition, not just in conjunction, because it is beneath the sun. And so, although all the stars are carried from the East to the West, they seem to move in the opposite direction; this is because the starry Heaven is revolved entirely and swiftly in 24 hours, while the planets themselves do not move as quickly and are left behind on the journey. Because they are overtaken by the Heaven, they seem to be moved backward. The Moon, however, being closest to us, is never seen to run backward in opposition or conjunction, but is then carried forward just a little, when it is filled with much light either from above or below. For the first heaven is of such speed compared to the Moon that it cannot be seen to be carried forward in such a way that it exceeds the 13 degrees by which it falls short of the heaven: therefore it does not move backward, but only slows down or accelerates forward and backward. 

From this, it is clear that they do not require Epicycles and eccentrics to explain why planets are elevated, depressed, move back, or grow sluggish. Indeed they affirm this: that the wandering stars <note>original: "sidera errantia"; the literal meaning of "planets".</note> find sympathy with supernatural things in certain parts of the world, and for that reason dwell there longer; therefore they are said to be raised into an <term>apsis</term> <note>original: "absidem"; the highest or lowest point in an orbital path.</note>. ...[the Sun] lingers longer than in the Southern region, they provide a physical reason: namely, that it is raised there to bake the earth where it has gained more strength while it exerted itself in the south, back when it was born along with the World. Therefore, they assert that the World began in our Autumn and in the Spring of the Southern region, agreeing with the Chaldeans <note>Ancient inhabitants of Mesopotamia known for their early advancements in astronomy and astrology.</note> and the more ancient Hebrews, and not as more recent thinkers believe. Thus, elevated so that it might restore what it had lost, it lingers for more days in the North than in the South, and seems to climb into an **eccentric** <term>eccentric</term> <note>original: "excentricum"; an orbital path that is not centered on the Earth, used here to explain the varying lengths of seasons.</note>. Despite this, they remain uncertain whether the sun is the center of the lower World, and whether the fixed stars are the centers of other planets, and whether those planets are orbited by other moons, just as our earth is. But they are still watchful in the investigation of this truth.

<margin>On Physics.</margin>
They assert two physical principles for all lower things: namely, the **Sun** as father and the **Earth** as mother. They say that the Air is an impure portion of the heavens, and that all fire is derived from the sun. The Sea, however, is the "sweat" of the Earth, or the fluid of the burnt and molten Earth within its bowels; it acts as the bond between air and Earth, just as blood serves the spirits and the body of animals. They believe the World is a vast living creature <note>This refers to the "Anima Mundi" or World Soul, a common Renaissance belief that the universe functions as a single biological organism.</note>. And they believe that we live in its belly, just as worms live in our own bellies. For this reason, we do not belong to the providence of the Stars and the Sun and the Earth, but to God alone. This is because, in respect to those celestial bodies—who intend nothing other than their own expansion—we were born and live by chance; but in respect to God, for whom the stars are merely instruments, we were created by foresight and order, and destined for a great end. Therefore, we are beholden to God alone as a Father, and are bound to acknowledge that everything comes from Him. They undoubtedly believe in the immortality of souls, and that after death, these souls are joined with either good or evil Angels, depending on which of the two they made themselves most like through their actions in this present life. For all things seek that which is similar to themselves. Concerning the places of punishment and reward, their views differ little from our own. They remain in doubt as to whether other worlds exist outside of ours, but they think it is madness to assert that "nothingness" exists beyond us; for they say that "nothing" exists neither inside nor outside the World. God, as an infinite being, does not allow "nothingness" to exist alongside Himself.

**GENOESE CAPTAIN.** Truly, if I had kept everything in my memory, and were I not troubled by the anxiety and fear of departing, I would pour forth wonders. But I will lose my ship unless I depart quickly.
