<margin>On the cause of worldly evils.</margin>
**GENOESE CAPTAIN.** They clearly confess that much corruption spreads through the world. They see that humans are not ruled by true, higher reason, but that the honest are tortured and slandered while the wicked dominate. However, they call the seemingly "blessed" life of these wicked people a misery. To them, it is a kind of annihilation—a hollow display of being what they are not: namely Kings, Sages, Vigorous men, and Saints, which in truth they are not. From this, they argue that a great **disturbance** <note>original: "perturbationem"; a central concept in Solarian philosophy suggesting the world has fallen out of its natural, harmonious order.</note> has arisen in human affairs due to some accidental event.

At first, they were almost inclined to say, following **Plato** <note>Likely referring to the myth in Plato's *Statesman*, where the universe occasionally reverses its rotation, leading to chaos and the need for divine intervention.</note>, that in ancient ages the celestial spheres revolved from the present West toward where we now call the East, and afterward assumed the opposite course. They also said it was possible that lower things were ruled by some inferior **deity** <term>deity</term> <note>original: "numine"; a lesser divine power or spirit.</note>, and permitted to be so by the Supreme Being; but they now consider this assertion foolish. They find it even more foolish to believe that **Saturn** ruled well at first, followed by **Jupiter** ruling less well, and then the other planets succeeding them—though they do admit that the ages of the World are ordered according to the sequence of the planets.

They believe that because of the movement of the **apses** <term>apses</term> <note>original: "absidum"; the points in an orbit where a planet is closest to or furthest from the center of its motion.</note>, every 1,000 or 1,600 years, worldly affairs undergo significant changes.

It seems to them that this current age of ours should be assigned to **Mercury**, even if it is interrupted by great planetary conjunctions; they believe that the regression of **anomalies** <term>anomalies</term> <note>original: "anomaliarum"; in pre-modern astronomy, these were irregularities or "loops" in planetary motion that defied simple circular models.</note> possesses a fated power. Finally, they affirm that the Christian man is happy, for he is content to believe that such a great disturbance happened because of the **sin of Adam**. They also hold the opinion that evils are passed down from fathers to sons more as a punishment than as a personal fault.

However, they believe the fault actually returns from the sons to the fathers, insofar as the fathers neglected **generation** <note>The Solarians practice a strict system of state-controlled breeding and eugenics to ensure the quality of their citizens.</note> and performed it outside the proper time, place, and choice of partners—or simply neglected their education.

This, they claim, is why all Cities in this age live in misery—and what is worse, they call these very evils "peace" and "blessedness" because they have not experienced true goods. To them, it seems the World is ruled by chance. 

But in truth, one who contemplates the construction of the World and **human anatomy** (which they often study in those condemned to death), as well as the structure of plants and beasts and the functions of their parts and smallest details, is compelled to acknowledge God’s wisdom and providence with loud acclaim. Therefore, man ought to give himself entirely to **Religion** and always venerate his own Creator. Yet, a man cannot achieve this well—or at least not easily—unless he searches out and comes to know the works of God, observes His laws, and philosophizes correctly regarding His creations. "Do not do to another what you do not wish for yourself" <note>original: "Quod tibi non vis, alteri ne feceris"; a variation of the Golden Rule found in many ancient traditions.</note>; and "whatever you wish that men should do to you, do also to them" <note>original: "quæ vultis vt faciat vobis homines, & vos facite illis"; referencing the words of Jesus in the Gospel of Matthew.</note>. From this it follows that, just as we require honor and good things from our children and from other men (to whom we grant very little), we owe far more to God, from whom we receive everything, through whom we exist, and in whom we are everywhere. Praise be to Him forever.

**HOSPITALLER.** Truly, since these people—who know only the **Law of Nature** <note>original: "naturæ legem"; the concept that moral and ethical truths are discoverable by human reason alone, independent of specific religious revelation.</note>—draw so near to Christianity (which adds nothing to the laws of nature except for the **sacraments** <note>original: "sacramẽta"; the formal rituals of the Church, which Campanella argues provide the spiritual strength to follow natural moral laws.</note> that provide help in observing them), I take this as a powerful argument for the Christian Religion, proving it is the truest of all. And I see that, once abuses are removed, it shall be the Mistress of the entire World, as the most distinguished theologians teach and hope. They say that the **Spaniards** discovered the **New World** <note>original: "nouum Orbem"</note> (although the first discoverer was our own **Columbus**, that greatest of Genoese heroes) for this reason: so that all Nations might be gathered under one law. Therefore, these people have philosophized as witnesses to the truth, chosen by God. From this I recognize that we do not know what we are doing, but are merely God’s instruments. Men seek new regions out of a greed for gold and riches, but God intends a higher purpose. The Sun strives to scorch the earth, not indeed to produce plants and humans, etc., but God uses...

# THE CITY OF THE SUN

...their struggle for the production of these things. To Him be praise and glory.

**GENOESE CAPTAIN.** Oh, if you only knew what they say through **Astrology** <note>The study of how the movements of stars and planets influence human affairs.</note>, and also from our own Prophets, regarding the coming age. They claim that our current century has more history in just one hundred years than the entire World had in four thousand. More books have been published in this century than in five thousand years before it. They speak of the marvelous invention of **Printing**, of **Muskets** <term>Harquebuses; early portable guns</term>, and the use of the **magnet** <note>The compass, which revolutionized navigation.</note>. These are illustrious signs, and at the same time, instruments for the gathering of the inhabitants of the World into one fold. 

They explain how these wonderful inventions occurred when great conjunctions took place in the "triplicity" <note>An astrological grouping of three zodiac signs of the same element.</note> of Cancer, with the apogee of Mercury moving through Scorpio. This happened because the Moon and Mars were powerful in this watery sign, leading to new navigation, new Kingdoms, and new weapons. But they say that soon, when the apogee of Saturn enters Capricorn, Mercury enters Sagittarius, and Mars enters Virgo—after the first great conjunctions and the vision of the **new star in Cassiopeia** <note>A famous supernova observed by Tycho Brahe in 1572, which challenged the idea that the heavens were unchanging.</note>—a new Monarchy shall arise, along with a reformation of laws and arts, new prophets, and a general renewal. They say this portends great benefit for Christianity. Yet, first, things must be uprooted and destroyed, and only then built and planted <note>original: "euelli, & extirpari, deinde ædificari, & plantari"; a reference to Jeremiah 1:10.</note>. 

But let me go, for I have things I must attend to. However, do not let this escape you: they claim to have already discovered the **Art of flying**, which seemed to be the one thing missing from the World. They also expect, in the near future, to have **eyeglasses** <term>Telescopes</term> through which hidden stars may be seen, and **hearing instruments** through which the harmony of the heavens may be heard.

**HOSPITALLER.** What? Ha, ha, ha! That is certainly pleasing. But Cancer is a feminine sign of Venus and the Moon; how could it do any good in the air, since it is a watery sign?

**GENOESE CAPTAIN.** They argue that the feminine brings about the fertility of things in Heaven, and that powers less robust than our own come to dominate. Thus we see that in this century, the **rule of women** has prevailed. For instance, the new Amazons appeared between Nubia and Monopotapa <note>Referring to reports of female warriors in Africa.</note>; and among Europeans, "The Russian" <note>Hürrem Sultan, also known as Roxelana, the influential wife of Suleiman the Magnificent.</note> ruled in Turkey, Bona in Poland, Mary in Hungary, Elizabeth in England, Catherine in France, Bianca in Tuscany, Margaret in the Netherlands, Mary in Scotland, and Isabella in Spain—the discoverer of the New World. Even the poet of this century begins his work with women <note>A reference to Ludovico Ariosto's epic *Orlando Furioso*, which begins: "Of ladies [Le donne], knights, arms, and loves I sing."</note>.

Yet, it was not merely for this that the trigon of Cancer (being a tropic, the exaltation of **Jupiter**, the apogee of the **Sun**, and the trigon of **Mars**) exhibited—through the Moon, Mars, and Venus—the new discovery of the hemisphere <note>The Americas.</note>, the wondrous journey of circumnavigating the whole Globe, and the rule of women. Furthermore, through Mercury and Mars, it brought about **typography** <note>The printing press.</note> and the **musket** <term>Archibugium; an early type of portable firearm</term>. It was also the cause of a great change in laws. For in the New World, and on all the southern shores of Africa and Asia especially, **Christianity** has fixed its roots through Jupiter and the Sun, which incline and act as signs in divine and voluntary matters, while in human and natural matters they also act as causes. In Africa, however, the **Safavid** <note>original: "Setifi" — Likely referring to the Safavid dynasty or related Islamic movements.</note> sect arose through the Moon and Mars. In Persia, the **Ali** <note>original: "Alle" — Referring to the followers of Ali, or Shi'ism.</note> sect was restored by **Ismail** <note>original: "Sosio" — Plausibly a reference to Shah Ismail I, founder of the Safavid Empire.</note> through Venus and Jupiter, coinciding with the change of Empire in those regions. 

But also in **Germany**, **France**, **England**, and almost the entire European North, a dire heresy runs rampant—a friend to lust and bestiality arising from Mars, Venus, and the Moon being powerful there—which seeks to expel human **free will** <note>A reference to the Protestant Reformation, specifically the doctrines of predestination held by reformers like Luther and Calvin, which Campanella (a Catholic) views as a denial of free choice.</note>. **Spain**, however, and **Italy**, because of **Sagittarius** and **Leo** (their respective signs), have remained stubbornly attached to the truth and purity of Christian law—would that they remained so in their morals as well! From the Moon and Mercury, these "Solar" peoples possess new arts, aided by the Sun’s position; for in the air, these stars enable the **art of flying**, just as that which is watery and floating in our regions becomes aerial under the equator.

# ON THE CITY OF THE SUN.

...and flying along because of the Earth's position relative to the more sunny Heavens. Indeed, they have established a new Astronomy, such that in the other hemisphere, from the equator to the South, the house of the Sun is Aquarius, that of the Moon is Capricorn, and so on; they invert all the signs and their powers. And they believe this is necessary by the force of Nature. 

O wonder! How much I have learned from these sages regarding the changes of the **apsides** <term>Apsides: The points in an orbit where a planet is closest to or farthest from the center of its orbit.</term>, eccentricities, and the **obliquity** <term>Obliquity: The tilt of the Earth's axis relative to its orbital plane (the "lean" of the planet), which Campanella believed changed over time.</term> of the equinoxes, solstices, and poles; and about the confusion of the Celestial figures in the immense space of the World's tottering machinery. I learned about the symbols of our earthly affairs in relation to those outside our world, and how much change follows after the "great synod" in Aries and Libra—the equinoctial signs—during the restoration of **anomalies** <term>Anomalies: In pre-modern astronomy, these were irregularities or deviations in a planet's predicted circular motion.</term>. These events, full of wonder, follow after the "great conjunction" to confirm its decree and bring about the change and renewal of the World. 

But I beg you, do not detain me any longer; many things remain for me to do, and you know the cares that trouble me. Another time, then. Yet I will not omit this: they strongly uphold human freedom. They say that if the forty hours during which a great philosopher <note>This is a veiled autobiographical reference to Tommaso Campanella himself. In 1600, he was subjected to a forty-hour torture session called the *veglia* (the vigil) by the Inquisition; he maintained his sanity by pretending to be mad and refusing to confess to heresy or rebellion.</note> among them was most cruelly tortured by his enemies could not compel him to utter even a single word of what they demanded—because he had resolved in his heart to remain silent—then surely the stars, which move so gently and from such a great distance, cannot compel us to act against our own will. 

However, because the stars produce an imperceptible and gentle change in our senses, whoever follows his senses more than divine reason will be subjugated by them. For the same constellation that drew foul vapors from the corpses of heretics also, at that very same time, drew out fragrant exhalations of virtue from the founders of the Jesuit order <note>original: "Iesuiniæ Religionis"</note>, the Minims, and the Capuchins. Under that same influence, Hernán Cortés propagated the Divine Religion of **CHRIST** in Mexico.

I shall tell you more in another conversation about the many things that now threaten the **WORLD**; for **HERESY** indeed...

#### *Concerning the elements, essence, purpose, division, and variety of the family, and its comparison with its whole and its parts.*

->C H A P T E R I.<-
->A R T I C L E I.<-

<margin>The goal of the head of the household.</margin>
<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' decorated with floral patterns and small figures.</image-desc>Since the family is a part of the city or the State <note>original: "Reipublicæ." While often translated as "Republic," in this context it refers to the organized political community or "commonwealth."</note>, and a part—insofar as it is a part—shares the same purpose as its whole, one must conclude that the Peripatetics <term>Peripatetics: The followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy, known for their focus on systematic observation and logic.</term> were incorrect. They claimed that wealth is the goal of the family and the householder <note>original: "œconomi"</note>, while a happy life is the goal of the city and the statesman. Instead, let a happy life be the goal of both.

2. A human being lives in himself, in his children, in his reputation, and in God. Since, however, all lives eventually fail except for that by which we are made eternal in God, it must be asserted that the statesman [directs] all these goals...

<summary>This page introduces Campanella’s treatise on Economics, defining the family as an essential component of the state that shares its ultimate goal: a happy life. He critiques the Aristotelian view that household management is merely about wealth, arguing instead for a broader spiritual and social purpose.</summary>

->F. TOMMASO CAMPANELLA<-
<meta>catchword: while (dum)</meta>

look back, but nevertheless to place all things after eternal life, and likewise to direct all forms of living toward this very thing; so also the Head of the Household <term>Head of the Household: original "Oeconomum." In this context, it refers to the person responsible for the management of the domestic unit.</term> procures goods useful for life in himself, in his reputation, and in his children, but he directs all these things toward the highest eternal good.

3. Although it is more convenient for one person to govern in a family, and several in a republic <note>original: "republica." Here meaning the state or political commonwealth.</note>; nevertheless, in both the former and the latter, several governors could be in charge. But it is better if one governs with the counsel and participation in government of many. Therefore, the wife has a part of the governance in the household management <note>original: "oeconomia."</note>, as do the steward <term>steward: original "architriclinus," a Greek-derived term for the master of a feast or a high-ranking household manager.</term>, the older children, and others, etc. Just as in a republic there is a king, queen, viceroy, judges, etc. A city can also be established in common so that the whole is like one family: as Socrates teaches, and St. Clement, and our *City of the Sun*, which we defended in the questions upon the third book of the *Epilogismi* <note>The *Epilogismi* was a work of Campanella's where he provided further philosophical defenses of his ideas.</note>.

<margin>Definition of the family based on the definition of the city.</margin>
4. Just as a city is a gathering and a union of families for the common preservation of the individual and the species, distributed into diverse duties for various uses and necessities, by which they procure necessary and useful goods for the present and future life; and if the diversity of duties were removed, it would no longer be a city; and if the purpose were removed—which is life or happy preservation—it would by no means be a city; and finally, if the useful goods by which it is preserved were removed, the city is lost: so the family (speaking regularly) is a unity of male and female, and of servants—both rational and irrational <note>In the 17th century, "rational servants" referred to human workers or domestic help, while "irrational servants" referred to livestock and beasts of burden.</note>—distributed into various duties for the various uses and needs of the individual and the species. Thus, if the variety of duties is removed, it is no longer a family; if the purpose—which is happy preservation—is removed, it is not a family; and if at last the external goods by which it is preserved are removed, the family is lost. For this reason, many soldiers in one house do not make a family, because they are like a single limb: as the Apostle says, *if the whole body were an eye, it would not be a body* <note>original: "si totum corpus est oculus, non erit corpus." A reference to 1 Corinthians 12:17, emphasizing that a community requires diverse roles.</note>. Nor do many scholars with their teacher in one house make a family: since their goal is not the preservation of their own gathering and community, but to learn the sciences. Likewise, if any society consists of a husband, wife, children, and servants, who [share] bread, clothing, and a home for living

<summary>Campanella defines the family as a miniature version of the state, sharing the same ultimate goal of eternal happiness while requiring a diversity of roles and duties to function. He argues that a true family is defined by its purpose of communal preservation and the presence of varied responsibilities, distinguishing it from other groups like soldiers or students.</summary>

# ON ECONOMICS <note>original: "OECONOMICORVM"</note> CHAPTER I.

...while it lacks [necessities], although a family is a society of this kind, it is nevertheless suddenly dissolved, with each individual departing to obtain food and other necessities for themselves wherever they may find them.

<margin>objection.</margin>
5. But truly, what shall we say of the monasteries of the mendicant monks <term>mendicant monks: religious orders, like the Franciscans or Dominicans, who took vows of poverty and lived on the charity of others.</term>? For these lack wives for the preservation of the species; nor do they possess property from which individuals may be nourished; nor do they have various offices <note>original: "officia," here referring to the specialized domestic duties or roles within a household</note> designated for procuring food. Likewise, if they even lacked a home, like the Gypsies <term>Gypsies: original "Zingari," referring to Romani people who were perceived by European writers of the time as nomadic and lacking fixed dwellings.</term>, just as many monks and hermits lived in the past; much less could they be said to constitute a family. Nevertheless, they are part of the state <note>original: "reipublicae."</note>. Therefore, etc. There are also in the kingdom of Fez and Morocco certain Muslim religious men, called Marabouts <term>Marabouts: original "Morabitæ," Muslim holy men or hermits in North Africa who often lived in fortified schools or monasteries.</term>, inhabiting monasteries enclosed on all sides by walls, in each of which one monarch rules with four wives and more than forty concubines, each confined in her own cell, and a multitude of children in the same place; and when the monarch dies, the firstborn succeeds in the government. What shall we say of these? Are they a family, or not? There exist other partial groups for living in various regions of the world; namely, the Brahmins <term>Brahmins: original "Brachmani," the priestly and scholarly caste of India.</term> in India, the Bonzes <term>Bonzes: original "Bongi," a term used by early European explorers for Buddhist monks in Japan and China.</term> in Japan, and the Amazon women within Nubia and the kingdom of Monomotapa <note>Monomotapa was a powerful medieval kingdom in Southern Africa, located in the area of modern-day Zimbabwe and Mozambique.</note>, who live without males. From this, it seems that either the philosophers—and especially Aristotle—have not spoken about every form of family, or these aforementioned forms do not constitute a family at all.

<margin>Response.</margin>
6. I respond. Just as the human body cannot exist in which all members are only hands, or only eyes, as the Apostle <note>A reference to St. Paul’s analogy of the "Body of Christ" in 1 Corinthians 12, where different members of the community have different functions.</note> rightly demonstrates, so neither can a city be made in which all are active, or all are contemplative. For it is established that man consists of soul and body. To preserve the body, he requires the active life, which procures food, clothing, and shelter. To preserve the soul, however, he requires religion, doctrine, and various sciences. These also contribute to the active life, so that one may truly know the reason why he ought to labor for the good of the body. The active life also contributes to the contemplative, while it governs the body—the vessel of the contemplating soul—and relieves the mind from the cares of external goods. For this reason, there are several families in the city [dedicated] to contemplation...

<sig>Nnn 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: alone- <note>original: "solum-"</note></meta>

<summary>Campanella examines whether non-traditional groups like celibate monks, nomadic Gypsies, or polygamous North African communities fit the definition of a "family." He concludes that just as a body needs different organs, a society needs diverse types of "families" to fulfill both material (active) and spiritual (contemplative) needs.</summary>
<keywords>family, monasticism, social structure, active life, contemplative life, Marabouts, Amazons, Aristotle, body politic</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 467 regarding how different social groups, like religious orders, function within the state (republic) even when they do not fit the traditional definition of a family unit.</meta>

->F. TOMMASO CAMPANELLA<-

...dedicated only [to contemplation]: such as religious gatherings, schools of learning, and temples. There are also families focused only on action, such as soldiers and farmers. Finally, others are mixed from both parts: just like the houses of philosophers. But indeed, the family is truly the basic element of politics <note>original: "elementum politicæ"</note>, sufficient for the preservation of the individual and the species. Therefore monks, being unable to preserve the species by themselves, gather for themselves the children of others as if by adoption and succession. Furthermore, lacking also the goods by which they might sustain the individual, they seek food and clothing from others, to whom they themselves communicate spiritual goods. Thus they provide for their own "family," by excluding the necessity of having wives for the sake of the species, and of possessing the goods of fortune <term>goods of fortune: material wealth or property</term> for the sake of individuals; and at the same time they devote effort to public utilities through contemplation and through doctrine, which they propagate by word and example. Furthermore, through prayers to God, they call down His help for us, and deify our nature in a most excellent way.

But the family of the Marabouts <term>Marabouts: Islamic holy men in North Africa, whom Campanella views through a highly critical and polemical lens</term> differs greatly from ours. For although it naturally looks out for the species, yet it does not profit that end for which it was instituted. Indeed, staying with several women shut up within the enclosures of the monastery, and delighting daily in their embrace and company—calling now this one, now that one to satisfy lust—overturns all contemplation and science. On account of these things, all Marabouts are most ignorant, full of superstition, and live a swinish life. Nor can they be called a part of the Republic <note>original: "Respublica," meaning the state or organized society</note> in the way a limb is part of a body; rather, they are like a worm born within the limbs or the belly, which devours the body and does not benefit the whole, but harms it by infesting it and taking away its food. 

This is surely proven by the fact that among them there is no true religiousness or knowledge, but only the most ignorant superstition; and they think it is permitted to them to copulate in the manner of beasts <note>original: "brutorum more subagitare"</note> with whatever woman they meet in the streets, even if she is not their own. Furthermore, just as men once adored the elements and beasts, so the African peoples worship these lazy and beastly men. Concerning other sects and families which are in the world, we read of somewhat better things in histories. But indeed, since neither souls [can be separated] from bodies, nor bodies...

<meta>catchword: pora:</meta>

7. Therefore, since the family is a part of the city formed in the likeness of the human body, it likewise possesses a man and a woman in the place of the soul; <margin>||</margin> in the place of the body, it has the home; in the place of external goods, it has servants, animals, and the estate. Just as, evidently, the city has its citizens for a soul; its dwellings and walls for a body; and its territory, animals, and servants in the place of external goods.

->*We must now speak of the establishment of the family and its governance, which is divided into acquisition, preservation, and enjoyment—or distribution.*<-

# CHAPTER II.
## ARTICLE I.

1. It is the duty of the statesman <term>statesman: original "Politicus," referring to one skilled in the art of governing a community</term> to first establish a family, and then indeed to govern it.

2. In this establishment, it is necessary to obtain a wife, a home, servants, and other external goods.

3. In governance, one must carry out duties as they have been established. And since to govern is to preserve and to lead the thing governed toward its proper end, it is therefore necessary to acquire goods for preservation, to keep those things which have been acquired, and finally to use and distribute them. Our discourse now turns to these actions.

<header>OF BROTHER THOMAS CAMPANELLA
On the establishment of the dwelling.</header>

### ARTICLE II.

1. A good Household Manager <term>Household Manager: original "Oeconomus," referring to the person responsible for the administration of a domestic estate</term> first prepares a habitation, just as nature first forms the body in which the soul is to dwell.

2. Therefore, in the foundation of a house, he shall consider several things. First, that the air be healthy and receive plenty of sun inside during the winter; and in the summer and other seasons, that it receive healthy winds, such as the northern <note>original: "boreales"</note> and western winds in our region. Nor should it be built in a lower part of the city, where thick air grows stagnant and the rains and uncleanness of the city lie and gather; nor where there is little light, a short day, and meager clarity.

Secondly, a place must be chosen in which the house can defend itself during civil unrest <note>original: "seditione," referring to riots or local uprisings common in Campanella's era</note>, when such occurs; and it should offer an easy entrance for things pertaining to food and supplies. Let it be near healthy waters, or have a spring bubbling up inside; likewise, let it be near the market, the temple, and other principal places. Also, if possible, let it be where the blows of hammers and the noises of craftsmen are absent: for although the air may be thinned by such activity, the senses and the work of contemplation are nevertheless disturbed by them.

Thirdly, let it be built so that it is convenient for all domestic duties and for the preservation of necessary things. Therefore, it shall have one large gate through which necessities may be brought in and through which entrance is open to all; and usefully, another small side-door <note>original: "ostiolum falsum," literally a "false door" or secret postern</note> that is hidden. Likewise, let there be a large courtyard. It will also be seen as a good thing if peristyles <note>A continuous porch formed by a row of columns surrounding a courtyard</note>, commonly called cloisters, like those of monasteries, adorn the walls on the inside.

Here, indeed, in the very lowest part of the dwelling—which is sometimes built underground—small rooms should be prepared for liquid things, such as oil, wine, and the like; for these require shade and cold for their preservation. Let there be a place for horses, but one that is less damp; likewise another for useful dogs. Both of these should face the south or the west, while the rooms for liquids should face the north. Furthermore, on the ground level or a little higher near the gate, there should be rooms for the common servants <note>original: "seruorum ignobilium," referring to laborers as opposed to high-ranking domestic officials</note> and the guards of the whole dwelling. Further inside, let there be the rooms for rustic tools, equestrian equipment, and arms. All things...

...so they will lie distinct so that they are immediately available to those searching for them. A little higher up, after ascending some steps, the masters' quarters should be built—namely, for the husband, wife, and children—facing every quarter of the sky: summer quarters to the north, winter to the south, autumn and spring to the east or west, as the opportunity of the air and location shall determine.

Larger halls should also be formed between them. Therefore, a square shape will be suitable for this house. In the highest part of the palace, quarters for the maidservants and boys should be built, but in such a way that they do not walk over the master's roof at any time; and places for some armaments and things hostile to thick humidity should be made, such as legumes, grain, gunpowder <note>original: "pulveris bellici," literally "war powder"</note>, and silks.

The Master of the House <note>original: "Aulae totius magister," referring to a Major Domo or head steward</note> and the nobler servants shall live in the second level of buildings, or on the same floor as the master's; but in such a way that access to the women and the masters is blocked, except for those who handle more private domestic affairs for the master.

Fourthly, it is necessary to have a cistern or fountain within the courtyard, or the passage of a river via a common aqueduct, which the Neapolitans call a *Formale* <note>original: "Formalem," the local name for the ancient Bolla aqueduct system in Naples</note>; likewise, places for washing; and consequently, ingenious machines through which water is carried from bronze aqueducts into all the rooms, but especially into the dining rooms <note>original: "refectoria, seu cœnacula"</note>, and most of all into the kitchen, by the slight movement of a single handle, as modern engineers <term>Engineers: original "mechanici," referring to those who design and build machines</term> actually demonstrate. 

But let no one ever enter the kitchen except the cook, his assistants, and those whom it concerns. The boys, however, should receive the dishes through a small window made in the wall or door of the kitchen. Let there also be a small window for the women, so they do not need to go out into the common hall; through this, by means of a built-in wooden wheel <note>original: "rotam ligneam," a "turn" or revolving cabinet used in cloistered monasteries to exchange goods without the parties seeing each other</note>, such as nuns <note>original: "sanctimoniales"</note> are accustomed to use in their convents, they may receive from the servants and provide necessary items.

3. Where so many requirements cannot be had, even a poor man should prepare a house for himself, as best he can, according to the pattern already described...

## *On the institution of the wife and marriage.*

### ARTICLE III.

1. Since the male and the female are the first elements of the commonwealth <note>original: "reipubl.", referring to the state or organized society</note>, upon whom almost every good and evil of the city depends, marriages should be managed so that they are celebrated only according to natural compatibility, so that the offspring may be of noble stock <note>original: "generosa," meaning well-bred or of high quality in a biological and moral sense</note>. It is fitting, moreover, for a thin man to be joined to a stout and plump woman, and vice-versa; for an angry woman, a mild male; and they should be of great physical size and fit for generating others, so that the commonwealth may be made eternal through a better succession. For marriage is a sacrosanct bond instituted by God, both for propagating the species and so that the male and female might be able to help each other and live with joy and honor. Therefore, God divided the sexes and made the woman charming, soft, timid, cautious, pious, and tenacious; namely, so that she might cherish the received seed, <margin>+</margin> give birth, and raise the offspring, and so that she might guard and preserve household affairs at home. Conversely, He made the male robust, confident, combative, and prudent; namely, so that he might sow, generate, instruct, and defend the offspring and the wife, and so that he might acquire household goods abroad and command. For this reason, only those who are fit for the aforementioned purposes should be joined in marriage, based on the consultation of physicians and wise elders; not according to dowries or external riches, but according to the goods of mind and body. Thus a king, for example, would better provide for himself and the commonwealth if he joined his son to a woman under his rule who was the most excellent, prudent, beautiful, robust, and fertile, rather than to another queen who was lazy, deformed, weak, and unfit for offspring. I say the same for all citizens proportionally. See *The City of the Sun* <note>original: "Ciuitatem Solis." This is Campanella's most famous work, a utopian vision where the state controls breeding to ensure the health of the population.</note>.

<meta>catchword: 2. Female-</meta>

<summary>Campanella argues that marriage is the foundational unit of the state and should be regulated by "natural compatibility" and physical health rather than wealth or social status. He defines traditional gender roles as divinely ordained functions intended to ensure the survival and strength of the community.</summary>
<keywords>marriage, eugenics, commonwealth, gender roles, City of the Sun, procreation, social stability</keywords>

473
<header>ON ECONOMICS, CHAPTER II.</header>

2. A woman is suitable for marriage when she is no less than nineteen years of the feminine lunar cycle <note>The Metonic cycle of 19 years, which Campanella links here to biological maturity.</note>. Indeed, before this age, she is not fit for producing robust offspring; her seed is weak, and when she swells <note>in pregnancy</note>, the outer skin of the belly is prone to rupture, and the womb is often damaged. The male will be suitable after his twenty-seventh year, although *Plato* and *Aristotle* assign the thirty-sixth year. However, their rule is difficult for our times, and is better suited to cold northern nations than to our climates. It is absolutely necessary for the male to be older in age, since according to nature he matures more slowly than the female; just as more robust plants mature more slowly than weaker ones. Likewise, the active power <note>original: "virtus actiua," an Aristotelian concept where the male provides the "active" principle in reproduction</note> is required to be more powerful and mature than the passive power. Furthermore, he must be fit for producing robust offspring and for ruling the family. *Aristotle*, agreeing with *Hesiod*, said that one ought to take a young girl as a wife so that you may accustom her to your manners from the beginning, and so she will not have tasted any other love. This saying is certainly true if only the reason of sexual pleasure and pleasant company is considered; but since the primary end of marriage is the generation and education of children—which is a fact known to everyone—this must be considered above all else. Indeed, *Aristotle* even contradicts himself: for in the first book of the *Economics* he wishes for a young girl alongside *Hesiod*, but in the seventh book of the *Politics* he suggests she be no less than eighteen years old, a point he took from *Plato*. Furthermore, *Hesiod* was speaking of a handmaid, not of a wife, and thus his reasoning follows that line. *Plato*, however, speaks of a wife, and his reasons in the *Politics* of *Aristotle* are better: namely, that for the sake of better generation, one ought to take a young woman, not a mere child, so that she does not become accustomed to sexual matters too early, lest they drink in incontinence and the manners of a harlot.

3. You shall not demand a dowry from a wife who is adorned with the strengths of body and mind. But if you are able to have that as well, consider yourself better advised. Among other nations, the male provides the dowry to the female. But following natural reason, we say that the one who has ought to give to the one who has not—whether male or female—so that the commonwealth <note>original: "respubl."</note> may everywhere procure equality, which is the preserver of itself. Destruction...

# *On the establishment of the country estate.*

## ARTICLE IV.

1. After the wife, the next thing required for the perfection of the family is the Countryside <note>original: "Rus," the rural territory</note>, or a villa, from which food and clothing are obtained. Furthermore, of all the arts, <term>Agriculture</term> and <term>Animal Husbandry</term> are the best. This is true first for the "goods of the soul," since they distract the mind from fraudulent arts—such as banking and trade—and from base ones—such as inn-keeping, the selling of delicacies, and similar trades. It is also true for the "goods of the body," because these labors make a man healthy, robust, and handsome with a manly rather than an effeminate beauty, and they make him fit for acquiring and defending a home. Moreover, it is natural for a human to receive nourishment from his own mother—which is the Earth—and therefore to cultivate her; for she provides food, water, wine, oil, and other liquids, just like milk from breasts. However, she must not be dug up and disemboweled so that metals and stones, which are only useful for the affliction of human nature, may be torn out. For this reason, the Romans religiously forbade the Italian soil from being gutted by mining, lest they appear like the matricide Nero <note>The Emperor Nero was infamously said to have ordered the womb of his mother, Agrippina, to be opened after her death so he could see where he had been conceived.</note>, eager to peer into what a mother carries in her womb. Furthermore, while all arts are useful to the state, a wise man will prefer those which are more useful to nature, justice, and the health of both body and soul.

2. Therefore, your estate shall be of such a size that it can provide sufficient grain for your family, and a little more. Likewise, it should be able to be divided into parts, so that one part may bear fruit this year while the other lies fallow; and in the following year, conversely, that part may bear—

He also justifies the use of dowries in marriage as a means for a wife to contribute to her own upkeep within the household.</summary>

...[is suf]ficient, let that land lie fallow. Likewise, separately within the estate, you should plant a double garden; in one, you will plant all medicinal herbs, and in the other, whatever is useful for human food, sufficient for your family.

You will choose another portion of land, suitable for a vineyard and adorned with hills, for Bacchus <note>original: "Baccho," the Roman god of wine, here representing viticulture</note>; or perhaps one planted with orchards. It is also necessary to have a wooded portion occupied by groves, which is profitable for oxen and other animals dedicated to farming, as well as for fowling and hunting. There shall also be a portion left fallow as a pasture for oxen and livestock; in this way, the land’s utility will not be entirely lacking, and for the following year, it will be fertilized much better by their manure. You should also have portable pastoral fences, woven from wicker <note>original: "viminibus"</note>, to be set up and taken down during the annual rotations of the land, both for the gathering of the animals and for their protection. You shall also establish an olive grove in drier, stony, and higher places. You will divide and decorate the land with fruit-bearing plants. Also, build granaries <note>original: "horrea"</note> in which certain crops may be stored, along with everything pertaining to the food, clothing, and bedding of the farmworkers. In the same place, you will also have a stable for horses and donkeys. Likewise, a small chapel <note>original: "sacellum"</note>, where they may gather especially on feast days to attend sacred rites, commend themselves and their work to God, and not allow themselves to forget these duties, but rather advise and teach one another. On the peak of the manor house they shall have a sort of banner <note>original: "vexillum," serving here as a weather vane</note>, a sign showing all the winds; from this they may know which wind is helpful or harmful to which things, and at what times they usually blow. The upper and more beautiful part of the buildings shall be properly furnished for the sake of the master and his children, should they ever wish to visit the countryside for pleasure, hunting, or for business. A fountain, cistern, or stream is also necessary in the courtyard of the house. Let everything be done according to the rules expressed above, as the nature of the circumstances permits.

## *On the organization of rational, irrational, and natural servants, etc.*

### ARTICLE V.

1. The best possession of a Householder <note>original: "Oeconomi," the person in charge of managing the household and its resources</note> are his servants. For they are his **rational instruments**; through them and by them, his power is spread across all household actions. Indeed, the master directly directs the rational instrument, which is the servant. The rational instrument, in turn, directs the **animal instruments**, namely oxen, horses, dogs, and sheep. These animal instruments then move the **artificial instruments**, which are the plow, the cart, the oil press, the mill, and so on. Finally, the artificial instruments move the **natural instruments** and their objects: which are the earth, grain, olives, vines, and other plants and things, according to a certain marvelous order. Nevertheless, rational instruments are capable of producing all effects without other instruments, except usually those of craft. For these reasons, the householder should take the greatest care to choose rational instruments through whom his power is communicated to every outcome.

2. Servants shall be as many as are sufficient for domestic and rural duties and exercises. Among the rural workers, there shall be a division of labor, so that some guard the livestock, others care for the dairy, others for agriculture, others for the beasts of burden, and so on. Let there be one head and master over them: who shall live in the rural manor, knowing how to record in a book the expenses, income, expenditures, and the fruits that are gathered. On the first of every month <note>original: "singulis Kalendis"</note>, he shall give an account to the master. He shall punish the others, especially the slaves <note>original: "mancipia"</note> and the young boys, for minor faults; but for great and more serious matters, he shall report to the master. He shall also note who works sluggishly and who works vigorously, as well as who they are and why they act so.

<note>original vocabulary: Householder, servants, rational instruments, animal instruments, man-made instruments, natural instruments, slaves, agriculture</note>

# ON ECONOMICS, CHAPTER II.

...wherefore they desist from work. Nor, unless by the counsel or testimony of two others of the best among them, should he <note>the overseer</note> undertake and handle this and many other matters.

3. In an urban household <note>original: "civili etiam domo," referring to a city residence as opposed to a rural farm</note>, the number of functions will determine the number of servants. Therefore, let there be one or more cooks, according to the size of the family, to prepare the feasts and all the food. Another should be the one who buys what pertains to sustenance: in a small family, the same person will be both cook and **purveyor** <term>expensor: the person responsible for purchasing supplies and tracking daily spending</term>; in the homes of the very poor, this is the maidservant or the wife herself. Another is required as a **clerk** <note>original: "scriba"</note>, who will keep the account of expenses: in small houses, he is also the master’s secretary, the writer and keeper of letters. Another, whom they commonly call a **steward** <note>original: "dispensatorem"</note>, will take care of the keys to the storerooms for oil, wine, grain, and legumes: or there will be several such people, according to the size of the family. A **valet** <note>original: "cubicularius," literally a chamber-servant</note> also seems necessary to care for the master’s clothing and person: but where women live together, they will perhaps better care for the clothes and the person of the wife; the valet, however, will attend to the master. It also seems necessary to have someone who manages the care of horses, just as there are carriages in Naples and gondolas in Venice: in a large house, one person is the **master of the stable**, and several serve under him. To these are added **footmen**, who are called *stafferii* <note>original: "pedissequi, qui stafferii vocantur," from the Italian *staffiere*, a groom or lackey who walks by the master's stirrup</note>; these precede the master as if announcing him, clearing the way and defending him: and boys <note>pages</note>, who follow behind, performing light services. This, however, seems to be a specimen of mere vanity. For one boy is enough to serve the person, and one footman for his protection and the care of the horse. In a well-ordered republic, such superfluities are not admitted.

4. The head of the family must be very careful that the number of servants does not become excessive; where one is sufficient for one function and service, two should not be employed. For they will perform the function more poorly, with one shifting the responsibility onto the other; and they are mostly idle, filling the house with wantonness, lewdness, games, lies, mockery, idleness, and other vanities and crimes that ruin a family.

5. On the wife’s side, it is necessary to have an elderly woman of good character from her own kin to serve as an exemplar...

...who lived honorably in her youth: let her be as a guardian of the wife, a mistress of the maidservants, and an overseer of their duties. Also, include a woman of lower status, or a purchased slave, to handle the menial chores. Furthermore, engage one or two higher-born maidservants—or even more, depending on the size and nobility of the family. It will be their duty to assist the mistress, to work on the household furnishings, and to weave and spin, just as Calabrian women do today and Roman women did in antiquity <note>Campanella, a Calabrian himself, often looks to his home region and classical Rome for models of industriousness</note>. Indeed, as both Solomon and Homer recommend for noblewomen <note>Referring to the "Virtuous Woman" in Proverbs 31 and Penelope in the *Odyssey*</note>, they should never live in idleness. Otherwise, they will devote themselves to love affairs and even entice the stable-hands. For nothing is worse than an idle girl.

6. Furthermore, just as it is fitting to have a mistress of the women, so too should one have a master of the servants, whom they commonly call a **Major-domo** <term>Maiordomus: the head of the household staff</term>. In distinguished families, there are also a cup-bearer, a baker, a carver <note>original: "qui in mensa secat in frusta carnes," a specialist who cuts the meat at the table</note>, a server of dishes, and a master of the hall. Moreover, there should be another to teach the servants their letters and the arts of service, as well as their purpose and good manners, and to punish failings and faults. Another is usually employed as a master of dancing, another for riding, another for handling weapons, and others for various noble exercises. Accordingly, care must be taken that they do not become accustomed to games of dice and gambling <note>original: "ludis taxillorum & alearum"</note> or others of this kind; for these breed greed, rapacity, perjury, fraud, and bad character. Instead, let there be games that add virtue and strength.

7. Having considered the number of servants, it seems necessary to speak of their character and condition. Aristotle <note>Referring to the Greek philosopher's *Politics*</note> advises against choosing servant classes that are too timid, because they cannot endure labor; nor those who are too strong, because they are not easily commanded; nor those of the same language, especially a foreign tongue <note>original: "barbarae"</note>, lest they form factions in the house. Indeed, I think such conditions can be wished for, but not easily obtained. I believe it is easy and useful for them to be of different languages; otherwise, if they all speak one language unknown to you, they might deceive the master and the children, and alert one another without your knowledge if they have decided to do something evil or to run away. Nor will there be strife and factionalism between them and your other household members. But, regarding their character, I would say...

<summary>Campanella outlines the hierarchy and moral education of domestic staff, emphasizing the need for constant labor to prevent vice and the strategic selection of servants from different backgrounds to prevent conspiracies.</summary>

# ON ECONOMICS, CHAPTER II.
<meta>catchword: Concerning</meta>

...servants of any condition are of use; and they are to be used, just like money, for what they are worth. Therefore, those who are more fearful will be useful for guarding the doors and the household property; for they do not dare to steal, nor to admit wicked people, and they are watchful because of fear. However, those who are stronger and bolder shall be grooms <term>Stafferii: footmen or grooms who accompanied a horse or carriage</term>, and rural guards, and honest hunters. Any agile and swift person will not be unsuited as a runner or a courier. Those strong in loyalty should be at the master's side and in his bodyguard. The more gifted shall be placed in charge of the others. 

The Swiss <note>original: "Heluetii"</note> and the French, therefore, are generally good at guarding household property, preparing provisions, managing expenses, and guarding the women—though not, however, at guarding the wine <note>A common humorous stereotype in early modern texts suggesting Northern Europeans were prone to drinking</note>. The Spanish are vigilant in supervising others, and are shrewd scouts and spokesmen; however, you should not entrust the household property, the women, or any business where the utmost trust is required to them, despite their naturally silent disposition. Neapolitans are suited for softer duties requiring little labor and much ceremony. Calabrians are for heavier tasks, where strength and labor, but not ceremonies, are required. Lombards are found to be the best masters of the halls. Let the Florentines and Genoese apply themselves to profits <note>Refers to their historical reputation as bankers and merchants</note>, etc. Thus you shall proceed by considering the customs of nations. But they sometimes deceive. Therefore, one must take account of individuals through physiognomy <term>physiognomia: the practice of judging a person's character or future from their facial features</term> and by knowing them through social interaction.

8. It is better to have purchased slaves of a boyish age, who do not know or may forget their homeland and parents, than those of a youthful or adult age. Likewise, it is better to buy servants than to hire them for a wage; for you can treat the former as you please, but the latter by no means. Likewise, for business requiring trust and for guarding property, Turks are more suitable. Where there is need of cunning and scouting others, Moors. You can manage Black people in laborious business as you please; you shall feed them with plenty of food, but with little or no wine. But it is good to have slaves from various nations and languages, mixed with servants of your own nation. Those who are more excellent shall be set over the others. Let food and freedom be the incentives for serving well for the base, and honor and dignity for the better ones, as the following discourses will teach.

FRIAR TOMMASO CAMPANELLA On the Governance of the Family.

# CHAPTER III.

## On the dominion of the head of the household according to nature and the state.

### ARTICLE I.

1. After we have explained what form and how many essential parts are appropriate for the institution of the family, it is now necessary to add a precise discussion concerning the governance of that same family and its individual parts.
2. The father in a family is the same as the king in a city-state. He possesses natural dominion over his wife and children; political dominion over his servants; and despotic dominion <note>original: "despoticum"; in this context, it refers to the absolute control a master has over property or "chattel" rather than a tyrant's rule</note> over his cattle, trees, estate, and buildings.
3. By nature, the male rules over the female and the parent over the children for three reasons. First, because he excels as the wiser; and wisdom is the foundation of natural dominion, just as the Apostle <note>A reference to St. Paul, specifically regarding 1 Timothy 2:12</note> teaches; for this reason, he generally takes away the authority of preaching and teaching from women. Second, because he is stronger: for nature is accustomed to subject the weaker to the stronger—though not in cases where the weaker might be the wiser. Third, because they are "something of him" <note>An Aristotelian concept that the family is an extension of the man's own body</note>: for the woman has her origin from the man and is, as it were, a part of him, although in relation to the children she is like a partner and a co-principle. From the male and female one perfect human being is made, capable of generating humans, which one part alone cannot do. Over the children, however, as if over their own property and a part and fruit of themselves, both parents have dominion, though the wife has far less.

Therefore, Aristotle is in error <note>original: "peccat"; literally "sins," but here used in the academic sense of making a philosophical mistake</note> when he denies that the father has perfect dominion over his son and wife. Indeed, he ought to have considered it more perfect than the dominion a king has over his vassals <term>vassallos: subjects in a feudal system who owe allegiance to a superior</term>, as is evident from the reasons for paternal dominion already stated: since [the dominion] of vassals...

<summary>Campanella defines the father's authority as a natural monarchy, justifying his rule over his wife, children, and property through arguments of wisdom, physical strength, and biological unity.</summary>

...some vassals are wiser and stronger than the king; moreover, none of the vassals are "something of the king" <note>original: "aliquid regis"; a philosophical concept meaning an extension of the ruler's person</note> in the way a wife and son belong to a father according to nature, but only according to the institution of the city. This city is many families gathered into one; and so that they may live conveniently, they place over themselves one common father called a King—a name derived from *ruling* <note>original: "regendo"</note>, not from *dominating* <note>original: "dominando"</note>. 

And although the father holds less power than the king, since he cannot kill his wife and children even when they commit a deed worthy of death, this does not happen to the father because of a lack of natural dominion, but because of a lack of political dominion. For men coming together into one established what is called "policy" in Greek <note>original: "politia"</note>, so that in enormous crimes, jurisdiction should belong not to the father of one family, but to the Father of all. This is because the fatherly devotion of a particular father does not always allow for a right judgment; indeed, he would most often, if not always, acquit his accused wife and children, or he would be so enraged against them that he would punish them cruelly and suddenly, outside the law. It was for this reason that Archytas <note>Archytas of Tarentum, a Pythagorean philosopher and statesman known for his self-control</note> refused to punish even a slave until the heat of his anger had cooled. 

Furthermore, in our own illnesses, we all flee to a doctor—not because we are all "something of him" or because we are not ourselves doctors, but so that we do not treat ourselves less correctly by being deceived by our own personal feelings. 

<margin>Genesis 2</margin>
Furthermore, God himself also subjected the wife to the husband, saying: *You shall be under the man’s power, and he shall rule over you.* The Apostle <note>St. Paul</note> teaches the same, subjecting children to the authority of their parents, just as Moses did in ancient times; Moses even passed a law allowing parents to sell their children <note>A reference to Exodus 21:7, though here used to illustrate the extent of ancient paternal authority</note>. 

But when Aristotle argues the contrary—on the basis that justice exists between two separate people, and likewise dominion, whereas a son is like a part of the father and a slave is like a tool—he proves nothing, except that paternal dominion is not acquired, nor is it "despotic" <note>referring to the rule of a master over property</note>, nor is it a civil thing established by the city or policy. Instead, it is natural, derived from nature, which is the foundation, the rule, and the strength of all forms of dominion. For this reason, the Senators of a Republic are called "Heads" and "Fathers" <note>original: "patres patritiique"; referring to the Roman Patricians</note>; and kings in ancient times were called "Fathers." The entirety of the Scripture of God and the works of the better Philosophers teaches that they are fathers and shepherds. Likewise, no one doubts...

### ARTICLE II.

1. Where the law of having only one wife prevails—as the Christian, ancient Roman, and Greek laws decreed—there the woman is more a sharer in governance, more honored, and is held as a part of the man and a "co-principle" <note>original: "comprincipium"; a philosophical term meaning a joint source or origin, suggesting the wife is a partner in the "originating" of the family</note>. This seems to have been proven by God when he built woman from the rib of man—and from one man, one woman. As the Scripture says: *Now they are not two, but one flesh.* This is for the purpose of the sexes, which is to produce other humans by coming together into one principle, or "joint-origination."

# FRIAR TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

## Laws for a husband toward his wife in household management.

### ARTICLE III.

1. **A** husband must treat his wife as a partner in life and as a co-principle <note>original: *conprincipium*; a philosophical term Campanella uses to argue that both parents are active sources of a child’s life, rather than the mother being a passive vessel.</note> of generation, through whom the life of both is made eternal. Likewise, he ought to love and honor her out of charity; and when she has sinned out of ignorance, he should admonish her privately. He should never punish her with a rod—except for the gravest faults—but rather with appeals to her sense of shame and with sober words. If, however, she should be stubborn, bold, or prone to lust, he should remove her opportunities for sinning and overlook many of her smaller faults. Nor should he pollute the marriage with the love of other women, or of those of lower character. For such an example would grant the wife license to do the same. Indeed, there is no greater grief for a woman than when she is defrauded in love. Furthermore, from such acts, spurious children <note>term: "spurious" (spurii); children born outside of a legal marriage, often called illegitimate.</note> will be born, who bring injury to the wife and the legitimate children, as well as disgrace to the father. Moreover, let there be decency in the sexual act with the wife; and before such acts, let him abstain from bad foods, shameful actions, and wicked thoughts, so that a good offspring may arise. He shall also 
<margin>+</margin>
teach his wife that the sexual act was not given by God for the sake of pleasure, but for the sake of generating others like themselves. This is a most sacred business, and it is to be handled with reverence. In this way, you will receive a worthy child, and you will discourage and extinguish in your wife any tendencies toward meretricious <note>meaning "characteristic of a prostitute" or shameful.</note> intercourse, impudence, and unrestrained, unregulated lust.

2. You shall give the wife authority over all the women of the household and over the preservation of the family's property. You shall not treat her dishonestly. You shall not introduce adulterous or shameful people into the home. Do not degrade her as if she were a servant girl. You should not display jealousy, but rather confidence in her. When, however, you wish to correct something wicked that you suspect in her, you should frame your speech as if talking about another person. For example: tell her how some man killed his wife because of her luxury <note>In this context, "luxury" often refers to sexual excess or infidelity.</note>, and how she paid the deserved penalties for it. Exaggerate the crime, adding that if you were in that man's place, you would have demanded a far more severe punishment. But at times it will be better...

He who devotes himself to this kind of spying will perpetually run into those pains which a physician is unable to dispel. Otherwise, you will show either that you wish to "sell" her <note>That is, putting her on display to attract others.</note>, or you will reveal a levity of spirit. You shall do the same with your children and other household members in a proportional manner.

## Laws for a wife toward her husband and family in household governance.

### ARTICLE IV.

A woman ought to consider that she has been "purchased" for her husband <note>This refers to the legal and economic nature of marriage contracts in the early modern period, where the transfer of dowry or bride-price defined the social contract.</note>. And because she is of lesser value <note>The author reflects the contemporary Aristotelian view that the male is the superior, active principle and the female the secondary, passive principle in a household.</note>, she herself gives a price and reward to the husband so that he may be her protection and guardianship. For wives also give their husbands a dowry where they are not held in the place of slaves. Elsewhere, however, the husband buys the women, as among the Chinese and Muslims <note>original: *Machometanos*</note>. A woman, therefore, must strive with all her might not to be worthy of servile subjection, but of lovable companionship. Furthermore, let her understand that the marital union was not established for the sake of pleasure, but so that they may bear a "tribute" of children to God and the state, and for themselves immortality, and for old age a recompense, help, defense, and nourishment from those children, as well as honor in heaven and on earth.

# FROM THE WORKS OF FRIAR TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

2. Raguel and Anna <note>These figures appear in the Book of Tobit, a text found in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles. Their daughter, Sarah, marries the younger Tobias.</note> depicted the **duties of a wife** when they joined Sarah to the younger Tobias in marriage, as sacred history <note>original: "historia sacra," referring here to the Bible.</note> testifies, saying: *The parents, taking hold of their daughter, kissed her and let her go. Warning her to (1) honor her in-laws, (2) love her husband, (3) rule the family, (4) govern the home, (5) and to show herself to be irreproachable.*

3. <note>The original manuscript repeats the number "3" for this and the following section.</note> You indeed owe, O woman, by the law of nature, honor to your elders; therefore, you owe it much more to your **in-laws**, as if they were your own parents, since they are the parents of your husband, with whom you are **one flesh**. <note>A reference to Genesis 2:24, a foundational concept in Christian marriage theology.</note> The husband owes the same to the wife’s parents. And in turn, each owes this to all blood relatives and relations by marriage. Indeed, among the virtues of marriage, that one is considered of no small importance by which differing families are gathered together, and those in discord are reconciled, and the seeds are sown for a noble offspring. For this reason, if a woman honors her husband’s parents less than she should, she goes against the virtue of marriage. It is also common for **jealousy** to arise between a mother-in-law and a daughter-in-law, because the love of the son is transferred from the mother to the wife. This also happens between a son-in-law and a mother-in-law, but not to such a great extent. Therefore, in this matter, a love that is patient, kind, and prudent is required to suffocate and remove the seeds of discord.

3. Regarding the second point, she must, after God, **love her husband above all else**. She should regard his will as a law given to her by God in matters that are good or indifferent <term>indifferentibus: "adiaphora" or matters not morally central to salvation, such as daily household choices</term>, but not in matters of vice, should he command anything evil. In this way, she will better satisfy both God and her husband; for once his wicked impulse has passed, the husband will love his wife more because she did not consent to his depravity. Furthermore, the more she experiences being loved by her husband, the more she ought to revere him. For excessive love often breeds contempt, contempt breeds hatred, and hatred breeds discord and contention; from these, one eventually arrives at the disgrace and ruin of one’s reputation, the family estate, and finally the home itself. Likewise, she shall not plot against the marriage for any reason. For this is the principal concern in marriage: namely, the **certainty of offspring** from one wife, known to none but the husband, by which he provides for his own immortality <note>Campanella views the fathering of legitimate children as a form of "biological immortality" or the continuation of the self through time.</note> with such certainty as he is able. Therefore, if he suspects or knows that another man might have a part in her embrace, the [purpose] of marriage is lost...

the goal, and in her the man finds rest. Therefore, she shall not defraud him, nor shall she give any occasion for **jealousy**. Indeed, the more she recognizes that her husband suffers from jealousy, the more she should increase her own holiness <note>In this context, "holiness" refers to the wife's purity, modesty, and religious devotion.</note>; in his presence, she should abstain from every look, word, or act that does not please her husband. For to a jealous man, even a fly—as the proverb goes—appears like a horse. <note>A traditional saying suggesting that for someone prone to suspicion, the smallest trifle is magnified into a major threat.</note> The true prudence of a wife is to ensure that her husband’s heart trusts her entirely, and that he believes that when he is away, no comfort is pleasing to her, whether at home or abroad.

Furthermore, she shall not admit anyone into the house whom the husband has not introduced. Aristotle <note>The author refers to the *Oeconomica*, a work attributed to Aristotle in the Renaissance, which provided guidelines for managing a household.</note> noted this well as a way to remove suspicion: if any fault should arise, it would not be blamed on the wife. Moreover, she ought not only to love but also to fear <note>This "fear" is intended as a deep, filial respect or "holy fear" rather than terror.</note> her husband, not demanding to be feared by him, but only to be loved, just as Paul concludes in his letter to the Ephesians, <note>A reference to Ephesians 5:33: "let the wife see that she respects her husband."</note> and Peter, that other prince of the church, praises Sarah for calling her husband Abraham "her Lord." <note>A reference to 1 Peter 3:6.</note> And she fulfilled this not only in voice, as is the custom in the present day, but in reality.

4. Furthermore, if any adverse fortune should befall the husband, she should show herself even more diligent, benevolent, sympathetic, and serving toward him. For misfortune is the test of true and prudent love. It is easy to love in prosperity, but to love in adversity is heroic. Rightly, therefore, Saint Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Archbishop of Constantinople known for his eloquent preaching.</note> praises Sarah because she followed Abraham through so many labors and adversities, and exposed herself to so many dangers for him—even the loss of her honor—in Egypt and in Palestine. 

A woman's love should also be such that it proves itself even after her husband's death. I certainly would not want her to bury herself alive with her husband, like the wives of the Scythians; <note>Ancient nomadic people of Central Asia; Greek historians like Herodotus claimed their widows were sometimes sacrificed.</note> nor to burn herself with him on a single pyre, as is the custom in Narfinga; <note>original: "Narfinga." This refers to the Vijayanagara Empire in Southern India, where European travelers often reported the practice of Sati (widow burning).</note> but let them instead imitate Judith, <note>The heroine of the Book of Judith, who remained a widow and a symbol of Jewish strength after saving her people.</note> who preserved her widowhood in chastity and was glorious for it; and Penelope, <note>The wife of Odysseus (Ulysses) in Greek mythology, famous for waiting twenty years for his return while fending off suitors.</note> who, while her husband was absent, admitted no union or pleasure, though she was solicited by suitors and urged otherwise by her father and father-in-law. Because of this, she deserved that Ulysses should reject the immortality offered by Circe for her sake. Ariosto <note>Ludovico Ariosto, author of the epic poem *Orlando Furioso* (1516). Isabella is a character who chooses death rather than breaking her vow of chastity to her late lover, Zerbino.</note> described a similar example in Isabella: who, to keep faith with the deceased Zer<meta>Catchword: bino</meta>

...before she would consent to the will of the one pursuing her, she obtained her own death by a clever trick. <note>original: "bino... mortem propriam astu, impetrauit." The text likely refers to a virtuous woman, possibly from a historical or hagiographical account, who chose death over a second marriage.</note> However, we by no means condemn second marriages—though they are "condemned by the turtledoves"—while we strive to uphold the slippery faith of women. <note>The turtledove was a traditional symbol of lifelong fidelity; it was believed that if its mate died, it would never take another.</note>

5. The third precept of Raguel <note>Raguel is a figure from the Book of Tobit in the Apocrypha, known for the instructions he gives to his daughter Sarah upon her marriage.</note> was: **To rule the family.** In this, much prudence is required of a wife: namely, that she keeps an account of the income and expenses of the estate, reports them to her husband, distributes goods rightly to the menservants and maidservants, and assigns specific duties to each, commanding in such a way that she is not held in contempt. Above all, she should nourish her daughters in the fear of God, forbid the company of base or wicked people, and appoint upright teachers for them. She should offer herself as an example to the others by being the first to take up any honorable task, and then committing the execution of it to the servants.

6. The fourth was: **To manage the house.** This means considering what is needed for importing, exporting, and preserving goods; providing conveniences for all functions, whether in the walls, the cupboards, or other places as she understands the need; and informing her husband of everything. Furthermore, she must inspect what items are lacking and order them to be bought, and see that what is superfluous is sold. She should distribute their proper portions to the **poor**; likewise, she must keep an account of how much is eaten and drunk daily and how much the daily expenses require. She must measure whether this equals the <term>census</term> <note>In this context, "census" refers to the family's total wealth, annual income, or registered tax status.</note> or exceeds it, or is less. She must strive to ensure it is always less, so that she can provide for her daughters' dowries, for household illnesses and misfortunes, and for extraordinary expenses. Moreover, she must see that flax, wool, hemp, and silk are purchased, and commit these to the spinners, or provide for them to be spun at home. She should increase the household furnishings, ensuring she has a sufficient and ready supply of clothes, beds, tablecloths, hand-towels, and other things of this kind. For this reason, Solomon, in the final chapter of Proverbs, <note>Campanella refers to the "Woman of Valor" in Proverbs 31:10–31.</note> commits all these things to be done by a strong and noble woman in her home and praises her; just as he praises sewing, working, decorating, and embroidering clothes with a needle. We read that the same was done by the Roman **Lucretia** in the writings of Titus Livius, <note>Livy, a Roman historian, describes Lucretia spinning wool late at night with her maids as a sign of her supreme virtue.</note> and even by the most illustrious queens in the works of Homer. For this reason, these things should not be left to craftsmen...
