### ECONOMICS, CHAPTER III.

A prudent woman will not entrust tasks to outsiders, nor will she buy things made by them: both to avoid greater expenses (for one who does these things at home profits more than double), and also to avoid idleness. For idleness corrupts women and provides them with the means for crimes, lusts, evil-speaking, vain laughter, mockery, slander, the desire to stare out of windows, to watch travelers, to pursue illicit loves, to discover new-fangled delights, and to paint the face and hair, etc. <note>original: "fucandi vultum capillosque" – literally "dyeing" or "painting," referring to the use of cosmetics and hair dyes which Campanella views as a sign of moral decay.</note> Furthermore, she ought to keep all domestic items in their proper places, workshops, and chests, so that she is not ignorant of where each thing is when it is needed; she should polish, clean, and inspect them frequently.

7. Fifthly, he adds: **That she should show herself irreproachable in all things.** This means in chastity, as has been said, and in honesty: and especially in the moderation of her own appearance and that of her home. Therefore, she shall not strive for luxurious clothes or those more beautiful than the law permits—indeed, always less so. Just as Plato and Aristotle rightly taught, so much more rightly did the apostles Peter and Paul, who forbade women gold, silver, precious garments, and the curling of hair; how much more, then, did they forbid painting the face so that it eventually withers. <note>original: "multo ergo magis fucationem vt flaccescant." Campanella argues that makeup actually ruins the skin it intends to beautify.</note> This is for several reasons. First, because much money and much time are consumed where it does no good but rather causes harm, and thus the family estate is ruined. Second, because these things provide an opening and occasion for lusts; those superfluous trimmings and paintings are like a laurel wreath hung before a tavern, which says to those passing by, "Wine is sold here." <note>In the Renaissance and antiquity, a "bush" or laurel wreath was a common sign for a tavern.</note> So it is with these women: "The wine of luxury and impurity is sold here"; it is a kind of invitation to evil. Third, because jealousy is stirred up in the husband by such things, when he is the only one she ought to please. Fourth, because in truth women appear more deformed from such adornment, and as if they were artificial (just as someone wearing a mask, no matter how beautiful the mask is, is immediately called "artificial"), and they generate nausea and anger when they seem to mock and deceive people, and to entice them to their love through fraud; for love ought to be spontaneous and pure above all things.

# BY BROTHER TOMMASO CAMPANELLA

To walk in sandals high by a palm’s breadth or more <note>Campanella is likely referring to "chopines" or *pianelle*, the high-platform shoes popular in the Renaissance which could reach extreme heights, making walking difficult without assistance.</note>, and to reshape the face by stripping the skin with litharge <note>original: "litargyrio"—lead monoxide, used as a skin whitener but highly toxic.</note>, and painting it with antimony <note>original: "stibio"—used as eyeliner or mascara.</note>, red ochre <note>original: "rubrica"—a red earth pigment used for rouge.</note>, deep pigments, and other ointments and filth; this is not only diabolical, as Chrysostom and Ambrose <note>Early Church Fathers who wrote extensively against vanity and the "correction" of God's handiwork.</note> teach—since they are "correcting" a divine painting—but it furthermore generates in themselves foul breath, headaches, blackening of the teeth, weakness, and distress. They become pale and scaly like corpses, which forces them to increase the application of these false colors again and again, ensuring the woman is no longer the same woman; this is the very annihilation of herself.

Add to this that when they kiss their husbands, they infect them with a face poisoned by pigments, stain their lips, and provoke nausea. Furthermore, the thickness, weight, and height of these sandals ensures that a woman cannot exercise her body; and when she moves anywhere, she requires a servant to lean upon, as if she were suffering from paralysis. To those watching, this creates contempt, aversion, and a sense of sluggishness, just as when we look upon a carcass or something shameful and sickly. 

From this lack of exercise, the woman becomes even paler, hence she has need of new applications of color. In this way, they render themselves withered and rotten, and their offspring small and sickly; they contaminate the republic and gradually make it degenerate. From this follow "painted" and false manners, and shameful examples both in the family and in the state. While they strive to show themselves as people of beautiful body and character through makeup, they become most foul, stunted, rotten, small, and sluggish in both body and mind, in both sexes. 

On the contrary, you see the Calabrian women <note>Campanella's own people; he was born in Stilo, Calabria, and often praised the vigor of his home region.</note>, who do not have thick sandals, makeup, or idleness; they are large of body, agile, robust, and lively in their actions, color, and voice. For these reasons, the mother of the family will eliminate such pests from her home, because of the many and great benefits that subsequently follow for herself, her home, her children, and the republic. Yet all these evils could be met with a single remedy: by ensuring that women are practiced in continuous and useful arts, and never live in idleness.

9. Finally, a woman ought to be silent and a keeper of secrets. She will not divulge the crimes and defects of her husband, nor what she knows about him...

# *On the generation and education of children.*
## CHAPTER IV.
### ARTICLE I.

<margin><unclear>s. ...</unclear></margin>
It was stated in the previous discourse that the greatest care must be given to offspring. Therefore, at the time of conception, husband and wife should not come together unless they have first abstained from intercourse for six or seven days to prepare a fertile, abundant, robust, and virtuous seed <note>original: "semen"—in early modern biology, this referred to the reproductive contributions of both parents.</note>. During those days, they should eat good foods; not delicate sweets <note>original: "saccaris"—sugar was often viewed as a luxury that "softened" the constitution.</note>, but the meat of older calves and of strong, noble animals, as we taught in the fourth book of *The Sense of Things* <note>Referring to Campanella's work *De sensu rerum et magia*, which explores the interconnectedness of nature.</note>. They shall then come together, but only after digestion is complete and under a favorable constellation <note>Campanella, like many Renaissance thinkers, believed that the position of the stars at the moment of conception influenced the child's temperament and destiny.</note>. ## *On the governance of rational servants.*

### *ARTICLE II.*

1. Some servants are purchased and are slaves <note>original: "mancipia"</note>, while others are voluntary, hired to serve for a certain wage. Of these, some are dedicated to honorable functions; for they are teachers of others and of the children, as well as chamberlains, secretaries, and the like. You shall treat these honorably, and distinguish them from the lowlier ones in their housing and at the table—unless you are a prince of the church, who takes food together with the servants as an example of humility. When you find a faithful servant, hold him as a brother or a son. Those who serve in a lower rank should be treated according to their condition. Although slaves <note>original: "mancipia"</note> may be treated more harshly, the master’s charity and prudence will nevertheless be vigilant in this, lest there be an Aesop, a Plato, or a Joseph among them <note>all three were famous historical figures who were famously enslaved: Aesop the storyteller, Plato the philosopher, and Joseph of the Bible</note>. For from among such as these, and not without merit, the King of the Turks <note>referring to the Ottoman Sultan, whose administration and military often consisted of highly trained men who were technically enslaved through the "devshirme" system</note> elevates his people.

2. The house of a patriarch <note>term: "patrisfamilias"—the male head of a household who held legal authority over all members</note> is to be regarded as a kind of school, in which those of his household may learn humanity, modesty, skill, and the method of serving and commanding. Otherwise, the purpose of the family—which is the same as that of the state <note>original: "reipublicae"</note>, namely the preservation of its own whole—will work against itself, having been turned into a school of vices and the ruin of the city. For this reason, those households are detestable in which people play with dice and gambling, engage in pimping, gluttony, the "pathic" arts <note>term: "pathicam"—referring to sexual submissiveness or passive homosexual behavior, viewed here as a moral vice</note> and the harlot’s art, or where they insult others and attack the weak...

...dice <note>original: "dos", likely a typo for "dos" meaning dice or gaming</note>, to occupy themselves with idle talk, and to become influential through assassination, impudence, curses, and insults—these are the things household members are taught. And the masters themselves will pay the most terrible penalties before God for the atrocious sins committed through their own example or teaching, both within their own home and later in the city when the servants are separated from it. We have discovered the shameful effects of this business in Naples <note>original: "Neapoli"</note>, where servants have almost no other purpose than to learn vices and to make themselves pleasing to their master through sins. It was better in the old days, when Neapolitan nobles maintained four or ten robust young men in place of such servants, with whom they later served their King in military campaigns. 3. Furthermore, let him have a common teacher for all the servants at home, from whom they shall seek a lesson twice a day. Let them learn what it is to serve, and what the purpose of it is; what integrity of life is; and how they serve God in the master given to them as God’s vicar, just as the Apostle teaches <note>referring to the biblical exhortations in Ephesians 6 or Colossians 3</note>. And let them perform their duty not for the sake of appearances <note>original: "ad oculum", literally "to the eye" or eye-service</note>, but in simplicity of heart, hoping for a true reward from the Lord of lords—and finally, let them learn whatever each is bound to observe in his own specific duties.

4. You shall not keep a servant in whom you have found a lie three times; nor one whom you recognize to take delight in lies (unless they are for a joke), or in vain and disparaging reports. Do not keep one who praises you to your face, especially falsely. When you catch a servant in theft <note>original: "latrocinio"</note>, you shall immediately remove him from your household. Consider also that gambling and whoring almost always make servants into thieves and liars.

5. Do not allow male servants to enter the chambers of female servants; let them have their exercises separately. Let them deliver necessary items to the women through a wheel <note>original: "rotam"; a revolving cabinet or hatch built into a wall, commonly used in cloistered convents to allow the exchange of goods without visual or physical contact</note>. You shall forbid the lowest rank of maidservant—commonly called *la vaiassa* <note>original: "la vaiaffa"; a Neapolitan term for a common domestic drudge, often associated in literature with loud or coarse behavior</note>—from dealing with the males, lest they carry "words of Cupid" <note>messages of lust or romantic advances</note> to the women. Castiglione, the "Great Courtier" <note>referring to Baldassare Castiglione, author of the influential 1528 book *The Courtier*</note>, permits and even encourages romances between male and female servants, so that marriages might eventually follow. But in this way, even a brothel is established...

# ON DOMESTIC MATTERS, CHAPTER IV.

...in the wife and daughters of the master: Therefore, this does not please me.

6. Let the master of the house <term>Herus</term> <note>The male head of the household</note> care for the males, and the mistress <term>Hera</term> care for the females in the family. However, let both groups be instructed by the master.

7. Slaves <term>Mancipia</term> <note>Specifically referring to those owned as property, distinct from hired servants</note> raised at home from infancy will be better for you. But you shall educate them with the discipline of a father, so that they become more obedient and more grateful to you.

8. Three things are appropriate for a servant, insofar as he is a servant: labor, correction, and food. And as it is said in Ecclesiasticus 33:
> Fodder, a whip, and a burden for the donkey; bread, correction, and work for the servant. <note>original: "cibaria & virga & onus afino, panis & difciplina & opus feruo"; quoting the biblical book of Sirach 33:25</note>
For without sufficient food, he is not able to work. Without labor, he becomes idle, difficult <note>original: "dyfcolus", from the Greek for peevish or hard to please</note>, proud, and a pimp; he becomes steeped in the other vices mentioned above. Without correction, however, he will be far worse, and will despise and attack his master. Therefore, it will be necessary either to dismiss him, if he serves of his own free will, or, if he is a slave, to do with him what the author of Ecclesiasticus teaches; namely:
> For a malicious servant, torture and shackles: put him to work, lest he be idle: for idleness has taught much malice. <note>Sirach 33:28-29</note>
(Terence and Aristotle said almost the same thing.) Then he adds:
> If you have a faithful servant, treat him as your own soul. <note>Sirach 33:31</note>
An example of this is Tyndarus in Plautus’s play *The Captives* <note>In this Roman comedy, the slave Tyndarus risks his life to save his master out of loyalty</note>.

9. It is also good to make them grateful and dutiful through the hope of freedom; likewise to bind them through marriage and the procreation of children: for thus they will not think of fleeing. And these shall be like the overseers of others on the estate, in the garden, with the herds, and so on. But those raised with you from childhood will become as obedient as sons, just like the Janissaries <note>original: "Ianizari"; the elite standing army of the Ottoman Sultans, composed of soldiers taken as children and raised in total loyalty to the ruler</note> of the King of the Turks.

10. The doorkeeper of the house, who observes what is brought in and out in large households—an old man, or one unfit for other tasks, such as a cripple—is considered useful. For such a person is fearful and cautious; he will neglect nothing, nor will he admit assassins.

# On the economic use and management of animals and plants.

## ARTICLE III.

1. Regarding irrational tools and servants <note>referring to livestock and draft animals</note>, and concerning agriculture and animal husbandry, a separate volume would need to be produced. But Virgil wrote the *Georgics* <note>original: "Georgica"; a didactic poem on farming</note> and the *Eclogues* <note>original: "Bucolica"; poems about the lives of shepherds</note> on these subjects; the former more for utility, the latter more in a poetic style, imitating Hesiod and Theocritus.

2. It is enough to say that this knowledge is necessary for the Head of the Household <term>Oeconomus; the person responsible for managing the domestic and financial affairs of a home or estate</term>. For even princes who take care of horses have a specific book for this purpose. Ancient kings also used to go out themselves and send their sons to care for the herds, as we read concerning Priam and his children. Therefore, the manager should not be ashamed to know these arts, but rather to be ignorant of them.

3. Dogs are useful as guardians of the herds, the countryside, and the home. Small dogs, which are kept for the sake of pleasure <note>lapdogs or pets</note>, are evidence of a shallow and lazy mind; they ought not to be kept. Indeed, the care spent on making their kind smaller is against nature, as is the "service" that is performed for them. Much more useful...

### CHAPTER V.

The principal manager <term>Oeconomus; the head of household management</term> is the father of the family <term>paterfamilias</term> himself. It is his responsibility to know all domestic and rural arts, as well as their uses and disadvantages. He must understand that he is a king within his own single house, so that he may lead it directly toward the goal of the commonwealth <note>original: "reipublicae"</note>, which is the common happiness. Through this happiness, he leads it toward God, the supreme good, the source of all things that sustain us, and our highest preserver and eternalizer.

...[stewards] they reject their stewards; these men very quickly suffer the loss of their property and their dignity. Poverty will come upon them like an armed man, as Solomon says <note>Referring to Proverbs 6:11 or 24:34: "So shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth, and thy want as an armed man."</note>. They will be scorned and held in contempt by their own servants, let alone by the citizens, and they will be abandoned by their friends. 3. There are three functions of this art <term>the "art" refers to Oeconomia, or household management</term>. First, to acquire. Second, to preserve what has been acquired. Third, to enjoy those things that are acquired and preserved, and to dispense them well.

4. Therefore, let the master distinguish his profitable property and estates from those that are unprofitable. Let him consider from which of them a more lucrative business may emerge.

5. Let him distribute duties and functions among the servants. However, let it be done so that no function is devoid of domestic utility. Therefore, let him eliminate all superfluous and useless roles.

6. Let him keep before his eyes the Persian proverb: *The eye of the master fattens the horse more than any fodder.* And that other Libyan proverb: *The footsteps of the master fertilize the field more than any manure.* If the head of the household <term>oeconomus</term> observes these, he will not be defrauded by his servants and will avoid thefts; no services will be handled with negligence. For this reason, on the Kalends <note>The "Kalends" refers to the first day of each month in the Roman calendar.</note> of every month, or when the servants are not expecting it, he should visit the workshops and the offices. He shall inspect what is missing and how diligently or negligently everything is being done. He should do the same for the countryside and the farmers. He should question everyone gathered together, and then each one separately, as to whether the services are being handled correctly; what is lacking and what is in excess in each office; and who is negligent or who is diligent in them. Let him then provide for whatever is needed with prudence. Let him admonish everyone with gravity. And by his own diligence, let him make the others diligent.

7. Since, in truth, all the members of a body naturally imitate the head, let the master realize that if he shows himself to be negligent in his own affairs, the servants will be much more negligent in the affairs of another. *The hireling, and he who is not the shepherd, sees the wolf coming and leaves the sheep,* as it is said in the Gospel <note>John 10:12</note>. Therefore, let him be an example to the others. Some say, not ineptly, that it is necessary...

This is both to ensure they are not stolen from him (forcing him to frequently replace the same things) and so that they are ready when needed, rather than being sought in vain. Great princes, moreover, will carry out these functions through the most faithful agents in small matters, but through themselves in great matters.

## On economic acquisition.
### CHAPTER VI.

In the matter of profitable acquisition, you shall consider, first, how much you have in your annual valuation <term>original: *census*; the total assessed value of one's estate and income</term>. For if you have two thousand gold pieces <note>original: *aureorum*; likely referring to the *scudo d'oro* or similar high-value gold currency of the period</note>, you should spend no more than a thousand for the food and clothing of the household and other provisions; or at most one thousand four hundred, calculating that which is given to managers, courtiers, the poor, and other extraordinary expenses. You should consider yourself as not even having the other six hundred, but you shall apply them to industrious pursuits and profits from the land and animals; and you shall set aside the profits for the needs of your children and for misfortunes. You must always apply yourself to increasing your estate, not knowing what the future day may bring forth. It is a true proposition: Whoever has as much going out as he has coming in cannot become rich; indeed, it is certain that he will be impoverished.

2. Let him consider how much he can spend on daily food, and prescribe this to the buyer: who should record the daily expenses in a book,

You shall not wait to buy daily: for almost double the money is spent that way; and there is less pleasure in it; and the items are less choice. Nevertheless, it is better to have everything from one’s own land.

5. Whatever surplus of goods, wine, oil, grain, etc., remains to you, you shall sell when it is more expensive: and in this, foresight through **Astrology** <note>In the 17th century, astrology was a practical tool used to predict weather patterns and harvest yields</note> is helpful. But you shall not wish for scarcity: nor shall you practice usury with your money. It is better to sell at a small price to neighbors than at a high price to those far away. For in this way you will gain goodwill, security, and protection: it is better to have convenient neighbors than inconvenient and needy ones. It is also better to sell to the poor when they have money at a low price, than when they have none at a high price.

For that which is not bought is more freely poured out. This is partly a good thing,**

<header>OF TOMMASO CAMPANELLA</header>

# On the distribution and enjoyment of goods acquired or preserved, in life and in death: and on the care of the householder when nature signals his death.

## CHAPTER VIII. <note>The original uses the Roman numeral IIX, a common archaic variant for VIII (8).</note>

The distribution and enjoyment of goods that have been acquired and preserved is the most important part of household management. For this is their ultimate purpose.

2. You shall avoid **avarice**, as it is the other extreme. For avarice is the fear of poverty, which makes a person live in continual poverty and servitude. He is a master and a rich man who enjoys his wealth and makes it serve him; not he who serves his wealth. You shall also flee the other extreme, **prodigality**. This is like stripping oneself of weapons in the midst of enemies. For riches are the weapons and the sustenance of life. He who counts them as nothing rushes headlong into poverty, mockery, blame, hunger, nakedness, despair, and sometimes even death. For this reason, a certain Marquis used to say that it is better for a nobleman to die than to become poor <note>original: "Viro nobili melius esse mori, quam pauperem fieri"</note>; a sentiment also found in *Ecclesiasticus 40*. <note>A reference to the biblical Book of Sirach 40:28: "My son, do not lead the life of a beggar; it is better to die than to beg."</note> Another writer indeed says that for a prince, it is better to lean toward avarice than toward prodigality for the sake of preserving his dignity and empire. <note>This reflects a common Renaissance political view, similar to Machiavelli's, suggesting that a "stingy" ruler is less likely to be forced to overtax his subjects.</note>

3. Weddings of great expense bring loss without honor. Spending on jousting matches, <note>original: *hastiludiis*; festive military games played with spears or lances.</note> and theatrical displays, and the applause of women and the common people, or in the presence of the prince, results in the honor of a single day but a hundred years of reproach. To give generously to parasites and thugs <note>original: *sicariis*; literally "assassins," but here referring to the violent or low-life hangers-on a wealthy man might keep as a retinue.</note> is an open disgrace, lacking even the mask of honor. The hunting of falcons and pampered dogs involves great expense for very little profit. He who gives to the poor lends to God. You shall feed your family first, over whom God has appointed you as guardian and ruler, before you feed monks and clerics who are in little need. In death, you should make bequests to your creditors and the servants who work for you before the church to which you entrust yourself. However, do not refuse to pay what you have vowed to the saints and to God, for you received it from Him. When wealth overflows for you, [give] first and more willingly for the honor of God and of holy places,

<meta>catchword: locorum, (of places)</meta>

<summary>Campanella argues that the purpose of wealth is its proper use, warning against both the slavery of avarice and the self-destruction of wasteful spending. He prioritizes providing for one's family and paying debts to servants over grand public displays or excessive donations to well-off clergy.</summary>

<keywords>avarice, prodigality, household management, charity, inheritance, social status, domestic economy, Ecclesiasticus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the specific advice of Chapter VIII regarding the management of household expenses and the display of wealth. While the previous page established the philosophical middle ground between greed and wastefulness, Campanella now provides practical instructions on clothing, servant liveries, and diet.</meta>

->### ON HOUSEHOLD AFFAIRS CHAPTER VIII.<-

3. [You should spend on the improvement] of places, rather than on games and displays, which are commonly called **liveries** <note>original: "libræas". These were the distinctive, often expensive uniforms worn by a nobleman's servants or used in public festivals to show off status.</note>; for these things pass away like smoke and leave no lasting fruit.

4. **Precious and glittering clothes** provide evidence of a shallow soul; they bring envy and disgust to your neighbor, and they create an obligation for him to do the same, resulting in his ruin as well as yours.

5. If you desire to display splendor in the attire of yourself or your wife, let that adornment not exceed local custom. You should add to it **solid gold and silver**, which remains, rather than drawn wire or spun thread, which is wasted away. Gold chains, beads, and buckles persist, but gilded items do not. Precious stones are less secure: for their value follows the whims of princes and is highest where money is abundant; but in times of necessity or misfortune, or among the common people, they are worth almost nothing or decrease in price.

6. One garment for winter and another for summer are sufficient. But by doubling them, so that you wear one on feast days and the other on workdays, there will be four. What if you add another two, for autumn and spring? You could then add a seventh for the countryside, for when you go to the fields or hunting, or travel elsewhere. I say the same regarding the clothing of women. However, you should take counsel with yourself according to your **rank and income** <note>original: "census ratione". This refers to the Roman-style assessment of wealth that determined one's social duties and legal status.</note>.

7. To spend money on precious liveries for servants is sheer vanity. When such a practice becomes common, it imposes a necessity upon everyone, as happens in **Naples**; where a common error has become a perpetual law. For this reason, the nobles are forced to retreat to their country estates, **flay their vassals** <note>original: "vasallos deglubere". A vivid metaphor for extreme taxation or exploitation of the peasants who lived on the nobleman's land.</note>, and soon return to Naples in turn, adorned in the skins of those miserable people.

8. Do not be ashamed to be the first to introduce **frugality and modesty** and to eliminate wicked and useless customs; through this, you will become better in both your condition and your character. For although this may seem absurd at first, eventually everyone will praise you. Only beware of this one thing: do not introduce bad customs yourself, even if they seem honorable, pleasant, or agreeable.

9. You shall feed your household with **coarse foods** rather than delicacies. For in this way, less money is spent, and they render the body more robust and fit for labor, but less inclined toward **lust** <note>original: "luxuriæ". In this context, it refers both to physical extravagance and the carnal desires thought to be fueled by a rich diet.</note>.

Sss
<meta>catchword: 10. Ser-</meta>

<summary>Campanella argues for investment in lasting goods like solid gold over ephemeral fashion and liveries. He specifically critiques the Neapolitan nobility for exploiting their peasants to fund their extravagant city lifestyles.</summary>

->FRIAR TOMMASO CAMPANELLA<-

**10. It is more beneficial to feed servants in a communal dining room than to feed them separately from one another. It will be more costly for you to distribute money for their daily food: for in this way you spend more, while they actually eat less, desiring to set aside and accumulate a little bit of money and to extort what is necessary—not to mention what is superfluous—for their own sustenance from your own table; and every day they will try to persuade you that your own table requires more provisions.**

11. On feast days, you shall provide them with more abundant, though not more delicate, food, both at home and in the country; and you shall command servants and animals to rest from their labors, just as the Lord God commanded; both so that they may attend to divine worship, and for their own benefit and yours, lest continuous labor destroy the "instruments of preservation" <note>original: "instrumenta conseruationis". Campanella views the bodies of servants and work animals as vital tools that require rest to remain functional.</note>.

12. You shall not pile up exquisite foods on your own table. You shall eat meat once, fish once, and legumes or greens with an egg once. For to always eat the same thing and in abundance is convenient for neither health nor the wallet <term>marsupium: a leather pouch or purse used for carrying money</term>. To eat well once, moderately once, and poorly once contributes most to health, as the proverb goes.

13. Make it so that the wallet argues with gluttony: and you should not become the advocate for one or the other, but the judge. Yet, you should not render a verdict in favor of the wallet too often. Gluttony produces cravings as witnesses, though they are not under oath. The wallet has evident witnesses: the cellar, the granary, and the chest, which are empty or soon to be emptied. You, therefore, shall prudently examine both. But when gluttony brings forward witnesses of infirmity or weakness, then let it go forth victorious. For he who spares money during illness or necessity suffers a greater loss in the subsequent trials.

14. **You shall not celebrate sumptuous banquets.** For parasites are fed by these. However, he who is prudent will disparage you, even after he has been filled by your bounty. No one will take pity on the poverty that will soon seize you, just as they do not for other misfortunes. Let Marius Deltuso <note>A contemporary figure known to Campanella, likely an example of a man who lost his fortune through excess.</note> be an example from our own age; he can be numbered among those whom Dante celebrates <note>original: Campanella quotes Canto XXIX of Dante's *Inferno*, where the poet ironically describes the "Spendthrift Brigade" of Siena.</note>:

->*Except for Stricca;*<-
->*Who knew how to make temperate expenditures.*<-

### CHAPTER VIII OF THE ECONOMICS

> *And Niccolò, who first discovered*
> *The costly fashion of the clove, etc.*
<note>original: "Et Nicolo, che la costuma ricca, / Del Garofano primo discoperso. &c." These lines are from Dante’s *Inferno* (Canto XXIX), referring to Niccolò dei Salimbeni and the "Spendthrift Brigade" of Siena, who notoriously wasted their fortunes on extravagant luxuries like roasting meat over fires of precious cloves.</note>

I would not deny, however, that friends should be received with splendid courses, but this should be done frugally and only when they have need of them. And you shall consider him a truer friend who offers you his money, rather than one who merely offers his life.

**15.** Your use of wine should be sparing. To purchased servants, you shall give wine only on feast days or when they are not feeling well, treating it as a medicine. To women, give little or none. To children, never give even a small amount. To robust and more serious persons, give it moderately. To your own children under eighteen years of age, you shall not allow wine unless illness compels it. For young men, it will be permitted, but diluted with water until the forty-fifth year; after this time, they may drink more freely. A small amount of wine sharpens the wit and is healthy for the body. Too much, however, clouds and dulls the mind; to the body, it brings heaviness, gout of the feet <term>podagras: a form of inflammatory arthritis, often associated with rich diets</term>, gout of the hands <term>chiragras: similar to podagra, but specifically affecting the joints of the hand</term>, stones, and obstructions, etc. To those who are afflicted and mourning, however, you may offer wine even to the point of intoxication. For as Solomon and Plato taught, it was given by God as a remedy for human miseries; and as David says, so that it may gladden sorrowful hearts and bring about the forgetfulness of pains and troubles, just as Homer shows through the character of Helen in the story of Telemachus.

**16.** While you are still healthy in body and mind, you should make a will regarding your goods. For your children, if they are nobles, the partitioning of the inheritance is harmful. Therefore, you shall bequeath everything to the eldest, who is to provide sustenance to the others proportionally. If they are laborers, let the division be made however you please; for it is easy for them to preserve and increase their wealth through their labors. If they are merchants, a division will be useful, so that the misfortune of one does not harm the others, and so that no part of the capital sits idle without generating profit.

**17.** In appointing a curator or guardian for your wards <note>In this context, "wards" or "pupils" refers to orphaned children under the care of a legal guardian.</note>, you will not do well to choose one of your blood relatives or in-laws, especially if that person also has children; instead, choose a friend from outside the family, and a religious man. You should, however, appoint the blood relatives as "preservers" of the wards and their inherited goods, but not as the administrators. In this way, neither the relatives nor the guardians will be able to plot against the property or the persons of the wards, as happens every day. Let the House of the Sforzas serve as an example.
<note>The Sforza family, rulers of Milan, were infamous for internal betrayals; Ludovico Sforza notably usurped the dukedom from his young nephew, the rightful heir.</note>

### FRIAR TOMMASO CAMPANELLA’S ECONOMICS

...under *Ludovico Sforza* <note>original: "Ludouico Sfortia." Ludovico Sforza (1452–1508), known as "Il Moro," was the Duke of Milan and a famous patron of Leonardo da Vinci. His reign ended in imprisonment after he was betrayed to the French.</note>; and the Count of *Casalduni*, who was oppressed and despoiled by his own kinsmen, who were <unclear>traitors</unclear>.

**18.** If your wife should die before you, and you remain a widower without an heir <margin>+ / \</margin>, it is good to marry again. But take care, as an old man, that you do not take a young girl whose lust you are unable to satisfy, lest she perhaps admit adulterers. Strive also that she be fertile and industrious. If you already have children of a younger age, it will be better to remain in widowhood and take care of them; but if they are adults, you shall spend your old age in a monastery in divine worship.

**19.** You shall celebrate the marriages of your children according to the rules previously stated. Strive, however, that the women—if they have a rich dowry—receive husbands from your own kindred <note>Campanella suggests "endogamy" here, or marrying within the extended family, to prevent the family's wealth (the dowry) from leaving the paternal lineage.</note>, but let the males take wives from outside the family.

**20.** Your wife, should you die first, if she is young and lacks children, would more usefully seek a monastery than a second marriage. It is better for her to marry if she is childless than if she has children. But if she is an old woman, it will be an evil thing if she marries; and may God give her a young husband, through whom she may pay the penalties for all her sins <note>A bit of Campanella’s dry humor; he implies that a young husband would be a source of grief or "purgatory" for an elderly widow.</note>.

**21.** Do not entrust your soul to one who loves you, but to one who loves his own soul. Before death, restore to everyone whatever you owe. Nor should you believe that your sons will satisfy your obligations for you, unless you have satisfied them yourself.

**22.** If you leave an immaculate soul to God, a whole body to the earth, an illustrious reputation to the world, and a splendid inheritance to your children, hope that it will be well for you on the last day, which is the beginning of the ages to come.

### *Response to those who contradict the doctrine of economics.*

You ask: what help is the present doctrine when Fortune is against us? I answer: that each man is the architect of his own fortune for the most part; but when one falls into hardships because of negligence and other vices, he casts the blame upon Fortune. But indeed, you will rarely see misfortune join itself to diligence and virtue, and even more rarely will you see it separated from negligence and vice. Do what you ought to do, and commend your affairs to God.

->T H E  E N D.<-

<summary>This concluding section of the Economics provides advice on late-life household decisions—remarriage, children's dowries, and estate settlement—before ending with a philosophical defense of personal agency over "Fortune." Campanella argues that most poverty and failure attributed to bad luck are actually the results of personal negligence.</summary>
